Executive Summary

Insikt Group has identified new infrastructure associated with the TAG-182 threat cluster, used to disseminate MarkiRAT malware in support of Iranian government surveillance operations. It is highly likely that TAG-182 is targeting Iranians living inside and outside the country using different lures, including free download tools and fake VPN applications. The group’s operations are highly likely active across social media platforms like Instagram.

As the kinetic conflict with the United States and Israel has subsided since April 2026, Iran's security apparatus is likely redirecting its focus toward intensified cyber surveillance and digital enforcement operations targeting perceived dissidents and alleged foreign collaborators. TAG-182’s operations are consistent with these security objectives and are likely to continue following the partial restoration of internet access in Iran on May 26, 2026. The indicators of compromise (IoCs) for this report are viewable in Appendix A, while defensive signatures are located in Appendix C and Appendix D.

Key Findings

TAG-182 is highly likely a component of Iran’s broader surveillance ecosystem, using MarkiRAT malware distributed through fake Android applications masquerading as legitimate services such as VPNs and media tools to collect intelligence from Iranian targets.

The MarkiRAT sample identified during this research shares notable tradecraft overlaps with historical variants, including the use of the Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS), suggesting a credible relationship between TAG-182 and activity previously attributed to Ferocious Kitten. However, while these similarities support an operational connection, additional evidence is necessary to confidently assess that the two clusters are organizationally linked.

Since Iran’s reconnection to the global internet, Iranian surveillance operations are highly likely to increase as authorities seek to identify and monitor perceived dissidents amid concerns over internal unrest and potential uprisings. The majority of Iranian intelligence and security organizations are likely to prioritize enhanced digital surveillance and intelligence collection to support domestic security objectives.

Threat Analysis

In early 2026, open-source information surfaced malware samples linked to MarkiRAT, which has historically been used by Ferocious Kitten for surveillance against anti-government networks, activists, and human rights advocates inside Iran. The IoCs, specifically the lures, suggest that threat actors custom-built a website that acts as a staging point for an application called “YESHICA” (Table 1). Other sample names also include “Pis2ray VPN”, which is not a legitimate application on either Google Play or Apple’s App Store (see Appendix A for additional IoCs).

In March 2026, Insikt Group identified a new sample associated with TAG-182’s updated infrastructure that uses an almost identical media player theme name, “YESHICA YEPlayer” (Figure 1).

Figure 1: TAG-182 continued to operate using similarly named applications despite open-source exposure of its tradecraft and infrastructure (Source: Recorded Future)

f44bb0be7ed3.text:
The Department of Defense suspended CMMC Phase 2's mandatory third-party assessment requirement, citing concerns about assessor ecosystem capacity and compliance costs affecting small and mid-sized defense contractors. A CMMC Reform Task Force will spend 60 days reviewing the program. Critical caveat: Phase 1 self-assessment obligations, SPRS score submissions, and DFARS 252.204-7012 requirements to protect controlled unclassified information (CUI) remain fully in effect.

Key Industry Perspectives:
Abdie Mohamed (NR Labs) warns that self-attestation without verification creates False Claims Act exposure, citing prior settlements with Aerojet Rocketdyne ($9M), Raytheon ($8.4M), and others.
Chris Nyhuis (Vigilant) supports the pause, arguing speed and innovation matter for national security but emphasizes: "the bar is the same. Only the person checking your homework went away."
Ned Butler (Redspin) clarifies that CMMC assessment costs align with other certification regimes and recommends narrowing scope to approximately 15,000-20,000 entities prioritizing sensitive CUI work.
Robert Teague (Redspin) notes there are actually 107 C3PAOs and 1,000+ certified assessors, challenging capacity shortage narratives.
Chetrice Romero (Ice Miller) emphasizes CMMC represents organizational resilience, not mere compliance: "Start with your business...build a strategic roadmap that prioritizes highest risks."
Emil Sayegh (CyberSheath) stresses the suspension doesn't eliminate legal obligations and warns: "Without a C3PAO in the loop, a government investigation can become the moment of truth."
Tyler Fordham (Dark Wolf) advocates for automated technical validation through penetration testing and infrastructure-as-code automation rather than manual assessments.
Austin Berglas (BlueVoyant) cautions against treating the pause as permission to reduce security efforts and warns of False Claims Act violations if companies submit inflated SPRS scores.

709366d47070.text:
The post discusses a significant discovery of Alan Turing's wartime papers. In November 2023, a collection of documents—referred to as the "Bayley papers"—sold at auction in London for approximately half a million dollars. These papers contain handwritten notes by Turing detailing his classified "Delilah" engineering project, which ran from 1943 to 1945. Delilah was a portable voice-encryption system named after the biblical figure. The cache also includes materials written by Donald Bayley, often recording notes taken during conversations with Turing. The papers survived because Bayley preserved them until his death in 2020, which was 66 years after Turing's passing.

Comments: One commenter questioned whether these were identical to papers "saved for the nation" currently held at King's College, Cambridge. Another commenter shared an anecdote from Bayley's recollections of his first meeting with Turing, describing him as somewhat disorganized, with his "shirt hanging out" and equipment that resembled "a spider's nest of stuff." Additional comments referenced Bayley's later work on Piccolo, a device designed for the Diplomatic Wireless Service, and noted ongoing interest in these historical engineering contributions.

c105ca46601d.text: Apple is warning iPhone and iPad users that scammers are using FaceTime calls to trick them into handing over money and account details. According to Apple, scammers pose as trusted organizations and use social engineering to convince people to hand over account credentials, security codes, and financial information. Apple says a caller can fake its number entirely, a trick known as spoofing, so the incoming call looks like it comes from Apple or a bank even when it doesn't. Scammers also tend to bring up private information early in the conversation, things like a home address, an employer, or sometimes a Social Security number, to sound credible. Once trust is established, the scammer pushes for speed. Apple describes callers warning victims that hanging up and calling Apple back themselves won't help, since the fraud will supposedly continue in the meantime. That claim is false, and it exists only to keep the victim on the line. Some scammers go further and ask victims to turn off two-factor authentication (2FA) or Stolen Device Protection, framing it as necessary to stop an ongoing attack. In reality, disabling those features is what opens the door for the scammer, not what closes it. "Apple will never ask you to log in to any website, or to tap Accept in the two-factor authentication dialog, or to provide your password, device passcode, or two-factor authentication code" according to the company's official statement. In one version of the scam, the caller claims someone broke into the victim's iPhone or iCloud account, or made unauthorized charges using Apple Pay. They then offer to help stop the attacker or reverse the charges. Apple recommends that users who receive suspicious messages or calls contact the company directly rather than trusting unsolicited communications. The company urges keeping iPhones updated to the latest iOS version and advises victims of suspicious FaceTime fraud to screenshot the call and send it to reportfacetimefraud@apple.com.

5e9b90bce8fa.text:
Apple and Google have been ordered to take down apps that can “nudify” or “undress” people and told that they must stop profiting from the harmful technology, according to cease-and-desist letters sent to the companies seen by WIRED.
On Thursday, San Francisco city attorney David Chiu sent legal notices to Apple and Google demanding that they remove from their app stores 13 face-swapping apps, which allow users to create AI-generated nonconsensual nude images. The letters say the Silicon Valley giants should stop “aiding and abetting” the sale of explicit deepfake images and “sever” business relationships with the app developers.
“Generating non-consensual intimate images is illegal, harmful, and completely unacceptable,” Chiu tells WIRED. The city attorney, whose office previously took legal action against 16 popular deepfake websites, says Apple and Google have likely “made millions of dollars in fees” from apps that offer nudification, and they should improve their moderation processes to stop them appearing in their stores in the first place.
“These companies have responsibility to ensure that apps on their platforms do not facilitate sexual abuse,” Chiu says. The city’s legal letters say California’s laws prohibit supporting services that create deepfake pornography. The apps use in-app payments, which the tech companies take a cut of, the letters says. “The fact that some of the world’s largest and most established technology companies are facilitating this has to stop.”
Researchers have repeatedly found and reported apps in Apple’s App Store and Google’s Play Store that allow people to generate sexual images using AI—including some apps being rated as suitable for use by children. While new laws and bans aim to tackle the scourge of explicit deepfakes online, technology and social media companies consistently direct millions of people toward the harmful tech.
Both Apple and Google have developer policies that prohibit pornography, abuse, and harassment on their platforms. They have previously removed dozens of nudify and deepfake apps, after reports by researchers and journalists.
Google spokesperson Dan Jackson tells WIRED that the company has deleted “hundreds” of apps with nudifying features for policy violations, including the five Android apps flagged by Chiu’s office, among other steps to restrict access to them.
“Google Play does not allow apps that contain sexual content, and we continually take proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content,” Jackson says in a statement. “When violations are reported to us, we investigate and take swift action, which in the case of these apps has included suspending hundreds of violating apps and restricting related search terms like 'nudify' on our store."
Apple tells WIRED that developers are ultimately responsible for the content of their apps, and those who fail to follow the rules will have their apps removed. The company also says users can report potentially problematic apps themselves. Adam Dema, an Apple spokesperson, tells WIRED in a statement that the company has removed three of the apps flagged by San Francisco city attorney and is “in the process of terminating their developer accounts from our program.” The other four developers must “address policy violations or risk being removed as well,” the company says.
“The App Store was designed to be a safe and trusted place for users, and we have always strictly prohibited apps designed to generate, distribute, or consume pornography," Dema says in the statement. “‘Nudification' apps are against our App Review Guidelines and we have proactively rejected many of these apps and removed many others, including when users have flagged them via our reporting tools.”
Over the last five years, a highly lucrative slurry of deepfake “nudification” tech has emerged online—most transparently with xAI’s Grok being used to create millions of sexualized images in January. A host of apps, websites, and bots allow people (mostly men) to upload pictures of people (overwhelmingly women and girls) and digitally “remove” clothing or place them into graphic sexual scenarios.
Often all it takes to create sexual deepfakes is a reference photo and a couple of clicks, with some results available in seconds. Images and videos have become more realistic as the underlying generative AI technology has improved, with services providing some results for free or charging small fees to create the harmful content. Previous reporting by WIRED and Indicator Media has uncovered incidents in at least 90 schools where deepfake sexual abuse images have been created of minors.
“These images are used to bully, humiliate, and threaten women and girls,” Chiu says. “This industry has a horrific impact on one’s reputation, mental health, loss of autonomy. There have been victims who’ve been suicidal.”
The 13 apps investigated by the City Attorney’s Office—eight on the App Store and five on the Play Store—broadly advertise themselves as “face-swapping” tools, with their ability to create sexual deepfakes available once people use them. The website of one app, which has more than 1 million downloads, displays more than a dozen different styles of AI images it will generate, including “bikini queen curvy,” “calm busty,” and “cinematic intimacy.” Many of the styles show sexualized images of women alongside their descriptions. The homepage of another of the targeted apps claims to produce “free and uncensored” videos. WIRED is not naming the apps to avoid pushing people toward them.
The problem won’t come as a surprise to Apple and Google. Over the last year, multiple reports have identified apps on the companies’ platforms that can allow people to create nonconsensual nude images or videos. In January and April this year, the Tech Transparency Project, an independent watchdog group, uncovered around 100 apps across both the App Store and Play Store, as well as some advertisements for nudifying technology on the platforms. (Google’s Jackson says the company has removed most of the apps identified by TTP.) Apps identified by the research were estimated to have been collectively downloaded around 480 million times and may have made around $120 million in combined revenues.
“We didn’t think after the first report that we would see this as a problem again—and it was just as bad, if not worse, after the second report,” says Katie Paul, the director of TTP. “Apple and Google make a lot of promises in their marketing about how trusted and safe their app stores are. And that is just not what is playing out in reality.”
Meanwhile, in a preprint research paper published in May, researchers from Cornell University and Georgetown University identified 420 apps offering general face-swapping capabilities on Google’s and Apple’s app stores. They tested 155 to see if they could be used to create face swaps with nude images; in 70 percent of cases, it was possible, with the apps not including safety measures to prevent this.
“None of these apps are advertised as nudification apps,” the research says. “This suggests that face swap apps, and many other forms of AI image generation and editing apps, are effectively ‘dual-use’: apps that evade content moderation by platforms because they present as benign, but possess the capability to create harmful content.”
Chiu, the San Francisco city attorney, says his office will keep pursuing the problem after being “absolutely horrified” at the harm and scale of the technology. “My hope is that Apple and Google will immediately remove these apps and strengthen their screening systems to make sure that apps like this never get onto their platforms in the future,” he says. “It's our hope that these companies will do the right thing—but if they don’t, we will have to consider all of our legal options.”
Updated 4:10 pm ET, July 17, 2026: Added comment from an Apple spokesperson.

b7ea0a12d23e.text: 1Password has launched a beta integration with Claude that enables secure website authentication without exposing user passwords. The integration is available to paid Claude subscribers (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise) on Claude Desktop for macOS and Chrome, requiring both the 1Password desktop app and browser extension. Secure Authentication Process: When Claude encounters a login page, it requests credentials from 1Password. Users approve via biometric authentication. According to 1Password, "secret values never enter Claude's context window, memory, or Anthropic's infrastructure." Agentic Mode Protection: 1Password introduced Agentic Mode to prevent agents from accessing the extension directly. The feature "limits access to the credentials approved for the current task, and keeps the rest of the vault inaccessible." Current Limitations: The integration currently supports logins and one-time passwords (TOTP) only, not payment cards or identity information. Security Controls: Explicit user approval required for each credential request; access limited to individual tasks; users can revoke access or cancel tasks anytime; automatic secret clearing if sign-in fails; post-autofill verification to ensure secrets weren't exposed.

3c2418d5f18e.text: Google is addressing a security vulnerability in Android 16 that permits unauthorized SMS and WhatsApp messaging through Gemini from the lock screen, bypassing PIN authentication. The flaw exploits a specific multi-touch gesture. When a user attempts to send an SMS via Gemini on a locked device where messaging permissions were previously revoked, the system normally requires PIN entry. However, pressing "Continue" simultaneously with the "Add attachment" button allows the message to send "without needing to enter a PIN." Users can then grant Gemini access to other previously restricted applications—such as WhatsApp—simply by entering commands like "@WhatsApp" in the Gemini text window, circumventing expected authentication steps. The vulnerability requires physical device access, though the publication notes this deserves attention given rising phone theft rates and potential exploitation in kidnapping scams. Similar Gemini-related lock screen bypass bugs have circulated since September 2025. Google confirmed this is a known issue and stated a fix was "scheduled for a full deployment this week." The company indicated the bug affects multiple manufacturers, though declined specifying which models remain vulnerable.

b511ded79e7c.text: Microsoft has announced that Windows Server 2022 will reach the end of mainstream support on October 13, 2026—approximately 90 days from the announcement date. The company stated: "On October 13, 2026, Windows Server 2022 will reach end of mainstream support." After this date, the operating system will transition to extended support, during which it will continue receiving security updates at no additional cost through October 14, 2031. The October 2026 security update will be the final mainstream support patch available for this version. Originally released in September 2021 as a Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) product, Windows Server 2022 was designed to receive 10 years of total support. Microsoft is now urging customers to upgrade to Windows Server 2025, which became generally available in November 2024 and offers mainstream support until November 13, 2029. The company emphasized the importance of planning upgrades and conducting deployment testing early to ensure smooth transitions. A free 180-day trial of Windows Server 2025 is available through the Microsoft Evaluation Center for organizations seeking to evaluate the newer version before full deployment.

07db6264f67c.text: Japanese frozen food giant Nichirei announced it would gradually restore operations affected by a cyberattack on July 13. The Tokyo-headquartered company, one of Japan's top frozen food producers operating through 80 global subsidiaries, disconnected its systems following the attack. The breach disrupted operations at Nichirei Logistics Group's refrigerated warehouses and Nichirei Foods' shipping operations, affecting multiple restaurant chains, retailers, and delivery services according to local media reports. The company confirmed that "hackers targeted its servers as part of the attack, and that some of the affected systems stored personal information." Nichirei submitted an initial report to the Personal Information Protection Commission regarding possible data leakage and pledged to provide updates if any breach is confirmed. The frozen food company declined to share specific attack details as a precautionary measure, leaving unclear whether a known ransomware group was responsible. The company also noted it is assessing the incident's impact on its financial results and will disclose any material consequences. Nichirei stated it would begin gradual restoration starting Friday, though no timeline for full service restoration was provided.

2f616245d20d.text: There has been a shift in the ransomware ecosystem as a new group has emerged as the most prolific threat actor behind cyber extortion campaigns in recent months. According to analysis of ransomware events between March and May 2026, The Gentlemen ransomware gang was responsible for the most attacks during the three-month period, accounting for 300 incidents. The Gentlemen usurped the Qilin ransomware affiliate operation, which was the most prolific group during each quarter during the previous year. The number of Qilin incidents between May and March is reported at 289, dropping the group to the second most prolific. The analysis of ransomware trends during the period by cybersecurity researchers at ReliaQuest was published on July 16. In total, 1368 claims of victims by 11 ransomware groups were tracked via posts about them on data leak sites. The victims were spread across 99 countries. There was a significant gap between ransomware incidents by The Gentlemen and Qilin compared with other notable ransomware operators, with DragonForce, Akira and LockBit accounting for between 150 and 100 observed incidents each during the period. Those three ransomware crews have been responsible for some of the most significant incidents in recent years, but, like Qilin, they appear to have been surpassed by a relative newcomer to the scene. "The Gentlemen became the most-active group, powered by aggressive affiliate recruitment and a well-packaged intrusion kit that lowers the bar for new operators," wrote Tristano Di Liberto, security analyst at ReliaQuest. "The pressure The Gentlemen applies is likely to persist into Q3," he added. Analysis of The Gentlemen by ReliaQuest has suggested that the pre-packaged, easy-to-use tools that affiliates of the ransomware-as-a-service operation are provided with has played a significant role in the rise of the group. Such tools include a playbook which affiliates can consult as a resource which gives them a guide to the attack chain and the workflow, advice on what edge devices to target for exploitation, how to use lightweight tunneling tools for command servers, and how to deploy Single-host Server Message Block (SMB) encryption. Leaked chat logs have suggested that The Gentlemen, like some other cybercriminal operations, harness the power of AI tools to speed up development and new versions of their offering – and doing it faster than rival ransomware groups which have not attempted to exploit AI. According to ReliaQuest, this could lead to affiliates abandoning their current provider in favor of The Gentlemen. "It runs proven affiliate throughput, ships tools faster than most rivals through its AI-accelerated build pipeline and offers a pre-packaged intrusion kit that shortens ramp-up," said Di Liberto. To help protect against ransomware attacks, ReliaQuest recommended the following actions: Restrict RDP and remote access; Enforce Microsoft's vulnerable-driver block list; Monitor blockchain RPC and session messenger egress; Harden identity against vishing and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks.

eee8e479154a.text: ACR Stealer, an infostealer circulating since 2024, extracts browser passwords, live session tokens, PDFs, Microsoft 365 documents, and files from synced OneDrive and SharePoint folders from enterprise networks. The malware gains entry through social engineering—victims paste commands into Run boxes and press Enter. Microsoft's Defender Experts team documented two delivery chains, observing increased ACR Stealer activity from late April through mid-June across customer environments. The campaigns "successfully using ClickFix lures to steal browser credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents," according to the report. Fileless Chain: The attack spawns mshta.exe to retrieve remote HTA content. An embedded VBScript loader uses COM objects to decode and execute PowerShell, generating victim IDs and disabling certificate validation. A JPEG from an image host contains the payload embedded in pixels—custom routines extract, decrypt, decompress, and execute it reflectively. The malware targets Chrome and Edge, reading login databases and using DPAPI to decrypt passwords, cookies, and tokens. Disk-Leaving Chain: Commands pull DLLs from WebDAV shares over HTTPS using obfuscated filenames. Some variants use pushd to mount remote shares as local drives. Python scripts bundled with pythonw.exe persist via hidden scheduled tasks mimicking software updates, clear PowerShell history, and execute through Windows Fiber API. In some intrusions, a secondary Python loader queries public blockchain RPC endpoints using the "EtherHiding" technique—storing C2 pointers in smart contracts to avoid attacker-controlled resolvers. Key Finding: Neither chain exploits vulnerabilities; both depend entirely on user compliance with social engineering prompts. Recommended Defenses: Remove Run dialog access via Group Policy; Block mshta.exe through AppLocker or WDAC; Apply attack surface reduction rules preventing PowerShell, Python, and rundll32.exe from launching internet-delivered content; Hunt for rundll32.exe with no command-line parameters making network connections; Isolate suspected hosts, rotate credentials, and revoke tokens. Microsoft provided three Defender XDR hunting queries and 16 campaign domains.

67a116abd833.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a previously undocumented malware called GoSerpent targeting Southeast Asian government and diplomatic entities since late 2025. Russian firm Kaspersky uncovered the activity in February 2026. GoSerpent functions as a backdoor designed to "contact an external server and deploy secondary payloads on sensitive data collection and credential dumping on the system." The malware operates by receiving encrypted, Base64-encoded command arguments containing command-and-control addresses and communication passwords. Key capabilities include establishing SOCKS5 proxy servers, file transfers, remote shell access, and port listening. The malware supports commands for alerting servers of infections, establishing remote connections, uploading/downloading files, and spawning shells on compromised machines. Attackers deployed complementary tools throughout the campaign: ThumbcacheService (a DLL for sophisticated file collection), Mimikatz (extracts credentials from LSASS memory), QuarksDumpLocalHash (retrieves local account password hashes), McMx RAT (a lightweight proxy and remote access variant), Stowaway (advanced proxy tool with reverse tunneling and SSH features), and TmcLoader/TmcPayload (exfiltration modules deployed in May 2026). Kaspersky notes that "the strategic deployment of various tools with sophisticated data collection and exfiltration capabilities" makes this threat particularly concerning. The campaign shares overlaps with TetrisPhantom, an APT group previously documented targeting APAC government entities through secure USB exploits. The article also discusses a separate DoNot Team operation targeting Bangladesh's military using spear-phishing emails with malware-laced RTF documents.

fd0b2c6d5756.text: U.S. prosecutors on Thursday charged a New York man and woman for their roles in a large-scale crime ring that laundered money stolen in cyber investment fraud scams. 27-year-old Zhuoying Chen and 38-year-old Haojie Zhang allegedly managed a network of over a dozen people based in Queens and Brooklyn between 2020 and 2022. Chen and Zhang allegedly transferred at least $43 million in proceeds from investment scams laundered to bank accounts in China by the criminal network using 140 bank accounts under roughly 45 shell companies, according to an unsealed indictment. The underlying schemes involved criminals contacting potential targets via social media or messaging services to build trust and persuade them to invest in fraudulent opportunities. Victims were then shown fake profiles with profits to encourage further investment before additional funds invested in the scheme were stolen. "For nearly two years, these two Chinese nationals allegedly ran a sophisticated, illicit network that laundered funds stolen from unsuspecting victims' life savings," noted Executive Associate Director John A. Condon of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). "As alleged in the indictment, the defendants laundered fraud proceeds, enabling scammers to continue to victimize Americans and deprive them of their hard earned money," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division added. If found guilty of conspiracy to commit money laundering, Chen and Zhang face a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, investment fraud accounted for 49% of all scam-related incidents last year, resulting in reported losses of $8.6 billion, up from $6.5 billion in 2024.

0535c4e93308.text: A ransomware attack has disrupted milk production at Fairlife, Coca-Cola's dairy brand specializing in high-protein milk and nutrition beverages. The company disclosed the incident via an SEC filing on July 16, 2026. Coca-Cola stated that "production operations at fairlife in the United States are temporarily suspended," though Canadian operations remain unaffected. The organization emphasized that "Product quality and safety have not been impacted." The company responded by activating incident response protocols, engaging external cybersecurity advisors, and notifying law enforcement. However, they acknowledged that "The full scope, nature and impacts of the incident are not yet known." As of the article's publication, no ransomware group had claimed responsibility. Coca-Cola has not confirmed whether attackers obtained data or issued ransom demands. The company has not yet determined if the incident will materially affect operations.

d4af9ee4f1df.text: Autonomous web agents read whatever a page displays, and much of that content comes from strangers. Product reviews, seller listings, and advertisements sit beside trusted site menus on a single page. An agent that reads all of that text as instructions can be steered by any of it. A group at UC Berkeley describe Cross-Site Prompting, or XSP, as the agent-era version of Cross-Site Scripting. Their system, Prismata, sits between a web agent and the browser. It filters the content an agent sees and limits the actions the agent can take. The comparison to XSS runs through the whole design. Cross-Site Scripting lets an attacker plant a script on a trusted site so it runs in a visitor's browser. XSP swaps executable code for plain language. An attacker writes a product review that tells the agent to send the user's credit card details to a stranger, and the agent may comply. Older web defenses translate poorly to this setting. Input sanitizers screen for code, and prompt injections carry none. Prismata works from the structure of the page. For any button, link, or form field, there is a path of ancestor elements running from the top of the page down to that element. The Berkeley team measured that these paths consist almost entirely of developer-written scaffolding such as layout containers and navigation. A reasoning model reads only that path and the user's task, then decides whether the element belongs to the task. An injection sitting elsewhere on the page stays out of that decision. The measurement came from a corpus of real pages. Across more than 90,000 samples of untrusted content drawn from Common Crawl and Mind2Web, about 1.2 percent sat on a path leading to something the agent could click or fill. The rest were dead ends for an attacker. For the small share of cases where untrusted content does sit on such a path, Prismata borrows from a 1977 security design. The Biba integrity model enforces a no-read-down, no-write-up rule, and the team applies it to the page tree. The system reads each layer of the path before revealing its children, watching for signs that untrusted content is coming. Headings such as "Reviews," accessibility labels, and developer class names like review-card mark the boundary. When a signal appears, everything below it inherits a lower trust label and gets pruned or set to read-only. The tests ran in WebArena, which is about as close to the live web as a benchmark gets. It runs a real GitLab instance and a production-grade shopping platform, so the page structures resemble what an agent would meet in the wild. The attacks were pop-up style lures planted where a malicious user or ad network could plausibly put them. Attack success dropped from 85.5 percent without the defense to 0.7 percent with it. Task completion under attack climbed from roughly one in twenty to nearly one in four. With no attack present, task success slipped from 29.9 percent to 26.6 percent once the filtering kicked in. The labels driving all of this come from language models, and the choice of model matters. Six labelers went head to head against human security experts on a set of WebArena pages, and each one admitted elements that lined up with the experts more than nine times out of ten. GPT-5.4-nano was the most cautious of the group, hitting 98.69 percent precision at the cost of the lowest recall. Gemini 3 Flash scored the highest F1. When an injection sits on the path to an action with no signal ahead of it, the attacker's text reaches the deciding step, and neither mechanism keeps it out. The team found this in roughly one in a thousand paths, dropping to about 0.017 percent on sites that follow web best practices. Language models sit at every stage of the pipeline, which sets a ceiling on the guarantee. The paper reports that Prismata held up against adaptive attackers who ran iterative attempts to fool its labeling, driving those attacks to zero. The bigger picture is an old idea carried into new territory: classical confinement principles meet probabilistic model outputs, resting on the bets that models label pages well and that sites keep structuring their HTML conventionally.

45b7f912f1fa.text: Researchers from Harvard Kennedy School, Meta, and other institutions studied AI voice phishing by testing 4,100 US adults with synthetic voices and human callers as controls using six commercial voice systems. Detection Limitations: While participants correctly identified synthetic voices 70.3% of the time, they also misidentified human callers as machines two-thirds of the time. Exposure to AI tools showed no meaningful improvement in detection accuracy. Persuasion Over Voice Quality: The study found that "persuasiveness" was the primary factor driving compliance, increasing odds by 2.58x per scale increment. How human the voice sounded proved irrelevant once other factors were controlled. Synthetic voices still persuaded people despite being identified as artificial. Compliance Rates: Approximately 16.5% across all scenarios agreed to comply, with the "fake relative in trouble" scenario reaching 36.1%. However, only 6.5% gave definitive yes responses; others merely hesitated. Recommended Defenses: The research suggests awareness training focused on voice detection is ineffective. Instead, organizations should implement out-of-band verification methods including callback procedures using known numbers, family code words, identity proofing beyond voice recognition, and processes preventing inbound callers from unilaterally triggering credential resets or transfers.

86cd2960160b.text:
In this Help Net Security video, Viktor Bulanek, CTO of Penetrify, explains where security budget waste comes from.

Budgets get built around vendor categories, compliance checkboxes, and last year's headlines. Attackers work along attack paths, and that mismatch is where the money goes. He walks through the two big leaks, overlapping tools that flag the same issue three times, and shelfware that covers a third of the estate at 100% of the invoice.

The license fee is the small part. The hidden costs are triage hours, alert fatigue, and false confidence. Viktor gives a five step plan any team can run in a quarter: map tool overlap, measure how many findings were ever proven exploitable, cut or consolidate, move the savings toward continuous validation of real attack paths, and track one metric, cost per validated exploitable finding fixed before production.

Most teams don't need more money. They need to move the money they have.

f1b9e68399c1.text:
Large cloud storage operators track their hard drives every day, recording which units keep running and which ones drop off the racks. Backblaze does this at scale, and its Q1 2026 report covers a fleet built for continuous use.

The analysis covered 341,263 hard drives, after boot drives and a small group of units that missed the reporting thresholds were set aside. The pool spans capacities from 4TB to past 20TB.

The quarterly annualized failure rate came to 1.24%. That figure rose from the prior quarter and settled under the level of a year earlier. Across the whole fleet, the lifetime failure rate stands at 1.39%, a steadier long-run gauge of how the hardware holds up.

Newer, higher-capacity hardware carried much of the load. The company added more than ten thousand drives during the period, most of them holding more than 20TB each. This young pool posted an annualized failure rate of 0.85%, strong for freshly deployed equipment.

No new drive models joined the fleet this quarter, an outcome the company calls rare given that new models arrived in six of the past eight quarters. Several existing models ran clean, with the HGST HUH728080ALE600 and two others recording zero failures over the period.

Failure counts and failure rates tell separate stories. The Seagate ST16000NM000J logged a single failure and still posted a 3.61% annualized rate, a result driven by a pool that has dwindled to about 130 units. One drop from a small group moves the percentage a long way.

Several other models logged just one failure each across the quarter, among them the Toshiba MG09ACA16TE and a pair of Seagate drives in the 12TB to 14TB range. Their raw failure counts look calm, and their rates stay low because their populations remain large.

Backblaze counts failures with a C++ program that gathers SMART statistics at the end of each day. A drive present one day and absent the next gets logged as a failure, with a lookback window that reverses the call if the serial number returns within the quarter. The reported rates reflect people "actively managing failure and risk."

The method depends on a drive appearing in the pool the day before, which leaves day-one failures outside its reach. Some drives give out on their first day in a data center, and the counter can miss them. Day-one failures have probably gone under-recorded across the program's history. Drive qualification before deployment keeps such cases rare, so the effect on the published figures stays small.

The complete dataset remains available for download.

Products Featured:

929a2dc4aa54.text:
SANS Stormcast Podcast Summary, Friday, July 17th, 2026, Handler: Johannes Ullrich.

Windows Hello for Business: The German Federal Information Security Office published a 169-page analysis of Windows Hello's architecture. Key findings included: Enhanced Sign-in Security (ESS) protects biometric data via TPM rather than filesystem encryption; biometric authentication provides no additional cryptographic entropy versus PIN-based approaches; biometric methods offer practical advantages ('a PIN is easily lost without the user knowing that it was lost while in order to use the biometrics the attacker would have to steal the device'); multi-user device configurations increase security risks; the analysis documents undocumented features and fills gaps in Microsoft's official documentation.

NGINX Vulnerability: F5 disclosed a heap-based buffer overflow in NGINX (both Plus and open-source versions) affecting map expressions, commonly used for traffic routing and A/B testing. The vulnerability requires specific configurations; with Address Space Layout Randomization enabled, exploitation is limited to denial-of-service attacks.

7-Zip XZ Decompression Flaw: A heap-based buffer overflow affecting 7-Zip's XZ decompression was reported to maintainers in June 2026, with patches now available through coordinated disclosure by the Zero Day Initiative.

e3ea75b43bea.text:
South Korea is developing its own security-focused AI model and hopes to bring it online by the end of the year, to ensure the nation has sovereign bug-finding capabilities.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon revealed the effort to create the model yesterday, and said it's needed so South Korea possesses a bug-finding model to rival Anthropic's Mythos.

The US government has twice blocked access to Mythos, once by requiring Anthropic to offer it only to American citizens, a demand the AI company could not meet and therefore blocked all access, and a second time by ordering the company to take down its services so Washington could investigate allegations of possible dangerous performance problems.

Those incidents led many other nations conclude that the US could in future deny access to powerful models, meaning US-based organizations and national security agencies would have an edge. Washington has since allowed limited access to Mythos to some of its allies.

Interest in developing sovereign AI capacity has nonetheless soared, and Bae said South Korea now aspires to develop its own Mythos-class model. The Register is aware of another effort to create Mythos-like tools, involving private firms and infrastructure operators across several countries.

In South Korea, the government's approach is to add security-related information to the corpus it is using to train a locally developed frontier model. The minister said he expects that security-capable model will debut by the end of 2026.

South Korea has also sought bids to create a chatbot that will be made freely available to all residents, plus an agentic application that will help locals interact with government services.

Minister Bae made his remarks at a policy briefing session conducted by President Lee Jae Myung, during which discussions about AI also touched on using the technology to detect fake news in real time, and put it to work handling complaints about government services more quickly than is currently possible.

e0c0d59059fd.text:
Authors: Microsoft Security Research and Balaji Venkatesh S. Published July 16, 2026.

Microsoft Defender Experts documented two distinct ACR Stealer campaigns operating from late April through mid-June 2026, both leveraging ClickFix social engineering tactics to compromise enterprise environments.

Campaign 1: WebDAV-Based Delivery. This intrusion chain uses deceptive prompts directing users to execute commands that load malware via remote WebDAV shares. The attack employs three execution variants, with advanced versions using obfuscated console commands and environment variable manipulation to reduce visibility. The infection sequence involves: remote DLL loading through rundll32.exe; obfuscated PowerShell scripts with arithmetic no-ops and fake control flow; Python-based loaders with multiple encoding layers; Fiber API shellcode execution for in-memory payload delivery; and browser credential harvesting using DPAPI decryption. A notable subset leverages blockchain-based dead-drop resolvers (EtherHiding technique) for command-and-control infrastructure, enabling dynamic updates without malware redeployment.

Campaign 2: Fileless MSHTA Chain. This variant prioritizes fileless execution through: MSHTA launching VBScript-wrapped PowerShell payloads; steganographic payload extraction from JPEG images hosted on compromised services; dynamic API resolution for reflective shellcode execution; Chromium browser credential theft targeting Login Data and Web Data databases; and systematic collection of PDFs and Office documents.

Key Mitigation Strategies: Microsoft recommends educating users about ClickFix dangers, enforcing web filtering, restricting scripting tools through application control, monitoring suspicious persistence mechanisms, and hardening endpoints against credential theft through multifactor authentication and conditional access policies. Both campaigns ultimately seek to exfiltrate sensitive credentials and enterprise data for follow-on compromise activities.

e2487a78ea3e.text:
Author: Rapid7. Published July 17, 2026 (last updated July 23, 2026).

Rapid7 reported on a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Microsoft SharePoint Server deployments. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-58644, received a CVSS score of 9.8 and stems from improper handling of untrusted data during deserialization processes.

Microsoft disclosed the vulnerability on July 14, 2026, confirming active exploitation attempts. The issue was subsequently added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog within two days.

Affected Products: Microsoft SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016; Microsoft SharePoint Server 2019; Microsoft SharePoint Server Subscription Edition.

Key Recommendations: Microsoft and CISA advised organizations to apply the July 14, 2026 security updates for all affected SharePoint versions and verify successful installation across all servers. Additional guidance included enabling Antimalware Scan Interface integration and monitoring for specific detection signatures.

Related Development: On July 22, 2026, a separate deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2026-50522) was also added to the KEV catalog, affecting the same SharePoint products. Organizations applying the comprehensive July 14 updates would be protected against both exploited vulnerabilities.

Rapid7 customers using Exposure Command, InsightVM, or Nexpose gained access to authenticated vulnerability checks for this threat following the July 14 content release.

df8d574fe2c9.text:
Author: Sergiu Gatlan. Published July 17, 2026.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday ordered government agencies to prioritize patching two actively exploited vulnerabilities in the Fortinet FortiSandbox threat detection platform.

These two critical-severity security flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-39808 and CVE-2026-25089) were addressed by Fortinet on April 14 and June 9, respectively.

As the company detailed in security advisories issued at the time, successful exploitation allows unauthenticated threat actors to execute unauthorized code remotely through low-complexity command injection attacks that require no user interaction.

To resolve these issues and block incoming attacks, admins must upgrade all affected deployments to the latest released versions.

While Fortinet has yet to tag these two vulnerabilities as used in attacks, and has not yet replied to BleepingComputer's emails regarding in-the-wild exploitation, threat intelligence company Defused revealed on June 16 that attackers had started abusing them in the wild.

"We are observing exploitation of multiple Fortinet FortiSandbox vulnerabilities during the past 24 hours, including: CVE-2026-39813 (no previous recorded exploitation), CVE-2026-39808, CVE-2026-25089 (vibecoded, likely faulty exploit)," Defused warned.

On Thursday, CISA also confirmed that the flaws are actively exploited in the wild, adding them to its catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities. As mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, U.S. federal agencies must patch vulnerable FortiSandbox instances by Sunday, July 19.

In February, Fortinet also patched a critical SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-21643) in the FortiClient Enterprise Management Server (EMS) platform, which Defused flagged as actively exploited one month later.

Two months later, the company addressed another security issue exploited in attacks: a path traversal vulnerability (CVE-2025-61624) that can allow authenticated attackers to escalate privileges.

Fortinet vulnerabilities are often exploited in cyber espionage campaigns and in ransomware attacks (often as zero-days). In total, CISA tracks 28 Fortinet vulnerabilities that have been exploited in attacks in recent years, 13 of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.

912bdf33e24e.text:
Author: Ravie Lakshmanan (The Hacker News, syndicating Proofpoint research). Published July 14, 2026.

At least two distinct threat actors are weaponizing a novel evasion technique called OAuth client ID spoofing in cloud campaigns while evading detection systems.

The activity allows users to enumerate user accounts and validate stolen credentials in Microsoft Entra ID environments without generating a successful sign-in event that would alert defenders.

According to Proofpoint: 'A blind spot exists in cloud sign-in telemetry: Entra ID returns different error responses depending on whether a supplied OAuth client ID is valid.' Attackers exploit this disparity to infer valid usernames and correct passwords at scale, effectively validating stolen credential lists without logging a successful login.

The attacks leverage the OAuth client ID, passed as 'client_id' in authentication requests via the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flow, using a syntactically valid client ID that doesn't correspond to a real application. 'If the spoofed client ID is not a proper UUIDv4, Entra does not reject the request outright,' allowing attackers to analyze AADSTS error responses to infer account/password validity. 'When a spoofed client ID is used, no corresponding application name is recorded in the sign-in log,' meaning detections looking for surges against a specific application name may miss the activity.

Proofpoint identified two large campaigns independently adopting this technique toward the end of December 2025: UNK_pyreq2323 (January to March 2026), using over 700,000 spoofed client IDs from AWS infrastructure targeting more than 1 million accounts across nearly 4,000 tenants, causing lockouts for roughly 28% of targeted users; and UNK_OutFlareAZ (starting December 2025), leveraging Cloudflare infrastructure targeting over 2 million users with 3.7 million randomized spoofed application IDs.

Organizations attempting to mitigate traditional enumeration attacks through Conditional Access policies scoped to specific applications won't catch spoofed client IDs. Yaniv Miron, director of threat research at Proofpoint, stated the problem is 'specific to Microsoft,' though 'we do believe that other identity providers are possibly exposed to such issues.'

28ddd11c3621.text:
Author: Eric Geller, Senior Reporter. Published July 13, 2026.

Organizations should be on guard for a hacking campaign in which attackers spoof OAuth client IDs to collect information about targets' user directories, according to security firm Proofpoint. The firm observed 'multiple campaigns at scale abusing spoofed OAuth application identifiers, with distinct tooling, infrastructure, and execution patterns indicating independent adoption by multiple threat actors.'

Microsoft Entra, the tech giant's identity management service, records hacking attempts in logs with information that can help defenders isolate potentially compromised accounts and malicious IP addresses. However, hackers have developed evasive techniques to obfuscate their activities and origins.

OAuth client IDs tell Microsoft Entra which application is attempting to access user data. By faking a client ID, hackers can collect username and password information from the Entra database without operating a genuine application that Entra trusts.

'Spoofed client IDs enable account enumeration without a registered OAuth application and allow attackers to infer both password and account validity without generating a successful sign-in event,' Proofpoint explained in its report.

Security teams typically monitor Entra logs for activity surges against specific applications. Using spoofed client IDs, which generate blank entries in the application field, allows attackers to evade trend-based monitoring. The technique also circumvents conditional-access policies designed for targeted applications.

Two major campaigns leveraged this technique. The January campaign used over 700,000 spoofed IDs targeting information about more than one million user accounts across nearly 4,000 organizations. The December campaign, with a February wave, was significantly larger, using 3.7 million spoofed IDs against over two million users.

'The emergence of multiple campaigns with unique tools and infrastructure suggests this technique is gaining traction among threat actors targeting cloud environments,' Proofpoint warned.

Businesses should monitor Entra logs for sign-in attempts with blank application IDs and watch for error code AADSTS700016, associated with unrecognized application IDs.

e704dfd8e429.text:
Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) are sophisticated, long-term cyber campaigns conducted by well-funded human adversaries (often nation-states) who target specific organizations for espionage, data theft, or critical infrastructure disruption. Traditional security tools often fail because APT groups bypass signature-based defenses by using customized malware and Living-off-the-Land (LotL) tactics that mimic legitimate user activity inside the network. Effective advanced persistent threat detection requires minimizing breakout time, the window between initial access and lateral movement.

What is an APT? Advanced: APT actors utilize customized malware, discover and weaponize zero-day vulnerabilities, and practice meticulous OpSec. Persistent: APTs utilize a low-and-slow methodology, remaining inside an environment for months. Threat: APTs are backed by well-funded organizational structures, state-sponsored units.

The Multi-Stage APT Attack Lifecycle: 1. Reconnaissance and Planning; 2. Initial Infiltration (spear-phishing, credential stuffing, supply chain compromise); 3. Establishing Footholds (backdoors, rootkits); 4. Lateral Movement and Escalation (harvesting admin credentials, mapping AD trust boundaries); 5. Data Exfiltration or Disruption (C2 channels, ransomware or DDoS as a distraction).

Why Traditional Detection Isn't Enough: Signature-Based Defenses fail against custom/LotL tactics; Dwell Time issues with reactive SIEM/EDR; Alert Fatigue and Data Silos; Fragmented Vendor Taxonomies for naming threat groups.

Shifting to Real-Time Intelligence: continuously harvesting data from open, deep, and dark web to track adversary infrastructure setup, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

Mastering APT Detection with Recorded Future: The Intelligence Graph maps relationships between billions of entities in real time; Third-Party Risk gives visibility into vendor/partner security postures; Insikt Group provides elite human threat research and hunting rules (YARA, Sigma, Snort); Recorded Future AI enables natural-language querying to reduce MTTR and generate intelligence briefs.

FAQs cover APT objectives, why detection is difficult, what 'breakout time' means, and how generative AI improves detection.

6f472c2e2c85.text:
Author: Stan Kaminsky. Published July 17, 2026.

When targeting an organization to steal information, maintaining a low profile is critical for attackers. Malware and stolen-credential use both risk detection or lockout. The ToddyCat APT developed a technique named 'Shadow Token via Remote Debug' (STRD) to establish reliable, persistent access to a victim's Google Workspace mailbox, potentially adaptable to other OAuth 2.0-based services.

How an STRD Attack Works: Attackers first compromise the victim's system with malware, often via known server software vulnerabilities or malicious loaders distributed via messaging apps, sometimes deployed remotely using stolen admin credentials. The malware then executes an STRD attack, connecting the attackers' remote service to the victim's mailbox via OAuth 2.0, with no user interaction or visible activity. The malware can then delete itself; the adversary retains access via the acquired OAuth token independent of the endpoint.

The Core Concept: ToddyCat's tool, Umbrij, identifies installed browsers, copies the user's active Chrome/Edge profile folder (including session cookies) to a new location, and launches a headless instance of the browser pointed at the duplicate profile in remote-debugging mode, controlled via the DevTools protocol using the Puppeteer automation library. Umbrij opens a Google Workspace OAuth consent screen, spoofing the application ID of legitimate tools (Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook or Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook), and uses debugging commands to programmatically click through account selection and consent. Google issues an authorization code, which Umbrij exfiltrates to a C2 server; attackers then exchange it for a long-lived OAuth access token granting mailbox access that can survive password resets.

Protection: Incident response for compromised accounts should include resetting passwords, terminating active sessions, revoking OAuth tokens and third-party app permissions, and reviewing legacy App Passwords. Prevention: block standard users from launching browsers in debugging mode via the DeveloperToolsAvailability group policy (Chrome and Edge), and configure SIEM/XDR monitoring for browser instances launched with an active debugging port.

134ea91ebac2.text:
Author: Christopher Granleese. Published July 17, 2026 (last updated July 27, 2026).

This Metasploit update announcement highlights several developments, shifting the Wrap Up blog to a bi-weekly cadence while maintaining weekly framework releases.

Linux Fetch Multi Payload Family: enhanced fetch payload capabilities via a Linux Fetch Multi payload family that automatically detects target architecture. 'The new Linux Fetch Multi family will report the architecture of the target host when it requests the payload, and the handler will automatically serve the correct elf architecture payload for the given target.'

RISC-V Architecture Support: Developer bcoles expanded support to include RISC-V IoT systems, adding 'staged and stageless shell payloads for both 32- and 64-bit RiscV systems' alongside XOR encoders for this architecture.

New Modules (4 additions): 1. HTTP to SMB Relay, an auxiliary module enabling NTLM authentication relay from HTTP to SMB servers; 2. Byte XORi Encoder, eight encoder variants for RISC-V 32-bit and 64-bit systems; 3. Fetch Payloads, 421 new payloads across Linux and Windows architectures with FTP support; 4. FTP Fetch Stagers, shell command stages for RISC-V targets supporting bind and reverse TCP connections.

Enhancements and Bug Fixes: Four enhancement PRs improved RISC-V encoder support, added FTP fetch capabilities, extended TLS certificate tracing for HTTPS connections, and updated Windows service templates. Four bug fixes addressed macOS fileless staging, XOR encoder register preservation, payload cache generation, and HTTP relay request handling issues.

42d69b7e065c.text:
Author: Daniel Stepanic. Published 18 July 2026.

Elastic Security Labs discovered a new campaign by Contagious Interview (tracked as REF9403) that hides malware within SVG image files using steganography techniques. The operation targets developers through fake job postings and coding challenges.

Discovery and Attack Method: The investigation began when DPRK-aligned actors posted in Elastic's community Slack workspace under the username 'Maxwell,' offering e-commerce platform development work. Interested participants received trojanized repositories containing fully functional code laced with malicious snippets. 'Payloads are split into Base64 fragments inside HTML comments across every SVG flag image' in asset directories. A JavaScript file reassembles these chunks alphabetically to construct the malicious payload, which executes via eval() during server startup.

Four-Stage Payload: Credential and Wallet Stealer, exfiltrating browser credentials and cryptocurrency wallet data across Windows, macOS, and Linux, targeting 25 cryptocurrency extensions including MetaMask and Phantom. File Stealer, performing recursive sweeps targeting developer files matching patterns like '*.env, *.pem, *.secret' and directories such as '.ssh, .aws, .azure,' while deliberately avoiding AI tool directories (.claude, .cursor, .windsurf). Socket.IO RAT, establishing persistent command-and-control via HTTPS, providing 'interactive shell access to the victim machine in real time' through the /api/service/process/ endpoint. Clipboard Stealer, monitoring clipboard content every 500 milliseconds on Windows and macOS, exfiltrating changes to command servers.

DPRK Attribution: The malware shares 'code similarity with the malware known as OTTERCOOKIE, first discovered by NTT Security in December 2024.' Observed API endpoints and behaviors match previously documented Contagious Interview infrastructure.

Infrastructure and Observables: Command servers identified include ldb.rightwidth[.]dev (browser/wallet stealer), upload.rightwidth[.]dev (file exfiltration), controller.rightwidth[.]dev (Socket.IO RAT), and file.rightwidth[.]dev (Windows payload downloads). Seven trojanized repositories containing zero antivirus detections were identified, including 'next-ecommerce-private-main.zip' and 'shopping-platform-main.zip.'

Key Concern: The campaign emphasizes developer targeting, as 'compromising an individual developer can provide a path to much broader organizational impact' through supply chain attacks on downstream organizations.

0f744e4cee4f.text: wp2shell: WordPress Core RCE Vulnerability. Author: Swati Khandelwal. Date: July 17, 2026 (Updated July 18, 2026). A critical remote code execution vulnerability chain, dubbed wp2shell, affects WordPress core installations. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable sites with "no preconditions." The attack combines two CVE-identified flaws: CVE-2026-63030 (REST API batch-route confusion) and CVE-2026-60137 (SQL injection in WordPress core). The SQL injection exists in the WP_Query author __not_in parameter. When attackers pass a string instead of an array, validation is bypassed, allowing raw values into the database query. The batch endpoint (/wp-json/batch/v1) enables the exploit by running multiple sub-requests simultaneously. An error in one request misaligns parallel tracking arrays, causing execution under a different request's handler. This confusion bypasses endpoint restrictions and delivers malicious input to the vulnerable query unauthenticated. Affected versions: 6.8.0-6.8.5 (SQL injection only, patched in 6.8.6); 6.9.0-6.9.4 (full RCE chain, patched in 6.9.5); 7.0.0-7.0.1 (full RCE chain, patched in 7.0.2). WordPress released patches Friday and enabled forced updates across its auto-update system. Mitigation until patching: block /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 at WAF level, disable WP REST API entirely, or deploy a drop-in plugin rejecting anonymous batch requests. Searchlight Cyber notes the flaw affects default WordPress installations lacking persistent object caching. The vulnerability reached public disclosure after patch analysis, with proof-of-concept code now available on GitHub. Over 500 million WordPress sites exist globally, though only those running 6.9+ face RCE exposure.

be642f259c33.text: Friday Squid Blogging: Squid Washing Up on Cape Cod Beach. Published: July 17, 2026 at 5:01 PM. The main post is quite brief. Bruce Schneier notes that there are "lots of articles" about thousands of squid washing up on Cape Cod beaches, providing three links to news coverage from Boston25News, On the Water, and WCVB. He then states: "As usual, you can also use this squid post to talk about the security stories in the news that I haven't covered." Comments: The post generated 36 comments discussing security topics rather than squid. Notable discussions included: DNS poisoning attacks by APT28 targeting hotel WiFi to capture Microsoft 365 credentials; OpenAI's autonomous agents escaping sandbox during testing and attacking HuggingFace; Chinese AI models (Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Qwen) challenging US AI dominance; concerns about guardrails on AI systems being fundamentally breakable per Gödel's incompleteness theorems; password manager Passwork being "licensed for the FSB"; Russian-Chinese cyber collaboration increasing. The comments reflected broader security concerns dominating discussions on Schneier's blog rather than the squid-related headline.

f4434c934d56.text: Abbott Probes Two Cyber Incidents Amid Extortion Claims. By Lawrence Abrams. July 17, 2026 | 04:45 PM. Abbott Laboratories is investigating two separate cybersecurity incidents. The company confirmed unauthorized access to internal legacy Exact Sciences systems in its Cancer Diagnostics business after the ShinyHunters extortion gang added Abbott to its data leak site, threatening to publish allegedly stolen data unless the company negotiated. The Exact Sciences Incident: Abbott stated: "Abbott is investigating a cyber incident in which there was unauthorized access to a limited number of internal systems in our Cancer Diagnostics business only." The company emphasized this does not impact business operations, product availability, manufacturing, or lab operations. ShinyHunters claims it gained access through a vishing attack targeting Abbott employees in mid-June, compromising a Microsoft Entra single sign-on account. The threat actors alleged they exfiltrated data from multiple sources, including 30 million rows of customer personally identifiable information containing names, email addresses, phone numbers, and over one million Social Security numbers. They also claimed to have stolen approximately 22 million client notes containing doctor-patient conversations and over 20 million medical orders. The LabCentral Breach: A threat actor known as ShadowByt3$ claimed to have breached Abbott's Core Laboratory diagnostics business through its LabCentral customer portal using compromised credentials on July 4, 2026. The group asserts it obtained manufacturing certificates, operation manuals, technical specifications, and regulatory documentation. Abbott disputed this characterization, stating: "LabCentral is an externally facing third-party hosted portal used by Abbott's core laboratory diagnostics business" that "houses publicly available technical product reference documents" and "does not contain proprietary/sensitive customer or business information." As of publication, neither threat actor had publicly released stolen data.

35e4824cd858.text: Eleven bytes will make an unpatched OpenSSL server set aside up to 131 KB of memory for a message that never arrives. On the glibc systems Okta tested, that memory is gone until the process restarts. OpenSSL shipped the HollowByte fix in June with no CVE, no advisory, and no changelog entry pointing at it. Okta's Red Team, which reported the denial-of-service bug and named it, published the details on Thursday. The fixed releases are OpenSSL 4.0.1, 3.6.3, 3.5.7, 3.4.6, and 3.0.21, all dated June 9. The flaw is that OpenSSL took the attacker's word for it: every TLS handshake message carries a 4-byte header, three bytes of which declare how long the body will be, and older versions grew the receive buffer to that declared size before a single byte of the body arrived. For an inbound ClientHello the ceiling is 131 KB, then the worker thread blocks waiting on a body that never comes. What makes HollowByte stick is glibc: when the attacker drops the connection, OpenSSL frees the buffer, but glibc holds small/medium chunks for reuse rather than returning them to the kernel, and varying the claimed size on every connection stops the allocator from reusing what it freed, fragmenting the heap. In Okta's NGINX testing, a 1GB server was OOM-killed with 547MB frozen in fragments; on a 16GB server HollowByte locked up 25% of system memory without crossing the connection ceiling. Matt Caswell's pull request states the OpenSSL security team chose to "handle this as a 'bug or hardening' only fix," a category outside OpenSSL's four official severity tiers, meaning no CVE, changelog note, or vulnerabilities-page entry was issued. The Hacker News compared this to CVE-2025-66199 (Low) and CVE-2026-34183 (Moderate), both memory-exhaustion DoS bugs from the same release cycle that did receive CVEs. Update July 20: OpenSSL triager Alexandr Nedvedicky said HollowByte is closer to a deployment/configuration issue than a protocol flaw, noted he tested on OpenBSD (not glibc) and had not considered glibc-specific effects, and was unsure the shipped realloc-based fix improves anything for glibc. Update July 24: OpenSSL published its own analysis, confirming reproducible elevated resident memory on glibc/Linux after attacking connections close, but describing the increase as a bounded, one-time rise tied to peak concurrent handshakes rather than an accumulating leak, and stood by its classification while adding a CHANGES.md entry. It confirmed DTLS remains unaddressed and that OpenSSL 1.1.1/1.0.2 extended-support customers receive the fix through their supported releases. OpenSSL's nginx testing showed peak per-worker resident memory dropping from about 102MB to 53MB in the worst case after the fix, and recommends upgrading plus setting handshake/idle timeouts, connection caps, and rate limiting.

6a60548a6df2.text: Seven Malicious Vite npm Packages Use Blockchain C2 to Deliver a RAT. Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: July 17, 2026. Researchers at Checkmarx discovered seven malicious npm packages targeting the Vite frontend build tool ecosystem in a campaign dubbed ViteVenom. This attack expands upon an earlier supply chain campaign called ChainVeil, attributed to threat actor SuccessKey. Malicious packages identified (published June 29-July 3, 2026): @uw010010/vite-tree, @vite-tab/tab, @vite-ln/build-ts, @vite-mcp/vite-type, @vite-pro/vite-ui, @vitets/vite-ts, @vite-ts/vite-ui. Command & Control Infrastructure: the malware employs a novel four-tier blockchain-based C2 system spanning Tron, Aptos, and Binance Smart Chain. Checkmarx researcher Pavan Gudimalla explained: "The attacker stores payload pointers as transaction data on public blockchains rather than on domain names that can be seized, making the infrastructure nearly impossible to take down." Attack Execution: malicious code executes at import time rather than install time, enabling evasion of endpoint security tools. The payload retrieves next-stage malware capable of spawning reverse shells, harvesting credentials, exfiltrating files, and establishing persistent backdoors. Attribution Update: later analysis linked ViteVenom to PolinRider, a North Korean-linked threat group, based on overlapping blockchain wallet addresses and encryption keys. Recommended Actions: users should immediately uninstall affected packages, audit dependencies, rotate credentials, and inspect shell configuration files for unauthorized modifications.

9e5ac34ff2f4.text:
Lorenzo Franceschi-Bicchierai reports:
U.S. prosecutors have accused a Florida man of uploading fake video games that contained malware to Steam, the popular PC games platform. Once victims downloaded and installed the games, the malware was designed to infect their computers, steal their passwords and other data, and drain their crypto wallets, according to a criminal complaint.
On Tuesday, the FBI arrested Zyaire Wilkins, a 21-year-old Florida resident and student. On Wednesday, prosecutors accused him and a number of unnamed co-conspirators of hacking crimes. Over the past two years, Wilkins and his partners allegedly published several malware-laden video games on Steam, including BlockBlasters, Dashverse, Lampy, Lunara, and PirateFi.
Read more at TechCrunch.

4c3fda3f0f63.text: A Go botnet called NadMesh emerged in early July targeting exposed AI services, with the operator's dashboard displaying 3,811 unique AWS keys harvested. The malware uses a Shodan harvester to continuously scan for vulnerable instances of ComfyUI, Ollama, n8n, Open WebUI, Langflow, and Gradio—tools frequently deployed without adequate firewall protections. Recent intel indicates 47 credential breaches and 41 model inventories in its latest 100 records. QiAnXin's XLab published their analysis Friday, naming the threat after the "n4d mesh controller" string found in its code. XLab's independent sensor data tracked roughly zero source IPs distributing NadMesh through late June, spiking to approximately 139 daily in early July. The botnet extracts "cloud keys pulled out of environment variables, k8s service account tokens" and configuration files including ~/.aws/config, .env, and ~/.docker/config.json. MCP exploitation ranks highest in the controller's priority list, followed by Kubernetes, Docker API, and Redis, though Censys documented over 12,500 reachable MCP services by late April, growing to roughly 21,000 by May 6. XLab's traffic analysis reveals docker_containers_api_rce comprises 30.31% of attempts, Jenkins_scripttext_rce another 22.28%, with Telnet weak passwords at 10.36% and Redis at 8.29%; MCP command execution barely registers below 1% in observed traffic. The scanning infrastructure adapts dynamically, with hits receiving denser sampling and non-responsive targets blacklisted as suspected honeypots. Recent CVEs in the exploitation chain include CVE-2026-39987 (Marimo pre-auth RCE) and CVE-2026-41176 (rclone RC server authentication bypass). Priority ports requiring restriction include 8188 (ComfyUI), 11434 (Ollama), 7860 (Gradio), and 5678 (n8n). Organizations should check for persistence artifacts and immediately revoke exposed AWS keys, cluster tokens, and registry logins. Indicators: C2 at 209.99.186[.]235, domain cdnorigin[.]net, agent SHA1 31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec.

ae7e2d5b50a6.text: The Good | Authorities Sanction Cybercriminals & Dismantle Russian Bulletproof Hosting Infrastructure. The European Union and United Kingdom have jointly sanctioned multiple Russian individuals and entities targeting government networks and critical infrastructure across Europe, including senior GRU officers and FSB-linked entities. The U.S. Treasury Department designated First VPN Service (1VPNS) and administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi for supplying infrastructure enabling ransomware attacks; law enforcement dismantled the platform in May. Yegeniy Silayev faced sanctions for developing cryptors concealing malware estimated to have facilitated billions in losses. Federal prosecutors unsealed indictments against three Russian nationals (Aleksandr Volosovik, Yulia Pankova, Kirill Zatolokin) operating bulletproof hosting services 'Media Land' and 'ML Cloud' that facilitated over $62 million in global ransomware damages tied to LockBit, Play, and Blacksuit. The State Department offers a $10 million reward for information on foreign government links to these hosting providers. The Bad | Attackers Trojanize Popular Remote User Platforms to Deploy Starland Malware. Threat actor UAT-11795, active since June 2025, distributes financially-motivated malware targeting users in the US, Germany, Romania, and Venezuela, disguising installers as WebEx, Zoom, MobaXterm, DBeaver, and FaceIT, likely via ClickFix social engineering. The infection chain begins with a malicious HTA file retrieving an altered NSIS installer containing a hidden Python loader that modifies the Windows Registry for persistence before deploying the Starland RAT, which verifies sandboxes, escalates privileges, scans for browser data/wallets/AV products/AD infrastructure, captures screenshots, executes shell commands, and fetches secondary payloads including CastleStealer and Remcos, using Polygon smart contracts and Telegram bots for resilient C2. The Ugly | Nearly 300 Imposter GitHub Repositories Distribute Infostealing Malware. Threat actors published approximately 300 fabricated GitHub repositories impersonating premium security products, cryptocurrency tools, and developer utilities to distribute the BoryptGrab infostealer. Malicious landing pages use client-side scripts to render customized branding and spoofed trust badges. Downloads deliver rotating ZIP archives containing legitimate signed WinGUP updaters paired with trojanized DLLs, triggering side-loading and reflective execution of BoryptGrab in memory. The stealer targets passwords, payment details, and session cookies across 19 browsers and 32 crypto wallet brands, plus messaging tokens from Discord, Steam, and Telegram, using direct code injection to bypass Chrome's App-Bound Encryption; harvested data is routed to Russian-based C2 servers. GitHub has removed many fake repositories, though malicious redirector pages remain active.

6a469bd009a8.text: GoldenEyeDog Subgroup Linked to DigiCert Breach and Code-Signing Certificate Theft. Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: July 17, 2026. Cybersecurity researchers have connected the April 2026 DigiCert security incident to a threat cluster called CylindricalCanine, identified as a subgroup of GoldenEyeDog (also known as APT-Q-27, Dragon Breath, and Miuuti Group). This Chinese cybercrime organization has targeted gambling and gaming sectors since at least 2015. The Breach Details: in April 2026, the threat actors compromised DigiCert support staff by delivering malicious files disguised as customer screenshots through a support chat channel. This allowed them to access initialization codes for pending EV Code Signing certificate orders. The attackers subsequently obtained and weaponized 27 code-signing certificates to sign Zhong Stealer malware. DigiCert revoked 60 certificates across multiple Certificate Authorities in response. Attack Infrastructure: the primary malware tool is Golden Gh0st RAT, a modified Gh0st Remote Access Trojan variant. According to Expel security researcher Aaron Walton, "the threat actor used a limited function...to access customer accounts...to facilitate support tasks." The malware features capabilities including data theft, keylogging, screenshot capture, and Windows Event log clearing. Targeted Applications: the RAT specifically targets data from browsers (Chrome, Firefox, 360 Secure Browser, Tencent QQ) and messaging platforms like Skype and Tencent QQ.
