8ff7539b35fc.text: Cybersecurity firm Barracuda has detected over one million retail-themed phishing attacks since April that employ "text salting"—a decades-old technique that embeds random, benign-sounding words into malicious emails to confuse AI-powered security systems. The technique works by peppering emails with harmless filler text designed to deceive automated scanners while remaining invisible to human readers. Attackers typically use three primary methods to hide this content: CSS cropping (reducing the visible window), text manipulation (moving content outside the visible screen), and zero-font techniques (inserting misleading words between visible phishing text). "Text salting and related techniques can be used to confuse AI-driven content analysis engines by flooding the email with random terms," Barracuda explained in its report, noting that AI systems struggle because they lack understanding of whether text is visible or hidden. While modern email security systems have largely adapted to these tactics through techniques like hidden text removal and anomaly detection, large language models typically process email text plainly without distinguishing between visible and hidden content. Barracuda suggests most tools probably aren't equipped with such training by default. Recommended Defenses: Barracuda recommends enterprises adopt a layered email security approach including sender reputation checks, authentication verification, URL inspection, HTML rendering analysis, and detection of discrepancies between visible and hidden content—potentially even abandoning AI-based filters altogether.

aa0d03c5fa91.text: Microsoft Security will present research and insights at Black Hat USA 2026 (August 4-6) focused on how threat actors exploit trusted systems and supply chains. The company highlights that attackers target "software, services, identities, tools, developer workflows, and AI systems that organizations already depend on." Main Stage Sessions: David Weston's keynote (9:15 AM PT, August 5) examines how security teams adapt when offensive capabilities become more accessible and scalable. "Poisoned at the Source" (2:30-3:00 PM PT, August 5): Aarti Borkar and Tanmay Ganacharya discuss Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigations into ongoing npm supply chain attacks. Black Hat Briefings: three peer-reviewed technical sessions will cover cloud, mobile, and software supply chain defense: GitHub security monitoring (Yossi Weizman), Samsung Bixby device compromise vulnerabilities (Dimitrios Valsamakas), and Azure Automation cross-tenant identity takeover risks (Shay Shavit). Booth Experience: Microsoft Security's booth (#2144) transforms into a community hub featuring connection circles and expert AMAs on threat intelligence and incident response, 13 Microsoft Intelligent Security Association partners demonstrating integrated solutions, live demonstrations of AI-powered defense tools, and custom security-themed swag. Microsoft Security Reception: hosted Wednesday, August 5 (6:00-9:00 PM PT) at Swingers mini golf venue. Pre-Event Skilling: the Microsoft Black Hat Skilling Challenge launches July 20, enabling remote participants to develop hands-on expertise with Microsoft Defender, Sentinel, and Security Copilot.

d1e52c22227c.text: Researchers at Comparitech have determined that government agencies worldwide experience ransomware attacks at an alarming rate—approximately one incident per day. Their analysis of attacks between January and June 2026 documented 187 ransomware incidents targeting government organizations, representing a 13% increase from the 165 attacks recorded in the latter half of 2025. This frequency is particularly concerning because government entities represent high-value targets. Rebecca Moody, head of data research at Comparitech, explained: "From weeks-long disruptions due to system encryption to extensive data breaches, governments are the ideal target for hackers." The vulnerability stems from the substantial disruption ransomware causes to public services and the sensitive citizen data these organizations hold, making ransom payment more likely than attempting independent system recovery. Geographic Distribution: the United States bore the heaviest burden, accounting for 31% of recorded incidents. Germany, Spain, and Italy followed with 7%, 4%, and 4% respectively. Ransom Demands: the average ransom demand reached $100,000, though outliers existed. The Land and Agricultural Development Bank of South Africa received a $3.1 million demand following a January 2026 attack, ultimately refusing payment. Perpetrators: the most prolific attackers included The Gentlemen (10%), Qilin (9%), and LockBit (7%). Defense Recommendations: Moody advised organizations to implement proactive cybersecurity strategies: "Keeping systems up to date, patching vulnerabilities as soon as they're flagged, carrying out regular backups, and making sure employees are regularly trained and are on high alert at all times are crucial to mitigating the risks of attacks."

0cb522f65700.text: Ernst & Young disclosed a significant data breach affecting its customers. The company discovered unauthorized access to a third-party support ticket system used by its IT personnel on April 23, 2026, prompting an investigation with external cybersecurity experts. The breach occurred between March 28 and April 12, 2026, during which attackers downloaded multiple documents. These files contained personal and financial information used in tax filings for affected clients. EY noted that "support tickets submitted through the platform may have included documents containing client tax information." As one of the world's largest professional services firms with 406,000 employees and $53.2 billion in annual revenue, EY serves major organizations across 150+ countries. The company has not disclosed the specific ticketing system vendor, the exact number of affected customers, or whether the breach extended beyond U.S. clients. EY states it is "not aware of any misuse or further exposure of the stolen files." In response, EY is offering affected clients 24 months of identity monitoring and restoration services through Experian, with enrollment required by October 31, 2026. The company notified federal law enforcement and secured its systems. At publication, no ransomware or extortion groups claimed responsibility, though later reports indicate the ShinyHunters gang took credit for the incident.

fb0944c6d3c8.text: A coalition of 42 US attorneys general, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, has reached an $18 million settlement with genetic testing company 23andMe following its October 2023 data breach. Additionally, 23andMe will pay over $705,000 to New York. The breach exposed information for more than six million individuals, including ancestry data. Initially, 23andMe attributed the incident to credential stuffing rather than direct network infiltration, citing customer password management failures and lack of multi-factor authentication (MFA) as contributing factors. After 23andMe filed for bankruptcy protection in March 2025, the attorneys general pursued claims related to the breach. In June 2025, James and a bipartisan coalition of 27 other attorneys general sued 23andMe to safeguard genetic information during bankruptcy proceedings. Following the bankruptcy, 23andMe's customer data transferred to TTAM Research, a nonprofit established by founder and former CEO Anne Wojcicki. The settlement imposes new security requirements on TTAM, including risk analysis, an advisory board focused on data security, and continued consumer rights to delete personal information. Attorney General James stated: "Companies have a duty to protect their customers' personal information from hackers, but 23andMe put millions of its customers at risk with its flimsy security measures." This settlement supplements a $46.75 million compensation award approved by a bankruptcy judge on July 7 for breach victims. Internationally, regulators have also penalized 23andMe. Spain's privacy authority fined the company €2.4 million ($2.75 million) in July 2026 for affecting 2,642 Spanish customers, while the UK's Information Commissioner's Office imposed a £2.3 million ($3.1 million) fine in June 2025.

1fc4159fdd6c.text: SecurityWeek's weekly roundup highlights significant cybersecurity developments across multiple domains: Major Incidents - Dutch authorities suspect domestic cybercriminals facilitated the Odido telecom breach affecting 6 million customers. A third-party vendor compromise exposed Lidl customer information in Belgium and the Netherlands. German textile manufacturer ZEGO Textilveredelungszentrum filed for bankruptcy after a six-week production shutdown caused by cyberattack. Japan's largest taxi operator, Nihon Kotsu, took systems offline following a suspected AiLock ransomware attack. Emerging Threats - Security researchers discovered CrashStealer, a C++ macOS information stealer disguised as a crash reporter that exfiltrates sensitive user data, credentials, and system information from compromised Apple devices. Iranian-linked actors leverage cellular roaming and advertising metadata to track U.S. military personnel smartphones. OpenClaw AI agents integrated with WhatsApp contain vulnerabilities enabling arbitrary code execution. Policy & Standards - CISA and international partners released guidance for establishing Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure programs, providing step-by-step instructions on handling external bug reports, establishing legal safe harbors. Additional Threats - Spirals ransomware targeted an Asian IT firm; The Gentlemen cybercrime group claimed a Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems breach involving 1TB+ of data exfiltration.

533f28c0c083.text: This guide addresses how traditional security reports fail executive audiences and proposes an alternative: executive cloud risk dashboards built around six key performance indicators. Core Problem: Organizations struggle to translate massive alert volumes into actionable business intelligence. Security teams generate enormous alert volumes, but translating that output into something a board can act on has historically required hours of manual work. Six Essential KPIs: 1. Overall Risk Score and Trend Direction - Consolidates posture into one metric factoring asset criticality and exploitability. 2. Critical and High-Severity Finding Count - Deduplicated issues prioritized by impact, not raw alert volume. 3. Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) - Measures operational effectiveness in closing security gaps. 4. Compliance Posture Across Active Frameworks - Expresses readiness as a single percentage across standards. 5. Attack Surface Exposure Score - Quantifies internet-exposed assets with unresolved critical findings. 6. Cloud Asset Coverage Rate - Tracks monitoring percentage across cloud environments. Design Principles: The article emphasizes four key principles: single-screen summaries with drill-down capability, trend visualization over point-in-time snapshots, segmentation by business unit, and audit-ready exportability. Key Distinction: Executive dashboards differ fundamentally from SOC dashboards. The former aggregates data for governance decisions; the latter surfaces granular alerts for incident response investigation.

a6995465efcc.text: Residential proxies have evolved from simple anonymity tools into sophisticated components of what criminals call an "identity-simulation stack." Flare researchers analyzed 2,889 underground posts across 545 discussion threads to understand how fraudsters currently evaluate and use this infrastructure. The research reveals that carders no longer view residential proxies as standalone solutions. Instead, they distinguish between "clean" and "dirty" pools, recognizing that addresses accumulate poor reputations through repeated misuse. One circulated guide titled "Getting the Cleanest Possible IPs for Carding" emphasizes that "even residential pools deteriorate as addresses are repeatedly used for abuse." Geographic Precision Expanding: Criminal actors have shifted from country-level IP matching to granular identity consistency. A January 2026 thread discussed aligning IP location with billing ZIP codes, device time zones, operating-system language, and browser characteristics. Users complained that major proxy providers removed ZIP-code targeting, fearing city-level selection would prove insufficient to evade fraud controls. Proxies as One Layer Among Many: The dataset repeatedly links residential proxies with antidetection browsers, WebGL fingerprints, cookie history, and user-agent consistency. One April 2026 guide warned that a "perfect residential proxy" fails if browser profiles expose contradictory information. Finance-Compatible Infrastructure: Several posts discuss restrictions imposed by established proxy providers on banks and payment processors, creating demand for services advertised as "finance enabled" or "bank compatible." The July 2026 FBI seizure of NetNut domains and the Popa botnet-which compromised two million devices-highlighted these contested ecosystems. Defensive Implications: Organizations should treat residential addresses as context rather than trustworthiness signals. Stronger indicators include session consistency across device history, account age, browser fingerprints, billing information, and transaction velocity.

8813dabea52e.text: North Korean threat actors connected to the Contagious Interview campaign have deployed a sophisticated attack using fake job postings and coding challenges to distribute malware. The malicious payloads are concealed within SVG image files using steganography. Attack Method: Threat actors posted job opportunities in the Slack workspace of a major security company, requesting developers for e-commerce platform upgrades. Interested candidates were directed to complete coding assessments containing trojanized repositories. "Any user who ran the project ended up with a four-stage payload aligned with OtterCookie," researchers note. Technical Approach: The malware embeds base64-encoded fragments within HTML comments across SVG flag images in asset directories. The repositories appear fully functional while executing malicious code silently in the background through a JavaScript file called "serverValidation.js." Payload Capabilities: The OtterCookie malware variant includes four distinct modules enabling: browser credential and cryptocurrency wallet theft; file exfiltration (targeting AI coding tools like Claude, Cursor, Gemini); Socket.IO-based remote access trojan functionality; clipboard content capture. Campaign Significance: Elastic Security Labs emphasized that "compromising an individual developer can provide a path to much broader organizational impact" through supply chain attacks. The persistent effectiveness of this social engineering approach demonstrates its viability as a vector for targeting software developers.

4b1f6245fb69.text: The article examines how enterprises often overpay for Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) solutions through integration overhead when components weren't architected to function as a unified system. Check Point's approach emphasizes that "Hybrid SASE is not a label - it is an architectural commitment." The piece distinguishes three maturity tiers for hybrid SASE implementations: 1. Hybrid in Name Only - Multiple user types supported but with siloed policies and inconsistent visibility. 2. Hybrid by Integration - Components work via connectors and workflows, improving coverage while increasing complexity. 3. Hybrid by Design - Unified operating model spanning agents, gateways, connectivity, and enforcement. Check Point SASE's architecture features three foundational capabilities: full mesh private connectivity across 85+ global Points of Presence, distributed security enforcement (endpoint agents and Cloud Edge Gateways), and unified operations through a single policy engine and console. The solution addresses common infrastructure limitations of retrofitted platforms, including "hub-and-spoke bias that adds latency" and "greater dependence on the public internet, with more exposure to jitter, packet loss, and routing variability." The platform achieved top rankings in the 2026 Miercom Hybrid Mesh Network Security Benchmark, earning "99.8% overall security effectiveness" across testing categories.

40dfc312a3ba.text: A previously undocumented ransomware variant named Spirals targeted an IT services company in South Asia, compromising systems in under 24 hours. According to Symantec's Threat Hunter Team, attackers progressed from initial access through data exfiltration to full network encryption within this timeframe. Technical Characteristics: Spirals is coded in Rust and employs AES-128 encryption with individual keys per file, each secured by an attacker-controlled ECDH P-256 public key. For efficiency, files exceeding 5 MB are "encrypted in chunks." Victims received a ransom demand through RECOVERY_SECTION.log, threatening data publication "within six days if no payment was made." Attack Methodology: The intrusion began with compromise of an internet-facing IIS web server via ASP.NET shell deployment. Attackers escalated privileges through UAC bypass techniques, enabled RDP, and established persistent access via local account creation. Credential harvesting involved dumping the SAM registry hive and LSASS memory across multiple systems. The attackers deployed multiple communication channels using Chisel tunneling (disguised as chrome.exe), reverse SOCKS proxy, and Cloudflare Tunnel client. Using PsExec as SYSTEM, operators distributed a PowerShell payload across numerous hosts, disabling Windows Defender and stopping services supporting 23 backup, database, and virtualization platforms including Veeam, VMware, SQL Server, and Oracle before deployment of ransomware. Symantec noted the operators demonstrated sophisticated capabilities, indicating capacity for broader campaigns.

c1b24117c08f.text: In this exclusive SecurityWeek interview, Brian "SchleiF" Schleifer sits down with Clint Bodungen, Director of AI/ML Engineering at Arcovo, founder of ThreatGen, and one of the industry's leading voices in industrial cybersecurity. Together they tackle why traditional governance often fails practitioners, how cybersecurity has evolved over the past two decades, and why the biggest vulnerability is still people not technology. Clint also shares, for the first time publicly, the story behind the MindStone Agent, his open-source agentic AI project designed to bring persistent memory, identity, and continuity to AI assistants. The conversation concludes with a real-world ransomware response where autonomous AI agents coordinated incident response, forensic analysis, recovery, and infrastructure migration with minimal human intervention.

72f3cbc01af9.text: Fortinet administrators face mounting pressure following CISA's confirmation that two critical FortiSandbox vulnerabilities are experiencing active exploitation in the wild. The two vulnerabilities-CVE-2026-39808 and CVE-2026-25089-both carry CVSS scores of 9.1 and impact FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS. These flaws represent OS command injection vulnerabilities permitting unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands through maliciously crafted HTTP requests. The attacks require no valid credentials or user interaction to succeed. Fortinet distributed patches for CVE-2026-39808 in April and CVE-2026-25089 in June. The company's security advisories warned at that time that successful exploitation could facilitate remote code execution through relatively simple attack methods. While Fortinet has not publicly acknowledged active exploitation, "CISA has now added both bugs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog." This listing signifies CISA possesses evidence of active real-world exploitation, though the agency typically refrains from attributing specific attacks or quantifying their scope. For federal civilian agencies, inclusion in the KEV catalog carries mandatory obligations. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, agencies must apply patches within CISA-established timeframes or discontinue use of affected products if adequate security cannot be maintained. The security research firm Defused reported observing exploitation attempts targeting both vulnerabilities this week, alongside a third FortiSandbox flaw (CVE-2026-39813). However, the organization noted that the exploit targeting CVE-2026-25089 appears ineffective, describing it as "vibecoded" and noting no functional public exploit has emerged. CISA's Thursday update to the KEV catalog also flagged Microsoft's newly patched SharePoint Server vulnerability, CVE-2026-58644. This critical deserialization flaw (CVSS 9.8) permits authenticated Site Owner-level users to execute arbitrary code remotely against vulnerable SharePoint installations with minimal complexity.

937badfa7ccd.text: The European Commission issued binding directives requiring Google to grant rival AI assistants the same access to Android hardware that Gemini currently enjoys. The order mandates access to cameras, microphones, screen contents, wake words functional when displays are off, and the ability to control other apps through simulated user interactions. Implementation is required by Android 18's release, with a deadline of August 1, 2027. Key Provisions: The decision addresses 11 operating system features split into two categories. Five "Restricted Features" requiring certification: centralized app data access, context-aware intelligence systems, structured on-device integration, screen automation, system integration (settings, media, notifications). Six "Unrestricted Features" with no certification barrier: ambient data (microphone, camera, screen, location, sensors), always-on hotword detection, long-press invocation, system-level models, third-party model implementation, background execution. Certification Requirements: Google must establish a Qualified AI Assistant Programme administered by independent Trusted Certification Authorities. Certification bars Google from imposing restrictions beyond reasonable security testing for user intent confirmation, data minimization, baseline app security, and agentic risk mitigation. The Commission emphasized that "higher integrity levels cannot apply to third parties than Google applies to itself." Search Data Sharing: A separate directive requires Google to share anonymized search data with competing search engines and AI chatbots. The anonymization process involves three passes: stripping direct identifiers, suppressing rare-term queries, and generalizing metadata until users exist in groups of at least 1,000. Google's Response: Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, contended the ruling "threatens device security by granting external apps sensitive and powerful device permissions," arguing that phone manufacturers currently vet assistants and this decision removes that safeguard. The article notes this concern isn't theoretical-researchers previously demonstrated that notifications could enable prompt injection attacks on Gemini's own utilities through indirect manipulation. Timeline: Draft terms: February 1, 2027. Final terms and applications open: May 1, 2027. Feature implementation: August 1, 2027. Concurrent hotword support: August 1, 2028.

072435ffec28.text: Cybersecurity startup Beacon Security has secured $13 million in seed funding led by Notable Capital, with participation from AlphaDrive Ventures, Holly Ventures, Jefferies Family Office, SVCI, and numerous angel investors. Founded in 2024 by IDF veterans Gal Tal-Hochberg (CEO), Or Mattatia (CPO), and Iddo Israely (CTO), the New York-based company developed an agentic security data platform designed to help organizations prevent, detect, and respond to threats. The platform normalizes and enriches telemetry from multiple sources for both AI agents and human analysts. It continuously maps sources against threats and compliance requirements to identify vulnerabilities before exploitation. Key capabilities include leveraging AI agents for building detections, investigations, and shadow AI analysis. The solution provides a library of specialized cybersecurity agents connected to a context layer designed to catch AI attacks and emerging threats that traditional tools may overlook. CEO Tal-Hochberg emphasized that the company built Beacon to address challenges arising from accelerated enterprise AI adoption, stating: "We built Beacon to solve these challenges by providing the trusted data layer that allows organizations to deploy security agents compliantly and effectively." The startup reports rapid adoption among enterprise customers, including Fortune 500 companies.

182a9c65b49a.text: Military forces face mounting pressure to deploy autonomous capabilities at unprecedented speeds. Across the U.S., UK, and NATO, new investment levels, shifting defense strategies, and expedited acquisition pathways are fundamentally changing capability delivery, with programs rewarded for achieving operational deployment at commercial velocity. The critical focus now centers on trusted information infrastructure enabling these systems to operate together at mission speed. As autonomous aircraft, uncrewed maritime vessels, ground systems, satellites, and AI-enabled mission applications become increasingly interconnected, so does the information powering them. Telemetry, intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance, command data, AI outputs, sensor-to-shooter workflows, and coalition intelligence must move seamlessly across platforms, domains, and partners. Defense has entered a new operational phase. The momentum behind military autonomy proves undeniable. The U.S. Department of War established dedicated leadership accelerating unmanned capability development. NSPM-11 reinforces AI's strategic importance across the National Security enterprise. The FY27 defense budget continues substantial investment in autonomous capability and modernization. The UK's Strategic Defence Review and Defence Investment Plan position autonomous systems centrally within future force design, backed by over £5 billion investment across four years. Programs are expanding autonomous testing and experimentation, while AUKUS Pillar II and NATO initiatives accelerate allied collaboration on autonomy and advanced defense technologies. The conversation is shifting. Current discourse emphasizes platforms: drone quantities, deployment speed, and AI's operational effectiveness. However, autonomous capability delivers maximum value operating within connected missions. Every autonomous system must exchange trusted information with operators, AI applications, command environments, and coalition partners. Mission data rarely remains within single platforms, networks, or classifications. The acceleration of defense innovation changes expectations across government and industry. Programs increasingly adopt commercial technologies through rapid acquisition pathways, adaptive procurement, and iterative delivery models. However, commercial speed shouldn't require bespoke information architectures consuming years for integration before operational capability realization. Rethinking trust establishment becomes essential as autonomous missions increasingly rely on software. While software plays critical roles across autonomous capability and AI systems, defense's highest assurance environments employ another solution: hardware-enforced separation. Hardware-enforced separation establishes trust within hardware logic rather than relying solely on software controls. Removing the operating system from the trust boundary reduces architectural complexity while supporting trusted information movement across secure environments. This approach has protected defense's most critical environments for years, now providing foundations aligning naturally with autonomous transformation's speed and scale. The future force measures success differently. It won't be judged simply by autonomous systems deployed, but by how effectively those systems exchange trusted information across land, sea, air, and space; how seamlessly they integrate with AI and command systems; and how confidently allied forces collaborate across security domains.

e2bffb42cec4.text: Armenian authorities detained a Russian tourist named Aleksandr Ermakov at Yerevan airport on June 28 based on a U.S. extradition warrant. However, his legal team contends that officials have apprehended the wrong individual. The U.S. is seeking "Aleksandr Gennadievich Ermakov," sanctioned by Australia, the US, and the UK in January 2024. This person stands accused of stealing 9.7 million records from Medibank Private, Australia's largest private health insurer, and posting some data on the dark web. He is currently serving a two-year Russian sentence barring him from leaving the country. The detained man is reportedly "Aleksandr Yuryevich Ermakov," a former prison-service lawyer from Omsk who speaks no English. His attorneys argue that U.S. paperwork contained only a given name and surname without the patronymic-the middle name field distinguishing one Aleksandr Ermakov from another in Russian passports-allowing an automated check to misidentify their client. The actual target allegedly participated in Sodinokibi/REvil ransomware operations from April 2019 through July 2021, affecting over 1,000 victims including private firms, law enforcement agencies, schools, and hospitals. The warrant originates from the Northern District of Texas federal court, dated June 26. The detained man remains held on a 30-day Interpol detention order while Moscow seeks consular access.

a676df0d5e18.text: This comprehensive guide compares AI agent runtimes and platforms across three distinct market layers: managed hyperscaler services, framework-native platforms, and sandbox/serverless runtimes. Key Definition: An AI agent runtime functions as the execution infrastructure layer that provisions, isolates, scales, and operates AI agents in production environments. As the authors explain, "the framework defines behavior and the runtime executes it." Three Market Layers: Managed Hyperscaler Runtimes: AWS Bedrock AgentCore, Google Vertex AI Agent Engine, and Azure AI Foundry Agent Service provide enterprise-grade infrastructure integrated with cloud identity systems. Framework-Native Platforms: LangGraph Platform and OpenAI AgentKit offer optimized deployment for teams standardized on specific frameworks, with built-in observability and state management. Sandbox & Serverless Runtimes: E2B, Modal, Daytona, Fly.io Machines, Cloudflare Agents, and Vercel Sandbox provide isolated execution environments optimized for code-executing agents with scale-to-zero economics. Six Evaluation Criteria: The guide emphasizes examining: sandbox isolation strength, state persistence mechanisms, multi-agent orchestration capabilities, observability and tracing, deployment models, and security governance features including identity scoping and audit logging. Use Case Matching: Selection guidance differentiates by workload pattern: code-executing agents require strong per-session isolation, autonomous long-running agents need durable execution with checkpointing, multi-agent systems benefit from orchestration platforms, and regulated enterprises should prioritize identity integration with existing governance controls.

5f93968e07f7.text: A critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting WordPress Core has been disclosed as CVE-2026-63030, dubbed "wp2shell." The vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code via the WordPress REST API batch endpoint. Affected Versions: WordPress 6.9.0 through 6.9.4; WordPress 7.0.0 through 7.0.1. Fixed Versions: WordPress 6.9.5; WordPress 7.0.2; WordPress 7.1 Beta 2. The advisory states the vulnerability "allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute code via the WordPress REST API batch endpoint," potentially compromising affected websites completely. Technical Details: The vulnerability combines two separate flaws. CVE-2026-63030 is a logic flaw in the REST API batch processor at /wp-json/batch/v1. The batch processor's validation and execution loops become desynchronized when URL parsing fails, causing subsequent requests to dispatch under incorrect handlers. CVE-2026-60137 is a SQL injection in the author__not_in parameter. The batch API desynchronization allows parameter validation bypass, enabling pre-authentication UNION-based SQL injection through recursive batch calls. Together, these vulnerabilities enable attackers to create administrator accounts, log in, and upload malicious plugins for code execution. Mitigation Guidance: Organizations should prioritize immediate upgrades to patched versions. WordPress has implemented forced updates for installations with automatic updates enabled. Temporary mitigations (if immediate patching is impossible): Block the /wp-json/batch/v1 endpoint at your WAF; Disable anonymous REST API access via plugin. Post-patch, defenders should review HTTP access logs for anomalous batch requests and check for unfamiliar plugins or PHP files. Current Status: As of July 21, 2026, both CVEs were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, confirming active exploitation in the wild. Public proof-of-concept exploits and full technical details have been released. (Published: July 17, 2026 | Updated: July 22, 2026 | Author: Rapid7 Labs)

d50d510e5573.text:
Hours of San Francisco Police Department drone video footage exposed on the open web illustrates a new era of incredibly granular—and consequential—urban surveillance. Meanwhile, the San Francisco City Attorney’s Office sent cease-and-desist letters to Apple and Google this week demanding that the tech giants delete 13 AI nudifying “face-swap” apps from their app stores that are almost exclusively used to target women and girls.
Since WIRED first reported in June about Meta’s NameTag face-recognition system, company executives have made opaque and conflicting comments about whether the feature even exists. We took a step back to lay out both the claims and the facts about the very real system.
In a speech on Thursday, President Donald Trump continued to push unsubstantiated and thoroughly debunked claims about interference in the 2020 US election. He even promised massive revelations in a trove of documents posted to the White House website, but the files did not prove his assertions—and in some cases actually contradicted Trump’s claims.
As adoption of AI tools rapidly expands and their capabilities increase, the tech giant Anthropic continued a push to get US states to regulate AI. Speaking about AI transparency requirements in California and New York from last year, Anthropic’s head of US state and local government relations, Cesar Fernandez, told WIRED this week, “The transparency-focused safety bills of 2025 were a really important start, but as the capabilities of AI systems continue to advance quickly—the policy responses need to match.”
And there’s more. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.
Mozilla Graded Period Trackers on Privacy. Only One Aced It
The astrology-themed period tracker Stardust sends users’ reproductive health details—birth control type, pregnancy status, moods, and symptoms as specific as tender breasts and stomach cramps—to a data firm not named in its privacy policy, according to the BBC, which first reported a Mozilla Foundation audit of six popular trackers produced in partnership with Harvard's Berkman Klein Center.
Stardust scored 2 out of 10, the worst of the group. Mozilla researcher Shoshana Wodinsky found the app pings third-party trackers from the moment it opens, before a user enters anything; the instant she logged a symptom, the details went to analytics firm RudderStack alongside a persistent user ID, with no in-app way to shut the sharing off. RudderStack is built to route data onward to destinations Mozilla couldn't observe. Stardust also hands Facebook an ad identifier that ties in-app behavior to the platform's existing profiles. The company told TechCrunch it has never received a legal demand for user data.
Euki, a nonprofit-run tracker, earned a perfect 10: no account required, health data never leaves the phone, and users can set a PIN, schedule automatic deletion, or pull up a decoy screen if someone forces the phone open. Its one soft spot is an in-app browser for educational pages that loads the usual web trackers, but it also resets identifiers between visits.
Russia’s FSB Sanctioned for Cyberattack on Polish Infrastructure
Russia’s FSB has long had a reputation for highly sophisticated cyberespionage, leaving disruptive cyberattacks to its fellow hackers in the country’s GRU military intelligence agency. But sanctions from the EU and UK this week, along with an advisory from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, and the NSA, pinned a cyberattack against the Polish electric grid on Center 16 of the FSB, a rare example of the Kremlin agency carrying out a cyberattack that nearly caused outages in the country’s electric and water utilities. The attack, which the Polish government has said came “very close” to causing a blackout, was initially attributed by cybersecurity firms Dragos and ESET to Sandworm, also known as Unit 74455 of the GRU, a more usual suspect in infrastructure hacking given its active role in Russia’s long-running cyberwar against Ukraine. But the Polish computer emergency response team at the time disputed that finding and tied the attack to the FSB, a conclusion now supported by a wide consensus of Western governments. The incident suggests that the FSB may be taking on some of the reckless, highly aggressive tendencies—and targeting—of its GRU coworkers.
An Alleged Russian State-Sponsored Hacker Worked for Kaspersky
For years, the Russian cybersecurity firm Kaspersky has been alleged to have ties to the Russian government, including by US officials who banned use of the company’s products within the US government and eventually by all American customers. Yet overt evidence of those connections has been scarce. Now Reuters reports that Denis Obrezko, a Russian man facing hacking charges in Boston and an alleged member of a hacker group known as Void Blizzard or Laundry Bear, spent two years working at Kaspersky. His stint at the company took place just before he joined another cybersecurity company, Yutek-NN, where he allegedly took part in the group’s hacking campaign that stole data and communications from numerous NATO governments and at least 11 US companies, according to US prosecutors. Prior to Kaspersky, Obrevko also allegedly worked at the FSB, neatly bookending his time at the company with apparent work for Russia’s intelligence services.
Obrevko has pleaded not guilty to the hacking charges. Kaspersky responded in a statement to Reuters that “the offenses charged cannot be related to the individual’s role or responsibilities during the employment at Kaspersky.”
A Real DHS Breach Was Twice Ruled a False Positive
In an incident that will induce anxiety in anyone responsible for assessing suspicious network activity, DHS officials ruled—twice—that signs of a hacker breach in its data-sharing Homeland Security Information Network platform were false positives when they were, in fact, signs of a very real intrusion. HSIN, used for sharing unclassified data between state, local, and federal agencies, as well as foreign partners, was breached by hackers two months ago, according to reporting from Nextgov/FCW. Analysts at the Federal Emergency Management Agency spotted signs of hacker activity in mid-May—altering files and code, hijacking a legitimate web server, and deleting logs of their behavior—but the findings were dismissed as a false positive.
In the weeks that followed, the hackers returned, were again detected, and were again dismissed as a mirage. It’s not clear why the signs of the breach were misjudged, but the incidents may represent federal analysts’ increasing challenges in detecting “living off the land” hacking techniques that use legitimate features of networks to access target assets on a network rather than planting more easily spotted malware. While the HSIN houses only unclassified data, the information is “highly sensitive,” Senate Intelligence Committee vice chair Mark Warner said in a statement following the report of the breach, and “its exposure risks national security.”
Hack Exposes an AI Music Generator’s Scraping Secrets
The AI music startup Suno scraped millions of songs, lyrics, and podcasts from YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius, and a string of stock-audio libraries to train its models, according to 404 Media, which reviewed internal data provided by a hacker who breached the company. The intrusion also exposed account information for hundreds of thousands of customers, including emails, phone numbers, and Stripe payment records.
Dataset notes in source code apparently from 2023 and 2024 tally 113,879 hours of YouTube Music audio alone, plus tens of thousands more from Pond5, Deezer, and other libraries—decades of music in total. Other files show Suno routing its YouTube scraping through Bright Data proxies and using PodcastIndex to target roughly 1 million hours of podcasts. The hacker, who goes by ellie.191, says they broke in by compromising an employee with the Shai-Hulud worm.
The files seemingly corroborate the record industry’s central allegation that Suno pulled songs directly from YouTube. The company, which argues that its training qualifies as fair use and settled with Warner Music Group last November, said the breach involved outdated code and no sensitive personal information—though customers whose data appeared in a sample shared with 404 Media said they were never notified.

8bc5a1fe1175.text:
Prompt injections, the malicious commands attackers embed into content to entice large language models to follow them, have been attackers’ go-to tool for turning AI platforms against their users. A well-phrased command sneaked into an email or calendar invitation is often all it takes to cause the LLM to exfiltrate sensitive data or follow other harmful actions.
Now, defenders are embracing the prompt injection, too.
Researchers from Tracebit on Monday said they found that placing prompt injections alongside passwords, cryptographic keys, and other secrets stored on Amazon Web Services was often all that was needed to shut down attacks from AI hacking agents. The prompts direct the attacking LLM to perform an action forbidden by its guardrails, the safety barriers AI developers erect to prevent it from taking harmful actions. The LLM responds by shutting down.
Examples are a prompt that orders the LLM to provide steps for developing inhalable Anthrax spores, or, in the case of LLMs from Chinese developers, make references to the iconic Tank Man from the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre. Once the LLM encounters these forbidden commands, it no longer follows its existing commands. The researchers have named the technique context bombing.
“Ultimately we’re triggering a refusal mechanism in the context,” said Andy Smith, cofounder and CEO of Tracebit, when explaining the name choice. “What we’re trying to capture is the fact that this does have a strong, sharp effect and one that can be difficult for the agents to come back from. Once they get that into their context they are going to keep refusing.”
Tracebit says initial testing suggests context bombing has great potential. They tested Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GLM 5.2, DeepSeek 4 Pro, and Kimi 2.6 by giving them instructions to perform routine developer tasks that led the models to enumerate resources and stumble onto the planted strings. They ran the models inside a simulated AWS environment.
“Across five leading models and 152 attack runs, planting one of these strings in a decoy secret cut the rate at which agents seized full account admin from 57 percent to 5 percent, and complete compromise (where they also left themselves a persistent foothold) from 36 percent to 1 percent,” Monday’s post reported. “The most capable agent in our tests, Opus 4.8, went from achieving admin access in 93 percent of runs to failing every single time when confronted with a context bomb.”
Averaged across the five models and the 152 runs, the results included:
- Admin privilege escalation fell from 57 percent to 5 percent
- Admin escalation with a persistent foothold fell from 36 percent to 1 percent
- Runs achieving any attack path fell from 91 percent to 15 percent
- On average, a run went from completing 1.53 paths successfully to just 0.16
- No runs were able to complete an attack path without at least triggering a canary detection
The research builds on findings from May, when Tracebit introduced a method for defenders to receive warnings when their infrastructure is under attack from AI agentic adversaries. It comes in the form of AWS resources that look like ones serving a legitimate purpose but, in fact, aren’t used at all. They sit alongside the resources that are used. When they are probed by agentic AI, defenders receive an alert. Like “canaries” taken into coal mines, these resources allow defenders to detect a threat before it has fatal consequences.
The Tracebit Canariens, on average, alerted the start of an attack within eight minutes. The motivation for developing context bombing came out of the need for something that stopped attacks, rather than simply warning of them. In the experiments, the agentic models needed, on average, 14 minutes to escalate to administrative control. The six-minute heads-up was cutting things uncomfortably close.
Attackers have already been using prompt injections to close down AI defenses inside networks. Researchers from security firm Socket, for instance, last month unearthed an LLM agent that directed target LLMs to provide instructions for building a nuclear bomb or biological weapons. The injections were designed to shut down AI-assisted malware analysis. Researchers from Check Point discovered a similar malware prototype.
Context bombing appears to be the first known case where defenders turned the tables.
“I’ve not seen anyone else use this technique as a defense, to the best of my knowledge,” Earlence Fernandes, a UC San Diego professor specializing in AI security, said in an interview. He said he had been toying with a similar approach, although in a slightly different context. “I wanted to be the first here, but I guess these guys beat me to the punch!”
To date, there is no known way to solve the root cause of prompt injections. That has left developers with no option other than to construct elaborate guardrails that prevent injected prompts from forcing LLMs to go off the rails. Defenders may now find a way to use this intractable problem in their favor.
This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

923f969e1b0e.text: Google's Gemini AI assistant contains a security flaw affecting locked Android 16 devices. The vulnerability permits someone with physical access to bypass authentication and send SMS or WhatsApp messages without entering a PIN. The attack exploits a specific multi-touch gesture. When users press "Continue" while simultaneously tapping Gemini's "Add attachment" button, the system bypasses PIN requirements. Attackers can then enable Gemini's access to other apps by typing commands like "@WhatsApp" with no authentication needed. As Cluley explains, "the changes are not temporary" — victims later discover unauthorized app connections in their Gemini settings. Key Details: The vulnerability requires physical device access; First reported in May 2026 via security research; Related bugs have existed since September 2025; Google confirmed awareness and scheduled a fix for that week. Recommended Protection: Users should disable Gemini on their lock screen by opening Gemini settings via profile picture, selecting "Gemini on lock screen," and turning off either "Use Gemini without unlocking" entirely or specifically disabling "Make calls and send messages without unlocking." (Author: Graham Cluley, Published: July 17, 2026)

41f09a1e0643.text: 7-Zip version 26.02, released June 25, addresses a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting the widely-used Windows archive utility. Researcher Landon Peng disclosed a flaw in how 7-Zip processes XZ-compressed data. According to the Zero Day Initiative advisory, "a specially crafted XZ data can trigger a heap-based buffer overflow, potentially allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code." The patch adds safeguards to prevent the decoder from writing beyond available buffer space during decompression of XZ files. Exploitation Requirements: The vulnerability requires user interaction—victims must open a malicious archive file or visit a compromised webpage. No active exploitation has been reported to date. Critical Limitation: 7-Zip lacks automatic update functionality. Users must manually install version 26.02 from 7-zip.org to receive the security fix. Users can also update via package managers like winget or unigetui. Historical Context: Archive utilities remain attractive targets for threat actors. In early 2025, Russian hackers exploited a different 7-Zip vulnerability as a zero-day attack against Ukrainian targets. (Article by: Lawrence Abrams, Published: July 18, 2026)

55421bdf9102.text: Critical remote code execution vulnerabilities affecting WordPress Core have received public exploit code, prompting urgent patching recommendations for administrators worldwide. The "wp2shell" attack chain comprises two vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-63030, a REST API batch-route confusion flaw in WordPress 6.9+; and CVE-2026-60137, an SQL injection vulnerability in the author__not_in parameter affecting WordPress 6.8+. These flaws can be chained together to achieve pre-authentication RCE against default WordPress installations running versions 6.9.x and 7.0.x, discovered by Adam Kues of Searchlight Cyber. WordPress powers over 500 million websites. The vulnerability chain affects WordPress 6.9.0-6.9.4 and 7.0.0-7.0.1. WordPress has enabled forced automatic security updates for vulnerable versions, recommending immediate updates to version 7.0.2 or 6.9.5. Security firm watchTowr reports: "we are beginning to see the first signs of in-the-wild exploitation." Temporary Mitigations: For systems unable to patch immediately, Searchlight Cyber recommends installing plugins blocking anonymous REST API access, and WAF-level blocking of /wp-json/batch/v1 endpoints. Cloudflare has deployed WAF protections across all plan tiers. (Author: Lawrence Abrams, Published: July 18, 2026)

12863879b1ae.text: WordPress 7.0.2 addresses two serious security vulnerabilities—one critical and one with high severity. The vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-60137, a facilitated SQL injection flaw discovered by TF1T, dtro, and haongo; CVE-2026-63030, a REST API batch-route confusion and SQL injection vulnerability enabling Remote Code Execution, reported by Adam Kues at Assetnote/Searchlight Cyber. Affected versions: WordPress 6.9 (patched in 6.9.5); WordPress 6.8 (patched in 6.8.6, affected by CVE-2026-60137 only); WordPress 7.1 beta (patched in beta2); Versions prior to 6.8 are unaffected. Temporary mitigation options include installing plugins blocking anonymous REST API access or using a Web Application Firewall to block /wp-json/batch/v1 and ?rest_route=/batch/v1 endpoints. Updates note: By July 21, over two dozen exploits targeting these vulnerabilities had surfaced, with attackers deploying webshells and creating backdoor admin accounts since late Friday evening. (Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security, Published: July 18, 2026)

58b574678ee4.text: Microsoft has identified a significant increase in ACR Stealer malware attacks targeting enterprise customers between late April and mid-June 2026. The malware operates as a malware-as-a-service offering, believed to be a rebranding of Amatera Stealer. Attack Methods: Threat actors employed two primary delivery chains. WebDAV-Based ClickFix Attacks: Attackers use social-engineering lures with ClickFix to execute malicious DLLs from remote WebDAV shares via rundll32.exe. The campaign involves obfuscated PowerShell scripts, Python loaders, and scheduled tasks disguised as software updates. Some variants leverage blockchain services as dead-drop resolvers for command-and-control infrastructure. MSHTA-Based Delivery: Attackers use ClickFix to launch Microsoft HTML Application Host, retrieving malicious content that executes obfuscated PowerShell downloaders. Encrypted payloads are concealed within steganographic JPEG images and executed in memory. Data Targeted: The malware targets sensitive information including passwords, cookies, session data, and authentication tokens; Chromium browser databases; PDF and Microsoft 365 documents; files from Desktop and Downloads folders; OneDrive and SharePoint directories. Recommended Defenses: Microsoft advises organizations to enforce web filters, block low-reputation domains, restrict access to unnecessary online resources, and implement application control rules limiting tools like PowerShell and rundll32.exe execution from user-writable paths. (Author: Bill Toulas, Published: July 18, 2026)

641e49972ec0.text: More than 30 age assurance laws are now in force worldwide. The UK is enforcing the Online Safety Act's "highly effective" age check requirement, with restrictions on under-16 access to social media planned for spring 2027. Australia's under-16 rules took effect in December, and the government has signaled its intent to double maximum fines to $99 million after early waves of non-compliance. Brazil's Digital ECA became enforceable in March 2026, and now half of U.S. states mandate some form of age verification. Facial age estimation has emerged as one of the most accessible compliance methods, requiring no government ID or database lookup. Incode's data shows users choose it eight out of ten times over other age assurance methods. However, nearly every implementation has historically captured faces, sent them to servers, and processed them remotely—creating significant privacy and security risks. The Problem with Server-Based Age Estimation: According to the Identity Theft Resource Center's 2025 Annual Data Breach Report, the U.S. recorded 3,322 data compromises last year—a 79% increase over five years—while supply-chain breaches doubled. Additionally, "63% of consumers have expressed serious concern over biometric data collection." Agentic fraud has escalated dramatically. In 2024, it represented 3% of fraud attempts; by Q1 2026, it reached 40%, with Incode estimating it will exceed 90% within 18 months. Privacy by Architecture vs. Policy: The industry standard has relied on privacy policies—legal documents that cannot prevent breaches, insider threats, or compromised vendors. Privacy by architecture offers a different approach: build systems ensuring sensitive data never becomes accessible. Incode's $100 Million Commitment: Last month, Incode announced a $100 million commitment to advancing privacy-preserving infrastructure, including its acquisition of Identiq, a company specializing in privacy-enhancing cryptographic solutions. On-Device Age Estimation: Launched in July 2026, it runs Incode's facial age estimation and passive liveness detection models directly on users' devices; the face is analyzed locally, never transmitted or stored. Incode compressed its models to approximately one-tenth of their original size using knowledge distillation. Server-Side Security Layer: session metadata travels to servers for fraud detection and session integrity analysis without accessing facial data; Incode claims 99% spoof detection across deepfakes, injection, replay, and physical spoofing, and flagged over 1 million face attacks in 2026. Fighting Fraud Without Pooling Data: Identiq's technology lets organizations share fraud signals without exposing customer data, per Co-Founder Itay Levy. Regulatory Compliance: Incode maintains SOC 2 Type 2, ISO/IEC 27001, HIPAA Attestation of Compliance, FedRAMP Ready, ACCS, and Kantara IAL2 certifications, and has processed over 7 billion trust checks. (Author: Ricardo Amper, Founder & CEO, Incode Technologies, Published: July 18, 2026)

c94c79ca9a5b.text:
There’s another update in the litigation involving 23andMe, below, but this won’t be the last update, as California’s Attorney General has also recently sued them under California’s privacy laws.
New York Attorney General Letitia James and a bipartisan coalition of 42 other attorneys general today secured $18 million from genetic testing company 23andMe for failing to protect customers’ private genetic data. In October 2023, 23andMe announced that it had discovered a data breach affecting 6.9 million consumers, including 305,245 in New York. The breach exposed a broad range of customer data, including genetic ancestry information. Some customers’ data was even published for sale on the dark web. As part of the settlement, Attorney General James and the coalition have secured new data protection requirements to secure 23andMe customer data. 23andMe will also pay more than $705,000 to New York.
“Companies have a duty to protect their customers’ personal information from hackers, but 23andMe put millions of its customers at risk with its flimsy security measures,” said Attorney General James. “New Yorkers trusted 23andMe with their sensitive and personal genetic data, only to find that data stolen and put up for sale on the dark corners of the internet. As a result of our coalition’s action, 23andMe will pay for violating the law and strict rules will be put in place to protect their customers.”
The October 2023 data breach of 23andMe exposed sensitive genetic information belonging to millions of customers. Some of this data was then listed for sale on the dark web, exposing customers to further hacks and identity theft. 23andMe learned about the breach months after impacted personal information was publicly available. The company first denied a breach and then, once it confirmed the breach, blamed costumers for how their accounts were set up or how passwords were used.
In the immediate aftermath of the data breach, Attorney General James and the coalition began a multistate investigation and found that 23andMe failed to take critical security measures, including:
- Safeguards against cyber-attacks utilizing stolen credentials including, comparing passwords against blocklists of known breached passwords or requiring multifactor authentication;
- Appropriate rate limiting or intrusion prevention;
- Logging, monitoring, or other tools likely to detect a data breach;
- Investigating or addressing unusual login patterns, including, for example, a massive spike in login attempts;
- Fixing known vulnerabilities; and
- Properly reviewing and testing design features.
In March 2025, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy protection and Attorney General James and the coalition filed claims related to the data breach investigation. In June 2025, Attorney General James and a bipartisan coalition of 27 other attorneys general sued 23andMe to protect Americans’ personal genetic information during the company’s bankruptcy.
As a result of the bankruptcy, 23andMe’s customer data was sold to TTAM Research (TTAM), a non-profit formed by 23andMe’s founder and former CEO. Attorney General James and the coalition have secured new information and data security requirements at TTAM to protect customers’ data and prevent future breaches. These measures include appropriate risk analysis, the addition of an Advisory Board on data security, and continuing to offer consumers the right to delete their information. These terms will ensure that TTAM, now reregistered as 23andMe Research Institute, will be a safer custodian of genetic data moving forward.
Joining Attorney General James in securing this settlement are the attorneys general of Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, North Dakota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia.
For New York, this matter was handled by Deputy Bureau Chief Clark Russell under the supervision of Bureau Chief Kim Berger of the Bureau of Internet and Technology. The Bureau of Internet and Technology is a part of the Division for Economic Justice, which is led by Chief Deputy Attorney General Chris D’Angelo and overseen by First Deputy Attorney General Jennifer Levy.
Source: NY Attorney General Letitia James

38cb0c8f78c0.text: This weekly security roundup covers major cybersecurity developments, including critical WordPress vulnerabilities, OAuth spoofing techniques, ransomware attacks, and advances in AI-driven security research. Key Highlights: Critical Vulnerabilities: WordPress 7.0.2 addressed one critical and one high severity security flaw requiring immediate patching. SonicWall Secure Mobile Access appliances face active exploitation through two zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-15409, CVE-2026-15410), prompting urgent firmware upgrades. Authentication & Access Threats: Attackers are spoofing OAuth client IDs to evade Microsoft Entra ID sign-in telemetry, exploiting how the system handles unfamiliar identifiers in security logs. Major Incidents: Coca-Cola's Fairlife milk production halted by ransomware; Lidl customers' data compromised via IT service provider breach; Spanish police dismantled a €140 million cybercrime network; Dutch authorities took down an investment fraud ring stealing €100 million monthly. Emerging Security Trends: Email and phishing now account for 50% of ransomware incidents, according to Sophos research. Meanwhile, 99.9% of fixable AI infrastructure vulnerabilities remain unpatched across organizations. Notable Product Developments: 1Password integrated with Claude AI to enable secure website authentication without exposing credentials. (Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security, Published: July 19, 2026)

32b970d7dc2c.text: F5 has patched a critical nginx flaw (CVE-2026-42533) affecting versions 0.9.6 through 1.31.2. The vulnerability enables remote attackers to trigger heap buffer overflow in worker processes through crafted HTTP requests, potentially causing denial of service or remote code execution. Technical Details: The flaw exists in nginx's script engine and surfaces under specific configuration: "a regex-based map whose output variable is referenced in a string expression after a capture from an earlier regex match." The overflow stems from a two-pass evaluation process. During the first pass, the engine measures required buffer size; the second pass writes data. When a map's regex evaluation occurs between these passes, it overwrites shared capture state, causing the buffer to be undersized for the actual data written. Impact & Scope: CVSS Score: 9.2 (v4) / 8.1 (v3.1). Fixed Versions: nginx 1.30.4, 1.31.3, NGINX Plus 37.0.3.1. Affected Products: NGINX Ingress Controller, Gateway Fabric, App Protect WAF, Instance Manager. Researcher Stan Shaw argues the flaw enables full remote code execution on default systems by supplying its own ASLR bypass, contradicting F5's conditions requiring disabled ASLR. Remediation: F5 recommends upgrading immediately. A temporary mitigation involves switching affected regex maps to named captures, though Shaw identified a narrower exploitation path remaining through this approach. (Author: Swati Khandelwal, Published: July 19, 2026)

804c86b9fe50.text: A threat actor tracked as UTA0533 exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) 1000 series VPN appliances prior to their public disclosure on June 22, 2026. Security firm Volexity discovered the activity during an incident response investigation. Key Vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-15409 (CVSS 10.0): A pre-authentication WebSocket bypass allowing unauthenticated requests to establish tunnels to localhost-only services; CVE-2026-15410 (CVSS 7.2): A path traversal flaw in the ctrl-service that enables privilege escalation. Attack Chain: The attacker chained these exploits to achieve root access by sending unauthenticated "/wsproxy" requests with specific User-Agent and bmID parameters, establishing WebSocket tunnels to CouchDB, reading the appliance UUID file to bypass authentication, and escalating privileges through the ctrl-service vulnerability. Malware Deployed: ROOTRUN (a setuid binary enabling unprivileged users to execute commands as root), KNUCKLEBALL (a Python script injecting two JAR payloads), Suo5 (an open-source HTTP proxy), and ORANGETAIL (a custom Java web shell enabling remote interaction). Consequences: With root access, the attacker could "access stored or cached credentials, capture network traffic, and potentially intercept credentials processed" by the appliances, per Volexity's analysis. However, evidence suggests limited lateral movement success. Updates: Rapid7 later identified that INC Ransomware emerged as a dominant threat actor weaponizing this vulnerability chain, with significant tactical overlap suggesting coordinated or single-actor responsibility. (Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, Published: July 19, 2026)

66f672251cb6.text: Ullrich reports detection of reconnaissance scans targeting the Hikvision Intelligent Security API (ISAPI), a REST-based interface for camera management and control. The scans specifically target the /ISAPI/System/status endpoint, which returns system information in XML or JSON format. Key technical details include: Authentication: The API uses Basic or Digest authentication. Encryption: Supports AES 128/256 in CBC mode, though the initialization vector is exposed in the URL. Security limitation: "The encryption does not provide any additional security if Basic authentication is used" since credentials transmit unencrypted over non-HTTPS connections. API age: While available since at least 2018, these reconnaissance scans represent newly observed activity. Ullrich notes the endpoint likely serves as a verification mechanism for ISAPI support (expecting 401/403 responses if accessible, 404 if absent) and could facilitate password brute-forcing attempts. Recommendation: The author advises against exposing these cameras to the internet and avoiding their placement in sensitive areas without proper security configurations. (Author: Johannes Ullrich, Ph.D., Dean of Research, SANS.edu, Published/Updated: July 19, 2026, 15:00:38 UTC)

7122a61c8b6a.text: An advanced threat actor is abusing the update mechanism for the ViPNet private networking product suite to target Russian organizations, including government agencies. Dubbed HelloNet, the campaign has been active since at least May, deploying a malicious payload that acts as a proxy and loader for additional malware. According to Kaspersky researchers, HelloNet has impacted organizations in the government, energy, transport, education, and logistics sectors. ViPNet is a family of Russian information-security products developed by InfoTeCS, providing VPN, endpoint, and network access protection, firewall, certificate management, centralized administration, and secure messaging and file transfer. The tool is commonly used in Russia, where it is certified by authorities for use in government and other regulated environments. In the latest campaign, attackers placed a malicious file (wtsapi32.dll, dubbed HelloInjector) inside the local ViPNet Update System directory to be sideloaded at system startup via the legitimate itcsrvup64.exe. This DLL is the first-stage loader that injects into the svchost.exe process, granting next-stage payloads elevated privileges on Windows and persistence across reboots. HelloInjector runs its embedded payload, which Kaspersky named HelloProxy, in memory and contacts the command-and-control server to receive additional modules. These include HelloExecutor (a backdoor for commands and network reconnaissance), HelloCleaner (removes ViPNet log data), and HelloBackdoor (Rust-based tool supporting file operations and command execution). Kaspersky tentatively attributed the campaign to an unidentified Chinese-speaking advanced persistent threat group, though researchers stressed this attribution has low confidence, relying primarily on unused strings referencing sina.com and a malware mirror hosted by China's University of Science and Technology. The firm recommends monitoring systems running ViPNet, particularly traffic on ports 5003, 5060, and 443. (Author: Bill Toulas, Published: July 19, 2026)

658595fbcabe.text:
Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: July 19, 2026.

Russian state-sponsored threat actors affiliated with Sandworm have deployed ClickFix social engineering tactics targeting Ukrainian users. The Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) attributed this campaign to UAC-0145, a sub-cluster within Sandworm, GRU's foreign military intelligence unit.

Attack Method: Threat actors compromised at least 10 websites between June and July 2026, injecting fake CAPTCHA checks that instruct victims to execute PowerShell commands. The attackers employed multiple sophisticated techniques: SMARTAXE tool to dynamically alter webpage content based on visitor characteristics; EtherHiding technique to retrieve malicious domain names from Ethereum smart contracts; Cloaking.House traffic filtering service to serve different pages to different visitors.

Malware Deployed: The campaign delivered various malicious programs: GHETTOVIBE, a VBS file saved to Startup autorun directory; SCOUTCURL, a PowerShell script performing system reconnaissance; FLUIDLEECH and LOADLOOP, loader programs (FLUIDLEECH disguised as antivirus software); FREAKYPOLL, a Python backdoor.

Mobile Component: Android devices were targeted through trojanized APK files disguised as security tools via messaging apps. The embedded COWARDDUCK backdoor collects contacts, specific file types, and real-time geolocation data, uploading findings via Dropbox APIs.

97c7d2c30c0a.text:
Anna Zhadan reports:
American healthcare giant Abbott Laboratories is investigating two cyber incidents that appear to be unrelated: one involving its Cancer Diagnostics business and another affecting its LabCentral portal.
Although unrelated, the two disclosures came within days of each other.
On July 16th, Abbott said it was investigating an incident involving unauthorized access to a limited number of internal systems in its Cancer Diagnostics business.
[…]
The ShinyHunters gang posted Abbott on its data leak site, threatening to publish the allegedly stolen data on July 18th unless Abbott negotiated with the group, although the deadline was later postponed to July 21st.
[…]
Separately, another threat actor has claimed to have breached Abbott’s LabCentral portal, which is a customer portal for core laboratory diagnostics. The ShadowByt3$ hacking gang told BleepingComputer that it gained access on July 4th using compromised customer credentials and a “weak point” in the environment.
The group claims it exfiltrated sensitive technical documentation related to Abbott’s laboratory diagnostic systems, including manufacturing certificates, operation manuals, technical specifications, and regulatory documents.
Read more at CyberNews.

dcef4577a279.text:
Author: Phill Moore. Published: July 19, 2026.

This weekly roundup covers digital forensics and incident response news across multiple categories.

Forensic Analysis: Coverage includes Tailscale artifact examination, AI framework comparisons, iOS/Android artifact analysis, and emerging detection methods for AI-generated imagery. Notable pieces examine PDF security history and Google Pay account artifacts.

Key threats discussed: ClickFix malware variants, AsyncAPI supply chain compromises, device code phishing abuse, and credential harvesting operations across multiple sectors.
