c7ece1d118f5.text:
Author: Ionut Arghire. Published: July 17, 2026 (2:23 AM ET).

Coca-Cola announced Thursday that it has suspended production at its subsidiary Fairlife following detection of a ransomware attack. Fairlife, a Chicago-based Coca-Cola wholly owned dairy company, distributes ultra-filtered milk in five flavors: chocolate, fat-free, reduced fat, strawberry, and whole milk.

In a July 16 filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Coca-Cola disclosed that hackers accessed a portion of Fairlife's systems, including production-related systems. The company stated: "After detecting the issue, the Company promptly activated its incident response and business continuity protocols."

According to the filing, the investigation into the incident's full scope, nature, and impact remains ongoing with assistance from outside advisors and cybersecurity experts. Law enforcement has been notified of the attack.

The company confirmed that "Product quality and safety have not been impacted. However, as a result of the incident, production operations at Fairlife in the United States are temporarily suspended. Fairlife's Canada production operations are not currently impacted."

Coca-Cola has not disclosed how the incident occurred, the identity of the attackers, or whether extortion demands have been received. As of publication, no known ransomware groups have claimed responsibility for the attack.

c12435cfc09f.text:
Author: Mike Lennon. Published: July 20, 2026 (6:25 AM ET).

Capital One has released VulnHunter, an AI-powered security tool designed to identify and remediate software vulnerabilities. Unlike traditional vulnerability scanners, VulnHunter uses agentic reasoning to reduce false positives that typically slow developer workflows.

The tool features capabilities to "identify potentially exploitable defects, map prospective attack paths, and propose highly targeted code remediations." It is available on GitHub with documentation and example workflows.

According to Chris Nims, Capital One's CISO, the company addressed "a massive industry pain point: overwhelming false positives that create friction and slow down daily workflows."

The tool requires access to Claude Opus 4.8 and a working Claude Code environment. Capital One notes that "no single organization can solve this challenge alone" and released VulnHunter to enable broader security improvements across the software industry.

Internally, Capital One used VulnHunter to efficiently identify and remediate vulnerabilities across thousands of repositories spanning multiple business areas.

878aa109dd2e.text:
Author: Sergiu Gatlan. Published: July 20, 2026, 05:29 AM.

Attackers have begun exploiting a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-6875) in the ServiceNow AI Platform, according to threat intelligence company Defused.

Formerly known as the Now Platform, ServiceNow AI Platform is an enterprise-grade Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) that helps businesses integrate AI into core enterprise workflows.

Cybersecurity company Searchlight Cyber, which found this critical vulnerability and reported it on April 1st, says that it allows unauthenticated threat actors to escape the sandbox and execute code remotely within the ServiceNow platform in high-complexity attacks.

ServiceNow addressed the flaw across hosted instances starting in April and released CVE-2026-6875 security updates for self-hosted instances one week ago, on July 13th.

Over the weekend, Defused security researchers confirmed that attackers have begun exploiting the vulnerability in the wild, with the first attempts being observed on Friday. According to Defused researchers, "the payloads hit the same pre-auth sink" as documented but "the sandbox-escape gadget reaches the same code-execution primitive by a different route."

ServiceNow has yet to flag this security as actively abused. However, the company advises all customers who have not already done so to secure their systems against attacks by upgrading to a patched release as soon as possible.

ServiceNow says that its AI Platform runs more than 100 billion workflows each year and powers over 100,000 enterprise AI apps at 85% of all Fortune 500 companies.

f4e36241b7de.text:
Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security. Published: July 20, 2026.

Microsoft has released Dusseldorf, an open-source out-of-band application security testing (OAST) platform designed to detect vulnerabilities that leave minimal traces within applications. The project addresses security gaps including server-side request forgery, cross-site scripting, server-side template injection, and XML external entity flaws.

The platform captures inbound network traffic across DNS, HTTP, and HTTPS protocols. Its naming convention references the German city Düsseldorf, which contains the letters SSRF—a fitting choice given the tool's purpose.

Dusseldorf operates by running listeners tied to a domain like *.yourdomain.net, logging every request to that domain and its subdomains as distinct entries called "zones." A graphical interface and REST API enable operators to view captured requests, customize responses, and establish filters.

The tool emphasizes private deployment, giving operators control over identity integration, infrastructure footprint, domains, and runtime policies. Deployment requires a machine with public IPv4 addresses and a domain with appropriate nameserver configuration.

Technical prerequisites include Docker, Docker Compose, Azure CLI, OpenSSL, Python 3 with pip, jq utility, and Helm. The codebase supports dual deployment paths: local setups for development and Azure cloud provisioning for production environments.

The open-source project is available on GitHub at no cost.

c852269f0544.text:
Author: Eduard Kovacs. Published: July 20, 2026 (1:21 AM ET).

Two critical WordPress security flaws are actively being exploited following their public disclosure. Identified as CVE-2026-60137 and CVE-2026-63030 and collectively called WP2Shell, these vulnerabilities affect WordPress versions 6.9.0-6.9.4 and 7.0.0-7.0.1.

According to Searchlight Cyber, which discovered the flaws, "The attack has no preconditions and can be exploited by an anonymous user in a stock install of WordPress with no plugins."

The first vulnerability is a high-severity SQL injection bug, while the second represents a critical arbitrary code execution flaw. When chained together, attackers achieve unauthenticated remote code execution capabilities.

WordPress released patches (versions 6.9.5 and 7.0.2) on Friday, with developers noting that forced updates were enabled through their auto-update system due to severity. Cloudflare has also deployed detection rules for customers.

Multiple security firms, including Patchstack, Hexastrike, and WatchTowr, have confirmed active exploitation attempts. Benjamin Harris, CEO of WatchTowr, emphasized the urgency: "This is going to hurt. WordPress runs on hundreds of millions of websites globally."

Harris highlighted an emerging trend, stating that proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours rather than the historical 24+ hour window, attributing this acceleration to AI-assisted vulnerability discovery tools.

436984be0e7e.text:
Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security. Published: July 20, 2026.

Open models are moving into production across more organizations, and the work of securing those deployments increasingly extends beyond the model weights. Mozilla's The State of Open Source AI 2026 identifies deployment, governance and operational tooling as persistent obstacles as model capability improves.

"Without investment in the infrastructure, tooling, and governance around open models, we risk locking in a system where only restrictive, closed AI can scale" – Raffi Krikorian, Mozilla's Chief Technology Officer.

The capability gap between leading open and closed models has narrowed to an average of 3.3 points on Chatbot Arena, giving organizations a wider choice for production workloads. The average hides differences across tasks: open models are at or near parity in coding, instruction-following and general knowledge, while closed models retain an edge in reasoning, long-context retrieval and agentic tasks.

The price of the cheapest model offering GPT-4-class performance fell 50-fold over 36 months, from about $20 to $0.40 per million tokens. This measure uses blended API list prices and does not represent every inference workload.

Open-weight models accounted for about one-third of all tokens routed through OpenRouter by late 2025. The figures cover routed traffic and exclude first-party services such as ChatGPT and Gemini.

Deployment continues to lag adoption: 79% of developers use open models, and 89% of organizations use open components somewhere in their software stack. Just over half of organizations using open models have moved them into production. Closed models continue to reach production more often, indicating that deployment barriers extend beyond model capability. Deployments completed with vendor partners reach production more frequently than internally developed implementations.

Community support, ease of adoption and model capability receive stronger scores than standardization and enterprise readiness. The weakest results appear in safeguards, where governance, operational consistency and production maturity trail other parts of the ecosystem.

Security and operations drive deployment friction: Developers identified infrastructure costs as a challenge, although security, privacy and compliance followed closely behind. Maintenance, deployment complexity and system integration also ranked as the most common operational concerns. Developers who stopped using open models reported these operational issues more often than developers who continue using them.

The harness becomes the next control layer: Mozilla describes the agentic harness as the next major development layer, including orchestration, tools, memory, execution environments, permissions, identity, evaluation, observability and governance. Model evaluation often focuses on capability, accuracy and benchmark performance, while production deployments introduce further requirements, including identity, permissions, auditability, budget controls and operational oversight across multiple AI components.

2ce941b8b7c1.text:
Author: Rapid7. Published: July 15, 2026 (Updated July 16, 2026).

Summary: Rapid7's Managed Detection and Response team identified two critical vulnerabilities in SonicWall SMA1000 appliances being actively exploited in the wild: CVE-2026-15409 (CVSS 10.0) - Server-side request forgery enabling unauthenticated attackers to tunnel to localhost services; CVE-2026-15410 - Local privilege escalation via path traversal in hotfix removal workflow.

Technical Details: The primary attack vector exploits a websocket proxy feature at /wsproxy on the SonicWall WorkPlace application. Attackers can "access local SonicWall appliance system services behind the firewall to send and receive arbitrary TCP traffic." This provides initial access to internal services like the Erlang process on localhost:1050. Following initial compromise, attackers leverage CVE-2026-15410 to escalate privileges to root by injecting malicious scripts into the hotfix removal process.

Attack Pattern Observed: Real-world exploitation involved harvesting credentials, session databases, and TOTP authentication seeds; lateral movement into corporate networks via compromised appliances; direct Active Directory authentication attempts from the appliance using service account credentials.

Mitigation: Organizations must immediately upgrade to fixed versions (12.4.3-03453 or 12.5.0-02835 platform hotfix or later). No workarounds exist. SonicWall recommends forensic review, credential resets, and TOTP token regeneration for affected organizations.

c4d324bedb5d.text:
Author: Sergiu Gatlan. Published: July 20, 2026.

Hugging Face disclosed a security breach involving an autonomous AI agent that infiltrated its production infrastructure, gaining access to internal datasets and credentials. The attack began through a malicious dataset that exploited code-execution vulnerabilities in the company's data-processing pipeline.

The attackers leveraged two security flaws—a template injection in dataset configuration and a remote code dataset loader—to execute code on processing workers. This allowed them to steal cloud and cluster credentials, enabling lateral movement across internal systems.

Hugging Face characterized the incident as matching "the 'agentic attacker' scenario the industry has been forecasting." The campaign involved autonomous agent frameworks executing "many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes."

Key Response Actions: Closed vulnerable code execution pathways; evicted the attacker and rebuilt compromised nodes; revoked and rotated all affected credentials; deployed enhanced malicious activity detection systems; reported incident to law enforcement.

The company found no evidence of tampering with public models or datasets, and verified its software supply chain remains clean. Hugging Face advised users to rotate access tokens and monitor account activity for suspicious behavior.

The platform has experienced multiple security incidents in recent years, including previous breaches of its Spaces platform and abuse for distributing malware.

3600ff74e58a.text:
Author: Eduard Kovacs. Published: July 20, 2026 (7:46 AM ET).

A longtime cybersecurity executive has built a website that tracks disclosed material breaches, aiming to give cybersecurity professionals, journalists, policymakers, and everyday citizens a resource that doesn't currently exist.

The tracker was created by Richard Bird, who is currently Chief Strategy and Chief Security Officer at enterprise AI governance company Singulr AI. He previously held leadership roles at JPMorgan Chase and several cybersecurity companies.

Unrelated to his role at Singulr AI, Bird is an author, and in preparation for his upcoming book — Built Wrong: Why Cybersecurity Keeps Failing and How We Can Rebuild It — he has launched a new project named The Hacker in a Hoodie (HIH) Index.

The core of the site is a pair of ledgers that update on what Bird describes as a daily or near-daily basis, pulled by pollers and tracers he built and runs himself. The first ledger draws from SEC EDGAR, the agency's public filing database, tracking the 8-K disclosures that public companies are required to file when they experience a material cyber incident — a requirement that has existed only since 2023. The second ledger is based on news articles and companies' own statements.

The data arrives as raw, inconsistent text, with some entries naming a dollar loss while most don't. Bird's ledger organizes those scattered records into one running list. At the time of writing, the index contains information on more than 100 incidents. The most current entries cover data breaches reported by Coca-Cola's Fairlife, Centers Lab, Mount Royal University, and Accenture.

The HIH Index grades every entry by how solid its sourcing is: a primary SEC filing counts as 'verified', a company's own statement as 'attested', and a news report as 'inferred'. That grading lets a reader tell at a glance how much weight a given entry can actually carry.

Separate from both ledgers, the site includes a static reference chart that pulls annual figures from the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (which shows nearly $20.9 billion in reported losses for 2025) and IBM's Cost of a Data Breach report (which shows an average of $4.44 million per breach). These reports provide context for the project's argument. They show that per-incident cost has barely moved in a decade, even as total reported losses have compounded at roughly 35% a year.

"This means only one thing — the hackers aren't making more money from the same number of victims," Bird told SecurityWeek. "More companies are failing (way more) at cybersecurity every year and the bad guys are functionally printing money by capitalizing on how poorly cybersecurity is actually being executed at these companies."

He added, "The [upcoming] book, and the index, are not pointing fingers of blame. What we've built in cybersecurity is rational. But it is rational based on the wrong data and inputs — we measure activity, we don't measure performance and outcomes."

Bird's case against summing the HIH Index data is straightforward: most of the ledger's entries are marked 'not yet quantified,' and the ones that do carry a figure come from different evidence tiers — a verified dollar loss in an SEC filing isn't the same as an inferred estimate drawn from a news report. Treating those as interchangeable and adding them together would produce a number that looks precise but is not backed by anything solid.

He points to the industry's favorite trillion-dollar cybercrime estimate, a controversial Cybersecurity Ventures projection, as exactly the kind of number his project aims to avoid manufacturing. "Summing the numbers creates a myth — it is no longer data; it becomes a prediction at best and a forecast at worst," Bird explained. "The losses are so grossly underreported that if I took that sensationalist approach, I'd be creating another version of the same problem. A bunch of guessing that is perceived as being better but only because it has more citations."

What makes the ledgers useful isn't the total — it's the ability to check. A reporter or analyst can look up what a specific company actually disclosed, how the filing was worded, and what evidence grade it carries. In an industry where cyber loss reporting leans heavily on marketing-driven estimates, having a citable, source-graded reference to check claims against fills a gap that has largely gone unfilled.

Bird maintains the entire project alone — no editorial team, no outside data vendor, just the scrapers he built to keep both ledgers current. He is also upfront about the dataset being young: the SEC requirement it's built on is relatively new, and he draws a direct comparison to Troy Hunt's Have I Been Pwned data breach notification service, which also started small and grew because there was nowhere else to look.

That absence is the point he's really making. Everything else in a company gets measured in dollars, except cybersecurity, which Bird says has been treated as overhead instead of a tracked outcome. In his words: "Business keeps score in dollars, governments keep score in dollars, consumers keep score in dollars — cybersecurity is the only business function that isn't measured in dollars from a performance perspective. It's treated as a 'cost of business'. There is only one other corporate 'cost of business' in the enterprise world — whether it is large, medium or small businesses. And that is taxes. We built cybersecurity as a tax, not as a value-added business function. The entire industry and practice has created an ecosystem over the last 30 years that not only emphasizes that truth, it actually rewards the continuation of the flawed model."

93aef628f7eb.text:
On March 18, 2026, Navigate360 learned that 8.3 million anonymous tips had been exposed. The company’s response—and the silence of the programs that depend on its platform—has persisted for months. We’re now seeking accountability through state and federal regulators.
A DataBreaches.net Editorial
In March 2026, the world learned that a hacktivist had acquired 8.3 million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers and programs like Safe2Tell and SandyHookPromise. The tipsters had all been assured that their tips would be anonymous, but investigations by DataBreaches and Straight Arrow News revealed that many tips were not anonymous, even though people expressed concerns for their safety if their identities became known. DataBreaches’ previous reporting on the Navigate360 breach (sometimes referred to as the BlueLeaks 2.0 breach) is linked at the bottom of this editorial.
Rather than forthrightly disclosing the breach and addressing concerns, Navigate360 and its subsidiaries P3 Campus and P3 Global Intel simply clammed up and wouldn’t answer any questions. Joining them in a conspiracy of silence, programs such as Safe2Tell, Safe2SaySomething, SandyHookPromise, and others also refused to answer any questions and responded to public records requests by claiming exemption from disclosure.
SuspectFile recently commented on the lack of transparency after three months. Had he waited a few more days, he could have said after four months. He wrote,
In the Navigate360 case, the most important question therefore remains unanswered:
When will all the people who entrusted such sensitive information to this platform be notified?
Perhaps the preliminary questions should be: “WILL all identifiable people who entrusted sensitive information to the platform be notified?” And “WILL all state regulators be notified of the breach, as required by state laws?”
In a new post about the Crime Stoppers data to be published this coming week, DataBreaches will report some statistics on tips provided to Crime Stoppers organizations and law enforcement tiplines. But before we turn to the Crime Stoppers data, and the lack of transparency concerning how Crime Stoppers may or may not have responded to the incident, let’s recap where we are so far with Navigate360 and referral programs that promised people their tips would be anonymous.
Have programs like Safe2Tell, Safe2SayPA, SandyHookPromise, and other programs notified anyone about the breach? Has Navigate360 or P3 notified anyone?
Have they notified any tipsters? There is no publicly available evidence that any of them have made any public disclosures about the breach. Why not? Have Navigate360 and P3 even given them all the information they need to make notifications?
It does not appear that many of the programs or schools have been given the information they need to make any required notifications.
On May 24, Navigate360 provided customers with instructions as to how to request their data (presumably because they had not already provided it). The information on how to request data was shared with DataBreaches by a recipient. It indicated that entities requesting data should expect the data to be provided in July. We do not know whether that has happened.
If you received data from Navigate360, when did you receive it, and was it sufficient to enable you to make the notifications you are obligated to make? We want to hear from you. You can contact us via Signal (Dissent.73), email to breaches@protonmail[.]ch, or Tox: A9C22FFAC38E535E79C0365F9847AA3286263A93A690337305B4F28400D9BA171565FA49E086
If any entity using P3 Campus requested data and was denied, please let us know and provide a copy of the denial reasons.
We Can Help (a Bit)
If you are school personnel and are still in the dark about who needs to be notified, and if you are being told to recommend people use programs that may not be secure, and if you have been given no proof that any security issues have been appropriately addressed, we want to hear from you. Contact us on Signal at Dissent.73 or via email to breaches@protonmail[.]ch
If school personnel still haven’t been notified by Navigate360, P3, or any programs, DataBreaches previously reported on the number of tips by school name. Table 4 provided a partial list of school names, in alphabetical order. In contrast, Table 3 provided a complete list of referrer names (including school domains and programs such as Safe2Say) and the number of tips associated with each referrer. The data we have published are not sufficient to make individual notifications, but it should give you some sense of how many students, parents, or staff may have their tips exposed in the dataset.
Have programs like Safe2Tell, Safe2SayPA, SandyHookPromise, and other programs notified any state regulators about the breach? Has Navigate360 or P3 notified any regulators?
We have not seen any public disclosures on state attorneys general websites that post notifications they have received. Many tipsters are California residents, yet it does not appear that California has been notified.
Because Navigate360 has not answered any of our questions and because programs have not answered DataBreaches’ questions and have exempted themselves from having to answer under states’ public records laws, DataBreaches has contacted the National Association of Attorneys General (NAAG) to make them aware of this breach and that no one appears to have been notified, even four months after the breach was discovered.
We urge state attorneys general to open investigations and enforcement actions into this incident and incident response. Navigate360, P3, and programs like safe2say assured people that their tips would be kept anonymous. They weren’t. People are reportedly still being told to use programs that were not truly secure and may still not be. States need to investigate and take enforcement action. DataBreaches will be following up on the overview email to NAAG with formal complaints to specific state attorneys general.

e2b721689e2c.text:
Author: Ionut Arghire. Published: July 20, 2026 (7:27 AM ET).

Professional services firm Ernst & Young (EY) has begun notifying clients that their personal and financial information was compromised in a data breach. The incident occurred on a third-party service management platform EY uses for tax-related work.

The breach was discovered on April 23, and attackers had access to the compromised platform between March 28 and April 12. During this window, hackers downloaded documents containing client tax information from support tickets submitted through the platform.

Compromised data includes names, addresses, Social Security numbers, account numbers, credit and debit card numbers, and other information used in tax filing preparation. EY stated: "Support tickets submitted through the platform may include documents containing client tax information."

The company says it has no evidence of misuse or further exposure of affected clients' personal information. As a remedial measure, EY is providing two years of complimentary credit monitoring, identity monitoring, and identity restoration services to impacted clients.

EY has not disclosed details about how the attack occurred or identified the responsible threat actor. No known ransomware or extortion group has claimed responsibility for the incident. The company engaged an independent cybersecurity firm to investigate the breach's nature and scope.

f672a079eb17.text:
Author: Bruce Schneier. Published: July 20, 2026.

A writer was mistakenly tracked, identified, and arrested using Flock Safety camera data after police entered an incomplete license plate number into the system. The stolen vehicle alert listed plate 34 DTM instead of the actual plate 34 10 DTM, but Flock's AI flagged the writer's vehicle because it matched the partial characters.

Flock's CEO claimed their system "worked correctly" and blamed law enforcement for not verifying matches, explaining: "The way that law enforcement likes to use these tools is, if any of the characters...get read, they want to get those alerts."

The incident revealed broader concerns: Systemic issues - other vehicles with similar manufacturer plates (34 ## DTM) were simultaneously tracked nationwide, suggesting the writer wasn't the first wrongfully flagged; Scope creep - police departments are using Flock cameras to track people, not just vehicles, with vague search terms like "heavy-set male with black and white hat"; Accountability concerns - the Flock CEO previously called privacy advocates "terrorists" but later apologized; Documented abuses - police have misused similar surveillance databases.

The incident demonstrates how surveillance technology, even when functioning as designed, can enable systemic errors and privacy violations at scale.

a33475951af8.text:
Microsoft is addressing a known issue impacting Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) servers, with synchronization problems persisting for over a week. WSUS, deployed nearly two decades ago, enables IT administrators to schedule updates for Microsoft products across enterprise networks from a centralized local server rather than having each endpoint update directly from Microsoft's servers.

By default, WSUS synchronizes with Microsoft Update servers daily to retrieve metadata for available Windows updates. However, affected servers experience broken synchronization, preventing administrators from deploying the latest Windows updates via WSUS or Configuration Manager.

The issue impacts both client platforms (Windows 10, version 1607 and later) and server platforms (Windows Server 2012 and later). According to Microsoft's Windows health dashboard, "Organizations might experience increased synchronization times or sync operation timeouts on WSUS servers," with heightened impact beginning July 13, 2026.

Microsoft deployed mitigation measures on Saturday to prevent sync issues on newly installed or rebuilt WSUS servers. However, the company continues working on additional mitigations for previously affected servers still experiencing synchronization problems.

The company noted: "Synchronization times and sync operations on WSUS servers have been restored and are operating normally for new WSUS installations and rebuilds."

This represents another in a series of WSUS-related incidents Microsoft has addressed, including similar problems in May 2024, July 2025, and August 2025.

(Author: Sergiu Gatlan)

55c870752167.text:
Microsoft released emergency out-of-band (OOB) updates to resolve shutdown issues affecting specific Dell computers running Windows 11. The problem stems from an incompatibility between a new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface and Intel's Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver.

The issue impacts Dell systems that installed the July 2026 security update (KB5101650) on Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 24H2. The root cause traces back to changes introduced in June's KB5095093 preview update, which created conflicts with Intel's power and thermal management driver.

Affected devices displayed a yellow warning icon in Device Manager and experienced "unexpected shutdowns, poor performance, increased heat, and battery drain," according to Microsoft's statement.

Microsoft distributed two emergency fixes: KB5121767 for Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2, and KB5121768 for Windows 11 Enterprise LTSC 2024.

The company had temporarily blocked the July update on affected Dell devices pending resolution. Devices using Windows Autopatch with hotpatch enabled received the emergency update automatically, while IT administrators could expedite deployment through Microsoft Intune.

(Author: Sergiu Gatlan)

a42c65f6318b.text:
The American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts says it’s releasing an online toolkit this week for criminal defense attorneys designed to uncover whether police used surveillance technologies—facial recognition, automatic license plate readers, gunshot detection systems, and more—to build the cases against their clients in secret.
The toolkit, which the group describes as the first of its kind, is built around handcrafted legal motions that, when granted by a judge, will force prosecutors to reveal whether surveillance technology was used against a defendant. It covers an array of technologies, from “stingray” phone trackers and location data sold by commercial brokers to AI-drafted police reports and forensic tools that crack phones and siphon data from car infotainment systems.
It also includes preservation motions—demands that surveillance data be saved before it is deleted automatically—aimed at government agencies and private vendors alike. The filings rest on a bedrock rule of American criminal law, established in 1963, that prosecutors are required to turn over all evidence that could help the defense. The motions will be distributed through a password-protected library, the ACLU of Massachusetts says, available only to verified defense attorneys.
The group is fighting a war against unregulated surveillance tools on two fronts, says Jennifer Herrmann, a staff attorney at the ACLU of Massachusetts and one of the toolkit’s authors. One front is pressuring cities to drop tools like Flock, the license plate reader network, and ShotSpotter, the gunshot detection system, outright. The other is arming defense lawyers to expose the surveillance in court.
“The amount of time that it can take for that initial use of technology and investigation to actually get to a court and constitutional challenge is long,” Herrmann says—so the motions give attorneys a way to “challenge what has already happened in the past,” building a record that carries over to whatever tool comes next.
The project responds to what its authors describe as a chronic lag between the moment police adopt a new surveillance tool and the moment courts finally decide whether using it is legal. Most Americans carried cell phones by the late 1990s and early 2000s, but the United States Supreme Court did not require police to get a warrant for cell phone location records until 2018. The lag isn’t just the result of slow-moving courts. The technologies with the worst disclosure records have faced the fewest court rulings precisely because a defendant cannot challenge a tool they were never told about.
In materials accompanying the launch, the ACLU of Massachusetts says police deploy these tools “sometimes without even disclosing their use to the prosecutors handling the case.” For years, the FBI required local police departments to sign secrecy agreements before using cell-site simulators—suitcase-sized devices, commonly called stingrays, that impersonate cell towers to secretly locate phones. In Baltimore, one such agreement instructed prosecutors to drop criminal cases entirely rather than reveal the device in court, even as the city’s police used it more than 4,300 times between 2007 and 2015. FBI records later obtained by the ACLU show the agreements persisted until at least 2020.
When Missouri investigators used Fog Reveal, a commercial tool that maps people’s movements using app-harvested location data, in the investigation of a 2017 murder, the Associated Press found no trace of it in the trial exhibits that helped convict the victim’s wife. And when Louisiana authorities obtained an arrest warrant in 2022 for Randal Quran Reid—a Georgia man misidentified by facial recognition and jailed for nearly a week—the warrant attributed his identification not to software but to “a credible source,” according to The Washington Post. The very document that authorized his arrest actively obscured how police came to suspect him.
The toolkit’s authors frame the problem slightly differently: Their central worry is not only evidence hidden from prosecutors but defendants who are never told a surveillance tool touched their case at all, and defense lawyers who don't know to ask.
Gideon Epstein, a Technology for Liberty policy counsel at the civil liberties group and the toolkit’s other author, points to Massachusetts's own leading license plate reader case, Commonwealth v. McCarthy, in which the defense sought records for only a handful of cameras rather than the statewide network. “A lot of the time they're not asking for the full scope of surveillance technologies in use,” Epstein says. The motions, he adds, are as much about prompting lawyers to demand everything as about forcing the government to cough it up.
The preservation motions target a separate and subtler problem: surveillance evidence that destroys itself. Axon's Draft One, an AI tool that writes police reports from body camera audio, discards the machine-written first draft by design. An Axon product manager told the Electronic Frontier Foundation in July 2025 that the choice avoids creating “disclosure headaches” for police customers and prosecutors. California legislators saw the matter differently and enacted a law last year that requires agencies to keep the original drafts.
Elsewhere, Flock Safety’s license plate reader network deletes its footage after 30 days by default, and Chicago’s contract for the ShotSpotter gunshot detection system declared the gunfire data the vendor's own property, not the city’s. In each case, the digital material a defendant would need to fight back against a claim can vanish—or sit beyond the government's reach—before a defense attorney is ever appointed to the case.
Flock Safety spokesperson Paris Lewbel says the company has procedures to preserve the integrity and authenticity of data stored in its system, and tools to confirm that an ALPR image or investigative report has not been altered since it was pulled from the platform.
Lewbel says Flock refers legal demands for ALPR data to the applicable customer—the agency that operates the cameras—and notifies that agency. Flock itself will not disclose the data, Lewbel says, unless required by law and permitted under its contract with the agency.
A spokesperson for SoundThinking, maker of ShotSpotter, says the company complies with subpoenas and court orders regardless of which side issues them, and cooperates with “reasonable requests” for data in criminal proceedings. When a subpoena covers material the company considers confidential, such as its own trade secrets, it asks courts to restrict that material's dissemination.
Epstein is careful to note the ACLU still generally wants this data to quickly disappear. It’s lobbying Massachusetts to cut license plate reader retention to as little as two days, from Flock's default of 30. But once someone is facing charges, he says, that same data can be the evidence that clears them, which is what the preservation motions are designed to protect.
If the approach sounds theoretical, Massachusetts's highest court has recently proven otherwise, twice. In 2024, the state’s Supreme Judicial Court permanently threw out drug and firearm charges against a Boston man—barring prosecutors from ever refiling them—after police defied a court order to turn over records of fake social media profiles that officers used to surveil him, built with predominantly Black and brown avatars. Last year, the same court ruled that defendants can demand a hearing forcing prosecutors to prove ShotSpotter actually works before its evidence reaches a jury. The rulings help explain why the toolkit is built on Massachusetts law, which the ACLU says can be adapted for other states: The state’s high court has run years ahead of the US Supreme Court on digital privacy, requiring warrants for cell phone location data back in 2014.
The ACLU’s timing is not incidental: Three weeks ago, the US Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that when police use a so-called geofence warrant—an order forcing Google to identify virtually all phones near a crime scene—they are conducting a “search” under the Fourth Amendment, triggering the Constitution's privacy protections. The justices sent the case back down for lower courts to work out what a valid geofence warrant looks like. The ACLU’s toolkit will ship a geofencing motion directly into those unsettled waters.
The motions are meant to be adapted and filed in real criminal cases, and the group is asking attorneys who use them to report back. The point, Herrmann says, is to take good lawyering that already exists and put it “at the fingertips of every attorney for every defendant,” while continuing to flag the gaps where new strategies are needed.
Updated at 1:10 pm ET, July 20, 2026: Added comments from Flock Safety and SoundThinking.
Updated at 9:25 am ET, July 22, 2026: WIRED clarified Flock's policy on notifications for legal demands and the timeframe during which mobile phones became mainstream in the US.

49bdd793abdd.text:
Following the sentencing of two young men for the 2024 Transport for London (TfL) hack, senior police officers have argued that the case strengthens the case for Cybercrime Risk Orders (CCROs)—tougher legal powers in the UK.

Owen Flowers, 19, and Thalha Jubair, 20, received five-and-a-half-year prison sentences for unauthorized computer access under Section 3ZA of the Computer Misuse Act 1990. Both are believed to be members of Scattered Spider, a cybercriminal group linked to major attacks including Marks & Spencer and Co-op incidents in 2025.

Paul Foster, deputy director of the UK National Crime Agency, called this "the largest cybercrime prosecution ever brought before the UK courts." The TfL attack cost an estimated £29m in damages and £10m in lost income, disrupting services for 7-10 million people.

Foster emphasized that the investigation "took nearly two years of painstaking work" involving the NCA, Crown Prosecution Service, City of London Police, FBI, Europol, and Australian Federal Police. He noted it surpassed the complexity of Operation Cronos, the 2024 Lockbit takedown.

This marks only the second conviction under Section 3ZA of the Computer Misuse Act, which applies to unauthorized acts causing serious damage.

Foster highlighted challenges prosecutors faced, particularly Flowers' age (17 at arrest) and two bail breaches. He explained that proposed CCROs—civil preventive measures to manage suspected or convicted cybercriminals—would "have allowed us to arrest Flowers sooner."

CCROs would create restrictions on individuals posing cyber threats before prosecution thresholds are met, operating similarly to sexual risk orders. Foster stated they would "provide law enforcement with a proportionate preventative tool" to protect the public and businesses during investigations.

Commander Ollie Shaw of City of London Police advocated for "digital prisons" restricting offenders' access to digital tools, with tech provider partnerships and account monitoring.

Cybersecurity consultant Adam Pilton cautioned about CCROs' effectiveness. He argued that highly skilled offenders could evade monitoring and warned: "Unless the people checking compliance have genuine technical capability, these orders won't be able to achieve what they promise."

Pilton criticized the "digital prison" terminology as "headline-grabbing marketing," noting that determined offenders would find ways to bypass restrictions regardless of supervision levels.

The Computer Misuse Act reform legislation is expected to be introduced in Parliament later in 2026 as part of a broader national security package, with CCROs potentially coming into force in late 2027 or early 2028.

(Author: Kevin Poireault, Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine)

0b0280b6113b.text:
A recent examination of hundreds of mobile apps marketed toward US military personnel found more than one in eight contained software built by companies in China, Russia, or other foreign nations, raising fresh concerns that adversary governments could harvest data revealing where service members live, work, and deploy.
According to researchers at Purdue University, the US Military Academy at West Point, and Florida International University, one popular app used by service members to rate living conditions on their own bases include code from Huawei, the Chinese telecom that US regulators flagged as a national security threat in 2020. Two others were built by Russian companies and incorporate the Russian ad service Yandex.
The largely unregulated advertising industry that tracks Americans online treats civilians and service members mostly the same—unless there is profit in telling them apart—despite evidence that exposure can reveal troop deployments, unit movements, and the routines of personnel within intelligence facilities and hardened shelters where nuclear weapons are believed to be stored.
WIRED investigations have previously shown location data harvested from ordinary apps tracing US service members to their homes, their children's schools, and off-base establishments where troops are prohibited from being seen. Experts have warned the same data could aid foreign spies in identifying personnel with access to sensitive sites, map when a facility is least guarded, or surface other compromising details.
The stakes are no longer hypothetical. In April, US Central Command acknowledged in a letter to Senator Ron Wyden that it had received multiple threat reports of adversaries exploiting commercial location data to target or surveil American personnel in the Middle East, where US forces remain locked in a standoff with the Iranian military over the Strait of Hormuz. Lawmakers called it the first official confirmation that troops in an active war zone were being hunted through the data-broker economy—a threat the Pentagon's own contractors and researchers had warned about for nearly a decade.
The new study takes a first look at one piece of that exposure: what actually sits inside the apps built and marketed specifically for the military.
"We are grateful for the opportunity to bring greater attention to these issues,” says Joshua Shinkle, a Purdue University PhD researcher and the study’s lead author. “We hope the research helps military-affiliated personnel, developers, and platforms make more informed privacy decisions and encourages continued discussion with developers, platforms, and policymakers about how to address these gaps.”
The researchers examined more than 220 such apps—from uniform guides and promotion-exam prep to banking and dating apps—pulled from the Google Play store and military subreddits. Nearly two-thirds—or 64 percent—contained third-party code, known as SDKs: prebuilt software components, typically used for analytics and advertising, that can also track user behavior, including their locations, and share that information with outside companies.
Forty percent of the apps collected or shared more data than they disclosed in their Google or Apple store listings, the researchers found.
The most common SDKs came from Google and Facebook, the two companies that dominate US digital advertising. But 76 turned up in all, including code traced back to China, Russia, Israel, India, Germany, and others. Roughly 7 percent of the apps carried third-party code from a nation considered adversarial by the Pentagon.
Twelve of the apps contained HMS Core, a Huawei software kit that advertises the ability to map user locations, deliver ads, and store images and video. Several were built for state National Guard organizations.
The researchers observed no data actually going to Huawei servers. But an SDK can be updated remotely at any time. Code that is dormant today can still be spyware tomorrow. In at least one case, noted by the study, the Huawei code arrived without the app’s developer’s knowledge, smuggled in as a dependency in a commercial notification tool.
The researchers also surveyed 103 military-affiliated Americans—active-duty service members, reservists, veterans, DoD civilians, and their families—about the data practices they encountered on their own phones. More than 83 percent used at least one app engaging in data practices they said made them uncomfortable. On average, those participants used more than three such apps.
Between 76 and 83 percent of participants said they were extremely uncomfortable with apps containing code from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea—the four nations the Pentagon designates as cyber adversaries. But no user has a straightforward way to know which apps carry such code. Neither Google's Play Store Data Safety section nor Apple's App Store Privacy Labels disclose the country of origin of the software running inside an app.
Participants reported being more comfortable with data collection when an app was branded for military use.
Meanwhile, nearly two-thirds said they had received little or no institutional guidance on personal app use. Of those who had received some, nearly three-quarters called it inadequate.
The Pentagon declined to comment.
Asked to weigh potential mitigations, participants ranked in-phone warnings—alerts when foreign or unknown third-party code is present in an installed app—as both the most effective and the most likely for them to support.
A federal law restricting data brokers from buying or selling data on military-affiliated personnel, independent audits of app privacy disclosures, and stricter bans on foreign code in military-marketed apps drew nearly identical support.

6bbafa2bf964.text:
A heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in 7-Zip could allow attackers to execute code when users open specially crafted XZ archives. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-14266, was detailed by Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative on July 15, with a patch released in 7-Zip version 26.02 on June 25.

The vulnerability stems from improper buffer handling in the XZ decoder. When processing XZ streams with output filters, the decoder received the full output-buffer length on each pass rather than the remaining available space. This created an out-of-bounds write condition. Version 26.02 corrects this by subtracting already-written bytes and terminating if that total exceeds buffer capacity.

The flaw received a CVSS 3.0 score of 7.0 (High severity), with vector AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. The local attack vector requirement means victims must actively open the malicious file—whether delivered via email, download, or webpage. As of the article's publication, no public proof-of-concept or confirmed exploitation existed.

The memory-safety issue appeared in 7-Zip source code dating back to at least version 21.07 (2021). The same codebase contains related flaws patched in April's version 26.01, including the higher-severity CVE-2026-48095 affecting the NTFS handler.

Users should manually update to 7-Zip 26.02 or later, as updates require manual installation from the official website.

(Author: Swati Khandelwal)

8f50d28b7b81.text:
A Russian-speaking threat actor known as "bandcampro" leveraged Google's open-source Gemini CLI artificial intelligence to manage malicious operations, including commanding a live botnet targeting dental clinic computers.

Trend Micro researchers analyzed 200 Gemini CLI session logs spanning March 19 through April 21, 2026. Their findings documented the actor using AI for password cracking, setting up residential proxies, compromising WordPress merchants, and orchestrating a phone-based cryptocurrency fraud targeting elderly Americans and Canadians.

The threat actor deployed AI to migrate a command-and-control server and control a botnet across eight dental clinic PCs. Researchers noted: "The entire C&C operation fits in three plaintext files totaling roughly 5 KB, making it highly replicable and effectively disposable."

The AI proactively suggested improvements 59 times without prompting. The actor contributed only 11% of generated text while the AI produced 89%, with the machine handling 80% of architectural design, 100% of coding, and 90% of problem diagnosis.

During a six-minute infrastructure migration, the AI independently resolved technical errors including fixing 502 gateway errors and identifying required User-Agent headers to bypass Web Application Firewalls.

Researchers warned that this portable skill-file model enables rapid infrastructure replacement, complicating takedown effectiveness and attribution efforts.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan)

3eebfbded3b1.text:
Following Microsoft's October 14, 2025 end-of-support date for Windows 10, significant security challenges persist. While Windows 11 now operates on 78.8% of Windows devices, Windows 10 still runs on 16.9% of machines that no longer receive security patches.

Microsoft offers a paid Extended Security Updates (ESU) program extending support until October 12, 2027, though consumers in the European Economic Area can access free ESU until October 14, 2026 without cloud backup requirements.

Small and medium businesses continue struggling with migration costs, with 21.4% of SMB devices still running Windows 10 compared to 16.6% at large enterprises. Healthcare, pharmaceuticals, retail, and manufacturing sectors face particular challenges due to specialized equipment incompatibility with Windows 11.

The report reveals that "Windows 10 devices carry nearly three times as many active CVEs as Windows 11 systems, averaging 1,903 vulnerabilities per device compared with 652." Approximately 66.6% of these vulnerabilities carry high or critical ratings.

Currently, 40.9% of Windows machines either lack support or will lose it within six months, creating compliance and cyber insurance complications for organizations.

(Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security)

b05323928645.text:
Google has released a Chrome 150 security update that resolves seven memory safety bugs, including critical and high-severity use-after-free vulnerabilities.

The browser refresh patches three critical-severity use-after-free flaws impacting Chrome's CameraCapture, GPU, and Network components. All three weaknesses were discovered by Google.

Additionally, the update fixes three high-severity use-after-free issues in Cast, Ozone, and Aura; Google discovered these vulnerabilities as well.

The seventh security defect is an out-of-bounds read and write flaw in the V8 JavaScript engine that was identified by OpenAI Codex Security. Google has yet to determine the bug bounty amount to be paid for the finding.

Google makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild, but users are advised to update their browsers as soon as possible, as "threat actors have targeted memory safety issues in Chrome."

For years, the internet giant has been hardening the browser against the exploitation of memory safety bugs, including by transitioning to memory-safe programming languages such as Rust.

Since April, the internet giant has patched over 1,400 Chrome vulnerabilities, including hundreds of memory safety flaws, most of which were discovered by Google, likely through the use of AI.

The latest Chrome iteration is now rolling out as versions 150.0.7871.128/.129 for Windows and macOS and as version 150.0.7871.128 for Linux.

(Author: Ionut Arghire)

12b4bb9c8269.text:
In this Help Net Security video, Thom Langford, EMEA CTO at Rapid7, discusses why accumulating additional security alerts reduces SOC response effectiveness.

The presentation highlights how attackers leverage stolen credentials and legitimate tools like PowerShell rather than deploying custom malware. Langford describes an incident where threat actors contacted a help desk, compromised a privileged cloud account, and subsequently exposed thousands of passwords within a three-minute window.

According to the video, ransomware operations can progress from initial access to payload deployment in under three hours. Langford proposes a solution centered on detection engineering, optimized tuning procedures, and artificial intelligence designed to augment human analysts rather than eliminate them.

The discussion emphasizes the importance of comprehensive visibility spanning both cloud and on-premises infrastructure, with success metrics focused on reducing dwell time and accelerating containment velocity. Langford concludes by advocating for managed detection and response services, where security professionals function as team extensions—revoking sessions, blocking access pathways, and containing threats expeditiously.

d52a10bec70d.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have identified a software supply chain attack targeting the Ruby ecosystem, using three malicious gems published to RubyGems to deliver additional payloads.

The attack involved three rogue gems: git_credential_manager (versions 2.8.0-2.8.3), published July 18, 2026; Dendreo (versions 1.1.3-1.1.4), published October 14, 2017; and fastlane-plugin-run_tests_firebase_testlab (version 0.3.2), published February 6, 2018.

According to StepSecurity analysis, "Each malicious release is a loader" that fetches second-stage payloads from an attacker-controlled Forgejo host, detecting whether it runs in build systems and skipping execution if detected.

The git_credential_manager package impersonates Microsoft's official tool, while the other two had remained dormant for years before receiving malicious updates. Notably, releases were published directly to the registry without matching commits or tags in source projects.

The git_credential_manager was added as a dependency to five packages, including Dendreo and fastlane-plugin, spreading the malicious code to existing users. Most packages (except fastlane-plugin) were maintained by the same account, suggesting multiple account compromises.

The embedded malware scans systems for approximately 30 environment variables related to CI/CD platforms (GitHub Actions, GitLab, CircleCI, Travis, Jenkins, Vercel). If detected, it exits—an intentional evasion mechanism targeting developer machines rather than ephemeral CI runners.

For git_credential_manager, malicious code downloads two payloads from a public Forgejo instance: a shell script and a native binary. Version 2.8.3 escalates the attack by launching the binary as a background daemon, establishing persistence through cron entries and systemd services.

If the user can run sudo without a password, the script re-executes as root, planting a setuid root shell copy at a path mimicking a networking utility.

Users who installed these gems should treat their machines and associated secrets as compromised. Recommended actions include removing the daemon at ~/.local/share/gcm/, erasing persistence mechanisms, checking for setuid shells at /usr/local/sbin/ping6, and rotating all credentials.

This attack reflects a broader pattern of RubyGems exploitation. In May 2026, RubyGems temporarily suspended new signups following coordinated spam campaigns. Recent incidents also included gems abused for data exfiltration and credential theft via browser extensions.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan)

8dfb2f7dd7ed.text:
Developers lean on AI coding assistants for a growing share of their daily work, letting the tools predict the next few lines and accepting many suggestions with a quick glance. Those tools learn from large collections of code, and some of that code can be tampered with before training starts. A poisoned example teaches a model to write insecure code when it sees a certain cue, and the flaw sits quietly until the right prompt sets it off.

Most defenses aim to catch this poisoning early, screening training data or scanning outputs for known problems. A team from the University of Louisville and the University of North Texas built a system called CodeTracer for the moment after those defenses let something slip. Their work starts from a model that has already produced a harmful completion. The job is to trace that completion back to the training examples that taught the behavior.

The researchers built the method for a setting that matches how large fine-tuning pipelines run in practice. Gradients from training are gone by the time anyone looks. The people running the check know only the fine-tuning corpus and the report of the bad completion, which includes the prompt and the code the model produced. A question guides the work: "Who planted the bug?"

CodeTracer runs in three stages. First it reads the harmful completion and builds a structured summary of the unsafe behavior, stripping away surface details like variable names. Second it searches the training data for code that carries the same underlying logic, narrowing a huge pool of files down to a small candidate set. Third it asks a language model to weigh each candidate against the summary and decide whether it holds the same unsafe pattern.

The default build uses GPT-4.1 for the reading and judging steps and a code encoder called UniXcoder for the search. The narrowing stage keeps the top 500 candidates, a slice small enough to review one at a time.

The evaluation drew on more than a million Python source files pulled from GitHub repositories that each carried at least a hundred stars. A small number of poisoned examples went into that pool for the test.

Three unsafe patterns sat at the center of the study: rendering templates with untrusted input, disabling certificate checks in web requests, and binding a network service to every interface on a machine.

Across a range of backdoor attacks and a field of competing methods, CodeTracer kept its false negative rate below 0.03, missing very few of the planted examples. Removing the files it traced drove the attack success rate close to zero.

The method ran in about 47 seconds per case, quicker than several of the tools measured beside it, and cost roughly a third of a dollar per completion. It held its accuracy on a much larger pool of eight million benign files, where spotting a few poisoned examples grows harder.

Two attacks went after CodeTracer itself. One padded malicious functions with filler code to hide them from the search. Another slipped comments into the code to steer the language model's judgment. Its miss rate stayed at a few percent under both.

The three unsafe patterns at the center of the study show up often in ordinary, benign code. A low false positive rate carries weight only when the benign test set includes code that resembles the poisoned kind. The pipeline leans on one model family for two of its three stages, with GPT-4.1 both writing the behavior summary and grading the candidates.

Post-incident attribution for poisoned code models has had few serious attempts, and CodeTracer gives a working option that runs cheaply and survives direct attacks in these tests. The researchers want to take the idea to AI agents next, where the trail runs longer and colder.

(Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security)

1452fd567436.text:
ZoneAlarm Mobile Security is a Check Point-developed app protecting mobile devices across iPhone, iPad, Android, and Apple silicon Macs. The application addresses threats including phishing, malicious websites, unsafe networks, and fraudulent links.

The onboarding requires notification permissions and Safari extension activation. The app conducts device configuration checks, OS status verification, SMS phishing protection assessment, and phone tampering detection.

The link scanning capability allows users to "paste a URL or scan a QR code before opening it." Each scan provides risk level verdicts, website categorization, and options to open, report, or dismiss results.

The system enables "blocking websites by category" with options including Security, Inappropriate Content, Streaming and File Sharing, Social and Gaming, and General Web Content. Users can customize subcategories within each group.

Features include encryption integrity monitoring, Wi-Fi encryption analysis, background security monitoring, and Wi-Fi Network Advisor functionality.

The reviewer highlights the application's "well-organized interface, phishing and link protection, and comprehensive content filtering system" as strengths for users seeking enhanced mobile security measures.

(Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security)
