Gartner's CTEM framework identifies five stages: scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, and mobilization. The first four now operate at machine speed, but mobilization remains stuck at organizational speed.

The core problem: security teams identify exposures while separate teams with different priorities, change windows, and approval chains must execute fixes. This handoff represents 'the soft underbelly of most CTEM programs.'

High and critical application vulnerabilities take an average of 55 days to remediate, with nearly half of enterprise vulnerabilities remaining unpatched after a full year. Legacy systems and production infrastructure complicate faster responses due to business impact concerns.

AI-driven discovery forces proactive security teams-traditionally measuring success through patch coverage-to adopt reactive-side metrics: dwell time, response speed, and containment velocity. Since no organization can eliminate all exposures at attacker speeds, focus must shift to attack paths connecting exploitable vulnerabilities to critical assets.

The blast radius-reachable assets from exploitable exposures-determines actual business risk. Attack path analysis identifies dangerous exposure routes while filtering dead-ends, narrowing mobilization scope from an impossible backlog to finite, prioritized paths.

d292e02fec4b.text:
Author: Ionut Arghire. Published: July 21, 2026 (7:12 AM ET).

Estée Lauder has notified employees that their personal information was compromised during a cyberattack on its Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS) system in August 2025. The breach occurred when the Cl0p cybercrime group exploited CVE-2025-61882, an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Oracle EBS.

The company's investigation determined in June 2026 that compromised data included 'names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, passport numbers, bank account numbers, health information, and employment-related data, including payroll information.' The EBS instance was used for HR management purposes.

The incident affected over 100 companies, with Cl0p leaking approximately 870GB of files allegedly stolen from Estée Lauder. The vulnerability was exploited starting August 9, 2025, according to CrowdStrike evidence, and was patched in early October 2025.

In response, Estée Lauder is providing affected individuals with 24 months of complimentary identity monitoring services and has notified law enforcement. The company has also implemented improved system protections. However, Estée Lauder has not publicly disclosed the number of potentially impacted individuals.

81d3de9dc988.text:
Author: Zeljka Zorz, Editor-in-Chief. Published: July 21, 2026.

Two SonicWall SMA 1000 vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) were actively exploited in zero-day attacks beginning June 22, 2026, weeks before public disclosure, according to Volexity researchers. Attackers gained the ability to 'install custom malware on vulnerable VPN appliances' and accessed cached credentials while capturing network traffic.

Attack Methodology: (1) Initial Access - attackers leveraged CVE-2026-15409 (an SSRF vulnerability) to tunnel from the internet to internal services, exposing a bundled CouchDB database with default 'admin:admin' credentials. (2) Privilege Escalation - they exploited hardcoded database access to reach vulnerable command injection endpoints, then deployed CVE-2026-15410 to execute arbitrary OS commands with root privileges. (3) Persistence - the group installed ROOTRUN (privilege escalation tool) and KNUCKLEBALL (Python loader), which injected malicious Java components into legitimate processes, including Suo5 (open-source proxy) and ORANGETAIL (custom web shell).

Defensive Recommendations: Security teams should patch immediately, re-image affected appliances, reset credentials and TOTP tokens, and review logs for compromise indicators. Volexity provided YARA signatures and indicators focusing on unexpected connections, suspicious files in /var/tmp and /tmp, modified nginx configurations, and unusual setuid binaries.

7d00acdf3cc9.text: The Qilin ransomware gang is actively exploiting a critical PAN-OS GlobalProtect authentication bypass vulnerability to infiltrate corporate networks, according to cybersecurity firm Arctic Wolf. Palo Alto Networks patched the flaw (CVE-2026-0257) on May 13 after Rapid7 documented exploitation attempts beginning May 17. The vulnerability enables attackers to bypass security restrictions and establish an unauthorized VPN connection without valid credentials. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-0257 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on May 29, mandating federal agencies remediate within three days. Arctic Wolf Labs documented multiple intrusions in June 2026 where threat actors leveraged this flaw against Palo Alto firewalls, resulting in Qilin ransomware deployment. The investigation revealed evidence points to multiple Qilin affiliates actively exploiting this flaw, with post-exploitation tactics varying from encryption-only operations to double-extortion schemes. The company assessed with moderate confidence that exploitation remains ongoing, citing extensive scanning activity and the ransomware-as-a-service model's tendency to distribute successful exploits among affiliates. Shadowserver tracks over 167,000 exposed GlobalProtect instances globally, while Shodan identified more than 172,000 IPs with GlobalProtect fingerprints, though patch status for these systems remains unknown. Qilin, which emerged as 'Agenda' in August 2022, operates as a RaaS platform claiming over 2,000 victims including Nissan, Asahi, Synnovis, and Lee Enterprises. (By Sergiu Gatlan, published July 21, 2026.)

b13f86017ece.text: Attackers have begun exploiting two critical vulnerabilities in WordPress that combine to enable unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and complete compromise of vulnerable websites. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, have been codenamed wp2shell. According to Jake Knott, principal security researcher at watchTowr, by the early hours of Saturday morning (UTC), successful exploitation was already well underway, initially using public exploit code to exfiltrate hashed credentials, with remote code execution following once additional details were made public. Telemetry data from KEVIntel shows 13 unique IP addresses from Switzerland, Germany, the U.K., Indonesia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, and Singapore have been linked to CVE-2026-63030 exploitation. Ryan Dewhurst, KEVIntel founder and CEO, noted attackers used multiple SQL injection techniques, including blind, UNION-based and Boolean-based payloads, and that AI-assisted analysis made reproducing the vulnerability and developing a working proof of concept trivial. The exploit chain was discovered by Searchlight Cyber using OpenAI GPT 5.6 Sol; the attack has no preconditions and can be exploited by an anonymous user in a stock install of WordPress with no plugins. Ben Marr of Intruder explained CVE-2026-63030 is a route confusion bug in the REST API batch endpoint that bypasses authentication. Cloudflare notes the RCE only triggers when persistent object cache is not in use; the SQL injection affects versions from 6.8 onward, the RCE from 6.9. Wiz reported 60% of organizations using WordPress initially had at least one vulnerable instance, with 25% exposing a vulnerable server to the internet. Observed post-exploitation includes uploading malicious plugins, harvesting admin credentials, LFI attacks against database credentials, and uploading PHP web shells. A 150KB web shell disguised as a plugin called CMSmap was identified as a full-featured attack platform. More than 100 backdoor admin accounts were created, with at least one case showing repeated attempts to install Overlord RAT, a Golang-based RAT. Defenders are advised to inspect for new admin accounts, malicious plugins, or suspicious files regardless of patch status. (By Ravie Lakshmanan, published July 21, 2026.)

4b098c478f1a.text: A critical remote code execution vulnerability recently patched in the ServiceNow AI platform is reportedly being exploited in the wild. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6875, has been described as a sandbox escape issue that unauthenticated attackers can exploit under certain circumstances to execute arbitrary code. ServiceNow announced patch availability on July 14, deploying security updates to hosted instances; self-hosted customers must install patches themselves. On the same day, cybersecurity firm Searchlight Cyber disclosed technical details and demonstrated exploitation methods. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported on July 18 observing in-the-wild exploitation leveraging Searchlight Cyber's released information. Defused initially indicated the exploit used a slightly different method than Searchlight's proof-of-concept, but later corrected this, determining the captured payload was actually identical. ServiceNow stated it has not observed evidence that this activity is related to instances that ServiceNow hosts, and encouraged both self-hosted and ServiceNow-hosted customers to apply relevant patches. No additional reports describing CVE-2026-6875 exploitation have emerged, suggesting the activity may involve cybersecurity industry members testing vulnerable systems. ServiceNow noted that vulnerabilities in their platform are uncommonly exploited by threat actors, with CISA's KEV catalog currently listing only two ServiceNow flaws, both patched in 2024. (By Eduard Kovacs, published July 21, 2026, 4:41 AM ET.)

37b677337463.text: A maintainer patches a library late at night that ships inside thousands of products, and no invoice follows. Sebastián Ramírez and Caleb Porzio spent years in that position. That gap carries a cost: critical projects lose their maintainers to salaried jobs elsewhere, security fixes slow down, and the software supply chain that companies ship on grows brittle. GitHub Sponsors has now moved more than $100 million to open source maintainers and projects. GitHub opened Sponsors in 2019 so any developer could pay the maintainers they leaned on; the program now supports over 70,000 maintainers and organizations, with a sponsor base past a quarter of a million. The first tranche of funding took nearly two years to gather; the latest stretch of the same size took five months. Organizations account for nearly 40% of sponsorship funding and that share keeps growing; each organization-funded sponsorship runs nearly 15 times the average individual one. Shopify began funding its dependencies at scale, and the program later added bulk sponsorships and invoice payments, more regions, and a Patreon partnership. Caleb Porzio said sponsorships allowed him to quit his job and work on his projects full time; Sebastián Ramírez routes some of his sponsorship money to sub-sponsor other open source tools. Mercedes-Benz Tech Innovation also funds maintainers through the program. Despite the milestone, the funding shortfall for open source stays large, with many critical projects still run on evenings and weekends and burnout continuing to pull maintainers away from code that companies depend on. (By Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security, published July 21, 2026.)

30845633f499.text: A recently disclosed Windows zero-day vulnerability called LegacyHive (CVE-2026-62832) allows non-administrative users to escalate privileges on updated Windows systems. The flaw was discovered by a security researcher operating under the handle Nightmare Eclipse and affects the Windows User Profile Service. The vulnerability enables attackers to mount other users' registry hives with full access, potentially extracting stored secrets or modifying registry values to execute malicious code when an administrator logs in. According to ACROS Security CEO Mitja Kolsek, the exploit works by allowing a regular non-admin user to mount any other user's registry hive in full access mode. Before Microsoft released official patches, ACROS Security, developer of the 0Patch platform, made free micropatches available for Windows 10 2004 and later, plus Windows Server 2022 and later, deployable via the 0patch agent without requiring restarts. Microsoft confirmed awareness of the vulnerability and stated it was actively investigating the claims and committed to updating impacted products to protect customers as soon as possible. Nightmare Eclipse has disclosed multiple zero-day exploits recently, including RoguePlanet, BlueHammer, and RedSun vulnerabilities affecting Microsoft Defender and Windows components. (By Sergiu Gatlan, published July 21, 2026.)

7ffd17f34907.text: Researchers at Sysdig have linked a second attack on the same Langflow server to JADEPUFFER, the AI-agent-driven operator documented earlier this month. The same operator has now deployed ENCFORGE, a new compiled Go ransomware designed to encrypt model weights, vector indexes, training datasets, and other AI infrastructure files across the host filesystem. The entry point remains unchanged: Langflow versions before 1.3.0 expose the /api/v1/validate/code endpoint without authentication, allowing remote attackers to execute arbitrary Python on the server (CVE-2025-3248, CVSS 9.8, in CISA's KEV catalog since May 5, 2025). The binary, retrieved from the attacker's C2 server hidden as /.lockd, is a UPX-packed static Go 1.22.12 ELF binary with zero threat-intel detections at analysis time. Its default extension list covers PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face SafeTensors, ONNX, GGUF/GGML, FAISS indexes, Parquet/Arrow datasets, NumPy arrays, and TFRecords, about 180 extensions total. ENCFORGE uses AES-256-CTR with an embedded RSA-2048 wrapped key, encrypting selected regions rather than whole files for speed, similar to LockBit and BlackCat. It kills processes holding files open, handles restarts without re-encrypting, drops ransom notes, and self-deletes after running. The recovered binary contains no networking, cloud storage client, or staging mechanism, and researchers found no evidence of exfiltration, a leak site, or payment portal; its only leverage is encrypted data. The extortion contact matches the prior JADEPUFFER campaign's Proton Mail address, the strongest attribution link between the two operations. After gaining code execution, the operator found the Docker socket, iterated through six Python scripts over about five minutes to reach the host, then used the Docker API to spin up a privileged container with host PID namespace and root filesystem mounted, copying and running ENCFORGE on the host via nsenter. Researchers estimate rebuilding a production AI model post-encryption could cost $75,000-$500,000 and recommend upgrading Langflow to 1.9.1+, rotating credentials, removing unneeded Docker socket access, alerting on privileged container creation, and keeping model artifacts in offline/immutable snapshots. (By Swati Khandelwal, published July 21, 2026.)

f3503e27d73e.text: Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-6875, a critical sandbox escape vulnerability affecting ServiceNow's AI Platform. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.5 and permits unauthenticated users to execute arbitrary code. According to threat intelligence firm Defused Cyber, exploitation efforts target the pre-authentication endpoint '/assessment_thanks.do' using HTTP POST requests. The vulnerability enables a complete compromise of ServiceNow instances and all connected proxy servers. ServiceNow released patches throughout June across multiple versions: Brazil EA and Brazil GA, Australia Patch 2, Zurich Patch 7b and Patch 9, and Yokohama Patch 12 Hot Fix 1b and Patch 13. Security researcher Adam Kues noted that ServiceNow is enhancing instance security by severely restricting the type of code that can run in sandbox contexts. Searchlight Cyber, which disclosed technical details, reported the issue on April 1, 2026. Defused initially noted exploitation attempts but later issued a correction, stating captured payloads matched Searchlight Cyber's proof-of-concept exploit. Update: following publication, a ServiceNow spokesperson stated they have not observed evidence that this activity is related to instances that ServiceNow hosts, and the company encourages customers to apply patches if not already deployed. (By Ravie Lakshmanan, published July 21, 2026.)

44b9df5a6eaf.text: Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse (aka Nightmare-Eclipse) has released a new proof-of-concept exploit called LegacyHive, a Windows User Profile Service arbitrary hive load elevation-of-privileges vulnerability. The PoC requires a second standard user's credentials and a third username (which can be an administrator account); if successful it mounts the target user's hive in the current user's classes root. The researcher stripped down the exploit to prevent public exploitation, noting the original was not limited to the usrclass.dat hive. The exploit works on all supported desktop and server Windows versions, including the latest July 2026 Patch Tuesday update. Chaotic Eclipse and Microsoft have been in dispute since at least April 2026, with the researcher releasing exploit details before patching, citing communication breakdown; three Microsoft Defender vulnerabilities came under active exploitation shortly after disclosure. Separately, Microsoft shipped patches for a record 622 flaws in July 2026 Patch Tuesday, including two actively-exploited privilege-escalation flaws in SharePoint Server (CVE-2026-56164) and Active Directory Federation Services (CVE-2026-56155), both added to CISA's KEV catalog with remediation deadlines of July 17 and July 28. CISA also flagged awareness of active exploitation of SharePoint flaws CVE-2026-32201 and CVE-2026-45659. Security researchers Kevin Beaumont, Will Dormann, ThreatLocker, and Cyderes' Howler Cell confirmed LegacyHive works and remains unpatched, describing how it chains offline registry hive modification, Object Manager symbolic link redirection, and a synchronized profile load. With LegacyHive, Chaotic Eclipse has released nine Windows exploits without coordinated disclosure in three months: BlueHammer, UnDefend, RedSun, RoguePlanet, YellowKey, GreatXML, GreenPlasma, and MiniPlasma. On July 20, 2026, 0patch released free micropatches for LegacyHive. (By Ravie Lakshmanan, published July 15, 2026.)

dffca0c74dda.text: Körber AG is the holding company of a diverse German technology and manufacturing organization with around 13,000 employees in 100 locations around the world. Andreas Gaetje is the CISO at Körber AG. He never planned a cybersecurity career, starting instead in economics and business politics before moving into IT via a consulting firm and then an insurance company as an auditor in the early 2000s, where ITsec and audit had a natural affinity focused on compliance. By the 2010s, large-scale attacks like WannaCry and NotPetya reframed cybersecurity as a serious business threat rather than a compliance issue. He became CISO at Körber IT Solutions in 2018 and CISO at Körber AG in 2019. His career advice: don't stay too long in a single company or industry sector, since different sectors carry different risk profiles and staying too long can leave your thinking stuck while attackers evolve. On leadership, he says it is a learnable skill built on trust and reliability rather than innate charisma. On hiring, he requires a desire to learn above all, and would hire white-hat but not black-hat hackers. His biggest current concern is the sheer pace of new technology, especially AI, which both attackers and defenders are using, with shadow AI proliferating. He believes the CISO role will become more important, not less, as AI's growth creates problems too broad for security teams alone to handle, requiring closer integration with product and development teams. He also worries that AI coding assistants and agentic SOC triage could erode junior staff's ability to build foundational analytical and programming skills over time. (By Kevin Townsend, published July 21, 2026, 7:30 AM ET.)

bbb9b810e64e.text: MIT is installing over 500 AI-enabled surveillance cameras across academic buildings, residence halls, and outdoor areas along Memorial Drive, with installation beginning in November 2025 and continuing through September 2026. The total investment exceeds $3 million. The cameras, primarily from Hanwha's Wisenet AI line, feature sophisticated capabilities: real-time face and object classification, detecting motion, loitering, crowds, and face masks, with people automatically classified by clothing color, gender, and age from up to 35 feet away, using Ai-RGUS software for continuous monitoring. MIT spokesperson Kimberly Allen stated collected data is retained up to 30 days, with exceptions possible. The cameras support resolutions from 2MP to 4K and can recognize faces, license plates, and vehicles in real time. The initiative coincides with MIT facing substantial budget cuts from federal actions, including hiring freezes, salary freezes, and library closures. Schneier's response to the announcement was simply: 'Yikes.' The comments section features debate about whether such surveillance actually prevents crime or merely documents it after the fact, with one security professional noting these capabilities are now standard across major manufacturers. (By Bruce Schneier, published July 21, 2026.)

80900385d4ca.text: The U.S. Justice Department has seized more than 1,000 websites and blocked 1,970 domains used to stream FIFA World Cup 2026 matches without authorization. Law enforcement authorities identified the seized domains using leads provided by U.S. authorities, FIFA, the Motion Picture Association's Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE), and multiple entertainment networks, including beIN Media Group, NBCUniversal, UFC, and Warner Bros. These seizures are part of Operation Offsides, a joint law enforcement action led by the IPR Center in coordination with HSI Washington and involving 14 partners across 54 countries, including nearly 400 web domains seized by the end of last month. Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said Operation Offsides is part of the Department's ongoing effort to protect copyright while reducing risk to American consumers from malicious software embedded in many illicit streaming services. HSI Special Agent in Charge Eric Weindorf added that these streamers not only violate copyright laws but also expose viewers to potential threats, including malware attacks and unsecure connections that can compromise personal and financial data. In coordination with the DOJ's International Computer Hacking and Intellectual Property program, authorities also carried out Operation Red Card, blocking hundreds of illegal streaming sites in Argentina, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and Colombia. A second phase launched July 10 in Colombia led to the arrest of four members of the Los Ciberinfiltrados cybercriminal group. The announcement follows a May FBI warning about fake FIFA ticket sites, and in June Mexican authorities shut down 44 domains linked to the PirloTV streaming platform. (By Sergiu Gatlan, published July 21, 2026.)

01a000177725.text: Shufti has launched the Shufti Glocal Platform, a compliance lifecycle management solution designed to help organizations manage identity verification, fraud prevention, risk assessment, and regulatory compliance through a single platform across every industry, region, and use case. For decades, global expansion has required companies to adopt different compliance providers for each new market; solutions built for one region often lack support for another region's regulations, document types, verification methods, or risk profiles, forcing businesses to combine multiple vendors, platforms, and workflows. This fragmented approach creates challenges including separate APIs, multiple contracts, different infrastructure, and separate billing. The Glocal Platform addresses this by providing one shared global infrastructure that adapts to each organization's compliance strategy, customer journey, and operational needs, supporting the entire customer lifecycle from sign-up and KYC through authentication, AML screening, ongoing monitoring, and remediation. According to CEO Shahid Hanif, after working with 2,000+ organizations worldwide, the same challenge kept appearing: businesses needed compliance technology that could adapt as they grew. Shufti supports identity verification across 240+ countries and territories, processing 10,000+ document types in 150+ languages with 99.7% OCR accuracy, including non-Latin scripts such as Arabic, Devanagari, Chinese, and Japanese. (Published July 21, 2026.)

acdb4beeb1bb.text: Scammers are impersonating FBI personnel who supposedly handle Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) complaints, using that disguise to deceive and revictimize people who already lost money once. The IC3 published the update on July 20, 2026, building on an earlier alert from April 2025; since then scammers have picked up new tricks, including AI-generated video of FBI officials and spoofed versions of the IC3 website itself. The FBI said complainants report scammers use a variety of methods to initiate contact, including email, phone calls, being approached directly, or seeing an advertisement via social media or forums. In one scheme, a victim who tells fraudsters they plan to file an IC3 complaint is soon contacted by someone claiming to be an FBI agent on Facebook Messenger, who moves the conversation to Telegram and sends a link asking the victim to 'update' their IC3 report; the agency warns the link may contain malicious code or collect more financial data to revictimize the person. In a second scheme, scammers circulate deepfake video clips of a senior FBI official urging people to file complaints through what looks like the official IC3 site; the fake page mimics ic3.gov's design but only accepts a single-step complaint form (name, phone, email, scam type, estimated loss), with every other link looping back to the home screen, after which victims receive a reference number and a promise of follow-up. The FBI points out that IC3 has no social media presence, never initiates contact by phone, email, or chat app, and never asks for payment to recover lost funds, advising people to type www.ic3.gov directly into the browser, skip sponsored search results, and confirm the domain ends in .gov. The FBI also shared advice for spotting deepfakes, such as distorted hands or facial features, mismatched shadows, lag in voice calls, and unnatural movement, urging people to verify surprising videos through reputable news sources or known official channels. (By Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security, published July 21, 2026.)

9cf9cd1c65c6.text: Independent security researcher Rony K Roy discovered a critical vulnerability in Meta's support infrastructure and received a $78,000 bug bounty from the company. Roy initially reported the flaw to Meta in January 2026, believing he had identified an authorization issue in Meta Horizon Managed Solutions, an enterprise platform for managing Meta Quest devices. Further analysis revealed the vulnerability was actually broader, affecting Meta's backend support infrastructure. The researcher's investigation uncovered vulnerabilities involving missing authorization, broken access control, and insecure direct object reference (IDOR) issues; when chained, these flaws could have been exploited to enumerate Meta support case numbers and obtain support requests. An attacker exploiting this vulnerability could have accessed email and chat conversations between users and Meta support, obtained support case details and submitted files, and accessed personal and contact information. Additionally, attackers could have created support requests on behalf of organizations using Meta Horizon Managed Solutions, modified support workflows, and added unauthorized subscribers to support cases. Meta patched the vulnerability in April 2026 and found no evidence of malicious exploitation. Roy disclosed his findings publicly last week and is listed among the top researchers on Meta's 2026 bug bounty leaderboard. Meta has not responded to confirm Roy's claims. (By Eduard Kovacs, published July 21, 2026, 6:19 AM ET.)

66e63d5d0a8d.text:
As modern cars have evolved into multi-ton computers on wheels, drivers are beginning to learn they need to install security updates for their vehicles' code, just as they would for a phone or laptop. Yet not even the most tech-savvy car owners would expect they'd need to install a patch for an insecure third-party component they never installed or requested—and likely aren't even aware of—that's been wired into some of the most sensitive systems of their vehicle, leaving it vulnerable to stealthy hacking, tracking, and even roadside paralysis.
That's the disturbing discovery of a team of security researchers at UC San Diego, who found that a model of aftermarket car alarm known as the KARR Security System, installed in more than 2 million vehicles across the US by their estimate, can let any hacker within Bluetooth range send radio commands to silently unlock the car at will, turn off its alarm, honk the car's horn or flash its lights, or even disable its ignition and leave a driver stranded.
The KARR alarm devices are typically installed by car dealers, not manufacturers or owners, and used as a measure to prevent auto theft from dealer lots. Yet when the cars are sold, the alarms typically aren't removed, even if the buyer declines to pay for it as an additional feature. That means car owners across the US have a hackable device under their hood whose code they'll need to update to protect their vehicle—but one that, in many cases, they never purchased and have no idea is there.
"This is a system added to cars by dealers, and unfortunately it has a severe vulnerability that allows anyone to gain access to any of these cars," says Aaron Schulman, the UCSD computer science professor who led the research. “It's designed to make cars more secure, but ultimately it's created a vulnerability that needs to be patched immediately across millions vehicles. We're trying to get the word out that you need to check your car for this device and manually patch it now.”
The company that sells the KARR Security System, Acrisure Protection Group, on Monday rolled out a firmware update for the vulnerable Bluetooth model of its aftermarket KARR alarm to fix the security issues UCSD uncovered. Car owners who already have the KARR Security smartphone app installed should receive an alert about the firmware update, the UCSD team says. Those who don’t have it installed will need to download the KARR Security System smartphone app (Android, iOS), connect it to their vehicle's KARR alarm, then tap “customer service” and “firmware update.”
Given that at least half of car owners who have the KARR device installed didn't ask for it to be in their vehicles, according to UCSD's estimate, you can check if your car has the device by looking for a KARR sticker on your car's driver-side window—or in some cases a sticker reading, “SWDS” for SouthWest Dealer Services, a subsidiary of Acrisure Protection Group—as well as a small button with a blinking light attached to the underside of your car's dashboard. Car owners in Southern California are most likely to have the device installed due to its popularity among car dealers in the region, but the UCSD researchers warn that they've found the devices installed in vehicles across the US and even in other countries.
That difficulty of getting word out to affected drivers, combined with the significant risk that the vulnerability could be used for theft, makes the KARR's security flaw “probably the worst” car hacking threat ever discovered, says Stefan Savage, another UCSD computer science professor who didn't work on the KARR alarm findings but did co-lead the first team to hack a car's steering and brakes in 2010 and 2011. “It affects a large number of vehicles, the manufacturer of your car can't fix it, and you don't even know you have the problem,” says Savage. “It provides all the elements a car thief would want, but you have none of the advantages we normally have in terms of defending it, because you're disconnected from the supply chain that put it there.”
Carjacking, Sabotage, and “Mayhem”
When WIRED reached out to Acrisure Protection Group about the KARR security flaw, a spokesperson responded in a statement: “The vulnerability described in [UCSD's] research is highly complex and presents a low risk to customers under real-world conditions. Nevertheless, we responded promptly and developed a firmware update to address the issue.”
The company added that it will be alerting car owners to its patch via the KARR Security app, the KARR Security website, and via “dealer communications." It didn't share more about how it will reach car owners who aren't aware that they have the device installed, including owners of affected vehicles that may have even been resold to drivers who can't be reached by dealerships.
Despite Acrisure Protection Group's claim to have patched the flaw “promptly," it actually took close to 18 months to push out its patch. The UCSD researchers told the company about the vulnerability in January of last year, but the company didn't offer a fix until just weeks ahead of UCSD's planned presentations about its findings at the Defcon hacker conference and the Usenix security conference next month.
Acrisure's claim that the vulnerability represents a “low risk” under “real-world conditions" also merits some skepticism. In a series of demos for WIRED, all captured in the video above, the researchers showed that they could use their own Android app to send Bluetooth commands to vulnerable vehicles with KARR installed to carry out a wide array of potentially disruptive or dangerous hacking. The demo exploits can, with the tap of a button, unlock a car at a stop light to enable theft or carjacking, instantly paralyze a parked car to prevent it from starting, or even—with a “mayhem” button they built into the app—hack a group of cars to simultaneously and repeatedly trigger their horns and lights, as the researchers demonstrated for WIRED in a UCSD parking lot.
The KARR Security System's vulnerabilities do not, fortunately, allow a hacker to start a car's ignition. But the UCSD researchers showed how a locksmith tool commonly available for resale online can, once a car thief is inside the vehicle, be plugged into a car's dash to create a working key within a few minutes and drive it away. Car thieves using that device would typically have to break a window or use car-door opening tools, potentially setting off a car alarm. But combined with the KARR vulnerability, they can stealthily get into the vehicle to carry out that theft technique.
The security flaw that makes all of those sabotage and intrusion tricks possible, the UCSD team found, is a single authentication key shared across all KARR devices. The UCSD researchers also spotted that key in the code of the KARR smartphone app, which customers who pay for the alarm can use to control it. With that key and a homemade app they created by reverse engineering the KARR app's code, they found they could spoof radio commands that would be accepted by any nearby Bluetooth-enabled KARR device.
The KARR device's insecurity is compounded by the fact that, even when a car buyer declines to pay for it as an add-on, it stays in the vehicle and continues to both beacon out and accept Bluetooth signals whenever the car is on, and also for as long as 10 minutes after the car is turned off. Though the KARR device is in a "deactivated" state for those drivers, the researchers found they could activate it with a radio command and then immediately carry out their menu of hacking techniques.
That activation does trigger a quick beep from the car's horn and a flicker of its lights, the only sign a car owner might have that someone has put their car into a hackable state. For the hundreds of thousands of KARR customers who did pay a dealer to enable the alarm system, they would receive no such warning.
Highways of Hackable Cars
A UCSD researcher, Nishant Bhaskar, first became aware of the KARR devices in 2018, while doing analysis of radio-enabled “skimmer” devices designed to steal credit card information from gas station point-of-sale terminals. He began to pick up Bluetooth signals from mysterious devices at the gas stations, and then soon realized that he was seeing the same radio signals on the highway from vehicles of all makes and models. That's when he began to search online for the text-based prefixes of those Bluetooth signals and saw in a Federal Communications Commission database that they came from the KARR alarm device.
Only years later, when then graduate researcher Jerry Yu was looking for a summer project in 2024, did Schulman suggest he take a look at the security of the KARR device whose signals Bhaskar had spotted. Yu quickly found the KARR app's universal authentication key, a glaring security flaw. “Once we reverse-engineered their application, we quickly realized after understanding their internal authentication protocol that it was so simple that we could extract it and re-implement it as our own application, which we did," Yu says. That app could, they discovered, unlock “every single car they've ever put this in.”
To get a count of how many vulnerable KARR devices are out there, UCSD researcher Yibo Wei used the open-source radio information database WiGLE, which crowdsources radio signals that contributors pick up with antennas all over the US and the world. He estimated as a result of those scans and extrapolating from the serial numbers of the devices that more than 2 million of the Bluetooth-enabled KARR devices have been deployed.
Those WiGLE results are, however, more than just a measurement tool. They also potentially allow a hacker to track the historical locations of vulnerable cars based on their KARR device's Bluetooth signature and find places where the vehicle is frequently parked—a disturbingly easy scouting mechanism for finding opportunities to hack them for theft or sabotage.
In the UCSD team’s own scanning, they also found KARR-enabled vehicles virtually everywhere they looked. At one point, the researchers took me for a short drive around the outskirts of the university's campus while using their app on a normal Android phone to scan for cars with beaconing KARR devices. They found 97 vehicles with the alarms in just 20 minutes.
Schulman and his team now feel a responsibility to warn every one of those drivers about the hidden, hackable gadget in the guts of their vehicle. "When you install something by default at a dealer in every car that's sold, the pervasiveness of that vulnerability is going to be unimaginable," he says. “This is why we need to publicize this and get it out there, because the only way this will eventually get solved is if we get everyone on board and to fix it themselves.”
Update: 7/21/2026, 11:42 AM EDT: WIRED clarified when the patch was introduced.

7ab5d7e7fc3a.text: Ukraine's computer emergency response team, CERT-UA, has warned that Russian hackers are using fake CAPTCHA checks to trick people into compromising their own PCs. The Kremlin-backed Sandworm hacking group is reportedly leveraging fake CAPTCHA checks on compromised websites that persuade users to execute a PowerShell command on their computers - tricking them into running malicious code. CERT-UA has attributed the attacks, which have surged this spring and summer against Ukrainian targets, to UAC-0145 - a branch of Sandworm, the hacking unit known for some of Russia's most destructive cyber attacks in the past 10+ years, including ones against Ukraine's power grid. The latest attacks begin when a user visits a compromised webpage, where they're greeted by a fake CAPTCHA claiming they need to complete an extra step to prove that they are human. But unlike normal CAPTCHAs it is not about picking out the traffic lights or ticking a box. Instead, the fake CAPTCHA instructs the user to copy and paste a PowerShell command into their Windows computer. The instructions tell the user to press a key sequence that opens the Windows Run dialog, pastes the contents of the clipboard, and hits Enter — all without the victim realising what they have just unleashed. Because what they've just executed could download malware, run PowerShell scripts, or install remote access software on their machine. A genuine CAPTCHA will never ask you to press Windows + R, open the Run dialog, paste a command, or press Enter to 'verify you are human.' The downloaded code run on targeted computers runs a reconnaissance tool called ScoutCurl that collects information about the infected computer. This includes details about system setup, installed software, files present, and browser data - all of which helps attackers determine whether the target is worth compromising further. At least ten websites are estimated to have been compromised as part of the campaign since the beginning of June. ClickFix attacks like this are not new. The uncomfortable truth is that ClickFix attacks persist because cybercriminals have found that they are very effective. They do not rely on users being tricked into clicking malicious links, but instead guide the victim through self-infection. The instructions are presented as 'helpful' technical advice and can too easily be trusted by the unwary. They exploit the widespread installation of legitimate tools like PowerShell, which are trusted in many corporate environments. ClickFix attacks are not just a problem for Ukraine, already navigating relentless cyberattacks from Russian hackers amid war. They are a problem for computer users worldwide. All computer users should heed Ukraine's warning about the rise in ClickFix attacks as a reminder that the most dangerous threats often do not arrive as zero-day vulnerability exploits. (Author: Graham Cluley; Published: July 21, 2026)

dc5d358951b1.text: Healthcare finance software provider Craneware disclosed a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to its data environment. The company confirmed the breach on July 20, stating that attackers viewed and exfiltrated 'a significant volume' of file names, though much consisted of non-sensitive or publicly available regulatory information. The breach also compromised some employee data alongside customer and partner records. Notably, no disruption to customer services occurred. Craneware notified both the UK's Information Commissioner's Office and the FBI. The company has not disclosed the attackers' identity or their method of gaining access. Craneware operates from Scotland and Florida, providing accounting and billing software to approximately 2,000 US hospitals and health systems, including its Trisus Chargemaster solution for billing information. Cybersecurity experts praised Craneware's swift containment but expressed concern about the incident's scope. Darren Williams of BlackFog stated that 'determined attackers can carry out data exfiltration with relative ease,' noting the healthcare sector's vulnerability. James Neilson of OPSWAT emphasized that 'the data it holds is an attractive target for cybercriminals,' given Craneware's central role in US healthcare infrastructure, despite much data being non-sensitive. (Author: Beth Maundrill; Published: July 21, 2026)

fb9cbe3c63ef.text: Healthcare technology company Clover Health Investments has disclosed a data breach impacting customers' personal and health information. Discovered on July 4, the incident resulted from a social engineering attack that compromised three non-managerial health plan employee accounts. Clover Health activated its response plan immediately upon discovery and engaged third-party cybersecurity experts to contain and investigate the intrusion. The compromised accounts belonged to 'employees who had member visit-scheduling and broker-facing sales functions.' These accounts had access to personally identifiable information and protected health information but lacked access to corporate financial or claims systems. The company stated it believes the incident has been contained and attackers evicted, though it has yet to determine the precise nature, scope, and extent of the breach. No details on the threat actor have been shared, and no known ransomware or extortion group has claimed responsibility. Founded in 2014, Clover Health Investments provides Medicare Advantage insurance plans and operates as a direct U.S. government contractor. The company filed disclosure details with the Securities and Exchange Commission. (Author: Ionut Arghire; Published: July 21, 2026, 5:36 AM ET)

13866bb907f7.text: Researchers at SOCRadar have uncovered a sophisticated social engineering operation attributed to the North Korean-aligned group Famous Chollima (also known as Wagemole). The campaign targets Web3 and cryptocurrency professionals through fraudulent job recruitment schemes. The threat actors initiate contact via LinkedIn, Telegram, Discord, and email, impersonating recruiters from legitimate firms or fictional companies. They lure candidates with lucrative salaries and career advancement opportunities, directing them toward skill assessment tests on attacker-controlled platforms. These malicious portals incorporate psychological pressure tactics, including countdown timers and automated warnings against tab-switching. The core deception leverages 'ClickFix' techniques—fabricating system errors claiming camera or microphone access failures, then instructing victims to paste diagnostic commands into their terminal. Windows systems receive PylangGhost, a Python-based remote access trojan compiled into native libraries using Nuitka to evade detection. macOS users encounter GolangGhost, written in Go, often deployed alongside a credential-harvesting helper designed to extract administrative passwords. Both employ modular architecture targeting over 80 browser extensions, specifically harvesting cryptocurrency wallet data from MetaMask, Phantom, and TronLink, plus passwords from NordPass. The group rapidly registers domains through budget registrars, prioritizing volume over infrastructure resilience, implementing precise targeting controls to block automated malware analysis. (Author: Kevin Poireault; Published: July 21, 2026)

95aad4c08272.text: Amazon has launched the GuardDuty investigation agent in public preview, an AI-powered tool designed to streamline threat investigation workflows. The feature analyzes GuardDuty findings across AWS accounts and organizations, delivering structured assessments that help security teams work more efficiently. During the preview phase, the tool is available at no cost across 10 AWS regions, with usage capped at 10 investigations per account daily (100 total per account during preview). The service provides 'structured assessments with risk levels, confidence scores and actionable recommendations,' according to Allan Holmes, Senior Specialist TAM – Security at AWS. Investigation Scope: Security teams can initiate investigations targeting individual findings, specific member accounts, or entire organizations. Results include risk assessments, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, affected resource identification, and remediation guidance. Access Methods: The feature integrates with the GuardDuty console, AWS CLI, and SDKs through three new APIs (CreateInvestigation, GetInvestigation, ListInvestigations). The CLI also supports natural-language prompts for simplified querying. Integration Options: The investigation agent works with Amazon EventBridge to route enriched findings to SIEM platforms, ticketing systems, and automation tools. It also supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling integration with AI assistants like Anthropic's Claude. Permission Model: Administrator accounts can investigate any account or the full organization; member accounts can only review their own findings. (Author: Anamarija Pogorelec; Published: July 21, 2026)

58f94c801d14.text: Microsoft has released manual mitigation steps to address a widespread Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) synchronization issue affecting both client and server systems. The problem prevents administrators from deploying the latest Windows updates through WSUS or Configuration Manager due to extended sync times and timeouts caused by accumulated publishing metadata. The company initially deployed a service-side fix on Saturday for newly installed or rebuilt WSUS servers after observing heightened impact beginning July 13. Microsoft subsequently released detailed manual remediation procedures for existing WSUS installations still experiencing problems. The fix requires IT administrators to: 1. Back up each SUSDB database. 2. Execute a cleanup query using SQL Management Studio against all SUSDB databases, including WSUS replicas. 3. Reset the MaxXMLPerRequest value to its default setting. Microsoft notes that 'the first Windows Update scan may take longer than usual, but subsequent scans will return to normal timing.' After cleanup, administrators should reindex the SUSDB, run the WSUS Server Cleanup Wizard, and recycle the WsusPool application pool. The company clarifies that 'the client-side DataStore.edb does not shrink automatically after the detectoids are removed. This is expected and does not affect scan performance.' Microsoft has addressed comparable WSUS deployment issues in May, July, and August 2025. (Author: Sergiu Gatlan; Published: July 21, 2026)

b2158c46002b.text: Kaspersky researchers documented a new communication component for Project CAV3RN, a sophisticated cyberespionage framework attributed to OilRig (APT34). The module, compiled with .NET Native AOT, uses an innovative dual-channel approach for command-and-control operations. Primary C2 Channel: Outlook Calendar - The AzureCommunication.dll component exchanges commands and results through Microsoft Outlook calendar events accessed via Microsoft Graph API. The module stores communications in a fixed time window (2050-05-13, 22:00-23:00 UTC) to avoid detection. Commands arrive as encrypted calendar event attachments with subjects formatted as 'Event ID: <agent-id>', while results use 'Boss Report ID: <agent-id>1500'. Communication employs layered encryption: RSA-OAEP-SHA256 protects AES keys, which then encrypt payloads using AES-256-GCM. Secondary Channel: DNS AAAA Recovery - When Microsoft Graph authentication fails, the module retrieves replacement credentials through DNS AAAA responses from actor-controlled nameservers under cloudlanecdn[.]com. The protocol uses specially crafted queries to recover TenantId, ClientId, ClientSecret, and UserEmail in 14-byte fragments. Attribution Evidence: Researchers assessed moderate confidence in OilRig attribution based on several factors: 'Microsoft-hosted services for C2,' use of compromised regional infrastructure (specifically an Israeli law firm's Microsoft 365 mailbox), and parallels with previously documented OilRig tooling like RDAT and OilBooster. Infrastructure Details: The domain cloudlanecdn[.]com, registered December 24, 2025, transitioned to custom authoritative nameservers on May 2, 2026, hosted at RouterHosting LLC (AS 14956). (Author: GReAT; Published: 21 Jul 2026)

92bb77569769.text: Zimbra announced patches on Monday for several critical-severity vulnerabilities, including a command injection bug disclosed in late June. The critical command injection impacts the SNMP monitoring component of the collaboration suite if SNMP notifications are enabled and the integrated Swatchdog service is running. An unauthenticated attacker could send crafted payloads to execute arbitrary OS commands in the background and compromise the email server. Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) version 10.1.20 includes a permanent fix for the bug. The update also patches four cross-site scripting (XSS) defects in the Classic Web Client (Classic UI) that could lead to script execution under certain conditions. The flaws can be exploited via malicious attachment filenames, crafted fields, and crafted attachments. Additional security fixes include CVE-2026-50055, a mail forwarding restriction bypass allowing authenticated attackers to exfiltrate emails despite forwarding restrictions; an access control vulnerability in the EWS extension (CVE-2026-10631); an authorization issue in mailbox delegation (CVE-2026-50054); and a server-side request forgery (SSRF) bug in Nextcloud integration. Zimbra urges users to update to ZCS 10.1.20 as soon as possible but reports no evidence these issues are being exploited in the wild. This update follows Zimbra's previous security patch from roughly two weeks earlier that addressed a critical XSS vulnerability in the Classic Web Client. (Author: Ionut Arghire; Published: July 21, 2026, 4:20 AM ET)

365cef55ec92.text: Troy Hunt describes a video demonstrating how Claude integrates information from UniFi, Home Assistant, and Pi-Hole systems. He emphasizes that AI's practical value lies in 'taking lots of noise and converting it into a useful signal.' Hunt recounts a specific incident where his Sonos units failed to connect to music services. Claude quickly identified the underlying issue: 'you know your Pi-Hole is dead, right?' A power cycle on the PoE port resolved the problem. He encourages readers to explore this application, calling it 'pretty awesome.' The piece positions this home network troubleshooting scenario as a genuine use case where AI provides tangible value by helping users identify root causes amid complex system interactions. (Author: Troy Hunt; Published: July 21, 2026)

399bc63b11e6.text: Benjamin Bachmann, Director Group Information Security at Bilfinger, discusses defending industrial plants in this interview. He explains that attackers prioritize operational control over data theft and challenges the notion that air gaps provide meaningful protection in OT environments. On Executive Misconceptions: Bachmann identifies two primary misunderstandings. First, executives believe attackers target data, when 'nobody breaks into an industrial environment to read the recipe' — the actual goal is operational disruption. Second, many assume air-gapped networks exist, but he describes this as 'the unicorn of industrial security.' On Security vs. Engineering: Rather than pitting containment against uptime, Bachmann advocates for negotiating response protocols during normal operations. He states that 'containment has to be cheap enough that nobody ever has to choose between safety, uptime, and defense,' preventing attackers from weaponizing security responses. On Legacy Equipment Visibility: Since older equipment lacks authentication features, Bachmann recommends network-based monitoring instead. He frames legacy systems positively: 'OT traffic is choreography. The same devices, the same conversations, the same cadence, every day.' On Ransomware Economics: Attackers calculate downtime costs to set demands, so defense requires enabling rapid, safe partial operations. Bachmann emphasizes rehearsing restarts rather than restores to minimize extortion leverage. On Human Risk Claims: He disputes that humans represent the weakest link, arguing 'trust is not a control.' Instead, he focuses on preventing click-to-controller pathways through architecture rather than awareness training alone. (Author: Mirko Zorz; Published: July 21, 2026)

d21b68bb9028.text: A drive ships with a label promising hardware encryption. You plug it in, set a password, and trust the chip inside to handle the rest. Millions of laptops and workstations run this way, on solid-state drives built to the TCG Opal2 standard. Milan Brož and three colleagues bought 38 of those drives and ran them through a test bench. Brož maintains cryptsetup, the tool that configures disk encryption on most Linux systems. The drives came from Samsung, Western Digital, Micron, Kioxia, and others, a mix of new stock and secondhand units pulled from laptops. The team treated each one as a black box and sent it only the commands the Opal2 documentation defines. What the drives got wrong: Two Lenovo OEM drives encrypt every sector with the same tweak value. AES-XTS relies on that value to make identical data look different depending on where it sits on the disk. With one value across the whole drive, identical content written to two locations produces identical ciphertext. A pattern in your files survives into the encrypted data. The same two drives ship a random number generator that returns a predictable counting sequence on every call. A SanDisk SATA drive leans toward one byte value, 0x8B. The drive emits it roughly double the expected frequency. Opal2 requires every drive to expose this generator and leaves its quality unspecified. The tweak flaw exposes residual pattern information about data a key change was meant to erase, and the researchers rate real exploitation as very limited. The weak generator matters for software that pulls keys from it, and the team searched for a product that does and came up empty. The encryption key itself lives on the drive and stays there. The reset tokens have their own problem. Every Opal2 drive carries a PSID, a code printed on the label that wipes the drive back to factory state. One batch of SanDisk drives generated those codes in sequence, sharing a prefix and a suffix. Recovering one drive's PSID hands you its neighbors' by counting up. Six other drives accept any garbage appended to a valid PSID and treat it as correct. Vendors buy hardware encryption, and no one checks it: Companies deploy Opal2 drives to satisfy a data-at-rest requirement. A purchasing officer sees 'hardware encryption' on a spec sheet and marks the box. The gap between that label and the chip's behavior went years unmeasured by any independent party. This is the first cross-vendor security comparison of Opal2 drives. The last major public work on self-encrypting SSDs landed in 2019. The disclosure went nowhere: Brož and his team reported every security issue to the affected vendors. Micron shipped a firmware fix for a sector-size bug on its Crucial T500. Every other report came back as already known and unpatched, out of support, or met with silence. What got fixed: The project shipped code. Opal2 support landed in cryptsetup. The team released the Opal Test Suite so anyone can point the same checks at their own drives. Three of the tested drives turned out unusable for real disk encryption. Cryptsetup now checks a drive's single-user-mode firmware before trusting it and drops to a safer configuration when the check fails. The practical guidance runs opposite to the original sales pitch. Layer software encryption over the drive's own, and let the hardware serve as a second wall. (Author: Anamarija Pogorelec; Published: July 21, 2026)

5e3d1bc8051f.text: Defensive cybersecurity frameworks traditionally document attacks after they occur. Organizations study breaches, record the methods used, and develop detections based on confirmed activity. This reactive approach creates a vulnerability window between when attackers develop new techniques and when defenders can identify and counter them. PR3TACK (Preemptive Tactics and Countermeasures Knowledgebase) seeks to narrow this gap. Built by Vishal Thakur of Atlassian, this open framework catalogs plausible attacker tactics and procedures 'that remain unobserved in the wild.' Key Distinctions from ATT&CK: While MITRE ATT&CK documents techniques verified in actual intrusions, PR3TACK focuses on techniques that could emerge from current system vulnerabilities and evolving attacker patterns. The framework highlights real attacks like Atom Table abuse and the Revix ransomware family's VM termination tactic that escaped ATT&CK documentation. Organizational Structure: Submissions fall into three priority tiers: High (validated proof-of-concept code), Medium (technical reasoning awaiting confirmation), and Low (academic research or investigation). The Seed Matrix organizes entries across seventeen tactic categories, including familiar ones like Execution and Persistence alongside original categories such as Pre-Positioning, Resilience Erosion, Governance Subversion, Cognitive Manipulation, and Digital Exhaust Manipulation. Tools and Contributions: A Navigator tool provides visual browsing capabilities with search, filter, and customization features. The project welcomes community contributions through an open intake process requiring technique descriptions, feasibility assessments, impact analysis, and preemptive defenses. Version 0.1 represents an early stage, with future value depending on community participation quality and volume. (Author: Mirko Zorz; Published: July 21, 2026)

4ad8c4660e8c.text: Most large companies run more than one AI platform at the same time. Developers pull up coding assistants, marketing teams lean on writing tools, and analysts query enterprise search across separate vendors. Single-provider setups keep giving way to mixed stacks as companies keep their options open. Sanctioned tools and personal accounts sit side by side inside many organizations. Anonymized sign-on data from more than 20,000 organizations on the Okta tracked this spread from June 2022 through June 2026. A Two-Speed Market: The Okta Enterprise AI Index sorts vendors into two groups by how fast their enterprise customer base grew across the study period. AI-native companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Cursor multiplied their corporate customers by more than four times. Established software makers such as Microsoft, Google Workspace, Figma, Slack, Adobe, and Notion grew under that mark and took the AI-enhanced label. From Chat to Action: The kind of AI landing in these companies changed along the way. The three phases trace a move from autocomplete to chat to agents. Anthropic passed OpenAI in enterprise accounts in March 2026 and led it in monthly active users the following month. Microsoft 365 still sits far ahead on raw volume. Credentials Scatter as Vendors Add Up: 'Our data shows that as the number of platforms grows, so does the risk of over-permissioned apps and orphaned tokens,' Fei Liu, Principal Emerging Tech Researcher at Okta, told Help Net Security. She calls for a change in mindset: 'Security teams need to stop thinking about this merely as adding a new software vendor and start treating it as an expansion of their identity fabric.' Agents Borrowing Human Logins: 'We're seeing a heavy reliance on traditional service accounts and static API keys, and unfortunately, we still see instances of shared human logins being used to authorize agentic workflows,' Liu said. 'When an AI agent inherits a human's login, you completely lose your audit trail — you can no longer distinguish whether a critical action was taken by an employee or autonomously by an algorithm,' she said. The Shadow AI Layer: 'For every enterprise-grade AI tool provisioned by IT, there are inevitably pockets of developers or marketing teams spinning up separate instances in their own cloud environments or using personal accounts,' Liu said. 'If an employee uses a personal account to access an unsanctioned LLM, and pastes proprietary source code or customer data into the prompt, the security team has zero visibility and no ability to revoke that access,' she said. Companies should 'provide paved roads to bring the most requested AI tools into the SSO and governance fold so employees don't feel forced to bypass IT in the first place,' Liu said. (Author: Mirko Zorz; Published: July 21, 2026)

b02f5e8fae35.text: French cloud provider OVH disclosed how it handled an emergency patch deployment for CVE-2026-53359 (Januscape), a critical Linux KVM vulnerability allowing guest-to-host escape attacks. The flaw permitted attackers with root access to guest VMs to execute code on the host system, crash machines, or compromise other virtual instances. OVH faced a nightmare scenario where attackers could breach cloud tenant isolation—the fundamental security model cloud providers depend upon. The company needed rapid remediation across tens of thousands of hosts running approximately one million virtual machines. Why Alternative Solutions Didn't Work: Disabling nested virtualization required knowing which tenants needed it (OVH didn't have this information); live patching risked introducing instability; live VM migration would take months to complete. OVH's Chosen Approach: The company backported a fix into their Debian distribution and conducted mass host reboots. This strategy meant deliberate customer downtime but faster comprehensive protection. The executive team approved this, prioritizing protecting the majority while accepting impact on minority customers lacking redundancy. Operational Secrecy: OVH deliberately withheld detailed information during patch execution to prevent customers from testing publicly available exploits against their unpatched systems. Testing Ground: Sydney's datacenter served as the initial deployment site—chosen for its smaller scale and convenient eight-hour time difference from France. Reboot Strategy: OVH implemented sophisticated wave-based reboots designed to prevent simultaneous failures of redundant customer workloads, using 'co-location graphs' ensuring instances from the same customer project never rebooted simultaneously. Complications Encountered: 20-30 hosts per 6,000 failed autonomous recovery due to faulty memory, BIOS issues, and inactive network interfaces; some VMs experienced data corruption during forced shutdowns; OpenStack API failures generated hours of HTTP 503 errors; one patching wave was postponed due to API traffic reaching '10 times the usual peak'; some machines required CMOS battery replacements. Outcome: OVH achieved what leadership termed 'a remarkable feat,' resulting in acceptable customer impact relative to the operation's massive scale. The company acknowledged room for improvement and committed to post-mortem analysis. (Author: Simon Sharwood; Published: Tuesday, July 21, 2026 // 04:52 UTC)

7ba825bb1282.text:
Frontier AI is fundamentally changing the pace of cybersecurity. For defenders and adversaries alike, it compresses the time required to discover vulnerabilities, assess exploitability, and act.

AI models can reason across entire codebases, identify complex vulnerability chains, and generate exploit paths at a speed and scale that was previously impossible. That's a breakthrough for defenders, but it's also a preview of how quickly adversaries will evolve.

At CrowdStrike, we wanted to answer a simple question: How do we turn frontier AI into better security outcomes?

Over the past several months, we've been working with frontier AI models, including Anthropic's Mythos Preview, to understand how their capabilities perform in real-world vulnerability research and other security use cases. Along the way, we uncovered a series of lessons that extend well beyond vulnerability discovery, from how frontier AI should be operationalized to how it will reshape adversary tradecraft to what organizations must do to continuously strengthen cyber defense.

This blog explores the first of those lessons: "The model is only part of the equation. The real differentiator is how it's harnessed."

Frontier AI Changes the Economics of Vulnerability Discovery

Security leaders are facing a fundamental shift. The number of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities has dramatically increased over the past decade, and the pace continues to accelerate. By late June 2026, the number of published CVEs this year had already reached nearly two-thirds of the total reported during all of 2025.

Defenders aren't simply managing more vulnerabilities; they're managing an expanding attack surface that is growing faster every year.

The window to respond is shrinking. The CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report found a 42% year-over-year increase in zero-day vulnerabilities exploited before public disclosure. Attackers are weaponizing vulnerabilities earlier in their lifecycle, giving defenders less time to identify, prioritize, and remediate risk before exploitation begins. Frontier AI will only accelerate this trend.

When frontier AI models first demonstrated breakthrough performance on software engineering and reasoning tasks, we wanted to understand what those advances meant for cybersecurity. Could these models fundamentally change vulnerability research? Could they help security teams discover vulnerabilities faster, understand exploitability more accurately, and ultimately improve defensive outcomes?

To answer those questions, we evaluated several frontier AI models, including Anthropic's Mythos Preview, across a range of real-world vulnerability discovery tasks.

The results confirmed what many in the industry are already seeing: Frontier AI represents a significant advance in vulnerability research. These models can reason across large codebases, identify subtle relationships between vulnerabilities, and explore potential attack paths with a level of sophistication that was previously difficult to achieve at scale.

Frontier AI models can reason across a wider aperture; as a result, they can recognize that what appears to be a low-severity information disclosure vulnerability becomes far more dangerous when combined with a memory corruption vulnerability and a privilege escalation path elsewhere in the application. It can evaluate whether existing mitigations can be bypassed, assess how an attacker might chain multiple weaknesses together, and produce a coherent attack narrative rather than a disconnected list of findings.

This capability has profound implications for defenders. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, it will compress the time between discovery and exploitation. Organizations can no longer assume they have days or weeks to patch before attackers move. They must separate meaningful risk from overwhelming noise and translate AI-driven discovery into actionable security outcomes. On the flip side, the same advances give defenders an unprecedented opportunity to move faster, prioritize more effectively, and respond with greater confidence, provided they harness AI properly.

The Harness Matters as Much as the Model

Our testing exposed another important breakthrough: Finding vulnerabilities is only part of the challenge. Security teams need to know which findings represent real risk and which can safely be ignored.

In our earliest tests, frontier AI models generated thousands of potential vulnerabilities. While many were legitimate, the majority proved to be theoretical, unreachable, or impossible to reproduce. The volume of findings quickly overwhelmed their value. So rather than asking which frontier model performed best, we began asking a different question: How do we operationalize frontier AI to gain a trusted view of vulnerability risk?

As we continued our testing, one conclusion became increasingly clear: "The frontier model wasn't the biggest differentiator. The way it was applied was."

Rather than treating the model as a standalone capability, we built a security harness around it, combining structured threat modeling, exploit validation, workflow orchestration, and the deep security expertise embedded throughout the CrowdStrike Falcon platform.

Each stage serves a purpose. Threat modeling focused analysis on code that was reachable by an attacker. Validation reduced theoretical findings before they reached analysts. Exploit verification determined whether vulnerabilities could be chained together and reproduced in realistic environments. Together, these steps transformed raw AI output into actionable vulnerability intelligence.

The results are profound. Using the same class of frontier AI models with different workflows produced dramatically different outcomes. A generic approach yielded false-positive rates approaching 80%. Applying CrowdStrike's security harness reduced that rate to approximately 20% while maintaining exceptional vulnerability discovery capability.

More importantly, the improvement wasn't model-specific. It came from combining frontier AI with structured workflows, rigorous validation, and deep security expertise. As the pace of model innovation accelerates and organizations gain access to an expanding ecosystem of capable frontier models, the differentiator won't necessarily be those with access to the newest and most powerful models. It will be the ability to operationalize AI to consistently deliver trusted security outcomes.

This lesson applies equally to defenders and adversaries. Sophisticated threat actors won't simply adopt frontier AI; they'll engineer workflows around it to accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Defenders must do the same by applying AI in ways that improve speed and confidence rather than simply increasing volume.

What We Found

Leveraging Mythos Preview along with proprietary harnesses optimized for vulnerability research, CrowdStrike analyzed nine categories of open-source software: network infrastructure, browsers, AI and developer tooling, virtualization platforms, search services, system software, databases, cryptographic libraries, and web sanitization tools.

The findings are significant in both volume and severity. Across these categories, the pipeline surfaced more than 2,400 vulnerabilities. More than one in four findings (26%) were rated high or critical severity. Approximately 50% of confirmed findings carried working proof-of-concept exploits generated or validated by the pipeline.

Vulnerability Distribution by Severity: Critical 72 (3%); High 552 (23%); Medium 888 (37%); Low 744 (31%); Informational 144 (6%).

The main takeaway is scale. In a matter of days, CrowdStrike's AI-driven vulnerability research pipeline surfaced more than 2,400 vulnerability findings across 43 different products and nine major open-source software categories. Frontier AI, when paired with the right harness, can materially change the speed and scale of vulnerability discovery, helping defenders find and prioritize risk faster.

A note on these findings: Results were generated through automated AI testing with human oversight, but not all have yet undergone full human triage with open-source maintainers and vendors. CrowdStrike is following responsible disclosure processes and will share additional details as this process is complete. Severity ratings, exploitability assessments, and proof-of-concept validity should be treated as informational at this stage.

Three Lessons for Security Leaders

1. Evaluate AI by outcomes, not models. The rapid pace of innovation in frontier AI means there will always be another model release, another benchmark, and another leaderboard. Those advances are only part of the equation. The real question isn't which model performs best in isolation; it's how effectively that model can be operationalized to solve real security problems. For defenders, success should be measured by outcomes: Can AI reduce false positives? Can it identify exploitable vulnerabilities with greater confidence? Can it integrate into existing security workflows and help teams make faster, more informed decisions? The organizations that realize the greatest value from frontier AI will be those that combine advanced models with security expertise, structured validation, and operational workflows that produce trusted, actionable results.

2. Prepare for AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery. Defenders and adversaries alike will benefit from faster discovery and better analysis. As AI compresses the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation, organizations can no longer assume they will have weeks, or even days, to remediate every critical vulnerability before attackers use them. Patching remains an essential security discipline, but it is no longer sufficient on its own. Security leaders should shift their focus from vulnerability management as a backlog exercise to continuous exposure management by understanding which assets are most critical, which vulnerabilities are most likely to be exploited, and where compensating controls can reduce risk while remediation is underway.

3. Build resilience, not just response. Frontier AI is not a cyber superweapon. It is an accelerator. The organizations best prepared for the AI era will build environments that are resilient by design. This means assuming sophisticated adversaries will eventually gain an initial foothold and designing security architectures that limit what happens next. It means protecting identities as aggressively as endpoints, reducing unnecessary privileges, continuously validating exposure, monitoring for policy changes, governing AI systems, and automating detection and response across the attack surface. Most importantly, it means creating a continuous feedback loop where offensive research strengthens defensive capabilities. This enables organizations to adapt as quickly as the threat landscape evolves.

Frontier AI represents one of the most significant advances in cybersecurity in decades. But the future of cybersecurity won't be defined by AI alone. The organizations that succeed will be the ones that combine frontier AI with deep security expertise, continuous validation, and a closed-loop approach that turns offensive discovery into stronger defense. That's the future CrowdStrike is building.

(Author: Joel Spurlock; Categories: Executive Viewpoint, Securing AI)

Author: Bill Toulas. Published: July 21, 2026.

Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-50522, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft SharePoint, to steal machine keys and maintain persistent access to compromised systems even after patching.

The vulnerability is a deserialization flaw that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. Once attackers obtain machine keys, they can "create valid authentication tokens to impersonate users and access available resources such as SharePoint sites and documents."

Microsoft addressed the issue in July 2026 security updates, though it wasn't initially marked as actively exploited.

Rapid Exploitation Timeline: July 17 - Defused detected undocumented SharePoint deserialization attacks. July 20 - watchTowr identified public proof-of-concept code; within hours, their honeypot network captured successful exploitation attempts. Researcher Janggggg published a PowerShell PoC on GitHub.

The exploit delivers a malicious .NET BinaryFormatter payload as a cookie in a forged WS-Federation sign-in response to SharePoint's endpoint, triggering remote code execution.

Mitigation Recommendations: watchTowr advises organizations to apply the latest SharePoint updates and "rotate credentials on any asset that may have been exposed."
