Author: Kevin Townsend. Published: July 21, 2026 (1:44 PM ET).

Cisco Foundation AI has announced Antares, a small language model (SLM) named after the brightest star in the Scorpius constellation. The Antares family currently comprises two models: Antares-350M and Antares-1B, both open-weight models available on Hugging Face.

Cisco describes Antares as "purpose-built for one of the hardest, most time-consuming and expensive problems in security: pinpointing where known vulnerabilities exist within a codebase."

When vulnerabilities are discovered, security teams must determine whether their code contains them and locate their exact position. Currently, this process is best assisted by AI, but organizations face a dilemma: expensive large language models from major providers versus cheaper open-weight general models that produce more false positives.

Antares addresses this trade-off by combining the advantages of both approaches. It functions as an open-weight model specifically designed for vulnerability detection, enabling organizations to maintain data sovereignty while achieving lower costs and reduced false positives.

The model's processing mimics human investigation methods, starting from vulnerability descriptions and searching for relevant code patterns. "Each model starts from a vulnerability description, searches for relevant code patterns, reads candidate files, incorporates new evidence, changes direction when a path is unhelpful, and narrows toward the files most likely to matter."

Antares targets budget-constrained security teams, particularly at "Universities, research institutions, nonprofits, and public-sector teams that still maintain important software."

To validate performance, Cisco released the Vulnerability Localization Benchmark—a 500-entry assessment requiring models to navigate unfamiliar codebases and recognize vulnerability patterns. Testing showed Antares completes tasks 172 times cheaper than OpenAI's GPT-4.5 and 15.2 times cheaper than Z.ai's open-weight alternative, while delivering comparable accuracy.

The output provides a ranked list of source files likely containing relevant vulnerabilities, enabling security teams to begin their triage process efficiently.

Stanford professor Amin Saberi commented: "Antares' results change that equation: near-frontier accuracy on secure code reasoning at a fraction of the cost, fast enough to run on every commit."

Author: Bill Toulas. Published: July 21, 2026, 12:41 PM.

Hackers are exploiting the "wp2shell" critical vulnerability suite (CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137) affecting WordPress Core to deploy persistent webshells and install malicious plugins on affected servers.

The critical exploit chain abuses the WordPress REST API's batch-processing feature, allowing remote attackers to execute code on vulnerable installations without authentication. Proof-of-concept exploits emerged over the weekend following SearchLight Cyber's disclosure of the wp2shell security issue.

Active exploitation was confirmed shortly after WordPress released patches in versions 7.0.2, 6.9.5, and 6.8.6, triggering automatic security updates for supported installations.

Cloud security company Wiz documented observed attack activities including mass-scanning for vulnerable WordPress installations, abuse of plugin upload functionality to install malicious add-ons, installation of PHP webshells ranging from simple backdoors to obfuscated shells disguised as plugins, querying the REST API to collect administrator usernames and emails, local file inclusion attempts targeting wp-config through admin-ajax.php to retrieve database credentials, deployment of malicious plugins exposing REST API endpoints for remote command execution, and successful access to WordPress administration panels. Wiz has not observed lateral movement or data exfiltration.

SANS Technology Institute's Johannes B. Ullrich described two-stage attacks starting with SQL injection probing before delivering PHP webshells to the "/wp-content/cache/" directory with randomized filenames used as passwords. The webshell code checked availability of PHP functions like "system()" and "exec()" to execute commands. Some attacks involved creating rogue administrator accounts.

WordPress security firm Defiant reported that exploitation probing began at 23:29 UTC on July 17, with SQL injection attempts following 13 minutes later.

Site administrators are urged to immediately update to patched versions, review logs for wp2shell-related requests, inspect installed plugins, and check for rogue PHP files or newly created admin accounts.

A tracking dashboard by Macnica researcher Yutaka Sejiyama reported an 81.6% patch rate from a sample of 124,580 websites evaluated.

SearchLight Cyber researcher Adam Kues published a follow-up report examining the wp2shell discovery and exploit development process, which involved AI tools.

Author: Connor Jones, Cybersecurity reporter. Published: Tuesday, July 21, 2026, 17:17 UTC.

German authorities have successfully neutralized the primary infrastructure supporting the Kratos phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit through an international operation involving the US and Indonesia.

The Frankfurt am Main Central Office for Combating Internet Crime (ZIT) and Federal Criminal Police (BKA) characterized Kratos as "one of the most widespread and dangerous PhaaS kits on the market." Indonesian authorities arrested the individual described as the platform's "developer and technical administrator," though no information was provided regarding additional suspects.

Operational Scope: Kratos functioned by enabling cybercriminals with minimal technical expertise to distribute convincing Microsoft-themed phishing pages designed to harvest credentials and session cookies, circumventing multi-factor authentication. The platform generated approximately 15,000 phishing campaigns monthly, with each campaign potentially affecting thousands of recipients worldwide.

Since 2024, the operation generated over €300,000 ($342,000) in revenue. An estimated 1,800 criminal enterprises utilized the kit to target hundreds of thousands of victims across more than 30 countries.

Technical Takedown: Authorities neutralized over 200 servers, though specific methodologies remained undisclosed. Historical precedents typically involve legal warrants to hosting providers or traffic null-routing through ISPs.

Historical Context: The kit operated under various names including SneakyLog and Sneaky 2FA. Security researchers documented its evolution from commercial trojans and infostealers. Manufacturing, retail, healthcare, law firms, and educational institutions in the US and Europe comprised primary targets.

Dr Benjamin Krause of the ZIT stated the approach demonstrates that "criminal online service[s]" can be effectively dismantled through coordinated enforcement efforts.

Author: Saeed Abbasi, Head of Threat Research Unit (TRU), Director of Product, Qualys. Published: July 21, 2026.

The Qualys Threat Research Unit identified a local privilege escalation vulnerability in snap-confine affecting Ubuntu Desktop versions 24.04, 25.10, and 26.04. The flaw exploits a race condition introduced during a security hardening transition from set-uid-root to set-capabilities model.

Attack Surface: snap-confine shifted to a capabilities-based model to enforce least privilege. However, this approach creates a vulnerability window where temporary directories under /tmp remain under unprivileged user control before root ownership transfer occurs.

Exploitation Method: The attack leverages two concurrent race conditions: 1) Mounting a FUSE filesystem over temporary scratch directories to bypass mount namespace isolation; 2) Creating symlinks targeting arbitrary files, allowing permission widening before snap-confine transfers ownership.

The exploit targets "/run/udev/*" paths to bypass AppArmor confinement, dropping malicious .rules files to force systemd-udevd execution as root.

Severity: Rated High.

Affected Versions: Ubuntu Desktop 26.04, Ubuntu Desktop 25.10, Ubuntu Desktop 24.04 (with current snapd packages).

Remediation: Organizations should "apply the latest snapd updates immediately," per Canonical's coordinated disclosure through the Ubuntu Security Team.

Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: July 21, 2026.

A third SharePoint Server vulnerability patched by Microsoft in July 2026 is now experiencing active exploitation. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-50522, carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8.

The vulnerability involves deserialization of untrusted data in Microsoft Office SharePoint, allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely across networks. Microsoft credited DEVCORE researcher "splitline" with discovering and reporting this issue.

Microsoft's advisory states: "In a network-based attack, an attacker authenticated as at least a Site Owner, could write arbitrary code to inject and execute code remotely on the SharePoint Server."

The company characterized the attack vector as having network accessibility with low complexity, meaning attackers need minimal prior system knowledge to exploit the vulnerability successfully.

Security vendor watchTowr detected active exploitation against on-premises SharePoint deployments following public proof-of-concept release. The firm warned that attackers are extracting SharePoint machine keys through single requests to maintain persistent access, advising that "Patching is not enough; defenders should rotate credentials on any assets that may have been exposed."

Defused Cyber disclosed threat actors are likely delivering .NET deserialization payloads to SharePoint sign-in endpoints without authentication credentials.

This marks the third SharePoint vulnerability experiencing active exploitation, following CVE-2026-56164 and CVE-2026-58644—both leveraged as zero-day exploits prior to patches.

CISA added CVE-2026-50522 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on July 22, 2026, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to apply fixes by July 25.

Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: July 21, 2026.

Threat actors have been observed exploiting a now-patched high-severity Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS vulnerability as an entry point to deploy Qilin (aka Agenda) ransomware on victim environments.

Arctic Wolf Labs said it investigated multiple intrusions in June 2026 that began with the exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw affecting the portal and gateway components of PAN-OS software.

Successful exploitation of the flaw allows unauthenticated remote attackers to sidestep authentication and establish VPN sessions without valid credentials when authentication override cookies are enabled with specific certificate configurations.

"Post-exploitation tradecraft varied across intrusions, from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion, possibly suggesting multiple affiliates operating under the Qilin ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) umbrella," according to Arctic Wolf's analysis.

Attackers demonstrated consistent operational patterns: staging ransomware at C:\PerfLogs\, using PsExec for lateral execution via administrative shares, deploying password-protected ransomware payloads, and implementing comprehensive log-clearing routines.

The threat actors weaponized the flaw to gain authenticated network access by establishing SSL VPN sessions, then escalated attacks to facilitate credential harvesting and lateral movement through Windows administrative shares via compromised administrative accounts.

Attackers deliberately cleared event logs and disabled Microsoft Defender Real-Time Protection prior to executing ransomware to minimize detection likelihood and avoid leaving forensic evidence.

Post-exploitation activities varied across victims, ranging from enterprise-wide encryption with no data exfiltration and reconnaissance via remote access tools like AnyDesk, Ngrok, or LogMeIn, to large-scale credential theft and data exfiltration to MEGA cloud service before ransomware deployment using Rclone, Proton Drive, and FileZilla.

This variability is consistent with RaaS models, in which multiple affiliates leverage shared initial access infrastructure and ransomware tooling while applying their own preferred post-exploitation methodologies.

Author: Swati Khandelwal. Published: July 21, 2026.

Researchers from Simon Fraser University, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shandong University, and QAX's Xingtu Lab demonstrated seven attack techniques against five open-source mobile agent frameworks: AppAgent, AppAgentX, Mobile-Agent-v3, Open-AutoGLM, and MobA.

Command Injection via Shell Metacharacters: The researchers found that AppAgent's controller executes model output directly without sanitization: subprocess.run(adb_command, shell=True). This allows injected shell commands to run on the host PC. A test payload launching calc.exe succeeded in 20 of 20 trials.

Screenshot Tampering (TOCTOU Vulnerability): Agents write screenshots to device storage before retrieving them, creating a 50-500ms window. Attackers can replace the PNG file before the agent reads it. This attack succeeded 19-20 of 20 times against four frameworks.

Invisible Text Injection: Vision models including GPT-4o, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GLM-4V read 2%-opacity text in at least 18 of 20 trials—"below typical human detection under normal viewing."

UI Spoofing and Credential Theft: An accessibility service overlay mimicking a login prompt deceived all five agents across 100 trials without hesitation.

Unauthenticated Input via Broadcast: Open-AutoGLM uses ADB Keyboard, a test tool accepting text broadcasts without authentication. Any app can register the same action and intercept keystrokes.

Researcher Response: First author Zidong Zhang stated: "the team has no evidence of the techniques being used outside a controlled setting." The researchers contacted maintainers privately before publishing, receiving no responses.

Recommended Fixes: Two frameworks show proper approaches: MobA streams screenshots over exec-out (eliminating file races), and Open-AutoGLM passes arguments as lists instead of concatenating strings, preventing command injection.

546c9516e6dc.text:
Author: Swati Khandelwal. Published: July 21, 2026. Category: Critical Infrastructure / Cloud Security.

Researchers from Zhejiang University have documented a novel attack called Bit2Watt that could allow cloud tenants to destabilize power grids through GPU workload manipulation, without requiring exploits or system breaches.

How the Attack Works: The technique exploits the direct relationship between GPU computational load and power consumption. By toggling GPU tensor cores between high-intensity and idle states on a precise schedule, attackers can create controllable power oscillations at the wall socket.

Two implementation methods were identified: SWMA (Synthetic Workload Method) uses a custom CUDA kernel that switches between compute-heavy and idle modes, producing power components ranging from 1.5 to 6 kHz across tested GPUs. LTMA (LLM Training Method) embeds modulation within legitimate AI training runs by adjusting hyperparameters, achieving 1.2 to 3 kHz frequencies while blending into normal training noise—making detection considerably harder.

Grid Impact Simulation: Testing a worst-case scenario with 1,000 synchronized GPUs on a 1 MW distributed grid showed concerning results: current total harmonic distortion reached 46.8% (well above the 13% safety guideline), and damping ratios fell to -0.27—indicating grid instability where disturbances amplify rather than dissipate.

Critical Limitations: The attack requires perfect synchronization across hundreds or thousands of cloud GPUs—a significant practical hurdle. Timing jitter of just 100 microseconds reduced aggregate amplitude by approximately 20%. Virtualization, scheduling delays, and device variability all add uncertainty that would likely require attackers to use substantially more GPUs or achieve better physical placement than the simulated scenario.

Detection Challenges: Standard monitoring infrastructure proves inadequate. Rack PDU counters sample once per second, while NVIDIA's NVML telemetry tops out at 450 Hz—both far below the attack's multi-kilohertz modulation. Dedicated electromagnetic interference sensing performed best, though LTMA consistently proved harder to identify than SWMA.

Secondary Threats: The same modulation creates a covert side-channel for data exfiltration, encoding information as two frequencies. Researchers recovered a 50-bit test sequence with zero errors using near-field antenna measurement—though exploitation requires physical proximity to target hardware.

Architectural Vulnerability: The fundamental issue stems from tight coupling between volatile GPU loads and increasingly inverter-dependent grids. No product vulnerability exists to patch; the exposure is architectural.

Research Scope: The physical experiments occurred in controlled testbeds; grid-scale damage projections came from simulation. No production systems were attacked, and no commercial product vulnerabilities were disclosed.

1687a3c3eefe.text:
Around 66,000 common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) are projected to be disclosed this 2026, according to the FIRST 2026 Mid-Year Vulnerability Forecast. Vulnerability researcher Jerry Gamblin revealed that disclosures in the first half of the year ran nearly 50% ahead of the same window in 2025, which itself finished at a record 48,185 CVEs. His analysis draws on National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and CVE Program data. The steep climb from the roughly 40,000 CVEs recorded in 2024 might make the “vulnpocalypse” panic justified.
The data: Volume vs. exploitable risk
Separating disclosure volume from dangerous risk is a key strategy in facing the forecasted overwhelming volume. As the raw count balloons, the share of critical vulnerabilities has roughly halved, falling from approximately 13% in 2024 to 7% in 2025 based on an analysis by Zafran that draws on National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Vulnerability Database data. The slice that is actively exploited in the wild remains remarkably stable at well under 1%.
| Metric | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 (Projected) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Total disclosed CVEs | ~40,000 | 48,185 | ~66,000 | 
| New CISA KEV entries | ~186 | 245 | ~290 – 300 pace | 
| Critical severity share | ~13% | ~7% | Trending lower | 
| Actively exploited | <1% | <1% | <1% | 
Table 1. Disclosure counts (NIST NVD) and CISA KEV entries (FIRST full-year projection)
According to the FIRST Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS), only around 5% of all published CVEs are ever observed being exploited. The CISA KEV catalog grew meaningfully, from 1,239 entries at the end of 2024 to 1,484 at the end of 2025, but that is a rounding error against the tens of thousands of new disclosures.
The challenge lies in the massive triage bottleneck that the vulnpocalypse will create; the NVD fully analyzed only about 28% of newly disclosed CVEs in 2025, but not a proportional explosion of exploitable risk, according to the Zafran analysis. NIST itself confirms the strain: the agency reported a 263% jump in submissions since 2020 and is now triaging enrichment by risk tier rather than analyzing every CVE.
Why the raw number is exploding
It should be noted that the surge in CVEs is not a sign that software suddenly became dramatically less secure, rather, it is driven by three structural factors:
AI-assisted discovery 
Autonomous bug-hunting is pointing frontier models at decades of legacy code. Models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI GPT 5.5 are highly effective at surfacing latent stability bugs. However, volume is not risk: the Linux kernel alone now accounts for more than 5,800 CVEs because its CVE Naming Authority (CNA) assigns an identifier to nearly every bugfix, even where no security impact is demonstrated. The real-world exploitation rate across that set sits near zero (on the order of 0.02%). Finding a flaw and having it weaponized are very different events.
Changes in structural reporting  
The discovery and cataloging infrastructure is catching up, inflating counts without changing actual exposure. This includes a roughly 449% year-over-year jump in GitHub Security Advisory volume and a large backlog of previously unassigned vulnerabilities finally being cataloged.
Product sprawl 
The number of distinct products with tracked vulnerabilities has grown by orders of magnitude. More software simply means more CVEs. This also applies to code: as more code is written into existence by AI and coding agents, more bugs are also written into existence. 
The real threat is speed, not volume
The metric that actually matters is speed. The window between disclosure and exploitation is collapsing from weeks to hours, and a rising share of exploitation now begins before a vendor patch is even public. In response, CISA recently retired its flat 14-day KEV remediation deadline in favor of a risk-based model that can demand action in as little as three days for the highest-risk combinations.
This is where AI Operational Excellence and proactive intelligence become mandatory. The TrendAI™ Zero Day Initiative™ (ZDI) exists to close this gap on the front end. Supported by more than 19,000 contributing researchers, TrendAI™ ZDI accounted for roughly 60% of the world’s coordinated disclosures in a 2023 independent tally, including 57% of critical-severity flaws, and turns those findings into protection that reaches customers an average of 115 days ahead of the vendor patch. When attackers weaponize zero-days against edge devices on day zero, pre-disclosure protection is no longer optional.
An action plan for security leaders
To weather what 2026 is set to bring, security programs must shift from counting raindrops to neutralizing the flood. Security leaders should be asking, “Are we still reporting CVE counts, or have we pivoted our metrics to exploitability?” The teams that succeed in 2026 will not be the ones who patched the most; they will be the ones who knew exactly what to patch first. The following best practices are recommended to minimize overwhelm and address vulnerabilities strategically:
Stop reporting raw CVE counts to the board 
Raw numbers frighten without informing. Report the actionable slices and trends based on the data on hand.
Triage KEV-first, then EPSS 
Confirmed exploitation is the sharpest filter available. Patch the top exploitability percentiles at zero-day urgency, and let the rest follow standard cadences.
Buy back time with virtual patching and containment 
When exploitation outpaces the fix or a vendor patch does not yet exist, shielding vulnerable systems at the network or workload layer neutralizes the exploit path without waiting on a code change. Virtual patching and containment turn the disclosure-to-patch gap from an open exposure window into a managed one, and they matter the most for exactly the small set of actively exploited flaws that triage surfaces.
Invest in automation, not a bigger patch treadmill 
Enrichment and triage loads are doubling while urgent live-system patching remains flat. Budget for intelligence that cuts through the noise.
Close the metadata gap 
A large share of new CVEs arrive without complete severity or product data. Lean on exploitability intelligence rather than raw catalog fields.

Description: This critical vulnerability in Langflow allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The flaw exists in handling of the exec_globals parameter at the validate endpoint, resulting from "inclusion of a resource from an untrusted control sphere." Attackers can achieve code execution with root privileges.

Severity: CVSS 3.0: 9.8 (Critical). Vector: CVSS:3.0/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. SSVC: Active exploitation, automatable, total technical impact.

Affected Product: Vendor/Product: Langflow / Langflow. Affected Version: 1.4.2 (confirmed affected through version 1.7.3).

Weakness Classification: CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere.

Key Dates: Published: January 23, 2026. Date Public: January 9, 2026. KEV Added: July 21, 2026. CISA Due Date: July 24, 2026.

References: ZDI Advisory: ZDI-26-036 (tracked as ZDI-CAN-27325). CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. Proof of concept available on GitHub. Fixed in Langflow v1.9.0.

Exploitation Status: Confirmed exploited with 80% confidence (vendor report). Listed in both CISA and KEVIntel known exploited vulnerability catalogs.

28ef2f4fa9b7.text:
Description: A vulnerability exists in DD-WRT's UPnP handling code (router/upnp/src/ssdp.c). An unsafe strcpy operation allows unauthenticated remote attackers to overflow an internal fixed buffer via M-SEARCH requests targeting the ssdp_msearch function. Exploitation requires UPnP to be enabled, which is disabled by default and typically limited to internal interfaces.

Severity: CVSS 3.1 Score: 8.1 (High). Vector: AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. CWE-121: Stack-based Buffer Overflow.

Affected Products: Vendor: DD-WRT. Product: DD-WRT. Affected Versions: All versions before build 45724.

Key Dates: Published: July 16, 2026. Updated: July 22, 2026. CISA KEV Added: July 21, 2026. CISA Action Due: July 24, 2026.

Exploitation Status: Active exploitation confirmed (80% confidence per CISA). Used by C0xmo botnet and related malware variants. Known exploited vulnerability in CISA and KEVIntel catalogs.

References: Patch: https://svn.dd-wrt.com/changeset/45724. SSD Disclosure Advisory: https://ssd-disclosure.com/ssd-advisory-dd-wrt-upnp-buffer-overflow/. CISA KEV: https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog?field_cve=CVE-2021-27137. Security coverage from Fortinet, BleepingComputer, and SecurityAffairs.

191d2a189316.text:
Description: This critical vulnerability affects WordPress versions 6.9.x before 6.9.5 and 7.0.x before 7.0.2. The flaw involves "a REST API batch endpoint route confusion issue which, combined with the author__not_in WP_Query SQL Injection (CVE-2026-60137), could allow an attacker to perform SQL Injection and achieve Remote Code Execution."

Severity: CVSS 9.8 (Critical): Full network-based exploitation without authentication or user interaction. CVSS 7.5 (High): Alternative scoring focusing on confidentiality impact. Status: Actively exploited in the wild.

Affected Products: Vendor: WordPress. Product: WordPress Core. Versions 6.9.0 through 6.9.4. Versions 7.0.0 through 7.0.1.

Key Details: CVE ID: CVE-2026-63030. Published: July 17, 2026. Updated: July 22, 2026. CWE: CWE-436 (Interpretation Conflict). Status: Listed in CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of July 21, 2026.

References: GitHub Security Advisory: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-ff9f-jf42-662q. WordPress Release Notes: https://wordpress.org/news/2026/07/wordpress-7-0-2-release/. CISA KEV Catalog Entry.

Mitigation: Immediate patching is required. If updates cannot be deployed, blocking unauthenticated access to /wp-json/batch/v1 via WAF is recommended.

68597a09b23d.text:
Microsoft halted its July security update for certain Dell devices following reports of serious hardware problems. The update, released as part of Patch Tuesday, contained a record-breaking number of CVE patches, including critical vulnerabilities under active exploitation.

According to Microsoft's support page, the company acknowledged that "this update might not be available for a limited number of Dell devices with Intel processors due to an incompatibility reported by Dell that can potentially cause unexpected shutdowns, poor performance, increased heat, and battery drain."

Rather than proceed, Microsoft stated: "We are working together with Dell to prevent the affected models from experiencing the issue and plan to release a resolution for affected devices in the coming days." The update became temporarily unavailable for impacted systems.

The timing proved particularly problematic given Microsoft's recent messaging emphasizing urgent patching needs. Just one week prior, the company had advocated strongly that users install patches immediately, citing the speed at which AI systems can detect and exploit vulnerabilities.

Microsoft later clarified that the issue affected Dell models with an Intel Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver and involved a new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface. The problem first appeared in preview updates on June 23.

The company indicated no workaround existed and promised a fix within days, maintaining the rollout pause for affected devices until resolution became available.

8473dec2a1e9.text:
Cybersecurity startup Empirical has raised $25 million in a Series A funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $37 million.

The new investment round was led by Brightmind Partners, with additional support from Costanoa Ventures, Hyde Park Angels (HPA), and other investors.

Founded in 2024, Chicago-based Empirical will use the fresh funding to accelerate the development of its two flagship products that help organizations predict and identify threats in the agentic AI era.

Empirical provides organizations with Foundation, a global cybersecurity model that monitors over 18,000 exploited CVEs for threat prediction, and Radiant, a predictive engine that can identify threats relevant to each organization's environment.

The predictive models deliver the intelligence that organizations need to discover risks within background noise. According to Empirical, its solutions provide security teams in technology, healthcare, and financial services with transparent, data-driven insights that enable them to measure and manage cyber risks.

Enhanced by AI and tailored to each organization's unique environment, the predictive models help prioritize remediation through deeper forecasting, evidence-based risk analysis, and actionable intelligence.

Empirical was co-founded by CEO Ed Bellis (co-founder of Kenna Security), CTO Michael Roytman (former Chief Data Scientist at Kenna), and Chief Data Scientist Jay Jacobs (co-creator of the Exploit Prediction Scoring System).

Bellis commented: "At Kenna we helped pioneer risk-based vulnerability management, but defending against AI threats needed a fundamentally new approach with predictive capabilities."

97a775d82ed2.text:
Fortinet announced it will use Intel Foundry to manufacture its sixth-generation Security Processor (SP6), representing a significant win for Intel's struggling foundry business.

The chips include dedicated accelerators for security and cryptographic operations required by modern hardware firewalls. Fortinet distinguishes itself by developing custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) rather than relying on commodity hardware like x86 and Arm processors, as many competing security vendors do.

Neither company disclosed production timelines or detailed specifications for the SP6. However, it's expected to exceed the capabilities of Fortinet's SP5 chips. The SP5, launched in 2023, supported layer 7 firewalling and IPsec VPN at speeds exceeding 30 Gbps. Performance decreased when advanced threat protection or SSL inspection was enabled, with throughput falling to 4.3 Gbps and 3.3 Gbps respectively.

The SP series targets smaller appliances including SD-WAN gateways rather than larger datacenter-focused systems using Fortinet's NP and CP-series processors.

Intel confirmed the SP6 will use the Intel 4 process node rather than the cutting-edge 18A technology. Fortinet may leverage "disaggregated semiconductor design and advanced packaging," potentially indicating a chiplet architecture for improved scalability.

The arrangement offers supply chain security advantages, as production occurs in an American facility by an American manufacturer—a rarity in advanced semiconductor manufacturing.

aeabb1e94ff8.text:
Virtual appliances play a critical role in cloud networks, providing services such as firewalls, secure gateways, and VPN connectivity. Yet, because they operate as "black boxes" that don't support traditional EDR agents, they represent a significant visibility gap for security teams. Wiz's Agentless Workload Detection addresses this by providing visibility into virtual appliances and enabling investigation of activity linked to high-profile threat actors, allowing detection and analysis of sophisticated attacks without requiring agent deployment.

The FortiGate Campaign Trail
FortiGate devices are high-value targets because they frequently face the internet and act as trusted gateways between external and internal networks. The research identified several critical exploitation patterns:
- CVE-2026-24858 Exploitation: Attackers exploited this zero-day to "create local super-user accounts and modify different settings, enabling lateral movement" and expanded impact.
- Credential Stuffing & FortiBleed: Coordinated campaigns using botnets targeted exposed admin panels, aligning with the broader FortiBleed campaign that compromised approximately 75,000 devices globally.
- Configuration Theft: Attackers downloaded full device configurations. Since FortiOS uses reversible encryption for stored credentials, stolen configs allowed actors to decrypt LDAP service accounts and VPN pre-shared keys for lateral movement.

Redis: Beyond Simple Cron Jobs
While Redis is secure by default when properly configured, exposed or misconfigured deployments remain frequently targeted in cloud environments. Most exploitation attempts focus on cryptojacking. The research detected attackers abusing replication methods like REPLICAOF to target Redis devices, where actors trick targets into syncing with malicious servers to inject shared object modules for remote code execution.

Threat detection rules include: "Redis suspicious replication target configured, Redis module loaded from unusual path" and "Attack Detected and Prevented by Redis."

Supply Chain Security: Detecting Malicious npm Packages
Supply chain attacks involving compromised npm packages represent a critical threat to modern application security. Agentless EDR successfully monitored and identified exploitation of npm dependencies in real time, capturing installation logs for malicious versions of @asyncapi/specs and enabling correlation of package activity with broader workload behavior.

Critical Vulnerabilities at Scale: PAN-OS and BeyondTrust
Recent years have featured high-profile RCE vulnerabilities in virtual appliances:
- PAN-OS: Actors successfully logged into admin accounts via CVE-2026-0257 in the PAN-OS VPN gateway. A spike in CaptivePortal URI traffic was observed shortly after CVE-2026-0300 disclosure.
- BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-1731): This critical pre-authentication RCE vulnerability affects BeyondTrust Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access software with a CVSS score of 9.9. Successful exploitation of these devices targeting unauthenticated administrative command execution was observed.

Case Study: The Zabbix API & Default Credentials
Agentless EDR provides visibility into HTTP and HTTPS endpoints, enabling detection of unusual activity and correlation with other cloud findings. An investigation beginning with an "Access To Unusual Executable File With HTTP GET And Query Params" detection led to identification of a Zabbix instance running from an unusual path with default credentials, allowing arbitrary code execution. This access proves dangerous because Zabbix manages hosts; with administrative permissions, attackers can create custom triggers executing arbitrary commands across managed instances.

CopyFail: Exploiting Linux Page Caches
Recent Linux LPE vulnerabilities, beginning with CopyFail, have been identified through Agentless EDR, which helped identify relevant workload activity consistent with successful exploitation using published techniques.

MongoBleed: Addressing Memory-Only Data Exposure
MongoBleed (CVE-2025-14847) is a critical unauthenticated memory leak vulnerability in MongoDB Server affecting handling of zlib-compressed network messages, allowing remote attackers to extract sensitive data from server memory without valid credentials. Following disclosure, the vulnerability was exploited in the wild almost immediately, and agentless visibility enabled identification of MongoDB activity associated with real-world exploitation attempts.

WordPress: Webshell deployed via wp2shell
HTTP access logs provide critical visibility into attack vectors targeting underlying web servers and hosted applications. Recently discovered was a webshell deployed on a WordPress instance by exploiting wp2shell vulnerabilities—a PHP webshell registering a custom REST API endpoint (/morning/v1/[REDACTED]) with permissive callback ('__return_true'), allowing attackers to send POST requests containing base64-encoded commands for execution.

Take Action: Unlock Agentless Visibility
To enable agentless workload detection:
1. Enable Defend Agentless Workload Detection through the Preview Hub
2. Verify workload/machine log ingestion is enabled in Event Management settings
3. Ensure Non-OS disk scanning is enabled for FortiGate log collection

Conclusion
Virtual appliances are no longer a blind spot. By automatically collecting local logs without deployment overhead, Agentless Workload Detection provides context to trace the full cloud kill chain. From zero-day exploitation in firewalls to misconfigured database APIs, this visibility enables investigation with greater depth and precision.

e203cb5bf4a6.text:
A large-scale operation dubbed 'FakeGit' is pushing SmartLoader and StealC malware through 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories that accumulated more than 14 million downloads.

Over 800 repositories pretended to be AI skills or MCP servers and appeared more than 600 times in public AI registries and catalogs. This increased the likelihood of being discovered by AI agents and developers, a technique that researchers call "agentbaiting."

The campaign is considered a continuation of an older operation that used Lumma Stealer and was attributed to a threat actor tracked as "Water Kurita" by researchers at cybersecurity company Trend Micro.

According to researchers at the enterprise browser platform Island, the AI focus was introduced in March and peaked in April, with the creation of 300 GitHub repositories linked to AI tools.

Researchers found that FakeGit grew to more than 1,400 repositories related to AI tools, agents, and workflows, all linking to SmartLoader or StealC malware downloads.

Many of the repositories imitate consumer and enterprise tools such as Gmail, WhatsApp, Databricks, Jenkins, and Docker, and include convincing documentation, fabricated stars and fork counts, copied project descriptions, and real developer account names.

Their README files direct visitors to download ZIP archives that pose as installers or project releases but are disguised Lua payloads that trigger SmartLoader.

Once SmartLoader is active, it establishes persistence through scheduled tasks, retrieves its command-and-control (C2) address through a Polygon smart contract, and downloads additional encrypted stages from GitHub, ultimately delivering the StealC information stealer.

The AgentBaiting Technique
Researchers at Island say the malicious repositories are part of an emerging technique they call AgentBaiting, designed to increase visibility to AI agents and improve chances of being used.

In a typical scenario, agents are likely to parse the README contents as legitimate documentation and recommend the repository or ZIP file to the human operator.

In Island's tests, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude surfaced various malicious repositories when prompted with related tasks, and sometimes relayed the installation instructions.

Island found in public registries and catalogs more than 600 listings for skills and MCP servers linked to the FakeGit campaign. Some included LobeHub, Glama, MCP.so, and MCP Market, indicating the operation has already penetrated the ecosystem and poisoned public resources.

The researchers could not determine if listings were submitted manually or indexed automatically, but said their presence made the repositories easier to discover and added to their credibility.

Island researchers told BleepingComputer that in limited, controlled testing, Claude Code cloned malicious repositories and downloaded the malicious files onto the test machine. However, the agent subsequently detected suspicious indicators and stopped before execution.

The tests were not designed to establish a detection rate, so they cannot provide conclusive results on whether coding agents can consistently recognize the danger during the execution stage.

Concerning the broader impact of the campaign, Island reports that GitHub's public download counters for 335 unique Release assets across 211 GitFake repositories recorded 14,084,688 cumulative download events.

Oleg Zaytsev, Lead Security Researcher at Island, clarified that this figure included repeated requests and automated activity, so it should not be interpreted as infections.

Island recommends that organizations maintain approved catalogs of skills and MCP servers, test new capabilities in isolated environments, and verify publishers and repositories independently.

Where SmartLoader execution is suspected, all secrets on impacted environments should be rotated immediately.

43623931b7cc.text:
Cisco has released two open-weight models designed to identify known vulnerabilities in existing code: Antares-350M and Antares-1B. These models are part of Cisco's new Antares family of security small language models (SLMs) and are available on Hugging Face, though access is restricted to vetted users.

DJ Sampath, Cisco's senior vice president and general manager of AI software and platform, explained that the company is carefully controlling access: "We're making sure we're gating that and appropriately granting access." The models are being made available to academic institutions, nonprofits, and smaller public sector security teams.

A key security advantage is that these small models run locally. Sampath noted that "you also need the keys to the source code" to scan for vulnerabilities, meaning attackers would need direct access to systems. Unlike cloud-based large language models, proprietary code remains on an organization's machines rather than being sent to external servers for processing.

The Antares name references a massive red supergiant star nearly 1,000 times larger than our sun. Amin Karbasi, Cisco's VP and chief AI scientist, explained the metaphor: vulnerabilities might affect only "a single file or a few lines of code in a million lines of code," yet carry enormous impact.

Cisco has created a new benchmark test measuring how efficiently AI models identify security flaws. According to the company, Antares-1B outperforms Google's Gemini 3 Pro and matches Z.ai's GLM-5.2. The unreleased Antares-3B reportedly surpasses GLM-5.2 and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 at vulnerability detection.

Performance metrics are dramatic. Karbasi stated: "Antares finishes the entire cohort of repositories in 15 minutes, whereas frontier models take five hours." Cost differences are equally striking—Antares costs under $1 to scan 500 repositories, while frontier models exceed $100-$150.

Karbasi emphasized Cisco's different approach: "Antares is inherently not a chatbot. It is an investigator. It is a search engine." The model employs multiple search strategies and adapts when one approach proves unfruitful. Its smaller size enables simultaneous searching across different methods.

Karbasi compared this efficiency to a bicycle on London streets versus a large truck, while Sampath offered another analogy: "Sometimes you don't need a private jet to go to a corner store, right?"

A future 3-billion-parameter Antares model will not be publicly released. Karbasi stated the company is "completely gating the 3B model to make sure that we responsibly release it to communities that need it."

306b2bfaa3de.text:
Oracle released its Critical Patch Update (CPU) for July 2026 on July 21, marking the third quarterly update of the year. This CPU contains fixes for 1235 unique CVEs distributed across 1449 security updates spanning 32 Oracle product families.

Severity Breakdown
Of the 1449 patches released, the distribution by severity was:
- Critical: 261 patches addressing 228 CVEs (18%)
- High: 763 patches addressing 613 CVEs (52.7%)
- Medium: 358 patches addressing 332 CVEs (24.7%)
- Low: 67 patches addressing 62 CVEs

Most Affected Product Families
Oracle E-Business Suite received the highest number of patches at 410, representing 28.3% of all patches. Oracle Fusion Middleware followed with 355 patches (24.5% of total).

The analysis provided a comprehensive table showing patch distribution across 32 product families, including counts of vulnerabilities exploitable over a network without authentication.

Recommendation
"Customers are advised to apply all relevant patches in this quarter's CPU." Tenable noted that a list of plugins to identify these vulnerabilities would be released through their standard channels.

ede5e89030ee.text:
Affordable government cloud security means meeting NIST SP 800-53, CISA's Binding Operational Directives (BOD), and compliance mandates without exceeding constrained public sector budgets. The core tension is straightforward: compliance obligations keep expanding while IT spending stays flat, and fragmented security tooling drives up both licensing costs and staff overhead.

Most public sector cloud security teams are managing too many tools, spending too many hours on manual compliance reporting, and still falling short on coverage for ephemeral cloud workloads. This article covers a four-part framework for reducing cloud security costs in government: consolidating your tool stack, adopting agentless architecture, mapping compliance obligations before procurement, and automating continuous compliance. Each part is designed to be actionable within existing procurement constraints.

Why Government Cloud Security Costs Have Become a Structural Problem
Public sector organizations face a unique cost problem. They must satisfy FedRAMP®, NIST SP 800-53, and GovRAMP™ mandates to operate cloud workloads, but their procurement cycles and budget allocations haven't kept pace with the complexity of modern multi-cloud environments. The result is a growing gap between what compliance requires and what budgets allow.

Tool sprawl is a major driver. According to Gartner research, large organizations commonly operate dozens of overlapping security products. Every additional tool adds licensing fees, integration work, maintenance windows, and staff training hours. A CNAPP consolidates these capabilities into a single platform, directly reducing both licensing overhead and the staff hours required for multi-cloud compliance reporting.

The Compliance-Budget Trap: FedRAMP Requirements vs. Flat IT Spending
This is a structural constraint, not a planning failure. Government agencies operate under procurement rules that allocate budgets annually or biennially, while compliance requirements from NIST and FedRAMP® expand on their own timeline.

Consolidate Your Security Tool Stack Before Adding New Tools
The highest-leverage cost reduction available to most government security teams is consolidation. Replacing a fragmented collection of CSPM, CWPP, vulnerability management, and compliance reporting tools with a unified platform eliminates redundant licensing and frees staff hours.

Prioritize Agentless, Instant-On Security to Eliminate Deployment Overhead
Agent-based security tools impose a hidden labor cost. Agentless architecture deploys in minutes and requires no per-workload maintenance, avoiding agent-based supply chain risk.

Map Your Compliance Obligations Before You Scope Your Platform
Government organizations frequently overspend by scoping platforms for frameworks they don't need, or underspend by selecting platforms that can't support required frameworks. A FedRAMP® Authorized platform has completed the full assessment process and received an Authority to Operate; a FedRAMP® Ready platform has completed a Readiness Assessment Report but cannot yet be procured for federal use.

Automate Continuous Compliance to Eliminate Manual Audit Overhead
Manual compliance reporting consumes significant staff time and introduces human error. Automated continuous compliance monitoring converts periodic audits into a persistent operational capability, including real-time framework mapping, automated evidence collection, drift detection, and pre-built audit-ready reporting.

How Orca Security Delivers Affordable Cloud Security for Government
Orca Security maps directly to each part of this framework, backed by both GovRAMP™ authorization and FedRAMP® Moderate authorization.
- Consolidation: Orca's unified platform combines CSPM, CWPP, vulnerability management, and compliance reporting.
- Agentless Architecture: Orca's patented agentless SideScanning™ technology deploys in minutes with zero agent overhead.
- Compliance Mapping: Orca supports over 180 out-of-the-box compliance frameworks, including FedRAMP® and GovRAMP™.
- Continuous Compliance: Orca's Agentic AI automates continuous compliance enforcement and evidence collection.

The University of Oklahoma case study demonstrates these capabilities in a government and education environment, where Orca replaced multiple point tools and delivered unified visibility across a complex cloud footprint.

FAQ section covers procurement vehicles (GSA MAS, NASA SEWP, agency BPAs), cost variability for small agencies, the definition and distinction of GovRAMP™ vs FedRAMP®, CNAPP consolidation benefits, and how agentless architecture reduces total cost of ownership for public sector agencies.

d0ecf7f33af6.text:
Microsoft's guidance on inbound and outbound mail routing for third-party email security has prompted a fair question from customers: how should organizations evaluate inline email security for Microsoft 365?

The answer depends less on whether a solution is inline and more on how that inline architecture is implemented. Microsoft is right to call attention to mail flow designs that can introduce unnecessary complexity, create authentication challenges, duplicate processing, or disrupt the expected Microsoft 365 experience. Those risks are real when a third-party service is bolted onto the environment without careful integration.

That is also why architecture matters. A modern enterprise email security layer should preserve authentication, maintain message integrity, respect Microsoft 365 mail flow, and give security teams stronger prevention without forcing users or administrators into a fragmented operating model. Check Point Email Security was designed with those requirements in mind.

Mail Routing Guidance Is Really About Implementation Quality
Microsoft's documentation is best understood as guidance for avoiding poor mail routing implementations, not as a blanket statement against inline security.

How Check Point Fits Into the Microsoft 365 Mail Flow
Check Point, a founding member of the Microsoft Intelligent Security Association, has been a Microsoft Partner for three decades. Microsoft Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender continue to apply their controls first, after which the message is inspected by Check Point Email Security before final delivery to the user.

This placement gives organizations an additional prevention point for advanced phishing, business email compromise, credential harvesting, QR code phishing, zero-day malware, and emerging AI-driven threats before the message reaches the inbox.

To help preserve authentication and message integrity, Check Point uses Authenticated Received Chain (ARC). Check Point also aligns with Microsoft routing practices through trusted connector and sender configurations.

Why Pre-Delivery Prevention Is Becoming More Critical
API-based approaches can be useful for finding and removing threats after delivery, but they still create a period of exposure. This is especially relevant as organizations adopt Microsoft Copilot and other AI-powered productivity tools, where techniques such as indirect prompt injection delivered through email can influence AI systems soon after a message arrives.

Complementing Microsoft Defender With Specialized Email Prevention
Check Point is not positioned as a replacement for Microsoft Defender. It adds an independent prevention layer that operates before delivery while preserving the Microsoft 365 experience.

What Enterprises Should Take Away
Microsoft's mail routing guidance reinforces that architecture matters. Check Point Email Security is designed to maintain clean mail flow while adding pre-delivery inspection against threats increasingly difficult for a single control point to catch alone.

4b3906976cf5.text:
AI models will do just about anything to complete the task you ask, including cheating to get there, according to new cybersecurity evaluations from the UK government's AI Security Institute (AISI). The group found that leading models often take shortcuts to achieve a particular result and then misrepresent how they obtained that result. And they won't always admit it when asked.

"Every model we have tested for this behaviour attempted to cheat," AISI said in a blog post on Tuesday. "Models did not reliably report this behaviour when asked, and often did not reason about it in their chain-of-thought, suggesting that detecting cheating will likely require robust monitoring methods."

Infractions included searching the internet for the answer, bypassing sandbox network restrictions, probing the evaluation harness, attacking a system other than the target, and guessing an answer.

Cheating in this manner has been widely documented by machine learning researchers. It doesn't necessarily imply malicious intent, AISI said, but it's nonetheless troublesome because it can produce misleading assessments of model capabilities.

When AISI evaluated five leading models, it found that all of them cheated. The results were as follows:
- GPT-5.4 cheated 67 times in 475 test runs (14.1 percent)
- GPT-5.5 cheated 54 times in 475 test runs (11.4 percent)
- GPT-5.6-Sol cheated 60 times in 475 test runs (12.6 percent)
- Claude 4.7 Opus cheated 43 times in 475 test runs (9.1 percent)
- Claude Mythos Preview cheated 37 times in 475 test runs (7.8 percent)

Asking models whether they cheated or did anything wrong proved an unreliable auditing mechanism because the models didn't always admit wrongdoing.

"In our experiments, models did not consistently acknowledge attempted cheating when asked, and described it as wrong less than 50 percent of the time," said AISI.

Existing vetting methods, such as self-reporting and chain-of-thought logs, proved similarly problematic because models don't always report their chain-of-thought. There were instances where a model would consider whether a proposed action amounted to cheating and then decided to take the action anyway.

Given the absence of reliable model cheating detection methods, AISI warns that its current approach – manual review coupled with LLM monitoring – may not be sufficient to catch deception, particularly as models become more sophisticated.

"A more fundamental fix would be to train the models not to cheat in the first place – but given this kind of behaviour was reported in frontier models more than a year ago, robustly aligning it away may not be easy," AISI concludes.

3d4530951c37.text:
Colin Wood reports:
At least one municipal government was among those to see their internet service disrupted after a cyberattack against a Maine telecommunications firm Sunday caused an outage affecting 23 towns along the state’s midcoastal region.
A local NBC affiliate reported that the government office of Damariscotta, a tourist town of roughly 2,300 inhabitants, known for its oysters, experienced unreliable or unavailable internet service following a cyberattack against Tidewater Telecom.
“The Town Office currently has spotty to no internet service,” read a public notice issued Monday by the town of Damariscotta, a name reputedly derived from an Algonquian word meaning “place of abundance of small fish.” “Since the majority of town office services rely on the internet, we are significantly limited in what we can accomplish this morning.”
Read more at StateScoop.

b343db126a97.text:
The Anubis ransomware gang has claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Coca-Cola's Fairlife dairy subsidiary, asserting they stole approximately one terabyte of corporate data and threatening to publish it unless the company negotiates by week's end.

Fairlife, which produces ultra-filtered milk products and protein shakes distributed across the United States, had its operations disrupted by the ransomware attack. Coca-Cola disclosed the incident on July 16, noting that attackers accessed production-related systems, though product quality and safety remained unaffected.

According to the threat actors, they "attacked their systems a week ago" and encrypted Fairlife's Nutanix infrastructure. The group stated the company "immediately reported the incident without attempting to follow the instructions we left on their network."

Anubis operates as a ransomware-as-a-service platform that emerged in December 2024, combining data theft with file encryption to pressure victims into paying ransoms. The gang previously added data-wiping capabilities to its toolkit.

Coca-Cola declined to comment when contacted about the claims, and BleepingComputer could not independently verify the gang's allegations regarding data theft, encryption scope, or the volume of stolen information.

(Author: Lawrence Abrams; Published: July 21, 2026, 2:50 PM)

dc31387ff37e.text:
Apple has addressed a security vulnerability in its Hide My Email service that allowed users' actual email addresses to be revealed, undermining the feature's privacy protections.

According to 404 Media, Apple deployed a fix on July 3, 2026, more than a year after the issue was initially disclosed to the company by Tyler Murphy, co-founder of EasyOptOuts.

Hide My Email generates unique, random email addresses that automatically forward messages to a user's personal inbox. This feature aims to protect privacy and reduce spam through disposable email addresses. The service requires an iCloud+ subscription and was introduced by Apple in June 2021.

The flaw made it possible to unmask a user's genuine email address hidden behind a Hide My Email address. The problem was first reported to Apple on June 13, 2025. The company attempted unsuccessful patches in March and again on June 30, 2026.

Simply sending a targeted Hide My Email user a message that got rejected as spam caused the person's real email address to appear in email logs.

Murphy and EasyOptOuts co-founder Ben Weiner noted that for many major email hosts, the leak was triggered by emails being automatically rejected as spam, even legitimate messages.

Real email addresses linked to Hide My Email addresses created before July 7, 2026, may have been captured in mail transfer logs when non-malicious emails were bounced.

Apple currently faces a class action lawsuit accusing the company of misleading customers about Hide My Email's privacy while charging for the feature and failing to fix the known problem for over a year.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan; Published: July 21, 2026)

6d443c83c400.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring the Department of War to establish new rules for mapping and securing critical defense supply chains. The order focuses on protecting defense systems against "physical, cyber, and economic subversion" and demands greater visibility into suppliers and subcontractors across all tiers.

Key Requirements: Within 180 days, the Secretary of War must develop policies requiring defense contractors to map critical supply chains. Contractors must submit a complete "indentured Bill of Materials" tracing components, equipment, software and materials through the supply chain to raw material sources.

The documentation scope extends beyond traditional software bills of materials, potentially connecting software dependencies with physical components, manufacturers, suppliers, maintenance information, countries of origin and raw-material sources. This could bring software developers, cloud providers and managed service providers within the regulations, even when several layers removed from prime contractors.

Supplier Vetting Requirements: Contractors must establish written procedures for proactively vetting suppliers, considering financial stability, foreign ownership or influence, and manufacturing risks. They must identify sole-source dependencies, inadequate production capacity and supplier concentration issues.

Significant supply chain risks must be reported to the Department of War within 15 days after vetting completion. Contractors then have 45 days to submit confidential corrective action plans.

Additional Provisions: Starting January 1, 2027, waivers allowing acquisition of covered materials from prohibited sources become more restrictive. Contractors whose supply chains depend on unreliable foreign suppliers must qualify and move to alternative sources promptly or risk contract suspension or termination.

The order directs the Department of War to use artificial intelligence and available tools to analyze contractor acquisition information and identify national security vulnerabilities and bottlenecks.

Cybersecurity Implications: The comprehensive supply chain maps required create potential cybersecurity risks themselves. Such detailed databases connecting defense systems to software dependencies, suppliers, and operational bottlenecks could attract foreign intelligence services and threat actors seeking single points of failure and vulnerable dependencies.

Defense contractors may need to implement strict access controls, encryption, audit logging, data loss prevention and compartmentalization to protect this sensitive information.

(Author: SecurityWeek News; Published: July 21, 2026, 2:16 PM ET)

602ff572409a.text:
Orca Extends AI Security Platform with Integration to Claude's Compliance API

Anyone who can prompt Claude is now a builder. Engineers are writing code with it. Analysts are drafting research with it. Operators are creating dashboards with it. Support teams are answering tickets with it. Whole business functions are quietly being rewired around it. Claude is enabling an explosion of builders inside organizations of all sizes.

Claude adoption is happening faster than most security programs can track. New users are being added, admins are configuring org settings, projects are being created and shared, and none of it is flowing through the tools security teams already rely on.

Today, we're closing that gap. Orca now connects to Claude's Compliance API, bringing Claude Enterprise organizations into the same platform Orca customers already use to secure the infrastructure, code, and AI assets in cloud-native apps.

Why this needs to live inside your cloud security platform: For the last decade, security teams have done the hard work of mapping identities, permissions, data stores, and workloads across cloud providers. AI platforms recreate every one of those problems in a new place: identities that can escalate, projects that can be over-shared, retention and training settings that can quietly change data exposure, network egress that can create exfiltration paths.

Treating that as a separate problem with a separate tool, a separate inventory, and a separate alert queue is how the last generation of cloud security ended up with 6+ point tools and no context to correlate them. Doing it again for AI is a step backward.

What Orca sees in Claude Enterprise: The integration uses a read-only Compliance API key. It deploys in minutes and never touches chat or file content. What Orca ingests today is the configuration and identity layer: organizations and org settings (SSO enforcement, IP allowlist, session-duration limits, data retention, content redaction, model-training opt-in, org-wide project sharing, code-execution egress); users; groups; roles and role bindings; projects (name, owner, visibility); and chat metadata (name, owner, model, timestamp, visibility — metadata only, never content).

Every one of these becomes a first-class asset in Orca's Unified Data Model, alongside existing cloud accounts.

Coverage and context to drive decisions: Identity and access — Orca surfaces privilege sprawl, shadow identity outside SSO/SCIM, and gaps in session and network scope. Data security — Orca flags how prompts, outputs, and files are shared, stored, and consumed inside Claude, covering project visibility, content redaction, retention, and model-training opt-in.

Secure Claude through your existing workflows: benefits described for security engineers (unified graph with AWS accounts/data stores), compliance leads (single-platform audit of access, SSO/retention enforcement), and IT/platform teams (visibility into project sprawl and configuration drift).

Getting connected: This integration requires a Claude Enterprise plan and a Compliance API key generated by the primary owner. Only two read-only scopes are needed: read:compliance_org_data and read:compliance_user_data.

About the Orca Platform: The Orca Platform identifies, prioritizes, and remediates risks and compliance issues across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Oracle Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, and now Claude Enterprise.

69ac54ec284e.text:
As AI tools proliferate and become deeply ingrained in software development around the world, new research from the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike shows how attackers are actively targeting the AI toolchain to steal access credentials, gain deeper access to a target environment, exfiltrate sensitive data, and even destroy target files and systems—all while finding new ways to cover their tracks.

Researchers discovered a worm in the wild while investigating AI software supply chain attacks. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work, says that the company has not yet attributed the activity to a specific actor, but that it fits into larger evolutions in how attackers like TeamPCP (which CrowdStrike tracks as “Altered Spider”) and North Korean groups are targeting the AI software supply chain.

“This is one of the campaigns that we’ve seen showing that this is an emerging attack class,” Meyers tells WIRED. “As AI coding agents become the development standard, supply chain threats are evolving to exploit those trust relationships. For the first time we’re experiencing how much AI and the AI toolchain has played into the broader tech ecosystem.”

The worm CrowdStrike identified works in phases. First it does reconnaissance to assess the target environment. Then it looks for access tokens and other sensitive data, like cryptographic keys and server access credentials that it can deliver to attackers. As the malware gains privileges, it further unpacks itself and continues to grab credentials, particularly “npm" tokens that give access to key software package management servers and other development capabilities like pull requests.

The deeper the malware bores into the system, the more sensitive data it can grab. At this point, the malware can also deploy its destructive capability, or what Meyers calls a “death switch,” to destroy files or block legitimate access to the compromised infrastructure.

The key finding, though, is that much of the worm's malicious activity takes place in what are essentially blind spots, because so much of its behavior mimics legitimate actions. “It's like a needle in a haystack, except this is a needle in a needle stack,” Meyers says. “This looks very much like a lot of the automation organizations are using to build code, so it’s very difficult to detect.”

Meyers adds, too, that in these AI software development pipelines, it is harder to gather the data points that security scanners and analysis tools traditionally use to detect potentially suspicious activity.

“There’s a lot of telemetry overlap because legitimate AI coding systems are operating the same way as this worm, so it becomes very difficult to discern from the telemetry you have available to you what is legitimate and what is illegitimate,” Meyers says.

To hide in plain sight even more insidiously, the authors of the worm included time delays where various capabilities will execute hours or even days after the groundwork is laid, making it even harder for defenders to establish a cause and effect of certain events leading to certain outcomes.

Meyers says that CrowdStrike has been working on strategies to connect more of the dots, but he emphasizes that as AI software development explodes, there is a pressing need for all players to collaborate on structural solutions.

“It’s a limited detection surface because only so much of this activity is actually going to produce any sort of telemetry signal for us to look at,” Meyers says, “so it becomes extremely onerous to determine what is legitimate and what is illegitimate behavior.”

08073abe0ca5.text:
Hidden text on a web page was enough to make Kiro, AWS's agentic coding IDE, rewrite its own configuration file and run an attacker's code on a developer's machine, with no approval step able to stop it.

Intezer, in research with Kodem Security, found that a request as ordinary as asking Kiro to summarize a page could end in remote code execution. AWS has patched the issue and says it is covered by CVE-2026-10591.

Kiro's safety model rests on a human clicking "allow." The agent can run shell commands, fetch URLs, and edit files, and the design assumes a developer reviews anything risky before it happens. That approval step is the security boundary, and the flaw let an attacker slip past it without the developer ever being offered a choice.

The weak point was the file that tells Kiro which external tools to load. Kiro reads its list of Model Context Protocol servers, and the exact command used to start each one, from ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json.

When that file changes, Kiro reloads it and launches whatever it describes, on the host, with the developer's privileges. At the time of the research, Kiro could write to mcp.json on its own with its fsWrite tool, no approval required, and reload it automatically.

Anyone who could influence the contents of that file could register a server whose start command was arbitrary code, and it would run the moment Kiro reloaded.

Getting text into Kiro's context is the easy part. The agent pulls in outside content whenever a developer asks it to fetch a URL, read documentation, or search the web. Intezer's proof of concept planted its instructions in one-pixel white text (color:#fff;font-size:1px) on an otherwise ordinary API documentation page.

The developer sees a clean API reference. Kiro reads the hidden block as a setup task, writes the malicious server into mcp.json, and reloads. Within seconds, the rogue server starts, and the attacker's code is running.

In Intezer's demo, the payload only phoned home with the machine's hostname, username, and platform every ten seconds, just enough to prove execution. The same primitive could run any command available to the developer, enough to steal credentials and source code, plant persistence, or pivot into whatever internal systems they can reach.

The researchers kept their callback pointed at localhost so no real Kiro users were exposed, and they note the attack is not perfectly reliable: the model is non-deterministic and may summarize the page and ignore the hidden block. In their testing, it worked within one or two tries. One success is all it takes.

Kiro did, in some cases, show a pop-up saying the MCP configuration had changed and asking for approval. It made no difference. The configuration reloaded regardless of what the developer clicked, so the warning offered no real protection. The only action the developer ever actually approved was fetching a URL.

Kiro had been here before: An agent able to write the file that governs what it is allowed to run has surfaced in Kiro before. On Kiro's release day in July 2025, Johann Rehberger of Embrace The Red showed the same mcp.json write-to-execution move: a prompt injection dropped custom code into an MCP settings file and ran it the moment the file saved.

He flagged a second route too, writing to .vscode/settings.json to allowlist shell commands. AWS's response, Kiro 0.1.42, added an approval prompt for those writes, but only in Supervised mode. The default Autopilot mode kept writing the file on its own, and that is the mode Intezer's 2026 chain used. No CVE was issued then either.

Others found neighboring versions of the same class. Cymulate reported that Kiro would auto-execute code written to .vscode/tasks.json when a folder was opened. AWS assigned it CVE-2026-10591 (8.8 under CVSS 3.1, 8.6 under CVSS 4.0) and fixed it in the 0.11 series.

Intezer's mcp.json chain was still live on versions 0.9.2 (macOS) and 0.10.16 (Ubuntu) when the company reported it in February 2026, and was confirmed patched in v0.11.130.

AWS's answer was to stop trusting the model's judgment on these files and move the check into the platform. Kiro now marks mcp.json, .vscode/tasks.json, the .git directory, and other sensitive files as protected paths, each requiring explicit approval before a write.

Its own documentation makes the point directly: "Supervised mode is a code review workflow, not a security control." The 1.0 release that followed leans harder on the same principle, with a capability-based permissions model that prompts for consent on anything a developer has not already allowed.

That combination closes the route Intezer took: Intezer confirmed the attack failed in 0.11.130, and, unlike the 2025 fix, the protected-paths check holds in both Autopilot and Supervised mode.

Intezer reported the flaw through HackerOne on February 11, 2026, and by April 3 AWS said the fix had shipped in its latest release without naming the version; the researchers confirmed it themselves in v0.11.130.

No separate CVE was issued for their report. Intezer reported no in-the-wild exploitation, and its testing covered Kiro IDE; it did not establish whether the separate Kiro CLI or Web builds shared the flaw.

Current builds are on the 1.0.x line, with 1.0.165 listed as the latest as of July 21, 2026, and anyone on an older version should update from Kiro's downloads page.

AWS told The Hacker News the mode gap was a separate issue rather than a fix that lapsed. The 2025 remediation, Kiro 0.1.42, "required human-in-the-loop confirmation for modifying in Supervised mode only," the company said, and "the default Autopilot mode was addressed in the 2026 remediation as a separate issue."

It pointed to bulletin 2026-037 and CVE-2026-10591 as where that work landed, and said every build before 0.11.34 was affected, with 0.11.34 the first to add mcp.json to the protected-paths list.

The published bulletin is narrower than that. It describes writes to execution-sensitive paths, gives .vscode/tasks.json as its example, credits Cymulate, and lists impacted versions as everything before 0.11. It does not mention mcp.json or 0.11.34, and Kiro's 0.11 changelog does not record the protected-path change.

Over roughly a year, three separate research efforts found the same shape of bug in Kiro: an agent quietly editing the files that decide what it is allowed to execute. Kiro is not alone: in December 2025, researchers catalogued more than 30 flaws across AI coding tools, Cursor and Copilot among them, all turning legitimate editor features into prompt-injection paths to code execution or data theft.

The current fixes all point to the same lesson: the control that works sits in the platform, enforced in every mode and outside anything the model can be told to change.

As more of the development workflow moves to agents that read the open web, a human in the loop only works as a control if the human is shown the step that matters, and the platform holds the line even after the model has been completely talked into crossing it.

c12f20c58fc1.text:
Most of us think privacy is a setting. Open a private browsing window. Clear your history. Reject a few cookies. Maybe install an ad blocker. Problem solved, right? Not exactly.

That is one of the central themes explored in a recent episode of Cybercrime: From the Frontline, The Privacy Illusion: What They Know About You.

Privacy: It's Complicated. The reality is that privacy in 2026 is far more complicated than most people realize. Information we share can be used against us in cybercrime or marketed for a profit in advertising. Every day, we generate enormous amounts of data through browsing, video, social media, navigation apps, Wi-Fi, shopping, and smartphone sensors—creating a digital footprint, or "digital exhaust." Much of this information isn't collected because we actively share it; it's collected because of how modern technology works.

Will Private Browsing Hide My Searches? Private/incognito mode mainly prevents your own device from storing history; ISPs, websites, ad platforms, and third parties can still observe traffic.

Am I Being Tracked Across Devices? Yes for most people, since ad networks and data brokers connect information across smartphones, laptops, tablets, smart TVs, wearables, and connected home tech to build detailed behavioral profiles.

What Is Real-Time Bidding in Advertising and What Is Shared About Me? Before an ad appears, information about your device, location, interests and behavior may be shared across a network of advertisers bidding for the impression—even losing bidders may receive data about you.

If I Disable GPS Is My Location Hidden? No—phones can often be located via nearby Wi-Fi networks and Bluetooth signals even without GPS, placing you within a small radius. Seemingly harmless posts (vacation photos, landmarks, routines) can also be aggregated into detailed profiles useful to attackers, advertisers, and data brokers.

Steps to Increasing Your Privacy: use privacy-focused browsers; review app permissions regularly; limit unnecessary applications; be thoughtful about what you post; learn how AI services use your information; monitor for data breaches; use identity monitoring tools where appropriate.

(Author: Bruce Sussman; Published: July 21, 2026)

98d6f581a699.text:
Cybercriminals are increasingly moving away from complex malware, relying instead on social engineering that exploits a common user habit: mindlessly clicking through endless digital rituals like CAPTCHAs, cookie consents, and authentication prompts. This habit is often targeted by various kinds of the ClickFix technique, which threat actors have been actively using lately. Researchers recently discovered a new variant of this technique, which they dubbed ConsentFix. It allows attackers to gain unauthorized access to Microsoft 365 accounts via OAuth—a highly popular vector right now—thereby completely bypassing the need to steal passwords. For organizations, these attacks present a severe risk of compromised corporate email, exposed documents, and breached cloud resources.

How ConsentFix Works: Attackers prompt the user to follow a seemingly harmless set of instructions that actually lead to compromise.
