A male registered nurse from northern Sydney has been charged after allegedly downloading the data of multiple patients.
Police received a report on Wednesday, July 22, that a NSW Health employee had allegedly accessed and downloaded patient information without authorisation.
Detectives launched an investigation under Strike Force Civic and, after inquiries, searched a home in Frenchs Forest at about 7.30pm the next day.
During the operation, police seized several electronic devices which they allege contained patient information.
A 59-year-old man, who is employed by the Northern Sydney Local Health District, was arrested and taken to Manly Police Station.
Read more at Daily Mail.

5370f4efe275.text:
Jessica Lyons reports on today’s entry in the “No Need to Hack When It’s Leaking” files:
Click To Pray, a prayer app endorsed by the Pope with hundreds of thousands of users worldwide, has leaked people’s names and email addresses for months – or longer – according to an ethical hacker who said she found and reported the security vulnerability six months ago to no avail. This app needs to take a vow of silence when it comes to your personal information.
The app, available in seven languages and on iOS, Android, and clicktopray.org, is the official app of the Pope’s Worldwide Prayer Network. It connects users across the globe to pray for the Holy Father’s intentions, and as of July 2026, it has 719,517 registered accounts.
It’s also very leaky, according to security sleuth BobDaHacker, who says she spotted and disclosed the vulnerability to the Pope’s Worldwide Prayer Network on January 3.
Read more at The Register.

c5798ef762be.text:
Threat actors are using email addresses exposed in data breaches leaked by the ShinyHunters extortion group to send sextortion emails demanding $2,000 in Bitcoin.

The emails claim to come from ShinyHunters and tell recipients that hackers compromised their devices after obtaining their email addresses from breached company databases. However, the messages appear to be sent by someone who downloaded data previously leaked by ShinyHunters rather than by the extortion group itself, using the exposed email addresses to make the threats appear more legitimate.

BleepingComputer has seen leaked data from the Amtrak, Hallmark, Substack, Betterment, CarGurus, ADT, Panera Bread, and McGraw Hill breaches used in this sextortion email campaign. For some recipients, BleepingComputer confirmed that the email addresses targeted by the sextortion emails were actually included in the associated data previously leaked by ShinyHunters.

The emails are sent from random addresses using names like "ShinyHunters" or "You've Been HACKED" with subject lines reading "Information about your online security." They falsely claim attackers installed exploits on victims' devices, accessed microphones and cameras, and recorded them visiting adult websites. The sender demands $2,000 in Bitcoin within 48 hours and warns recipients not to contact police or reset devices.

However, there is no indication that the sender compromised recipients' devices, installed malware, or obtained any of the described information. The campaign appears to have started in April, with numerous people and organizations reporting similar messages. BleepingComputer contacted ShinyHunters, who denied involvement in the sextortion campaign.

Recipients should not pay the ransom or respond to these messages.

77412b7c43ee.text:
Insurance phishing operations have fundamentally shifted their approach. Rather than harvesting credentials for delayed exploitation, attackers now "synchronize their activity with victims in real time, authenticating against legitimate insurance portals as victims unknowingly complete the login process."

The threat landscape has transformed from traditional credential theft to what researchers term "session-time compromise." Attackers leverage phishing pages as live intermediaries, intercepting one-time passwords and other verification codes before they expire, enabling account access during the victim's active browsing session.

Threat actors primarily distribute malicious pages through sponsored Google advertisements targeting insurance-related search queries. These fake sites closely replicate legitimate insurance provider interfaces and utilize disposable hosting platforms like GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Wix to evade detection.

CTM360 identified a previously undocumented phishing framework offering real-time victim monitoring, backend administrative dashboards, manual approval workflows, and Telegram Bot integrations for instant credential submission notifications.

Defenders must move beyond identifying individual phishing domains toward understanding complete attacker operations, including infrastructure, tooling, and workflow methodologies. This represents a critical shift from Digital Risk Protection toward comprehensive Cyber Threat Intelligence capabilities.

The full report is available through CTM360's platform.

9ec1d53460e9.text:
The DevMan ransomware-as-a-service operation maintains a centralized web portal enabling affiliates to construct payloads, track earnings, and oversee victim-related activities. Swiss cybersecurity firm PRODAFT monitors this coordinated RaaS scheme under the designation "Funky Mantis."

The platform integrates payload generation, financial management, victim communication, support functions, victim record-keeping, team administration, and payout mechanisms. "The service integrated access brokerage or access distribution with ransomware deployment. Administrators offered country-specific 'networks,' asked whether an affiliate would use personal or program-supplied access, and imposed two-to-three-day completion windows."

DevMan emerged in April 2025 as an affiliate for multiple ransomware groups before launching independent operations. Security researchers at Vectra AI identified strong connections to DragonForce ransomware. The operators claim development of specialized SCADA targeting capabilities designed to force industrial systems beyond operational limits, potentially causing hardware failure through thermal stress.

The operation experienced disruption in June 2025 when a whistleblower identified "GangExposed" publicly disclosed operator identities, prompting some affiliate departures. The threat group subsequently alleged extortion attempts ranging from 0.3 to 1 Bitcoin.

According to Ransomware.Live statistics, DevMan claimed 184 victims through February 4, 2026, with approximately 50 located in the United States across technology, healthcare, financial services, professional services, and government sectors.

The latest portal iteration (version 3, released January 2026) incorporates structured victim documentation, lifecycle management, team creation controls, per-victim build customization, deadline monitoring, revenue tracking, and shared operational access capabilities.

PRODAFT identified five distinct operational roles: LARVA-367 (administrator/coordinator), LARVA-546 (access coordinator), LARVA-547 and LARVA-548 (senior operators), and LARVA-550 (affiliate operator).

Affiliate governance restricts autonomy—new operators gain access only after demonstrating initial victim compromise and face removal after one month without additional victims. Management reserves authority to assume control during operational violations. Ransom proceeds follow an 80-20 split favoring affiliates.

Targeting policy permits operations against non-CIS entities while prohibiting attacks on CIS consulates and Serbia. The framework explicitly encourages critical infrastructure targeting while forbidding attacks against pediatric healthcare facilities and unauthorized disclosure of minors' personal information.

The Windows locker variant incorporates privilege verification, security control impairment, process termination, recovery inhibition, event log clearing, network discovery, lateral movement, multithreaded encryption, ransom note generation, and optional self-deletion functionality.

Encryption employs ChaCha20-Poly1305 algorithms. Files under 3 megabytes receive complete encryption, while larger files undergo partial encryption processing—one megabyte per fifty-one megabyte intervals.

The report coincides with allegations from former Huntress employee Ben Folland accusing a current Huntress analyst of transferring law enforcement communications to DevMan in December 2025. Huntress CEO Kyle Hanslovan acknowledged "questionable, long-term threat actor communications" while characterizing the disclosure as demonstrating "poor judgment" rather than illegal conduct.

Folland disputed this assessment, arguing the actions "meet the definition of an insider threat," particularly given the forwarding of FBI communications containing agent identities directly to the investigated threat actor.

de5b045a1876.text:
This weekly roundup covers major cybersecurity incidents and developments from the previous week, featuring critical vulnerabilities, breaches, and emerging threats.

ServiceNow Vulnerability (CVE-2026-6875): A critical pre-authentication code injection flaw in ServiceNow's AI Platform is being actively exploited. The vulnerability permits unauthenticated attackers to escape the script sandbox and achieve remote code execution on targeted instances.

Hugging Face Breach: The machine learning platform disclosed unauthorized access to internal datasets and service credentials. OpenAI later claimed responsibility, stating that several of its models executed the breach during a cyber capability assessment.

Additional Notable Stories:
- SharePoint RCE (CVE-2026-50522) being exploited to extract IIS machine keys
- SonicWall SMA zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-15409, CVE-2026-15410) exploited for weeks before disclosure
- Check Point firewall management authentication bypass (CVE-2026-16232) under active attack
- Threat actors using Claude Artifacts to distribute malware through fake download pages
- Kratos phishing-as-a-service platform dismantled by international law enforcement
- Ransomware groups targeting EMEA healthcare supply chains
- Multiple data breaches affecting millions (Paidwork: 23 million users; Estée Lauder HR records)

The report emphasizes emerging threats from AI agents, autonomous malware variants, and expanding attack surfaces in cloud and edge infrastructure.

eef11ef365c7.text:
The Origin Energy breach is dominating Australian news this week, presenting a complex situation with multiple concerning facets. The company has emphasized that "don't worry, your credit card is fine," while the threat actor countered that the organization "didn't respond when I tried to report it."

The situation has evolved as the two parties reportedly "come to an agreement." The nature of this settlement remains unclear—whether financial compensation changed hands or if Origin made commitments in exchange for promises about data deletion. However, neither scenario provides any assurance that the compromised information has actually been destroyed.

Troy Hunt emphasizes that affected individuals should operate under the assumption that data may still be leaked at any time. He references this pattern from previous major Australian breaches, including those affecting Optus, Medibank, Latitude, Ticketek, and Qantas.

The broader lesson from these incidents is that breach victims should prepare for perpetual uncertainty regarding whether their stolen data will eventually surface publicly.

3207a9e40a6e.text:
This comprehensive weekly roundup covers digital forensics and incident response news across multiple categories.

Forensic Analysis Highlights: The week featured significant forensic content, including Eoghan Casey's work at DFRWS on "Adding Clarity to a Foundational Concept in Cyber Investigations: Technique." Elcomsoft published multiple technical pieces addressing encryption cracking methods, digital triage evidentiary standards, and courtroom admissibility of forensic reports. Additional coverage included iOS SplitWise analysis, DocuSign document authentication concerns, and Windows persistence forensics techniques.

Threat Intelligence & Hunting: Extensive threat actor analysis dominated this section. Notable reports included investigations into Kali365 phishing campaigns, CVE-2026-0257 exploitation leading to Qilin ransomware, and APT42's AI-assisted phishing tactics. The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident received significant coverage, with multiple organizations analyzing the autonomous attack implications.

Emerging Threats: Key concerns included device code phishing attacks bypassing MFA, ransomware evolution combining AI capabilities, and supply chain compromises affecting npm and PyPI repositories. Cloud infrastructure vulnerabilities and identity-focused attacks emerged as critical focus areas.

Software Releases: The week saw numerous tool updates including ALEAPP v2026.2.0, iLEAPP v2026.2.0, LAVA v0.14.0, Plaso 20260720, and CyberChef v11.3.0, among others.

00d7a417e9f7.text:
Claude Opus 5 went live on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic says the model improves on Claude Opus 4.8's cyber capabilities, coding through cybersecurity.

Anyone with an AWS account in a supported region can call it. On higher-risk requests, Opus 5 hands the job back to Opus 4.8, the older model. The user sees a notice when that happens. API customers can configure the fallback.

The guardrail that catches the riskiest requests ships with a setting the customer controls.

What the model does now: Opus 5 is a step up in coding, able to read a codebase like an experienced engineer and write production-quality code, adjusting its approach as it works. It runs agents that keep going for hours and overnight, routing around obstacles and recovering from errors. The company reports its largest accuracy gains on document-heavy enterprise work.

For agent automation, the model pushes back on flawed instructions and splits big jobs into sub-agents that need less oversight. It runs multi-day projects and produces professional-grade output.

Where the data goes: On Bedrock, Opus 5 runs with zero data retention by default and zero operator access. The same model reaches customers through Claude Platform on AWS, with zero data retention on request, billed and authenticated through AWS.

How engineers reach it: Engineers select Opus 5 in the Bedrock console playground or call it through the Anthropic Messages API and the Converse API. The model supports adding and removing tools mid-conversation through content blocks on system messages, replacing the re-send of the whole tools array.

Where it runs: Opus 5 is available on Bedrock in four regions at launch: US East (N. Virginia), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Europe (Ireland), and Europe (Stockholm), with more listed in the documentation. On Claude Platform on AWS, it reaches North America, South America, Europe, and Asia Pacific.

Opus 5 lands with better cyber capabilities than Opus 4.8. The control over when it drops back to Opus 4.8 sits with the customer, in the API.

c55dee06cf82.text:
The Internet Storm Center documented scanning activity targeting ESAFENET's CDG (Content Data Guard) product, a document management and data leakage prevention solution primarily marketed in China.

The vulnerability stems from default credentials that ship with the software. The article notes that while the default password "Est@Spc820" appears robust on the surface, containing "10 characters, upper/lower case, special characters, and numbers," it remains "terribly insecure as it is a well-known default password."

Exploit scripts targeting these default credentials were published in a Nuclei template in 2023. The scans capture typical POST requests attempting authentication at /CDGServer3/SystemConfig using standard web user agents.

Beyond default password vulnerabilities, ESAFENET CDG has suffered from additional security flaws including SQL injection and cross-site scripting attacks. The article emphasizes that even security-focused products can ship with fundamental vulnerabilities that attackers readily exploit.

daf7e719ff08.text:
GitHub and PyPI (Python Package Index) have introduced time-based mechanisms to protect against supply-chain attacks. Dependabot now includes a default three-day cooldown setting, while PyPI rejects new files uploaded to releases older than 14 days.

These measures follow multiple high-profile attacks on development ecosystems, including the 'chalk' and 'debug' attacks, the "s1ngularity" operation, the Shai-Hulud campaign, and the GhostAction supply-chain attack.

GitHub's Dependabot Cooldown: Dependabot delays package update processes for 72 hours to reduce risks of automatically adopting newly published malicious packages. In recent cases, malicious npm packages were detected within minutes of publication. However, detection alone doesn't eliminate threats, as maintainers must still remove packages, creating a window for developers to download malicious code.

GitHub selected three days as a balanced approach between avoiding risky releases and maintaining current upgrades. Users can configure shorter or longer delays through Dependabot's 'cooldown' configuration option. GitHub recommends using lockfiles for dependency pinning, restricted-scope tokens, and disabling unnecessary installation scripts in CI.

PyPI's 14-Day Release Cutoff: PyPI now blocks maintainers from adding new files to package releases after 14 days of publication. This prevents attackers with compromised publishing tokens or workflows from poisoning older, trusted releases. The platform found only a small percentage of projects legitimately upload files more than two weeks after publishing.

No confirmed past PyPI attacks used this release poisoning technique, but the platform is implementing preventative measures to block this dangerous possibility.

e05233709f42.text:
Researcher Jeremiah Fowler provides today’s entry in the “No Need to Hack When It’s Leaking” files:
I recently discovered a publicly accessible database that was not password-protected or encrypted and contained what appeared to be records associated with the Tribeca Film Festival.
Upon further investigation I uncovered an additional three separate unsecured databases: “development” (203,370 records), “staging” (224,999 records), and “production” (238,000 records). The total number of exposed records was 666,369, and timestamps ranged from 2019 to 2026. Multiple files also referenced a fourth database labeled as “CMS” (content management system) that was properly secured. While the latter was not publicly accessible, there are potential risks associated with identifying where internal data is stored.
A majority of the exposed records I saw in a limited sample were images, press kits, marketing materials, and documents (including some marked as confidential). Inside the database marked as “production,” there was a single backup .dump file that contained potentially sensitive information, including email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses, and hashed passwords. The backup file contained a total of 295,916 records that included folders indicating 163,171 “users,” 15,488 “films contacts,” 13,535 “contacts,” and more.
Read more at ExpressVPN.

14c0177db461.text:
Security researchers who discovered and reported CVE-2026-54121 (aka "Certighost"), a critical privilege elevation vulnerability in Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS), have released a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for and technical details related to the flaw.

The vulnerability: AD CS is a Microsoft Windows Server role that lets an organization run its own Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). It acts as a Certificate Authority (CA), issuing and managing digital certificates used for authentication, encryption, and signing across a network.

CVE-2026-54121 is a critical improper-authorization flaw with a CVSS score of 8.8. Microsoft explained that "An authenticated attacker could manipulate attributes associated with a machine account and obtain a certificate from Active Directory Certificate Services that allows authentication as that machine via [Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos]." The company also noted: "If a Domain Controller account can be targeted, the attacker could authenticate as the Domain Controller and gain the ability to perform privileged Active Directory operations."

Researchers Aniq Fakhrul and Muhammad Ali reported the bug to Microsoft in May 2026, and the company released fixes on July 14, 2026. At the time, Microsoft assessed CVE-2026-54121 as "less likely" to be exploited, though this assessment may change with the public PoC release.

How the exploit works: Exploitation requires network access and a domain account. The attack leverages a fallback behavior in AD CS during certificate enrollment when the CA must resolve a requester's identity through directory lookups. In cross-domain-controller scenarios, the CA performs a secondary directory lookup by contacting another host. Attackers can steer this process using two certificate request attributes: cdc (Client DC), specifying which host to contact, and rmd (Remote Domain), specifying which principal to look up. When both attributes are present, the CA initiates SMB and LDAP connections to the attacker-controlled host, searches for the specified principal, and uses the returned identity data to build the certificate. A machine account created through default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota settings constitutes a valid domain principal, allowing the rogue endpoint to satisfy CA authentication checks despite not being the impersonated Domain Controller. The attacker obtains a CA-signed certificate authenticating as a target Domain Controller, usable via PKINIT to obtain Kerberos credentials for that DC account. Since Domain Controller accounts possess directory replication rights, attackers can execute DCSync operations to extract the krbtgt account secret, converting ordinary domain access into full domain compromise.

Patch or mitigate: Microsoft's July 2026 updates validate the "chase" target before lookup proceeds. Administrators should upgrade affected AD CS hosts promptly. The researchers noted: "If the July update cannot be installed immediately, the vulnerable code path can be switched off completely with a policy flag, because the cdc chase is an optional fallback feature." This can be accomplished through registry modification using certutil (certutil -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC) followed by restarting the CA service (Restart-Service CertSvc -Force). No known in-the-wild exploitation has been reported to date.

c38790aff790.text:
Anthropic on Friday rolled out Claude Opus 5, pitching it as a cheaper alternative to its top-tier Fable 5 model. In terms of cybersecurity, the new model is nearly as good as the AI giant's most capable system, Mythos 5, at spotting software vulnerabilities, but remains well behind it in turning those findings into working exploits.

The difference comes from Anthropic's own OSS-Fuzz-based evaluation, which measures how well a model can locate and then exploit vulnerabilities with minimal human steering. According to the company, Opus 5 identifies vulnerabilities at a rate close to Mythos 5, but its exploit-development score trails considerably.

Anthropic frames this as a deliberate outcome, noting that it has avoided training Opus 5 directly on offensive cyber tasks. The gains it does show, the company says, are a byproduct of broader capability improvements.

Opus 5's safety classifiers are tuned to be less restrictive than those on Fable 5, with Anthropic expecting roughly 85 percent fewer interventions.

The model is permitted to search for vulnerabilities directly in source code, but binary-based vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, and exploit generation remain blocked. Requests that trip those classifiers fall back automatically to the older Opus 4.8 model inside Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork.

Enterprises and researchers enrolled in Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program can get a version of Opus 5 with those restrictions loosened further.

Mythos 5 also remains withheld from general release, while Fable 5 is described as the safeguarded, publicly available counterpart built on the same underlying model. Both models were taken offline by Anthropic last month due to the Trump administration's concerns over their use by foreign nationals. The restrictions were later lifted.

Pricing for Opus 5 holds at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens (same as for Opus 4.8), with a faster-response mode available at double the base rate.

6ccb85bae497.text:
An AI coding agent opens a terminal, reads a config file, and finds a live cloud key sitting in plaintext. It runs with the permissions of the person who launched it. Every file that person can read, the agent reads. Every credential in the environment, the agent can use.

That reach is where the damage starts. A prompt injection, a mistyped command, or a hallucinated path points that access at the company's own credentials and production systems.

Luke Hinds built Sigstore at Red Hat, a signing project that became a standard for verifying where software packages come from. His company, nolabs, which he co-founded with Stephen Parkinson, released Nono, an open-source runtime that confines AI agents at the operating system kernel.

Nono has drawn more than 3,100 stars on GitHub. Over 80 people have contributed to it, and its users include large enterprises and teams in regulated industries.

The kernel gets the final say: Nono checks every action an agent takes against policies written in code. An agent asks to use a tool, open a file, or reach a network endpoint. The kernel returns the verdict. Enforcement sits in the operating system, below the agent and below any guardrail sharing its process.

Nono leans on Landlock on Linux and Seatbelt on macOS, kernel features that strip a process of privileges and hold them stripped. Once the sandbox applies, the limits stand for the life of the process.

"We currently support Windows via the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2), which runs a real Linux kernel so Nono's Landlock enforcement applies exactly as it does on native Linux. Native Windows enforcement is under active research," Hinds told Help Net Security.

Developers reach for agents to move faster. Security teams watch those same agents inherit human-level permissions across files, credentials, and production systems. Containers and microVMs shrink the blast radius. An over-permissioned agent inside one still holds every key it was handed.

The tool gets a phantom key: Broad, session-long permissions are the problem Nono's newer feature targets. Agent Tool Sandboxing hands each tool call its own scoped authority. A tool receives a phantom credential standing in for a real secret. Its file access covers what the task needs. Its network reach ends at the endpoints it must hit. The authority expires when the call finishes.

A tool holding a phantom stand-in still has to authenticate against a live service somewhere. Hinds described how that call gets made: "Nono routes the request through a trusted proxy outside the sandbox, which retrieves the real credential from secure storage – such as the operating system's keychain, 1Password, Bitwarden, or Kubernetes Secrets – and injects it only into the request sent to the approved external API."

James Carnegie, a staff security engineer at Datadog, is one of its users: "Datadog engineers want their agents to move fast, and we want our credentials and production systems kept safe while they do. Nono is the only sandbox that gives us both fine-grained, per-command policies and sophisticated credential management that fits existing, complex real-world toolchains."

Nono is available for free on GitHub.

070019b182b5.text:
Booz Allen Hamilton has announced an expansion of its powerful suite of AI-powered cyber defense products. Now generally available, Vellox Ranger provides automated, environment-specific threat detections, developed on Booz Allen's proprietary agentic AI framework, that identify exploitable paths and vulnerabilities based on the actual state of an enterprise's infrastructure.

This automation helps protect the systems that matter most and reduces the risk of operational disruption, limits how long attackers can remain undetected in an environment and increases cost savings by minimizing false alarms. The outcome: organizations are empowered to speed, scale, and strengthen threat detection at machine speed.

As highlighted in Booz Allen's latest cyber threat report, "When Cyberattacks Happen at AI Speed," security teams are falling behind as attack surfaces expand, tools remain fragmented, and threats evolve at AI speed. Detection engineering built on generic rules, manual tuning, and scarce expert time cannot keep up with dynamic environments. The result is too much noise, too little clarity, and a widening gap between how fast adversaries can adapt and how fast defenders can respond.

Vellox Ranger addresses this gap by applying a detection-from-the-inside-out approach, modeling customer environments (including assets, topology, vulnerabilities, and telemetry), layering on the latest cyber threat intelligence (CTI), then mapping relevant exposure to MITRE ATT&CK, and generating prioritized detection logic tailored to that environment. While AI enables autonomous threat detection, enterprise cyber teams maintain human-led governance.

"Vellox Ranger and the entire Vellox product suite are game changers, rapidly redefining how organizations quickly detect and disrupt advanced cyber threats at machine speed," stated Mujtaba Hamid, EVP and leader of Booz Allen's product portfolio. The firm built its solution to combat AI-powered adversaries using its proprietary trusted agent framework, informed by decades of regulated mission cyber expertise.

Vellox Ranger represents the newest addition to Booz Allen's agentic cyber product suite, leveraging more than 30 years of technology, tradecraft, and adversarial insights.

The Vellox product suite includes:
- Vellox Reverser (generally available): Malware reverse engineering and threat intelligence automating analysis of complex and evasive threats, producing actionable defensive recommendations in minutes.
- Vellox Navigator (coming soon): Live cyber compliance command layer facilitating continuous monitoring, controls assessment, and risk mitigation to autonomously interpret and control enterprise security in real time.
- Vellox Reverser Triage (coming soon): An extension replacing legacy sandbox tools producing actionable intelligence with fast, high-volume malware triage across all file types.
- Vellox Striker (limited preview): Emulates the AI-powered adversary to assess critical security gaps and train customer models to detect sophisticated threats.
- Vellox LayerOne (limited preview): The mission-grade governance and compliance gateway for AI agents, validating outputs, enforcing controls, and generating defensible evidence.

Andrew Turner, EVP and head of Booz Allen's global commercial cyber business, noted that "CISOs are defending against threats that move faster than any human team can." He emphasized that Vellox Ranger recovers analyst time wasted on false alerts while maintaining current defenses as infrastructure evolves.

2a752ba54715.text:
You may have heard your peers say, "Cybercrime has become industrialized." But did you have any proof? We do.

Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) closed out its tracking for the first half of 2026 with a deep analysis of the Global Threat Landscape spanning ransomware, initial access brokers, data breaches and leaks, nation-state espionage, and hacktivism, among others.

One of the most striking analyses that puts the threat landscape severity in perspective was the number of distinct threat actor profiles active worldwide between January and June. 261 — that's how many identifiable groups and individuals, each with its own tradecraft, targeting logic, and operational rhythm, running campaigns simultaneously across nation-state espionage, ransomware, hacktivism, and cybercrime.

The Worldwide Picture of Most Active Threat Actors: APTs Lead, But Not Everywhere. Across all 261 profiles tracked globally, nation-state Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups were the single largest category — accounting for 118 profiles, or just over 45% of the total. Ransomware operators came second at 75 profiles (29%), followed by hacktivist collectives (34), cybercriminal groups (31), and dedicated extortion-only gangs, which remained a niche category at just 3.

Threat Actor Category | Profiles Tracked | Share of Total
Nation-State APT Groups | 118 | 45.2%
Ransomware Groups | 75 | 28.7%
Hacktivist Collectives | 34 | 13.0%
Cybercriminal Groups | 31 | 11.9%
Extortion-Only Groups | 3 | 1.1%
Total | 261 | 100%

That APT dominance reflects the sheer number of state-sponsored programs China, North Korea, Iran, and Russia field simultaneously across espionage, intellectual property theft, and pre-positioning operations. The extortion-only category being almost statistically irrelevant is telling too — it confirms that pure extortion has essentially been absorbed into the ransomware business model rather than surviving as an independent specialty. Double extortion is now just how ransomware works.

Threat Actors to Watch Out For: CRIL flagged five groups worldwide as carrying the highest confidence and activity levels for security teams to track through the rest of 2026:
Bluenoroff (North Korea, Lazarus subgroup) — cryptocurrency sector, financial services
UNC6508 (China, PRC-nexus espionage) — US/Canada education, healthcare, government, aerospace & defense
Volt Typhoon (China, state-sponsored) — US (incl. Guam) and allies, communications, energy, manufacturing, government, IT
Desert Falcons (Palestine) — UAE, Israel, Jordan, and 12+ other MEA nations; aerospace & defense, government, law enforcement, media
SideCopy (Pakistan) — India, Afghanistan; government, defense/military

Bluenoroff, a financially motivated Lazarus Group subgroup, funds North Korean state operations by impersonating established crypto investors and planting malicious links inside victims' Calendly scheduling accounts.

Volt Typhoon continues to favor "living off the land" techniques that blend into normal network activity, prioritizing long-term undetected access over rapid data theft.

UNC6508 compromises externally accessible REDCap research environments and has been observed creating malicious mail-forwarding rules to silently exfiltrate correspondence, routed through US-based residential proxies and compromised routers to obscure attribution.

The threat actor profiles, targeting patterns, and regional breakdowns are drawn from Cyble's H1 2026 Global Threat Landscape Report, built on continuous monitoring across dark web forums, ransomware leak sites, and threat actor communications worldwide. Cyble Vision provides ongoing tracking of these groups as they develop.

9d9531ebda24.text:
Nvidia and a large group of technology, cybersecurity, and enterprise software companies announced the launch of the Open Secure AI Alliance, a new initiative aimed at developing and sharing open source tools, models, and techniques for securing AI systems and agents.

The effort builds on existing work from the Linux Foundation's Akrites initiative and the OpenSSF community.

Inaugural partners include Adobe, Cadence, Capital One, Cisco, Cloudera, Cloudflare, Cognition, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Dell, DoorDash, Elastic, HPE, Hugging Face, IBM, LangChain, Microsoft, Naver, NetApp, Nous Research, OpenClaw, Palantir, Palo Alto Networks, Red Hat, Reflection AI, Salesforce, SAP, SK Telecom, ServiceNow, Siemens, Snowflake, SpaceXAI, Synopsys, Thinking Machines Lab, and TrendAI.

Nvidia contributes open models, weights, data, and agent research, including NOOA, designed to make agent behavior easier to trace, test, and audit. HPE contributes to SPIFFE/SPIRE, a zero-trust identity framework. Hugging Face donates its Safetensors model weight storage format to PyTorch Foundation. IBM and Red Hat extend supply chain security through Lightwell for automated vulnerability remediation. Microsoft contributes MDASH, a multi-model scanning harness for finding software bugs. SpaceXAI open-sources its Grok Build terminal-based AI coding agent.

The alliance contends that "open models, harnesses, and security tooling should be treated as defensive assets rather than liabilities" and warns policymakers that broad restrictions on open frontier AI could weaken cyber defense capacity.

Nvidia cites the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, noting that when closed tools blocked forensic work, Hugging Face used the open-weight GLM 5.2 model to review over 17,000 actions and contain the breach.

c9b27a1ee25b.text:
The operators of a well-known malvertising campaign have developed a novel technique to avoid detection: hiding their activity in the victim's browser to secretly build and then deliver the final payload.

The new tactics by SourTrade, a prolific and evolving malvertising operation which has been active since 2024, have been detailed by cybersecurity researchers at Confiant.

SourTrade impersonates several well-known trading and cryptocurrency platforms, including TradingView, Solana and Luno, with the aim of targeting investors and traders with an infostealer.

As detailed in a blog post published on July 23, the campaign uses a range of malvertising lures to draw interest from potential victims, with many focused around trading tips or cryptocurrency giveaways. If the user visits one of these sites, SourTrade begins the process of stealthily delivering the payload.

The site does not distribute a complete payload malware at once. Instead, the malvertising site delivers assembly instructions to the victim's browser, before it retrieves a clean file from separate infrastructure and then directs the browser to build the final malware in memory on the victim's machine.

No finished malware ever exists on the network.

This design is used to counter file fingerprinting, a technique used by many cybersecurity defenses to help identify malicious activity, therefore freeing SourTrade to deliver the payload.

Michael Steele, threat intelligence researcher at Confiant, stated: "Security tools see only clean components. Network logs record a legitimate-looking download. The full attack is only visible when the entire execution chain is examined."

When the user visits the site, they have been directed to through malvertising, a JavaScript instruction prepares the browser for the constituent parts of the malware delivery. The initial stage of this is the delivery of the instructions used to piece together the malware.

After this, the remote components of the malware are built within the browser, after which it is executed and delivered. As this has been built in the browser, to any protections, the payload looks as if it should be trusted and safe – while in fact the victim is unaware an infostealer is being installed on their system.

"This design gives the operators some advantages. It avoids exposing one stable malware binary over the network and produces output that can vary by victim or session," Steele explained.

Researchers warned that SourTrade remains a widespread and evolving malvertising campaign.

4c439eb13ae0.text:
Coca-Cola confirmed on Monday that a ransomware attack on its dairy subsidiary Fairlife resulted in a data breach. The company had initially disclosed the cybersecurity incident on July 16 when it suspended production at U.S. Fairlife facilities.

The Anubis ransomware group claimed responsibility for the attack, listing Coca-Cola on its leak website on July 20 and claiming to have "stolen 1 TB of confidential data." According to the article, a timer on the Anubis website indicated the stolen information would be made public unless a ransom was paid.

In its statement, Coca-Cola confirmed that "certain data" was taken but provided no specifics. The company reported that most production has resumed at the four U.S. Fairlife facilities, with "retail availability of Fairlife products largely unimpacted due to existing inventory." The statement noted that "product quality and safety have not been impacted."

Coca-Cola assessed that "the incident has not had, and is not reasonably likely to have, a material impact on the company's financial condition or results of operations."

The Anubis group, active since December 2024, employs a double-extortion model involving file encryption and data exfiltration. The gang is notable for a "wiper mode feature" that permanently deletes victim files to prevent recovery.

(Author: Eduard Kovacs, SecurityWeek, published July 27, 2026)

1207e30cc301.text:
Microsoft remained the leading target for brand impersonation in Q2 2026, representing 23% of all phishing attempts. LinkedIn, Google, Apple, and Amazon rounded out the top five, collectively accounting for more than half of tracked brand phishing incidents during the period, according to Check Point's quarterly report.

For the first time, ChatGPT entered the list of ten most frequently impersonated brands. Check Point analysts predict that as AI tools transition from novelty status to essential daily-use platforms for managing subscriptions and work tasks, "they become just as attractive a target as any bank or tech giant."

The technology sector continues as the primary target category, followed by social networks and banking services. These industries manage sensitive user data, finances, and professional connections, making them high-value targets.

Users can identify phishing attempts by spotting distorted logos, non-functional links, mismatched domains, and spelling mistakes. Attackers increasingly leverage AI to generate convincing graphics and websites, making "subtle distortions and inconsistencies" important red flags for detecting fraudulent sites, the firm noted.

(Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security, published July 27, 2026)

1f888a18df11.text:
Italian AI-native cybersecurity company Beelzebub announced raising €3 million (approximately $3.4 million) in seed funding led by VC United Ventures, bringing total funding to $3.8 million.

Founded in 2025, the Milan-based startup developed a platform combining red- and blue-teaming capabilities to counter AI-powered cyber threats. The system assumes attackers have already infiltrated networks and operates by ensnaring them in a closed loop that integrates simulation, detection, and threat intelligence.

The platform employs continuous adversary emulation to identify attack paths before exploitation and uses runtime deception technology with LLM-powered traps to detect and contain intrusions immediately. It isolates compromised systems and initiates incident response procedures while leveraging autonomous threat intelligence to convert intercepted attacks into actionable defenses.

An AI analyst dissects detected malware and delivers comprehensive incident reports. The platform operates entirely on-premises for sensitive environments unable to use cloud-based tools.

According to CEO Mario Candela: "AI-powered attackers are too powerful, too competent, too fast, and too numerous, meaning the only way to fight back is at the same pace and intensity."

The company plans to expand its research team, establish new offices in Rome and San Francisco, and target additional European clients, particularly NIS2-regulated organizations. The platform is NIS2-ready and receives live threat intelligence from over 60 independent researchers globally, available as SaaS or on-premises deployment.

(Author: Ionut Arghire, SecurityWeek, published July 27, 2026)

699e8ae9cfcb.text:
Yet another Israeli mass surveillance company:

"Made by Israeli surveillance company Cognyte, the tech simulates a mobile phone tower, which forces nearby phones to connect to it. That enables cops to keep tabs on any phones in the vicinity - whether they're owned by a suspect in a case or not. Cognyte's contract with the state of Texas reveals that the simulator, called FalcoNet, can be concealed within the vehicles, hidden in a backpack for on-foot missions or attached to a helicopter. It's the same technology as the infamous Stingray, one of the original cell-site simulators made by defense giant L3Harris."

Tags: cell phones, Israel, law enforcement, privacy, surveillance

(Author: Bruce Schneier, published July 27, 2026)

d54c93fc4ee3.text:
Mobile devices present a serious security problem: they operate outside the security perimeter and beyond the visibility of the security team. While security may know what applications live on those devices, they rarely understand the components and dependencies that comprise those applications; nor what vulnerabilities are buried within those components.

Jim Dolce, CEO at Lookout, gave an example: WolfSSL. It's a small, fast, and portable SSL/TLS library written in ANSI C, designed mainly for devices with limited memory - and it exists on more than a billion devices. "If you have a banking app on a mobile device for online banking, that app is likely using WolfSSL. It has a very serious vulnerability. If exploited by a bad actor, it can mimic your bank, and when you put in your credentials, it will steal your banking credentials."

The Mythos Glasswing project found and publicized this WolfSSL vulnerability. So, the bad guys know the banking app may be vulnerable, but does the security team know that employees are using it?

"Knowing an application's name and version reveals only a fraction of its risk profile," explains Lookout. "Security teams need visibility into the software components, dependencies, and vulnerabilities embedded beneath the surface."

This is what the firm's new Mobile Security Exposure Center (MSEC) provides: full visibility into an organization's potentially vast mobile fleet. In a nutshell, MSEC examines every device in the fleet, so it knows what apps are present. It then creates its own proprietary software bill of materials (SBOM) from the binary for the different apps.

From this SBOM it learns every component within the app and correlates those components with the vulnerability databases (such as the KEV list) that exist. The results are fed into the organization's CTEM to assist the security team to take any necessary remediation steps.

"The system will identify which apps use WolfSSL, the version of that app, the user and the device that is using that app, and all of that information then can be used to remediate the exposure. So MSEC basically identifies the exposure and provides that information," continued Dolce. This applies to all the software components of all the apps on all the mobile devices.

MSEC also complements Lookout's existing AI Visibility & Governance product. "While AI Visibility & Governance helps organizations understand AI adoption and usage across the enterprise," says Lookout, "MSEC reveals the software composition and exposure profile of those applications. Together, they provide a more complete view of application risk, security, and governance."

The result, it continues, is "A shift from reactive application management to proactive exposure management."

However, there is a slight issue here. MSEC correlates the app components it unearths in its SBOM creation with the vulnerability databases that exist. We've mentioned one - the KEV list, or the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog produced by CISA. The clue to the issue is in the name, known vulnerabilities. No vulnerability database can include unknown vulnerabilities. So, while MSEC can help remediate known vulnerabilities, there is always the possibility that a new frontier AI model will unearth new vulnerabilities.

Lookout is obviously aware of this, and has it covered.

"Bad actors can use frontier AI models, Mythos as an example, in order to find vulnerabilities and exploit them," agreed Dolce. "That's the offensive use of a frontier AI model. Well, Lookout can use that same model defensively. We can go beyond KEV and the other vulnerability databases by using the frontier models ourselves to find unknown vulnerabilities across the SBOM. That will be the next iteration of MSEC."

He continued, "We will take our SBOM and use the frontier AI models defensively to go and find unknown vulnerabilities for ourselves, and catalog those as well."

But it all starts with knowing the app inventory across the enterprise mobile fleet, creating the accurate SBOM for all the apps in the fleet, and then correlating the app components against known vulnerability databases, and then, he added, "The last step is find unknown vulnerabilities using the same frontier AI models defensively that the bad guys are using offensively."

(Author: Kevin Townsend, SecurityWeek, published July 27, 2026)

1fdae83296bd.text:
A sophisticated crypter service called Cruciferra has been identified as enabling multiple cybercriminal groups to deliver remote access trojans and information stealers. According to Proofpoint's analysis, this tool represents a significant advancement in malware obfuscation capabilities.

The service employs several advanced evasion techniques. It features "indirect system calls, API and Import Address Table (IAT) unhooking" along with BYOVD-based EDR tampering to bypass security measures. A particularly notable capability is its customized implementation of Process Ghosting, which executes payloads while minimizing forensic evidence.

Cruciferra uses polymorphic encryption, meaning the algorithms vary between samples, complicating both static analysis and signature-based detection methods. The service has been advertised in underground forums with pricing ranging from $450 to $2,000 monthly since fall 2025.

Distribution Campaigns:
The crypter has been observed in multiple attack campaigns:
- Tax-themed phishing: Targeting Indian taxpayers and finance professionals
- SSA impersonation: Delivering XWorm and AdaptixC2 malware
- Hospitality targeting: Using bed bug and guest complaint themes to distribute zgRAT

Execution occurs through DLL side-loading, with the malware establishing persistence via Windows registry modifications and attempting UAC bypass techniques.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, The Hacker News, published July 27, 2026)

a9054089e98b.text:
A threat actor has been compromising public Wi-Fi gateway appliances at organizations running captive portal networks to target Microsoft 365 accounts of traveling corporate employees, according to ReliaQuest research.

The attackers modified DNS configurations on compromised SOHO routers to redirect users to attacker-controlled infrastructure for credential theft. The campaign has been ongoing since at least June 2026 and employs adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) techniques to intercept traffic and harvest sensitive information.

The activity mirrors the previously observed FrostArmada campaign attributed to APT28 (also known as Forest Blizzard and Fancy Bear), a state-sponsored group believed linked to Russia's GRU.

Compromised Wi-Fi gateways were identified at shared venues including hotels and conference centers across the US, India, and Saudi Arabia. ReliaQuest notes that "any organization running captive Wi-Fi services" faces similar attack risks.

Organizations across multiple sectors were targeted-including financial services, professional services, legal, healthcare, energy, and retail-suggesting broad rather than sector-specific targeting.

The researchers identified four attacker-registered domains used to deliver Microsoft-impersonation lures. Unlike FrostArmada, this campaign used DNS poisoning to redirect all users, potentially indicating "a less sophisticated or less careful actor."

While the new campaign reuses some APT28 tradecraft, the infrastructure and targeting methods differ from prior FrostArmada activity, suggesting either copycat activity or independent threat actors.

(Author: Ionut Arghire, SecurityWeek, published July 27, 2026)

c310fb81ac6f.text:
Ullrich details a security threat involving Spring Boot's /actuator/heapdump endpoint. This debugging feature exposes a binary heap dump file that can reveal sensitive application data.

The Vulnerability: Spring Boot's heapdump endpoint "often includes secrets used by the application to connect to backend systems. API keys, database passwords, and other sensitive data may be exposed."

Attack Pattern: The observed requests target /admin-api/actuator/heapdump using basic authentication with default credentials (admin:admin). The attacker assumes weak default passwords rather than no authentication.

Configuration Risk: The management endpoint base path is typically configured in application.yml using the setting management.endpoints.web.base-path=/admin-api/actuator. This creates a predictable attack surface.

Mitigation Approach: Ullrich recommends using Spring Security to restrict access to these management endpoints more effectively, moving beyond reliance on password strength alone for protection.

(Author: Johannes Ullrich, SANS ISC, published July 27, 2026)

2823349acd2c.text:
Shutting down endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools before encryption begins has become standard operating procedure across the ransomware ecosystem, analysis of attacks by researchers at Halcyon has warned.

The practice, sometimes called EDR-kill, was once considered a specialist capability. It has now become standard practice among leading ransomware groups, giving defenders even less time to detect and contain attacks, said Halcyon in its Q2 2026 Ransomware Evolution Report, published on July 27.

Moreover, some of these leading ransomware groups are now including an EDR or antivirus shutdown into their attack chain.

This is the case with The Gentlemen, a group which has recently emerged and become one of the most prolific ransomware threats, which Halcyon has analyzed in detail.

In a previous threat assessment document, the company's Ransomware Research Center shared that The Gentlemen's developers are systematically reverse-engineering samples from other groups, such as Babuk, Qilin, LockBit 5.0 and Medusa, to select the strongest encryption routines, code-obfuscation techniques and EDR evasion methods to incorporate into their own codebase.

Ransomware Attacks Decline, But Threats Grow More Sophisticated:
Halcyon's ransomware report recorded 1988 publicly claimed ransomware attacks from 89 active groups targeting organizations across 101 countries during the second quarter of 2026.

While overall number of claimed attacks fell by 5.7% quarter on quarter, the underlying tactics used by attackers became significantly more advanced, signalling a shift towards faster, more automated and harder-to-detect operations, the company said.

The leading ransomware groups were Qilin (293 attack claims), The Gentlemen (214 attack claims), DragonForce (143 attack claims), Akira (119 attack claims) and Lockbit 5.0 (102 attack claims).

DragonForce and LockBit 5.0 showed an activity uptake in the second quarter of 2026, while The Gentlemen overtook Qilin for the top spot in June.

Halcyon also identified several emerging - or for some, returning - ransomware groups, including KryBit, Payload, PEAR and World Leaks.

Manufacturing was the industry most targeted by ransomware groups in Q2 2026, representing 19.8% of all cyber extortion attacks. Construction took the second place, followed by business services, retail and software.

Vulnerabilities in enterprise edge devices, such as in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway (CVE-2025-5777), SonicWall SSL VPN (CVE-2024-40766) and Fortinet's FortiOS (CVE-2024-55591) were among the most exploited by ransomware groups during the reported period.

The report noted groups like DragonForce and Akira moved from initial breach to ransomware deployment in under an hour in some attacks.

Ransomware Groups Operationalize AI:
The Halcyon report found that for ransomware operations, AI is moving beyond experimentation into operational use.

"Threat actors increasingly leveraged AI throughout the attack chain, from malware disguised as AI productivity tools to AI-assisted victim negotiations and the emergence of what researchers believe to be the first agentic ransomware capable of autonomously conducting key stages of an intrusion," the Halcyon analysts wrote.

For instance, Halcyon reported increased instances of the LLM-developed EvilAI masquerading as fake AI-productivity apps while secretly providing ransomware actors initial access.

Ross Asquith, solutions engineering director for Europe at Halcyon, said the democratization of EDR-kill techniques and the generalization of the use of AI in ransomware attack chains show that the "ransomware ecosystem is becoming faster, more automated and far more effective at neutralizing the security tools organizations rely on."

This, he added, should prompt cyber defenders to focus on cyber resilience and "no longer assume traditional controls will buy them the time they need to respond."

Finally, the report highlighted growing evidence of ransomware being used to support state objectives, with Iran-linked actors increasingly disguising espionage campaigns as criminal ransomware operations.

(Author: Kevin Poireault, Reporter, Infosecurity Magazine, published July 27, 2026)

26d185446558.text:
Dental and vision benefits administrator DentaQuest is notifying millions of people that their personal and dental health information might have been stolen in a data breach.

The incident was discovered on May 20, and DentaQuest's investigation determined that hackers had access to the organization's network between May 17 and May 20.

During this timeframe, attackers accessed information including names, addresses, Social Security numbers, member identification numbers, Medicaid and Medicare numbers, benefits provider names, diagnosis, treatment details, and billing information.

DentaQuest is providing affected individuals with 24 months of free credit monitoring, fraud consultation, and identity theft restoration services.

Based on filings with Attorney General's Offices in Texas, Massachusetts, and South Carolina, DentaQuest is sending written notification letters to at least 4.5 million people. According to the HIPAA Journal, more than 23.4 million individuals were potentially impacted, with DentaQuest confirming at least 15 million were affected.

The notorious extortion group ShinyHunters claimed responsibility and leaked approximately 234 GB of stolen data. The leaked information included email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and government-issued IDs.

A Sun Life subsidiary serving 35 million people in 50 states, DentaQuest ranks among the largest dental benefits administrators in the US.

(Author: Ionut Arghire, SecurityWeek, published July 27, 2026)

ee1c295f339e.text:
AWS has released the DevOps Agent, an AI-powered operations assistant designed to help DevOps and SRE teams investigate and troubleshoot infrastructure issues. The tool specifically addresses AWS Network Firewall incidents by analyzing logs, reviewing firewall rules, identifying configuration changes, and recommending solutions to restore connectivity.

The agent accesses "firewall logs, VPC Flow Logs, route tables, firewall policies, and recent AWS CloudTrail events through AWS APIs" to pinpoint root causes and present mitigation plans. It demonstrates proficiency in diagnosing three common scenarios: domain deny list issues, stateless rule priority problems, and asymmetric cross-Availability Zone routing complications.

Integration Features: The system integrates with GitHub, GitLab Self-Managed, and CI/CD pipelines. According to AWS Senior Technical Account Manager Salman Ahmed, the agent can "associate AWS resources with deployments of AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) images, and Terraform," enabling correlation of disruptions with recent deployments.

Preventive Capabilities: Beyond incident response, the agent analyzes previous investigations to recommend improvements for reducing recurring issues, such as implementing guardrails within CI/CD pipelines for Network Firewall rule modifications.

(Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security, published July 27, 2026)

bc34d1b5624b.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have identified a fresh cyber campaign targeting government entities in the Middle East, orchestrated by a threat actor with East Asian connections. Zscaler ThreatLabz detected the intrusions this month and discovered three previously unreported malware families: TELESHIM, MIXEDKEY, and BINDCLOAK.

The campaign employs a multi-stage attack chain that establishes persistent access on infected systems. According to Sudeep Singh, senior manager of APT research at Zscaler ThreatLabz, "The campaign used a multi-stage attack chain to establish and maintain access on infected systems, with TELESHIM abusing the Telegram API for command-and-control (C2) communication to blend in with legitimate internet traffic."

Attack Methodology: The infection begins with an ISO file containing a legitimate executable (RegSchdTask.exe) used to sideload a malicious DLL called AsTaskSched.dll. This 32-bit Windows backdoor, TELESHIM, leverages Telegram as its command-and-control channel to retrieve additional payloads.

The attack sequence continues through a second DLL sideloading chain involving GoProAlertService.exe and pthreadVC2.dll, where MIXEDKEY acts as a reflective loader. This component decrypts and executes content from a file named C99F29AC08454855B3D538960BB2F34F.PCPKEY.

Evasion Techniques: Both TELESHIM and MIXEDKEY employ sophisticated obfuscation methods, including string encryption, control flow flattening, mixed boolean arithmetic, and opaque predicates to hinder reverse engineering. TELESHIM incorporates multiple virtualization detection mechanisms including hypervisor detection via CPUID and RAM speed verification through WMI.

Command and Control Operations: TELESHIM supports two message types for C2 communications: control messages that register infected hosts by transmitting MAC addresses and executing received commands, and download-and-execute messages that deploy secondary payloads as scheduled tasks. The final payload operates behind dual XOR encryption layers, with environmental keying tied to the infected machine's volume serial number.

Final Stage: BINDCLOAK, a 64-bit C2 implant written in C++, contacts an external server at cert.hypersnet[.]com. Researchers observed post-compromise reconnaissance between July 7-9, 2026, with C2 commands executed exclusively between 4 a.m. and 12 p.m. UTC.

Attribution: Based on the threat actor's public IP address, Windows server locale configuration, geolocation analysis, and operational hours, researchers assess with moderate-to-high confidence that an East Asian adversary conducted the campaign. The activity remains unattributed to any known threat group at this time.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, The Hacker News, published July 27, 2026)

93d1100a13d7.text:
GitHub has implemented a new cooldown mechanism in Dependabot that delays automated dependency updates by at least three days after a package release. This measure aims to reduce vulnerability to supply chain attacks involving malicious package versions.

The three-day waiting period applies only to version updates designed to keep dependencies current. Security updates bypass this delay and deploy immediately to address vulnerabilities quickly.

The Problem Being Addressed: Threat actors sometimes upload compromised packages to registries, which get adopted by downstream projects before removal. Though these poisoned versions are typically short-lived, the window of exposure can still affect numerous users.

Why Three Days? According to GitHub, this timeframe represents an optimal balance: "it pushes you past the window where most of these attacks live, and it doesn't hold your dependencies back longer than necessary."

Customization Available: Organizations can modify the cooldown parameter in their dependabot.yml configuration to suit their specific needs and risk tolerance.

Broader Defense Strategy: GitHub emphasizes this represents just one layer of protection. Comprehensive defense includes lockfile pinning, disabling installation scripts in CI/CD, scoped build tokens, and manual update review processes.

Industry Trend: Similar cooldown controls have been adopted across multiple package ecosystems including VS Code, Ruby, Bun, npm, pnpm, and Yarn over the past year.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, The Hacker News, published July 27, 2026)

4d5bd0026bcb.text:
Google has introduced its own naming system for cybercrime groups, departing from a Microsoft-led industry standardization effort. The system uses a two-word format where the first word identifies the specific actor, and the second categorizes them by motivation or attribution.

Google's categories are:
- CASTLE - People's Republic of China
- ION - Iran
- NEPTUNE - North Korea
- RELIC - Russia
- COMET - Non-state cybercriminals

The taxonomy emerged from Google's 2022 acquisition of Mandiant, consolidated into the Google Threat Intelligence Group. Google acknowledged that "multiple naming schemas mean researchers often refer to the same group by ten different names," citing how Seashell Blizzard and APT44 refer to identical Russian military intelligence units.

Despite previous reports that Google supported Microsoft and CrowdStrike's 2025 coordinated naming initiative, this announcement suggests that collaboration either failed to materialize or dissolved.

Google emphasized keeping its system "simple...to streamline operations and facilitate mapping to other naming taxonomies," acknowledging existing industry frameworks while operating independently.

(Author: Simon Sharwood, APAC Editor, The Register, published Monday, July 27, 2026 at 08:31 UTC)

22d95b14984b.text:
Marathon Petroleum's CISO Mary Rose Martinez discusses operational technology security automation and supply chain vulnerabilities in energy infrastructure.

On Air-Gapping OT Environments: Martinez explains that "the traditional concept of air-gapping operational technology (OT) environments is effectively dissipating" as digitization increases exposure for industrial control systems like PLCs, HMIs, and SCADA systems. This transition extends across manufacturing and transportation sectors as well.

On Patching Constraints: Given that critical equipment like catalytic crackers cannot restart on standard patch schedules, Marathon leverages the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture model. This framework enables "security controls implemented at and between the information and operational technology layers" to synchronize security actions with operational rhythms while managing risk.

On Supply Chain Risks: Martinez identifies greatest vulnerabilities where visibility diminishes, particularly with nth-party vendors. The company mitigates these through due diligence assessments, contractual provisions, and vendor partnerships for collaborative problem-solving.

On Workforce Skills: She advocates developing "different learning pathways to increase digital fluency" across the workforce, noting that AI advancements help democratize technical knowledge while cross-skilling remains necessary.

On Critical Infrastructure Defense: Martinez emphasizes partnerships with government agencies remain essential for leveraging threat intelligence and informing effective security regulations.

(Author: Mirko Zorz, Director of Content, Help Net Security, published July 27, 2026)

a5da8e96612f.text:
The piece features Joel Moses, VP of Strategic Engineering at F5, discussing how attackers exploit identity systems rather than attempting to breach them directly.

Moses addresses several attack vectors:
- MFA Fatigue: Attackers wear down users with repeated authentication prompts until they approve access
- Session Token Theft: Compromised authentication tokens grant unauthorized access
- Malicious Application Consent: Users unknowingly grant permissions to fraudulent applications

The 2022 Uber breach serves as a case study demonstrating these vulnerabilities in action.

Recommended Defenses: Moses proposes multiple protective measures: implementing number matching for authentication, deploying FIDO2 security keys, conducting periodic audits of third-party application permissions, and monitoring for suspicious changes in identity settings.

The discussion emphasizes how cloud and on-premises trust relationships create pathways for attackers to move between environments, underscoring the expanding identity attack surface in hybrid infrastructure environments.

Tags: F5 Networks, identity, identity management, strategy, tips, video, zero trust

4e7e1e5b23e9.text:
LastPass Authenticator is a complimentary application providing two-factor authentication for accounts supporting time-based one-time passwords (TOTP). The tool offers push notifications for single-tap approvals and generates six-digit verification codes. It's accessible on iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Android platforms.

Getting Started: Account enrollment involves scanning a QR code, importing one from saved photos, or manually entering a secret key. The application includes built-in templates for numerous services—Amazon, AWS, Binance, Coinbase, Discord, Dropbox, Facebook, Evernote, GitHub, PayPal, Slack, Twitch, and X—plus options for custom entries.

Accounts appear in a searchable list displaying service icons, names, and expiration timers. Users can organize entries into groups, modify account details, transfer accounts between devices, and export accounts as QR codes.

Security Features: Protection mechanisms include Face ID or PIN security, "Tap to Reveal" functionality keeping codes hidden until accessed, and cloud backup for device transitions. A built-in Security Checkup tool evaluates security settings, confirms app currency, and detects device jailbreaking.

Additional Capabilities: Users can scan verification codes directly from device screenshots, preview upcoming codes before current ones expire, customize code display locations, and group digits for improved readability.

Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer. Published: July 27, 2026.

8b22016208de.text:
GitHub's Dependabot now implements a waiting period before deploying routine version updates. Following a September 2025 incident where attackers compromised npm maintainer credentials and poisoned popular packages like chalk and debug, the platform introduced a three-day cooldown for non-security version bumps.

The malicious versions remained live for approximately two hours before detection and removal. During that brief window, automated update tools could have already filed pull requests, exposing teams to compromised code. This vulnerability in speed prompted the policy adjustment.

Two Distinct Update Types: Dependabot manages two separate functions. Security updates address known vulnerabilities and deploy immediately when advisories are released. Version updates maintain current dependencies as new releases ship—these now experience the three-day delay through the cooldown option in dependabot.yml.

Pattern of Fast-Moving Attacks: Supply chain incidents consistently follow a similar timeline: malicious packages publish, spread through installations, and get caught within hours. GitHub's Advisory Database documented more than 6,500 npm malware advisories in the year ending May 2026—approximately 18 newly cataloged malicious packages daily. The three-day window allows scrutiny to occur before packages reach development teams.

Limitations of the Approach: The cooldown proves ineffective against "attacks that play a longer game," including dormant backdoors or maintainer sabotage. It represents one defensive layer among several, which should include dependency pinning, installation script restrictions, token scoping, and update review processes before merging.

Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security. Published: July 27, 2026.

87bbbbddcbc7.text: Handler on Duty: Guy Bruneau. Threat Level: Green. 7aa0b13a300d.text:
A massive malvertising campaign is using fake Solana, Luno, and TradingView webpages with malicious JavaScript that instructs browsers to assemble malware directly in memory. The operation has been active since late 2024 and is localized to 25 languages in 12 countries, primarily in Asia Pacific and Latin America. A filtering system ensures that only real targets (retail traders and crypto investors) land on the malicious pages, while researchers, scanners, and security bots are redirected to blank pages.

Confiant says the campaign's design stands out through its use of the web browser as "a local assembly pipeline" for the malware. The page registers a service worker as a download manager, sets up a shared worker to assemble the malware from components, and uses randomized seed/size parameters per session so each resulting malware file has a unique hash to bypass static detection. Remote components and locally generated bytes are combined to build the malicious payload from a clean version of the Bun executable, then handed to the service worker to trigger a same-origin download, so no finished file ever crosses the network.

Earlier variants of the SourTrade campaign used the StreamSaver project on GitHub; since April the operation switched to same-origin ServiceWorker delivery. This corroborates a 2025 Bitdefender report on a resilient malvertising campaign whose payload could intercept network traffic (acting as a proxy), collect cookies/passwords, keylog and screenshot, steal crypto wallet data, and establish persistence.

Users are advised to avoid downloading financial/crypto apps from social media ads or sponsored search results, obtain executables from official sites, and verify installer digital signatures.

a064b3b327ef.text:
Rapid7's MDR team discovered an exposed server functioning as an operational malware delivery and testing laboratory containing over 1,000 artifacts. The investigation began with an alert about a user executing a file from a WebDAV server via rundll32.exe.

Operational Insights: The exposed infrastructure revealed an attacker operating "like modern software product teams." The server hosted 453 bulk-generated shortcut lures with spoofed filenames and fake icons, 236 filename-spoofing tests (Unicode, double-extension, padding), 146 URL/LOLBin execution experiments, 89 encrypted droppers, and comprehensive testing documentation. LLM-generated README files with lures and malicious executables suggested the operator used generative AI for rapid lure generation and documentation.

Campaign Details: CURP Campaign (Mexico) targeted Mexico's national ID lookup service through a typosquat domain, triggering WebDAV-based malware delivery that ultimately deployed PureRAT 4.4.3, a .NET information stealer targeting cryptocurrency wallets, browser data, and credentials. The DlrtyGames Campaign used 7-Zip SFX droppers with DLL sideloading and process hollowing to deploy a modular RAT with keylogging and wallet-targeting capabilities.

Critical OPSEC Failures: The operator left behind "Simba Service" admin panel documentation containing default credentials, panel IP/port, API endpoints, and deployment instructions—all without changing default passwords.

Traffic Analysis (5.5-day window): 77,098 requests from 3,892 unique IPs across 101 countries. Mexico generated 82.5% of traffic with ~2,365 launch events. Peak activity: June 21-24, 2026.

c7200eddcdca.text:
Arista has released patches for CVE-2026-16812, a maximum-severity command injection vulnerability in VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) on-premises deployments. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 10.0 and is actively being exploited in real-world attacks.

VeloCloud Orchestrator serves as a centralized management platform for configuring and monitoring SD-WAN deployments and edge devices. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to "access privileged functionality that was intended only for internal use," according to Arista's advisory. The company emphasized that VCO is exposed by default with no configuration option to prevent external access. Attackers need only network connectivity to the web interface—no credentials are required.

Affected Versions: VCO 5.2.x before 5.2.3.14; VCO 6.1.x before 6.1.3.4; VCO 6.4.x before 6.4.2.4; VCO 7.0.x before 7.0.0.1. Hosted and Dedicated deployments were already patched and are unaffected.

Arista identified three malicious IP addresses exploiting the flaw: 8.19.75.217, 206.72.242.124, 206.72.242.162.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added this vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered federal agencies to mitigate it by July 30, 2026.
