Angel Marchena, Director of Technical Operations at Western Governors University, explained: "Dynatrace helps us reduce manual effort by providing automation that is grounded in real-time context, which allows our teams to focus on higher-value work."

Key Capabilities

Autonomous SRE Agent automatically activates when issues are detected, determining whether they relate to existing investigations and enriching findings with additional context.

Cloud SRE Agent manages remediation across AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, centralizing results for auditable autonomous operations.

Agent Builder lets organizations develop custom AI agents without programming expertise, customizing automation for their specific needs.

Enhanced Dynatrace Assist extends natural-language investigation and agent workflows to broader user groups.

Expanded Integration Ecosystem connects with major cloud providers, platforms like ServiceNow and PagerDuty, and developer tools.

Steve Tack, Chief Product Officer at Dynatrace, stated: "Most observability platforms stop at data – leaving humans to find answers, determine what to do, and execute."

The approach differentiates itself by grounding decisions in deterministic, real-time environmental understanding rather than probabilistic outputs. Every action remains transparent, auditable, and governed.

Cloud SRE Agent, Enhanced Dynatrace Assist, and expanded integrations are presently accessible to SaaS customers. The Autonomous SRE Agent and Agent Builder are expected in August.

(Published: July 27, 2026.)

4739d8cef727.text:
Zenity has announced a major expansion of its platform, positioning itself as "the AI security platform for autonomous AI built around a new security architecture designed to govern AI decisions before they become enterprise actions, including those made by long-horizon agents operating autonomously across extended, multi-step workflows."

The platform now includes Exposure Management and Runtime Boundaries capabilities, both designed to enforce security at the decision point where agents make choices before taking action.

The company identifies a critical shift: while first-generation enterprise AI required understanding where it was used and who could access it, autonomous AI presents different challenges—particularly regarding long-horizon agents that execute multi-step tasks over hours or days. "Risk can emerge across a sequence of individually legitimate decisions as their context, access, tools and actions evolve throughout the workflow."

Zenity's approach centers on a "decision layer" that evaluates every AI action before it becomes an enterprise action, rather than merely alerting after an agent has already acted. The platform operates through three integrated capabilities:

Surface: Continuously discovers AI agents, validates attack paths, and prioritizes exposure.

Enforce: Runtime Boundaries evaluate AI actions in real time, determining whether they should proceed, be blocked, or terminated before business impact occurs.

Protect: AI-powered Digital Forensics and Incident Response closes the loop, with Guardian Agents continuously learning from investigations to strengthen future policies.

Runtime Boundaries analyze agent intent, identity, requested actions, accessed data, tools, previous activity, and enterprise policy. The system enforces policies across multiple platforms including Claude Code, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot, Salesforce Agentforce, ChatGPT Enterprise, Amazon Bedrock, and custom AI agents.

VP Product Tomer Teller stated: "The future of AI security won't be defined by what an AI agent already did. It will be defined by what AI is allowed to do before it acts."

The company emphasizes creating a continuous security loop where exposure analysis informs runtime decisions, investigations improve policies, and each decision strengthens future protection.

(Published: July 27, 2026.)

fd460f07ef31.text: JetStream Security has announced the release of an AI Kill Switch that allows organizations to shut down compromised AI agents on-demand without impacting other AI operations. This new control plane for AI agents solves the inability to stop a single agent that falters, begins overspending, or needs to be taken offline for compliance reasons without affecting other agents. JetStream's AI Kill Switch solves a problem many businesses have not faced up to this point: AI systems are becoming increasingly capable and as evidenced by the recent OpenAI/Hugging Face incident, can cause significant collateral damage as they seek to attain their goals in ways that we cannot predict. This new reality means that every organization needs to have the ability to continuously monitor its AI systems and have the ability to precisely halt malicious actions using a kill switch. "Not being able to stop a runaway AI system without impacting other production systems is one of the chief" reasons companies hesitate on AI deployment, according to JetStream Security CEO Raj Rajamani. He notes that only 17% of organizations operate AI at production scale, constrained by insufficient confidence and governance rather than model limitations. The Kill Switch reduces client concerns about system reliability. JetStream's approach integrates multiple factors: the person initiating action, the AI agent identity executing it, the system's intended purpose from its AI Blueprint, and the product owner responsible. Access permissions documented in AI Blueprints ensure every agentic action traces back to accountable personnel, enabling targeted revocation and component shutdown. Since each agent maintains independent entitlements, the Kill Switch affects only that specific agent, and these actions remain reversible. The platform records all activities with timestamps, providing organizations audit trails for post-incident examination and regulatory compliance. Regulatory frameworks increasingly demand shutdown capabilities. The EU AI Act mandates safe-halt mechanisms for high-risk systems, while NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 require organizations to disengage AI operating beyond approved parameters.

f2d9b811ccab.text: 7AI has announced two major platform capabilities: 7AI Federated SIEM, which lets security teams query, investigate, and act on data wherever it lives, including within 7AI, and 7AI Build, which lets enterprises and partners define agentic workflows, skills, and AI-native security services on top of the 7AI platform. Lior Div, CEO of 7AI, stated: "Three out of five customers we have talked to in the past year tell us the same thing: they want to stop putting everything into the SIEM." He explained that when AI agents can query and investigate data where it resides, customers prefer a federated approach that separates detection from storage and enables reading and acting on data across multiple locations. Div further noted that agents built on context graphs connecting federated data access, enterprise insights, and customer-defined skills can investigate based on organizational workflows rather than default vendor settings. The announcement follows 7AI's June launch of Threat Hunt, Threat Intel Hunt, and Skills capabilities. Over one year at enterprise scale, 7AI's agents have completed more than nine million investigations, reclaiming over one million analyst hours. 7AI Federated SIEM allows enterprises to connect security data across existing SIEMs, data lakes, and cloud platforms. Detection is abstracted from storage, enabling customers to migrate data on their own timeline without duplication. 7AI Build enables security teams and partners to create agentic workflows and custom skills. Teams can encode organizational context and investigative techniques into the platform. The platform supports three operational models: direct deployment, combined deployment with 7AI expertise through PLAID ELITE, or building custom offerings on 7AI's foundation. Yonatan Striem-Amit, CTO of 7AI, emphasized: "AI security platforms cannot be rigid. Every enterprise has its own tools, policies, workflows, risk tolerances, and institutional knowledge."

119f196c6134.text: C1 has launched shadow AI discovery to eliminate the massive security blind spots created by unauthorized AI agents, tools, and credentials. By automatically discovering and folding every AI-adjacent identity into C1's existing identity governance platform, organizations can finally ensure that the governed path is the fastest path to safe AI adoption. Shadow AI discovery works across two surfaces. In the cloud, C1 uses connectors to find unowned agents and map every MCP server, API, and data store that agent can reach. It flags long-lived keys and over-permissioned service accounts on sight. On the endpoint, C1 scans devices for local MCP configs, unsanctioned copilots, and API tokens sitting in plaintext in .env files. Cloud and endpoint findings land directly in the C1 platform, answering the question: what AI is running, and who owns it? AI has multiplied the number of non-human identities (NHIs) inside the enterprise. The fastest-growing and least-governed NHI is the AI agent that authenticates on its own and accumulates its own credentials. Existing tools miss it. Privileged-access tools guard human sessions, endpoint tools watch processes, and data-loss tools watch sanctioned apps. Each one assumes an identity is a person or an approved app. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 found that "one in five organizations reported a breach due to shadow AI, and among those breached through an AI model or application, 97% lacked proper AI access controls." For much of the market, governing shadow AI stops at detection. In C1, discovered agents become real access items on the same fabric as employee access. Teams assign owners, route approvals, certify in reviews, and de-provision stale credentials. Governance becomes a lifecycle rather than a one-time action, with complete audit logging. CEO Alex Bovee stated: "Every CISO knows shadow AI is happening in their environment, and now especially on the endpoint." He emphasized the necessity for "complete visibility into AI, harnesses, and MCP use across cloud and end user environments" to maintain control. With shadow AI discovery, security teams can protect against future attacks and prepare for emerging threats while enabling organizations to scale AI adoption confidently.

74bb1435a63b.text: Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has implemented a new naming convention for tracked threat actors following the merger of Mandiant and Google's Threat Analysis Group into a single unit. Previously, these organizations maintained separate naming schemes, creating confusion with mixed sequential identifiers like APT1 and independently developed names. The new system assigns every tracked threat actor a two-word cryptonym. The first word identifies the specific group—either retaining recognized names from prior public reporting or using randomly generated words reviewed by analysts to avoid bias. The second word denotes the threat actor's category, reflecting assessed country attribution, criminal motivation, or activity type. Google established these category classifications: CASTLE for People's Republic of China groups; ION for Iran-linked groups; NEPTUNE for North Korean groups; RELIC for Russian groups; COMET for cybercriminal groups. Google stated: "Transitioning to a convention that is simpler to follow and remember is a practical step toward managing a highly intricate tracking problem." As an example, Sandworm (APT44), the Russian state-linked group, now carries the designation SANDWORM RELIC. GTIG has begun renaming several dozen active threat groups, with additional actors to follow. Previous names remain searchable in the Google Threat Intelligence platform alongside MITRE ATT&CK mappings and aliases from other security vendors. The organization will continue using "UNC" (uncategorized) designations for threat clusters under early investigation.

7fa038f817c1.text: n8n has patched a high-severity expression-sandbox escape allowing authenticated workflow editors to execute operating-system commands on the server running the automation platform. Security Joes discovered the flaw while investigating n8n's February fix for CVE-2026-27577. The affected versions are those below 2.31.5 and versions 2.32.0 through 2.32.0. n8n resolved the issue in versions 2.31.5 and 2.32.1, tracking it as GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m with a High CVSS 4.0 score of 8.7. No CVE had been assigned as of the publication date. Administrators should update installations rather than relying on interim guidance to restrict access to trusted users only. The advisory describes such controls as incomplete short-term mitigations. No patched 1.x release exists, and n8n Cloud's status remains undisclosed. Exploitation requires valid account credentials with workflow creation or modification permissions. A successful attack executes commands with n8n process privileges, potentially exposing encryption keys and decrypting stored credentials. The vulnerability exploited two distinct gaps in n8n's sandbox implementation: arrow functions bypassed identifier rewriting, and Reflect.get() calls accessed restricted properties dynamically. Security Joes accessed process.getBuiltinModule, loaded child_process, and executed host commands. The researchers tested their proof-of-concept against n8n 2.30.4 successfully. The fixed rewriter now includes dedicated arrow-function handling routing bare identifiers through the data context. Security Joes reported the flaw July 15 after discovering it July 14. n8n published fixes July 22. Defenders should review workflows for unexpected arrow functions and monitor for suspicious shell command execution spawned from n8n processes.

448257458c4f.text: Threat actor names can sound simple. LockBit. Fancy Bear. BlackCat. Scattered Spider. Anonymous Sudan. Each name gives the impression of a clear group with a defined identity. In threat intelligence, however, the name is rarely the whole story. Some names are chosen by attackers. Others are assigned by researchers, security vendors, governments, or public databases. One name may represent a ransomware brand, a hacktivist identity, a research label, a campaign, a malware family, or an activity cluster observed across different incidents. For security professionals, this distinction is important. Confusing attacker created identities with researcher assigned labels can lead teams to overestimate certainty, miss relationships between aliases, or focus on the name instead of the behavior behind it. Who Gets to Name a Threat Actor? Threat actor naming usually starts with either visibility or investigation. When a group wants attention, it may introduce itself publicly through a leak site, Telegram channel, ransom note, cybercrime forum, or public claim of responsibility. This is common among ransomware groups and hacktivist collectives because recognition can support their goals. Researcher assigned names start from a different place. Analysts may see repeated malicious activity across victims, environments, tools, infrastructure, or techniques and need a way to track it. MITRE ATT&CK describes groups as 'activity clusters tracked by a common name in the security community,' and notes that different organizations may use different names for similar activity. When the Name Becomes the Brand: For ransomware groups, a name can carry business value, building credibility and increasing fear during negotiations. Hacktivist groups use names to point to a cause, region, ideology, or target, framing attacks as political or social statements. Researcher Assigned Names and Activity Clusters: A group name may be based on repeated infrastructure, shared tools, malware families, C2 patterns, IOCs, targeting, victimology, or TTPs. This does not always mean researchers know the real people behind the activity; often the name describes a cluster of behavior rather than a confirmed organization. APT29 shows how quickly naming can become complicated, collecting labels from multiple vendors and reports. Why One Group Can Have Many Names: Different teams see different parts of the same picture (phishing infra vs malware samples vs IR data), and public databases attempt to map aliases. Rebrands add another layer, as groups may change names after law enforcement attention, sanctions, leaks, internal conflict, or reputational damage while continuing similar tools and tactics. Rebrand, Offshoot, or Reused Code? Shared code does not automatically prove two groups are the same, since malware can be sold, leaked, reused, or shared through affiliate programs; analysts must compare timing, infrastructure, victim patterns, affiliates, language, and behavior. From Threat Actor Name to Action: Threat actor names help organize intelligence and communicate risk, but the real value comes from the evidence behind them. Exposure management brings threat intelligence into focus by helping security teams move from a name to the assets, weaknesses, identities, and paths that could create risk in their own environment.

a7b0f3768048.text: MedusaHVNC is a remote access trojan (RAT) being sold as malware-as-a-service (MaaS). It is promoted through its own website and a Telegram channel. It was found and analyzed by BlackFog, with the analysis finding a hidden virtual network computing (HVNC) module that opens a legitimate browser on a separate hidden Windows desktop. Since it operates from a hidden desktop, its operation is invisible to the user. The malware uses a 5-stage infection chain. It starts when the legitimate wscript.exe executes a JScript launcher. The script waits for just over 7.5 seconds and then builds its embedded files under %TEMP%\Nx2981Okkr2\. Several files are written to disc, including an encrypted payload and a .bat in the Startup folder to maintain persistence. Windows AutoIT is used to decrypt the payload and start charmap.exe (the Windows character map utility). The loader, now inside charmap.exe, contains two further layers of encryption. "The first applies a 16-byte repeating XOR operation to 1,009,152 bytes from the .data section. The second uses ChaCha20" with specific cryptographic parameters. The final payload communicates with the operator's C2 at hardcoded address 51.89.204.28:4444. The operator can create a browser (Chrome, Edge, or Firefox) within the hidden desktop. Legitimate Windows functions support screen capture, synthetic input, and clipboard operations, providing complete control without user visibility. The only obvious mitigation is detecting unexpected data exfiltration, as the RAT's covert operation still requires data to leave the network.

640a65bd987e.text: Security researchers have identified a phishing campaign leveraging Microsoft Teams themes to distribute remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools. The operation, dubbed Operation BlueDash, uses fake "secure document" lures to trick victims. Attack Method: The campaign directs victims through compromised infrastructure to a counterfeit Microsoft Store page claiming Teams requires an update. According to ZeroBEC researchers: "The victim was directed through compromised web infrastructure to a counterfeit Microsoft Store page claiming that Microsoft Teams had to be updated before the shared document could be opened." Payload Delivery: A malicious executable named "supportdev.exe" acts as an Inno Setup loader that launches hidden PowerShell commands, fetches Level RMM installer, and deploys ConnectWise ScreenConnect in parallel. This dual-deployment strategy appears designed to establish redundant remote access capabilities. Attribution: ZeroBEC attributes the operation with moderate-to-high confidence to Nigerian threat actors based on infrastructure analysis, code history examination, and GitHub environment investigation. Reconnaissance Activities: Post-compromise, attackers ran commands to assess system state, firewall configurations, and local administrator privileges, suggesting structured operational procedures. The campaign represents an ongoing trend of threat actors abusing legitimate RMM tools for persistent unauthorized access.

67f9bf539f59.text:
Dan Raby reports:
A former accountant has been sentenced to years in federal prison after he was convicted for taking part in a scheme to laundering more than $5.3 million stolen from Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta.
Ronald Deabler, a 66-year-old Atlanta business owner and former Certified Public Accountant, was found guilty by a jury earlier this year.
According to information presented in court, the situation began when an unnamed hacker was able to get access to the email system of one of Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta’s furniture vendors. The hacker then pretended to be one of the vendor’s employees and tricked the healthcare institution into sending what they believed to be a legitimate payment. Instead, prosecutors say $5.3 million went an updated bank account belonging to Deabler.
Read more at CBS.
Update: This post was corrected post-publication to delete a comment that the accountant had been employed by the hospital. Thanks to a sharp-eyed reader, Adrian Sanabria, for catching my error.

1518711bcf55.text:
From the Information Commissioner’s Office:
A council worker who unlawfully accessed hundreds of personal records has been handed a suspended sentence.
Geoffrey Smith, 31, from Ledbury, Herefordshire, was a new employee at Herefordshire Council working in the Children and Young People directorate. His unlawful conduct was discovered after concerns were raised within the council about potential unauthorised access to a referral case, prompting an investigation into other records he had accessed.
That investigation revealed that, over a four-day period, Smith unlawfully accessed approximately 490 records and downloaded 94 documents. The records related to his family members and families known to him and included children and adults. The records accessed involved highly sensitive material such as medical records, social worker reports and child and family assessments.
On 27 May 2026, Smith pleaded guilty to an offence under Section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990, relating to the unlawful accessing of personal data held on computers. Smith was sentenced at Worcester Magistrates’ Court following a hearing on Friday 17 July to two months imprisonment suspended for 12 months, 120 hours unpaid work, £2000 costs plus a victim surcharge of £154.

42ab31089336.text: Elastic InfoSec operates fourteen AI agents for triaging security alerts. These agents were making 19 LLM calls to complete work requiring only 8 calls. The team developed a five-step optimization methodology that reduced LLM calls to 7-9 per task on the same workload. Core Distinction: Agent Optimization vs. Prompt Engineering: Agent optimization differs fundamentally from prompt engineering. While prompt engineering aims to get a model producing correct answers, agent optimization focuses on "getting an agent to produce the right answer consistently, thousands of times, at a predictable cost." The primary cost driver in agentic workflows is not prompt length but rather the quantity of LLM calls. Three optimization priorities exist: LLM call count reduction (primary lever), tool-call discipline (eliminating redundant queries), and behavioral consistency. The Five-Step Optimization Loop: Step 1: Measure the Baseline using the Agent Builder consumption endpoint, tracking LLM calls, round counts, total tokens, and run-to-run variance. Step 2: Capture Representative Test Conversations (2-4 covering distinct input types) using the Converse API. Step 3: Analyze Conversation Traces for Inefficiency Patterns — vague call budgets, redundant queries, excessive reasoning-only calls, unnecessary schema exploration, overly broad default time ranges. A concrete example replaced "Target 5–10 rounds for this investigation. Hard cap: 12 rounds" with a specific checklist, reducing calls from 14-19 to 7-9. Step 4: Revise and Verify, either via direct prompt editing or an AI-assisted analyzer template, then verify in QA before production. Step 5: Monitor for Drift — watching for token increases exceeding 20% above baseline, rising LLM calls, spikes, and reappearing variance, returning to Step 2 when drift appears. The article provides a diagnostic table and a reusable prompt template covering ten optimization patterns, and positions the methodology as an ongoing maintenance discipline: measure before changing, analyze actual behavior, verify improvements, and monitor afterward.

c538bba68a2d.text: AI pentesting (AI penetration testing) leverages reasoning-capable AI models to autonomously discover, exploit, and validate security vulnerabilities in running applications. It specifically targets context-dependent flaws like broken authorization and business-logic abuse that traditional scanners cannot detect. Unlike pattern-matching scanners, AI pentesters reason about intended application behavior and attempt to subvert it. How AI Pentesting Works: a reasoning model planning assessments through recon, hypothesis formation, probing, exploitation, and chaining; deterministic tools handling well-understood work; an independent validator confirming genuine exploitability; and contextual knowledge of existing tools' discoveries. Vulnerability Classification: heuristic-detectable (SQLi, XSS, misconfigurations) vs context-dependent (BOLA/IDOR, cross-tenant leakage, auth bypasses, privilege escalation, chained business-logic exploits) — AI pentesting addresses the latter. Comparison table: Manual Pentest (deep, novel scenarios, point-in-time 1-2x/year), DAST (heuristic classes at scale, continuous/CI-CD, blind to intent), AI Pentesting (context-dependent flaws, continuous, needs independent validation). The Validator Problem: "A model asked to find and certify its own findings is inconsistent"; independent validation separates proposer and validator roles. Reliability and Limitations: strongest benchmarked model achieved 61% overall but fell below 26% on harder system-exploitation tasks; systems without validators produce approximately 30% hallucinated findings. Current State: non-experts using coding agents solved CTF challenges in under an hour for under $20 (RAND 2026); valid AI-generated HackerOne reports rose 210% YoY with prompt-injection reports up 540%; frontier-model programs found tens of thousands of vulnerabilities in open source (Anthropic; Mozilla 2026); the first in-the-wild AI-assisted zero-day was assessed (Google GTIG 2026). Evaluation Criteria: independent validation, context-awareness of existing findings, continuous operation, verifiable output, low false positives, complementary positioning. FAQ covers differences from AI-powered DAST, why it doesn't replace human pentesters, best-performing vulnerability classes, production safety governance, and pricing models (per-assessment or subscription vs. $20K-$50K manual engagements).

53b7de8eb336.text: JetBrains has fixed a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-63077) affecting TeamCity On-Premises and is urging admins to upgrade self-hosted servers as soon as possible. "For those who are unable to do so, we have released a security patch plugin," noted Daniel Gallo, Solutions Engineering Lead at JetBrains. TeamCity as a possible target: JetBrains TeamCity is a widely used CI/CD server solution, available as TeamCity Cloud or self-hosted TeamCity On-Premises. State-sponsored hacking groups and ransomware affiliates have leveraged vulnerabilities in unpatched TeamCity On-Premises servers previously. About CVE-2026-63077: Discovered and privately disclosed earlier this month by security researcher Antoni Tremblay, CVE-2026-63077 is exploitable via the TeamCity agent polling protocol and may allow attackers to bypass authentication checks and execute OS commands with the privileges of the TeamCity server process. "Depending on the privileges granted to the TeamCity server process, a successful attack could expose TeamCity data, configurations, and stored credentials, modify server state, and potentially compromise the integrity of build artifacts and downstream CI/CD pipelines," Gallo explained. JetBrains has already implemented the fix for TeamCity Cloud deployments, and is now advising customers to do the same on their self-hosted instances, as CVE-2026-63077 affects all TeamCity On-Premises versions. The company checked TeamCity Cloud environments for signs of exploitation attempts and found none. "At the time of publishing this advisory, we are not aware of any active exploitation of this vulnerability," they added. What to do? TeamCity On-Premises customers should upgrade to version 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3, or implement the security patch plugin if they still run v2017.1+. Those running TeamCity v2017.1 to v2018.1 must restart the server after installing the patch, but starting from TeamCity v2018.2 admins can enable the plugin without that step. To mitigate risk, JetBrains advises limiting network access to TeamCity servers to trusted networks, or requiring VPN connections or an additional security layer for internet-facing servers, and running the TeamCity server with minimum OS privileges. UPDATE (August 6, 2026): CISA has added CVE-2026-63077 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered US civilian federal agencies to remediate it by August 8, 2026.

130574b71157.text: A critical flaw in Arista's VeloCloud Orchestrator has gone from zero to KEV in short order, with the networking giant confirming attackers are already exploiting it. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-16812, carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and affects VeloCloud Orchestrator On-Prem, the self-hosted version of the software that enterprises use to centrally manage VeloCloud software-defined wide area networks (SD-WANs) connecting branch offices, datacenters, and clouds environments. According to Arista's security advisory, the flaw is an OS command injection vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to reach privileged internal functionality that was never meant to be exposed externally. Worse, Arista says the on-premises orchestrator is exposed by default, with no configuration capable of removing that exposure entirely. Exploitation requires access to the web interface but no credentials. Until administrators can patch, Arista recommends restricting that interface to trusted management networks and blocking IP addresses associated with observed attacks. "Successful exploitation may compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the orchestrator and data managed by the orchestrator," Arista warned. "Compromises to the VCO platform may allow attackers access to the VeloCloud Edge devices as well." Arista published three IP addresses observed conducting attacks, but otherwise kept its cards close to its chest. The company hasn't said who's exploiting the bug, when the attacks began, or how many customers have been affected, and didn't immediately respond to The Register's questions. Even without those details, the admission of in-the-wild exploitation was enough for CISA to add the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The issue affects only on-premises deployments. Customers using Arista's hosted or dedicated VeloCloud Orchestrator service had already been patched before the advisory was published, the company said. Fixes are available in VeloCloud Orchestrator versions 5.2.3.14, 6.1.3.4, 6.4.2.4, and 7.0.0.1. Arista urged customers running earlier releases to upgrade immediately. Arista is far from the first vendor to issue a patch after attackers had already begun exploiting the flaw. Over the past year, a steady stream of networking gear, VPNs, firewalls, and other edge-facing enterprise software has followed the same pattern: by the time customers learn there's a problem, somebody else has already proved it's worth exploiting.

26eab7862334.text: STAR Labs has published a Linux kernel exploit that turns an ordinary local user into root on the CentOS Stream 9 build it targeted. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-53264 (CVSS score: 7.8), is a use-after-free race in the kernel's network traffic-control subsystem. Researcher Lee Jia Jie said artificial intelligence (AI) helped him find the bug and speed up exploit development. This is local privilege escalation, not remote code execution, so an attacker needs a foothold on the machine before any of it applies. The demonstrated exploit also requires unprivileged user namespaces, the CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT and CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER kernel options, and a kernel-specific return-oriented programming (ROP) chain containing hardcoded offsets. Those conditions narrow the immediate exposure, but full exploit source code is now public. The upstream fix landed on June 1, 2026, and has since been backported to several stable kernel branches: 5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.94, 6.18.36, and 7.0.13, with the mainline fix entering 7.1-rc7. No entry exists in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and no official exploitation reports in the wild as of July 28, 2026. Lee stated that AI assisted with vulnerability discovery, KASAN proof-of-concept development, and race window optimization. "AI still has many blind spots and lapses in reasoning ability," Lee explained, emphasizing that human judgment stayed necessary throughout the work. The vulnerability involves concurrent RTM_NEWTFILTER and RTM_DELTFILTER operations that can leave one thread reading an action object after another thread has freed it. The exploit creates its own user and network namespaces, providing namespace-local CAP_NET_ADMIN without host administrator rights, reaching the vulnerable path through a clsact qdisc and flower filter. Lee reported the exploit succeeded in all 10 test runs, taking between 9 and 111 seconds on a laptop running CentOS Stream 9, though those figures lack independent verification. Kyle Zeng (KyleBot) was credited as the original reporter, having reported the flaw shortly before TyphoonPwn 2026; Lee found it independently and published later technical analysis and exploit code. Distribution status remained uneven as of July 28: Debian lists fixed kernels for supported releases, Ubuntu still marks multiple maintained kernel packages vulnerable, and SUSE lists the issue as pending across multiple products.

4cd6a3cfa212.text: Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Fastjson, a popular JSON processing library for Java developed by Alibaba for serialization and deserialization tasks. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-16723 with a CVSS score of 9, affects all deployments running as Spring Boot executable fat-jars—the most common deployment model. According to Alibaba's advisory, this vulnerability is exploitable "under fastjson's stock default configuration — no AutoType enablement required, no classpath gadget required." The vulnerability impacts Fastjson versions 1.2.68 through 1.2.83 (the final 1.x release), which are no longer supported. Fastjson 2.x versions remain unaffected. Attackers exploit this flaw by crafting malicious JSON files containing a @type value that manipulates the library into performing resource lookups while bypassing restrictions. According to Imperva, "FastJson 1.x can treat the presence of a @JSONType annotation as a trust signal during type resolution." Imperva observed attacks against organizations across business, computing, financial services, healthcare, and retail sectors in the US, with additional incidents in Singapore and Canada. Most attacks originated from browser impersonators, with roughly 30% from Ruby and Go-based tools. Since no official patch exists, organizations should migrate to Fastjson 2.x, enable SafeMode, block specific JSON requests, or use modified builds without vulnerable code. (Author: Ionut Arghire; Published: July 28, 2026, 3:27 AM ET)

166d338bc17c.text: A maximum-severity security vulnerability affecting on-premises versions of Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) is being actively exploited in the wild. Tracked as CVE-2026-16812 with a CVSS score of 10.0, this flaw involves operating system command injection that could enable arbitrary code execution. Arista disclosed that the issue "may allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality and impact the VCO host." The company noted this capability was "intended to be for internal use only and is not intended to be remotely accessible." Affected Versions: VCO 5.2.x releases prior to 5.2.3.14; VCO 6.1.x releases prior to 6.1.3.4; VCO 6.4.x releases prior to 6.4.2.4; VCO 7.0.x releases prior to 7.0.0.1. Arista has already patched hosted and dedicated VCO versions. The company provided three IP addresses associated with the attacks: 8.19.75.217, 206.72.242.124, 206.72.242.162. The firm recommends immediately restricting VCO web interface access to trusted administrative networks, monitoring for connections from known malicious IPs, checking for unexpected outbound activity, and reviewing administrator logs for suspicious changes. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added this vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to apply patches by July 30, 2026. (Author: Ravie Lakshmanan; Published: July 28, 2026)

6c52db12855d.text: Hackers are actively exploiting a critical vulnerability in FastJson, an open-source Java library developed by Alibaba, to conduct remote code execution attacks against US-based organizations across multiple industries. CVE-2026-16723 affects FastJson versions 1.2.68 through 1.2.83 and was discovered by FearsOff, an offensive security company. The flaw stems from the library's type-resolution logic, which "performs attacker-controlled resource lookups before enforcing AutoType restrictions." The vulnerability impacts Spring Boot fat-JAR deployments specifically. As Alibaba noted, "the target runs as a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (i.e., launched via java -jar xxx.jar)." Security researchers at Imperva confirmed that attacks are "targeting a wide range of organizations, across Financial Services, Healthcare, Computing, Retail, Business, and other industries." Currently, nearly all attacks focus on US organizations, though incidents in Singapore and Canada have been recorded. No patch currently exists for CVE-2026-16723. FastJson 1.x is no longer actively maintained, making a future security update unlikely. Organizations should either enable SafeMode or migrate to unaffected versions. FastJson2 uses a safer allowlist-first model and is not vulnerable. (Author: Bill Toulas; Published: July 27, 2026)

316a8f9759e3.text: The cybersecurity industry has long prioritized detection capabilities, investing heavily in telemetry, visibility, and faster response times. However, this focus has created an unintended consequence: attackers now deliberately target these very security systems. Modern threat actors employ tactics including Living-off-the-Land (LOTL) techniques, identity abuse, telemetry tampering, trusted process abuse, and sensor deception. The central theme uniting these approaches reflects a crucial realization: "Visibility has become a target." Bitdefender will host a featured session titled "You Can't Detect What You Can't See: Why Detection-First Security Has Blind Spots by Design" on Wednesday, August 5, from 1:30–2:15 PM at the Pulse Stage 3, Mandalay Bay Convention Center in Las Vegas. Nicholas Jackson (Bitdefender Director of Cyber Security Services) and the article's author will examine how attackers manipulate endpoint security tools. The presentation emphasizes that "many security architectures implicitly trust operating system telemetry," which attackers exploit. Solutions discussed include prevention, attack surface reduction, anti-tampering measures, least privilege access, telemetry validation, and continuous security verification. Research from Bitdefender Labs reveals that "84% of the attacks investigated relied on legitimate tools already present inside victim environments." Organizations increasingly face attackers using native capabilities rather than malware, making traditional detection-focused strategies insufficient. At booth #5135, Bitdefender will showcase the GravityZone unified security platform through an interactive virtual reality experience demonstrating prevention of LOTL attacks, supply chain attacks, and ClickFix techniques. The company emphasizes that AI should empower analysts rather than replace human decision-making in security operations. (Author: Yasser Fuentes; Published: July 27, 2026)

a0255f31baeb.text: Across Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg, organizations are accelerating digital transformation through AI, cloud adoption, and increasingly connected business operations. These investments are creating new opportunities for innovation, but also reshaping the cybersecurity landscape. In this dynamic environment, Rapid7 is excited to announce an expanded strategic distribution partnership with Exclusive Networks across the Benelux region. Why now? Because as organizations grow, so too do the expectations of security teams. As attack surfaces expand, more sophisticated AI-enabled threats emerge; as compliance requirements evolve, leaders expect security to scale right along with the business – all without adding unnecessary complexity. In this chaotic environment, cybersecurity customers are demanding experiences that create more calm. This means no more disconnected security tools or reactive approaches, but integrated security operations, trusted expertise, and partners who can help them improve visibility and build long-term cyber resilience. The Benelux region has long been at the forefront of digital innovation. As organizations continue modernizing their infrastructure, they're also preparing for increasingly rigorous cybersecurity requirements through regulations such as NIS2 and DORA. Meeting these expectations requires partners who understand the regional market and can provide specialist expertise. Exclusive Networks has established itself as one of the region's leading specialist cybersecurity distributors, combining deep technical expertise with a partner-first approach. Rapid7's AI-powered cybersecurity operations platform helps organizations simplify security operations by unifying exposure management, threat detection and response, managed services, and security automation into one platform. Combined with Exclusive Networks' cybersecurity expertise, technical enablement, and regional support, partners are better positioned to expand managed security services and deliver integrated cybersecurity solutions. (Author: Claudia Zoon, Senior Manager, Channel Sales at Rapid7; Published: July 28, 2026)

6ac5e6a7a720.text: Microsoft has launched MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, its inaugural cybersecurity-focused artificial intelligence model designed to identify complex vulnerabilities in code. The model has been integrated into Microsoft's MDASH system, which orchestrates more than 100 specialized AI agents across multiple AI models. According to Microsoft's testing within the CyberGym cybersecurity evaluation framework, MAI-Cyber-1-Flash—when combined with MDASH and GPT-5.4—outperformed competing systems including Google's 3.5 Flash Cyber, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, and Anthropic's Mythos 5 in vulnerability discovery capabilities. The company explained that MAI-Cyber-1-Flash was engineered to "efficiently handle up to 90% of all tasks, enabling MDASH to use the larger and most costly models in our fleet (in this case GPT-5.4) for the 10% of exceptionally hard tasks that truly need them." This architectural approach yields "a 50% cost saving when compared against our best offering in MDASH today." The model will be offered through Project Perception, an agentic security platform that enables organizations to simulate attacks, detect threats, investigate incidents, and remediate vulnerabilities. Project Perception entered public preview on August 3. (Author: Eduard Kovacs; Published: July 28, 2026, 7:11 AM ET)

c60e2e82a7bc.text: Schneier discusses municipalities switching from Flock Safety's license plate readers to Axon's system, questioning whether this change actually improves privacy protections. He quotes a Jalopnik article comparing the switch to "a gambling addict trying to kick the habit by switching from FanDuel to DraftKings." The core argument is that both systems collect extensive personal data beyond license plate information. Switching vendors does not necessarily reduce citizen privacy loss—it merely replaces one surveillance infrastructure with another. Schneier emphasizes the limited substantive difference between the two companies' capabilities, suggesting that municipal governments are engaging in surface-level change rather than addressing fundamental surveillance concerns. The post is tagged with: cars, law enforcement, privacy, and surveillance. (Author: Bruce Schneier; Published: July 28, 2026)

581a8ca53f1d.text: The AI models, datasets, and automated systems researchers depend on can be compromised in ways conventional cybersecurity tools aren't designed to detect. A new project called VERITAS (VERified Infrastructure for Trustworthy AI in Science) aims to close that gap by establishing AI Assurance as a core function of scientific research infrastructure. Led by Anita Nikolich, research scientist and director of research and technology innovation at the University of Illinois School of Information Sciences, the initiative has received a three-year, $896,000 grant from the US National Science Foundation's Cybersecurity Innovation for Cyberinfrastructure program. The project brings together experts in adversarial AI, research cyberinfrastructure, data science and workforce development to address security risks unique to AI-powered science. Nikolich emphasized that "when a poisoned dataset or backdoored model produces an answer that looks plausible but is subtly wrong, no firewall or virus scanner is likely to catch it." The project will pilot standardized model cards and dataset datasheets for large scientific computing allocations, creating traceable records of origin, construction, intended use, and limitations. A new AI Assurance Engineer position will be piloted at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications to review novel AI projects, scan for malicious behavior, check software vulnerabilities, and evaluate agent autonomy levels. Through the National Data Platform Education Hub, VERITAS will develop hands-on challenges teaching students to identify poisoned data, inspect models, evaluate permissions, and find vulnerabilities in scientific AI pipelines. The project represents one of the first applications of AI red-teaming to scientific research infrastructure. Nikolich noted that "AI systems can fail in ways that are difficult to distinguish from legitimate scientific results." (Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security; Published: July 28, 2026)

319720657fd3.text: Advanced AI capabilities are compressing the time between vulnerability disclosure and active exploitation. As tasked by the White House Executive Order on Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security, CISA released Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk to modernize the federal government's approach to vulnerability management. The Directive transitions vulnerability prioritization away from static CVSS severity scores to real-world risk signals, requiring remediation timelines from the next system upgrade to as little as 72 hours based on threat characteristics and exposure status; for the highest risk vulnerabilities, CISA also requires forensic triage to determine whether an asset has been compromised. Wiz addresses this challenge with a unified CNAPP approach, using Wiz Exposure Management to automate vulnerability categorization and validate public exposure, and Wiz Defend to accelerate forensic triage and discover indicators of compromise. BOD 26-04 requires evaluating findings against four criteria: Asset Exposure, Known Exploitation (CISA KEV), Automation Potential, and Technical Impact. Wiz syncs continuously with the KEV catalog against full cloud inventory (VMs, containers, serverless, AI), and its Attack Surface Management (ASM) capability validates which exposures are truly exploitable and maps ownership via the Wiz Security Graph. Wiz maps findings to the mandatory 3-day, 14-day, 60-day, or next-upgrade response workflows, provides AI-driven fix guidance, traces vulnerabilities back to source code repositories for shift-left remediation, scans IaC and container images via Wiz Code, and helps validate exposure isolation to lower risk tiers. For forensic triage mandates, Wiz provides full-stack workload context, telemetry aggregation (processes, network connections, identity permissions), and targeted investigation routing to accelerate incident response. (Authors: Aviram Ben Kalifa, Bryan Rosensteel; Published: July 28, 2026)

922610c2685d.text: Coca-Cola Company's dairy subsidiary Fairlife experienced a ransomware attack in July that resulted in both data theft and production disruptions. On July 27, Coca-Cola announced that the Chicago-based company had "resumed the majority of production" at its four US facilities. The incident, discovered on July 16, "involved access by an unauthorized third party to a portion of the company's systems and taking of certain data," along with production outages. Fairlife generates over $1 billion annually from ultra-filtered milk and protein shakes. The company implemented incident response protocols and engaged external experts. Production was temporarily halted in the US before being restored. According to social media posts, ransomware group Anubis claimed responsibility for the breach, allegedly obtaining 671GB of data including HR records, engineering documentation, and production information. The group claimed to have published this data on its ransomware blog. Ross Filipek, CISO at Corsica Technologies, warned that "that information creates options. Criminals could impersonate executives or vendors" and exploit operational details to identify vulnerable supply chains. Coca-Cola stated that retail availability remained largely unaffected due to existing inventory, and "Product quality and safety have not been impacted." The company asserted the incident was "not reasonably likely to have[,] a material impact on the company's financial condition or results of operations." (Author: Phil Muncaster, UK/EMEA News Reporter; Published: 28 July 2026)

651cb300ed5b.text: Tal Kollander's history divides neatly into two halves: first as an active hacker and then as the block that stops hacks. Based in Tel Aviv, Israel, Kollander defines a hacker as anyone who accesses a computer without proper authorization, subdividing them into white, black, and grey hats based on subsequent actions, and noting that nation-state actors and unauthorized pentesters are hackers by this definition regardless of patriotic motive. She began hacking as a curious child playing Flash games, later building cheat tools with a friend and selling them to companies, then moved into hacking social media accounts as a teenager. During compulsory Israeli military service she joined the IDF's Mamram computer unit and then Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, using offensive hacking skills to protect critical infrastructure like Iron Dome, which shifted her mindset from breaking to protecting systems. After leaving the IDF in 2011, she held CISO and security architect roles at MalamTeam, Avnet's Israeli subsidiary, and EMC/Dell EMC. In May 2019 she co-founded Gytpol (renamed Remedio in September 2025) with Gilad Raz and Yaakov Kogan, raising a first external round of $65 million; she is CEO and CISO. Remedio's premise is that attackers move laterally by abusing configuration and compliance drift even when EDR tools are in place, and the company aims to both find and fix these drifts rather than just report them. (Author: Kevin Townsend; Published: July 28, 2026)

52171374f60f.text: Act Security has emerged from stealth with $60 million in total funding—a $20 million seed round led by Team8 and Bessemer Venture Partners, plus a $40 million Series A led by Notable Capital. Founded in 2025 and based in Tel Aviv, the company addresses the escalating challenge of vulnerability management in cloud environments. The core problem: AI's ability to discover vulnerabilities is outpacing patch deployment. The Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams projects approximately 59,000 new CVEs in 2026—roughly 161 daily discoveries. Recent patch releases underscore the scale: Oracle announced over 1,400 patched vulnerabilities in July 2026, while Microsoft patched a record 622 vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome 149 included patches for 429 vulnerabilities alone. Rather than attempting to patch everything, Act Security reduces exploitability by minimizing unnecessary cloud access. According to CEO Jonathan Langer, "close to 97% of cloud access sits dormant and unused," creating pathways for attackers and uncontrolled AI agents. The platform enables enterprises to remove exposed attack paths, safely deploy AI agents with enforced boundaries, and achieve compliance with standards including NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, and HIPAA. The founding team—Jonathan Langer (CEO), Stephan Goldberg (CPO), Itay Kirshenbaum (CTO), and Ilai Fallach (VP R&D)—previously founded Medigate, which was acquired by Claroty for $400 million in January 2022. (Author: Kevin Townsend; Published: July 28, 2026, 7:00 AM ET)

daac3d6e00d9.text: Cybersecurity startup Hush Security announced a $30 million Series A funding round, bringing total raised to $41 million. Investors include Akamai Technologies, Battery Ventures, and YL Ventures. Founded in 2024 and based in Tel Aviv, Hush Security emerged from stealth in September 2025 with a machine access platform for controlling enterprise AI agents and their infrastructure. The platform features a central agent registry with scoped just-in-time permissions, credential elimination, complete action logging, and centralized kill-switch capabilities. The solution enables organizations to identify agents in their environments and map model context protocols, tools, and accessed resources. It provides centralized control and security management from a single panel, permission mapping, and policy enforcement for each action, along with comprehensive audit trails for investigations and compliance. The company plans to use the investment for hiring engineering and sales talent, accelerating IAM and ecosystem support, and expanding partnerships. CEO Micha Rave stated: "Every company already knows how to manage identity for its people and its applications. But now software acts autonomously, on its own initiative, inside your most sensitive systems. AI agents need strict identity, not just API keys." (Author: Ionut Arghire; Published: July 28, 2026)

707cd010e558.text: Phishing emerged as the dominant initial access method in Q2 2026, appearing in over half of all Cisco Talos Incident Response engagements—a significant increase from roughly one-third the previous quarter. Threat actors refined delivery techniques using QR code-embedded PDFs to circumvent email gateways and leveraged trusted cloud platforms for hosting malicious links. Authentication abuse surged dramatically, observed in 65% of engagements compared to 35% last quarter. Attackers defeated multi-factor authentication through adversary-in-the-middle proxies, session-token theft, MFA fatigue attacks, and self-enrolled devices. Ransomware incidents comprised over 20% of engagements, with Talos IR encountering Sinobi ransomware for the first time alongside Nitrogen and Warlock variants. Notably, operators weaponized legitimate remote monitoring tools—trojanized MeshAgent binaries and Zoho Assist—for covert access. A persistent QR phishing campaign beginning in April targeted Australian organizations by compromising Microsoft 365 accounts; the threat actor, designated UAT-11764, distributed victim-tailored PDFs with QR codes directing to credential-harvesting pages, then created inbox rules for evasion and hosted malicious documents on SharePoint. Researchers uncovered ARToken, a sophisticated PhaaS platform linked to EvilTokens, exposing 80+ API endpoints for device code phishing, token persistence, and SharePoint exfiltration, bypassing MFA using OAuth device authorization flows. Sinobi operators deployed trojanized MeshAgent as a covert SYSTEM-level backdoor, maintaining undetected access roughly three days before encryption, moving laterally via RDP and WinRM using weak service account credentials from ntds.dit. Warlock actors (Storm-2603) deployed Zoho Assist Unattended Agent for persistent remote control. Healthcare organizations led targeted sectors at 17% of engagements, followed by public administration and manufacturing at 14% each. Authentication abuse was the most prevalent weakness (65%); insufficient logging and visibility affected 42% of engagements, up from 18% last quarter; exposed infrastructure vulnerabilities appeared in 31%; unrestricted outbound email enabled propagation in nearly 15% of engagements. (Authors: Lexi DiScola, Dave Liebenberg; Published: Tuesday, July 28, 2026)

7173f23a938d.text: Grafana Labs has announced general availability of six AI capabilities that transform Grafana Assistant into an agentic operations layer for detecting, investigating, and remediating production issues. The new releases include Grafana Assistant Investigations, Grafana Assistant Workspace, Grafana Assistant Automations, the Grafana Cloud MCP server, gcx, and Grafana Agent Observability. The company notes that observability traditionally begins only after code reaches production. However, as engineers ship code more rapidly and AI agents accelerate change rates, organizations must implement observability earlier in the development lifecycle. According to Grafana Labs' 2026 Observability Survey, "92% of practitioners say they'd get real value from AI catching anomalies, yet only 57% say they're currently implementing observability for their own AI systems." Grafana Assistant Workspace, now generally available, provides a centralized location for chat history, live canvas, and investigation reports, allowing teams to evaluate architectures before services are built. The gcx CLI manages dashboards, alert rules, and data sources as code, while the Grafana Cloud MCP server grants MCP-compatible clients direct access to dashboards, alert rules, incidents, and data sources. Both Grafana Assistant Investigations and Grafana Assistant Automations are now generally available, enabling engineers to query telemetry in plain language, correlate technical data with business outcomes, and run saved prompts on schedules. Grafana Agent Observability extends monitoring to AI systems themselves, capturing token usage, costs, and conversation data for forensic-level debugging, with built-in evaluators to test conversations for hallucinations, drift, or policy violations. (Author: Industry News; Published: July 28, 2026)

7af1d86cee70.text:
NVIDIA has assembled nearly 40 technology companies behind a new initiative to build open source security tools for AI, although the coalition launches without participation from several of the industry's most influential AI developers.

Announced on July 27, the Open Secure AI Alliance members including Adobe, Cisco, Microsoft, CloudStrike, Space X, SAP and the Linux Foundation.

However, big-name AI vendors including Google, Anthropic and OpenAI were notable absences from the initial list of signatories.

The alliance – which builds on the Linux Foundation's Akrites initiative and OpenSSF community work – will focus much of its effort on finding, fixing and disclosing vulnerabilities in AI products.

"Across the alliance, contributors are building an open defense stack for agents – from identity and isolation to safe model formats, multi-model scanning and secure coding workflows," said NVIDIA in a blog post.

"Defenders need both frontier closed models and frontier open models, working together, so they can choose the right system for the job and ensure that transparency, adaptation and sovereign control are available wherever security demands them."

While it is not clear why Google, Anthropic and OpenAI are not part of the initiative, one industry CISO noted that broader participation and clearer accountability is needed to improve the NVIDIA initiative's chances of success.

Exabeam CISO, Kevin Kirkwood said, "The major frontier model developers need to be at the table, and the industry needs agreed rules for liability when an agent exceeds scope."

Hugging Face Incident Reinforces Open Source Message

The move comes just days after a serious and unprecedented incident in which two OpenAI models autonomously broke out of a sandbox and hacked Hugging Face's production systems.

Hugging Face revealed that it was forced to use an open-weight Chinese model to repel the attack because safety filters on proprietary US equivalents limited their usefulness.

As the Trump administration mulls whether to restrict access to such models, the NVIDIA alliance is arguing for more openness.

"The right response is not to deny defenders access to capable open systems. It is to pair openness with strong safeguards, clear rules against malicious misuse, rigorous evaluation and rapid remediation," it said.

Experts Remain Skeptical

Gene Moody, field CTO at Action1, said the launch of the alliance is recognition of the fact that "the technology is advancing faster than many organizations can responsibly govern it."

However, he questioned whether it would have the required impact.

"Open source models already exist by the thousands, many capable of running entirely on local hardware, disconnected from any cloud service or vendor oversight," Moody explained. He noted that once isolated, safety controls become vulnerable to modification.

Black Hills Information Security owner, John Strand, was similarly skeptical about whether such efforts would prove sufficient as AI systems continue demonstrating unexpected behaviors.

62e4e16c4435.text:
AWS Shield Advanced is introducing an Anti-DDoS managed rule group designed for application-layer (L7) DDoS protection. This addition will be deployed to eligible web access control lists in Count mode, preserving traffic flow while operating alongside existing mitigation and AWS WAF rules. The rule group is available to all AWS WAF customers and included with Shield Advanced subscriptions.

Migration Timeline

Between July 27 and August 7, 2026, AWS will add the Anti-DDoS managed rule group in Count mode to eligible Shield Advanced web ACLs. The company recommends customers evaluate the rule group before an automatic upgrade in October. During evaluation, organizations should review the new Anti-DDoS dashboard, compare DDoSDetected and DDoSAttackRequests metrics, and leverage AWS WAF labels for request analysis.

AWS notes that "existing automatic mitigation remains active throughout the process" until the rule group assumes responsibility. Beginning January 1, 2027, AWS will discontinue Shield Advanced application-layer automatic mitigation, meaning resources not migrated will lose automatic protection.

Rule Group Capabilities

The managed rule group expands protection by learning normal traffic patterns and responding to attacks independently of health checks. It introduces a Challenge action alongside Block and Count options, with configurable sensitivity levels. The update reduces web ACL capacity requirements from 150 to 50 Web Control Units and adds a dashboard with DDoS events and traffic insights.

Blocked DDoS requests during active mitigation are excluded from AWS WAF and Shield Advanced charges.

Monitoring Features

The rule group introduces CloudWatch metrics and labels for attack monitoring. New DDoSAttackRequests metrics track application-layer attacks, while existing DDoSDetected metrics report Layer 3 and 4 events. Every inspected request receives labels indicating detected events, suspicion levels, and mitigation decisions for use in AWS WAF rules and logging platforms.

Infrastructure Requirements

Organizations using CloudFormation, AWS CDK, Terraform, and similar infrastructure-as-code tools must update templates. AWS Firewall Manager users should add AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet to WAF policies since application-layer protection is transitioning from Shield Advanced policies to AWS WAF.

Pricing

Shield Advanced includes the rule group for up to 50 billion requests monthly. Blocked DDoS traffic is excluded from charges during active mitigation. Web ACLs updated automatically between July 27 and September 30, 2026, incur no per-request fees or WCU consumption during evaluation, though this waiver doesn't apply to manually added rule groups.

dd3d21388be5.text:
Medical Computer Business Services (MCBS), a regional healthcare billing and practice-management company based in Augusta, Georgia, disclosed a significant data breach affecting 1,261,464 individuals.

The breach occurred between September 22-26, 2025, though the company didn't publicly announce details until late June. Investigation concluded May 28, 2026.

Compromised Data

Exposed information includes: "Full name, Physical address, Social Security number, Date of birth, Health plan beneficiary number" and medical records containing diagnosis, treatment, and mental health information. The extent of exposure varies per individual.

Business Context

MCBS provides "billing, coding, accounts receivable, financial, and administrative services" to healthcare organizations, functioning as a data aggregator processing patient records for multiple providers.

Attribution

The PEAR ransomware group claimed responsibility, alleging they exfiltrated 3.3 terabytes of data including HR files, business operations, payment information, and databases. Data has been fully leaked online, though BleepingComputer couldn't verify authenticity.

Recommendations

The company advised affected individuals to place fraud alerts and security freezes on credit files. Those who received medical services in Georgia should contact their providers to determine exposure.

363afc524ce7.text:
Cybersecurity industry body CREST has added additional standards to accredit AI penetration testing services.

Unveiled on July 28, the AI-Enabled Penetration Testing requirements are optional add-on requirements for cybersecurity service providers wishing to demonstrate responsible AI usage, both within their businesses and when delivering services.

This AI-Enabled Penetration Testing accreditation is a new optional module integrated into CREST's existing Penetration Testing Accreditation Standard.

The new AI standards allow accredited providers who actively integrate AI into their daily operations to undergo independent assessment and formally demonstrate responsible, secure AI governance to clients and regulators.

The new module will not affect standard memberships, but it gives providers using AI a way to verify their practices and earn an extra layer of trusted assurance.

Applications are now open for existing CREST members and cybersecurity service providers who wish to obtain additional recognition for the use of AI within their accredited penetration testing services.

CREST AI Penetration Testing Standards Follow Industry-Wide Adoption Surge

This new module launch follows the launch of CREST's AI in Penetration Testing report, released in March.

The report found that over three-quarters (76%) of cybersecurity providers have increased their AI usage over the past year and that 69% are already integrating it into daily service delivery.

The report led CREST to publish a set of AI Principles in March and an AI Charter in June, which was publicly signed by over 100 cybersecurity organizations.

Like the AI principles and the charter, the AI additional standards have been developed by CREST's AI Working Group, which will continue evolving them.

The optional AI-Enabled Penetration Testing requirements form part of the CREST Penetration Testing Accreditation Standard and provide independent assurance of responsible AI usage.

First Accreditations Coming Within a Month

Nick Benson, CEO of CREST, stated the initiatives address a gap where "AI adoption outpacing governance." He explained: "We recognize that buyers increasingly demand AI-enabled services have independent assurance. We believe these additions provide a practical framework to restore market trust."

Speaking to Infosecurity, Benson noted that while no organization has achieved the new accreditation at launch, "the industry body expects the first accredited organization within the next month."

"Unlike voluntary agreements, this formal accreditation integrates directly into CREST's existing complaints and discipline processes. This allows CREST to take action and enforce compliance across the ecosystem," he added.

Chris Oakley, SVP of assurance services for the Americas at LRQA Cybersecurity, stated the new standards are "based on the collective experience of cyber industry leaders" and deliver "a consistent answer to AI governance in cybersecurity."

William Wright, CEO of Closed Door Security, noted that advanced AI systems are "steadily moving towards becoming critical infrastructure" and organizations require "a framework approach for responsible usage that this new standard brings."

1e551e3b5f01.text:
Google has announced that Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) is adopting a new cryptonym-based naming convention for tracking threat actors.

According to the internet giant, the schema moves away from sequential numbers and disparate identifiers, relying instead on two-word combinations for each activity cluster.

The first word is a unique and memorable term that may have been used in public reporting and which is meant to represent the threat actor. A randomly generated term will be used if none exists.

The second word is meant to place each threat actor into a specific category based on motivation, attribution, or activity type.

As an example, Google will use 'Castle' as the second word for threat actors from China, 'Ion' for those from Iran, 'Neptune' for North Korean groups, 'Relic' for Russian threat actors, and 'Comet' for cybercrime gangs.

Under the new naming scheme, Russia's notorious Sandworm group, which has been tracked by Google as 'APT44', will become 'Sandworm Relic'. Within the community, the APT is also tracked as Blue Echidna, Electrum, FrozenBarents, G0034, Iridium, Iron Viking, Quedagh, Seashell Blizzard, TEMP.Noble, TeleBots, UAC-0082, UAC-0113, and Voodoo Bear.

Google states: "We know there are many threat actor tracking schemas in the industry, so we are intentionally seeking to keep this system as simple as possible to streamline operations and facilitate mapping to other naming taxonomies."

According to the company, the issue that remains is the visibility that each cybersecurity organization has into the threat landscape, which prevents direct comparisons between threat actors in most cases.

To kick off the transition, Google has renamed several dozen of the most active threat actors. The process will continue on a rolling basis.

"Previous names will remain indexed and searchable in the Google Threat Intelligence (GTI) platform, with MITRE ATT&CK mappings and other vendor aliases preserved," the company said.

Google will continue to use the UNC designation for uncategorized threat clusters.

685ca1972d2b.text:
JetBrains has issued an urgent security advisory regarding CVE-2026-63077, a critical flaw affecting TeamCity On-Premises installations. The vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating system commands.

Vulnerability Details:
The flaw exploits TeamCity's agent polling protocol to bypass authentication mechanisms. According to the advisory, "this flaw may enable an unauthenticated attacker with HTTP(S) access to a TeamCity server to bypass authentication checks and execute arbitrary operating system commands with the privileges of the TeamCity server process."

Affected Versions & Patches:
- Fixed in versions 2025.11.7 and 2026.1.3
- TeamCity Cloud instances already updated
- A security patch plugin available for versions 2017.1+

Potential Impact:
Successful exploitation could expose TeamCity data, configurations, stored credentials, or enable modification of server state, depending on process privileges granted.

Discovery & Status:
Researcher Antoni Tremblay reported the vulnerability on July 10, 2026. JetBrains confirmed no evidence of active exploitation in the wild.

Recommended Mitigations:
Organizations should require VPN connections or implement additional security layers for internet-facing TeamCity servers, as even the login screen presents potential attack vectors.

f7d09a13e5bc.text:
Kaspersky's threat research team documented a previously unknown malware toolkit developed by Mirage Kitten (also known as UNC1549, Smoke Sandstorm, and Nimbus Manticore), an APT group targeting aerospace, aviation, defense, and telecommunications sectors across the Middle East and Africa.

NightLedger Backdoor

The research identified a Windows backdoor that masquerades as SspiCli.dll and exploits DLL search-order hijacking against AppVShNotify.exe. This implant establishes HTTPS connections to command-and-control servers and supports 14 distinct commands including process execution, file operations, screenshot capture, and process discovery. The backdoor "uses custom delimiter (#%%#) to parse server responses," similar to the group's previous TWOSTROKE tool.

Tunneling Tools

Two WebSocket-based tunnelers were discovered:

BridgeHead: Deployed in Egypt and Pakistan, implements SOCKS5 tunneling with Windows SSO proxy authentication support
ArcBridge: Identified in April 2026, supports tunnel creation and hostname resolution commands

Both tools demonstrate sophisticated evasion techniques, including username-based execution validation to prevent analysis environment execution.

Geographic Impact

Victims span multiple countries including Egypt, Jordan, Tanzania, Pakistan, Ethiopia, and Burkina Faso across government, aviation, telecommunications, and financial sectors.

ef60ae51b015.text:
This security analysis discusses a malware campaign distributing malicious payloads through fake banking emails. The attack chain begins with a RAR archive containing a VBS script that decodes and decompresses a Base64-encoded payload.

Infection Chain Overview

The initial VBS script executes PowerShell commands to decompress gzipped files and write three additional files to disk: an AutoIT3 interpreter executable, an AutoIT script, and encrypted shellcode.

The malware establishes persistence by adding a registry entry: "reg add HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run /v Windows32..."

Payload Injection Technique

The AutoIT script performs process injection into charmap.exe (Windows Character Map utility) using Windows API calls:

OpenProcess
VirtualAllocEx
WriteProcessMemory
CreateRemoteThread
CloseHandle

The shellcode undergoes XOR decryption (key 0xEC) before injection. The final payload is identified as VIPKeylogger malware, which communicates with cphost17[.]qhoster[.]net.

Key Observation: The analysis notes this AutoIT-based approach mirrors techniques described in concurrent malware research, suggesting a broader campaign trend.

261b680f3e5f.text:
In this Help Net Security interview, Brandy Wityak, VP of Complex Matters at LevelBlue, explains what happens in the hours after a shadow AI incident.

She describes how quickly logs roll over, why firewall records of outbound traffic to AI platforms are often gone before responders arrive, and what regulators look for when they assess whether a company did enough. Wityak also discusses the gap between an AI policy in a wiki and a control a company can defend, and when documentation helps or hurts.

When you walk into an organization after a shadow AI incident, what is the first artifact you ask to see, and how often does that single request surface a gap the company didn't know it had?

The very first artifact to be requested should be the user's endpoint being secured. Any logging, which might show any user action should also be preserved to prevent rollover.

Typically, this will lead to an organisation not knowing or understanding which logs they have or indeed where they keep them.

On numerous occasions we have asked for logs only for the organisation to come back three days later saying they can't find them, or that they don't actually store them even though they thought they did. In some cases they weren't logging certain events at all, despite believing they were. "The gap between what an organisation thinks its logging environment looks like and what it actually looks like is one of the most consistent things we see."

How long after an incident does the evidence window begin closing, and what specifically is the first thing to disappear?

It starts closing the moment the incident occurs. Logs have limited retention periods and will begin to roll over immediately. "The first thing likely to have already gone is firewall logging showing outbound connections to AI platforms — api.openai.com, claude.ai, gemini.google.com."

Those connections are often the clearest evidence of what data left the organisation and when, and they are frequently no longer available by the time we are engaged.

If the data never left the endpoint at all, the situation is even more time-critical. The window further shortens, if evidence exists only on the user's endpoint and is held in memory. Every action the user takes on that device after the incident, risks overwriting that data permanently. In those situations, the speed at which the endpoint is secured is everything.

Walk us through the difference between a regulator who concludes an organization was unlucky and one who concludes it was negligent. What specific piece of evidence, or absence of it, tends to tip that judgment?

It is unlikely a regulator would conclude an organisation was simply unlucky. The incident will be measured against the regulatory standards the organisation is bound by. Under UK and EU GDPR, that means whether appropriate technical and organisational measures were in place relative to the risk.

The use of shadow AI by an employee is never unlucky from a regulatory perspective — the organisation may be found to have failed in its duties and held accountable. "The central question in shadow AI incidents is likely to be whether the organisation took measures within its power to restrict employee activity and mitigate risk."

Plenty of companies have an AI usage policy sitting in a wiki. How does a regulator distinguish a policy that merely exists from a control that demonstrably functions, and which side of that line do most companies fall on?

Currently, we believe most companies are at the start of the maturity journey around AI governance and technical controls. The question is not simply, do they have a particular control – whether that be a written policy, governance plan, or technical restriction. It's whether the actions of the organisation to mitigate shadow AI risk was appropriate.
