Wiz Research made several disclosures: GhostApproval (a trust-boundary flaw affecting six AI coding assistants), a critical Amazon Q Developer VS Code extension flaw allowing credential theft via malicious Git repos, the Miasma supply-chain attack compromising 30+ Red Hat Cloud Services npm packages with the Mini Shai-Hulud worm, threat intelligence on cryptocurrency-targeting social engineering, a GitHub RCE (CVE-2026-3854), analysis of the Axios NPM supply-chain compromise, and 2026 Threat & Security Reports on shared dependency risk and AI-driven cloud exploitation economics. The post closes thanking customers, the Wiz team, and Google colleagues, stating the Wiz mission remains to protect everything organizations build and run.

5c43d38910b8.text: Microsoft has released the KB5101684 preview cumulative update for Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2, featuring 42 bug fixes and feature improvements. This optional non-security preview update is part of the company's monthly testing schedule, released at month-end to trial fixes before the following month's Patch Tuesday. Unlike regular security updates, monthly non-security previews don't include security patches and remain optional for users. Users can install KB5101684 through Settings > Windows Update > 'Check for Updates.' Since it's optional, a download prompt appears unless 'Get the latest updates as soon as they're available' is enabled. The update is also available via the Microsoft Update Catalog. The update advances Windows 11 24H2 to build 26100.8973 and Windows 11 25H2 to 26200.8973. The update resolves several issues: File History backup failures with false credential errors, newly enrolled devices remaining incorrectly noncompliant, and files on DFS mapped drives incorrectly marked as internet-sourced. The rollout includes Voice Isolation for Voice Access, which filters out other speakers and background noise to improve speech recognition. Additional features include improved File Explorer navigation, enhanced search for misspelled app names, and Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security expansion to external fingerprint readers. Microsoft reports no known issues with this update.

897b6b676b75.text: A new Mirai-derived IoT botnet discovered by Nozomi Networks Labs can force infected Linux devices to reboot when its main process is killed, enabling persistence mechanisms to relaunch the malware. The threat, named Tengu, was identified using machine-learning technology designed to detect previously unknown malware families. The dropper initially reached honeypots via Telnet credential brute-force attacks. Tengu includes encrypted command channels, traffic relay functionality, payload delivery, system reconnaissance, and multiple denial-of-service methods. The malware features multiple persistence and self-defense mechanisms designed to keep the malware running on compromised Linux-based devices and make recovery more difficult. It maintains Mirai traits like plaintext registration and reused DDoS code, while adding SOCKS5 proxy functionality, shell execution, and the ability to download ELF binaries or Android APKs via an IPFS gateway. The malware supports 25 DDoS techniques and targets Android TV boxes. Beyond systemd and init.d persistence, Tengu deploys a hidden guardian process checking every 60 seconds whether the main process runs, restarting it if necessary. It also abuses Linux hardware watchdogs - a background process feeds the watchdog only while Tengu operates, triggering device reboot within 30 seconds if terminated. Additional defenses include overwriting reboot/shutdown binaries, terminating competing botnets, string decryption during execution, memory-only operation, debugger detection, and timing analysis to detect emulation. Nozomi advises applying security patches, replacing default credentials, network segmentation, and monitoring Linux and IoT devices for suspicious activity. The organization published indicators of compromise and MITRE ATT&CK mappings.

14c865c2685e.text: Security researchers at Tenable suspect the Iran-linked group CyberAv3ngers orchestrated cyberattacks disrupting more than 30 Minnesota water facilities. While neither state nor federal authorities have formally attributed the attacks, Tenable noted the operational patterns align with the group's previous activities and timing relative to recent government warnings. CISA released an advisory on July 22 alerting about Iran-linked attackers targeting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) across critical infrastructure - four days before Minnesota reported its water system disruptions. On July 26-27, coordinated cyberattack attempts targeted operational technology at over 30 community water systems statewide. Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) confirmed the Department of Health is collaborating with affected facilities to maintain public safety. No communities have mandated water conservation changes. Braham initially restricted water use but issues resolved the same day; Maple Plain declared a local emergency for resource coordination flexibility; Plymouth and South St. Paul confirmed cyber-related disruptions without usage modifications. MNIT's assistant commissioner John Israel said cyberattacks against critical infrastructure require a coordinated, whole-of-government response. Identified around 2020, CyberAv3ngers maintains suspected connections to Iran's IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command, initially functioning as a propaganda persona before its first substantive campaign in November 2023 compromising PLCs at Pennsylvania's Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa. Tenable documented at least 75 Unitronics Vision Series PLC compromises across the US, Israel, UK, and Ireland exploiting default passwords. Between 2024-2025 the group developed IOCONTROL malware targeting OT/IoT devices, with OpenAI documenting use of ChatGPT during development. 2026 marked escalated targeting of US critical infrastructure via Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley PLCs beginning March, and CISA's July update expanded potential targets to Schneider Electric and Siemens equipment. Experts emphasize small and rural water facilities are particularly vulnerable, lacking dedicated cybersecurity personnel and often managing systems through remote-access software like TeamViewer and AnyDesk or exposing PLCs directly to the internet, bypassing enterprise security controls. Poor IT/OT segmentation enables single intrusions to propagate across extensive networks.

aea7b8697d50.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a large-scale fraud campaign involving the creation of lookalike websites impersonating major Russian companies to siphon funds from international firms over more than nine years. According to Russian cybersecurity vendor F6, threat actors have established clone websites of Russian companies across multiple sectors including fertilizer manufacturers, petrochemical companies, metallurgical plants, logistics operators, and banks. The operation began in 2017. Most of the content on these fraudulent websites was copied from the legitimate company websites; some also used lookalike domain names. These fake websites, available in English, French, Arabic, and Russian, were used to target international customers and steal advance payments for goods that did not exist. The phony prepayment scheme primarily targeted organizations in Commonwealth of Independent States countries, focusing on the B2B sector and international trade. Attackers initiated contact through cold calls, phishing email campaigns, and fraudulent corporate websites, sometimes hiring unsuspecting sales representatives to pass customers to a 'senior manager' who then sent commercial offers, contracts, and invoices with bogus banking details. An Azerbaijani company lost an estimated $150,000 in April 2025 through such a fraudulent transaction. F6's investigation identified nearly 100 counterfeit domains, most associated with IP addresses 212.127.73.235 and 167.86.100.68, sharing common DNS records and registration data indicating a single coordinated campaign, per F6 threat intel lead Elena Shamshina. The campaign traces back to 2017 when a Russian chemical company received calls from farmers about delayed fertilizer deliveries they had prepaid for via a fraudulent site ('www.agrocenter-eurohem.ru') that was a near-perfect copy of the legitimate site with only bank/contact details changed, including convincing forged commercial proposals on company letterhead. Earlier iterations relied on local .ru domains while newer ones use .com/.org/.net TLDs. F6 also found fraudulent business documents with fake corporate emails and banking details. In a particularly brazen twist, after victim companies published fraud warnings on their real sites, the threat actors copied those warnings onto the fake sites, replacing references to the legitimate domain with the fake one. F6 recommends due diligence on business partners via trusted sources and government registries, verifying subsidiary legitimacy, checking supplier domain/registration dates, and confirming payment details before transferring funds.

98bab11eb4c1.text: The U.S. Federal Communications Commission is banning imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots and power inverters, citing national security risks, in a move that targets China. Beijing quickly accused the U.S. of protectionism. The measures are likely to test relations with Beijing ahead of a planned U.S. visit by Chinese leader Xi Jinping to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump in September. China dominates the global market for humanoid robots with an estimated market share of roughly 85%. The FCC's ban also includes new imports of quadruped robots, often referred to as four-legged robot dogs. The agency said imports of advanced robots pose cybersecurity and other national security risks, and offshore production leaves U.S. supply chains vulnerable to disruptions. The ban on power inverters, used to convert DC to AC electricity in renewable energy systems, data centers and household appliances, could have sweeping ramifications. FCC chairperson Brendan Carr said the move was to secure America's critical supply chains, noting the bans apply to 'new versions' of such imports. The bans follow restrictions on imports of Chinese products including drones, and on exports of U.S. advanced technology to China; the U.S. is also weighing controls on Chinese open-source AI models. Analyst Samm Sacks called it 'a steady drumbeat of potential flashpoints' heading into the Trump-Xi summit. China has been rapidly expanding robot use, with Morgan Stanley forecasting its humanoid market could reach $15 billion by 2030; of roughly 15,000 humanoid robots shipped globally in 2025, Unitree and AGIBOT each shipped more than 5,000 versus a few hundred or less for Tesla and Figure AI. China's Foreign Ministry accused Washington of overstretching the concept of national security to suppress Chinese companies and vowed to take all measures necessary to defend Chinese businesses. Analyst Lian Jye Su noted the bans could interfere with U.S.-China tech collaborations, citing Nvidia's June reveal of a humanoid robot design using China's Unitree chassis; the Pentagon recently included Unitree and other Chinese tech firms on its list of companies with alleged ties to the Chinese military, which Beijing rejected.

1ad9dffbbd43.text: Stairwell announced the availability of Backstory, an agentic investigation platform designed to identify malware variants, locate affected systems, and determine the complete scope of security incidents within seconds. The platform addresses a significant challenge: AI-generated malware is proliferating, creating numerous variants that traditional alert-based tools struggle to detect. While many security tools focus on reducing alert noise, Backstory emphasizes risk reduction by revealing what actually exists in environments and mapping incident spread. Stairwell's Hidden Malware Report revealed that malware families are substantially larger than public reports indicate. Analyzing 1,085 public threat reports, researchers discovered each published malware hash corresponds to an average of 2.4 additional malicious variants - uncovering over 46,000 related malicious files absent from original research. 'Closing tickets faster does not mean you contained the threat,' stated Mike Wiacek, founder and CTO. 'What else looks like it, where did it land, how long has it been here?' Backstory operates on Stairwell's ground-truth architecture, which continuously collects all executable files from customer endpoints. The platform leverages over 1.5 billion preserved executable files, AI trained on 110,000+ detection rules, intelligence from 20+ public threat sources, and 8.7+ billion historical rule matches. Stairwell exhibited Backstory at Black Hat USA 2026, booth 5006.

1d222b99514b.text:
Attackers Are Turning Microsoft’s Trusted Login System Into Their Latest Phishing Weapon
Attackers are increasingly abandoning fake Microsoft login pages in favor of abusing Microsoft’s legitimate authentication infrastructure, allowing phishing campaigns to bypass many of the warning signs employees have been trained to recognize.
Starting on June 25th through the second week of July, we identified more than 200 phishing emails targeting users across approximately 120 organizations, spanning a wide range of industries and countries worldwide. The messages impersonated Microsoft Teams task notifications from HR and directed recipients to a legitimate Microsoft sign-in page. Victims were then prompted to grant permissions to an attacker-controlled application, allowing the campaign to abuse Microsoft’s trusted authentication flow while concealing its malicious intent.
The Lure
The message impersonates a Microsoft Planner task-assignment notification. The sender name is “There’s New Activity On Team,” and the subject line is “HR@[company].com Sent 3 Messages Via Teams Chat”. The body closely mimics Teams styling and references a “Payroll, Compensation + Benefits Update,” alongside a “4 Overdue Employee Tasks” counter intended to create urgency and encourage a quick click. Every link in the message, including both call-to-action buttons, leads through the same redirect. The visible sender address also belongs to the target’s own organization, meaning the email is sent to the same person it appears to come from.
The Attack Flow
- The user clicks the link.
- The link opens a legitimate login.microsoftonline.com OAuth authorize URL — not a look-alike domain, which is exactly why it doesn’t look suspicious.
- Signing-in walks the user into a permissions prompt — “Approve permissions” or “Accept on behalf of your organization.”
- If approved, Microsoft redirects the browser to the redirect_uri specified in the original request. In this campaign, that’s an AWS API Gateway endpoint — attacker-controlled infrastructure, not Microsoft’s.
- The authorization code (or token) is delivered to that endpoint, and the attacker exchanges it for access — scope and impact depend entirely on what permissions were granted and whose account approved them.
This technique is already common and becoming increasingly widespread. It is a named and tracked technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and in 2026 it evolved from a targeted, manually built attack into a service that virtually anyone can rent.
Impact to the individual or business
Depending on the permissions the user approves on the consent screen, the attacker-controlled app can operate across the victim’s entire Microsoft 365 environment:
- Email — read, search, and send from the victim’s mailbox (a common springboard for follow-on BEC fraud from a trusted internal address)
- Files — any documents the user can open, download, or share
- Teams — chats, channel messages, and shared conversations
- SharePoint — company sites, document libraries, and internal content the user can reach
- OneDrive — the user’s personal cloud storage
- Calendar — meetings, invites, and attendee details (useful for reconnaissance and timing convincing follow-up lures)
Among customers whose locations could be classified, the geographic distribution was as follows:
- North America – 98.3%
- Asia – 0.9%
- LATAM – 0.9%
Among customers whose sectors could be classified, the leading sectors were as follows:
- Industrial / Manufacturing — 39 emails (19.3%) across 15 organization
- Legal / Professional Services — 28 emails (13.9%) across 21 organizations
- Nonprofit / Associations — 22 emails (10.9%) across 16 organizations
- Government / Public Sector — 18 emails (8.9%) across 9 organizations
- Healthcare — 14 emails (6.9%) across 11 organizations
- Other (the above doesn’t add up to 100% so we should use “other” for the last option.
Based on the findings, Check Point Email researchers believe that attackers have stopped forging Microsoft’s front door and started walking through it. Every screen the victim sees is authentic, the only fake thing in this entire chain is the intent behind the app requesting access.
The campaign is no longer active, but it’s yet another example of how attackers have fundamentally changed how they’re bypassing traditional phishing defenses.
Recommendations
- Hover over links before clicking and check whether the destination matches the service referenced in the message. Be suspicious when different buttons lead to the same URL.
- Verify that the sender name, sender address, and sending domain are consistent. In this campaign, the message appeared to come from the recipient’s own email address, while the display name claimed to represent Teams activity.
- Do not trust an email simply because it appears to come from an internal address. Display names and sender addresses can be spoofed or manipulated.
- When uncertain, open Teams or other applications directly through the official app rather than using links in the email.
Report suspicious messages immediately. Early reporting allows security teams to investigate the application, revoke malicious consent, identify affected accounts, and block related campaign activity.

8d20a2c683f9.text: Wiz has announced that Red Agent, its AI-powered security tool, is now generally available. The platform helps organizations identify exploitable security risks through continuous, autonomous penetration testing. During the preview period, Red Agent demonstrated significant impact: over 10,000 validated critical exploitable risks were discovered, consisting of externally facing vulnerabilities requiring no authentication; 70% of organizations that enabled Red Agent discovered previously unknown High or Critical vulnerabilities; 35% of organizations found their first verified Critical vulnerability within 1 hour of activation; and at peak capacity, Red Agent scanned 350,000 assets and processed 480 billion tokens daily. The platform comprises three main components: the Web API Crawler, which uses client-side code analysis to discover hidden APIs and map endpoint structures; the API DAST Attacker, which continuously identifies logic-driven vulnerabilities by analyzing application behavior dynamically rather than relying on static patterns; and Secrets Blast Radius, which validates exposed secrets' impact by testing their active status and determining precise access scope. The article emphasizes that adversaries now use frontier AI models to discover vulnerabilities in hours rather than months, and that traditional scanners miss logic flaws through signature matching, manual penetration testing doesn't scale, and point-in-time testing creates security gaps. Real-world examples cited include SSRF-to-Local-File-Read attacks extracting GCP credentials, broken object-level authorization in airline GraphQL APIs exposing passenger data, and unreferenced parameters bypassing credit system monetization models.

1a98bfcdaeca.text: AI-powered Security Operations Center (SOC) startup Mate Security has announced raising $35 million in a Series A funding round that brings the total raised by the company to over $50 million. Led by Canaan Partners, with additional support from Insight Partners, Microsoft's Venture Fund M12, and Team8, the investment round comes eight months after the company emerged from stealth mode. Founded in 2025 by former Wiz and Microsoft veterans, Tel Aviv-based Mate has built an open, agentic platform that relies on AI to transform security operations into continuously learning defense systems. Mate's agentic SOC creates a unique security context graph for each organization, based on assets, business processes, users, and data, which is then used to build detections, triage and investigate incidents, and perform threat hunting and incident response. By using unique context graphs, Mate's agents operate within each organization's context to provide tailored, up-to-date defenses. They operate in a Continuous Detection, Continuous Response (CDCR) framework, retaining knowledge with each investigation to improve detections that feed the next investigation. Planning to double its workforce by the end of the year, Mate will use the fresh investment to expand its customer support, sales, and R&D teams, as well as its market presence. CEO Asaf Wiener stated: 'When we started Mate, we knew we had to invest in the foundation: context and trust, and build them deeply into our product. We will continue moving fast and stay laser-focused on our customers, as we expand into new markets and categories to build the Open Security Operations foundation of the future.'

a4c3a61b7ad1.text: Florida-based zero trust security company ThreatLocker announced Wednesday that it has raised $190 million in a Series F funding round. The company previously raised $20 million in Series B funding, $100 million in Series C funding, $115 million in Series D, and $60 million in Series E funding last year. With the latest round, the total reaches nearly $500 million. According to a source familiar with the matter, ThreatLocker was valued at $1.6 billion in its previous funding round, with the latest raise significantly increasing that valuation. The Series F round was led by Elephant, with support from D. E. Shaw Ventures, Arthur Ventures, and Koch Disruptive Technologies. The investment will fund product enhancements and international expansion, beginning with a new office in the United Kingdom. Over the past 18 months, ThreatLocker expanded to Australia and the UAE. ThreatLocker provides endpoint, network, and cloud security through a zero trust model that blocks unauthorized software and AI tools by default. The platform restricts actions approved applications can take, limits access to storage, manages user privileges, and regulates network traffic based on application identity. It includes policy-based endpoint detection and response capabilities monitoring for indicators of compromise with real-time automatic responses. The company reports its solutions serve more than 70,000 organizations worldwide. CEO Danny Jenkins stated: 'Most cybersecurity tools are still built around identifying malicious activity after it has already entered an environment,' emphasizing their approach of defining what is permitted while denying everything else by default.

6f697c6c583d.text: The article argues that while AI-accelerated exploit tooling (referred to as Mythos) speeds up exploit timelines, the real vulnerability management problem predates AI. Security teams were already struggling with prioritization long before faster exploit tools arrived. The core thesis: 'A CVSS 9.8 with no path to a critical asset is less urgent than a CVSS 5.5 sitting one hop from your customer database. That was true before Mythos. It's just more expensive to get wrong now.' Most enterprise security teams rely on CVSS-sorted vulnerability backlogs of 50,000+ findings without meaningful context. Security leaders consistently report lacking identity context (account privileges), reachability data (internet exposure), and path continuity (confirmed exploit chains to critical assets). Individual tools (Okta, Wiz, CrowdStrike, Qualys, Splunk, etc.) generate excellent isolated signals, but none of them see the chain that connects all four into a viable attack path. Rather than replacing existing tools, the recommended playbook shift is to implement a unified intelligence layer correlating identity, cloud, endpoint, and vulnerability data to identify confirmed attack paths to crown-jewel assets before prioritizing remediation.

22a7f5fab8d4.text: Nebula Security says a patched Firefox JIT flaw could be triggered by simply visiting a malicious webpage and was also used to compromise Tor Browser. Tracked as CVE-2026-10702, the bug provides arbitrary code execution inside the browser's renderer process. Mozilla rated it High and fixed it in the Firefox 151.0.3 update. 'No settings or additional user interaction are required,' Eten Zou, CEO of Nebula Security, told The Hacker News. 'Visiting a malicious webpage is enough to trigger it,' Zou said every Tor Browser release that incorporated a vulnerable Firefox version was affected, though researchers have not identified the exact Tor releases. On its own, the bug runs code only inside Firefox's sandboxed content process. Nebula released public exploit material and used the flaw as the first stage of IonStack, a browser-to-kernel chain built for an ARM64 device running Android 17. The released end-to-end code targets one supported Google build, although Zou said the browser flaw itself is not ARM-specific. The public code contains Firefox 151.0 offsets for the supported ARM64 Android 17 build; Zou described the x86 path as more stable, although Nebula has not completed the full chain for that architecture. Firefox users should update to the latest release. The Hacker News traced the faulty alias declaration through Mozilla's source history to Bug 1995077, which landed for Firefox 147; the override is present in Firefox 151.0.2 and absent from Firefox 151.0.3, placing the affected stable-release range at Firefox 147 through 151.0.2. Mozilla's advisory does not list Firefox ESR, and the faulty override is absent from Firefox ESR 140.12. As of July 28, 2026, the available primary-source record does not establish exploitation in the wild. In its technical analysis, Nebula traces the issue to MObjectToIterator when it runs with skipRegistration set to true. Firefox's JIT compiler turns frequently run JavaScript into native machine code, and to do that safely it tracks which operations can touch memory; Firefox treated the operation as a read even though resolving a lazy property can allocate a replacement dynamic-slots buffer and free the old one. Global value numbering then treated a later slots-buffer load as redundant and reused the earlier pointer after it had become stale. Nebula's exploit reclaims the freed allocation, leaks a hidden-class pointer, builds a fake object, and corrupts a Uint8Array to gain arbitrary memory read and write; the Android code then changes memory protections and redirects a WebAssembly function entry point to ARM64 shellcode. Mozilla's source-level fix removes the custom read-only alias handling from ObjectToIterator and adjusts the related iterator operation. IonStack's second stage is CVE-2026-43499, a separate Linux kernel futex flaw Nebula calls GhostLock; CVE-2026-10702 provides the remote browser foothold while CVE-2026-43499 carries it to root on the supported Android build. Zou said GhostLock is invoked directly from Firefox, and that Android's weaker sandbox makes exploitation easier, though Nebula does not believe a stronger desktop sandbox would prevent the attack. Updating Firefox blocks the documented browser entry point but does not patch GhostLock itself.

2afe43315693.text: Most organizations have incident response plans, security tools, and technical teams in place. Yet new research suggests that many still lack the coordination, visibility, and executive alignment needed to withstand a serious cyberattack. According to The State of Incident Response Readiness 2026, based on a survey of 600 senior IT security decision makers conducted by Vanson Bourne in January and February 2026, 73% of organizations admit they would not be 'fully ready' if a significant cybersecurity attack occurred tomorrow. The findings point to a critical gap between having incident response capabilities and being able to execute them effectively under pressure. The report also found that cyberattacks are already a recurring business risk: 76% of organizations experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, and 32% experienced more than one. Incident Response Readiness Remains a Weak Point: Fewer than 40% of respondents described key incident response components as 'highly effective,' including documented plans, tabletop exercises, threat hunting, digital forensics, and 24/7 monitoring. Coordination Breakdowns Slow Response: 90% of organizations expect difficulty coordinating stakeholders during a significant incident; 75% agree delays or uncertainty around legal and communications team involvement slow decision-making; 89% cite limited executive or board involvement in incident response readiness and decision-making. Visibility Gaps Increase the Risk of Repeat Incidents: 78% agree blind spots in their environment create persistent attacker access and increase the risk of repeated incidents, spanning on-premises, cloud, endpoints, SaaS, identity, and OT environments. OT and ICS Environments Add Business Risk: 84% of organizations are concerned about attackers crossing from corporate IT into OT/ICS environments, particularly serious for manufacturing, energy, healthcare, transportation, and critical infrastructure. Cyberattacks Are Already Causing Business Damage: impacts included operational shutdowns, data loss, reputational damage, customer loss, lost revenue, and executive disruption, varying by sector and region (e.g., retail most likely to report shutdowns/lost revenue; manufacturing/financial services more likely to report data loss; North America highest attack incidence; APAC highest data loss/reputational damage). Ransomware and Cloud Attacks Lead Future Concerns, alongside identity abuse, third-party risk, and AI-enabled threats. AI Adoption Is Rising, but It Is Not a Substitute for Readiness: nearly one-third of organizations report extensive AI use in detection/response, up from 25% last year, with 63% expecting AI embedded by 2027; however, AI cannot resolve unclear decision rights, fragmented coordination, or incomplete visibility on its own. Organizations Are Re-Evaluating Incident Response Support Models, with many expecting to switch IR/MDR providers for more proactive readiness support, better cross-environment coverage, and reduced overreliance on single-vendor ecosystems. Recommendations: define decision rights before an incident, test cross-functional coordination via tabletop exercises, validate visibility across critical environments, use AI to support (not replace) response processes, and assess internal/external response capacity. The report concludes that incident response readiness should be treated as an ongoing operational discipline rather than a static plan or annual compliance exercise.

1f4cc6af4a93.text:
Cyber Threats
Tracking Over 35,000 Fake Sites in the 2026 World Cup Scam Wave
Between January and June 2026, TrendAI™ tracked more than 35,000 fake sites exploiting the 2026 FIFA World Cup, spanning counterfeit merchandise shops, cloned ticket pages, and bogus free-streaming sites, which together drew roughly 1.48 million visits from Japan.
Key takeaways
- Between January and June 2026, TrendAI™ identified 35,538 malicious sites tied to the FIFA World Cup, which together drew roughly 1.48 million visits from Japan alone.
- The activity falls into three main types: fake shops selling counterfeit merchandise, near-perfect clones of official ticket sites, and fake live-streaming pages that never actually show a match.
- The cloned ticket sites are the most dangerous, harvesting credit card details and one-time passwords in real time so attackers can push through fraudulent payments even when multi-factor authentication is in place.
- The best defense is caution: users should navigate directly to official websites, treat words such as "free" and "official" with suspicion, and never enter a one-time password on a page reached from a search result or ad.
Introduction
From June 11 to July 19, 2026, the 2026 FIFA World Cup took place, co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico, drawing attention from fans around the world. Large-scale events like this are prime targets for cybercriminals, and online scams exploiting the tournament have been observed worldwide. This article explains the scam techniques TrendAI™ has identified and what internet users should watch out for.
It bears emphasizing that these scams merely impersonate FIFA, its affiliated organizations, official tournament partners, and legitimate broadcasters and video streaming services, none of which are in any way involved in the scams themselves.
Tens of thousands of scam sites, millions of visits
In May 2026, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) issued a public service announcement (I-052726-PSA) warning of scams exploiting the tournament.
Between January and June 2026, we identified 35,538 malicious sites (scam, phishing, and similar sites), as well as suspicious sites whose safety could not be verified, all containing the keywords "fifa" or "worldcup." We also confirmed that these sites were accessed approximately 1.48 million times from within Japan. That traffic surged as the tournament got underway, showing that Japanese users are among the primary targets.
In May 2026, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) issued a public service announcement (I-052726-PSA) warning of scams exploiting the tournament.
The following sections examine the fake and scam sites we identified more closely.
Fake shops selling fake merch
Between January and June 2026, we identified 6,251 fake shopping sites containing the keyword "FIFA" or the Japanese terms for "World Cup" (ワールドカップ, W杯) or "Japan national team" (日本代表). Many of these had been set up well before the tournament began. To draw users in, attackers rely on techniques such as SEO poisoning, which pollutes search engine results.SEO poisoning, which pollutes search engine results.
These sites display soccer jerseys, tournament merchandise, and other goods, and their overall appearance and layout closely resemble those of legitimate Japanese online stores, but the attackers use various tricks to defraud users of their personal information and payments. Items purchased on these sites often never arrive, and when they do, they may be counterfeit or shoddy goods.
Bogus ticket sites and card-skimming clones
We found a fake website that almost completely replicates the official FIFA hospitality site, where fans can purchase match tickets and hospitality packages. The fake site copies the official site's brand logo and page design, and it goes further: to appear more credible, it loads videos and images directly from the official site's servers and links to FIFA's official social media accounts and policy documents. It even has a built-in automatic translation feature, meaning users across many languages (including Japanese) are potential targets.
The fake site has a login page, but it has no real connection to FIFA's account system. If a user is tricked into entering their email address and password, the credentials are sent directly to the attackers.
Going through with the checkout on this fake site can expose the user's credit card details and lead to direct financial loss. The whole process is designed to look and feel just like a normal online purchase, so it is hard to notice anything is wrong.
- The user enters their credit card details on the fake site's payment page
- The attacker obtains the card details in real time
- The attacker uses the card details to attempt a fraudulent payment elsewhere
- The user receives a one-time password for identity verification from their card company or bank, via SMS or other means
- The user enters the one-time password on the fake site's payment screen
- The attacker immediately uses the one-time password to complete the fraudulent payment
- The user is shown a fake order-confirmation screen
Identity verification with one-time passwords (multi-factor authentication) is an effective defense against payment fraud, but this technique bypasses it because victims enter the one-time password into the fake site themselves.
Fake match streams, real profits for scammers
We confirmed that results for the Japanese search phrase "fifa ワールドカップ 2026 無料配信" (FIFA World Cup 2026 free streaming) led users to fake live-streaming sites. Here too, the attackers used SEO poisoning to game search rankings. Near the top of the video results sat the compromised website of a research institute at a US university. Those results were packed with Japanese-language titles posing as Japanese broadcasters and streaming services, and a single compromised site held multiple embedded fake pages, one for each match.
What the fake-stream operators are really after
Clicking one of these search results carries the user from the compromised website, through relay pages hosted on blogging platforms, and on to a fake live-streaming site. The destination site poses as a sports-focused streaming service and offers pages named after real matches in the actual tournament schedule. A video-player mock-up on the page makes it look as though the match is about to start, but throughout our investigation we never saw any actual footage play.
The fake live-streaming sites have a malicious ad network (an advertising delivery network) built in, so each time the user clicks or taps the fake play button, they are redirected to a different site. The destinations included account-opening pages for legitimate financial trading services and major e-commerce sites. These legitimate businesses are themselves likely unwitting victims of ad fraud, with their affiliate advertising abused through the same malicious ad network.
Some of the fake streaming sites also flash a message that "registration is required to watch," sending users to a sign-up page. That page then harvests personal information and credit card details, or quietly enrolls victims in unrelated subscriptions that keep charging them on an ongoing basis. Whenever a major tournament, concert, or other high-profile event comes around, the attackers swap out their infrastructure and tactics and run the same fake live-streaming scam all over again.
Staying a step ahead of the scammers
Cybercriminals exploit whatever topics and news attract the most public attention to deceive users. Don't take words such as "free" or "official" at face value. With a bit of calm judgment and the right security measures, they can protect their personal information and assets.
- Shoppers should buy tickets, merchandise, and other goods by navigating directly to the official website, not through links in search results or social media ads.
- When users do land on a site from a search, they should check the URL (domain) carefully. They should be wary of listings with unnatural titles, such as those stuffed with symbols.
- Viewers should watch matches through official broadcasters and video streaming services. If an unofficial site advertising "free streaming" asks them to register an account or enter credit card details, they should not comply.
- Even legitimate payments may redirect users to their card company's page for identity verification (3-D Secure) and ask for a one-time password sent by SMS. They should check that the merchant and amount in the SMS match the purchase they are actually making. If anything looks off, such as an unfamiliar amount or merchant, they should stop without entering the code and contact their card company or bank.
- Users should use a different password for each service. If they reuse the same password across multiple services, a single password entered into a fake site can lead to the takeover of their other accounts.
- Installing trusted security software, and making use of its advanced anti-scam features, is another effective safeguard.
Proactive security with TrendAI™ products
Trend Micro ScamCheck, a mobile app dedicated to scam protection, combines several AI technologies to protect users from increasingly sophisticated scams.
Its Web Threat Protection feature blocks access to malicious websites, including fake and scam sites. Its Scam Check feature uses generative AI to assess scams for users: from a screenshot of a suspicious email, advertisement, or social media post, it can determine whether a scam site is likely involved. For PC users, the same Web Threat Protection feature is built into Trend Micro Maximum Security.
TrendAI™' security products help stop constantly evolving, increasingly sophisticated scams before they cause harm, letting defenders move toward proactive, AI-powered security.
- Shingo Matsugaya (TrendLife Threat Research)
- Makoto Shimamura (TrendLife Threat Research)

71e0497b5dd4.text: Elastic automatically translates your Microsoft Sentinel detection rules into Elastic Security. Export your Scheduled and Near Real Time (NRT) analytics rules from Sentinel, upload them, and Elastic picks up the mapping and translation from there using an LLM you choose. Watchlists and severity mappings carry over. This is the first automatic migration path off a modern SIEM, available now in Tech Preview in 9.5, and it works across multiple cloud providers and regions so you can deploy closer to where your data lives. Automatic Migration focuses on the rules that carry your detection logic: Near-real-time (NRT) detection analytics rules, Scheduled Analytic Rules, Watchlists to ES|QL Lookups, and Severity Mapping. Migration steps: On the Security Launchpad, open Manage Automatic Migrations, select your AI provider, and expand Migrate your existing SIEM rules to Elastic. Select the Microsoft Sentinel option, export rules from Sentinel and upload into Elastic Security; Elastic scans for watchlists and prompts for upload when found. Rules show status as Installed, Translated, Partially translated, Not translated, or Failed, with the ability to view, edit, and install rules. On sequencing: Rules first (translate Sentinel rules first if data sources aren't yet prioritized, so Elastic identifies needed integrations), Data first (onboard log sources before migrating rules to improve translation quality and enable immediate rule activation), or Custom data (use Automatic Import for proprietary/non-standard log sources). After migration, Workflows lets you build automation triggered by rule firing, using natural language via Agent Builder. Elastic Security integrates generative AI (RAG, agentic frameworks) alongside Automatic Migration, Automatic Import, and Agent Skills. The author frames rewriting detection rules by hand as the switching cost that keeps teams on a legacy SIEM, and positions Automatic Migration as removing that barrier while keeping watchlists and severity levels intact.

27b0cde33795.text: Cisco Talos has discovered a new Rust-based remote access trojan attributed to the Chaos ransomware group, named 'msaRAT' after binding names found in the binary: 'msaOpen,' 'msaClose,' 'msaError,' and 'msaMessage'. The malware uses the Tokio asynchronous runtime with capabilities for browser-leveraged remote code execution and covert command-and-control tunneling. Notably, msaRAT never directly accesses the network. Instead, it manipulates Chrome or Edge exclusively through Chrome DevTools Protocol, offloading all external communications to the browser itself. Infection Process: Attackers download an MSI installer file ('update_ms.msi') impersonating a Windows update. Upon execution, a custom action extracts lib.dll, containing the RAT payload, directly into memory. Browser Hijacking: The malware searches for Chrome or Edge installations via environment variables and registry, then launches the browser in headless mode with debugging enabled. It establishes a DevTools Protocol session, bypasses Content Security Policy, and injects JavaScript code. WebRTC Communication: The injected JavaScript retrieves STUN/TURN configuration from Cloudflare Workers, establishing a WebRTC DataChannel. The malware deliberately omits ICE candidates, forcing all traffic through Twilio's TURN relay, effectively masking the attacker's actual infrastructure. Communications use double-layer encryption: DTLS plus ChaCha-Poly1305. Strategic Advantage: By routing traffic through legitimate services (Cloudflare and Twilio), the malware evades detection. Network monitoring observes communications as originating from a standard browser process at 127.0.0.1, blending C2 traffic within normal web activity. Detection: ClamAV and Snort signatures are available for threat detection and blocking. Authors: Jordyn Dunk, Michael Szeliga, Takahiro Takeda.

074dcb059a87.text: A static credentials vulnerability (CVE-2026-20316) affecting Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC)—a centralized platform for managing multiple Cisco Secure Firewall devices—is now being actively exploited by attackers, according to CISA warnings. The vulnerability, reported by Jimi Sebree of Horizon3.ai, exists in the FMC's web interface and involves low-privileged account credentials. Attackers can use these credentials to log in and potentially access sensitive information. Cisco noted the flaw could be combined with other vulnerabilities to elevate privileges and enable deeper system compromise. CISA added CVE-2026-20316 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on July 29, directing U.S. civilian federal agencies to remediate by August 1, 2026, and investigate whether their systems were compromised. Cisco's Product Security Incident Response Team confirmed active exploitation began this month. The company provided hotfixes and identified a compromise indicator: the presence of package_info.pl execution referencing /var/tmp/license.tmp suggests potential exploitation. The company strongly recommends rotating all user credentials, keys, and certificates on the Cisco Secure FMC device because active exploitation of this vulnerability has been ongoing. Cisco also updated guidance for CVE-2026-20079, a related authentication bypass flaw discovered in March 2026 that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute scripts and gain root access. No active exploitation of this second vulnerability has been reported. The FMC's web-based management interface represents the primary attack vector. Cisco advised that restricting public internet access to this interface reduces exposure risk. Author: Zeljka Zorz, Editor-in-Chief, Help Net Security.

18e7155f6e5c.text: Rapid7 reported on two critical vulnerabilities in VMware vCenter Server disclosed by Broadcom on July 29, 2026. Both CVE-2026-59309 and CVE-2026-59310 carry CVSS scores of 9.8 and can be exploited by unauthenticated attackers with network access. CVE-2026-59309 represents an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service enabling attackers to gain unauthorized management plane access without credentials. CVE-2026-59310 is a directory traversal vulnerability in the vCenter Syslog server permitting arbitrary code execution for network-accessible attackers. The article emphasizes that vCenter Server compromise grants attackers significant control over the virtualized environment and its associated workloads. At publication, no exploitation evidence or public proof-of-concept code existed, though vCenter has historically appeared on CISA's KEV vulnerability list multiple times. Broadcom provided version-specific patches across multiple product lines (vSphere Foundation 9.1.x, 9.0.x, vCenter 8.0, and others). The advisory notes there are no workarounds for either vulnerability, making patching the only remediation option. Rapid7 customers using Exposure Command, InsightVM, and Nexpose gained unauthenticated vulnerability check access via the July 30 content release. Published July 30, 2026 (last updated August 4, 2026).

3a61bc72010b.text: South Korean authorities and four security firms have disclosed a state-sponsored campaign that compromised trusted domestic websites. The attackers used those sites to exploit locally installed financial-security software and infect targeted visitors with SIGNBT or COPPERHEDGE backdoors. A compromised page could infect a system running a vulnerable AnySign4PC version without a prompt or user-initiated download. KISA says AnySign4PC versions 1.1.4.4 through 1.1.4.6 are affected and lists version 1.1.5.0 as the fixed release. AhnLab refers to two exploited products only as financial-security software A and I and does not disclose their identities or versions. AhnLab identified evidence of related attacks at 72 organizations in 2026 and found 15 legitimate websites used as watering holes, with overlap to attacks ending in Gunra ransomware (shared initial-access vulnerability, malware filenames/execution patterns, SSH key fingerprint 'Qr1to32lQHxEu6phzNyrTZrU0iElrOfVWMBLnqoen24', and network infrastructure including reverse-tunnel address 176.65.128[.]26 and domain jshosting[.]me), though evidence does not establish a single actor ran both. The joint advisory (KISA, NIS, Police, Financial Security Institute, with AhnLab, S2W, ENKI Whitehat, Plainbit) describes spear-phishing lures (resumes, recruitment, investment material, surveys) and compromised news/healthcare/education/manufacturing sites. ENKI identified AnySign4PC exploitation as a zero-day observed since second half of 2025, before KISA's June 2026 patch notice. AhnLab's Operation Double Barrel report describes an exploit chain using four PNG images for key exchange, version-checking, exploit delivery, and success reporting, communicating via WebSocket to trigger a buffer overflow and inject payloads (Struggle/SIGNBT 3.0 or Brandoor/COPPERHEDGE) into legitimate Microsoft processes, supporting remote command execution, file theft, reconnaissance, and further payload delivery. Plainbit reconstructed a watering-hole incident showing webshell installation, JavaScript injection into a news page, in-memory DLL creation without prompts, injection into svchost.exe, and subsequent use of privilege escalation, Mimikatz, RDP, and NLBrute. S2W found DLL side-loading, encrypted registry blobs, and in-memory PE loading across three malware clusters. A March 2026 Gunra ransomware intrusion used the same compromised healthcare website and vulnerability in 'software A,' also injecting into SyncHost.exe, with shared filenames (net.tmp/inet.tmp) and SSH fingerprint, though AhnLab could not determine the relationship between operators (possible shared tools, access broker, or limited collaboration). Neither the government advisory nor the Operation Double Barrel report formally attributes the full campaign to Lazarus, though AhnLab attributed a related March 2026 AnySign4PC attack to Lazarus separately, and Kaspersky previously documented Lazarus using similar techniques (Operation SyncHole). Recommendations include patching to AnySign4PC 1.1.5.0 and hunting for suspicious DLL loading, encrypted registry data, in-memory PE execution, injection into SyncHost.exe/svchost.exe, and unexpected SSH tunnels. As of July 30, 2026, only an unrelated CVE (CVE-2020-7882) is publicly associated with AnySign4PC; no CVE has been published for this specific flaw. Author: Swati Khandelwal.

f7ae161c7226.text: Russian threat actors linked to previous Zimbra exploitation have been observed targeting U.S. and European government entities, telecommunications, financial, hospitality, and aerospace sectors by exploiting CVE-2026-42897 (CVSS 8.1), a cross-site scripting vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook Web Access. The campaign began July 22, 2026, and has been attributed to Laundry Bear (also tracked as TA488, CL-STA-1114, UNK_PitStop, and Void Blizzard). These actors previously exploited CVE-2025-66376 in Zimbra, deploying a malware payload called ZimReaper that harvested 90 days of victim communications and other sensitive data. The current OWA attacks employ 'half-click' exploitation methods where merely opening an email triggers compromise. Threat actors send messages from compromised addresses containing vague, generic lures about supply chains, research updates, and market metrics—deliberately excluding URLs or attachments to increase the likelihood of opening. The weaponization culminates in deployment of OWAReaper, a sophisticated JavaScript-based implant executed within OWA's reading pane. After execution, the malware rewrites emails on the Exchange server to remove exploit traces. Critically, it leverages Outlook APIs and add-in permissions to establish persistent mailbox access that survives credential rotation and device re-imaging. The malware employs dual command-and-control mechanisms: querying GitHub's Commit Search API every 24 hours for commands, and parsing inbound emails for instructions. It also creates hidden iframes in offline message caches, enabling re-infection even after system restoration. Data exfiltration occurs primarily via HTTPS with AES-CTR encryption. When this fails, the malware tunnels data through DNS queries to attacker-controlled domains. Proofpoint researchers note the earliest infrastructure was established in March 2026, two months before Microsoft disclosed this vulnerability, suggesting potential zero-day exploitation. No TA488 activity was detected between February and the July 22 campaign launch. Author: Ravie Lakshmanan.

f8553d1f2476.text: Cisco announced patches Wednesday for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting its Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) product. The security flaw, identified as CVE-2026-20316, involves static credentials for a low-privilege user account. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit default credentials to gain access to vulnerable devices and retrieve sensitive information. Cisco rated the vulnerability as high severity, noting it can be combined with additional FMC flaws to achieve privilege escalation. 'If the FMC management interface does not have public internet access, the attack surface that is associated with this vulnerability is reduced,' per Cisco's advisory. The company detected active exploitation of CVE-2026-20316 in July and released indicators of compromise to assist organizations in detecting attacks. A researcher from Horizon3.ai reported the vulnerability, though the firm has not yet disclosed details about CVE-2026-20316. The U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA added this vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Wednesday, directing federal organizations to address it by August 1. Cisco also updated its advisory for CVE-2026-20079, a critical FMC vulnerability patched in March, and released detection indicators despite no disclosed in-the-wild exploitation. Recent months have seen Cisco address exploitation of vulnerabilities across multiple products, including Catalyst SD-WAN Manager and Unified Communications Manager. Author: Eduard Kovacs, published July 30, 2026 (2:31 AM ET).

bb1d08f96fdf.text: [Note: proofpoint.com URL 301-redirected to https://therecord.media/zimbra-webmail-zero-click-phishing-russia-laundry-bear] Russian state-aligned hackers have been compromising governmental and commercial organizations throughout the West through zero-click phishing emails, federal agencies in the U.S., U.K., Europe, Australia and New Zealand warned on Thursday. The campaign, carried out by the advanced persistent threat (APT) group Laundry Bear, targets Zimbra Collaboration Suite's webmail platform and exploits a vulnerability that was patched in November 2025. According to the advisory, the hackers carried out 'extensive' targeting of Ukrainian entities before training their sights on U.S. and NATO organizations — evidence of 'an increasing trend within Russian cyber threat groups to target Ukrainian users first.' 'The covert and persistent nature of this activity, along with the absence of any known financial extortion, almost certainly indicates this group's involvement in espionage activities with Russian government backing,' the agencies concluded. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 said the hackers targeted the defense and transportation sectors, as well as financial organizations in NATO member states, Ukraine, CIS countries and Africa. Proofpoint reported the group had compromised 'government, high science, and defense industrial base targets in the United States.' Laundry Bear was first identified in May 2025 by Dutch intelligence agencies, active since at least 2024, previously using 'unsophisticated' techniques like password spraying. Since at least July 2025, the group deployed a novel exploit against CVE-2025-66376, hiding malicious JavaScript in emails from previously compromised accounts that executes immediately when opened. Hackers attempted to exfiltrate the last 90 days of emails, passwords, contact lists, two-factor authentication tokens and other passcodes. In March 2026, Seqrite described a related zero-click Zimbra campaign compromising a Ukrainian maritime agency, attributed with medium confidence to Fancy Bear; Dutch intelligence said Laundry Bear's tactics overlap with but are distinct from Fancy Bear. The agencies urged organizations to immediately patch Zimbra webmail software or switch mail clients if patching is infeasible. Author: James Reddick, published July 23, 2026.

a5c8d8a6a2d0.text: Organizations face a relentless stream of emerging threats, from zero-day exploits to rapidly evolving adversary tactics. CrowdStrike is introducing Falcon Platform Indicators of Attack (IOAs) to provide and maintain detection content across the CrowdStrike Falcon platform — a new category of CrowdStrike-managed, adversary-driven detections designed to detect attack activity by correlating telemetry across CrowdStrike modules and third-party data sources. They will first be delivered in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, where they are now generally available. This expands how CrowdStrike delivers IOAs: historically endpoint IOAs and cloud IOAs; Falcon Platform IOAs build on these by surfacing detections across all modules customers use. They are maintained at scale and continuously refined by CrowdStrike detection engineers working alongside incident response experts, Falcon Adversary OverWatch threat hunters, and Falcon Complete MDR team. Advantages cited: fast protection against emerging threats without waiting for manual rule creation; reduced operational overhead since CrowdStrike manages the full detection lifecycle; detection content informed by frontline expertise; and stronger cross-domain detection through platform consolidation, using telemetry across endpoints, identities, and cloud. Falcon Next-Gen SIEM already provides layered detection: high-confidence sensor-based detections, automated leads for environment-specific anomalies, real-time correlation rules, and scheduled detections. Falcon Platform IOAs complement this with continuously updated coverage for emerging threats. Customers can also use the Emerging Threats dashboard for rule templates and investigation guidance. The piece concludes that as the threat landscape evolves faster than organizations can build/maintain detection content, Falcon Platform IOAs operationalize CrowdStrike's expertise at scale to help organizations adapt with greater speed and consistency. Author: Paola Miranda, published July 29, 2026.

e1d700f4f6f3.text: Orca Security has unveiled two AI-powered capabilities designed to address the expanding landscape of application development. Orca AI AppGen Security identifies and secures AI applications built outside traditional development pipelines on platforms like Claude, Supabase, and Lovable. Simultaneously, AI Code Security Auditor provides deep AI-driven static analysis for code developed within conventional pipelines. The company's State of AI Security Report 2026, analyzing data from over 1,200 production cloud environments, revealed that 52% of organizations now build custom applications with AI. As business teams deploy AI-generated applications connected to APIs, cloud resources, and sensitive data, security visibility has become fragmented. IBM research indicates that breaches involving shadow AI cost organizations an average of $670,000 more than other incidents, underscoring urgency around comprehensive software security. CEO Gil Geron stated: 'Everyone is a builder now...Organizations need security that can keep pace with this shift without slowing innovation.' Orca AI AppGen Security capabilities: discovering AI-generated applications and builders; mapping application risk across APIs and data access; prioritizing high-risk exposures based on business impact. Orca Code Security Auditor capabilities: identifying vulnerabilities traditional tools miss; full repository scanning for frontier model vulnerabilities; prioritizing exploitable risks for focused remediation. Sisense CISO Sangram Dash noted: 'Seeing exploitable code and the AI apps our employees stand up in one platform lets us say yes to builders instead of slowing them down.' Published July 30, 2026.

48d4af95366a.text: Your phone rings, you pick up and say hello. On the other end: total silence. No one answers, and the call abruptly disconnects. In most cases, these are scam calls. Who's calling? Actual person: microphone issues, muted accidentally, Bluetooth connection problems, or carrier glitches, or an unavailable call-center agent overwhelmed by predictive dialing systems. Robot or AI: Silence on the line is a common sign of robocalls testing whether a number is active before passing it to a human; legitimate call centers use the same tools. AI agents may analyze responses to decide if a number is active and worth a live follow-up. Unwanted caller: scammers use quick silent calls as groundwork for elaborate attacks (loans, government impersonation, law enforcement); debt collectors may use silence as psychological pressure; stalkers may use silent calls to induce anxiety. Why do they call and stay silent? Even a single spoken word like 'Hello' can reveal region/accent/location, approximate age and gender (AI is better at detecting nuances than humans), times you're available, and likelihood of a successful attack based on how you respond. The main reason for silent calls is to harvest biometric voice data — a few seconds of recorded audio, stitched together from multiple silent calls, can help build a believable voice deepfake used later to impersonate a relative, colleague, or boss and request money or 2FA codes. What to do: don't answer unknown/hidden numbers; don't rush to call back; don't speak first (wait for the caller to greet you); block unknown numbers even after the call; don't share your number everywhere; consider getting a second phone number for online use. Author: Alexey Sadylko, published July 30, 2026.

c1a9b5932b5f.text: CrowdStrike announced updates to Falcon Cloud Security designed to reduce operational friction in cloud security management. The release focuses on four main areas: Infrastructure as Code Security — the platform now integrates directly into Visual Studio Code and IntelliJ, providing immediate feedback on misconfigurations; security teams can create Custom Rego Rules for IaC scanning to enforce organization-specific policies alongside built-in detections. Identity Governance Improvements — new capabilities include Permission Querying in Graph Explorer, allowing analysts to explore cloud identity relationships without relying solely on security findings; the system can generate least-privilege IAM policies based on observed usage patterns. Application Context Enhancement — Admin Actions correlate code analysis with cloud infrastructure insights to identify what control plane actions applications perform; API Findings automatically discover REST APIs, gRPC services, and serverless functions directly from source code. Workload Protection — Agentless VM Scanning expands to Microsoft Azure, complementing existing AWS support; a new Kubernetes Deployment Wizard guides administrators through deploying protection across multiple Kubernetes platforms in minutes. The release aims to help security teams spend less time managing security operations while focusing on risk reduction. Author: Dana Raveh, published July 29, 2026.

00d18e7b41b2.text: Attackers are moving away from fake Microsoft login pages in favor of abusing Microsoft's own authentication system, letting phishing campaigns slip past the warning signs employees are trained to spot, according to Check Point. Between June 25 and the second week of July, researchers found over 200 phishing emails targeting around 120 organizations in a wide range of industries and countries. The email masquerades as a Microsoft Planner task-assignment notification, claiming that HR has shared payroll and benefits updates while displaying several overdue employee tasks to create a sense of urgency and encourage recipients to click the embedded links. 'Every link in the message, including both call-to-action buttons, leads through the same redirect. The visible sender address also belongs to the target's own organization, meaning the email is sent to the same person it appears to come from,' Check Point explained. How the Attack Works: Once the user clicks the link, they are taken to a genuine login.microsoftonline.com OAuth authorization page, so the URL itself does not raise suspicion. After signing in, the user is presented with a permissions request asking them to approve access for themselves or their organization. If they agree, Microsoft redirects the browser to the address registered by the application. In this campaign, that redirect points to an AWS API Gateway endpoint controlled by the attackers rather than Microsoft. The endpoint receives an authorization token that the attackers can exchange for access to the victim's account, with access level depending on the permissions approved. Check Point warned the technique is already common and becoming increasingly widespread: 'It is a named and tracked technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and in 2026 it evolved from a targeted, manually built attack into a service that virtually anyone can rent.' An attacker-controlled app can reach into the victim's entire Microsoft 365 environment, including email, files, Teams chats, SharePoint, OneDrive, and calendar data. Check Point advises hovering over links before clicking, treating multiple buttons leading to the same URL as a warning sign, and checking that sender name/address/domain line up. 'The campaign is no longer active, but it's yet another example of how attackers have fundamentally changed how they're bypassing traditional phishing defenses,' researchers concluded. Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security. Published July 30, 2026.

05ff2a895994.text: Analog Devices, a Massachusetts-based semiconductor manufacturer with approximately 24,000 employees and $12 billion in annual revenue, has disclosed a data breach affecting its systems. The company detected unauthorized access on June 23 and subsequently discovered that hackers had stolen certain files during an investigation conducted with external security experts. The breach involved the theft of unspecified files, though Analog Devices stated that "the incident did not disrupt its operations" and the company remains unaware of any public leaks or malicious use of the stolen data. The firm indicated the cybersecurity incident would have no material impact on its business or financial condition. Notably, Analog Devices separately disclosed awareness of "a disparate cybersecurity matter" on July 26 regarding public reports it was assessing. This likely refers to ExfilSquad, a data-theft extortion group claiming to have stolen 570,000 records from the company. ExfilSquad operates without file-encrypting ransomware and maintains a leak website listing other victims including Microsoft and various government entities. Interestingly, Analog Devices no longer appears on the group's victim list at the time of reporting. (Author: Eduard Kovacs, Published: July 30, 2026 7:16 AM ET)

294a889e1d99.text: Author: Bruce Schneier, Published: July 30, 2026, originally appeared in The Guardian. Schneier proposes a "work versus gym" framework for deciding whether to use AI on tasks. He contrasts work—tasks that simply need completion regardless of method—with gym activities, where the process itself builds skills and capacity. The distinction draws from AI researcher Daniel Meissler: "if your job is to move heavy things from one side of the room to another, you should use assistive tech...But at the gym, it makes no sense for that robot to lift weights for you." Schneier uses student writing assignments as his primary example. He argues these represent "gym tasks, not work tasks" because "the very act of writing...will help develop the critical thinking skills they will need in their future careers." He observes that AI-generated work typically appears "catchy, plausible, grammatically perfect" yet lacks logical coherence—distinguishable to trained readers but not necessarily to students lacking developed writing skills. The framework extends to professional creative work. While much writing serves as pure work—instruction manuals, legal briefs, disclosure documents—some writing functions as art, where process matters fundamentally. Historically, humans performed both categories; AI now enables society to separate them, potentially reducing demand for human writers. Schneier emphasizes AI reliability remains essential: "There's no point giving an AI something that it can't do reliably."

77c1c1ee3239.text: Authors: Saurabh Sharma and Yaroslav Kikel, Published: July 30, 2026. Kaspersky researchers identified two sophisticated backdoors—OctLurk and SilkLurk—deployed in cyber-espionage operations targeting government organizations across Central Asia since January 2025. Victims span Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Syria, operating in healthcare, research, foreign affairs, law enforcement, and educational sectors. Shared Operations: The same threat actor operates both backdoors. Evidence includes victims infected with both malware families using identical staging directories and deployment patterns, suggesting a unified operation. Sophisticated Obfuscation: Both families employ victim-specific encoding mechanisms. OctLurk uses C: drive serial numbers, while SilkLurk uses computer names to decrypt payloads, complicating reverse engineering and automated detection. Extensive Capabilities: The backdoors support plugin architecture enabling command shells, file system manipulation, credential harvesting, keylogging, browser password theft, network scanning, and remote access through Pandora FMS agents. Technical Architecture: OctLurk operates through loader DLLs using double-XOR encryption and zlib decompression, communicating via hardcoded C2 addresses and collecting comprehensive victim fingerprinting data. SilkLurk employs DLL side-loading of legitimate binaries (NVIDIA, Realtek utilities) combined with victim-specific decryption algorithms; its configuration stores multiple C2 addresses and proxy settings. LurkProxy, a supporting tool with architecture similar to OctLurk, functions as a reverse proxy enabling both SOCKS5 and transparent proxy modes for C2 communication. Post-Compromise Activities: Operators deployed standard reconnaissance tools including Impacket's secretsdump for credential extraction, FSCAN for network enumeration, and PlugX for persistent remote access. They harvested event logs, extracted browser credentials, and collected emails via IMAP commands. Attribution: "We assess with medium confidence that the same actor is behind both backdoors, and that they are Chinese-speaking," though the researchers cannot attribute activity to a known group. Historical PlugX associations with Chinese-speaking actors support this assessment.

a857a84db3b6.text: Published: July 30, 2026. Dropzone AI has launched AI Threat Hunter, a proactive threat hunting agent designed to automate security investigations. The platform enables security teams to execute structured hunt packs across their environments to discover concealed threats and security gaps that conventional alerts might overlook. Traditional threat hunting requires substantial time investment—typically 10 to 20 hours per hunt—making it rare or reactive. This new tool operationalizes hunting by automating the investigative process. The solution includes over 270 hunt packs aligned with MITRE ATT&CK frameworks and actual attacker tactics. Key capabilities include: federated investigations across Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, CrowdStrike NG-SIEM, Elastic, and Panther; bundled hunt packs (5-10 hunts per pack) returning results in 1-2 hours; posture insights including visibility gaps and misconfigurations; transparent, repeatable scheduled operations. CEO Edward Wu stated that the solution enables teams to "identify undetected intrusions at the same speed" as attackers operate, transforming hunting from an occasional activity into routine practice. Customer examples demonstrate measurable impact: Zapier reduced triage time by 85%, UiPath saved 700+ analyst hours while cutting false positives by 86%, and Assala Energy achieved complete alert investigation with 5x faster response times. Additional features planned for late 2026 include custom hypothesis-driven hunts and tighter integration with Dropzone's AI SOC Analyst for response automation.

908ebdd9bc02.text: Published: July 30, 2026. PortSwigger has launched Burp AT in public beta, integrating agentic AI capabilities into Burp Suite for professional penetration testing. The tool enables security testers to assign investigative tasks to AI agents while maintaining human oversight and control. Agent Autonomy with Human Control: Penetration testers can delegate work to AI agents that operate through Burp Suite's established tools and project context. The testers maintain authority over scope, permissions, and approval requirements. According to Dafydd Stuttard, Burp Suite creator and PortSwigger CEO: "Agents also need reliable execution, relevant engagement context, structured testing methodology and boundaries they cannot reinterpret or bypass." Built-in Security Framework: The system enforces scope and permissions at Burp's tooling layer, architecturally separate from the AI model itself. Agents can propose actions but cannot execute anything Burp prohibits. All activities are recorded within the project for inspection and accountability. Specialized Testing Skills: Burp AT includes task-specific pentesting methodologies developed with PortSwigger Research, allowing agents to apply validated testing approaches without requiring users to construct custom prompts or workflows. Human testers retain full access to traditional Burp tools and can assume direct control whenever needed.

69ba5c28fdd9.text:
AI has introduced a new class of network traffic.
Prompts, file uploads, model calls, and agent actions carrying sensitive business context now traverse the network as organizations race to adopt AI and achieve their business goals.
Traditional firewalls were never built to understand these connections, AI activity often looks like ordinary web traffic, leaving the firewall unable to determine whether a prompt contains sensitive data, an agent is calling a tool it should never access, or an application’s AI model is subjected to a malicious prompt.
These challenges demand comprehensive protection, which is why Check Point created the AI Defense Plane—a full-stack approach to securing AI across the enterprise. Today, we are extending that protection to the network: the connective tissue of enterprise AI and the point where users, applications, models, and agents converge.
With the introduction of the industry’s first AI Network Firewall, Check Point brings AI security for users, applications, and agents directly into the firewall organizations already own—turning the network into a real-time control point for AI security.

73c3e3ea3a6b.text: Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, Published: July 30, 2026. Chinese cybercriminal group SilverFox has launched a sophisticated attack against a Japanese industrial manufacturer, deploying a multi-layered malware framework combining vulnerable driver exploitation with remote access capabilities. The campaign chain begins with phishing emails featuring invoice-themed lures that direct victims to attacker-controlled content hosted on legitimate QQ and Tencent Cloud services. This triggers a complex infection sequence involving DLL sideloading that ultimately delivers ValleyRAT (also known as Winos 4.0). According to Cato Networks researchers, the group "combines new vulnerable-driver abuse, newly observed abuse of legitimate applications for DLL sideloading, defense evasion, and layered recovery mechanisms." The malware employs three vulnerable drivers for the BYOVD technique: BootRepair.sys (previously unreported), EnPortv.sys (previously unreported), and wsftprm.sys (used in prior campaigns). The malicious DLL gets sideloaded through legitimate Zeon Corporation applications (ConvertToPDF.exe or PDFDirect.exe), creating a modular framework allowing operators to swap drivers while maintaining operational continuity. Defense evasion features include NTDLL unhooking to remove security software hooks, process injection with thread-context hijacking, and dual watchdog mechanisms ensuring persistence even if components are terminated separately.

ff8446ad5bdc.text:
The age of rogue AI hacker agents has arrived—but it didn't have to happen this way.
After an OpenAI agent breached the Hugging Face platform earlier this month, the two companies said this week that the hacking spree was more extensive than previously thought and also involved intrusions into multiple third-party accounts and services as part of the attack on Hugging Face. The incident has made waves in the cybersecurity community amid broader discussions about how evolving AI capabilities are changing both offensive hacking and digital defense. But as more information emerges, many researchers have concluded that rather than elucidating AI’s next frontier, the episode simply highlighted long-standing cybersecurity problems that are more consequential than ever in the AI age.
“People are YOLO-ing really hard. It’s shocking how little people have really thought about a scenario like this,” says Alex Zenla, cofounder and chief technology officer of the cloud security firm Edera. “I consider all AI and anything AI touches to be fully untrusted—which is fine, you just need to build against that. And this situation proves the point. The fact that OpenAI wasn't more paranoid about this seems kind of reckless."
OpenAI did not provide comment for this story ahead of publication.
The company said in its original disclosure about the Hugging Face hack that one of the two models that broke containment and made its way to the open internet for days was an experimental prototype that was never meant for release.
