dc5142ce2a70.text:
Microsoft Teams Vishing Attacks Lead to Chaos Ransomware

Author: Lawrence Abrams
Published: July 30, 2026

Threat actors are impersonating IT support staff in Microsoft Teams calls to gain remote access to corporate devices and deploy Chaos ransomware. Security firm Sophos tracks the campaign as STAC4749, targeting dozens of organizations between February and June 2026, primarily in North America (50% Canada, 45% US).

Attack Method: The attackers create fake IT-themed domains using the '.top' top-level domain (examples: sequrityupdate.top, scan-security.top) with personas like 'Anthony Brooks' and 'Dylan Harper.' Through Teams calls lasting 90 seconds to 20+ minutes, they convince employees to launch remote sessions via Microsoft Quick Assist or RemSupp remote management tools.

Once accessing devices, attackers deploy PowerShell backdoors into the %AppData% folder, establish persistence through disguised registry entries (masquerading as Realtek audio components), and install backup access tools like DWAgent or AnyDesk.

Ransomware Connection: At least three compromises led to Chaos ransomware deployment, with one case showing progression from initial Teams contact to encryption in under 17 hours. Ransomware notes appeared as 'readme.chaos.txt' files claiming data theft and threatening leaks if ransom isn't paid.

Sophos assesses this as 'financially motivated' and links Chaos ransomware to former members of BlackSuit and Royal ransomware operations, themselves spinoffs from the Conti cybercrime syndicate.

b8899d9596ae.text:
AI Threat Detection: A Complete Guide to Modern Security

Author: The Orca Security Team
Published: July 30, 2026

AI threat detection applies machine learning models to security telemetry to identify attacker activity that traditional rules cannot catch. Rather than a single capability, it comprises four interconnected techniques: anomaly detection, behavioral analytics, supervised classification, and agentic AI for investigation and triage.

How It Works: The detection pipeline flows from telemetry collection through baseline creation to alert scoring. Security teams gather control-plane API logs, network flows, DNS queries, authentication events, and process activity. Models then learn normal patterns for specific entities across dimensions like timing, volume, and resource access. When new events arrive, the system measures deviation from baseline and generates a confidence score, creating a precision-recall tradeoff.

Core Techniques: Anomaly Detection identifies unusual activity without labeled attack data but most anomalies are benign, creating alert fatigue. Behavioral Analytics tracks entities across sources over weeks but newly created workloads lack historical profiles. Supervised Classifiers excel on known attack classes but cannot recognize novel threats. Agentic AI layers LLM-based reasoning over detections to provide investigative context, though fluent narratives built on false positives can mislead analysts.

Real-World Applications include identity threat detection (impossible-travel scenarios), cloud activity detection (role enumeration followed by secret extraction), and phishing detection combining message analysis with threat intelligence.

AI Versus Traditional Approaches: Signatures and rules outperform ML on known threats; models excel where threats cannot be pre-specified. The most effective pipelines combine both.

Implementation Challenges: Baseline poisoning, cold start for ephemeral infrastructure, initial alert volume escalation, and explainability gaps.

Best Practices: Fix telemetry collection before tuning models, re-baseline after incidents, map detections to MITRE ATT&CK, rank findings by exposure and attack paths, integrate into existing incident response workflows.

Orca's Approach: Orca connects detections to asset, identity, data, and exposure context within a unified data model, with agentless scanning, runtime sensors, and a Threat Investigation Agent that contextualizes findings and proposes root causes.

FAQs cover whether AI replaces SIEM (no), how to validate AI detection, what to ask vendors, and detection without full packet capture.

e7d893c812ea.text:
Timeless Compliance: Why Better Questions Beat Bigger Frameworks

Author: Matt Honea
Published: July 30, 2026 (11:46 AM ET)

In 2009, a surgeon named Atul Gawande and a team backed by the World Health Organization demonstrated that a 19-item surgical checklist could significantly reduce complications and deaths across eight hospitals worldwide. Yet today, security teams send AI vendors questionnaires with 300 questions, half beginning with 'describe your approach to…' and almost none that would catch a real failure.

The timing is significant: the EU AI Act's enforcement provisions for general-purpose AI arrive this August, ISO/IEC 42001 now appears in third-party risk questionnaires, and NIST's AI RMF has become the default in North America. Published crosswalks show substantial overlap between ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, and the EU AI Act, so an organization can satisfy all three with one set of processes.

The Questionnaire Problem: Free-text prompts like 'Describe how your AI system ensures fairness' cannot be answered with evidence, only prose; they ignore that LLMs are stochastic systems where a point-in-time attestation goes stale the moment a model version changes; and they don't scale with risk, sending the same 300-question addendum to a marketing chatbot and a clinical decision support system.

What Usable Actually Looks Like — five tests for any AI assessment question: (1) Answerable with an artifact — a log, config, eval report, or diagram, not an essay. (2) Scoped to risk tier — classify the system first, then ask proportionate questions. (3) Measurable or binary where possible. (4) Decision-relevant — if a bad answer wouldn't change the decision, cut the question. (5) Mapped once, reused everywhere via published crosswalks.

The Questions That Actually Matter: where the model is deployed and who the upstream provider is; what data flows in/out and where it's logged; what inference parameters are logged and whether an incident can be replayed; what the eval suite covers and how often it runs; where human oversight points are; the incident process; and how model swaps are tested and communicated.

Standardize the Model Card: The article proposes a standardized model card—covering model version/lineage, training data provenance, retention, a common core of eval benchmarks, safety mitigations, default inference parameters, and a change log—modeled on SOC 2's success in giving one artifact that can answer many customers at once.

Key Insight: 'compliance is an evidence problem, and for AI, evidence is an observability problem.' Organizations that pass audits easily are those whose logging, evals, and documentation let any reasonable question be answered in minutes with an artifact rather than weeks with an essay. This is Part 4 of a multi-part series on securing generative AI.

Jailed Flock Vandal Wipes Out Three Cameras, Racks Up Thousands in Damages

Author: Connor Jones
Published: Thursday, July 30, 2026 at 16:28 UTC

A California man learned a costly lesson about surveillance camera destruction: disabling license plate readers while leaving other CCTV systems intact is a poor strategy for evading arrest.

Marcus Bee, 40, of Pismo Beach, was arrested by the Monterey County Sheriff's Office on Tuesday for allegedly attacking at least three Flock automated license plate readers (ALPRs) in Lockwood and Bradley, California—communities roughly 25 miles apart.

According to deflock.org, which tracks Flock camera deployments, only three ALPRs operate in these two areas. Police allege Bee caused 'thousands of dollars' worth of damage to public safety infrastructure.'

The suspect's downfall came through other surveillance. The Monterey County Sheriff's Office stated that 'his actions were captured by other surveillance cameras located nearby,' along with additional investigative leads. Bee was jailed with bail set at $30,000.

Sheriff Tina Nieto issued a statement declaring: 'This arrest sends a clear message that anyone who intentionally damages public safety equipment will be identified, arrested, and held accountable.' She emphasized that the cameras help solve crimes, recover stolen vehicles, locate missing persons, and protect communities.

Broader Context: This case exemplifies a growing trend of Flock camera vandalism across the United States. Similar incidents include a Georgia incident (July 2026) where two ALPRs were set on fire with suspects unidentified, and a Virginia case where Jeffrey Scott Sovern, 41, was accused of damaging multiple ALPR cameras between April and October 2025, claiming the technology violates constitutional rights.

The Flock Controversy: The ACLU notes that 'less than 1 percent of the cars scanned are connected to crime,' yet all scanned vehicles are logged with details including manufacturer, model, color, and license plate number. The Institute for Justice has documented at least 26 cases where police misused license plate reader data to stalk romantic interests. Reports suggest ICE and CBP have accessed Flock data for immigration enforcement, despite company denials of direct contracts with these agencies. Flock CEO Garrett Langley claims the cameras addressed approximately 1 million crimes nationally last year and maintains no constitutional violations exist.

f547c036a1ca.text:
Data risk management treats data as a distinct risk category requiring four foundational attributes: classification, ownership, lifecycle, and business impact rating. Organizations typically manage data risk through compliance projects that become outdated as ordinary operations - exports, backups, test refreshes - create undocumented copies across systems.

Core Framework Components: The approach separates from vulnerability management and cloud risk management by focusing specifically on data assets. According to the article: "a store's tier sets its impact rating and its retention period sets the date after which continued existence is a finding."

Three recurring data risk categories exist: Exposure and Access Risk involves data accessible to unintended parties - e.g. "a customer export created for a one-off analysis two years ago still sits in a shared drive." Lifecycle and Retention Risk occurs when data outlives its intended purpose, such as deleted records persisting in restore points. Third-Party and Sharing Risk encompasses data beyond organizational control, such as vendor-held customer records or partner-accessible buckets.

Implementation Strategy: Start with discovery across one high-value domain rather than attempting comprehensive estate coverage immediately. Classification should precede control assignment, using FIPS 199 standards rating confidentiality, integrity, and availability as low, moderate, or high. Named individual ownership is critical: "A high-impact store with no owner has nobody to approve an exception."

Key Distinctions: Data risk management operates continuously alongside governance, which establishes policies; risk management measures production reality against those policies, reporting discrepancies back to inform governance decisions.

Published: July 30, 2026. Author: The Orca Security Team.

American semiconductor company Analog Devices announced that an unauthorized party accessed some of its systems and exfiltrated certain files. The company detected the incident on June 23 and activated incident response protocols to limit the breach, engaging external cybersecurity experts to assist with containment and investigation activities.

Analog Devices designs analog, mixed-signal, power management, and digital signal processing chips used in industrial automation, automotive systems, communications infrastructure, healthcare equipment, aerospace, and data centers. The company states it has no knowledge of stolen data being leaked online or used for fraudulent purposes but will continue monitoring the situation. Law enforcement authorities have been informed, and affected parties and regulators will receive notifications about the compromised information.

Analog Devices reports that business operations were not affected by this incident and does not believe the event will have any material impact on its operations or financial condition.

The company is also separately assessing an unrelated cybersecurity matter that surfaced in public reports on July 26, potentially related to the data extortion group ExfilSquad, which briefly listed Analog Devices on its leak site before delisting the company. This sponsored article by Huntress Labs examines a real security incident from June 2026 where attackers gained initial access via SQL injection vulnerability and subsequently entrenched themselves deeply within a compromised system.

Initial Access: Attackers exploited an unvalidated input field on a webpage, leveraging SQL injection to access the underlying Windows machine running Microsoft SQL Server. As noted, "SQL injection remains one of the most common (and most preventable) web application vulnerabilities."

Post-Breach Activities: Rather than immediately deploying ransomware or stealing data, the attacker methodically performed reconnaissance by running Windows service enumeration commands; created persistence mechanisms including enabling Remote Desktop, creating administrative user accounts, and disabling Windows Defender; deployed malicious payloads including BadIIS modules (used for search-engine fraud and traffic manipulation) and XMRig cryptocurrency miners disguised with hidden file attributes; and downloaded additional tools via PowerShell scripts executed with silenced execution policies.

Key Defensive Lessons: The article emphasizes that remediation must address root causes: "If a team had removed all the attacker's tools and accounts but never fixed the underlying SQL injection flaw, the attacker could have simply walked back in." Recommended practices include maintaining system inventories, reducing attack surface, enforcing multi-factor authentication, and conducting thorough root-cause investigations rather than surface-level cleanups.

For years, the cybersecurity industry's understanding of software supply chain compromise has been anchored by a few watershed events, including Russian cyber espionage actor ICE RELIC's (formerly known as APT29) 2020 compromise of SolarWinds and North Korean cyber espionage actor UNC4736's 2023 compromise of 3CX. However, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has been tracking growth in threat activity targeting open source software repositories to conduct supply chain compromises over the past several years.

Notable Campaigns: UNC6780 (TeamPCP), February-May 2026, conducted extensive open source supply chain compromises targeting PyPI, npm, and Docker Hub, abusing the pull_request_target GitHub Actions trigger and deploying credential stealers (SANDCLOCK). Axios Package Compromise, March 2026: a malicious dependency was introduced into the legitimate axios npm package after a maintainer account was compromised via social engineering; it dropped the WAVESHAPER.V2 backdoor attributed to North Korean actor MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE (formerly UNC1069); axios has over 100 million weekly downloads and customers in 15 verticals/13 countries were affected before removal within three hours.

AI Likely to Accelerate Compromises: GTIG anticipates AI, including 'vibe coding,' will increase attacker opportunities, citing cases of malicious MCP packages and an AI coding agent unwittingly co-authoring a commit that integrated a malicious cryptocurrency-themed package. OpenSSF data shows malicious open-source package identification rose 1,444% from 2024 to 2025.

Traditional Supply Chain Compromise Remains Rare: cases include UNC4899's 2025 Bybit hack ($1.4B stolen via compromised developer machine and frontend code injection), the Notepad++ compromise (UNC6688), and DAEMON Tools installers (UNC6863, deploying SLICKDEMON/BADFALL/QUIC RAT).

Mitigation Recommendations span administrative oversight (SBOM/ABOM inventories, Wiz SDLC Infrastructure Threat Framework, vendor risk registers), identity/access controls (short-lived OIDC tokens instead of PATs, FIDO2 SSH, ephemeral CI/CD runners), infrastructure protection (zero trust, network segmentation), secure development practices (ignore-scripts, OSV-Scanner, HSM-backed code signing), and continuous monitoring/incident response playbooks for upstream takeovers, dependency confusion, and pipeline poisoning. It also notes new native platform guardrails: Dependabot's three-day cooldown, PyPI's 14-day upload immutability, and npm v12 disabling lifecycle scripts by default.

Authors: Kelli Vanderlee, Stuart Carrera (Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant). Published: July 31, 2026.

9378e04e2b9b.text:
A vulnerability in Azure Cosmos DB, dubbed CosmosEscape by researchers at Wiz, exposed a platform-wide signing secret that could grant attackers access to any customer database.

The exploit chain began with a crafted query targeting a Gremlin database controlled by an attacker. This led to code execution on a multi-tenant gateway, revealing both a platform-wide signing secret and a regional account directory. Armed with these credentials, attackers could locate targets and retrieve their primary account keys.

According to Wiz, the attack required only a standard Azure account with a Cosmos DB Gremlin database - no special permissions or insider access necessary. "The query returned the platform-wide master key," which could then be used across Cosmos DB's public endpoint to compromise other customer accounts.

The vulnerability exploited a flaw in Cosmos DB's custom Gremlin engine, which failed to account for .NET reflection when translating queries into code. This oversight created file-read and file-write primitives leading to arbitrary code execution.

Microsoft patched the vulnerable Gremlin entry point within 48 hours of the November 2025 report and completed a permanent fix across all regions by July 2026. A Microsoft spokesperson stated they found "no evidence of customer impact" and that no customer action is required.

The researchers plan to present the complete exploit chain at Black Hat USA on August 6, 2026.

Author: Swati Khandelwal. Published: July 30, 2026.

5d53d85eef74.text:
According to Action1's latest survey of over 1,000 system administrators worldwide, AI and automation have underperformed relative to expectations from two years prior. The Action1 2026 Survey Report: AI Impact on Sysadmins compares predictions made in 2024 against current 2026 reality, revealing significant adoption gaps.

The most substantial disparities between forecasts and implementation include: patch management optimization (67% predicted full automation versus 16% current implementation), server CPU and memory monitoring (70% predicted versus 20% actual), vulnerability prioritization (66% versus 17%), incident detection and remediation (67% versus 19%), compliance analysis (62% versus 28%), and log analysis (83% versus 50%).

Gene Moody, field CTO at Action1, characterizes this shift differently, noting that "sysadmins are comfortable using AI to analyze information, reduce noise and recommend actions," indicating adoption follows a more cautious model where experienced professionals retain decision-making authority over high-impact operations.

Supporting this narrative, nearly half of surveyed sysadmins employ AI for troubleshooting focused on recommendations rather than autonomous resolution. Organizations mandating AI use doubled from 15% in 2023 to 34% in 2026, while administrator competency in AI integration increased from 24% to 58%.

Primary concerns persist regarding privacy and accuracy (74%), control loss (58%), costs (55%), and job displacement (24%).

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and co-authoring partners released updated 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), succeeding 2021 guidance from the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA).

An SBOM functions as "a list of the components that make up a software package and their supply chain relationships," enabling organizations to understand software composition, evaluate supply chain security risks, and make informed decisions.

Key Updates: The revised guidance incorporates input from a 2025 public comment period and extends minimum elements to all software SBOMs. New elements include component hash algorithms, component licenses, the name of the SBOM generation tool, and generation context. Several existing fields were renamed "to improve clarity and consistency" in automated supply chain and vulnerability management.

Future Development Areas: The document addresses four emerging challenges: cloud and SaaS products present complications due to shared responsibility and continuous updates. AI systems require additional descriptors like model cards beyond traditional SBOM elements, with CISA currently directing users to separate G7 AI SBOM guidance from May 2026.

The guidance also incorporates a digital signature field to verify SBOM authenticity and recommends connecting SBOMs to security alerts using formats like VEX and CSAF to identify vulnerable components.

2d61b223fe4e.text:
A dangling DNS takeover occurs when a DNS record points to a deleted cloud resource, leaving a "dangling" link vulnerable to exploitation. Security firm Silent Push investigated how AI could amplify this known vulnerability at nation-state scale.

The research, called "DangleGeddon," demonstrated that AI serves as a significant force multiplier. Using Claude Opus 5, researchers automated subdomain discovery across 12,500 domains and generated context-enriched takeover scripts. AI filtering reduced datasets to hundreds of exploitable targets, identifying vulnerabilities beyond human-discoverable scope.

The team safely tested their approach and disclosed findings to affected organizations, including major entities: U.S. Federal Government - a dangling Azure blob storage record enabled creation of phishing pages bypassing government trust filters on .gov domains; Banking - Societe Generale had an unassigned Azure Blob storage resource accessible through a dangling record; Manufacturing - Ford's dangling DNS record pointed to a developmental Azure VM, potentially exposing developer credentials and API keys; Pharmaceuticals - Eli Lilly left a record pointing to an Apple device guide.

Silent Push projected catastrophic downstream impacts: "government systems disruption with severe national security implications," banking paralysis affecting "online banking and real-time payments," manufacturing supply chain compromise, and pharmaceutical sector losses "in the hundreds of billions."

The researchers concluded that while financially motivated cybercriminals might exploit this locally, nation-states represent the true threat, seeking "cost and chaos at massive scale."

By Kevin Townsend, July 30, 2026 (8:15 AM ET).

833d5e785ca5.text:
Organizations increasingly rely on multiple business applications to manage critical functions. As the article notes, "There are more employees with access to critical business application than ever before." Typically, companies operate 10-15 different applications handling financial transactions, HR operations, and customer data across interconnected systems.

This complexity creates challenges for security teams. The volume of roles and permissions generates what the author describes as "analysis paralysis: You know something needs attention, but not what, or where."

The Four-Step AI Analysis Approach: 1) Identify the specific problem and decision needed. 2) Export relevant source data (user assignments, licenses, telemetry, change logs). 3) Craft prompts specifying the AI's role, desired format, and applicable rules. 4) Validate results before implementation. The author emphasizes that "AI is a powerful assistant, not a rubber stamp."

Three Practical Examples: Segregation of Duties Review - AI analyzes layered role and privilege data to flag users holding conflicting access combinations that create fraud risks, providing prioritized findings for audits. Security and Licensing Optimization - the system identifies unused roles, unassigned users, and over-provisioned access that unnecessarily inflates licensing costs through a phased remediation roadmap. Anomaly Detection - using telemetry and change-tracking data, AI establishes baseline behavior patterns and surfaces deviations indicating suspicious activity or unused granted access.

The conclusion emphasizes integrating these AI-driven processes into existing access governance tools.

Published: July 2026. Written by: Alex Meyer. Read time: 6 minutes.

c37456eb08a6.text:
A recent hacking campaign impersonated notifications from Microsoft Teams and abused Microsoft's legitimate authentication infrastructure to compromise corporate Outlook, SharePoint and OneDrive accounts.

In a blog post published on July 29, cybersecurity researchers at Check Point warned that attackers are increasingly abandoning fake Microsoft login pages in favor of abusing Microsoft's legitimate authentication infrastructure.

By employing this tactic, attackers hope that their phishing campaigns have a higher chance of being successful by avoiding some of the telltale signs of suspicious activity which users may be aware of.

The campaign started in the final weekend of June and continued into July, targeting users at 120 organizations including manufacturing, legal and healthcare, with emails designed to look like a notification alert for Microsoft Teams from the company's HR department.

Disguised as Microsoft Planner task-assignment notification, the sender's name on the email was "There's New Activity On Teams" and claimed HR had sent messages to the user on Microsoft Teams. The body of the message also referenced "overdue tasks" in an attempt to employ social engineering to pressure the user into interacting with the fake request.

If the user clicked a link in the message, they were taken to legitimate OAuth authorize URL.

If the user attempted to sign-in, the page provided them with a prompt to accept to "Approve permissions" or "Accept on behalf of your organization." If the user did this, the login attempt was redirected to attacker-controlled infrastructure, and the attacker also received an authorization token.

With all of this done via their infrastructure, the attackers had the ability to access the account and could exploit this to do anything a legitimate user could do with their Microsoft 365 suite.

"Attackers have stopped forging Microsoft's front door and started walking through it. Every screen the victim sees is authentic, the only fake thing in this entire chain is the intent behind the app requesting access," Check Point said in the blog post.

With this access to the email account secured, researchers detailed that as well reading messages and exfiltrating data from the victim's inbox, attackers could use this access to a legitimate, trusted account as a springboard for Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks.

While this specific campaign is no longer active, Check Point noted that it is "yet another example of how attackers have fundamentally changed how they're bypassing traditional phishing defenses."

To help identify and protect against campaigns which use these techniques, Check Point recommended implementing the following advice:

- Hover over links before clicking and check whether the destination matches the service referenced in the message. Be suspicious when different buttons lead to the same URL
- Verify that the sender name, sender address, and sending domain are consistent. In this campaign, the message appeared to come from the recipient's own email address, while the display name claimed to represent Teams activity
- Do not trust an email simply because it appears to come from an internal address. Display names and sender addresses can be spoofed or manipulated
- When uncertain, open Teams or other applications directly through the official app rather than using links in the email

Author: Danny Palmer, Contributing Writer, Infosecurity Magazine. Published: July 30, 2026.

b30bf3a50b9f.text:
Hidden instructions embedded in Word documents can manipulate Microsoft 365 Copilot into altering financial figures in reports, then copying those same instructions into the generated file. Security researcher Håkon Måløy disclosed this technique on July 28, following a 144-day responsible disclosure period after notifying Microsoft on March 31.

In Måløy's proof-of-concept demonstration, the initially created file subsequently triggered identical behavior when used in another Copilot drafting session. Microsoft deployed two mitigations after confirming the issue: one blocked the original prompt wording, while the second updated the underlying model to GPT-5.5.

The attack demonstrated continued success with modified instructions on GPT-5.6 the following day. "The vulnerability class therefore remains exploitable at the time of publication," Måløy stated.

The technique is not zero-click and requires an active Copilot drafting or editing operation. The malicious document must enter the model's context either as an attachment or through a OneDrive source selected by Work IQ, Microsoft 365 Copilot's intelligence engine.

No exploitation in the wild has been documented. Måløy withheld the complete payload but recommends treating external documents as untrusted, reviewing files before starting generation or editing operations, and checking files before reuse or sharing.

The exploit functions by leveraging document text that Copilot reads to determine draft content. The tool can misinterpret instructions within source files as user requests. Specifically, the proof-of-concept halved financial figures, embedded the full prompt in white eight-point text, and concealed both modifications.

Måløy explains that Word removes color and font size before sending document text to the language model, allowing white-on-white instructions to remain legible to the AI. The payload contained two components: one altered the document content, while the other instructed Copilot to copy and hide the instructions by framing them as source-tracking and readability requirements.

Microsoft indicates that Word can ground drafts on up to 20 files, emails, or meetings, while Edit with Copilot can utilize Work IQ. During Måløy's testing, Copilot searched OneDrive for a quarterly report, discovered the malicious market analysis outside the folder containing other sources, and included it.

With the original malicious document absent and only the infected quarterly report attached, Copilot halved the figures in a subsequent quarterly draft and appended the prompt again. This newly created file represented an ordinary internally generated document.

The chain does not self-propagate; each subsequent hop requires another Copilot operation. Once Copilot copies instructions into internally generated documents, the original source is no longer present in the next session, complicating efforts to trace manipulation back to its source.

As of publication, no public CVE or standalone Microsoft advisory was identified through NVD, CVE.org, or Microsoft's Security Update Guide searches. Microsoft references jailbreak and cross-prompt injection attack classifiers that help block high-risk prompts, though availability varies across Copilot scenarios.

Defender for Office 365 implements mail-flow inspection for inbound email. Microsoft describes Copilot's runtime safeguards as addressing injected instructions from grounded content. Neither Microsoft nor Måløy confirmed detection of this specific payload at either layer.

According to Måløy, no complete customer-side remediation exists. He argues that payload-specific blocks cannot adequately address this vulnerability class, since determining malicious content requires the model to process attacker-controlled information.

Author: Swati Khandelwal. Published: July 30, 2026.

caf958d1a7ad.text:
Network firewalls are the workhorses of modern cybersecurity. They are trusted to protect the network, blocking malicious traffic and preventing intrusions and breaches. And for decades, network security teams have built controls around a relatively stable model: users connect to applications, applications exchange data, and security tools inspect packets, protocols, and destinations. Firewalls became exceptionally good at understanding where traffic was going and whether it should be allowed.

But just as AI is reshaping every aspect of the business world, it's also had a monumental impact on how security teams view network traffic and the firewall.

AI is driving new network dynamics that traditional security policies were never designed to govern. Employees, applications, and agents send prompts, call models, connect to services, and trigger actions across the environment, all activity most firewalls can't see, let alone understand. AI agents interact with external services, retrieve information, execute actions, and increasingly communicate with other agents autonomously.

Reinventing the Firewall for the AI Era: The network is the central hub for AI use and the one control point where it can be secured in real time. And this new reality calls for a new kind of network security rooted in AI and designed to protect your network from today's ever dynamic threat landscape.

Check Point introduced the industry's first AI Network Firewall to deliver comprehensive AI security at the network level that protects employee AI use, AI applications, and AI agents directly from the firewall organizations already run. The AI Network Firewall is fully integrated into Check Point's AI Defense Plane, turning the existing firewall into an Intent-aware enforcement layer for detecting, inspecting, and controlling AI activity across the enterprise including every network, cloud, branch, and AI data center.

Addressing the Visibility Gap in the AI Enterprise: The challenge facing organizations today is twofold: not only is AI being adopted rapidly, it has also fundamentally changed the nature of network activity. Traditional security controls were designed to inspect connections, applications, and traffic flows. They can identify where traffic is going and whether a connection should be permitted, but they were never built to understand the context and intent behind AI interactions.

This visibility gap is a growing problem. Employees are sending prompts to generative AI platforms, applications are making model calls behind the scenes, and autonomous agents are increasingly communicating with other systems and services without human involvement. Much of this activity traverses the enterprise network, yet conventional firewalls cannot inspect a prompt, determine whether sensitive information is being exposed, govern agent-to-agent interactions, or identify malicious AI-driven activity.

The answer to this challenge is an evolution of the firewall itself. To secure the AI enterprise, security controls must move beyond traffic inspection and become intent-aware. By understanding prompts, model interactions, file uploads, API calls, and agent behavior in real time, an AI Network Firewall provides the visibility and control organizations need to safely adopt AI at scale.

Rather than treating AI as an isolated technology stack, it embeds governance directly into the network control point that already sits in the path of enterprise activity. This allows security teams to prevent prompt-injection attacks, stop data exfiltration, detect API abuse, govern MCP servers, and maintain centralized oversight of AI usage across employees, applications, and autonomous agents.

Security That Operates at AI Speed: The speed at which AI is being adopted is creating a second challenge: operational complexity. Security teams are straining to keep pace with a constant stream of new AI applications, changing business requirements, and emerging threats. Traditional security operations often depend on translating business requests into technical policies, manually coordinating changes across multiple systems, and maintaining consistency across disparate environments. At AI speed, that approach becomes increasingly unsustainable.

This is where intelligence must extend beyond enforcement into operations. Modern AI security requires platforms that can simplify policy creation, automate analysis and remediation, and integrate directly with the business context organizations have already established. Human-language policy management, automated event analysis, and agentic orchestration enable security teams to respond faster while reducing the risk of human error.

Rather than duplicating policy across multiple tools, organizations can leverage existing labels, tags, identities, and asset classifications from across their technology ecosystem to enforce a single, consistent access-control model. The result is greater efficiency, fewer operational mistakes, and stronger alignment between security objectives and business priorities.

Scaling Security Across the Modern Enterprise: The final challenge is scale. Enterprise environments are more distributed than ever, spanning data centers, public clouds, branch offices, SD-WAN deployments, SASE architectures, and AI infrastructure itself. Security teams must protect this growing footprint while maintaining prevention-first security, minimizing downtime, and avoiding operational bottlenecks.

An intent-aware AI firewall provides a foundation for consistent security across every environment. Through centralized management, unified policy enforcement, automated lifecycle operations, and continuous monitoring, organizations can extend the same level of visibility, control, and protection across their entire infrastructure. Security operations become easier to manage as environments grow, while policy remains consistent and auditable regardless of where AI workloads or users reside.

Protecting What Comes Next: AI, Intelligence, and Trust: The next generation of firewalls will not simply secure connections. They will understand AI interactions. Led by the new AI Network Firewall, this security layer will identify prompts, model calls, agent requests, and AI-driven workflows, apply policy dynamically based on business context and security intent, and bring governance directly into the infrastructure that organizations already depend on to protect their networks.

Ultimately, the value is not just stronger security. It is empowering organizations to embrace AI confidently and completely, without unnecessary risk. Employees can innovate, developers can build AI-powered applications, and agents can automate business processes, all under governance models that provide visibility, accountability, and protection.

In an era where AI is transforming how work gets done, the firewall must transform with it. The network is becoming more than a transport layer. It is becoming the control plane for AI security.

And the organizations that recognize this shift first will be best positioned to embrace AI safely, securely, and at scale.

Author: Aviv Abramovich, VP Product Management, Network Security at Check Point Software. Published: July 30, 2026.

ffa88a3bfc8f.text:
In June 2021, DataBreaches reported on a ransomware attack affecting OSF Healthcare by a little-known gang called Xing Team. Our reporting noted OSF’s lack or response to inquiries and lack of timely notification. When OSF issued a statement in October, DataBreaches reported on that, too, commenting that we did not find their incident response timely or accurate. It appears that HHS OCR also noted their noncompliance with HHS’s Security Rule and HITECH. They issued the following press release yesterday about a settlement that includes a monetary penalty of $552,250 and a corrective action plan. As is usually the case, there is no admission of guilty by the covered entity:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Oﬃce for Civil Rights (OCR) today announced a settlement with OSF Healthcare System and its Affiliated Covered Entities (OSF), concerning potential violations of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) Privacy, Security, and Breach Notification Rules. OSF is headquartered in Illinois and has providers located in Illinois and Michigan.
“An accurate and thorough HIPAA risk analysis is not only required by law, but it is also necessary to protect health information and prevent or mitigate ransomware attacks,” said OCR Director Paula M. Stannard. “If a HIPAA regulated entity doesn’t know what threats and vulnerabilities exist to its electronic protected health information (ePHI), they will often learn the hard way when their systems are hacked.”
OCR enforces the HIPAA Privacy, Security, and Breach Notiﬁcation Rules, which set forth the requirements that covered entities (health plans, health care clearinghouses, and most health care providers), and business associates must follow to protect the privacy and security of PHI.
The settlement resolves an investigation that OCR initiated after OSF ﬁled a breach report in October 2021. In April of 2021, OSF discovered that its files had been infected with the “Nephilim” variant of ransomware. The PHI of 53,907 individuals was exfiltrated by the threat actor. Affected PHI included driver’s license numbers, diagnosis and treatment information, prescription information, medical record numbers, provider names, dates of services, financial account information, and health insurance information. OCR found that OSF had potentially violated provisions of the Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules, including:
- Failing to conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the ePHI held by OSF;
- Impermissibly disclosing the PHI of 53,907 individuals;
- Failing to provide timely breach notification to affected individuals; and
- Failing to provide timely breach notification to the Secretary of HHS.
Under the terms of the resolution agreement, OSF agreed to implement a corrective action plan that OCR will monitor for two years and paid $552,250 to OCR. Under the corrective action plan, OSF has committed to taking steps to ensure compliance with the HIPAA Rules and protect the security of ePHI, including:
- Conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis to determine the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the conﬁdentiality, integrity, and availability of its ePHI; and
- Develop and implement a risk management plan to address and mitigate security risks and vulnerabilities identified in its risk analysis.

854f7b774fda.text:
Two years after a malware incident that was not handled in accordance with South Korea’s requirements, KT has been fined. Lee Jin-seok reports:
KT has been fined more than 53.9 billion won [USD $37,630,484.43] over a personal data breach and unauthorized micropayment damages caused by the exploitation of illegal small base stations (femtocells). The government also decided to file a complaint against KT for obstructing the investigation, including by submitting false materials during the data breach probe.
The Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) said on the 30th that at a plenary meeting held on the 29th, it resolved to impose a fine of 53.979 billion won on KT, along with corrective orders and recommendations to inspect vulnerabilities, strengthen safety measures, and improve data protection standards, as well as a publication order.
According to the investigation, hackers implanted certificates extracted from a lost KT femtocell into a self-built femtocell and then accessed KT’s mobile network without authorization. By combining this with personal information such as names, gender, and dates of birth, they requested mobile micropayments and then intercepted automated response system (ARS) calls and text messages (SMS) containing payment authentication codes to execute unauthorized micropayments. As a result of the incident, the personal information of 16,647 KT users was leaked, and unauthorized micropayment damages worth approximately 240 million won occurred against a total of 368 people.
During the investigation, it was additionally revealed that in March 2024, 38 servers within KT’s IT service network were infected with malware through hacking, leaking the names, phone numbers, and accounts of company employees and partner company workers. It was confirmed that KT recognized this but handled it internally without reporting it to the government, and systematically concealed the breach by deleting the logs of 10 servers where the breach occurred.
In October 2025, KT’s chief indicated that he would take full responsibility for the micropayment incident. KT also allowed dissatisfied customers to apply for early termination refunds.
Read more at Seoul Economic Daily.

The United States faces sustained threats from homegrown and domestic violent extremists over the coming year. Since July 2025, there has been a significant rise in mass-casualty attacks by Islamic State supporters, assassinations of government officials by anti-government extremists, and plots by anarchist groups targeting infrastructure.

Key Assessment: The Iran War's primary threat stems not from direct Iranian operations but from secondary sociopolitical and economic consequences. While Iranian authorities seek to guide attacks through American proxies, their actual capabilities remain limited, relying on low-sophistication actors disrupted early in planning stages.

Major Threat Categories:

Homegrown Violent Extremists (HVEs): Islamic State supporters represent the most severe HVE threat, with arrests increasing dramatically—twelve cases in twelve months versus two previously. The group maintains sophisticated propaganda networks and encourages mass-casualty attacks, particularly during October 2026-January 2027 holiday periods.

Iran-Nexus Actors: Despite heightened motivation from the conflict and leadership deaths, Iran lacks capacity for sophisticated US operations. Attempts rely on financially motivated criminals rather than ideological supporters.

Domestic Violent Extremists (DVEs): Neo-Nazi accelerationists continue conducting mass-casualty attack plots despite organizational disruption. Anti-government extremists target high-profile officials with increasing frequency. Anarchist groups employ increasingly destructive methods against immigration facilities and infrastructure.

Elevated-Risk Entities: Organizations face heightened threats if associated with: US foreign policy decision-making, immigration enforcement, Israeli government/military, critical infrastructure provision, or AI development.

Secondary Effects: The conflict amplifies existing extremist grievances around Middle East policy, US-Israel relations, economic conditions, and corporate involvement in military operations—issues likely to intensify during 2026 midterm elections.

Plain language. Live data. A fix decision in one conversation.

Dashboards answer the questions someone already decided to build a screen for. Every other question — the one a new CVE just made urgent, or the one no vendor anticipated — waits until someone writes a report or files a ticket. Anyone who has lived through a critical CVE disclosure knows the drill: The board wants an exposure answer in hours, and the honest answer is "we're still pulling the data." Vulnerabilities are now weaponized within 10 hours of disclosure, and a manual exposure assessment often takes longer than that. The team burns days reconciling scanner exports against deployment reality, spending their time finding the answer instead of fixing the problem.

That's the ceiling of dashboard-driven security. The SysQL Skill removes it.

The SysQL Skill brings Sysdig's security graph into Claude Code so you can ask any question in plain language and get back a validated query, real blast-radius data, and a prioritized fix decision. No query language to learn. No console to navigate. This skill works in whatever language your team thinks in. It's one of the latest agent skills in Sysdig's headless cloud security platform.

From plain language to fix decision: What it looks like. The demo starts with a single question: "Find the vulnerabilities with a known exploit." The skill writes the query — MATCH Vulnerability WHERE v.hasExploit = true … ORDER BY cvssScore DESC — runs it live against your environment, and returns results ranked by severity. CVE-2024-41110, a Docker escape at CVSS 9.9, sits at the top.

That's not a dashboard widget. That's your live environment, answering the question you actually asked.

The more important moment comes next. It's a natural follow-up question: "How many workloads are affected by CVE-2024-41110?" The answer is zero KubeWorkloads, and the skill tells you why. The flaw lives in a Go dependency, not a directly linked workload. So the skill reasons about graph relationships, re-queries on its own, and finds the CVE in three sysdig/vuln-host-scanner images on quay.io. This is runtime insights at work: vulnerabilities linked to images, and images to workloads. The result is a real blast radius instead of a flat scan result.

One more question: "Should I fix this CVE? Look for an available fix." The response is yes, and it comes with the exact fixed-in version for every affected image.

Three questions, no pre-built reports, and a prioritized fix decision, all in one conversation.

The question you didn't plan to ask. Every cloud-native vulnerability management platform eventually hits the same wall: You can only see what the vendor decided to surface. SysQL exposes the underlying security graph directly, so vulnerabilities, images, workloads, running containers, and exploitability signals are all connected and queryable. The most important question in an investigation is usually the one you didn't plan to ask. Now you can ask it.

Not only that, but you can ask this question with control intact. Queries run through the Sysdig Secure MCP server with read access to the security graph, so every question is governed and auditable just like any other access to your Sysdig environment.

This is part of what Sysdig calls headless cloud security: Security stops being a destination your team navigates to and starts running where they already work. Earlier posts in this series covered the Runtime Investigation Skill, custom cloud security controls, and onboarding at cloud speed. SysQL extends the same principle to the full security graph. This is what CNAPP looks like when it stops requiring you to go somewhere to use it.

The bigger shift. Security investigation has always had a hidden constraint: You can only ask what the vendor built a screen for. SysQL removes that constraint. Your data comes to you, answers the question you actually have, and ends the conversation with a fix, not a ticket to find one.

d3b9b6c43b90.text:
UPDATE: More than 30 Minnesota community water systems were attacked between Sunday and Monday.
Original post:
On June 16, media reported that Iran-linked Handala had attacked Cal Water. There was no evidence that they tampered with the water supply, but the group warned it would be increasing attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure. On July 23, the Iran-linked WANA News reported:
Following a cyberattack by the hacking group “Handala” on Maryland’s Operational Technology (OT) infrastructure, the group issued a warning statement declaring that critical U.S. infrastructure is on the front lines of their future attacks.
Handala emphasized that tampering with Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and SCADA systems is only part of the group’s offensive capabilities, and broader threats are facing water, electricity, and transportation networks.
This warning comes as the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) recently acknowledged in a security advisory that cyber actors are targeting industrial equipment from Rockwell Automation, Schneider Electric, and Siemens.
Days later, at least four water utilities in Minnesota reported having been attacked. DysruptionHub has been compiling news reports from Maple Plain, South St. Paul, Braham, and Plymouth. A statement from Braham suggests there may be a fifth locality that has not yet been publicly named.
There is no evidence at this point that water has been tampered with. While no group has claimed responsibility for the attacks, Handala is suspected in light of their recent activities and threats.

b10233fef80c.text:
Dan Raby reports:
A former accountant has been sentenced to years in federal prison after he was convicted for taking part in a scheme to laundering more than $5.3 million stolen from Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta.
Ronald Deabler, a 66-year-old Atlanta business owner and former Certified Public Accountant, was found guilty by a jury earlier this year.
According to information presented in court, the situation began when an unnamed hacker was able to get access to the email system of one of Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta’s furniture vendors. The hacker then pretended to be one of the vendor’s employees and tricked the healthcare institution into sending what they believed to be a legitimate payment. Instead, prosecutors say $5.3 million went an updated bank account belonging to Deabler.
Read more at CBS.
Update: This post was corrected post-publication to delete a comment that the accountant had been employed by the hospital. Thanks to a sharp-eyed reader, Adrian Sanabria, for catching my error.

c5f5786b2df8.text:
From the Information Commissioner’s Office:
A council worker who unlawfully accessed hundreds of personal records has been handed a suspended sentence.
Geoffrey Smith, 31, from Ledbury, Herefordshire, was a new employee at Herefordshire Council working in the Children and Young People directorate. His unlawful conduct was discovered after concerns were raised within the council about potential unauthorised access to a referral case, prompting an investigation into other records he had accessed.
That investigation revealed that, over a four-day period, Smith unlawfully accessed approximately 490 records and downloaded 94 documents. The records related to his family members and families known to him and included children and adults. The records accessed involved highly sensitive material such as medical records, social worker reports and child and family assessments.
On 27 May 2026, Smith pleaded guilty to an offence under Section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990, relating to the unlawful accessing of personal data held on computers. Smith was sentenced at Worcester Magistrates’ Court following a hearing on Friday 17 July to two months imprisonment suspended for 12 months, 120 hours unpaid work, £2000 costs plus a victim surcharge of £154.

17a5a4da582b.text:
Researcher Jeremiah Fowler provides today’s entry in the “No Need to Hack When It’s Leaking” files:
I recently discovered a publicly accessible database that was not password-protected or encrypted and contained what appeared to be records associated with the Tribeca Film Festival.
Upon further investigation I uncovered an additional three separate unsecured databases: “development” (203,370 records), “staging” (224,999 records), and “production” (238,000 records). The total number of exposed records was 666,369, and timestamps ranged from 2019 to 2026. Multiple files also referenced a fourth database labeled as “CMS” (content management system) that was properly secured. While the latter was not publicly accessible, there are potential risks associated with identifying where internal data is stored.
A majority of the exposed records I saw in a limited sample were images, press kits, marketing materials, and documents (including some marked as confidential). Inside the database marked as “production,” there was a single backup .dump file that contained potentially sensitive information, including email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses, and hashed passwords. The backup file contained a total of 295,916 records that included folders indicating 163,171 “users,” 15,488 “films contacts,” 13,535 “contacts,” and more.
Read more at ExpressVPN.

3993f251a464.text:
Security researchers at Zenity Labs discovered a vulnerability they dubbed "AgentForger" in OpenAI's workspace agents. The flaw allowed attackers to create malicious AI agents within a victim's ChatGPT workspace through a single deceptive link.

The attack exploited ChatGPT's agent builder feature, which constructs AI assistants capable of operating across email, chat, calendars, and business applications. The vulnerability accepted attacker-supplied instructions embedded in ChatGPT URLs. Upon clicking, the builder would automatically configure the malicious agent, activate the victim's connected services (Outlook, Teams, Slack, SharePoint, Google Drive), disable approval prompts, publish the agent, and schedule its execution.

The compromised agent functioned as an autonomous corporate infiltrator. Rather than requiring traditional command-and-control infrastructure, it monitored the victim's inbox for messages containing "TASK" in the subject line, executing each instruction whether that involved searching files, collecting documents, or exfiltrating data.

Michael Bargury, Zenity's co-founder and CTO, stated: "With one click, an attacker gets a fully autonomous agent inside your company that has your people's identity and access, with the guardrails off."

Zenity's proof-of-concept demonstrations included mapping organizational structures, hunting for embedded credentials, and conducting phishing impersonations via the victim's own Teams account.

Zenity reported the issue to OpenAI on June 4, 2026. OpenAI acknowledged the report the following day and patched the vulnerability four days later by removing the problematic URL parameter before public disclosure.

Author: Carly Page. Published: Thursday, July 23, 2026 at 14:02 UTC.

63519bac3a3d.text:
It’s been a longtime feature of the annual Defcon hacker conference that attendees come away not only with knowledge of new software vulnerabilities and hacking techniques but also an elaborately designed conference badge—often electronic masterpieces embedded with intricate puzzles, complex crypto challenges, hidden Easter eggs, and even the mechanical gear trains of a watch.
Each year’s badge creator endeavors to top previous designs and blow the minds of hard-to-impress hackers. But this year’s badges take a different tack. Instead of the badge designs being the star, it’s what is inside the hardware that will really stand out.
This year, Defcon asked legendary hardware hacker Andrew “bunnie” Huang to create the badges—revealed here for the first time—and they include an innovative open source chip that Huang designed and that aims to do no less than advance the state of security, transparency, and trustworthiness in computing.
But the chip isn't just part of the badge. Its core module can be removed and used after the conference as a hardware security token, giving the badge a second life beyond Defcon.
The chip—called the Baochip-1x—is a “mostly” open source microcontroller that has been three years in the making and fulfills Huang’s years-long dream of making a chip whose security is verifiable. Huang has published the source code for the Baochip’s operating system, firmware, processor core, cryptographic engines, and input-output system, on GitHub, making these components available for inspection and use.
The chip is also packaged so that researchers can peer inside to check the silicon itself and compare what they see against the published design, rather than having to trust that the manufactured chip is what the designers intended.
Computer chips are traditionally black-box components with an opaque casing that obscures their circuitry. Even previous open source chips that made their specs and code available for users to examine were encased in impermeable plastic, creating a supply-chain problem. Users had to trust that nothing changed during the manufacturing stage of the chip, such as a backdoor component being added to it.
Unlike conventional chips encased in opaque plastic, the Baochip is packaged so that infrared light can be shone through the back of the silicon, allowing the chip's internal structures to be visually inspected.
Huang plans to demonstrate the technique at the conference, allowing attendees to inspect the chip under an infrared light.
“I've been doing a bunch of stuff along the lines of trust and silicon and verification transparency” for years, Huang tells WIRED. "It's all … this kind of story arc I've been on … to try and get a chip that we can trust down to the very core, down to the transistor … You can actually … see the RAM arrays … on the chip.”
Build-a-Chip
Building a new chip is an expensive project that can cost millions of dollars for fabrication. But Huang got a big break three years ago when a company called Crossbar reached out to him. The company wanted to create a new open source and secure chip but didn’t know how to go about it. Huang agreed to assist on one condition: that they let him piggyback on their manufacturing run by placing his CPU on their chip wafer, allowing both designs to share the same manufacturing run rather than requiring Huang to fund a separate run.
"They look at it as, if they put me on the chip, they get two products for the price of one,” Huang says. This kind of piggybacking is not unusual, he adds, though it’s not something the industry likes to discuss publicly.
The result is a Crossbar chip that includes both Crossbar’s microprocessor and Huang’s. The Baochip is essentially the same chip but with the Crossbar microprocessor disabled, since Huang doesn’t have the rights to distribute it.
The Crossbar version of the chip uses a proprietary ARM core, whereas Huang’s version uses a RISC-V core whose implementation is open source. The RISC-V instruction set is also open and publicly documented. The two versions can use the same underlying infrastructure and peripherals while activating different CPU cores.
There are some closed-source elements on Huang’s chip. Some low-level physical-design and manufacturing elements, including those associated with TSMC's 22-nanometer fabrication process, are proprietary. “But … if you look on the spectrum of how open you can get things, this is … very, very far beyond any [other] security-oriented chip,” Huang says.
Badge Beginnings
Past Defcon badges have used commercial off-the-shelf chips rather than custom-designed open source silicon. The idea for using the Baochip was sparked by a meeting late last year when Huang spoke with Defcon founder Jeff Moss about his progress in developing his open source chip. He told Moss that he planned to release it this summer through his company, Baochip.
Moss realized the concept behind it matched perfectly with the conference theme this year—agency—which Defcon defines as the technologies we use and the choices we make that increase self-determination. And he and Huang realized it would be a great opportunity to help bootstrap the chip’s adoption. Until now, the Baochip has been distributed only in a small development release; the 27,000 Defcon badges represent its first major distribution.
Moss had one requirement for the badges. He wanted them to have a life beyond the conference and not be something that people would just throw in a drawer or a landfill after the event. He’s long been frustrated with the design and limitations of hardware security tokens and crypto wallets that, at the hardware level, can be cracked, so he thought Huang’s chip could be a more secure alternative to existing authentication tokens and wallets.
"I've always kind of dreamed of this idea where you can take your secrets, put them in hardware, and then if an attacker gets in, they can't quite get your secrets,” Moss tells WIRED.
The badge's detachable module can serve as a FIDO hardware security token. Its software supports time-based, one-time password systems and password management. Huang says it is "probably the world's first open source security token that you can fully inspect all the way down to the bootloader [and] transistors.”
The removable module also includes a camera for scanning QR codes to register them to authentication systems. But in keeping with Defcon’s privacy practices and its ban on surreptitious photography at the conference, the camera is very low resolution and nearsighted, and the chip by default only utilizes the black and white data from the camera and doesn’t support photo storage.
"It's … great at scanning QR codes and pretty much bad at everything else,” Huang says.
The badges, whose artwork was designed by Dutch firm Cheeso, don’t eschew conference life. Huang still included features designed to encourage attendees to interact. The badges, for example, have LED lights that flash in different color palettes and patterns depending on the type of badge—there are different ones for general attendees, speakers, and goons (the small army of volunteers who run the conference) as well as the special black Uber badges that go to contest winners and special VIPs, which give them free Defcon attendance for life. Each badge type starts with a specific color and flashing pattern, but users can add to their colors and build more complex flashing patterns when their badges communicate with other badges.
How Secure Is It?
The chip runs an operating system written in Rust and includes secure boot, a true random number generator, and hardware features intended to harden it against attacks. Huang believes it will be particularly resistant to remote, nonphysical attacks.
The chip also uses resistive RAM, or RRAM, a type of nonvolatile memory that Huang says is designed to make physical extraction of stored data more difficult than conventional flash memory. With flash memory, he says, "if you de-layer it down to the actual flash cells … you can just see the ones and zeros literally on these chips.”
Huang is cautious, however, about overhyping the chip’s security capabilities. He estimates that it could withstand attacks involving tens of thousands of dollars in resources, but says an adversary with millions of dollars and a sophisticated hardware-analysis lab could likely defeat it.
“I actually think it's one of the most secure chips you can get out there, but I [also] think most chips have been oversold in terms of security,” he says.
Huang says he likes the fact that the chip will be stress-tested by Defcon attendees and knows they will likely hack them and expose flaws that will help him make them even more secure.
"I fully expect there will be zero-days [that people find in the code]. It's actually … one of the features … of launching at Defcon,” he says of designing an open source chip capable of being examined.
Today the chip can function as a YubiKey-like security token; but in the future, he says, it could become an HSM or run other software such as Linux. The hardware uses a 350 MHz RISC-V processor with 2 megabytes of SRAM and 4 megabytes of RRAM, which he says puts it “on the edge of being able to run Linux,” and it has 4x 700MHz PicoRV32 cores for doing input-output. It already runs MicroPython and has C and Rust development kits.
Huang plans to expand the chip’s features himself, but he also expects DefCon participants to build on what he’s provided and make the chips their own.
Updated 8/4/2026 at 12:35 pm ET: Added details about the badges’ art design.

0f80bde6a591.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a newly disclosed security flaw impacting Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) Software to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following reports of zero-day exploitation.

The vulnerability, assigned CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS score: 5.3), allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to log into affected devices using low-privilege account credentials to access sensitive data within susceptible systems.

According to Cisco's alert, "This vulnerability is due to the presence of static user credentials for a low-privileged account." Attackers can exploit this by using the account to log in to affected systems. A successful exploit permits attackers to access sensitive data as the low-privileged user.

Cisco noted the attack surface is reduced if the FMC management interface lacks public internet access. The company assigned a Security Impact Rating of High rather than Medium because the vulnerability can be chained with other Cisco Secure FMC Software vulnerabilities to escalate privileges.

Security researcher Jimi Sebree of Horizon3.ai discovered and reported the flaw. Cisco acknowledged active exploitation earlier this month but did not disclose when attacks began, who conducted them, or exploitation methods.

Patched versions are available for FMC versions 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7, and 10.0. Cisco recommends using "cat /var/log/messages | grep license" to detect exploitation indicators showing "/var/tmp/license.tmp" in command output.

Cisco also updated its advisory for CVE-2026-20079 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical authentication bypass flaw in Cisco Secure FMC Software, with identical indicators of compromise and hotfixes. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must apply fixes by August 1, 2026.

Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: July 30, 2026.

af7829dfff10.text: Resecurity has announced native integration availability with IBM QRadar SIEM, a widely-used Security Information and Event Management platform adopted by Fortune 100 corporations globally. The plugin can be activated through IBM Application Exchange. The integration utilizes open standards STIX and TAXII (including version 2.1) to ingest, normalize, and correlate indicators of compromise (IOCs). It provides configurable data ingestion and processing workflows, allowing security teams to set up log sources for continuous infrastructure visibility. According to the announcement: "This approach helps enrich security events with additional context and supports more informed analysis within Security Operations Centers (SOCs)." The company emphasized that customers benefit from seamless integration and industry best practices for threat intelligence implementation with IBM Security's SIEM product. Resecurity stated it continues expanding its integration ecosystem to support interoperability with widely-adopted technology platforms, enabling organizations to operationalize threat intelligence within existing workflows. (Note: appears to be sponsored content, as indicated by the "Resecurity Sponsored" label on the article.)

d72398c026fc.text: Device code phishing—exploiting OAuth 2.0 device authorization flows to steal access tokens—has transformed from a specialized red-team technique to an industrial-scale threat within six months. Originally designed for input-constrained devices like smart TVs and printers, the device authorization login flow has expanded to applications it wasn't originally intended for, particularly CLI logins. While researchers documented this attack vector in 2020, nation-state actors didn't begin deploying it until 2024. By 2025, criminal groups like ShinyHunters targeted Salesforce at scale. The arrival of the EvilTokens kit in February 2026 accelerated criminal adoption dramatically. Microsoft reported detecting "10 to 15 entirely new campaigns every 24 hours" by April, while Barracuda documented "7 million attacks in four weeks." Six Key Takeaways: 1) Defeats All MFA Forms, Including Passkeys - The attack targets the authorization layer post-authentication rather than the login process itself; users authenticate normally, then copy a device code and approve access on legitimate provider URLs, so passkeys and hardware security keys provide no protection because the attack exploits the separation between identity verification and application access. 2) PhaaS Industrialization - Device code phishing is now a standard feature in phishing-as-a-service platforms such as Tycoon2FA and Kali365; advanced kits like ARToken include PRT persistence, mailbox access, BEC automation, and SharePoint exfiltration. 3) Rapid Kit Development - Push Security tracks over 25 distinct device code phishing kits; AI-assisted development has collapsed barriers to entry, with many kits sharing structural similarities due to LLM-generated code. 4) Beyond Microsoft - While 99% of current attacks target Microsoft, the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant is cross-platform; GitHub, AWS, and Salesforce all implement device flows and represent future targets. 5) Broader Authorization Attack Shift - Device code phishing is part of a wider trend toward attacking authorization mechanisms rather than authentication; related techniques like ConsentFix target OAuth consent flows and similarly bypass passkeys. 6) Detection Must Occur in the Browser - Since phishing pages can be delivered through any channel and users interact with legitimate provider URLs, traditional email gateways and network proxies cannot block these attacks; browser-based detection of behavioral signatures offers the most effective defense.

9c62e7150b1b.text: Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reported that a Chinese-speaking threat actor used DeepSeek through the open-source Hermes Agent framework to conduct autonomous cyberattacks. After receiving an initial Telegram instruction, the agent independently identified internet-facing systems and selected public exploits without requiring further operator intervention. The operator, tracked under the aliases knaithe and KnYuan, launched exploitation attempts targeting over 460 victims using both autonomous and manual attack workflows. Unit 42 documented seven distinct exploit tracks involving eight CVE identifiers. The n8n attack chain combined two separate vulnerabilities. Exploitation attempts against Langflow and n8n systems ultimately failed because exposed targets lacked required configuration elements. In parallel manual operations, the threat actor exfiltrated data from three organizations via the NetScaler memory-overread flaw CVE-2026-3055 and achieved command execution on 11 Marimo instances through CVE-2026-39987. However, Unit 42 could only confirm three successfully compromised targets across the entire campaign. The agent demonstrated sophisticated capabilities: it enumerated vulnerable versions, downloaded exploits, abandoned unproductive attack paths, and selected alternative vulnerabilities based on severity and deployment scale. An exposed HTTP server running on port 8888 inadvertently exposed the actor's model configurations, API keys, exploit scripts, and target lists. DeepSeek served as the primary reasoning model within Hermes Agent, which provided terminal access and unattended execution capabilities. Limited use of Claude Code and Qwen Code was detected. Organizations should patch exposed Langflow, n8n, and Marimo systems, update NetScaler ADC or Gateway appliances configured as SAML identity providers, and restrict public access to workflow and notebook interfaces. Unit 42 assesses the operator to be based in Zhuhai, China, though publicly available information—including GitHub profiles and blog posts—cannot independently verify legal identity or state connections.

8ec88649ab96.text: Madison Square Garden uses facial recognition technology to scan all visitors and flags activists opposing this surveillance practice. The system was deactivated during Taylor Swift's event at the venue. Evan Greer, an activist monitored by the system, highlighted the disparity: "Ironically, Swift herself has reportedly used facial recognition at her own concerts to identify stalkers. This 'privacy for me, surveillance for thee' attitude..." exemplifies how wealthy individuals can afford privacy protections unavailable to ordinary people. The contrast is stark—while Swift's privacy measures prevented photo leaks from her private event, average citizens face constant surveillance. Swift has previously employed facial recognition technology herself to identify potential stalkers at her concerts, yet benefited from having the surveillance system disabled during her own gathering. The incident underscores growing concerns about surveillance disparities, where elite figures can opt out of monitoring systems while regular attendees cannot.

15d98b2be061.text: Google confirmed this week that an unprecedented surge in Chrome vulnerability discoveries has been driven by artificial intelligence. The company built an AI agent harness leveraging Gemini to identify security flaws across Chrome's codebase with significantly greater efficiency. The results have been striking. Chrome 149 and 150 releases patched 1,072 security defects, "surpassing the total number of security bugs fixed across the prior 23 milestones combined." Year-to-date, Google has patched over 1,800 bugs, with July's Chrome 151 release alone containing 370 security fixes. A notable discovery validated by the AI system was CVE-2026-3545 (CVSS 9.8), a sandbox escape vulnerability that had remained undetected in Chrome for 13 years. Tracked as "insufficient data validation in Navigation," the flaw could have allowed "a compromised renderer to trick the browser into reading local files." The company patched this vulnerability in Chrome 145 in early May. Google's agent harness includes support for model interoperability, was trained on previously identified CVEs and Chrome's entire Git history, and leverages developer-supplied SECURITY.md files. The company emphasizes it analyzed source code "strictly at rest, operating on locked-down machines that lack general internet access." To address the patch gap, Google is piloting twice-weekly Chrome security releases and working to automate CVE description generation. Additional initiatives include dynamic patching (eliminating restart requirements), memory safety hardening, and transitioning Chrome to memory-safe languages like Rust.

b7444fc2ad3f.text: Once attackers breach corporate networks, they often exploit standard domain infrastructure protocols to avoid detection by traditional security tools. Kerberoasting and DNS tunneling have become standard attack methods because they blend seamlessly with legitimate network traffic. Traditional network security tools struggle when attacks lack distinct indicators. Network Anomaly Detection (NAD) analyzes all traffic for suspicious artifacts deviating from typical host behavior, rather than searching for explicit attack signatures. Kaspersky's Anti Targeted Attack (KATA) platform implements this technology to detect domain controller attacks, traffic tunneling, C2 communications, and other infrastructure compromise indicators. NAD isn't based on universal indicators—each attack scenario requires tailored detection models accounting for specific protocol behavior and baseline deviations. Kerberoasting Detection: Kerberoasting exploits standard Kerberos protocol operations; attackers request Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) tickets for service accounts with Service Principal Names (SPNs), then attempt offline password cracking; legitimate TGS requests are indistinguishable from malicious ones.
