Australia's Broader CMS Campaign Warning: The Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) issued an alert warning of a global exploitation campaign targeting various CMS vulnerabilities and plugins. The agency stated: "As part of this campaign, malicious cyber actors are actively scanning websites for opportunities to deploy web shells, leveraging various vulnerabilities affecting CMS software and plugins."

Once deployed, web shells serve as conduits for remote access and control of targeted web servers. Identified vulnerabilities include those affecting Sneeit Framework, WPBookit, Gravity Forms, Craft CMS, Ninja Forms, MaxSite CMS, Breeze Cache, WavePlayer, MetInfo CMS, and Joomla JCE.

The ACSC concluded: "This highly scaled global exploitation campaign demonstrates the rapidly evolving cyber risk facing organisations. Advances in AI are accelerating the speed and scale of cyber operations, reducing the time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation."

83e0574356ff.text:
Organizations are building and deploying AI infrastructure in cloud environments at rapid pace, but cybersecurity fundamentals are often neglected to prioritize speed, according to Orca Security's 2026 State of AI Security Report.

Building AI Without Security: The report reveals that 56% of AI adopters have deployed agent frameworks into production, while 51.5% leverage AI to create custom applications. More concerning, 81.2% of companies running AI packages contain at least one known vulnerability, with 99.9% of fixable AI vulnerability alerts remaining unpatched.

API-based AI is integrated into development workflows with access to codebases, terminals, environment variables, and credentials—creating expanded attack surfaces. Each production AI agent represents a new non-human identity with distinct permissions and potential blast radius. Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines enable large language models to access internal documents and proprietary knowledge at query time.

More than half of AI cloud service users operate four or more distinct AI service types. Across major cloud providers, between 87% and 98% of organizations have not configured customer-managed encryption keys for their AI services.

Securing the AI Supply Chain: The report identifies five attack layers: package registries, model hubs, developer tools, agent frameworks, and brand trust. Notably, 74.1% of companies running AI packages have at least one critical CVE.

Managing AI Agents and RAG: Sixty-four percent of AI adopters have deployed vector databases connecting language models to internal documents and proprietary knowledge. Organizations using retrieval-augmented generation operate an average of 3.78 vector databases.

Governance and Compliance: Governments are expanding AI regulation. The EU AI Act introduces requirements for high-risk AI systems beginning August 2, 2026, while Colorado's amended AI law takes effect January 1, 2027. Nearly 30% of AI adopters store at least one AI key insecurely.

Infrastructure and Encryption: Common exposure issues include missing encryption, broad access privileges, and internet-facing services. Most organizations have not enabled customer-managed encryption keys for their AI services.

6461c8496c2b.text:
The European Union and the United Kingdom jointly sanctioned dozens of Russian individuals and entities, accusing Russia of coordinating a network of hacking groups responsible for attacks across Europe.

The Council of the European Union announced sanctions on nine individuals and four entities, including Russian military intelligence (GRU) officers and cybercriminals. The UK separately sanctioned 24 individuals and entities, including senior GRU figures Vyacheslav Stafeyev, Ivan Senin, and Ivan Kasyanenko, whom officials say directed cyber and hybrid operations.

Sanctioned individuals include Vitaly Nikolayevich Kovalev (known online as "Bentley," "Alex Konor," and "Stern"), identified as leader of the Trickbot and Conti cybercrime gangs; Alexander Volosovik, owner of Media Land bulletproof hosting service; CARR hackers Denis Degtyarenko and Yuliya Pankratova; Lumma Stealer developers Maksim Voronin and Maksim Gordienko; and Unit 29155 members Evgeniy Bashev and Roman Puntus.

The UK additionally sanctioned members of IMPULS, accused of recruiting hackers from Russian universities, and individuals linked to Lumma Stealer malware operations, which affected at least 2,100 domestic victims over six months.

The Council publicly identified the FSB's 16th Centre as controlling several cyber threat groups, including the Turla hacking group. The unit has targeted government networks and critical infrastructure in France, Germany, Poland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Austria, Slovakia, Romania, and Finland since 2010. FSB hackers tracked as Static Tundra, Berserk Bear, Ghost Blizzard, and Dragonfly were linked to a failed strike on Poland's critical infrastructure.

A December cyberattack on Poland's energy grid affected approximately 30 facilities using DynoWiper malware and potentially could have disconnected power to roughly 500,000 people during winter, though it caused no actual disruptions. Cybersecurity companies ESET and Dragos attributed the incident to Russian state-backed Sandworm, while CERT-PL linked it to Berserk Bear.

Poland also blocked a cyberattack targeting the National Centre for Nuclear Research (NCBJ).

The Council stated: "We strongly condemn Russia's behaviour and misuse of this cyber ecosystem, targeting public services and critical infrastructure, causing disruptions and financial losses." The sanctions represent a response to malicious activities destabilizing the EU and international partners.

ad1f8c8771d3.text:
Opposition to AI data centers has emerged as a primary theme in US politics, cutting across party lines. While communities raise legitimate concerns about land misallocation, energy costs, and environmental impact, the authors argue these local battles obscure a larger issue: the concentration of power and wealth among AI companies.

The authors note that data centers produce relatively few jobs compared to their resource consumption. Opposition has been particularly fierce in lower-income communities, where residents see tech companies profiting while offering minimal returns. Globally, the carbon footprint poses sustainability concerns if AI usage accelerates.

However, Schneier and Sanders contend that focusing exclusively on data center opposition may play into corporate hands. While $750 billion is being invested in US data center infrastructure annually, this pales compared to enterprise software markets and represents just a fraction of what AI companies ultimately seek: "capturing all the value created by entire industries."

The authors predict demand for centralized computing may decline as Chinese labs innovate smaller, cheaper models and as on-device AI capabilities improve on phones and computers. This could resemble the early-2000s fiber optic bubble.

Rather than opposing data centers alone, the authors advocate broader action: state AI regulation, taxing AI computation so the public captures profit share, and supporting Public AI—an alternative ecosystem developed under public control prioritizing public benefit over private profit.

A significant concern involves AI company campaign spending. Anthropic and OpenAI, though industry rivals, spent millions in New York congressional races supporting opposing viewpoints on "AI safety"—ultimately benefiting both by maintaining the mystique that their products represent the world's most critical challenge.

The authors conclude that corporate concentration of wealth poses the greatest existential risk. Solutions must extend beyond limiting data center development to include public financing of campaigns and meaningful state regulation to counteract Citizens United effects.

116da435a79a.text:
Cybersecurity agencies from 12 countries have issued a fresh warning that a Russian state-sponsored cyber unit is actively targeting vulnerable routers worldwide.

The joint advisory detailed how Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16 cyber actors have been observed hunting for vulnerable routers by scanning the internet for devices that still use default or weak Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) passwords and community strings.

Center 16 is also known as Berserk Bear, Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Ghost Blizzard and Static Tundra.

Sectors most at risk from this global targeting, including communications, defence, energy, financial services, government and healthcare, are being urged to take action. This includes using SNMPv3, as it provides built-in authentication and encryption capabilities that help protect management traffic from interception and tampering.

SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 rely on community strings transmitted in plaintext, making them vulnerable to network sniffing. If an attacker obtains a valid community string and gains successful SNMP access, they can use Object Identifiers (OIDs) to command the router to copy its configurations and send it via Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP). These exfiltrated files are then sent to a virtual private server leased by the threat actor or a compromised file transfer protocol server.

As well as hunting for vulnerable routers via scanning for weak SNMP passwords and community strings, the Russian threat actor has also been known to occasionally exploit common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) in Cisco devices.

In 2025, Cisco warned that a seven-year-old vulnerability (CVE-2018-0171) in the Smart Install feature of unpatched, often end-of-life Cisco devices, was being exploited by Center 16/Static Tundra. Customers were urged to apply the patch for CVE-2018-0171 or to disable Smart Install if patching is not an option. The patch was first issued in 2018.

The joint security advisory noted that many of the TTPs used by this Russian threat actor overlaps with that of other groups, such as China-linked group Slat Typhoon.

The advisory has been co-authored by agencies from Australia, Canada, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Italy, New Zealand, Poland, Sweden, the UK and US.

EU, UK Blame Center 16 for Poland's Energy Grid Cyber-Attack: At the same time as the publication of the joint advisory, the coordinated cyber-attacks which targeted Poland's energy infrastructure in late 2025 have been officially attributed to FSB Center 16 by the UK and European Union (EU).

In a statement issued on July 13, the UK government said: "This reckless attack failed but could have caused 500,000 citizens to lose electricity in the depths of winter. It is another example of the Russian state's irresponsible attempts to sow chaos across Europe."

The EU and UK have also issued a joint sanctions package targeting 24 individuals and entities behind the destructive cyber and hybrid operations including cybercriminals involved in proxy networks linked to the Russian Intelligence Services.

The UK is also sanctioning individuals behind Lumma Stealer. The UK government said that Russia has used Lumma Stealer's stolen credentials to conduct cyber espionage operations against targets globally to support the Kremlin's objectives.

According to the National Crime Agency, within the last six months, there have been at least 2100 Lumma Stealer victims in the UK.

e4a33e75dd4e.text:
Progress Software has instructed some ShareFile customers to shut down their on-premises servers following detection of what it describes as a "credible external security threat" targeting the ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers component.

The emergency notification, distributed via email and obtained by The Register, directed organizations operating ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers to manually power down their Windows servers hosting the software. Notably, no patch or configuration fix has yet been released as an alternative.

Progress stated: "We have reason to believe there is a credible external security threat targeting Progress Software's ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers." The company emphasized that disabling ShareFile account access was insufficient and warned that immediate manual server shutdown was necessary.

The vendor characterized the action as precautionary while conducting investigations with internal and external security experts. Progress representatives contacted affected organizations directly to reinforce the directive.

A subsequent weekend statement offered limited new information. Progress claimed "no indication of unauthorized access to any ShareFile customer account or data" and stated it had not "identified any active threat," yet maintained that Storage Zone Controllers must remain powered down during the investigation period.

Critical details remain undisclosed, including the threat's nature, affected software versions, customer compromise status, and when systems can safely restart.

Progress provided The Register with a statement: "Protecting our customers' data and maintaining the security of our services remain our highest priorities...Storage Zone Controllers must remain turned off while we complete our investigation."

The information gap has generated speculation. One Progress customer posted on Reddit theorizing that a complete server shutdown directive suggests "it's almost certainly an unauthenticated RCE being exploited in the wild."

Storage Zone Controllers represent the on-premises component allowing organizations to maintain files locally while leveraging Progress's cloud platform for authentication and management. Their typical internet-facing Windows server placement makes them attractive exploitation targets for serious, remotely exploitable vulnerabilities.

This incident emerges months after Progress addressed two critical ShareFile Storage Zone Controller v5 vulnerabilities permitting unauthenticated remote code execution when chained together, though the company hasn't connected the current situation to those previous bugs.

Progress has a substantial history with security incidents, spending much of 2023 and 2024 addressing consequences from mass MOVEit Transfer exploitation by the Clop ransomware gang, which evolved into a significant supply chain breach affecting thousands of organizations.

d175839591bc.text:
Zimbra has released patches for a critical stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability affecting its Classic Web Client. The flaw allows malicious code embedded in specially crafted emails to execute when users open those messages.

According to Zimbra's announcement, "a specially crafted email could run malicious code when the email is opened." If exploited, the vulnerability could grant attackers access to mailbox information, session data, or account settings.

The company resolved this issue in version 10.1.19, released on July 7. Zimbra strongly recommends all customers using the Classic Web Client upgrade immediately to obtain the latest security patches.

Customers migrating from older versions (10.0.x, 9.0.x, or 8.8.15) should update SNMP mitigation settings and reapply them following the upgrade.

The vulnerability has not yet been assigned a CVE identifier. It was reported by Google's Threat Analysis Group (GTIG), an organization known for identifying security flaws targeted by state-sponsored actors and commercial spyware developers.

This represents a zero-click attack vector, as users need only open an email to trigger the malicious code execution, posing a significant risk to Zimbra deployments.

0f721bf822c7.text:
Just after noon on a Saturday last month, a Skydio X10 quadcopter hovered about 200 feet over a San Francisco apartment complex, watching police chase a man hiding behind a parked car. The target of this manhunt lay down on the pavement, apparently unaware that he remained in full view of the flying eye overhead. The 5-pound drone had, in fact, already followed him across the city, zooming in on his black SUV’s license plate, keeping the vehicle locked at the center of its video frame until he pulled over. Now it watched the police as they closed in and surrounded him.
As the officers approached, the man adjusted his hiding spot, moving to the other side of the parked car. At that moment, however, another Skydio drone zoomed in on his location, one of four Skydio quadcopters that had followed the man in just the prior hour. This one had been called away from a nearby McDonald’s, where it had been watching two people who’d exited the suspect’s car a few minutes earlier—and now began watching him from a second angle.
Within seconds, three officers converged on the man, two pointing weapons at him, then tackled him as half a dozen more police arrived on the scene. Police records provided to WIRED by the San Francisco Police Department show the entire street-and-sky response followed from what the SFPD described as an alleged “auto boost/strip” incident—the suspected theft of car parts or another object from a vehicle.
This glimpse of modern drone-enabled police surveillance, including the highly sensitive video of the man’s physical takedown, wasn’t voluntarily released by the SFPD—which, like most US police departments, rarely releases drone videos even in response to public records requests. Instead, it was accidentally livestreamed onto the open internet via Skydio’s website. That’s where two security researchers, Sam Curry and Maik Robert, discovered that the SFPD was leaking all of the real-time footage from five of its surveillance drones, including both color and thermal imaging, accompanying location metadata, and the drone pilots’ names and email addresses, to anyone who merely found the public web address where the videos were hosted.
Curry and Robert say they reported their discovery to Skydio around two days after discovering it, and it was quickly taken offline. By then, though, the researchers had watched police carry out what appeared to be multiple arrests and searches as well as tracking cars and individuals from the sky, all visible at a fully public web address.
“There’s a certain trust given to the police to use these things correctly,” says Curry. “When you're watching a drone feed live, you can look into dozens of different apartments, you can see police zooming in on people, you can see arrests. The fact that all of this was exposed feels like a really big issue from a privacy perspective.”
The leaked feed of video captures two forced detentions—whether any actual arrests were made is unclear from the footage—a police visit to an apartment in a high-rise apartment building, and an apparent search of an alley populated with homeless people, as well as numerous other more ambiguous instances where police used drones to surveil individuals, vehicles, or buildings. While the feed remained live, Curry and Robert began archiving the public stream of data and videos and later shared the results with WIRED.
The archive Curry and Robert captured offers a detailed record of SFPD drone operations over about 48 hours in mid-June. It includes 60 videos from 20 separate flights, with each mission recorded from three feeds: a color camera, a thermal camera that renders people as heat signatures, and a third view from the drone’s rooftop dock. WIRED analyzed all 20 color videos with software that detects people, vehicles, and other objects in images. The review found that the cameras had filmed hundreds of people and vehicles across the 20 flights. In a single frame, as a drone hovered over a downtown intersection, the software counted 34 people crossing the street or standing on the sidewalks. Across all of the videos the footage showed clear faces of dozens of people.
Together, the videos amount to more than three hours of aerial color footage and roughly the same amount of thermal footage. The archive also includes second-by-second telemetry logs for every flight—more than 5,000 GPS points in all tracing over some 44 miles—recording each drone’s latitude and longitude, altitude, speed, heading, and battery level from takeoff to landing. Six SFPD pilots’ names and email addresses also appear across the logs.
Skydio, based in nearby San Mateo, is one of the leading American drone companies selling to police departments, fire departments, government agencies, and the military. Its X10 drones are part of SFPD’s drone program, which began in 2024 and is authorized for vehicle pursuits and active criminal investigations. Since then, the program has grown quickly: SFPD’s fleet has expanded from six drones to 98, and officers logged more than 1,400 launches between May 2024 and March 2026, according to a 2025 SFPD annual report and reporting from the San Francisco Chronicle.
The city maintains a transparency portal that publishes information about police drone flights, including logs, after they occur—without video. The link Curry and Robert found was not part of that transparency system.
Curry and Robert say the drone videos were exposed not as a result of any error on the part of Skydio, but rather by what seems to be a misuse of Skydio’s software by the SFPD. Skydio allows users to generate shareable links to videos or access to drones’ data streams in real time, known as ReadyLinks, with the ability to limit access to users with an authentication code or an expiration date. Someone with access to the SFPD’s instance of Skydio’s software, however, appears to have created a link last December to five of its drones’ feeds with no authentication requirement and an expiration date of one full year.
That link was then somehow added to an open-source collection of archived web URLs known as AlienVault Open Threat Exchange, typically used by security researchers, where Curry and Robert found it. In other words, the link appeared to have already exposed the drone feeds for six months by that time, with no assurance that Curry and Robert were the only ones who had been watching.
When WIRED reached out to the SFPD, it responded in a statement calling the exposed drone video web address an “internal restricted link that is for SFPD law enforcement purposes only,” of the kind that “allow SFPD to coordinate on law enforcement and public safety operations,” and that it had been “improperly obtained and accessed by individuals without authorization.” (Curry and Robert point out that they didn’t bypass any security or authentication of any kind to access the stream, which is the typical legal definition of “unauthorized access.”)
“After being made aware of the vulnerability, SFPD has put more restrictive sharing protocols in place to ensure unauthorized individuals will not be able to access our footage,” the statement continues. “At this time, we do not have information that other individuals were accessing the live drone feed. This matter remains under investigation.”
Skydio didn’t respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
In the footage WIRED reviewed, drones capture dramatic moments like police chasing and restraining targets of the aerial surveillance. In other videos, officers can be seen through the window of an apartment in a high-rise, which police records describe as both a “check on well-being” or a “missing person” investigation in different drone flights filming the same incident. In another, police can be seen talking to homeless people in an alley, what police records describe as a “person with a knife” investigation.
The innocuous appearance of many of the videos raises questions about whether the surveillance was necessary. In one “auto boost/strip”-related call, the drone follows two young men in their car, at least one of whom is described in police records as having been identified as a “suspicious person in a vehicle.” Then the two men emerge onto a basketball court and start playing, and the drone departs.
A drone flight in response to what police records describe as a “person with a gun” investigation seems to fixate on a seemingly intoxicated man stooped on a sidewalk. Another drone, called in response to an alleged “prowler” incident, hovers over a young person wearing headphones and sitting on the roof of a building, zooms in on them, then flies away. “That one felt like an invasion of privacy, just so uncomfortable,” Curry says. “Like this person thinks they’re by themselves on this roof and has gotten away from everybody, and then there's a police drone watching them.”
In its statement, the SFPD notes that it adheres to a “strict policy” around drone use, and that “drones can only be used to assist with active criminal investigations, to assist with or in lieu of vehicle pursuits, and for training exercises.”
Curry and Robert say they first became curious about Skydio last month after seeing an announcement from a Florida police department that it was adopting the company’s drone system, and then learning how widely the company’s drones have been deployed across the US. As web-focused security researchers, they decided to check out the company’s systems. In one routine step, they used the tool GetAllURLs, which pulls all archived web addresses for a given domain from sources including AlienVault Open Threat Exchange, requesting all Skydio links. Almost immediately, they found the San Francisco police drone feed.
Soon they were watching live footage of scenes like a man with a hand wrapped in a bloody white cloth talking to police and then a detention of a suspect at a gas station by a group of plainclothes policemen. At that point, it started to become “pretty clear that this probably shouldn't be public,” as Robert put it. “Like, I don't think there's any reason that someone from the public should be able to watch in real time as someone is getting grabbed by undercover cops.”
In fact, police departments have very often treated drone footage as too sensitive to release, even under freedom of information laws. Chula Vista, California, whose police department pioneered the “drone as first responder” model, spent years fighting a public-records lawsuit seeking access to its drone videos, arguing that the footage is investigatory and could expose private details about people caught on police cameras. (A California appeals court rejected the city’s position that the videos could be categorically withheld, a ruling that became statewide precedent after the California Supreme Court declined to review it. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine which videos, if any, must be released.)
The fact that so much San Francisco drone footage was potentially exposed online is “shocking, but not surprising,” says Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project who focuses on drone surveillance and privacy. The videos, he says, demonstrate why privacy advocates consider any law enforcement surveillance data a “toxic asset” that’s always at risk of a security breach, and recommend minimizing the data and video recorded and retained from drone flights. “That means not recording when you don't need to record,” Stanley says.
SFPD’s drone policy says operators must keep cameras trained on areas necessary to a mission and minimize the inadvertent collection of data about uninvolved people or places. It also instructs operators to take reasonable precautions, including turning cameras away, to avoid inadvertently recording or transmitting images of places where people have a reasonable expectation of privacy. But the exposed Skydio feeds reviewed by WIRED showed full missions from takeoff to landing, capturing not only detentions and searches, but also streets, apartment buildings, rooftops, cars, courtyards, and bystanders who did not appear to be the subject of any police operation.
“Watching these videos, it was just a reminder of what a powerful technology this is, and the amount of city life that is swept up in these videos,” Stanley says. The potential for privacy violations based on that broad video collection only becomes greater in the age of AI, he notes. “Maybe no human has the time to pore over every frame of these videos, but an AI can do that, and it's scalable to vast amounts of video,” Stanley says.
After each mission, the SFPD policy says, drone footage must be reviewed for evidentiary value and uploaded to the department’s digital evidence database; footage with no evidentiary value must be deleted within 30 days. Since the URL Robert and Curry found made real-time drone data available but not historical data, it’s not clear if the exposed videos violated that policy.
Curry and Robert were struck by the fact that, in all the videos they watched, no one ever looks up at the drone or makes an attempt to hide from it—perhaps evidence that, given their size and altitude, the flying cameras are virtually invisible to the targets of their surveillance. “You’re just watching from above, and no one is aware that the drone is there,” Curry says. “It felt kind of creepy.”
Curry says watching the videos has changed his sense of his own privacy as he walks around an American city—or, at least, San Francisco. “This was the first time I'd seen drones used in a city like this, and looking at these streets, they’re the same streets I walk down when I’m visiting,” he says. “I guess it just makes me feel more observed.”

c1b9f234c284.text:
The European Union imposed sanctions on Russian military intelligence officers, hackers, and private companies on Monday, targeting what it called a yearslong cyber espionage campaign designed to undermine the bloc.

The action focused on nine individuals and four entities with alleged connections to an online spying network that has targeted governments and conducted sabotage operations against critical infrastructure including heating and power plants since 2010.

According to the European Council, those targeted "contribute to Russia's efforts to destabilize the EU, its member states and international partners." The espionage and attacks have affected at least nine countries.

France, Germany, Poland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Austria, Slovakia, Romania, and Finland have been targeted, among others. The specific names of individuals and entities were not disclosed in the statement.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot indicated France would summon the Russian ambassador soon. He explained the cyber activities aim to either "capture information, or sabotage the operation, for example, of railway infrastructures as it was the case in Poland."

The EU focused its measures on the 16th Centre of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), which the bloc said has been "controlling a variety of cyber threat groups" and conducting "a wide range of malicious cyber activities with growing severity."

The announcement follows prior warnings from officials in Sweden, Poland, Norway, Denmark, and Latvia about Russian cyberattacks targeting European critical infrastructure.

db160383da54.text:
Cybersecurity agencies from the United States and eight allied nations have jointly warned that Russian state-sponsored hackers are targeting vulnerable routers to breach critical infrastructure networks.

The joint advisory, authored by the NSA, FBI, and CISA along with 15 additional agencies from Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, New Zealand, Estonia, Finland, France, and Italy, attributes these attacks to hackers from Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16.

This hacking group—tracked under multiple names including Berserk Bear, Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Ghost Blizzard, and Static Tundra—exploits routers by scanning for devices accepting default or common SNMP authentication credentials. The attackers then issue commands using spoofed IP addresses to extract device configuration files via Trivial File Transfer Protocol to their servers.

The most vulnerable sectors include energy, communications, defense industrial base, healthcare, financial services, and government services. The UK National Cyber Security Centre noted: "Centre 16 has been seen hunting for vulnerable routers by scanning the internet for devices that still use default or weak SNMP passwords."

The advisory recommends upgrading to SNMPv3, disabling Cisco Smart Install, enforcing strong passwords, blocking TFTP and SNMP traffic at firewalls, updating software and firmware, and replacing end-of-life devices.

This follows a separate international operation that disrupted FrostArmada, attributed to Russian military intelligence group APT28, which had compromised 18,000 routers across 120 countries.

da50a68978db.text:
An Armenian national extradited from Ukraine has pleaded guilty to charges related to his role in notorious ransomware outfit Ryuk.

Karen Serobovich Vardanyan, 34, pleaded guilty to conspiracy and computer fraud in a federal court in Portland on July 8.

The Justice Department claimed that between November 2019 and April 2020, he illegally accessed computers belonging to various U.S. organizations to install Ryuk. These victims included a Michigan company that paid 200 bitcoin—over $1.1 million at the time—to restore network access. Vardanyan was also accused of hacking a company in Wilsonville, Oregon, and a school in Texas.

The DOJ stated that "Vardanyan and his co-conspirators hacked and deployed ransomware on hundreds of compromised servers and workstations over the period," receiving approximately 1,610 bitcoins in ransom payments valued at over $15 million at the time of payment.

As part of a plea deal, Vardanyan agreed to pay over $1.1 million in restitution. He faces a maximum sentence of five years plus a $250,000 fine for conspiracy, and 10 years plus another $250,000 for computer fraud.

Brief Ryuk Background: Ryuk operated as one of the most prolific ransomware groups from 2018 to 2020, targeting defense contractors, hospitals, IT service providers, and other sectors. The group disbanded in 2020, with members reportedly joining the Conti group.

2bb39332313c.text:
FastNetMon is introducing Netomics, a self-hosted BGP routing intelligence platform that combines live routing data, registry information, RPKI validation, routing history and AI-assisted querying into a single application.

Built for internet service providers (ISPs), cloud providers, Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) and enterprises operating large IP networks, Netomics provides complete visibility into global internet routing without relying on third-party lookup services.

Network engineers often need to consult multiple public tools to investigate routing incidents, validate prefix ownership, check route origins or review historical routing changes. Netomics brings this information together in a single platform that runs entirely within the customer's own infrastructure, creating an internal source of truth for routing intelligence.

Pavel Odintsov, Founder of FastNetMon, stated: "Internet routing has become critical operational infrastructure, yet many organisations still depend on multiple external services to understand what is happening in their own networks. We built Netomics to give operators complete ownership of their routing intelligence while making it easier to troubleshoot incidents, automate workflows and improve routing security."

Netomics combines live BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) feeds with global routing data, Internet Routing Registry (IRR) information, WHOIS records, Regional Internet Registry (RIR) data, geofeed information, RPKI validation and historical routing data to provide comprehensive internet routing visibility.

The platform operates entirely on-premises, ensuring routing intelligence remains private, always available and under organizational control. It eliminates external rate limits and integrates directly with existing network infrastructure.

Netomics provides access via web interface, REST APIs, Prometheus metrics and native Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, enabling integration into automation workflows and AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude.

4f0b257dc250.text:
Anthropic has extended a limited-time promotion that increases weekly usage limits in Claude Code by 50% through July 19, 2026, at 11:59 PM PT. When the promotion ends, weekly usage limits will return to their standard levels without any changes to users' plans or billing.

The promotion is available to Pro, Max, and Team plans, as well as legacy seat-based users on Enterprise plans. Free plans and consumption-based Enterprise seats are not eligible.

What's Included: "No action is required to participate. If you're on an eligible plan, the increased weekly limit is automatically applied to your account," Anthropic stated in their announcement.

The 50% increase applies only to Claude Code across all supported environments, including the CLI, IDE extensions, desktop app, and web. Usage limits for other Claude products—including Claude (web, desktop, and mobile) and Claude Cowork—remain unchanged.

The promotion does not affect 5-hour usage limits. Additionally, the offer is non-transferable, has no cash value, and cannot be combined with any other offer.

5fbd546fc51c.text:
Healthcare diagnostics company Centers Laboratory (Centers Lab NJ LLC) has informed the US government that a data breach discovered nearly one year ago affects more than 540,000 individuals.

According to a data breach notice posted on its website, the New Jersey-based provider of testing and laboratory services for healthcare organizations discovered an intrusion in its IT environment in August 2025.

An investigation showed that threat actors had gained "limited access" to Centers Laboratory systems between August 9 and August 14, exfiltrating personal and protected health information, including names, dates of birth, SSNs, driver's license or state identification numbers, passport numbers, and health insurance and medical information.

The healthcare data breach tracker maintained by the Department of Health and Human Services revealed last week that the data breach affects 542,377 individuals.

Centers Lab was targeted by the WorldLeaks cybercrime group, which listed the organization on its website in October 2025. The hackers leaked more than 1.6 million files totaling 720 GB, allegedly stolen from Centers Lab systems.

WorldLeaks, which previously targeted major companies such as Nike and Dell, emerged in 2025 following the shutdown of the Hunters International ransomware group. Following the transition to WorldLeaks, the cybercriminals stopped using file-encrypting malware and have focused on data theft and extortion. More than 170 organizations are listed on the group's website at the time of writing.

6c49a20ba760.text:
An attacker running a live Microsoft 365 phishing operation left a Python web server listening on a public port with directory listing switched on. The command that did it: python3 -m http.server 8080, was still sitting in the readable .bash_history.

From that one lapse, French security firm Lexfo lifted the operator's entire toolkit and pivoted through it to two more phishing operators, three campaigns in all. Each ran a custom fork of the open-source Evilginx proxy, cloned from public GitHub.

The largest of the three had been running for more than a year, its victims overwhelmingly corporate mailboxes.

The three got past MFA in two mechanically different ways, one by proxying the live login, one by abusing a legitimate Microsoft sign-in flow. The two need different defenses, which is the part that matters most if you run Microsoft 365.

Directory listing on a working attack server is close to a full confession. The listing exposed phishing configs, credential-harvesting logs, RMM installers, combolists, backup archives, and the operator's own Telegram session files.

Behind it ran an Evilginx adversary-in-the-middle proxy and a SimpleHelp remote console on the same host, at 185.163.204[.]7 in Budapest, cataloged in late April 2026 during a routine internet scan.

The bash history and a set of public repos pointed straight at the operator: an Egyptian actor the firm tracks as codemado, active in VoIP and hacking forums since 2018, now running a Microsoft 365 AiTM platform on picis[.]net and monetizing access through a bulk mailer he wrote called MaDoO Blaster.

His campaign went live on April 20 and kept running past the day the directory was found on April 30, with fresh subdomains and a renewed wildcard certificate turning up weeks later. His own bot logged captures against two corporate M365 accounts, one French, one North American.

The repeated captures of the same accounts from different IPs are consistent, the firm says, with the operator refreshing stolen tokens as they aged out.

Where the kits came from: codemado did not build the framework he runs. He cloned it, and his bash history shows him comparing kits side by side. The server held four Evilginx variants pulled from two other GitHub developers, and both turned out to be active operators in their own right.

The first, red-queen, comes from a Nigerian operator the report calls mail-argenta, and it shows how much polish gets bolted onto a public framework. His fork renames the crossorigin and integrity HTML attributes to defeat Subresource Integrity checks and adds a URL-rewriting engine to http_proxy.go to dodge path-based detection. It pre-fills the victim's email address to cut abandonment.

It also sets a one-year TTL, 31,536,000 seconds, on the captured Microsoft session cookies. The report says an intercepted login can then outlast a password reset and, without a CAE-capable Conditional Access policy, stay usable for months.

A pre-compiled evilginx2.exe is committed to the repo, so a buyer never has to build anything. One captured M365 cookie sitting in the repo carried an expiration date of June 30, 2027.

mail-argenta got caught the way his own victims do. The firm found his email and a password in infostealer logs, the kind of harvested-credential data his phishing panels exist to produce. That leaked password matched the one hardcoded as the MySQL password in his Kraken panel and reused across his accounts.

The quiet one: The third fork, black-queen, logged far more captures than the other two, and it never touches a password. Its author, whom the researchers could not identify past the handle saroula01, built it around Microsoft's OAuth device code flow, a legitimate sign-in path meant for input-constrained devices.

The attack generates a real device code, wraps it in an Authenticator-themed lure page, and tells the target to enter it at the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin. The victim signs in on a real Microsoft page and clears MFA themselves. saroula01's backend polls the token endpoint and takes the token the moment they do.

Calling this "MFA bypass" misses how it works: nothing gets bypassed. The lure page is Authenticator-themed and attacker-built, but the device code and the Microsoft page where the victim finishes are genuine, so the MFA prompt the victim satisfies is real.

A passkey or FIDO2 key does not help either, because the victim clears it on genuine Microsoft infrastructure while authorizing the attacker's session; the origin binding that stops Evilginx passes cleanly when the origin really is Microsoft.

Microsoft documented the technique in February 2025, in a campaign it assessed with medium confidence as Russia-aligned. It has since spread well past state-backed use, into campaigns hitting hundreds of Microsoft 365 organizations.

saroula01's version ran quietly for over a year. The firm counted 218 distinct captured accounts in the campaign's Telegram bot logs across a dozen countries between June 2025 and July 2026, around 94 percent of them corporate mailboxes. Those are logged captures, not scan targets.

A token file briefly committed to the repo and then deleted, still readable in the git history, held 97 live Microsoft tokens tied to three of those victims, every one set to autoRefresh and some refreshed as many as 25 times. The framework was keeping the sessions alive on its own.

Both phishing domains, picis[.]net and romnor[.]ca, were offline when The Hacker News checked ahead of publication, though the report's timeline shows picis[.]net still provisioning new subdomains as late as May 2026. The Lexfo CTI team told THN that the domains had already gone offline before it took any action, and reads that as the operators rotating infrastructure or pulling back rather than a coordinated takedown, though it cannot confirm which.

Built with help: The report found signs of AI-assisted development across all three operations, though they vary in strength. saroula01 left two git commits co-authored by Claude models. mail-argenta committed an instructions.txt that is a verbatim save of an AI coding session, references to earlier prompts and all, documenting how the URL-rewriting feature got built.

codemado's is thinner: one of his scripts credits CyberNeurova, a paid "uncensored" code-generation API, the report says, which advertises itself with the prompt "Build me a keylogger in Python." Two of the three put a model directly in the code; the third is a credit line, and none of them shows how much of each build the model did.

It is not confined to these three either. Microsoft has separately documented device-code phishing built on AI-driven backend automation and generative-AI lures.

The Hacker News asked the report's authors how much of the tooling AI actually produced across the three operations. The Lexfo CTI team said the Evilginx forks carried only minor changes to the core, and that the clearer signs of AI use sat in the glue code around them, the scripts and phishlets, several of which read as direct model output. It was less the framework itself, the team said, than the code built around it.

What defenders can actually do: The two techniques do not share a fix. Phishing-resistant MFA, FIDO2, or passkeys still shut down the Evilginx side by binding the sign-in to the real domain. It does not stop device code abuse. For that, the lever is Conditional Access.

Microsoft's own line is to block device code flow wherever possible. A handful of setups genuinely need it, mostly input-constrained hardware like Teams room devices and some command-line tools. Inventory that uses the sign-in logs, blocks the flow everywhere else, and tests the policy in report-only mode before enforcing.

Layer IP-based Conditional Access location policies and Continuous Access Evaluation on top, so that on supported Microsoft 365 workloads, a stolen token seen from outside your allowed ranges gets reevaluated instead of riding out its lifetime.

For detection, the report flags refresh-token grants from the Microsoft Office client ID d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c in Entra sign-in logs as worth watching, where that desktop client is not in normal use; cross-check them against unfamiliar source IPs.

The same Microsoft guidance flags a catch: a session that started with device code flow stays tagged on later refreshes even when the current event no longer shows it, so hunt on the sign-in's Original transfer method field, not just the live authentication protocol.

On endpoints, hunt for the RMM tooling these operators drop for persistence; codemado's kit reaches for XEOX, so start with the agent at C:\Program Files (x86)\XEOX\xeox-agent_x64.exe and scheduled tasks matching *XEOX*Agent*Watchdog*. The domains and IPs are in the report, but that infrastructure rotates, so treat it as containment, not a fix.

The Hacker News also asked Microsoft about the abuse of its device code flow, and had received no response by the time of publication. This story will be updated with any reply.

None of this took much: three operators, none of whom built the frameworks they ran, stood up working campaigns off public repositories, kits that sell for a few hundred dollars, and a model helping with the custom parts.

The report reads that the barrier to a working campaign has fallen to near zero, and the Lexfo CTI team expects this class of attack to become significantly more common over the coming months.

One cheap ecosystem now supplies two ways around MFA, and that is the part that outlasts any single campaign here: a shop hardened against reverse-proxy phishing is still open to device-code abuse. Blocking that second path is one Conditional Access policy, no passkey rollout adds for you, and it exists only once someone writes it.

Update (July 16, 2026): Lexfo has issued an erratum to the report. Three entries it originally listed as malicious indicators, agent01.xeox.com, ws01.xeox.com, and 80.80.250.0/24, are legitimate XEOX vendor infrastructure, shared across all XEOX customers. Anyone who blocked them off that list should reverse that.

The corrected guidance is to alert and audit XEOX activity only where XEOX is not an authorized tool, and the same qualifier applies to the endpoint artifacts above: XEOX is a product some environments run on purpose.

5265e659a86f.text: We have made real progress in software supply chain security, improving visibility into software components, authenticity and build integrity. Much of this progress traces back to Executive Order 14028, which pushed agencies, contractors and enterprises to invest in SBOMs, signing and provenance. All of that matters, but it is not enough. The current software trust model still stops short of the question that determines risk at execution: What is this code capable of doing if it runs? This blind spot is becoming harder to ignore as AI changes the speed, scale and variability of malicious software. University of Toronto research demonstrated an AI-powered worm capable of adapting its attack strategy as it moves through a network. Unlike traditional worms that exploit a fixed vulnerability, this prototype can reason through new attack paths and tailor its behavior to different systems. The June 2026 AI executive order on cybersecurity reflects federal concern. But the issue is broader than policy: traditional trust models are insufficient when AI generates, modifies and deploys code faster than human review can keep up. We can no longer trust software based primarily on what it is, where it came from or whether it resembles something seen before. Visibility is not trust: SBOMs answer an important question: What is inside this software? Organizations cannot manage dependencies, open-source exposure or known vulnerable components if they do not know what is inside a build. But composition is not behavior. A package can have a clean dependency tree and still perform dangerous actions. An application can include expected libraries and still attempt credential access, persistence, lateral movement, file modification or data exfiltration. SBOMs help security teams understand ingredients, but they do not predict what software will do once it executes. Context matters. File deletion may be legitimate in a disk cleanup utility and catastrophic in an office macro. Credential access is expected in a password manager, but not in a package dependency. That is the limitation of composition-based trust: knowing what software contains does not tell you what it can do once it runs. Authentic does not mean safe: Signing and provenance answer different questions. Can we verify who published this software? Can we confirm where it came from? Can we determine whether the build followed expected steps? Those controls improve integrity, accountability, compliance and auditability. But authenticity is not the same as trustworthiness. Signed software can still behave maliciously. A trusted vendor update can be compromised. A legitimate build process can produce an artifact that violates enterprise policy. An AI coding agent can generate code that functions correctly while introducing unintended security consequences. Most security programs still assume that if software is signed, came through an approved pipeline or originated from a known repository, it is safe. That may be reasonable as a first filter, but it is a dangerous final decision. This approach made sense when software changed slowly and malicious code had recognizable indicators. AI is now generating, modifying and deploying code at unprecedented speed. Validating where software came from does not tell us whether it should run. The missing fourth pillar: Government supply chain security frameworks have helped formalize essential controls around software origin, integrity and build process. What they have not fully addressed is behavior. Software supply chain security must now answer four questions: What is inside the software? Can we trust where it came from? How was it built? What can it do? The fourth question increasingly determines security outcomes because software inherits the privileges of the user, workload, service account or automation context that launches it. Once code executes, it can access data, modify systems, communicate externally, establish persistence, disable controls or move laterally. Traditional malware defense often makes that decision after execution begins by collecting telemetry, generating alerts and enforcing containment. Those capabilities remain necessary, but AI makes the timing problem worse. When attackers can instantly generate variants and alter payloads, the observable surface of malware becomes unstable. Waiting for recognizable signatures, known indicators or post-execution alerts to make trust decisions is too late. Moving from software identity to software behavior: The next step is adding behavioral verification to existing software supply chain controls. A stronger model evaluates behavior before execution wherever possible, especially for high-risk artifacts such as third-party packages, installers, scripts, containers, CI/CD outputs and AI-generated code. The practical question should change from 'Do we recognize this?' to 'Is this behavior authorized?' That requires assessing actions such as privilege escalation, persistence, credential access and unexpected network communication in context. Years ago, Zero Trust changed security by rejecting implicit trust in networks, devices and identities. The same principle now needs to apply to software execution. No artifact should be trusted solely because of its origin, signature or reputation. In a Zero Trust for Code model, trust is not inherited from supply chain evidence alone. Those controls remain foundational, but they do not answer the final execution question. Most enterprises can answer what is inside software, where it came from and how it was built better than they could five years ago. The harder question is determining what it can do once it runs. (Author: Ken Ammon, CEO, CodeHunter; Published: July 13, 2026)

288e0fc047fd.text: Microsoft released guidance explaining its Windows servicing model through comments by Chris Morrissey, Senior Director of Communications. The guide covers monthly security updates, preview releases, hotpatch updates, and feature rollout mechanisms. Patch Tuesday (Monthly): Released on the second Tuesday each month, these cumulative updates combine security and non-security content. As Morrissey explained, 'optional non-security preview updates...give IT teams and early adopters an opportunity to validate upcoming fixes' before inclusion in regular monthly releases. Optional Preview Updates: Released during the fourth week of monthly cycles, these allow testing of upcoming fixes and early access to selected features on the latest Windows versions. Hotpatch Updates: Security-only fixes that install without requiring device restarts. A quarterly baseline update (delivered as a regular monthly update) requires a restart and installs all new features; the following two monthly updates can install restart-free. Out-of-Band Releases: Emergency updates deployed outside regular schedules to address immediate security concerns or known issues. Feature Rollouts: Windows 11 receives features through annual updates, monthly patches, or Microsoft Store. Microsoft uses Controlled Feature Rollout to introduce capabilities gradually, with features typically disabled by default on managed devices. (Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer; Published: July 13, 2026)

47a2f0d6f821.text: Chip designers license blocks of circuitry from outside vendors and drop them into larger products. A single processor can carry components from a range of suppliers, each written by a company the buyer may never deal with directly. A malicious supplier can bury a hidden circuit in a working design, and that circuit can stay quiet until a specific input wakes it up. Researchers at the University of Florida built a tool aimed at this problem. Called VeriChat, it works as a conversational assistant for hardware security engineers. The system answers technical questions about chip security and runs verification tools directly on a design file that a user uploads. General chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini give confident answers that sometimes contain invented facts, and in hardware security a wrong answer can send an engineer down a costly path. The Florida team recorded one case where 'a widely used chatbot described three side-channel analysis frameworks, and one of the three was entirely fictional.' VeriChat addresses this gap with a retrieval-first design. Three agents pass work sequentially. The first rewrites user questions for search. The second pulls matching passages from a curated library of 28,221 hardware security papers and live web results. The third writes answers using only gathered evidence, declining to elaborate when support is insufficient. VeriChat's distinguishing feature is its link to verification tools. Researchers demonstrated it using a planted attack: they embedded a Trojan in an AES S-Box encryption component. The malicious circuit 'watches the data stream for one exact three-byte sequence, 0xDE, 0xAD, 0xBE' and leaks encryption keys through a status light when triggered. A user without knowledge of the hidden circuit uncovers it through conversation. VeriChat runs automated checks including syntax verification, synthesis analysis that 'flags several extra' memory elements, simulation feeding the exact trigger, and formal verification proving potential data leakage. Experienced hardware security researchers created benchmark test questions. VeriChat retrieved relevant supporting material far more frequently than baseline systems. 'A blind review by a human expert scored its factual accuracy at 87.73 percent, well ahead of the next system.' When tested with false premises and invented technologies, 'VeriChat refused to go along with the fabrications 92 percent of the time,' compared to commercial models accepting them more readily. Several limitations warrant consideration. The Trojan came from the same research team that built VeriChat, meaning they designed, planted, and discovered it -- a known-attack scenario. Unknown attacks remain untested. Scoring relies partly on AI models as judges, including GPT-4o ranking answers. The 87.73 percent accuracy means 'close to one claim in eight still comes back wrong,' requiring engineers to verify results in a field demanding absolute correctness. The broader significance addresses supply chain vulnerabilities. Hardware buyers face challenges similar to software library purchasers -- dependency on unvetted suppliers. A tool enabling engineers to question suspicious designs conversationally while running verification checks offers one approach to narrowing this security gap. (Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security; Published: July 13, 2026)

00ade71a3b7d.text: A security analysis of 14 days of server logs revealed systematic, distributed scanning targeting AI infrastructure. The researcher identified three primary threat categories: MCP Server Reconnaissance -- the scanners performed legitimate Model Context Protocol handshakes using valid JSON-RPC 2.0 calls. As the article notes: 'The scanner is not blindly requesting a URL. It is speaking the protocol.' This indicates attackers actively search for exposed MCP servers that could grant access to databases, filesystems, and internal APIs. AI Assistant Credential Harvesting -- attackers targeted configuration files from coding tools, requesting paths like /.claude/mcp.json and /.cursor/mcp.json. The use of HEAD requests suggests mature, efficient scanning operations across large host populations. LLM Endpoint Probing -- scanners searched for unauthenticated inference endpoints using OpenAI-compatible and Ollama signatures (/v1/models, /api/tags). Recommendations: Organizations should audit logs for MCP handshakes, verify AI config files aren't deployed to web roots, test for exposed LLM endpoints, review fetch-style endpoints for SSRF vulnerabilities, and enable metadata service protection on cloud platforms. (Author: Manuel Humberto Santander Pelaez; Published: 2026-07-13)

b718cf442165.text: Growing demand for compute capacity, power, cooling and low-latency connectivity is prompting organizations to reassess where AI applications run, according to CoreSite. Public cloud continues to support experimentation and rapid deployment, while colocation is increasingly used for workloads that require predictable performance, dedicated infrastructure or close proximity to cloud services and enterprise data. More than half of organizations have implemented or are upgrading AI technologies, an increase from the previous year. Generative AI, chatbots, predictive analytics and agentic AI have reached production environments at many organizations, indicating that AI deployments are moving beyond pilot projects. Hybrid environments have become the preferred location for AI and machine learning workloads, while interest in on-premises deployments continues to decline. Colocation is emerging as a preferred environment for AI workloads that require additional power capacity and direct connections to cloud platforms. Juan Font, President and CEO of CoreSite, observed that 'CIOs may not currently have accurate reporting on how widespread the usage is within their organizations' and noted growing token usage costs are prompting IT leaders to evaluate AI project ROI more carefully. Colocation gains ground: Enterprises are expanding colocation's role within their infrastructure, deploying web applications, HR systems, security workloads and augmented AI applications in these environments. Organizations increased public cloud deployments of mobile applications, websites, chatbots and content delivery services compared with the previous year. Some workloads migrated away from public cloud as organizations reassessed placement based on performance, security and infrastructure needs. Organizations prioritize security, uptime and predictable performance when selecting colocation providers, valuing direct cloud connections, scalable infrastructure and support for AI systems' power and cooling requirements. Connectivity becomes a priority: Direct connectivity between enterprise infrastructure and major cloud providers has become important for hybrid deployments. Seventy-nine percent of IT leaders indicated that 'native, direct cloud connections are a very important capability for colocation providers.' These connections enable lower-latency cloud access, reduce public internet reliance and streamline data movement between enterprise and cloud environments. Organizations increasingly evaluate provider ecosystems combining cloud platforms, network carriers, AI services, security products and managed services supporting workloads across multiple infrastructure environments. (Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security; Published: July 13, 2026)

0c3b3d34fc56.text: The provided webpage is primarily a navigation and header structure for the SANS Internet Storm Center. No substantial article body text is present -- the page consists mainly of: Navigation menu items (Diaries, Podcasts, Jobs, Data sections); Links to resources like TCP/UDP port activity, SSH scanning data, and threat feeds; References to Johannes Ullrich's SANS classes; Footer information with social media links and copyright notice. The actual podcast content or detailed commentary for the 'ISC Stormcast' episode is not included in the extracted webpage content provided. (Handler on Duty: Guy Bruneau; Threat Level: Green; Published: Monday, July 13th, 2026)

8efbd25eb924.text: OpenAI has temporarily removed usage restrictions for its GPT-5.6 Sol model following a surge in demand over a 48-hour period. The company eliminated the standard five-hour usage cap for Plus, Pro, and Business plan subscribers while issuing a one-time usage reset for all users. OpenAI product lead Tibo announced the changes on X, stating: 'temporarily removing the 5 hour usage limit restriction for all Plus, Business and Pro plans.' The model typically tracks messages and cloud-based tasks against shared usage limits with rolling five-hour windows. By removing this restriction temporarily, users can work continuously without hitting the threshold that previously forced them to pause. Additionally, OpenAI is optimizing GPT-5.6 Sol's efficiency to reduce token consumption. This improvement allows the model to 'take you further' before reaching usage limits, though it doesn't make the service completely unlimited. The changes address increased demand for coding and agentic work capabilities, though the exact technical methods behind the efficiency improvements remain undisclosed. (Author: Mayank Parmar; Published: July 12, 2026)

d953f645abe7.text: Microsoft has cautioned that customers should expect more security patches going forward due to AI-powered vulnerability detection. Pavan Davuluri, executive vice president for Windows + Devices, stated: 'As AI helps defenders discover more issues, customers will see a higher volume of security updates included in each security release.' Davuluri's announcement explained that Microsoft is leveraging artificial intelligence to identify software vulnerabilities more effectively through internal process changes. He noted that customers utilizing Microsoft's automated patching tools will be better equipped to manage the increased patch volume. The executive positioned investment in automated patching solutions as justified because the expanded patch releases improve overall security outcomes. According to Davuluri: 'By applying AI across security analysis, we can identify patterns faster, prioritize risk and scale vulnerability discovery across the Windows codebase.' Microsoft employs a tool called the multi-model agentic scanning harness (MDASH), which incorporates multiple AI models, including third-party vulnerability discovery systems. The infrastructure includes dedicated cloud resources for scanning operations. The process involves a scanner pipeline that examines critical binaries and validates candidates using multi-model analysis across different model families, followed by a separate Windows-specific validation pipeline that eliminates false positives before findings reach engineering teams. Davuluri emphasized that this approach 'handle a larger volume of potential vulnerabilities and shortens the review window for new ones, shrinking the attack window for zero-day exploits.' Oracle has similarly announced that AI-driven bug detection will enable it to add monthly critical patch releases to its existing quarterly security update schedule. The article notes that while increased vulnerability discovery is beneficial, IT administrators face a practical challenge: expanded patch windows haven't materialized proportionally. VMware has responded by introducing 'Express Patches' that release independently and more frequently than standard product updates, deployable in any sequence without requiring prior upgrades. (Author: Simon Sharwood, APAC Editor; Published: Friday, July 10, 2026)

7417a44137e0.text: A former ransomware negotiator at incident response firm DigitalMint has been sentenced to 70 months in prison after admitting he shared confidential client information with the BlackCat ransomware group and later helped carry out ransomware attacks. Prosecutors say Angelo Martino, 41, abused his role at DigitalMint beginning in April 2023 by providing BlackCat operators with sensitive information gathered during ransomware negotiations. The information included victims' negotiating positions, insurance policy limits, and internal assessments, helping the group maximize ransom demands against five organizations. 'He was hired to help victims in a moment of crisis. Instead, Martino betrayed them, fed their confidential negotiating positions to ransomware criminals, and helped squeeze them for more money,' stated U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida. Alongside Martino, Ryan Goldberg of Georgia and Kevin Martin of Texas were also involved in the scheme. All three worked in the cybersecurity industry and used their positions and expertise to support the criminal activity. Martino and Martin worked as ransomware negotiators at DigitalMint, while Goldberg was an incident response manager at Sygnia Cybersecurity Services. In one case, the conspirators received about $1.2 million in Bitcoin after a victim paid a ransom. The Justice Department said the money was divided among the participants and later laundered through cryptocurrency transactions designed to hide its origin. Federal investigators also seized more than $10 million in cryptocurrency and other assets linked to Martino. The forfeited property included luxury vehicles, a fishing boat, and a food truck. A restitution hearing will determine how much he must repay victims. Martino pleaded guilty on April 14 to a one-count information charging him with conspiring to interfere with interstate commerce through extortion. On May 1, his co-conspirators, Kevin Martin and Ryan Goldberg, were each sentenced to 48 months in prison for their roles in the conspiracy. In late 2023, law enforcement disrupted the BlackCat/ALPHV ransomware group by seizing control of its data leak site. (Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security; Published: July 13, 2026)

057067c4c4e8.text: Thirty-seven cybersecurity-related merger and acquisition deals were announced in June 2026, according to SecurityWeek's M&A tracking. Major Deals: 1Password acquires Apono -- The password and access management provider purchased Israel-based Apono for a reported $250-$300 million. Apono specializes in just-in-time access governance for humans, machines, and AI agents. Accenture acquires majority stake in Dragos, full ownership of runZero and NetRise -- These transactions total $4.175 billion and create an integrated operational technology/industrial cybersecurity platform for critical infrastructure operators. Cisco acquires WideField Security -- The California-based identity threat detection firm strengthens Splunk's Agentic SOC capabilities. This represents Cisco's third security acquisition in 2026. Databricks to acquire Panther Labs -- The data intelligence company acquired the San Francisco cloud-native SIEM and AI SOC platform, expanding its security lakehouse strategy. F5 acquires SurePath AI -- The Denver startup specialized in network-based shadow AI detection, supporting F5's newly launched AI Security Platform. Rubrik acquires Strata -- The Colorado identity orchestration company enables Rubrik's new Identity Continuity feature for automatic failover during cyber incidents. SailPoint acquires Entro -- Completed acquisition of the Tel Aviv-based non-human identity and credentials security specialist for approximately $200 million. Additional Transactions: Twenty-seven additional cybersecurity M&A deals were announced, involving companies across various specializations including GRC, SASE, identity management, and security consulting services. (Author: Eduard Kovacs; Published: July 13, 2026, 8:20 AM ET)

d6909d71333d.text: Attackers targeting Microsoft cloud tenants have developed a technique to evade detection by spoofing OAuth client IDs during account enumeration attacks. By using fake application identifiers in authentication requests, threat actors can probe for valid credentials without leaving traces in sign-in logs. Proofpoint researchers demonstrated that when attackers submit false client IDs to Microsoft's OAuth 2.0 token endpoint, Entra ID responds differently depending on the identifier type. A spoofed client ID leaves the application name field blank in logs, which allows detection systems tuned to specific applications to miss the activity entirely. The technique enables attackers to confirm valid username-password pairs using error code AADSTS700016, which indicates an unrecognized application identifier. This response reveals successful credentials without generating a sign-in event that defenders would typically monitor. Campaign Details: Proofpoint tracked two separate campaigns: UNK_pyreq2323 (January 2026) -- Used over 700,000 spoofed client IDs generated from the Exchange Online application prefix, impacting 1 million accounts across 4,000 tenants. UNK_OutFlareAZ (December 2025-March 2026) -- Deployed 3.7 million randomized UUIDs, reaching 2 million users. Defensive Implications: Experts emphasize that 'a successful sign-in event should no longer be treated as the definitive source of truth when determining whether credentials have been compromised.' Organizations should investigate blank application IDs and AADSTS700016 errors as potential indicators of client ID spoofing attacks. (Author: Mirko Zorz, Director of Content, Help Net Security; Published: July 13, 2026)

7bdb6d483791.text: Progress Software notified customers on July 10 of 'a credible external security threat targeting Progress ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers.' ShareFile is the company's enterprise file-sharing service, while Storage Zone Controllers enable private data storage for customers. The company initially stated it had no evidence of unauthorized access to accounts or data but confirmed temporarily disabling access. Customers were instructed to manually shut down their Storage Zone Controller servers. By July 12 at 5 p.m. ET, Progress restored cloud service access for affected customers. However, the company mandated that Storage Zone Controllers remain offline during its investigation. Progress stated: 'At this time, we have no evidence of unauthorized access to any ShareFile customer account or data.' The company launched both internal and external security investigations but provided limited details about threat detection or resolution timelines. Some users speculated the incident involved recently disclosed vulnerabilities or zero-day exploits, though Progress neither confirmed nor denied these claims. This marks another security incident for Progress, following the 2023 MOVEit Transfer breach and an April 2026 critical vulnerability in MOVEit Automation. (Author: Kevin Poireault, Reporter at Infosecurity Magazine; Published: July 13, 2026)

f88755c10224.text: Security researchers at Hudson Rock discovered that attackers claiming to represent 'All Egyptian Cyber Warriors' compromised the Argentine Football Association's systems, likely motivated by frustration over Egypt's World Cup elimination. The breach traced back to an infostealer malware infection from September 8, 2025, on a device belonging to an AFA software developer employed there for nearly a decade. Attackers either retained stolen credentials dormant for months or specifically sought them after Egypt's controversial loss to Argentina in the tournament's round of 16. Once authenticated, the threat actors gained 'profound administrative control,' including access to phpMyAdmin panels, database root access, training facility management portals, media systems, and competition management infrastructure. Hudson Rock identified critical security weaknesses: weak, reusable passwords across multiple systems, and some credentials stored in plaintext rather than hashed. Stolen data advertised on cybercrime forums included staff information, professional club details, email addresses, phone numbers, and user roles. The AFA acknowledged the incident Friday, stating: 'There is a possibility that our account has been subject to unauthorized access. We are currently working to clarify the situation and implement necessary security measures.' Hudson Rock characterized this as 'a textbook example of how devastating a single, unmitigated infostealer infection can be.' (Author: Connor Jones; Published: Monday, July 13, 2026 at 13:02 UTC)

131d29395787.text: A critical vulnerability in RabbitMQ (CVE-2026-57219, CVSS 8.7) allows unauthenticated attackers to retrieve the broker's OAuth client secret from an obsolete management endpoint. This flaw enables potential full system compromise. The vulnerability affects RabbitMQ deployments configured with OAuth 2/OIDC authentication through providers like Auth0, Azure AD, Keycloak, or UAA. Attackers accessing the management port can 'fetch it, then...impersonate the broker to the identity provider and obtain an administrator token,' granting control over users, messages, queues, and settings. The flaw was introduced in version 3.13.0 in early 2024 and patched in versions 4.3.0, 4.2.6, 4.1.11, 4.0.20, and 3.13.15. A secondary vulnerability (CVE-2026-57221, CVSS 5.3) allows authenticated users to enumerate queues and exchanges, potentially enabling reconnaissance for future attacks. Recommendations: Organizations should immediately update deployments, restrict management interface access, implement network segmentation, and rotate OAuth secrets. No in-the-wild exploitation has been documented. (Author: Ionut Arghire; Published: July 13, 2026, updated July 14, 2026)

09e3b1d0e1f6.text: Meta has filed a patent application (US 2026/0182881) for an AI system capable of monitoring voice throughout the day to analyze emotional states and maintain timestamped logs of detected feelings paired with contextual data like location and activity. The system analyzes speech patterns -- including tone, pace, sighs, and laughter -- to generate emotional assessments. As described in the filing, it can produce summaries like: 'You sigh most frequently before bed, and you're happiest when with friends.' Key Technical Features: The technology extends beyond voice analysis to incorporate biometric signals (pupil size, blink rate, eye moisture) and device usage patterns (posts viewed, screen time, app-switching speed). The patent also includes a fitness coaching component that adjusts encouragement based on detected emotional state. Regulatory Context: The EU's AI Act has already banned emotion-reading AI in workplace and school settings since February 2025, with fines reaching €35 million or 7% of global revenue. Critics note that emotional expression varies significantly across individuals and cultures, questioning the scientific validity of such systems. Amazon's similar Halo wearable, which featured emotion detection from voice alone, was discontinued in 2023 following privacy concerns raised by Senator Amy Klobuchar. (Author: Swati Khandelwal; Published: July 13, 2026)

2b2e78dcad9f.text: A few days ago, I was sitting with the CISO of a Fortune 50 company, walking through how his security team was thinking about AI agents in the SOC... [Full text retrieved: discusses Kahneman's System 1/System 2 framework applied to SOC design, citing analysis of 25 million enterprise alerts finding 98% can be resolved autonomously with under 2% requiring human review, and that a 450K-alert/year enterprise can expect 54 real threats hidden in low-severity alerts.
