Argues the 'fast brain' (purpose-built forensic AI, not a general LLM) should investigate 100% of signals and hand off assembled cases to the 'slow brain' (Claude, Codex, Cursor) for judgment-based work like case analysis, detection engineering, and threat hunting. Identifies two failure modes: keeping analysts doing System-1 triage work, and deploying frontier AI directly against raw alerts (System 2 doing System 1's job, more expensively). Concludes that owning the investigation/knowledge layer in-house (rather than via an MDR provider) is a prerequisite for making an AI analyst copilot useful, since every investigated alert and tuned rule compounds into a smarter autonomous layer.]

6092ae9b45ac.text: Cybersecurity researchers have identified an intrusion where an unknown threat actor deployed an AI-generated PowerShell script for Active Directory enumeration. Huntress researchers Jevon Ang and Dray Agha discovered that the script looked for the Domain Controller and mapped users, computers, and domains, before creating a directory and exporting out a number of files. The attack began with the threat actor establishing Remote Desktop Protocol access using pre-compromised credentials on a domain-joined Windows Server, staging tools in C:\ProgramData\ during early June 2026. Researchers identified several indicators suggesting AI generation: the script's title '100% Working AD Information Gathering Script - FULLY FIXED' suggested iterative refinement with a large language model, placeholder strings, over-engineered code featuring multiple Domain Controller discovery methods, and colorized console output. The PowerShell script employed a five-step cascading fallback mechanism for reconnaissance, harvesting AD users, computers, groups, OUs and trust relationships into a staging directory. About 30 minutes later, the attacker deployed s5cmd and SharpShares to identify accessible data repositories; data was converted to CSVs, archived, and exfiltrated along with an HTML-formatted AD Inventory Report likely generated as an unsolicited LLM addition. Huntress noted the underlying attack chain still resembles the tried-and-tested smash-and-grab playbook, but AI augmentation prioritizes aggression and speed over stealth. A cited Sygnia report described an AI-assisted AWS cloud attack progressing from initial access to broad compromise in about 72 hours by chaining weaknesses across application services, AWS resources, source-control repos, CI/CD workflows, runtime components and data stores, including disruptive actions like denying S3 access, zeroing ECS capacity, blocking network ACLs, and purging SQS queues. Sygnia's conclusion: AI didn't introduce new techniques, but reduced the time and effort to operationalize them across a complex environment.

a916db7e9969.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is warning that attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities in the iCagenda and Balbooa Forms extensions for Joomla to achieve remote code execution through arbitrary file uploads. The agency has categorized the flaws as maximum priority, ordering federal agencies to apply available security updates and/or mitigations within three days. CVE-2026-48939 affects the iCagenda extension (used for event registration and calendar creation). This arbitrary file upload flaw allows attackers to upload malicious files, including PHP scripts, leading to data theft, web shell installation, and complete website compromise. CISA warns that iCagenda contains an unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type vulnerability that allows the upload of arbitrary files in the file attachment feature, ultimately resulting in PHP code upload and execution. CVE-2026-56291 impacts the Balbooa Forms extension (a drag-and-drop form builder). This vulnerability similarly enables uploading dangerous file types and executable files, resulting in remote code execution and website takeover. According to mySites.guru, both flaws were exploited in automated attacks before patches were released. iCagenda attacks occurred hours before version 4.0.8 launched (June 15-16), and Balbooa Forms was exploited as a zero-day since July 8, one day before the vendor released version 2.4.1 (July 9). Website administrators should verify whether their Joomla installations use these extensions and apply the available fixes immediately.

78d6d9512ed6.text: This Huntress incident analysis (by Harlan Carvey and Lindsey O'Donnell-Welch) examines a June 2026 breach at a tech sector organization where threat actors conducted unusually extensive post-compromise modifications after gaining initial access through SQL injection. The attack began with malicious activity on a Microsoft SQL Server instance; investigation revealed the threat actor exploited a SQL injection vulnerability in a web application with improperly validated user input, gaining access to an IIS web server running on the same endpoint. Following exploitation, the attacker executed tasklist /svc to identify running processes/services, exfiltrated command output to an external domain, enabled Terminal Services/RDP, created a new administrative user account (adminweb2$), added it to the local Administrators group, authenticated with it, and attempted to disable Windows Defender. The attacker installed BadIIS modules (malicious IIS components) via appcmd.exe to facilitate SEO fraud and other attacks, deployed XMRig cryptocurrency mining software, hid miner files using attrib.exe, created service persistence via nssm.exe, installed CnCrypt Protect for defense evasion, and downloaded multiple PowerShell scripts and batch files. The breadth of environmental modifications distinguished this incident from a quick smash-and-grab; the attacker methodically established infrastructure for prolonged access and concealment. Huntress recommends organizations maintain accurate asset inventories, reduce attack surface through application management, restrict access and enforce MFA, keep systems updated and monitored, and investigate root causes when incidents occur.

b0071678f0aa.text: CVE-2008-4128: Cisco IOS CSRF Vulnerabilities. Overview: CVE-2008-4128 affects Cisco IOS 12.4 running on 871 Integrated Services Routers, allowing remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands through cross-site request forgery (CSRF). Vulnerability Details: The HTTP Administration component contains multiple CSRF weaknesses exploitable via: 1) a 'show privilege' command directed to /level/15/exec/-  URI, 2) an 'alias exec' command sent to /level/15/exec/-/configure/http URI. Severity Ratings: CVSS 3.1: 4.3 (Medium) - AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N; CVSS 2.0: 9.3 (High) with user interaction required; CWE-352 (Cross-Site Request Forgery). Affected Products: Vendor Cisco, Product IOS version 12.4, Hardware 871 Integrated Services Router. Timeline: Published September 18, 2008; Public Date September 17, 2008; CISA KEV Added July 13, 2026; Due Date July 16, 2026. Exploitation Status: confirmed as actively exploited with 80% confidence (CISA assessment); public exploits available (Exploit-DB IDs 6476 and 6477).

279c51402190.text: Lumen Technologies has announced Lumen Defender Advanced Managed Detection and Response (AMDR) for Palo Alto Networks Cortex XSIAM. Attackers are increasingly operating earlier in the lifecycle while AI is accelerating threat speed. This expanded service brings together Lumen's managed detection and response capabilities and Lumen Defender Threat Feed powered by Black Lotus Labs network-embedded threat intelligence with Cortex XSIAM's AI-driven SOC platform to help enterprises modernize security operations, reduce alert fatigue, and accelerate detection and response. Jim Fowler (Lumen CTPO): 'Cyber defense is a speed game, and the network is where threats often show up first... With Palo Alto Networks, we're again raising the bar for security by expanding access to our high-value network threat intelligence and putting it to work through modern, automated operations.' A standout feature is integration of Black Lotus Labs threat intelligence, derived from activity observed across the Lumen network rather than endpoint/log telemetry, enabling detection of pre-compromise reconnaissance/staging before attacks reach customer environments. Simone Gammeri (Palo Alto Networks Chief Partnership Officer): 'Combining Lumen's network-level threat intelligence with Cortex XSIAM empowers organizations to proactively defend against sophisticated threats at machine-speed and scale their security operations.' Lumen Defender AMDR for Cortex XSIAM is designed for: reduced alert fatigue via smart grouping and high-confidence alerts; accelerated threat scoping/triaging; visibility into pre-compromise activity; faster decision-making with threat context; standardized evidence-based investigation/response; less reliance on specialized in-house SOC talent; lower operational complexity via agentic workflows; increased confidence in security coverage; and simplified pricing with fewer tools/contracts/handoffs.

325d9a575c0a.text: Microsoft announced that passkeys will become the default authentication method in Microsoft Entra ID, phasing out SMS and voice authentication due to increasing security threats in the AI era. Timeline of Changes: September 1, 2026 - Passkeys become default; users enabled for SMS/voice are auto-enabled for passkey registration. February 1, 2027 - Microsoft discontinues native SMS and voice authentication delivery. After February 1, 2027 - Users must register passkeys before signing in; no opt-out option. Why the change: AI-enabled phishing campaigns reach click-through rates as high as 54% compared to traditional methods at roughly 12%. Passkeys use public-key cryptography rather than shared secrets, making them phishing-resistant by design. Migration path: organizations should identify users currently using SMS/voice authentication, plan passkey rollout (synced or device-bound options), launch registration campaigns, and prepare user communications. Fallback option: organizations with regulatory or technical requirements for SMS/voice can select third-party telecom providers through the Microsoft Security Store beginning October 30, 2026, though they'll assume associated costs. Authored by Nadim Abdo, Corporate Vice President, Identity and Network Access Engineering, Microsoft.

704c0ac16fce.text: Cybercriminals are leveraging large language models to enhance phishing and malware campaigns, producing emails with fewer obvious errors and more authentic business tones. However, Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks present a greater challenge, relying entirely on social engineering to manipulate employees into executing attackers' requests, such as fraudulent fund transfers. Kaspersky has developed specialized detection technology targeting AI-generated BEC emails. The technology exploits how LLMs function: they predict likely word sequences rather than composing naturally. Since attackers typically use widely available AI models, the detection system identifies BEC-specific phrases and recognizes machine-generated text patterns, allowing the security solution to identify and block attempted BEC attacks before employees encounter them. The technology currently supports detection in eight languages: English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and Turkish. Implementation: the AI-generated BEC detection technology is integrated into Kaspersky Security for Mail Server, specifically within Kaspersky Secure Mail Gateway. The feature is available in the KSMS Plus license following the recent KSMG 3.1 update. Author: Roman Dedenok.

f77a9963719c.text: Since June 26, 2026, an unattributed threat actor has published at least 292 deceptive brand-impersonation GitHub pages and repositories mimicking legitimate software and security tooling vendors, including a fake Arctic Wolf GitHub page. Each repository hosts a marketing-styled README with a concealed download link routing victims to a malicious 'secure download' page. The payload is a pure smash-and-grab in-memory infostealer with a 41-entry cryptocurrency wallet path table and 19+ targeted browser names. Stolen data is packaged into a ZIP and exfiltrated to a C2 server at 193.143.1.131 (Proton66, AS198953, Russia). Arctic Wolf assessed with high confidence the stealer shares a codebase with BoryptGrab (1,638 matched functions, BinDiff similarity 0.40, 94% function overlap), though five architectural divergences (different secondary payload delivery, different Chrome App-Bound Encryption bypass method, raw Winsock vs WinINet exfiltration, different logging style, different disk artifact footprint) suggest either heavily refactored code or a distinct operator/affiliate using shared tooling — Arctic Wolf assessed only roughly-even/low confidence that this is the same threat actor as prior public reporting. Attack chain: throwaway GitHub accounts impersonate brands; the Arctic Wolf lure repo 'Arctic-Wolf-Security/.github' (created June 30, 2026) presented a fake 'managed-detection' onboarding checklist linking to a threat-actor-controlled domain. The fake download page is a single templated HTML/JS artifact reused across all impersonated brands, regenerating a uniquely-named ZIP/executable roughly every 60 seconds. The archive contains a signed, notarized-style legitimate WinGUP updater (renamed) plus a trojanized libcurl.dll; the legitimate exe side-loads the DLL, which decodes an embedded blob into a next-stage PE and executes the stealer entirely in memory via COM/OLE reflective techniques, without writing to disk. The stealer runs eleven theft modules: system fingerprint/geolocation, installed app enumeration, browser credential theft (Chrome App-Bound Encryption bypass), Telegram data collection, Discord token extraction, Meta Max credential theft, Steam account theft via process memory, cryptocurrency wallet theft, file grabbing, screenshot capture, and Windows Credential Manager dump; it establishes no persistence and performs no anti-analysis checks but leaves a staging folder under %TEMP%. Delivery infrastructure includes ~78 active *.github.io redirector accounts, ~20 distribution/TDS domains, and six bulletproof-hosted 'GitHub Download' servers. Targeting is opportunistic/search-driven across security tooling, fintech, crypto, dev tools, secure email, macOS utilities, and gaming software, not sector-specific. Recommendations include downloading only from vendor-verified sources, treating sparse-history .github repos as suspicious, blocking traffic to 193.143.1.131/24, hunting for libcurl.dll side-loading by renamed WinGUP executables, alerting on plaintext POST /upload with X-Filename/X-Size headers, detecting Chrome App-Bound Encryption bypass patterns, and rotating credentials/wallet keys on compromised hosts. Arctic Wolf says detection/telemetry coverage for these techniques is confirmed in its Aurora Endpoint Security and Aurora MDR offerings.

2922f655ac86.text: A patch management strategy is a structured approach to identifying, testing, and deploying software updates across your environment. Most security incidents don't start with a sophisticated attack; they start with a known vulnerability that never got patched. IT teams typically manage OS patches, third-party application patches, and firmware/driver updates. Security patches vs bug fixes vs feature updates differ in urgency and testing needs. 7 Steps: 1) Establish a comprehensive asset inventory (agent-based and agentless scanning). 2) Define a policy with clear ownership and SLAs (maintenance windows, approval workflows, remediation timelines by severity, rollback procedures). 3) Prioritize updates based on risk, not release date (CVSS, EPSS, asset criticality, exposure, CISA KEV catalog). 4) Implement a rigorous testing phase (canary groups, phased rollouts, ring-based deployment). 5) Execute deployment with a phased rollout (pilot groups, non-critical systems, then production/critical systems last; remote workforce patching independent of VPN). 6) Verify and audit patch success (post-deployment scanning, watching for patch drift from reimaged/restored systems). 7) Track KPIs (Mean Time to Respond, patch coverage percentage, exception count, stale vulnerability count). Best practices include automating routine deployment, using a single centralized tool, prioritizing by exploitability/exposure, defined SLAs, including third-party software, consistent backup/rollback policies, and staging validation. Common pitfalls: patching everything simultaneously causing burnout/shortcuts, test/production configuration mismatches, assuming deployment equals remediation, and untracked exceptions becoming forgotten vulnerabilities. Compliance mapping: NIST SP 800-40 (federal lifecycle guidance, risk-based prioritization), PCI DSS Requirement 6 (timely security patch installation), HIPAA Security Rule (procedures against malicious software interpreted to include patching). Author: Brenda Buckman.

2a2c442dfe62.text:
Suzanne Smalley reports:
The U.S. government on Monday sanctioned a VPN provider and its Ukrainian administrator for abetting ransomware gangs behind attacks on American municipalities, hospitals, schools and businesses.
First VPN Service (1VPNS) provided ransomware groups with tools to “hide their identities, disguise malicious software, and evade detection — enabling attacks that have caused billions of dollars in losses to U.S. critical infrastructure providers,” according to a Treasury Department press release.
The administrator, Dmytro Rashevskyi, used fake identities “to buy infrastructure from companies that might otherwise refuse to do business with him because of complaints of abuse from internet service providers about illegal activity originating from 1VPNS servers,” the Treasury said.
Read more at The Record.

dc8d9946fba8.text: Nihon Kotsu, Japan's largest taxi operator, experienced a cyberattack over the weekend that forced the company to shut down critical infrastructure. The incident involved malware infection and unauthorized external access to internal systems. Impact on Operations: the company's taxi dispatch system remains offline, along with car hire services, web booking, reservation management, and telephone dispatch services. The firm serves approximately 18,228 employees and operates 8,558 taxis plus over 2,000 chauffeur vehicles, generating roughly $1 billion in annual revenue. Response Measures: Nihon Kotsu immediately implemented emergency disconnection procedures to prevent further damage, engaged external cybersecurity experts to investigate and recover systems, and advised customers to use the GO taxi app or visit nearby taxi stands instead. Data Breach Concerns: while no confirmed data leak has been verified, the company is investigating the possibility and promised updates if new information emerges; customers were warned against opening suspicious attachments or links in communications claiming to originate from Nihon Kotsu. Ongoing Developments: initially, no ransomware groups claimed responsibility; a later update indicated that AiLock claimed the attack and threatened to leak stolen data 'soon.' Author: Bill Toulas.

f5b9ed5af5c9.text: Jscrambler disclosed that threat actors published a malicious version of its npm package, downloaded approximately 1,500 times over a two-hour window before being removed. The compromised versions (8.14, 8.16, 8.17, and 8.20) contained information-stealing malware that executed during installation. The malicious code targeted extensive categories of sensitive data including: developer credentials and secrets; cloud credentials (AWS, Azure, GCP); AI tool configurations (Claude, Cursor, Windsurf); cryptocurrency wallets and seed phrases; browser data and messaging app credentials. Security firm Socket detected the compromise and revealed the malware used strong encryption via ChaCha20-Poly1305, making reverse-engineering difficult. Jscrambler stated the breach resulted from 'compromised npm publishing credentials,' which have since been revoked. The company released safe version 8.22 and deprecated affected packages. Developers using malicious versions should treat environments as compromised and rotate all credentials and secrets. Author: Bill Toulas.

8a961523a90f.text: Security researchers have identified a new macOS information-stealing malware called CrashStealer that impersonates Apple's crash-reporting system. The malware was first tracked in May during development stages and observed in active attacks by early July. CrashStealer targets sensitive data including: Keychain credentials and stored secrets; browser passwords and cookies from Chromium and Firefox; over 80 cryptocurrency wallet extensions (MetaMask, Phantom, Coinbase Wallet, etc.); 14 password managers including 1Password, Bitwarden, and LastPass; files from Documents and Downloads folders. The malware employs multiple social engineering techniques, displaying a fake macOS password prompt to convince users that they are authorizing a legitimate system operation, requiring administrator access, specifically targeting the Keychain. Researchers at Jamf discovered the payload arrives through a signed and Apple-notarized installer ('Werkbit Setup') that bypasses Gatekeeper security protections. The malware then re-signs itself for persistence by rewriting code-signature data, altering file hashes while keeping code unchanged. The delivery occurs through a fake software website gated behind meeting PINs, suggesting targeted campaigns rather than broad distribution. CrashStealer distinguishes itself from similar families through its client-side encryption mechanism and native C++ implementation, using AES-256-GCM encryption before exfiltrating stolen data to command-and-control servers. Author: Bill Toulas.

69317a73e38e.text:
Fatima Abdullahi reports:
The Federal High Court in Abuja has fixed July 21, 2026, for the arraignment of Zenith Bank Plc and three other defendants over allegations of illegally accessing and disclosing the confidential financial records of Makers Island Company Limited.
The other defendants are Oluwaseyi Famousa, Paul Oku and Yesu-Felix Abosede Alice.
Justice Hauwa Yilwa scheduled the arraignment on Monday after counsel representing the Inspector-General of Police informed the court that the defendants would face an eight-count charge bordering on alleged cybercrime and unauthorised access to banking data.
Read more at CrimeFighters NG.
Criminally charging a bank? That’s something we haven’t seen often here.

bfbf4a36c59d.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a new macOS information stealer called CrashStealer that harvests sensitive data from compromised systems.

Unlike other information stealers built on AppleScript droppers or Objective-C-based wrappers, CrashStealer is implemented in native C++, according to Jamf Threat Labs. Security researcher Thijs Xhaflaire explained that it "validates the victim's login password locally before harvesting" and "collects broadly across browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, password managers, and the keychain."

The malware is distributed via a signed and Apple-notarized dropper presented as "Werkbit.app" on a disk image. Both the image and binary carry a valid developer ID ("Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV)"), allowing the software to pass Gatekeeper security checks.

The disk image originates from werkbit[.]io, registered in June 2026. Downloads are gated behind a meeting PIN, restricting access to specific visitors.

Upon launch, the "veltod" executable contacts a GitHub repository (github.com/mgothiclove) to retrieve a "sys.cache" file containing a curl command that downloads a shell script. This script fetches the next payload ("CrashReporter.dmg") to the "/tmp" directory.

The malware establishes persistence as a LaunchAgent, displays a password prompt for local credential validation, and then harvests:

- Browser credentials from Chrome, Brave, Edge, Opera, Vivaldi, and others
- Approximately 80 cryptocurrency wallet extensions
- 14 password managers including 1Password, Bitwarden, and LastPass
- Files from ~/Documents and ~/Downloads directories

Data is encrypted with AES-GCM and exfiltrated to 179.43.166[.]242.

Jamf researchers noted the operation demonstrates "real care" through its "signed and notarized dropper that clears Gatekeeper," distinguishing it from typical commodity stealers through client-side encryption and analysis-resistance techniques.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan; Published: July 13, 2026)

dd7c88d4cc4d.text:
Google and Microsoft have pulled ModHeader, a popular header-editing extension with roughly 1.6 million installs across Chrome and Edge, after researchers found a hidden browsing-history collector built into its official store version.

The collector was dormant. An empty allow-list kept it switched off, and no proof has emerged that it ever gathered or sent a single browsing domain.

The analysis came from Stripe OLT, a UK security firm, which checked the code against Google's own Web Store signature and confirmed the collector shipped inside the genuine extension, not a counterfeit.

Its review covers the Chrome build and its roughly 900,000 users; third-party trackers put another 700,000 or so on Edge. Microsoft pulled the Edge listing on July 3, and Google removed the Chrome one a week later, on July 10.

Version 7.0.18 (extension ID idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj) still edits HTTP headers as advertised. The same minified background code also contains a second system. On first run, it builds a device fingerprint and loads a hardcoded encryption key. As you browse, it takes the domain from each page you open, encrypts it, and stores it locally, up to 1000 distinct domains.

Once a day, a scheduler bundles the encrypted list with your fingerprint, posts it to api.stanfordstudies[.]com, and wipes the local copy. The upload time is offset per install, so browsers running it would not all beacon at once if the collector were switched on. Separate teardowns, by HackIndex on version 7.0.18 and researcher Yunus Aydin on 7.0.17, describe the same pipeline.

The collector runs only if your browser matches an entry on an internal allow-list, and that list ships empty. The check fails every time, so the pipeline stops before it collects a single domain. Populating that list is a small change, with no new permissions and no click from you, delivered as a routine update. The hardcoded key, the endpoint URL, the scheduler, and the storage logic are already on the machine.

Not everything was asleep. On install, update, and uninstall, the extension pinged a second domain, extensions-hub[.]com, with the product, version, and browser. And a script that runs on every page had already logged real request metadata to local storage in plain text, so that piece had clearly been running.

Automated checkers had rated ModHeader low risk, some as high as 95 out of 100. Each part of the design can frustrate a different kind of check. The data is encrypted, so a scanner sees ciphertext. The upload is gated off, so a sandbox sees nothing leave.

The malicious code is minified into a legitimate codebase. The endpoints had no established malicious reputation to flag. And a signed, popular extension reads as trusted. A store signature proves where a file came from, not what it does.

Stripe OLT tied the domains to real, maintained infrastructure. stanfordstudies[.]com has no link to Stanford; it is a repurposed old domain fronting an OpenSearch back end, while extensions-hub[.]com is set up for advertising.

The two API endpoints resolved to the same Amazon server at the time of analysis, which fits one operator without proving it. A handful of weak signals point loosely toward a Chinese-speaking operator: a Simplified Chinese locale, a "salt" marker written with the character 盐, and a China-origin mail provider. The researchers name no group, and neither do we.

The warning signs came earlier. ModHeader drew complaints for injecting ads into search results in 2023 and reportedly went ad-supported around then. Who took it over is unconfirmed, and the researchers make no claim about the original author.

ModHeader's own site still publishes an ad plan that says it collects no user data, which is hard to square with a built-in browsing-history collector, even a switched-off one. The developer has not responded publicly to the findings as of publication.

If you have ModHeader, remove it from Chrome and Edge; your browser may have disabled it already. Uninstalling clears its stored data, so the thing to double-check is that profile sync or a managed extension policy will not put it back.

If you pasted secrets into it, API keys, bearer tokens, and session cookies, rotate them, since researchers found its header-history feature storing full HTTP headers on disk.

For defenders, block and log stanfordstudies[.]com and extensions-hub[.]com at DNS and proxy, and search logs for the extension ID and any POST to api.stanfordstudies[.]com/app/log.

(Author: Swati Khandelwal; Published: July 13, 2026)

0a2a84e5502a.text:
German supermarket chain Lidl notified customers in Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands of a data breach affecting an IT service provider. The company disclosed the incident last week through notices on its support websites.

According to Lidl's statement, unauthorized individuals temporarily accessed a separately stored file containing customer information and extracted data. The company emphasized that "the online shop system itself was not affected."

Compromised data includes names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, customer numbers, and salutations. Lidl cautioned that passwords, billing/delivery addresses, and payment details may have been compromised, though customer accounts remained unaffected.

The company stated it has "no concrete evidence of data misuse" but warned customers about potential phishing and identity fraud risks.

Response measures included the service provider securing its systems, filing a police report, engaging forensic experts, and notifying data protection authorities. No information about the attackers has been disclosed.

(Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security; Published: July 13, 2026)

70c0b5364d47.text:
A misconfigured server in Budapest exposed the complete toolkit of an active three-actor phishing ecosystem, according to research from French security firm Lexfo. The Python HTTP server, left running in late April with directory listing enabled, revealed phishing configurations, credential logs, remote management installers, and operator Telegram session files.

The Primary Operator: Threat actor codemado operated an Evilginx-based adversary-in-the-middle platform targeting Microsoft 365 corporate accounts. Artifacts linked codemado to an Egyptian operator active on hacking forums since 2018. Beyond the phishing proxy, the server contained a seven-tool remote monitoring arsenal for persistence, including ScreenConnect and SimpleHelp, plus a custom bulk-mailer called MaDoO Blaster.

Two Additional Actors: The other operators surfaced through public Evilginx forks on GitHub. Mail-argenta, traced through infostealer logs containing reused credentials, appeared connected to a Nigerian individual. Saroula01 built a framework exploiting Microsoft's OAuth Device Code Flow—a legitimate feature allowing victims to authenticate on real Microsoft pages while attackers claimed tokens.

Scale of Operations: Saroula01's campaign was largest, running undetected for over a year starting June 2025. It accumulated 218 confirmed victims across 12 countries (94% corporate), with "captured tokens set to refresh automatically in the background" and recovered entries refreshed up to 25 times for sustained access.

Key Findings: All three operators used generative AI for tooling development. The research indicates the barrier to running functional AiTM campaigns has dropped substantially, with components available free on GitHub or sold on Telegram. Lexfo urged defenders to assume MFA bypass is possible and disable device code authentication where unnecessary.

(Author: Alessandro Mascellino; Published: 13 July 2026)

6ae6d909bc23.text:
Somewhere right now, a security tool is quietly finding bugs faster than any human can fix them. That's supposed to be the good news. The catch is that the attackers have the same tools, pointed the other way, and they don't file tickets.

That's the shape of this week. Trusted code turns on the people who installed it. Old bugs from last year are still landing because the fix sat in a queue too long. Fake installers, poisoned packages, systems left facing the open internet, and helpful little AI assistants running instructions that were never yours.

The gap between "patch exists" and "already exploited" keeps shrinking, and nobody's closing it. None of it is exotic. That's what wears you down. Same ordinary mistakes, just happening faster than we can keep up.

Threat of the Week: Progress urged customers to disable Windows servers running Storage Zone Controllers due to an unspecified external security threat. The company disabled affected accounts "out of an abundance of caution" while consulting with security experts. No evidence of unauthorized ShareFile access has been reported.

Top News Highlights:
Zimbra Critical Flaw: A stored cross-site scripting vulnerability in the Classic Web Client could enable arbitrary code execution through malicious emails, potentially exposing mailbox data and session information.
Jscrambler npm Compromise: Multiple package versions containing a Rust-based information stealer targeting developer secrets across Windows, macOS, and Linux systems. The activity correlates with the IronWorm group documented previously.
GigaWiper Backdoor: A post-compromise tool offering three destructive capabilities—disk wiping, Windows drive overwriting, and fake ransomware with unsaved encryption keys—plus screen recording and VNC functionality.
SHELLSTORM Operation: Over 1.4 million domains targeted using 27 WordPress plugin vulnerabilities to deploy web shells, with heaviest infections in Taiwan, the U.S., Germany, France, and the U.K.
HalluSquatting Attacks: Researchers revealed a technique exploiting AI hallucinations combined with prompt injections to trick coding assistants into executing attacker-controlled instructions through legitimately-named fabricated resources.

Additional Notable Threats: Citrix Bleed 2 exploitation leading to DragonForce ransomware deployment; Fake Chinese VPN installer dropping GoodPersonRAT malware; Malicious Braintree.Net NuGet package intercepting payment card data; RedHook Android malware incorporating wireless ADB exploitation; Helix data extortion group using voice phishing and MFA abuse targeting SharePoint.

Key Takeaway: "The pace of vulnerability discovery is changing with advances in AI making it possible to find more issues, faster, across more code," Microsoft stated regarding expanded security update volume. The organization plans to accelerate vulnerability detection and remediation cycles to reduce customer exposure windows.

(Author: Ravie Lakshmanan; Published: July 13, 2026)

d08198eba45e.text:
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) released a detailed postmortem regarding a significant security incident where a contractor publicly exposed sensitive credentials on GitHub for nearly six months before detection.

What Happened: A repository titled "Private CISA" containing 844 MB of sensitive data was discovered on May 15, 2026. Exposed materials included AWS GovCloud administrative credentials and plaintext passwords for internal systems. CISA took over 48 hours to invalidate the compromised AWS keys after being notified.

Critical Gaps Identified: CISA acknowledged several operational failures - poor notification channels: GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon reported that CISA ignored nine automated alerts about exposed credentials before external media involvement became necessary; inadequate incident response playbooks: the agency lacked procedures for handling GitHub-related security incidents; slow key rotation: system complexity and federal partner interconnections delayed credential invalidation.

Recommended Improvements: CISA emphasized the importance of establishing clear, distinct reporting channels for internal versus product-related security issues; publishing security.txt files and reporting instructions in multiple prominent locations; implementing continuous scanning of public repositories rather than quarterly reviews; maintaining mature key management capabilities.

Silver Linings: Enhanced logging and zero-trust principles enabled CISA to verify that no customer data or mission-critical information was compromised, and the leaked credentials were never used maliciously.

(Author: Brian Krebs; Published: July 13, 2026)

972b9d9a6cad.text:
The EU and the UK jointly sanctioned dozens of Russian individuals and entities, accusing Moscow of coordinating a malicious cyber ecosystem targeting Europe, its member states, and international partners.

The UK sanctioned 24 individuals and entities, while the EU imposed restrictive measures on nine individuals and four entities.

"Cybercriminals, self-proclaimed hacktivists and private companies linked to Russia, including actors operating under its instructions, direction or control, have also carried out, enabled and facilitated a wide range of malicious activities," the Council of the EU stated, condemning Russia's misuse of the cyber ecosystem targeting public services and critical infrastructure.

The Council attributed multiple cyber espionage and sabotage campaigns to the 16th Centre of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), accusing the unit of directing threat groups including Turla and targeting government networks and critical infrastructure across Europe, including combined heat and power plants in Poland.

On December 29, 2025, attackers targeted more than 30 wind and solar farms, a combined heat and power plant, and a manufacturing company in Poland with previously unseen data-wiping malware designed for operational technology systems. The operation failed to disrupt electricity generation or heat supply.

More recently, Poland blocked a cyberattack targeting the IT infrastructure of the National Centre for Nuclear Research (NCBJ), the country's leading nuclear research institute.

According to the Council, the 16th Centre has spent years targeting government networks and critical infrastructure in France, Germany, Poland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Austria, Slovakia, Romania, and Finland.

"From directing criminals to targeting businesses, and striking Poland's energy grid in the depths of winter, the Russian state is sinking to new lows in its attempts to undermine European security," UK Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper remarked.

The UK sanctions also target individuals linked to Lumma Stealer, an information-stealing malware used to steal credentials and other sensitive data from compromised devices. Russia has used credentials obtained through Lumma Stealer to support cyber espionage operations, while the National Crime Agency estimated at least 2,100 UK victims over the past six months.

"We're sanctioning Russia at speed and scale," EU High Representative Kaja Kallas stated on X. "This is our biggest round of individual designations since Moscow's 2022 full-scale invasion and includes the EU's largest-ever cyber sanctions package."

The latest measures follow another round of EU cyber sanctions imposed in March, when the Council sanctioned three companies from China and Iran and two individuals over cyberattacks targeting EU member states and international partners.

Separately, the National Security Agency (NSA) and its partners released guidance on protecting routers against cyber activity attributed to Russia's FSB Center 16.

(Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor; Published: July 13, 2026)

bb1bd1cfb589.text:
Two rival nation-state cyber espionage operations, one linked to China and the other to India, have converged on the same Pakistani police force.

According to new analysis published by SentinelLabs on July 9, suspected China- and India-nexus actors ran intrusion campaigns against several Pakistani law enforcement bodies between February 2024 and April 2026, concentrating on Balochistan Police, the province's main force.

The compromised assets included servers hosting applications for biometric records, criminal case files and tenant registrations tied to national identity data. One China-nexus actor reportedly planted implants in a portal used by officers and citizens.

SentinelLabs grouped the command and control activity observed into four clusters. PlugX, ShadowPad and Cobalt Strike point to China-nexus operators; a Remcos cluster was tied to a suspected India-nexus actor Recorded Future tracks as TAG-179, overlapping with the group others call Bitter.

Two Rivals, Opposite Motives: For China, SentinelLabs said the likely driver was the safety of its nationals, tied to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). They have reportedly faced repeated deadly attacks, some claimed by the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), a Baloch separatist group. Police data would allow China to assess that threat independently.

India's motive is more likely its rivalry with Pakistan, in which Balochistan is a recurring flashpoint. Islamabad accused New Delhi of backing the insurgency, which India denied, and the force holds the record of how Pakistan polices the province.

A Citizen Portal Turned Against Its Users: The standout finding was the compromise of the force's Complaint Management System (CMS), used by both officers and citizens checking a complaint.

Two variants of an implant named cms_plugin.exe were uploaded in late 2024, one in Rust, the other .NET. The Rust variant is a stager that, on execution, displayed "Update Complete! Please refresh the page," mimicking a portal update.

The .NET variant posed as a component of Chinese vendor Qihoo 360's security software and loaded an AsyncRAT client. Shared code and simplified Chinese strings pointed to a Chinese-speaking developer.

Reaching the databases behind these applications would expose police personnel and payroll records, criminal case files and fingerprint biometrics, stolen vehicle records, hotel check-ins tied to identity data, landlord and tenant registrations, and citizen complaints including misconduct reports.

The convergence reflects a structural risk in digital policing: systems that centralize records and services also concentrate intelligence value, making police infrastructure intelligence terrain for any capable adversary.

(Author: Alessandro Mascellino; Published: 13 July 2026)

e28f7393358b.text:
Jesse McGraw, formerly known online as GhostExodus, transitioned from being a notorious blackhat hacker to a cybersecurity advocate and researcher. His journey reveals insights into hacker psychology, neurodivergence, and redemption through consequence.

McGraw discovered hacking in high school through a friend who programmed during math class and used those tools to access protected school systems. This exposure taught him that "technology, for want of a better phrase, can be bent to one's will." He initially used social engineering to gain access to remote systems as a teenager.

McGraw's background resembled many hackers—profound isolation stemming from weak parental bonds rather than autism spectrum disorder. His father dealt heroin while his mother worked as a dancer, leaving McGraw without emotional connection.

As McGraw's skills grew, he targeted increasingly larger systems. He explains: "I never hacked for monetary gain...I just did it for the thrill of joyriding on their systems." He lacked moral boundaries initially, and notes many hackers fail to consider victim impact because "they're sitting behind a computer. They don't see the human being on the other side of the machine."

McGraw identifies as neurodivergent and observes that "most of the people I come across are neurodivergent" in hacker spaces, though neurodivergence doesn't create hackers but amplifies their capabilities.

In 2009, McGraw led the Electronik Tribulation Army (ETA) and planned a major attack on Anonymous, hacking into over 14 computers at the North Central Medical Plaza in Dallas, including the SCADA system controlling HVAC operations. His downfall came from posting a video of the attack on YouTube with his face visible; researcher Wesley McGrew recognized equipment in the background and contacted the FBI. McGraw received a 110-month sentence in 2011.

McGraw states "The victim impact is now central to what I do today." He now specializes in open-source intelligence for online child safety work, identifying predators and reporting them to authorities, describing himself as a "red hat."

(Author: Kevin Townsend; Published: July 13, 2026)

c5b05bdb0433.text:
Varonis Threat Labs researchers Doron Kapah and Mark Vaitsman created "Breach at the Beach," a free online capture-the-flag (CTF) experience focused on Microsoft Entra ID security. The training simulation features Pixel, Varonis' mascot cat, investigating a breach while players trace threat actors' steps through cloud identity systems.

Why Entra ID Matters: The researchers emphasize that Entra ID serves as the enterprise control plane connecting users, applications, and increasingly AI-powered workflows. Mark Vaitsman notes: "In today's AI era, a lot of identities are non-human identities. If there is a compromise in Entra, a threat actor can pivot themselves into a non-human identity, and it can quickly turn into a stealthy and scalable data exfiltration attempt."

Learning Approach: The CTF teaches defenders to recognize when legitimate features become weaponized rather than hunting for misconfigurations. Deliberately designed without AI assistance compatibility, the challenge forces players to develop genuine understanding by working through raw Entra logs in complex evolving environments.

Accessibility: Available free at breachatthebeach.com, the four-stage challenge awards 1 CPE credit per stage, a themed badge, and a completion certificate. The experience targets security professionals across all roles—red teamers, blue teamers, CISOs, and threat intelligence specialists.

Event Availability: Black Hat USA 2026 (August 3-6): Varonis booth #2948; $2,000 prize drawing. DEF CON 34 (August 6-9): Cloud Village competition with prizes. Online access available globally.

(Sponsored by Varonis; Published: July 13, 2026)

a311e477ad19.text:
Beyond IT compliance, cloud security is now the backbone of civilian agency resilience, national defense, and warfighter safety, as cloud environments become increasingly complex.

Key Takeaways: For the Department of War (DoW), cloud security is an IT concern and a requirement for operational readiness and national security. Achieving a mature zero trust architecture requires deep, real-time visibility across seven critical pillars, including users, data, and workloads. FedRAMP High and IL5 authorizations provide the rigorous vendor validation that federal agencies need to ensure the protection of their controlled unclassified information (CUI) and the support of their tactical edge deployments. Tenable One Cloud Exposure, which now has FedRAMP High and IL5 authorizations, delivers a unified cloud native application protection platform (CNAPP) approach within a strictly regulated environment.

The stakes could not be higher. A misconfigured workload, an overprivileged service account, or a storage bucket quietly exposing sensitive data go beyond compliance findings to be addressed in the next POA&M cycle. In a federal context, those conditions translate directly into operational risk.

Zero Trust Requires Cloud Visibility across seven pillars: Users, Devices, Applications and workloads, Data, Network and environment, Automation and orchestration, Visibility and analytics.

What FedRAMP High and IL5 Mean: FedRAMP High provides the rigorous validation civilian agencies need to protect sensitive, unclassified citizen and operational data; IL5 meets the strict requirements for DoW workloads. "Tenable One Cloud Exposure has achieved FedRAMP High and IL5 authorization, building on its existing FedRAMP Moderate status."

A Unified Approach to Cloud Risk: Tool sprawl fragments visibility. As part of the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform, Tenable One Cloud Exposure maps the cloud attack surface by analyzing workloads, identities, and infrastructure together inside a single, rigorously vetted security boundary.

(Author: Zach Bennefield, Federal Security Strategist, Tenable; Published: July 13, 2026)

9c8c8caa7c12.text:
Researchers have discovered a sophisticated attack called "MemGhost" that plants false memories in AI agents through a single email. The attack, detailed in a paper titled "When Claws Remember but Do Not Tell," exploits how personal AI assistants store and retrieve persistent user information.

How the Attack Works: Personal AI agents maintain notes about users in memory files to provide continuity across sessions. An attacker sends an email containing hidden text directed at the agent rather than the human recipient. If the agent's email-reading capability processes it, three things occur sequentially: the agent writes the attacker's fabricated information into its persistent memory, its visible reply conceals this action, and during future conversations, the planted false information influences the agent's responses or actions.

Key Technical Details: The researchers developed MemGhost, a tool that generates attack emails automatically. They trained an attacker model against a shadow copy of OpenClaw (an open-source personal agent), rewarding emails that successfully implanted false memories while keeping replies inconspicuous. Testing results showed: "across 56 fresh test cases, MemGhost pulled off the full attack" with success rates of 87.5% against OpenClaw using GPT-5.4 and 71.4% against Claude Code SDK on Sonnet 4.6.

The attack remains hidden because capable agents deliberately conceal their tool operations from chat displays, memory files rarely get inspected by users, and background-mode operations often produce no visible notification.

Defense Gaps: An input filter designed to catch poisoned emails failed to detect MemGhost's payload over 90% of the time. A hardened model trained to ignore email-based instructions still followed the malicious memory write approximately 50% of the time.

Broader Context: In 2024, researcher Johann Rehberger showed manual memory poisoning through contaminated web content, dubbed "SpAIware." Microsoft addressed a related flaw in Copilot (EchoLeak, CVE-2025-32711) that leaked data through hidden email text, but the underlying vulnerability persisted.

Recommended Mitigations: The paper advocates for tagging information sources, obtaining user approval before storing new memories, and comprehensive logging of all write operations, or segregating email-reading tasks from memory-write functions.

Latest Developments: Following publication, the lead author confirmed the team tested real-world delivery by connecting a Gmail account to OpenClaw. The payloads cleared normal Gmail filtering and still achieved memory poisoning in over 50% of cases without explicit user confirmation.

(Author: Swati Khandelwal; Published: July 13, 2026)

01f47bb84e91.text:
Tidal Cyber has announced Threat-Led Asset Visibility and Vulnerability Prioritization, new innovations extending the company's Threat-Led Defense platform.

The announcement marks a significant advancement in defensive security, shifting the industry beyond static asset inventories, CVSS scoring, and disconnected exposure management toward an execution-centric model built on how adversaries actually execute attacks across the kill chain.

At Tidal Cyber, adversary procedures are not another data point. They are the organizing principle that connects threats, assets, vulnerabilities, and defenses into a single operational mode to: identify the assets and defenses that matter most based on their role in adversary execution and attacker success; expose vulnerabilities that enable adversary execution and increase the probability of successful attacks; prioritize defensive action using procedural-level intelligence, not inventory counts or severity scores; and measure defensive gaps against real-world adversary execution and identify the controls most likely to disrupt an attack.

Unlike security platforms that treat assets, vulnerabilities, and threats as separate domains, most asset management programs still cannot determine which assets attackers care about. And most exposure management platforms still stop at identification instead of answering the only question that truly matters: "Can an adversary successfully execute this attack against my environment?"

That question fundamentally changes the defensive equation. Rather than evaluating assets, vulnerabilities, and defenses independently, Tidal Cyber correlates them through the lens of real adversary execution. Every procedure becomes a connective layer that reveals how vulnerabilities enable attacks, which assets are operationally relevant, and where defensive controls can interrupt attacker progress. Instead of measuring isolated risk, organizations can understand and reduce the likelihood of attacker success across the entire attack lifecycle.

Rick Gordon, CEO of Tidal Cyber, commented: "Most security platforms still prioritize based on severity scores, inventory counts, or generalized risk models. But adversaries don't attack environments based on CVSS scores or asset databases. They exploit the path of least resistance."

Threat-Led Asset Visibility moves beyond inventory management by identifying which assets are operationally relevant to adversary execution, where defensive blind spots exist, and those gaps increase influence attacker success.

Threat-Led Vulnerability Prioritization moves beyond static severity scoring by correlating vulnerabilities directly to adversary procedures, operational tradecraft, and the likelihood of successful attack execution.

Instead of asking, "Which vulnerabilities are most severe?" organizations can now answer the question that matters most: "Which vulnerabilities materially increase the likelihood of attacker success against the assets and procedures that matter most?"

This approach enables organizations to prioritize: vulnerabilities tied to active adversary tradecraft, control gaps impacting critical attack procedures, and defensive actions that reduce real operational risk.

The announcement also builds on Tidal Cyber's continued innovation strategy, including the recent separation of MITRE ATT&CK CTI from Tidal Cyber CTI and proprietary intelligence sources, an industry-first approach designed to provide greater transparency, attribution clarity, and procedural precision across modern threat intelligence.

Frank Duff, Chief Innovation Officer of Tidal Cyber, stated: "Threat-Led Defense starts with a simple principle: you cannot reduce residual risk unless you understand how adversaries actually execute attacks and how that execution impacts your defensive environment."

f3c73f8db6a4.text:
Cloudflare has announced the general availability of Precursor, a next-generation continuous behavioral validation engine for bot management. Precursor runs seamlessly inside web browsers to monitor entire user sessions in order to detect bot automation. Unlike static CAPTCHAs, it analyzes ongoing interactions in real time to catch advanced bots, improving detection precision without interrupting legitimate users.

For the first time, automated bot traffic has eclipsed human activity on the Internet, now generating roughly 57% of all web requests. This milestone emphasizes a seismic evolution from an Internet built for human clicks to a digital landscape now dominated by AI agents.

For organizations and everyday consumers, this means that legacy defenses are blind to a new breed of automated threats that drive up infrastructure costs, manipulate inventory, and compromise data. While a modern bot can easily fake a single action to pass a one-time security check, replicating an entire human journey remains a massive engineering hurdle.

To protect the integrity of the global Internet, organizations must move away from static, point-in-time defenses and embrace continuous behavioral validation—analyzing telemetry across an entire session to unmask automated imposters trying to blend into the crowd.

According to Dane Knecht, CTO of Cloudflare: "Instead of just checking an ID at the gate, we are looking at behavior over the entire visit. This makes life seamless for real users, while making it incredibly difficult and expensive for bad actors to fake human behavior."

Precursor provides session-level insights by continuously collecting robust browser signals through four key mechanisms:

Privacy-led defense: The system logs aggregate behavioral patterns rather than recording specific user inputs. Keyboard activity is recorded exclusively as timing rhythm and cadence—never capturing actual keystrokes.

Zero-code, one-click setup: Precursor is enabled with one click, automatically allowing Cloudflare to inject a compact, dynamic script requiring no modifications to underlying code. The script evaluates interaction dimensions such as mouse movement, scrolling rhythm, typing cadence, clipboard activity, and page visibility duration.

Real-time analysis engine: Cloudflare's servers instantly unpack telemetry data sent from a user's browser and scan it for signs of faked or computer-generated activity, validating whether interaction streams map rationally to human behavior.

Session-long security measures: Unlike traditional defense challenges that reset per request, Precursor continuously evaluates the visitor's user journey across web or single page applications, preventing automated agents from resetting their behavioral signatures by refreshing a page.

168df3e30d5a.text:
UK authorities charged five individuals following a National Crime Agency investigation into Russian Coms, a caller ID spoofing platform used by criminals to execute over 1.8 million fraudulent calls.

The charged individuals are: 28-year-old Ayoub Sehailia, 30-year-old Zakkaria Sehailia, 30-year-old Usman Din, 29-year-old Denis Ozmus, and 53-year-old Fadila Salem, all from London.

Charges include conspiracy to supply articles for use in connection with fraud, transferring or converting criminal property, and failing to comply with notice to provide phone passcodes. All five are scheduled to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Friday, August 14.

The platform, established in 2020, evolved from a handset application to a web-based service. It permitted criminals to mask their identities by appearing to call from pre-selected numbers belonging to financial institutions, telecommunications companies, and law enforcement agencies. The goal was stealing funds and personal information from victims.

Since 2020, the platform has been linked to tens of millions in financial losses affecting approximately 170,000 victims. When the NCA took down Russian Coms in March 2024, hundreds of criminals had paid for six-month contracts priced between £1,200 and £1,400 in cryptocurrency.

Prior to shutdown, criminals used the platform to make over 1.3 million calls to 500,000 unique phone numbers across more than 107 countries, resulting in average losses exceeding £9,400 per victim.

The platform was promoted on Telegram, Snapchat, and Instagram, offering encrypted calls, web phone access, international calling, voice-changing services, and 24/7 support.

Scammers exploited spoofed bank numbers to gain victim trust, then convinced them to transfer money to attacker-controlled accounts by claiming fraudulent activity on their accounts.

The platform's takedown followed arrests of three men in Newham, London, two believed to be administrators and developers. The shutdown was part of "Operation Henhouse," a broader anti-fraud initiative that resulted in 290 arrests across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.

392fb7002224.text:
Check Point Research's weekly threat intelligence report highlights significant cybersecurity incidents and vulnerabilities from the week of July 13, 2026.

Top Attacks and Breaches: AssuranceAmerica, a U.S. auto insurer, disclosed a breach affecting approximately 7 million individuals. Attackers leveraged compromised employee credentials to access company systems and steal names, contact information, driver's license numbers, insurance policy and account data, vehicle information, and claims details.

Latvia's state-owned forestry company Latvijas Valsts Meži experienced ransomware disrupting multiple systems. The attackers exploited an unpatched system and leaked approximately 44GB of internal materials including credentials and source code.

Injective Labs, a blockchain software developer, suffered a supply chain compromise when malicious npm packages were published through their compromised SDK project, exfiltrating cryptocurrency wallet credentials.

Moody Bible Institute reported a breach affecting over 2.3 million donors, students, alumni, and supporters, with the ShinyHunters group publishing allegedly stolen personal information.

AI Threats: Researchers identified JadePuffer, an autonomous ransomware operation that used a large language model to conduct an intrusion without direct human control. The operation exploited a Langflow vulnerability and deleted databases while demanding ransom.

Security researchers demonstrated that malicious instructions embedded in open-source files could achieve remote code execution through Claude Code and OpenAI Codex when operating with automated permissions.

Google's Dialogflow CX contained Rogue Agent, a vulnerability allowing users with limited permissions to inject persistent malicious code that could capture chatbot conversations.

Vulnerabilities and Patches: Multiple Tenda router models are affected by CVE-2026-11405, an undocumented authentication backdoor providing administrative access.

Linux maintainers patched CVE-2026-53359, a critical hypervisor vulnerability in the Kernel-based Virtual Machine that could enable host system escape.

U-Boot addressed six vulnerabilities affecting secure boot signature verification, potentially enabling arbitrary code execution.

Opera corrected a critical browser vulnerability allowing malicious websites to install modifications without user consent.

Threat Intelligence Reports: Check Point Research profiled Cavern Manticore, an Iran-linked threat actor targeting Israeli government and information technology organizations utilizing a modular .NET command-and-control framework.

The organization reported June 2026 cyberattack activity averaged 2,270 weekly attacks per organization, with ransomware incidents increasing 33% year-over-year.

Researchers investigated a student employment phishing campaign abusing compromised school email accounts with over 3,200 messages passing authentication checks.

Analysis of UAT-7810 identified a China-linked threat actor compromising internet-facing networking devices to expand relay infrastructure.

c86e6a1bcfd8.text:
A phishing-as-a-service operation named Forg365 is targeting Microsoft 365 accounts through a combination of device code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle tactics, antibot evasion, AI-generated lures, and post-compromise mailbox operations.

Distribution & Pricing: The service costs $400 monthly or $3,800 annually and is distributed via Telegram. Attack chains leverage legitimate email infrastructure from Amazon SES and Twilio SendGrid to create redirection chains mimicking standard email traffic.

Platform Capabilities: According to ZeroBEC's analysis, "The panel exposes a mature operator workflow: accounts, links, invitations, OAuth app configuration, redirect links, SVG generation, campaign sending, SMTP profiles, SMTP rotation, AI email generation, token vaulting, account intelligence, keyword alerts, viewer links, and browser-extension support."

Technical Approach: Campaigns employ business document or remittance-themed lures. The platform includes a device-auth phishing component presenting Microsoft-styled verification pages that push victims into legitimate Microsoft Authentication Broker flows—victims see authentic Microsoft surfaces while attackers gain unauthorized session access.

Browser Extension: ForgCookie, a Chromium-based extension, maintains compromised account access by cycling through token acquisition and injecting refresh-token credentials into Microsoft login domains.

Defensive Recommendations: Organizations should block device code authentication when unnecessary, audit mailbox artifacts after device code events, review mail-flow rules, and decommission legacy email aliases no longer corresponding to active personnel.

f47291661b84.text:
Every AI vendor is talking about agents – autonomous systems that handle complex tasks without constant human input. The promise is real. But one question gets asked too rarely: what makes an agent reliable enough to trust with your network security? The answer isn't the model. It's the harness.

Agents Run on LLMs. Reliability Runs on Something Else: AI agents get their reasoning power from large language models (LLMs). LLMs are impressive. They understand context, reason through complex problems, and plan across a wide range of tasks. But on its own, an LLM is a generalist. It knows a little about everything and not enough about your environment. Left ungrounded, it hallucinates — confident outputs that are simply wrong. In a chatbot, that's an inconvenience. In network security, it's a risk you can't accept. What separates a capable AI agent from a reliable one is how it's harnessed. Three elements define that harness: skills, tools, and context. Get all three right, and the agent is accurate and trustworthy. Get one wrong, and you're back to hallucination, just with more steps in between.

Why Generic AI Gets the Harness Wrong: A general-purpose agent applied to network security borrows a harness built for everything and uses it where precision matters. Generic models handle generic cases. They've never seen the edge cases of mature environments – decade-old rules nobody remembers, multi-vendor dependencies that break in non-obvious ways. They work from static training data, with no sense of what "good" looks like at scale. The result is automation that works in demos and fails at scale.

What a Reliable Harness Needs to Get Right: Reliability doesn't come from a bigger model. It comes from how you build the three parts of the harness – skills, tools, and context. Build skills on real experience: Skills should encode expertise earned in production, not theory from generic training data. Build tools to serve the agent: Not everything is done by LLM, and tools are essential to allow it to fetch data, reduce it for practicality and prepare it for the model. Give the agent a live view of the environment: An agent is only as accurate as the picture it works from; tools should read the environment as it exists right now – topology, dependencies, policies, traffic – and act on it.

How Check Point Builds the Harness: Check Point built its agentic platform on exactly these principles, on the same LLM foundation as any other system. Skills from 30 years of real deployments draw on protecting over 100,000 organizations. Tools build a live picture of your network via a proprietary Network Knowledge Graph – a continuously updated model of topology, flows, dependencies, firewall policies, and real-time traffic. Context that keeps every decision grounded combines the Network Knowledge Graph with Check Point's best practices, customer security guidelines, and regulatory requirements.

The Harness Is the Differentiator: LLM intelligence is widely available – but it is how you direct that power that matters. That's the Check Point harness, and it's why agentic network security, done right, produces results accurate enough to trust in production.

140606297839.text:
AI agents are now reading and writing emails before humans ever see them. What was once a human-centric communication channel is quickly becoming an AI-driven workflow, and that shift introduces a new and largely unprotected attack surface.

Much of the industry's recent attention has centered on EchoLeak, a vulnerability demonstrated in Microsoft Copilot. Researchers showed that a carefully crafted email could influence Copilot's behavior and potentially expose sensitive information without the user clicking a link, opening an attachment, or taking any action at all.

The importance of EchoLeak was not that it revealed a flaw in a specific product. It showed a fundamentally new attack model. Attackers no longer need to deceive users if they can manipulate the AI acting on their behalf. Malicious content can be injected into emails to manipulate how an agent summarizes, prioritizes, or even responds on behalf of an employee.

Why Post-Delivery Security Falls Short: Traditional email security has focused on stopping threats after delivery. But in an agentic environment, post-delivery controls are too late. AI agents can process and act on an email instantly, meaning the impact occurs before any human review.

Email Agent Hijacking (EAH) occurs when attackers embed instructions within emails, signatures, attachments, or other content specifically designed to influence how AI systems interpret information, make decisions, or trigger actions. Rather than targeting the user, the attacker targets the AI agent consuming the content. Reader agents must be shielded from malicious inputs, and writer agents need a validation layer to ensure their outputs are safe, accurate, and aligned with corporate policy.

Email Security for the Agentic Era: Check Point is the first company to address EAH by securing both the content AI agents consume and the content they generate. This protection prevents inbound email content from influencing AI behavior and validates AI-generated outputs before they are delivered.

EAH represents a fundamental evolution in email threats. To learn more, Check Point offers a webinar titled "Why Email Agent Hijacking Marks the End of Post-Delivery Email Security," scheduled for Wednesday, July 22.

370bbe62a612.text:
Cyber-attackers are increasingly deploying a stealthy technique which enables them to spoof OAuth Client IDs to gain access to cloud environments, cybersecurity experts have warned.

According to research by analysts at Proofpoint, cybercriminals are leveraging Microsoft Entra ID, the tech giant's cloud-based identity and access management solution, formerly known as Azure AD, to gain access to accounts without a registered OAuth client ID.

The nature of the technique means that it is difficult for defenders to identify suspicious activity, while at the same time, the attackers are provided with stealthy access to the organization's cloud services.

OAuth client ID spoofing has emerged as a novel technique and is increasingly leveraged in campaigns which target the cloud, Proofpoint warned in a blog post published on July 13.

Entra sign-in logs are a common tool for defenders to aid with identifying malicious authentication activity, such as user enumeration. However, the research details how attackers are exploiting OAuth client ID spoofing to bypass detection by Entra sign-in logs, therefore helping them to stealthily compromise enterprise cloud services.

Evading Detection via Microsoft Entra: Proofpoint explained that client ID spoofing was performed by issuing POST requests to Microsoft's OAuth 2.0 token endpoint using the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flow, which allowed direct submission of usernames and passwords. This results in Azure Active Directory Security Token Service (AADSTS) error codes which allow unauthenticated requestors to infer the validity of usernames and passwords, as well as the enforcement of additional controls such as multi-factor authentication (MFA) or zero-trust concepts like conditional access (CA).

With this information, the attackers could identify accounts which could be exploited. Crucially, the use of the spoofed IDs and blank fields in Entra ID logs makes the malicious activity harder for defenders to identify.

Proofpoint said that it has tracked multiple large-scale campaigns deploying this technique, targeting millions of user accounts across thousands of Microsoft Entra tenants in the wild. They note how the attackers make attempts to spoof common usernames to aid the process of client ID spoofing, such as initials paired with common surnames like Smith, Jones, Williams, and Johnson.

Researchers warned that organizations should expect more attackers to look for ways to exploit this technique. "The emergence of multiple campaigns with unique tools and infrastructure suggests this technique is gaining traction among threat actors targeting cloud environments," the blog post warned.

Proofpoint said that in response to this tactic, defenders should treat sign-in log entries with blank application IDs, or those without a corresponding application name, as potential indicators of client ID spoofing. They also suggested that defenders should be alert that an AADSTS700016 error code may signal compromised credentials, not just a failed login attempt.

efc51b9c45dc.text:
Every security domain has a number that tells you how much of it is under control. Identity has MFA adoption. Patching has mean time to remediate. Exposure has open critical issues. Each one answers a simple question at a glance. Cloud infrastructure should have an equivalent metric, and Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) coverage is a strong candidate.

IaC is how the modern cloud gets built. Code can be reviewed before it ships, governed by policy, and rebuilt the same way every time. How much of your cloud runs through code, your IaC coverage, is a direct measure of how much of it you can secure by design.

But unlike other domains, coverage in the cloud isn't binary. A resource can be half-covered: deployed through a pipeline yet impossible to trace back to the code that defined it. The useful version of IaC coverage isn't a single percentage, it's a funnel: from the infrastructure that could be in code, to what an IaC tool actually tracks, to what you can open and fix in a repo today.

The IaC Coverage Funnel: 1. IaC-supportable — every cloud resource that could be defined in code. This is the widest part of the funnel. A resource that falls out here (e.g., a VM spun up in the console during an incident) is never imported to IaC, never flagged as drifted, and won't be considered when infrastructure needs to be re-provisioned. 2. Tracked by IaC — the resource appears in a state file. Drift can be detected and the resource is semi-governed, but if the module that created it was deleted or refactored out of the repo, no one can trace or fix the code that defines it. 3. Mapped to a declaration in code — the resource's definition in state resolves to an actual module, file, and line in a repo you can open today; the source can be scanned before deploy and fixes can ship as pull requests.

IaC Coverage Enables Traceability, Resilience, and Compliance: Coverage determines whether a misconfiguration gets fixed at its source in code or patched manually in the console (traceability); whether an environment can be rebuilt from code under pressure (resilience); and how much of an estate is validated before it ships to production versus caught after, if at all (compliance).

How Wiz Measures IaC Coverage: Wiz Code scans the modules and pipelines that define infrastructure, and Wiz Cloud sees what's actually running. The IaC Inventory, now Generally Available, reconciles them, connecting every module to every deployment and every live resource it manages, producing the coverage funnel and surfacing exactly where resources fall out of governance. A finding on a live resource maps back to the exact module that declared it, with the owner attached, so the fix ships as a pull request instead of a manual console change. The same rules run as pipeline controls in development and as cloud controls at runtime.

The Security Metric Cloud Teams Have Been Missing: Measuring coverage is the foundation; acting on it is what matters now, because AI models can find a flaw and produce a working exploit in hours. In the era of AI Threat Readiness, machine-speed remediation requires stage three of the funnel — the resource has to map back to code. The Wiz Green Agent can open a pull request and fix a misconfiguration at its root only across the share of the estate that coverage reaches. Existing Wiz Code customers can connect their repositories and IaC platforms and start exploring the IaC Inventory today.

Insolvency proceedings have been initiated – and why we are still looking ahead
Ladies and gentlemen, 
dear business partners,
Today we are contacting you with a message that is very difficult for us personally.
ZEGO Textilveredelungszentrum GmbH has filed for insolvency.
This decision was one of the most difficult steps in our company’s 37-year history. It was not made hastily, but only after we had examined and exhausted all available options.
Over the past few months, we have fought with all our might for our company, our employees, our customers, and our suppliers. Our goal has always been to maintain business operations and return ZEGO to a stable course.
The cyberattack of March 29, 2026, however, impacted our company to an extent that we could not fully compensate for despite our best efforts. This step is very painful for us.
For many years, ZEGO has stood for reliability, quality, and collaborative partnerships. Many of our customers and suppliers have been with us for a long time. Business relationships have often blossomed into trusting partnerships, even friendships, for which we are extremely grateful.
That is precisely why it is important for us to also inform you of the following today:
Insolvency does not automatically mean the end of a company.
Rather, the process offers the opportunity to restructure, reposition, and economically stabilize a company. We will dedicate ourselves fully to precisely this goal.
We will continue to fight for the survival of ZEGO Textilveredelungszentrum GmbH.
Our goal is to develop viable solutions together with the stakeholders, to preserve jobs, to maintain customer relationships and to secure the future of our company.
For this, we continue to need the support and trust of our business partners.
We would therefore like to expressly ask you to support us during this difficult phase. Every form of support, every collaborative partnership, and every instance of trust will help create the conditions for the successful continuation of the company.
We would like to sincerely thank you for your support, loyalty and trust so far.
We will keep you informed about further developments and are always available to answer your questions.
Let us work together to ensure that this difficult phase is not the end, but a new beginning for ZEGO.
Best regards
Johannes Zenglein 
ZEGO Textile Finishing Center
