Lang Khuong Duy of Viettel IDC discovered two high-severity Avi Load Balancer bugs that can be exploited for directory traversal attacks (CVE-2026-47871) and privilege escalation (CVE-2026-47870). Both Lang and Waeytens have been credited by Broadcom for responsibly reporting CVE-2026-47869, a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability that can be exploited by an authenticated attacker with network access. Broadcom's advisory does not mention in-the-wild exploitation for any of these vulnerabilities. However, organizations should install the latest updates, as threat actors regularly exploit VMware product vulnerabilities in attacks. Author: Eduard Kovacs.

2203f492ffed.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed two access control flaws in RabbitMQ message broker service. Miggo's security team discovered these vulnerabilities, which could allow attackers to leak OAuth client secrets, expose enterprise messaging infrastructure, and bypass tenant boundaries. CVE-2026-57219 (CVSS 8.7): An obsolete HTTP API endpoint ('GET /api/auth') reveals client secrets on RabbitMQ installations with OAuth 2 configured. According to researchers, 'leaks the broker's confidential OAuth secret to an unauthenticated attacker in a single request, a direct path to full broker takeover in the configurations that use that secret.' The endpoint's authorization check was hardcoded to always allow requests, unlike other sensitive management endpoints. CVE-2026-57221 (CVSS 5.3): Missing authorization allows any authenticated user connecting to a virtual host to enumerate queue and exchange names, read message counts and consumer counts, regardless of actual permissions. Impact & Timeline: Both flaws existed in the codebase since early 2024, affecting RabbitMQ 3.13.0 and later. Patches are available in versions 4.3.0, 4.2.6, 4.1.11, 4.0.20, and 3.13.15. No active exploitation prior to disclosure has been reported. Recommended Actions: Organizations should rotate OAuth secrets if management interfaces are internet-accessible, limit port 15672 access, separate tenants by virtual host, and implement firewall rules blocking vulnerable endpoints. Author: Ravie Lakshmanan.

a74ab06bdec9.text: Jamf Threat Labs discovered a new macOS infostealer called CrashStealer that impersonates Apple's crash-reporting tool to steal passwords, Keychain data, and cryptocurrency wallets. The malware was initially detected during development in May and entered active use by early July. The threat distinguishes itself through a native C++ implementation around an internal class the authors named MacOSData, allowing it to validate login credentials locally before harvesting data from browsers, password managers, and digital wallets. The infection begins with a disk image named 'Werkbit Setup' containing an application signed with Developer ID 'Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV).' This signature, along with a stapled notarization ticket, enables the dropper to bypass Gatekeeper protections on first execution. Following initial launch, the veltod executable contacts a GitHub repository to retrieve commands that fetch additional scripts from a separate server. These scripts download CrashReporter.dmg, which mimics Apple's legitimate crash-reporting component. CrashStealer displays a fake macOS password dialog and validates credentials using the dscl command. Upon receiving the correct password, it unlocks the login Keychain and extracts data from user directories while targeting approximately 80 cryptocurrency wallet extensions and 14 password managers including 1Password, Bitwarden, LastPass, Dashlane, and Keeper. Collected files are encrypted individually using AES-256-GCM before being packaged into hidden ZIP archives and uploaded to command-and-control servers. The malware copies itself to a new location with a fresh ad hoc signature, then installs as a LaunchAgent named 'com.apple.crashreporter.helper' to maintain access across login sessions. Anti-analysis techniques include flattened control flow, runtime string decryption, and multiple debugger checks.

2356a8b854c8.text: Two new phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, have been discovered targeting Microsoft 365 accounts using techniques designed to circumvent multi-factor authentication defenses. Jalisco employs device-code phishing methods, while OmegaLord disguises itself as a PDF reader to harvest login credentials and phone numbers. Cybersecurity researchers at ReliaQuest analyzed both toolkits, noting that while device-code phishing has grown increasingly prevalent, traditional phishing approaches continue evolving to bypass modern security measures. The device-code phishing technique exploits OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant flows by convincing victims to authorize attacker-controlled devices accessing their Microsoft accounts. Attackers initiate sign-in requests to Microsoft services, generating device authorization codes. Through social engineering, they trick victims into entering these codes on legitimate Microsoft login pages, granting unauthorized access without requiring usernames or passwords. Jalisco generates fresh OAuth device codes automatically when victims access phishing pages, circumventing Microsoft's 15-minute validity window established to combat device-code attacks. The toolkit includes a web portal enabling operators to manage captured sessions and compromised accounts. ReliaQuest researchers observed attackers registering multiple rogue devices on compromised accounts, sometimes using innocuous names containing 'Microsoft' or 'Windows' to avoid detection. Following account compromise, attackers search SharePoint and other SaaS services for sensitive data—customer/employee personally identifiable information, financial records, and internal communications—exfiltrating information within minutes before defenders identify breaches. Attackers subsequently demand extortion payments, threatening data leaks. OmegaLord represents more conventional phishing, using fake PDF Reader login pages to collect email addresses, passwords, and phone numbers. Jalisco joins other device-code phishing tools including EvilTokens, Kali365, Tycoon2FA, Venom, and Forg365. ReliaQuest recommends reducing Entra ID device-registration limits from the default 50 to one or two, blocking device-code authentication through Microsoft Entra Conditional Access, restricting OAuth Device Authorization grants in Okta, and auditing unnecessary app registrations.

cd65b6b8ed7c.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 11 old, Microsoft-signed, Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) applications that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using the modern firmware standard. 'An attacker exploiting one of these vulnerable applications can execute untrusted code during system boot, enabling deployment of malicious UEFI bootkits or other malware,' ESET researcher Martin Smolár said in a report. The UEFI shim bootloaders expose any UEFI-based machine that trusts Microsoft's 'Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011' third-party UEFI certificate authority certificate, irrespective of the installed operating system. The certificate expired June 27, 2026, and has been replaced by Microsoft UEFI CA 2023 and Microsoft Option ROM UEFI CA 2023. The shim is a lightweight, open-source UEFI bootloader that acts as an intermediary between firmware and Linux, allowing Linux distributions to boot when Secure Boot is enabled. The UEFI firmware loads the shim and validates its signature against the Microsoft CA; the shim validates the second-stage bootloader (usually GRUB 2); GRUB 2 validates the kernel. The outdated-but-trusted shims can be exploited to execute arbitrary code at boot, deploying bootkits like Bootkitty, HybridPetya, or BlackLotus even with Secure Boot enabled. Affected shim loaders (version 0.9 or lower) include those from Spyrus, Red Hat (RHEL/CentOS 7.2), Baramundi, WhiteCanyon/Blancco WipeDrive, Finland's Matriculation Examination Board, NTC IT ROSA, Oracle Linux, PC-Doctor, and openSUSE. These were revoked by Microsoft in the June 2026 Patch Tuesday update following responsible disclosure in February. An attacker could use bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver (BYOVD) techniques with these shims to run arbitrary code during early boot, before the OS initializes. Linux's Machine Owner Key (MOK) allowlist and denylist mechanisms can be subverted: an attacker could replace an up-to-date shim with an older Microsoft-signed shim to bypass MOK denylist enforcement, since the allowlist still trusts the old certificate, enabling arbitrary code execution. The attack also subverts Secure Boot Advanced Targeting (SBAT), which revokes vulnerable boot components by generation rather than blocklisting hashes. CERT/CC noted that vendor-specific bootloaders were not updated after upstream fixes became public, creating a long-term supply chain exposure where outdated components remained trusted because they were not added to the Microsoft-signed DBX revocation list. Because this occurs before the OS and security products initialize, malicious code can sidestep EDR and other built-in controls. The issues are tracked as CVE-2026-8863 and CVE-2026-10797 (the latter a long-patched shim certificate-revocation bypass via modified bootloader signature headers). ESET said the expired 2011 CA certificate has no bearing on Secure Boot verification as long as bootloaders signed with it are not explicitly revoked by hash: 'What makes these old shims dangerous is not a novel vulnerability, it's that no new vulnerability is needed to bypass UEFI Secure Boot. An attacker needs no complicated exploitation primitives – only a copy of an old, still-trusted, but unrevoked shim binary and a basic understanding of how UEFI shims work.'

6475dde9d2b1.text: Researcher Cereblab discovered that Grok Build, SpaceXAI's command-line interface, was transmitting entire user repositories to Google Cloud Storage without consent. The tool uploaded complete codebases as Git bundles, including full Git histories containing secrets deleted months earlier, rather than just uploading files necessary to answer user prompts. Cereblab's investigation tested this by instructing Grok Build to simply reply with 'OK' without opening any files. The tool uploaded the entire repository anyway. Other users reported similar findings, with one experiencing exposure of their entire user directory containing SSH keys and password manager databases. The behavior differed significantly from competing CLIs: 'SpaceXAI's data retention went far beyond that of other CLIs, such as Claude Code, Gemini, and Codex, which open individual files rather than entire repos before uploading them.' Following public disclosure, SpaceXAI implemented a server-side fix by setting disable_codebase_upload to true, which stopped the uploads. Cereblab criticized the company's response: 'What actually stopped the upload was a silent global flag – disable_codebase_upload: true – that applies whether you opt in or out.' SpaceXAI's public statement emphasized that zero-data-retention customers were protected and offered a /privacy command to disable data collection, but Cereblab clarified this command was merely a per-session retention toggle, not the switch that fixed the issue. Elon Musk promised deletion of all previously uploaded user data, stating that data collected prior to the fix 'will be completely and utterly deleted.' The Register notes it cannot independently verify this deletion claim. Cereblab remained critical of the default settings: 'No developer should have to run an opt-out after every session to keep their own code off someone else's servers. The right default is off.'

0b1c28be41c9.text: Tracebit researchers have developed a defensive technique using 'context bombs'—injected text designed to trigger safety guardrails in AI agents—to protect corporate environments from autonomous attacks. The researchers tested this approach against leading AI models including Anthropic's Opus 4.8, Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro, Zhipu AI's GLM 5.2, DeepSeek's DeepSeek 4 Pro, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.6. They deployed canaries containing context bombs in simulated AWS environments with ten possible attack paths. Results proved striking: across five leading models, planting a single context bomb in a canary secret had a significant impact on attack success. Opus 4.8 achieved full admin access in 93% of baseline runs but failed completely with context bombs deployed. Gemini 3.1 Pro similarly went from 60% success to failure. The technique leverages prompt injection—the same vulnerability attackers exploit. Instead of defending against injection, researchers weaponized it defensively. Western models responded to sensitive biological topic references, while Chinese models halted when encountering politically sensitive Chinese-language content. The researchers acknowledged limitations: they haven't tested 'abliterated' models stripped of safety guardrails, leaving questions about effectiveness against fully unrestricted systems.

6ed4a8364e6f.text: A jailbroken Google Gemini completed 90 percent of the work in a credential- and cryptocurrency-stealing operation, including deploying a new command-and-control (C2) server in merely six minutes, per a TrendAI report shared exclusively with The Register. The solo operator—a Russian-speaking individual known as 'bandcampro'—oversaw the cyber-fraud operation targeting Trump supporters and conspiracy theorists, while the AI agent handled most hacking tasks: migrating botnets, writing and deploying C2 servers, and executing 59 unprompted behaviors during migration. According to Tom Kellermann, TrendAI's VP of AI security, 'Persistence is evolving because of AI' through dynamic C2 shifting and steganography via invisible prompt injection. The attacker jailbroke Gemini by claiming to be an 'authorized pentester' requiring disabled safety features. The AI still refused some requests—declining to create network-scanning malware—but complied with most instructions provided in conversational Russian. When the attacker's old Cloudflare tunnel-based infrastructure encountered blocking, he requested Gemini redesign the architecture. On March 23, after instructing Gemini to 'study the C2 migration,' the AI launched the new C2 server, diagnosed and fixed deployment errors, and successfully controlled eight computers at a dental clinic—all within six minutes. The AI designed 80 percent of attack architecture, 100 percent of coding and command execution, and 90 percent of problem identification and debugging. The entire operation fit into three plain-text files totaling four pages: jailbreak instructions, C2 framework code, and a C2 migration guide. Kellermann emphasized that defenders must view jailbroken AI as command-and-control infrastructure, implementing multi-layered guardrails, behavioral anomaly detection, and least-privilege mechanisms following OWASP and NIST frameworks. He highlighted that Russians excel at jailbreaking and persistence, distinguishing their tactical destructiveness from Chinese espionage-focused operations. Though this attacker operated independently, Kellermann noted that Russian cybercriminals typically become absorbed into organized crime cartels over time.

7cf9edd58805.text: Researchers at KU Leuven tested 85 of the most popular crypto wallets that run as browser extensions and found that the wallets themselves leak enough to link and track the people using them. The way these wallets talk to websites and blockchain servers can tie a person's separate addresses together and let outsiders follow them from site to site. This is not a hack; the wallets behave exactly as they were built to. The 85 extensions together have about 35 million users listed on the Chrome Web Store. The team, from the university's DistriNet security group, posted the paper this month for presentation at the PETS 2026 privacy conference in Calgary in late July. Problem 1: Seventeen wallets exposed connections between a user's separate addresses—13 by bundling two addresses into one request, four by firing separate requests within milliseconds of each other—covering about 23 million installs. Problem 2: A website can fingerprint which wallets a user has installed (36 of 85 wallets do this, ~82% of installs studied); of 30 popular Web3 apps tested, only 11 sent a real revoke command on disconnect, and 22 of the 36 fingerprintable wallets still let a site read the user's address after a revoke request, surviving cookie clearing and browser restarts. Problem 3: Of those same 36 wallets, 23 will hand out a user's address from inside an invisible cross-site iframe if the user previously connected to an app embedding that tracker, potentially linking a wallet address (and thus balances/transactions) to a real identity already known to the tracking site. The researchers disclosed the cross-site issue to vendors before publishing. By a February 2026 retest, Coinbase Wallet and Coin98 had fixed it, and Hana Wallet did so later; of eight vendors that replied via bug bounty programs, most declined to treat it as a bug—MetaMask called it a known issue with no plans to change its provider injection, Rabby called the attack 'virtually impossible,' OKX called it informational since no funds are stolen, and Bybit, Backpack, and Core called it low-risk. The paper builds on 2023 research on wallet address leaks and went up on arXiv July 7.

f38c9e1d54d7.text: AI security agents are starting to influence real security decisions, but most still rely on fragmented risk signals: scanner output, severity scores, threat intelligence, configuration findings, and exposure data. That fragmentation matters because attackers chain exposures across identities, networks, cloud assets, applications, and security controls; if an AI workflow only sees isolated findings, it cannot determine whether those findings create a real attack path. Security validation tests whether exposures, misconfigurations, credentials, and controls can actually be leveraged in a real attack path, producing evidence of what is exploitable rather than estimating risk. Pentera's AI-powered security validation platform safely emulates real-world attack techniques against production environments to determine which exposures can actually be leveraged, generating validated attack paths with evidence of technique used, systems reached, credentials obtained, privileges gained, assets at risk, and objective achieved. To bridge the gap between validation data and AI workflows, Pentera introduced an MCP (Model Context Protocol) Server making Pentera validation data available directly to MCP-compatible AI assistants, letting agents retrieve findings, review validated attack paths, access test results, and initiate validation activities via natural language (e.g., 'Show me all validated attack paths from the latest Pentera test that resulted in privileged access'). This changes workflows from passive analysis to validation-driven action: validating before ticketing, prioritizing exploitable attack paths over highest-severity findings, enriching remediation tickets with attack evidence, and revalidating after fixes are applied. Pentera's MCP Server runs locally as a Docker container using STDIO communication, opens no inbound ports, requires no external management interface, inherits existing Pentera RBAC permissions, and logs interactions for auditability, letting organizations use validation data in AI workflows without exposing a new network service or bypassing governance controls.

b62d5d084b3f.text: Thank you to AI Breakthrough Awards for naming Vectra AI the AI Security Solution of the Year in the 2026 AI Safety, Security & Compliance category. For Vectra AI, the AI story has always started in the same place: trusted signal intelligence. AI does not change the need to understand what happened, who or what was involved, how activity unfolded, and why it matters; it raises the bar for it, because 'without trusted signal, agentic AI just accelerates noise.' As a 2025 and 2026 Leader in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Network Detection and Response (NDR), Vectra AI signal intelligence helps explain what happened (network communications, protocols, lateral movement, command-and-control, data movement), identity data helps explain who or what was involved (user, service account, machine identity, workload, cloud identity, privilege, access pattern), and signal intelligence brings those together so teams can understand why activity matters. For teams building their own Agentic SOC, Vectra AI gives domain-specific detections, network metadata, identity context (Identity Threat Detection and Response, Account Association), entity attribution, API-accessible signal, and MCP-ready access. For teams adding agentic capabilities to an existing SOC, Vectra AI provides AI triage, correlation, and prioritization, attack graphs, investigation and hunting capabilities, and AI-Assisted Search for plain-language queries. A third path is operationalizing AI with help from Vectra AI experts via Vectra MXDR, Managed Services, the Threat Hunting Methodology guide, and platform reporting. The author frames AI security as fundamentally a trust conversation — can defenders trust the signal, understand the context, see the evidence, and keep people in control — and presents the award as validation of Vectra's continued work on signal intelligence.

1ec56b6a485f.text: The Sysdig Threat Research Team observed an attacker who started with a single leaked service-principal credential and by the next morning owned the entire tenant, achieving Global Administrator ownership of the directory and root-level access over every resource, then planting persistence across dozens of identities and compromising the telemetry pipeline meant to detect the attack. In Azure, permission lives in at least five disjointed systems that Azure doesn't unify: Entra directory roles, Azure RBAC, Key Vault access policies, bearer keys/SAS tokens, and Graph API application permissions. These systems don't share identifiers, maintain different logs, and use different data models, letting an attacker hop between them undetected. Attack timeline: Phase 1 (03:27–03:50 UTC) — service principal signs in from a Netherlands hosting provider, self-grants Global Administrator within 2.5 minutes, adds attacker-controlled client secrets to 26 application registrations. Phase 2 (04:32–04:37 UTC) — calls elevateAccess to gain User Access Administrator at root scope, self-assigns Owner-class roles, harvests storage account keys from four accounts, steals root access keys for Event Hub namespaces carrying audit telemetry, and gains access to three Key Vaults. Phase 3 (through ~09:57 UTC) — confirms backdoor access using planted secrets, then goes quiet. The bridge between Entra roles and Azure RBAC is elevateAccess, a single API letting a Global Admin grant themselves root-level User Access Administrator, an action invisible in the RBAC blade and absent from the AzureActivity log. Key Vault access policies form a parallel authorization model to RBAC; the attacker used both. Bearer keys and SAS tokens grant access to whoever holds them with no attached identity, and data-plane use of resulting keys is invisible unless diagnostic logging is explicitly enabled (off by default). The leaked service principal held RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory, a tenant-takeover-equivalent Graph API permission invisible from an app's own roles pane. Non-human identities account for ~97% of managed identities per Sysdig's 2026 Cloud-Native Security Report and are the worst-instrumented part of the permission estate; removing the original GA grant does nothing to the 26 backdoored app registrations. The investigation succeeded only because control-plane logs were captured to immutable, off-tenant storage the attacker couldn't reach. Recommendations include inventorying all five planes as one estate, treating NHIs as first-class identities, watching for elevateAccess and similar cross-plane bridge events, disabling shared-key storage access, and enabling several diagnostic logs (MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs, storage/Event Hub/Key Vault data-plane diagnostics) that are off by default, then correlating everything into a single identity-centric timeline.

4eea0de29a4c.text: Microsoft released patches for 570+ vulnerabilities in July 2026 Patch Tuesday, including two actively exploited vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-56155 and CVE-2026-56164) and one previously disclosed flaw (CVE-2026-50661). Following the release, researcher Nightmare Eclipse published a proof-of-concept exploit for an unpatched Windows elevation of privilege vulnerability called LegacyHive. CVE-2026-56155 is an elevation of privilege flaw in Active Directory Federation Services with documented wild exploitation; Microsoft bundled fixes into Windows updates and began hardening the AD FS Distributed Key Manager container's Access Control List. Dustin Childs from TrendAI's Zero Day Initiative noted AD FS is exactly the kind of identity infrastructure attackers target for pivoting after initial access. CVE-2026-56164 is a remotely exploitable SharePoint Server elevation of privilege flaw reported by Google's incident responders, already under active exploitation; enabling AMSI provides partial mitigation, but security updates remain essential, particularly for related SharePoint RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-50522, CVE-2026-58644) and a critical security feature bypass (CVE-2026-55040). Rapid7's Adam Barnett explained CVE-2026-55040 is the first in a pair of exploits which, when chained, enable unauthenticated remote code execution against vulnerable SharePoint servers; the second vulnerability remains embargoed pending August 2026 patches. CISA urged SharePoint hardening due to concurrent exploitation of recently patched CVE-2026-32201 and CVE-2026-45659. CVE-2026-50661 is a Windows BitLocker security feature bypass that CrowdStrike suggested may be the patch for GreatXML, a BitLocker bypass exploit previously released by Nightmare-Eclipse. Microsoft pre-announced the high vulnerability count, confirming AI-accelerated internal vulnerability discovery, and stated that if critical updates aren't delivered within a couple of weeks of release, attackers gain adequate time for exploitation; it updated deployment recommendations to require patching within three days, with zero-to-one day deadlines and maximum two-day grace periods for the most severe issues. Tenable's Satnam Narang highlighted that CVE-2026-45659 was originally marked 'exploitation less likely' yet was added to CISA's KEV list July 1, and noted Anthropic's Red Team found its Mythos Preview model able to produce proof-of-concept exploits for 13 of 14 vulnerabilities rated 'Exploitation Less Likely.' Five Eyes cybersecurity agencies recommended organizations integrate AI tools for earlier vulnerability detection and faster incident response, while also reducing attack surface, accelerating patching, and strengthening identity controls. Update: Microsoft updated CVE-2026-58644's advisory on July 16, 2026, confirming active exploitation.

a77a9d164423.text: Progress Software has confirmed that a zero-day vulnerability was responsible for the recent ShareFile Storage Zones Controller disruption, with access being restored following service interruptions. The company disabled access to ShareFile accounts for Storage Zones Controller customers two days prior, citing concerns about 'a credible external security threat.' Progress stated that as of Tuesday, July 14th, access had been restored for customers who applied security patches. The vulnerability affects versions 5.x and 6.x of the Storage Zones Controller product. Progress characterized it as high-severity and released patched versions to customers, stating it has 'no evidence of unauthorized access to any ShareFile customer account or data.' In private communications to customers, Progress described the security defect as a path traversal bug exploitable by administrative users, allowing them to 'read arbitrary files accessible to the application's service account, write threat actor-controlled content to arbitrary directories, or enumerate the server filesystem layout.' WatchTowr founder Benjamin Harris questioned the aggressive response to an admin-only vulnerability, suggesting there may be undisclosed details about the vulnerability or attacker activity, and advised organizations to assume exposed systems may have been compromised and to update immediately rather than assuming a patch resolves all concerns.

3ffff7da34ef.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned Tuesday that attackers are actively exploiting three vulnerabilities to hack Internet-exposed on-premises SharePoint Server instances. These security flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-32201, CVE-2026-45659, and CVE-2026-56164) affect all supported self-hosted SharePoint Server versions, including SharePoint Server Subscription Edition. As detailed in a Tuesday advisory, attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities to bypass authentication, gain remote code execution, and carry out post-exploitation activity, including stealing Internet Information Services machine keys and gaining persistence to deploy malware on compromised systems. CISA also flagged two more SharePoint Server vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-55040 and CVE-2026-58644), which Microsoft patched on Tuesday and tagged as attractive targets for attackers, although they are not yet known to have been exploited in the wild. Shadowserver currently tracks nearly 10,000 Internet-exposed Microsoft SharePoint servers, with over 800 of them unpatched against the CVE-2026-32201 and CVE-2026-45659 vulnerabilities. CISA urged security teams to closely monitor affected servers for signs of exploitation and recommended applying Microsoft's latest patches, verifying successful installation, shortening patching cycles, enabling Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) integration for SharePoint web applications, and using Microsoft Defender Antivirus detections to detect and remediate compromise. Additional hardening measures include hunting for and remediating intrusion artifacts before rotating IIS machine keys, establishing tailored logging to monitor for anomalous activity, avoiding direct internet exposure of SharePoint servers unless necessary, and reviewing Microsoft's official SharePoint Server security-hardening guidance. It is also advisable to block external access to SharePoint Central Administration and restrict farm and database communication to required systems, placing servers behind a Layer 7 reverse proxy where exposure is required. CISA added the three actively exploited vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on April 14 (CVE-2026-32201), July 1 (CVE-2026-45659), and July 14 (CVE-2026-56164). Federal agencies have until July 17 to secure SharePoint servers affected by CVE-2026-56164 under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04 or discontinue them if mitigations cannot be applied. In total, since November 2021, CISA has flagged 11 Microsoft SharePoint vulnerabilities that have been exploited in attacks, with 7 also exploited in ransomware attacks.

04a413158a2b.text: Industrial control system manufacturers released critical security updates in July 2026. The three major vendors addressed numerous vulnerabilities across their product portfolios: Siemens published nine advisories covering six critical vulnerabilities. A token invalidation flaw in Opencenter X received a CVSS score of 10, "allowing an attacker to bypass authentication and gain full access to the application." Additional critical issues were patched in Mendix, Sidis Secured SmartPlug, Simatic S7-1500, Cadra, and Desigo CC. High-severity vulnerabilities were also addressed in multiple other products. Schneider Electric released two advisories. One addressed a high-severity vulnerability in IGSS that enables "arbitrary code execution" through specially crafted files. The second covered an authentication bypass in EcoStruxure Cybersecurity Admin Expert exploitable by local attackers. Rockwell Automation published 12 advisories including two critical vulnerabilities. A critical flaw in the 1715 Redundant IO product allows "unauthenticated attacker access to intrusive CLI commands," enabling file manipulation and memory modification. Three additional critical DoS vulnerabilities affecting controller products were patched. Additional vendors including ABB, Mitsubishi Electric, and organizations like CISA and VDE CERT also released related security notifications during the same period. Author: Eduard Kovacs, Published: July 15, 2026 (5:19 AM ET).

dd2e6ab2afce.text: SingGuard-NSFA is an open-source guardrail framework designed to address operational threats in agent workflows. The framework includes four models with parameters ranging from 0.8B to 9B, all built on Qwen3.5 base backbones. Risk Taxonomy: The NSFA risk taxonomy organizes threats using the CIA triad framework—confidentiality, integrity, and availability. It defines 185 risk variants grouped into a smaller set of categories, cross-validated against three OWASP guidelines. The taxonomy covers seven top-level domains: five addressing query-side threats including "prompt injection and jailbreaks, malicious code and cyberattack requests, sensitive information stealing, dangerous operations and tool abuse, and resource abuse," plus two covering response-side threats. Operational Modes: The system operates in two modes: a generative mode producing chain-of-thought analysis for compliance auditing, and a real-time classification mode with latency of 45-57 milliseconds—suitable for production deployment. Performance Results: Benchmarks report F1 scores exceeding 94% across all four models on three multilingual test sets, spanning 133 languages. Testing included datasets from AgentDojo, InjecAgent, and AgentHarm. The system demonstrated compatibility with other guardrails, achieving 17.6 F1 point improvements when integrated with Llama Guard 3. Extensibility Features: New risk categories can be added without retraining the backbone model, maintaining real-time performance requirements. The project is available on GitHub. Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security, Published: July 15, 2026.

b877e379e798.text: SonicWall disclosed active exploitation of two critical zero-day vulnerabilities affecting Secure Mobile Access (SMA) 1000 series appliances. CVE-2026-15409 (CVSS 10.0): A server-side request forgery flaw allowing remote unauthenticated attackers to potentially "cause the appliance to make requests to an unintended location." CVE-2026-15410 (CVSS 7.2): A post-authentication code injection vulnerability in the Appliance Management Console permitting authenticated attackers to "execute arbitrary operating system commands as administrator." Patches and Indicators: Available patches include versions 12.4.3-03453 and 12.5.0-02835. Organizations should check logs for suspicious indicators including requests to /__api__/login or /__api__/logout, requests to /wsproxy, and unusual hotfix rollbacks. Attack Chain: Security researchers from Rapid7 observed threat actors chaining both vulnerabilities to gain device control. Once compromised, attackers "extracted high-value credentials, active session databases, and Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP) multi-factor authentication seed configurations" to establish persistent access and conduct lateral movement into corporate networks. CISA added these flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, requiring federal agencies to patch by July 17, 2026. Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, Published: July 15, 2026.

a2f1baf06dbb.text: SonicWall is urging customers to immediately update SMA1000 secure remote access appliances, which are being targeted by threat actors via two new zero-day vulnerabilities. The vulnerabilities are tracked as CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, and they affect SMA1000 versions 6210, 7210, and 8200v. Enterprises using these products have been instructed to update to hotfix releases 12.4.3-03453 or 12.5.0-02835. CVE-2026-15409 has been described as a critical server-side request forgery (SSRF) issue affecting the Appliance Work Place interface. It allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to cause the targeted appliance to make requests to unintended locations. CVE-2026-15410 is a high-severity code injection issue affecting the Appliance Management Console (AMC), and it can allow an attacker with admin privileges to execute arbitrary OS commands. "SonicWall PSIRT has investigated multiple cases indicating the active exploitation of the vulnerabilities" noted in the advisory. The vendor shared indicators of compromise to help enterprises detect potential attacks. The two vulnerabilities may be chained together. Volexity assisted SonicWall's investigation into the zero-day attacks but has not released details. CISA added both CVE identifiers to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, urging government agencies to address them by July 17. SonicWall products have a history of exploitation by threat actors, including cybercriminals. CISA's KEV catalog currently includes 17 flaws affecting SMA1000 appliances. Author: Eduard Kovacs, Published: July 15, 2026 (1:19 AM ET).

460ee4cefdb5.text: A newly discovered macOS infostealer called CrashStealer is deceiving users by masquerading as Apple's crash-reporting tool. The malware was first detected in early July and delivered through a disk image named "Werkbit Setup" that carries a valid Apple developer ID and notarization ticket. The attack chain involves directing users to a signed dropper that bypasses Apple's Gatekeeper security feature. Once executed, the application contacts GitHub APIs to download and decode a malicious script that fetches the CrashStealer payload. The malware then displays a fake macOS authorization prompt to harvest system login credentials. According to Jaron Bradley, Director of Jamf Threat Labs, "The presence of a Developer ID shows us that the application was signed by a developer who purchased a signing certificate" that authenticates the malicious application and reduces security warnings to victims. Once installed, CrashStealer steals usernames, passwords, cryptocurrency wallet credentials, and keychain data. The malware distinguishes itself through client-side AES-GCM encryption and anti-analysis techniques including control-flow flattening and anti-debugging measures. After Jamf Threat Labs reported the compromised developer account to Apple, the company immediately revoked the developer ID. Author: Danny Palmer, Contributing Writer, Infosecurity Magazine, Published: 14 July 2026.

b7c8aa9fcb84.text: Three major software vendors released security patches addressing 15 vulnerabilities across their product portfolios on Tuesday. ServiceNow addressed a critical remote code execution flaw in its AI platform, tracked as CVE-2026-6875 with a CVSS score of 9.5. The vulnerability could be exploited without authentication. The company stated: "ServiceNow addressed this vulnerability by deploying a security update to hosted instances." Ivanti released fixes for two security defects in its Xtraction data aggregation tool (CVE-2026-14902 and CVE-2026-14903), including a medium-severity open redirect and a high-severity path traversal vulnerability that could expose arbitrary files. Fortinet published 11 security advisories detailing 12 vulnerabilities across multiple products including FortiOS, FortiProxy, FortiSASE, FortiSIEM, and others. The most severe flaws were high-severity bugs in FortiAuthenticator and FortiSandbox allowing remote attackers to retrieve sensitive information. All three vendors reported no evidence of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities in the wild. Author: Ionut Arghire, Published: July 15, 2026 (7:02 AM ET).

9dc81e5c40ba.text: Fortinet has announced new capabilities for its unified endpoint platform, FortiEndpoint, designed to help organizations securely adopt AI, protect sensitive data, and reduce risk. By bringing AI visibility and control, native data security, endpoint risk scoring, and FortiAI-assisted operations into FortiEndpoint, Fortinet enables security teams to better govern AI usage, reduce sensitive data exposure, enforce risk-aware access, and simplify security operations across distributed environments. Michael Xie, President and CTO at Fortinet, stated that "Organizations need a simpler and more effective way to manage security as their environments become more complex and AI-enabled." He emphasized the company's strategy to consolidate security functions through one agent, one console, and one license. Key Innovation Areas: Securing AI use at the endpoint: FortiEndpoint provides centralized visibility over sanctioned and unsanctioned AI applications and agents, allowing organizations to identify tools in use, monitor adoption, and detect shadow AI. Granular guardrail policies enable security teams to allow, restrict, monitor, or block applications based on organizational requirements. Reducing AI-driven data exposure: The platform now natively supports Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to inspect sensitive data exchanged with AI applications, automatically preventing leakage of personally identifiable information, intellectual property, and financial data. Built-in user coaching provides real-time policy guidance. Unifying endpoint security and operations: FortiAI-Assist simplifies administration by allowing security teams to investigate events using natural language, generate investigation summaries, and identify high-risk devices. Adaptive zero-trust capabilities provide dynamic risk and compliance scoring. Chris DePuy, Technology Analyst at 650 Group, noted that Fortinet addresses "visibility into AI usage, control over sanctioned and unsanctioned tools, protection against sensitive data leakage, and real-time coaching" through an integrated platform approach. Published: July 15, 2026.

fc38d1d8ca0d.text: Delinea has redesigned its partner program to address the emerging challenge of securing machine identities and AI agents. The company's research reveals a significant gap: "Machine identities outnumber human identities by as much as 50 to 1," and 46% of organizations lack adequate identity governance for AI systems. The new Delinea Partner Advantage Program responds to partner feedback about shrinking margins, channel conflict, and unclear engagement terms. The program offers measurable customer outcomes, including "$2.2M average annual ROI per customer" and "70% reduction in standing privileges across cloud and on-premise environments." Program Features for Sell Partners: Deal registration with 30% discount at Select tier; Teaming protections (20-25% discounts across tiers); Renewal protections for partners investing in customer relationships. The platform includes AI-powered capabilities for streamlined onboarding, intelligent deal registration, personalized partner hubs, and automated incentive claim validation. The program launches with three tiers—Elite, Premier, and Select—designed to scale with partner growth. Future phases will introduce tailored engagement models for MSPs, ISVs, GSIs, and other partner types, positioning Delinea as a comprehensive identity security partner solution. Author: Scott Goree, Published: July 2026.

20ea6b899bf5.text: Researchers from ETH Zurich have created a new type of pixel called a "Fourier pixel" that can simultaneously display video and capture images. This pixel manipulates light's intensity, oscillation phases, and polarization to generate and sense arbitrary light fields. Schneier draws a troubling parallel to George Orwell's 1984, where the telescreen served as both receiver and transmitter: "Any sound that Winston made, above the level of a very low whisper, would be picked up by it; moreover, so long as he remained within the field of vision which the metal plaque commanded, he could be seen as well as heard." The development was published in Nature and represents advancement toward ubiquitous dual-function display technology that could simultaneously entertain and monitor viewers without their awareness. The comment section reflects widespread concerns about privacy implications, data collection, advertising surveillance, and the absence of protective legislation to prevent misuse of such technology. Author: Bruce Schneier, Published: July 15, 2026.

7285d9a34cad.text: Security firm Mindgard discovered a critical vulnerability in Cursor, an AI-powered code editor, that allows arbitrary code execution on Windows systems simply by opening a malicious repository. The Vulnerability: When a developer opens a repository folder in Cursor on Windows, the application searches for a Git binary in multiple locations—including the workspace root directory itself. If an attacker places an executable named git.exe in the project's root, Cursor automatically executes it without user confirmation or warning. As security researcher Peter Garraghan explained, "git rev-parse --show-toplevel" commands trigger execution, and Cursor repeats this operation continuously while the project remains open. The attack requires no prior system access or user interaction beyond opening the folder. Attack Prerequisites and Impact: The exploit works exclusively on Windows; macOS and Linux are unaffected. The attacker needs only to commit a malicious binary to a public repository. When cloned, the executable runs with the developer's full privileges, gaining access to source code, SSH keys, and cloud authentication tokens. Disclosure Timeline: Mindgard reported the flaw on December 15, 2025, but received inadequate responses from Cursor's security team. After seven months without a patch or official advisory, Mindgard published complete technical details on July 15, 2026—employing full disclosure as a last resort. Vendor Responses: Cursor dismissed the finding as "out of scope," arguing it requires malicious input already present in the workspace. The company acknowledged poor communication but offered no timeline for fixes. Similar vulnerabilities affected GitHub Copilot CLI, Google's Gemini CLI, and OpenAI's Codex—none of which had been patched as of June 2026. Defensive Measures: Until patches arrive, security experts recommend opening untrusted repositories in disposable VMs or Windows Sandbox, inspecting cloned repositories for suspicious executables (git.exe, node.exe, npx.exe), implementing AppLocker or Windows App Control restrictions, and deploying Workspace Trust features where available. Author: Swati Khandelwal, Published: July 15, 2026.

73fe13f0f663.text: ClickFix has evolved from an isolated social engineering technique into a sophisticated Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) ecosystem, according to research from ReversingLabs. The attack method emerged in late 2023 and gained its name from Proofpoint in mid-2024. How ClickFix Works: The technique bypasses traditional exploits by presenting fake webpages mimicking CAPTCHA checks, browser updates, or meeting errors. Users are instructed to open Windows Run or macOS Terminal and paste a command. JavaScript has already copied malicious code to the clipboard before instructions appear. The command executes through trusted system tools like PowerShell, mshta, or curl. Users encounter ClickFix pages through compromised websites, malvertising, SEO poisoning, and phishing campaigns impersonating IT teams or vendors. Industrialized Attack Model: Complete ClickFix packages range from "$250 per month to $1,800 for a lifetime license" with included updates. Premium packages provide pre-built lure templates for major targets like Cloudflare and SSL errors, domain rotation, AV-bypass guarantees, and Telegram support channels. This structure allows attackers with minimal malware expertise to launch campaigns at scale. Evolving Payloads: Lumma Stealer remains the most common payload, but remote access trojans including DarkGate, XWorm, AsyncRAT, NetSupport, and SectopRAT are expanding the attack catalog. Notable Variants: A January 2026 variant called CrashFix deliberately crashes browsers before deploying recovery lures. Related attacks include FileFix, PromptFix targeting AI tools, and ConsentFix exploiting OAuth screens. Defense Strategies: ReversingLabs developed a structural YARA rule analyzing lure pages themselves rather than payloads. Testing flagged 123 confirmed ClickFix lures that "evaded every antivirus engine tested." The rule is available as open-source software. Additional protections include PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, script block logging, Windows Defender Application Control, AppLocker, and employee training. Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security, Published: July 15, 2026.

713136cb45c5.text: The White House announced the launch of Gold Eagle, a new coordination mechanism designed to accelerate the detection, prioritization, and patching of vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure. The initiative pairs open source software maintainers with critical infrastructure operators through a shared reporting and remediation pipeline, utilizing existing federal authorities and resources. Gold Eagle involves collaboration among CISA, the Treasury Department, and the Department of War, alongside private-sector partners. The program aims to eliminate duplicate vulnerability scanning across agencies and companies while delivering prioritized remediation guidance to defenders in government and industry. The initiative stems from Executive Order 14409, "Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security," signed by President Trump on June 2. The executive order called for an AI-enabled clearinghouse to identify and fix software vulnerabilities, with Gold Eagle now serving as the operational implementation. According to the White House, Gold Eagle has begun receiving and triaging vulnerability reports "from across industries and sectors" and coordinating scan verification, though participating companies, specific AI models used, and vulnerability prioritization methods remain unspecified. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stated: "GOLD EAGLE serves as the vanguard of America's cyber defense. We are leveraging frontier AI alongside top American innovators to safeguard our critical infrastructure." The launch follows the Trump administration's removal of restrictions on Anthropic's latest AI models. Reports indicate CISA is using Anthropic's Mythos to scan and audit government software for vulnerabilities. Author: Eduard Kovacs, Published: July 15, 2026.

13dad2bfa561.text: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers identified TuxBot v3 Evolution, a previously undocumented modular IoT botnet framework. The malware developers leveraged an LLM to accelerate code development, which introduced several critical bugs that rendered key features non-functional. Notably, the LLM included safety disclaimers in the source code that developers failed to remove before deployment. While the framework's core infection mechanisms work—including Telnet brute-forcing with 1,496 credential pairs and encrypted C2 communications—exploit systems and several fallback channels are broken due to implementation errors traceable to AI-generated code. Framework Architecture: C-based bot agent compiling for 17 architectures (ARM, MIPS, x86_64, PowerPC, RISC-V, etc.); Go-based C2 server with DDoS-for-hire panel and multi-user admin interface; Custom exploit virtual machine with modular .expl file format; Docker-based test infrastructure including a 'battle arena' for testing DDoS methods; Automated build system cross-compiling payloads for multiple architectures. Development Timeline: January 3, 2025 developer clones MHDDoS from GitHub, revealing Iranian origin via hostname leak; August 6, 2025 domain registered; January 2026 benchmark reports and first VirusTotal submission; March 2026 C2 first observed on Xpanse; April 2026 six new production samples detected. LLM-Assisted Development Issues: raw LLM chain-of-thought reasoning left in source comments; C2 authentication module falsely claims Argon2id but uses PBKDF2 with SHA256; every bot file carries an unremoved AI-generated safety disclaimer. Functional Status: Working: multi-architecture compilation, primary encrypted C2 (X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305), Telnet/SSH/HTTP/ADB scanners, UDP/TCP/DNS DDoS floods, persistence, stealth, DGA, P2P gossip. Non-functional: exploit engine, exploit VM, IRC/HTTP C2 fallback (XOR key bug), Layer 7 HTTP DDoS methods, 16 native C exploits. XOR Encryption Key Bug: string table encrypted with two different keys causes garbage output for nine entries including IRC credentials, HTTP C2 URLs, and exploit payloads with dropper IP 185.10.68.127; researchers used LLM prompts to fix this, restoring functionality. C2 Infrastructure: 209.182.237.133 (bot protocol, SSH admin, JSON API), 185.10.68.127 (dropper, FlokiNET Iceland, also serves Kaitori v3.9 tying it to Keksec/AISURU). Scanner uses 1,496 Telnet credential pairs; successful HTTP credentials are never reported to C2 (stubbed out). DDoS framework registers 78 attack vectors but 47 Layer 7 HTTP vectors incorrectly redirect to TCP SYN handler. Overall assessed ~70% functional; operator likely possesses corrected variants given active infrastructure and April 2026 new sample detections. Authors: Chris Navarrete, Doel Santos, Published: July 15, 2026.

e5d24bf8cac7.text: Kaspersky researchers identified a comprehensive malware framework called OkoBot that targets cryptocurrency users through a sophisticated multi-stage infection chain. The campaign, active since January 2026, represents an evolution of the previously documented TookPS downloader. Key Findings: Initial Infection Vectors: The malware spreads through ClickFix attacks and fraudulent GitHub repositories. One notable example involved a fake SQL Server Management Studio package that was actually the legitimate Audacity audio editor with embedded malicious code. Attack Architecture: The framework comprises over 20 malicious payloads working in concert. As researchers note, "this campaign differs from previous activity in that it uses a new framework to deliver all malicious modules and orchestrate them via an SSH tunnel." Core Capabilities: Browser extension installation and concealment; Cryptocurrency wallet seed phrase harvesting; Keystroke logging with screenshot capture; Video recording of wallet application windows; SSH tunnel establishment for remote access. Malicious Components: SeedHunter (targeting Ledger and Trezor wallets), MC Keylogger (capturing clipboard and USB device data), OkoSpyware (recording video and keystrokes), and ext_daemon (managing browser extensions). Geographic Impact: Hundreds of victims identified across 25+ countries, with highest concentrations in Brazil, Vietnam, Canada, Mexico, and Turkey. Attribution Notes: No confirmed attribution to known threat actors, though Russian-language comments in code and geoblocking techniques suggest Russian-speaking threat actors. Author: Yaroslav Kikel, Published: July 15, 2026.

969344923cad.text: Four compromised npm packages within the @asyncapi namespace have been distributing a multi-stage botnet loader, according to security research from OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, and StepSecurity. Affected Packages: @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1, @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/specs (v6.11.2, v6.11.2-alpha.1). Attack Mechanism: The poisoned packages contain obfuscated first-stage payloads that download encrypted second-stage payloads identified as Miasma from IPFS. Unlike typical supply chain attacks using install hooks, this malware executes when the infected module loads in Node.js, launching a detached background process. The second-stage "sync.js" loader downloads from an IPFS hash and contains encrypted components that decode to the Miasma tasking framework. Malware Capabilities: The framework includes 744 modules supporting six C2 communication channels via HTTP, Nostr relay, IPFS, BitTorrent DHT, libp2p GossipSub, and Ethereum smart contracts. Features encompass credential theft, AI tool poisoning, LAN lateral movement, and propagation across npm, PyPI, and Cargo registries. A persistence mechanism establishes systemd, crontab, macOS launchd, and Windows Registry autostart keys. Evasion Tactics: The malware incorporates a dead man's switch monitoring stolen tokens and triggers directory wipes if revoked. It avoids systems identified as sandboxes or virtual environments and skips machines with Russian language settings or security tools from CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender, CarbonBlack, Cylance, Osquery, Tanium, and Qualys. Attack Vector: According to StepSecurity, the attacker gained push access to repositories and exploited GitHub Actions release pipelines, publishing packages with valid OIDC provenance attestations without stealing npm tokens. The compromise originated from a pull request vulnerability in the asyncapi/generator repository using misconfigured "pull_request_target" workflows. A researcher had submitted a proof-of-concept demonstrating the vulnerability in April 2026, but the fixing pull request remained unmerged when the attack occurred July 14, 2026. Attribution Uncertainty: While the malware shares technical similarities with previous Shai-Hulud and Miasma campaigns, definitive attribution remains unclear. Microsoft tracks the artifacts as MiasmStealer and Supychain. Mitigation Note: The malware executes at module-load time rather than during installation. Therefore, the common mitigation of running "npm install --ignore-scripts" does not prevent execution of this particular threat. All five malicious versions have been unpublished from the npm registry. Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, Published: July 15, 2026.

46c19ff390e6.text:
AWS has expanded Security Hub with new capabilities for AI workload protection and Microsoft Azure security monitoring. The centralized security platform now enables organizations to collect and prioritize security findings across multiple cloud environments.

Azure Security Monitoring: Security Hub now discovers and evaluates Azure virtual machines, container images, Function Apps, and identities for misconfigurations and vulnerabilities. It performs posture assessments using the CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark. Azure findings integrate with existing AWS workflows, allowing teams to assess risk through a unified interface.

AI Workload Protection: Amazon GuardDuty AI Protection is now generally available, providing threat detection for Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker. The service identifies unusual model usage patterns and detects cost harvesting attacks where compromised credentials are exploited to run expensive AI inference. GuardDuty's AI-powered investigations feature (currently in preview) analyzes findings automatically, providing confidence scores and MITRE ATT&CK mappings to help teams distinguish malicious activity from benign events. Security Hub includes a new AI inventory tracking AWS-managed services, self-hosted models on EC2/ECS/EKS, and external model endpoints, correlating assets with security findings across the infrastructure.

f07989dcea0e.text:
The UK government has added several new cyber-related scenarios to its National Risk Register; some of which could theoretically result in mass casualties.

The register is based on the government's internal, classified National Security Risk Assessment, and considers malicious risks like terrorism and cyber-attacks alongside non-malicious risks such as severe weather incidents.

In the latest edition, published on July 14, the government added new scenarios anticipating what might happen in the event of cyber-attacks on digital infrastructure, water infrastructure, and police systems, as well as a mass CrowdStrike-style outage impacting IT systems.

There's also a new section devoted to interference in democratic processes, which could come from: "attacks on election infrastructure, deterioration of the online information space, harassment and intimidation towards candidates or voters, the hack and leak of sensitive information relating to a party or a prominent individual, and any element of foreign interference in any of these."

New Identified Risks:

Cyber-attack on data infrastructure: A sophisticated attack against UK colocation datacenters allowing data exfiltration. Recovery could take "several days to weeks," with information restoration potentially taking years. Rated as having 5-25% likelihood ("highly unlikely") and "moderate" impact: up to 200 fatalities, 400 casualties, and costs reaching hundreds of millions of pounds.

Cyber-attack on water infrastructure: Malicious actors infiltrate operational technology systems, deploying destructive malware causing loss of system visibility and control. Major disruptions could take months to recover from, resulting in physical and mental health casualties. Same likelihood and impact scoring as above.

Cyber-attack on policing infrastructure: Could result in compromised investigations, staff safety risks, reduced intelligence access, and diminished frontline policing effectiveness. Most severe impacts likely last several days; ongoing disruption could persist for months. Same likelihood and impact scores.

Digital outage: Key impacts include shutdown of communications, emergency services, transport, border control, financial systems, and broadcasting, plus widespread smart device failures. Government assesses likelihood between 1% and 25%+, with impact ranging from moderate to catastrophic.

Government Response: Chief Secretary to the Prime Minister Darren Jones stated that updates were necessary given "proliferation of AI and the growing dependence of critical infrastructure on IT and OT systems."

The government announced plans for a "landmark national resilience campaign" later in 2026, designed to encourage households to adopt simple measures improving their resilience to cyber-attacks and other risks.

81b451235d32.text:
FreeRDP is a free implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol, released under the Apache license, and it runs on a large share of workstations and servers through the many tools built on it. The 3.29.0 version is a security, bugfix, and maintenance update that resolves 22 advisories.

What the fixes address: The commits encompass hardening efforts distributed across the codebase. Multiple patches introduce bounds and length checks to media and channel code, including AV1 decode output limits, region rectangle checks matching existing AVC handling, and an H.264 decoder fix for surface dimension inconsistency. The camera channel received data validity checks and a fix for config descriptor reading.

Cryptographic and connection pathways received attention as well. One patch ensures the core rejects abbreviated server random values during key establishment. Another enhances handling of embedded null bytes in X.509 certificate processing. The update implements endpoint FedAuth token authentication and a server response size check in the Windows client. Resource limits and general runtime hardening complete the security commits.

These improvements reach clients across multiple platforms. This release cycle also included iOS build fixes, Android build corrections, and clipboard MIME format handling improvements in the SDL client.

A quick release cadence: FreeRDP maintains frequent releases. Version 3.29.0 shipped one week after 3.28.0, with earlier releases appearing every few weeks throughout spring. Version 3.28.0 introduced features including a revived iOS client and new server-side smartcard API. Version 3.29.0 prioritizes security following "a very rigorous review since our last release by a couple of security researchers," according to maintainer Armin Novak.

The library functions as the RDP engine within many downstream tools. Vulnerabilities in widely-embedded components affect far more than direct users, making coordinated fix batches particularly valuable.

Users can obtain FreeRDP 3.29.0 from the project's release server.

060ef73f1e65.text:
Microsoft is blocking this month's Windows 11 security updates on some Dell devices because they are causing shutdowns and performance issues.

This known issue affects only Dell systems after installing the KB5101650 cumulative update released Tuesday for Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2 devices.

"After installing the June 23, 2026, Windows preview update (KB5095093), a limited number of Dell devices might display a yellow exclamation point in Device Manager next to the Intel Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver," Microsoft stated.

"These devices can potentially experience unexpected shutdowns, poor performance, increased heat, and battery drain."

The root cause is a change in the June 2026 KB5095093 preview cumulative update that creates a conflict between the new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface and the Intel Innovation Platform Framework (IPF) Processor Participant driver.

"This issue was reported by Dell during testing and identified as an incompatibility between the Intel driver and the new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface introduced in the June 23, 2026, Windows preview update."

The Intel IPF Processor Participant driver manages system power and thermals by adjusting processor cooling, power consumption, and thermal performance.

Due to this incompatibility, Windows displays a yellow exclamation mark beside the Processor Participant driver in Device Manager.

Microsoft is working with Dell to resolve the issue and has halted pushing KB5101650 to affected systems. "Microsoft plans to release a resolution for affected devices in the coming days."

e5a26dc17d63.text:
U.S. federal prosecutors have unsealed charges against three Russian nationals accused of operating bulletproof hosting services that supported ransomware gangs causing over $62 million in damages globally.

The defendants are: Aleksandr Volosovik (alias "Yalishanda"), owner of Media Land; Yulia Pankova, owner of ML.Cloud who handled legal and financial matters; Kirill Zatolokin, who collected customer payments.

These hosting services provided infrastructure across multiple countries—including China, Finland, the Netherlands, and the United States—used for malware delivery, command-and-control operations, phishing attacks, and hosting illegal content.

According to prosecutors, "The victims in this case are not only in Ohio, but also in 20 other states...They include banks, schools, government entities, hospitals, and media companies."

The services supported major ransomware operations including Lockbit, Blacksuit, and Play. Infrastructure was also used for distributed denial-of-service attacks against U.S. companies and critical infrastructure.

The State Department is offering up to $10 million through its Rewards for Justice program for information about the defendants or their associates. The European Union and UK have also announced sanctions against the individuals and companies involved.

a6709234134c.text:
Strike Graph's Trust Chain is a third-party risk management (TPRM) solution that fundamentally shifts how organizations assess vendor security. Rather than relying on vendor self-reporting through questionnaires, the platform requires submission of actual compliance evidence that undergoes automated validation.

Verify AI Technology: The platform's distinguishing feature is its patent-pending Verify AI engine. When vendors submit compliance documents, the system tests whether evidence actually demonstrates the required controls. As noted in the article, "A vendor submitting a penetration test that covers a narrower scope than required by the requesting company, or a policy document that addresses only a subset of the relevant controls, will have those deficiencies surfaced automatically rather than accepted as complete." The technology reduces compliance team workload by 92%—from over 40 hours per vendor to approximately 3.5 hours—by automatically identifying gaps and discrepancies.

Continuous Monitoring: Rather than annual assessments, Trust Chain implements ongoing supply chain monitoring. Compliance teams set evidence expiration schedules, and the system automatically requests updates before documents expire, maintaining real-time visibility into vendor compliance status.

Vendor Portal Experience: Vendors benefit from a centralized submission platform rather than completing redundant questionnaires for each customer. The platform achieves an 84% vendor response rate compared to industry averages around 67%.

Regulatory Context: The article emphasizes that questionnaire-based TPRM increasingly conflicts with regulatory frameworks like CMMC Level 2, where named officials bear personal responsibility for vendor compliance attestations. Self-reported assertions alone do not satisfy regulatory evidence standards.

c0f950d2bba8.text:
Google and Mozilla have released fresh Chrome 150 and Firefox 152 updates that resolve critical-severity vulnerabilities.

Mozilla rolled out Firefox 152.0.6 with patches for two critical security defects, warning that exploit code has been published for both.

The bugs are tracked as CVE-2026-15718 and CVE-2026-15719, and are described as an invalid pointer in the 'JavaScript: WebAssembly' component and a site isolation issue in the 'DOM: Navigation' component.

"We are aware that exploit code for this is public however we are not aware of any attacks in the wild abusing this flaw," Mozilla notes for both weaknesses.

Google fixed 15 vulnerabilities with the latest Chrome update, including two critical use-after-free flaws in Ozone, tracked as CVE-2026-15764 and CVE-2026-15765.

The browser refresh also resolves 12 high-severity bugs across Skia, Libyuv, HTML-in-Canvas, Linux Toolkit Theming, V8, Media, GPU, Core, and UI, including uninitialized use, heap buffer overflow, insufficient policy enforcement, insufficient validation of untrusted input, and use-after-free issues.

Only three of these security defects were reported by external researchers, while the rest were discovered by Google. The internet giant has yet to disclose the bug bounty amounts paid to the researchers.

Google makes no mention of any of the patched vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild. The latest Chrome iteration is now rolling out as versions 150.0.7871.124/.125 for Windows and macOS and as version 150.0.7871.124 for Linux.

7fc22e8c164e.text:
For most of the past decade, the managed detection and response (MDR) decision was straightforward: teams lacking 24/7 SOC capacity outsourced to providers who offered it. This solved resource constraints, with limited alternatives.

However, security leaders now approach MDR renewals differently. Agentic AI SOC platforms can perform substantial analytical work previously requiring human analysts—not just triage and enrichment, but threat reasoning and determination.

MDR Model Limitations: While quality MDR providers offer mature detection libraries and experienced analysts, the model itself creates structural challenges. MDR economics depend on detection content generalizing across hundreds of customers, producing three consequences: Custom detections fall outside scope, representing "10 to 30 percent of alert volume" in mature enterprises. Investigation depth is rationed, with lower-severity alerts receiving minimal enrichment. Organizational context has limitations—analysts cannot maintain intimate knowledge of each customer's unique environment.

AI SOC Advantages: Agentic AI platforms decouple investigation capacity from analyst headcount. They investigate every alert—custom or vendor-generated—with full enrichment at machine speed. Benefits include compressed response times, expanded coverage of previously uninvestigated alerts, and sustained threat hunting capabilities without additional headcount.

Trade-offs: Organizations lose external human oversight, existing detection libraries, threat intelligence relationships, and vendor accountability. AI systems cannot replace digital forensics engagements or provide executive-level human interaction during incidents.

Implementation Strategy: Rather than immediate replacement, teams should migrate incrementally: route out-of-scope alerts first, run parallel systems comparing depth and accuracy, and maintain MDR as backup until confidence builds. Some organizations adopt deliberate hybrids, combining AI SOC with retained MDR or incident response services.

10de67c693c4.text:
Robots that read the world through cameras now lean on large vision-language models to interpret what they see and decide what to do next. These models handle images and text together, so any words that fall inside the camera frame become part of the input. A stop sign, a street name, a sticker on a wall.

Researchers at Michigan Technological University have shown that this reading habit opens a door for attackers, and the door leads to a denial-of-service problem that looks nothing like the ones most defenders track.

The work targets a behavior called overthinking. Reasoning-oriented models sometimes generate long chains of deliberation even for simple questions. Because inference time rises roughly in step with the number of tokens produced, a response that balloons from a sentence to several paragraphs also balloons in latency. The researchers turn that tendency into a weapon. They craft short passages of scene text that, once placed in view of a robot's camera, push the model into extended reasoning and delay its decision.

Think about how most AI security stories go. Someone tricks a model into leaking data it should guard, or coaxes it into saying something it should refuse. This one plays a different game. It goes after availability, the third leg of the classic security triad, and the goal is to keep the system too busy to answer in time.

The idea itself is ancient. Flood a target with more work than it can handle and watch it grind to a halt. What changes here is the delivery. The overload arrives as ordinary words on a sign, the kind a person would read and walk past without a second thought.

The attacker gets no access to model weights, no peek at the developer's hidden prompt, no fancy pixel tricks or sensor meddling. The whole capability is a readable sign placed where the camera will catch it, sized and printed so a human could parse it too.

Not just any text will do this. The researchers tried dropping random paragraphs into a scene, and the robots shrugged them off, answering about as fast as they did with nothing there at all. The triggers that work have to be built on purpose, and figuring out how to build them is the real contribution here.

The recipe turned out to be a stack of demands piled into one sign. A physics word problem. A life-or-death moral choice. A request to write out pseudocode. An order to explain the reasoning before committing to an answer. Any one of these nudges a model toward longer output. Combine them, and the model tangles itself trying to satisfy everything at once, second-guessing and circling back instead of just deciding.

Building those combinations by hand would take forever, so the team automated the search. They let the strongest ingredients breed and mutate across generations, keeping whatever produced the biggest slowdowns, a kind of survival of the most confusing. The clever shortcut is how they scored each candidate. A full overthinking response takes a long time to play out, which makes testing thousands of them painfully slow. The researchers found they could judge a trigger from just its first few dozen words, since the tell-tale signs of a spiral show up almost immediately. That let them screen a huge pile of candidates cheaply and only run the slow, complete test on the handful that looked most promising.

The big number in this paper is a slowdown of nearly seven times, and it comes with a footnote worth reading. That result landed on a model called Gemma3, which happens to be closely related to the one the researchers used to build their triggers in the first place. So it's really a best-case picture, the kind an attacker gets when they already know the target intimately. The more telling question is whether these signs work on models they were never tuned against. On two of those, Kimi-VL and Qwen3-VL, they did, but the effect was milder, somewhere in the range of one and a half to three and a half times slower. Still a real drag, and nowhere near seven.

The team also carried the attack out of the lab and into a room. They bolted a camera onto a small robot, printed a trigger on a sheet of A3 paper like a regulatory sign, and propped it in view. One model slowed to a crawl under the live camera feed, running close to five times slower than normal. The others roughly doubled. The robot never moved during any of this, so what the test proves is delay under real optics, and nothing about crashes or anyone getting hurt.

One last check gives the result some spine. When the researchers took attack prompts from earlier text-only research and simply printed them onto signs, most of them did nothing. A prompt that ties a chatbot in knots turns out to be almost harmless once a robot has to read it off a wall and weigh it against what its camera sees. The triggers had to be designed for this setting to work in it.

Here is the reassuring part. The defense costs almost nothing. Cap the token budget, set a hard timeout, and switch to a bounded fallback policy when a response runs long. A lightweight monitor can watch the opening tokens and pull the plug before a full blowup, since the warning signs tend to show up right away.

That simplicity puts the stakes in perspective. The attack only bites systems that run unbounded reasoning models inside a time-sensitive loop, and any team building one can close the gap with a budget and an early-warning check.

b0ae952026c9.text:
Over the past twelve months, researchers documented intrusions in which AI ran exploitation workflows autonomously, generating thousands of commands across dozens of sessions with minimal human direction, according to Check Point's AI Security Report 2026.

AI-powered cyber attacks: The attackers posing the greatest risk are those orchestrating AI across multiple stages of the attack chain without requiring human intervention. They achieve this by obtaining capable AI models and removing their safety controls. Attackers gain AI capabilities by abusing commercial models, using stolen AI credentials, self-hosting freely available open-source models, or purchasing access to AI tools built for cybercrime.

Jailbreaking removes the safeguards that prevent AI models from following malicious instructions. Attackers use carefully crafted prompts to bypass safety controls, although these techniques are regularly patched. A more persistent approach targets AI coding agents by placing malicious instructions in files such as CLAUDE.md, which are automatically loaded at the start of every session. Once planted, the jailbreak remains active until the file is removed.

AI is widely used to develop malware by generating, refining, and debugging code, allowing less experienced attackers to produce more capable tools. Criminal groups and nation-state actors increasingly rely on AI-assisted development. A smaller but growing category of malware also communicates with AI models during execution to generate commands or adapt its behavior in real time.
