That Nichirei Group is unable to provide some services suggests a ransomware attack has made some data unavailable. The mention of "further damage" suggests that discussing whatever happened could divulge clues about security weaknesses that would allow further attacks, perhaps directed at the Group's clients. KFC Japan hasn't posted any information about store closures. Indeed, the company continues to promote seasonal menu items such as a Japanese-style citrus and chicken combo that the chain says is refreshing to eat even in the heat of summer. (Author: Simon Sharwood, APAC Editor; Published: Thursday, July 16, 2026, 03:01 UTC)

ba5d31723327.text: Published: July 15, 2026. Authors: Microsoft Security Research, Ravikant Tiwari, Sagar Patil, Suriyaraj Natarajan, and Arvind Gowda. Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated supply chain attack targeting the @asyncapi npm organization on July 14, 2026. The compromise affected five package versions across four packages, with malicious code executing at import-time rather than through installation hooks. Affected Packages: @asyncapi/specs (versions 6.11.2-alpha.1 and 6.11.2), @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1. Attack Vector: The attacker exploited a vulnerable GitHub Actions workflow using pull_request_target, stealing a bot personal access token (PAT). This enabled unauthorized code commits that triggered legitimate release pipelines, publishing poisoned packages with valid provenance signatures. Execution Method: Code executes when modules are imported via require() or import, spawning a detached child process that downloads "sync.js" from IPFS. Traditional npm --ignore-scripts mitigation does not prevent this attack. Malware: The payload contains the Miasma runtime (M-RED-TEAM v6.4) with capabilities for persistence, command-and-control communication, and credential harvesting targeting over 100 environment variables and credential files. Detection: Microsoft Defender identifies artifacts as "Trojan:JS/MiasmStealer.SC" and "Trojan:Script/Supychain.A". Recommendations: Organizations should immediately remove compromised versions, purge caches, hunt for suspicious NodeJS directories, block IP 85.137.53[.]71 on ports 8080-8091, and rotate all credentials from affected environments.

6421e7bc4334.text: Author: Unit 42. Published: July 15, 2026. The security of the npm ecosystem reached a critical inflection point in September 2025. The Shai-Hulud worm, a self-replicating malware that automated the compromise and redistribution of malicious packages, marked the end of the "nuisance" era of npm attacks and the beginning of a high-consequence threat landscape. Since that watershed moment, Unit 42 has tracked an aggressive acceleration in the frequency and technical depth of supply chain compromises. Attacks have evolved from a series of isolated typosquatting incidents into systematic campaigns by various threat actors to weaponize the trust that powers modern software development. April 2026 Campaigns: Two campaigns emerged in April: the first started April 22, 2026 and included the string Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming. The second started April 29, 2026 and is known as Mini Shai-Hulud. May 2026 Campaigns: In May 2026, the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign continued with two new waves attributed to TeamPCP. These campaigns introduced credential-free initial access techniques and generated the highest single-hour package count of any Shai-Hulud worm to date. Copycat activity has complicated future attribution to TeamPCP. June 2026 Campaign: A new supply chain attack on June 1, 2026 compromised at least 32 packages published under the @redhat-cloud-services npm namespace. The attacker bypassed code review entirely, pushing a payload named Miasma. July 2026 Campaign: Attackers compromised the release pipelines of four core AsyncAPI GitHub repositories on July 14, 2026. In a campaign calling itself miasma-train-p1, they published five trojanized packages to npm, with payloads appearing to be descendants of the Miasma remote access Trojan (RAT). [Note: full article content exceeded retrieval length; remainder of the piece (titled 'The New Baseline for npm Threats' and mitigation guidance) was truncated in the fetch.]

4aaeb0f3b918.text: Authors: Lior Samuni, Todd Stansfield. Published: July 15, 2026. A software bill of materials (SBOM) functions as "a machine-readable inventory of every component, library, and dependency in a piece of software" with version, supplier, and license details. The concept borrows from manufacturing BOMs but catalogs code components rather than physical parts. The article emphasizes that an SBOM differs fundamentally from software composition analysis (SCA). While SCA represents a scanning activity that identifies vulnerabilities at a point in time, an SBOM serves as a persistent inventory. This distinction matters operationally: "An SCA scan gives you a point-in-time list of issues to fix now. The SBOM persists after the scan." Key Components: According to NTIA guidance, an SBOM must include seven required data fields: supplier name, component name, version, unique identifiers, dependency relationships, SBOM author, and timestamp. These enable automated vulnerability matching and component tracking across software estates. Dominant Formats: Two standards dominate: SPDX (a Linux Foundation ISO standard emphasizing license compliance) and CycloneDX (an OWASP standard built for security with native VEX support). A third format, SWID tags, appears mainly in asset management contexts. Real-World Applications: Security teams deploy SBOMs for four primary purposes: vulnerability management paired with Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) data, license and compliance management, incident response to zero-day vulnerabilities, and procurement risk assessment during M&A activities. The Log4Shell vulnerability exemplifies SBOM value: teams with current inventories identified affected systems in minutes, while those without spent weeks reverse-engineering their own software. Compliance Requirements: Multiple regulatory frameworks now mandate SBOMs: US Executive Order 14028 requires them from federal software suppliers, the EU Cyber Resilience Act mandates them for products containing digital elements, and FDA rules require them for certain medical devices. Frameworks like NIST SSDF and PCI DSS expect component inventory maintenance without always naming SBOMs explicitly. Generation and Management: SBOMs should be generated at three possible points: source analysis (fast but incomplete), build-time (most accurate), or binary/runtime analysis (necessary for legacy software). The article stresses automation: "An SBOM should be regenerated every time software is built or released" to prevent staleness. Best Practices: Effective SBOM programs automate generation in CI/CD pipelines, capture transitive dependencies, standardize on established formats, and correlate inventories to live vulnerabilities rather than treating them as static documentation.

a353d7c8e4e6.text: Published: July 16, 2026. Author: Research Special Operations. Four Microsoft SharePoint Server vulnerabilities are under active exploitation, prompting CISA to issue a hardening alert. An additional high-severity flaw recently patched adds pressure for organizations running on-premises deployments. Key Takeaways: CISA confirmed active exploitation of three on-premises SharePoint Server vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-32201, CVE-2026-45659, CVE-2026-56164), which attackers have used to gain unauthorized access, establish remote code execution, steal IIS machine keys and deploy malware for persistence. Two additional SharePoint Server vulnerabilities disclosed on July 14, 2026 (CVE-2026-55040 and CVE-2026-58644) were not yet observed as exploited at publication time, though Microsoft flagged CVE-2026-58644 as exploited on July 15. Microsoft released patches for all five vulnerabilities and Microsoft Defender Antivirus detection signatures are available to identify exploitation activity for three of the actively exploited flaws. Vulnerability Details: CVE-2026-32201 - Spoofing (CVSSv3 6.5, VPR 7.2); CVE-2026-45659 - RCE via deserialization (CVSSv3 8.8, VPR 9.4); CVE-2026-56164 - Elevation of Privilege (CVSSv3 9.8, VPR 9.5); CVE-2026-55040 - Security Feature Bypass (CVSSv3 9.1, VPR 7.3); CVE-2026-58644 - RCE via deserialization (CVSSv3 9.8, VPR 7.9). Attackers combined CVE-2026-32201, CVE-2026-45659 and CVE-2026-56164 to gain entry, extract IIS machine keys, establish persistence, and deploy malware; stolen machine keys can be used to forge requests for further exploitation, and key rotation alone is not sufficient remediation without removing key-harvesting artifacts. As of July 16, 2026, no threat actor attribution or public PoC exists. Detection signatures include Exploit:Script/SuspSignoutReqBody.A, Exploit:Script/ToolPaneAuthBypass.A/.C, and Backdoor:MSIL/LeakFang.A!dha. Tenable has classified all four actively exploited CVEs under Vulnerability Watch and released plugins for all five CVEs, plus an Attack Surface Management subscription to identify exposed SharePoint assets.

0d8ce1c6138e.text: Author: Jules Czarniak. Published: July 17, 2026. Category: Threat Intelligence. As highlighted in the Mandiant M-Trends 2026 report, the mean time-to-exploit (TTE) has dropped to -7 days, meaning vulnerabilities are often exploited a week before a patch even exists. To keep pace, many security teams are exploring how to integrate large language model (LLM) agents into their codebases, development environments and CI/CD pipelines for automated vulnerability discovery and remediation. This blog provides guardrails including: Pre-agent data security and defense-in-depth (agents should not access PII/PHI, treat codebase as untrusted input for prompt injection); Cloud provider limitations and Zero Data Retention agreements; Workload isolation in unprivileged containers; Red Teaming of AI agents themselves; Least-privileged machine identities tied to human controllers with JIT tokens; Supply chain resilience for third-party skills/MCP servers; Toxic Flow Analysis and observable logging of agent actions. It also stresses human-led threat modeling (PASTA framework) since RAG-fed LLMs can hallucinate on stale documentation. Track 1 (Enterprise Vulnerability Management) covers Risk-Based Vulnerability Management using a formula: Final Score = (W1*S_vuln) + (W2*S_asset) + (W3*S_threat), incorporating CVSS, asset exposure/sensitivity (optionally FAIR), and threat context/EPSS. It recommends EASM, CSPM, and CTEM for foundational discovery alongside AI deployment, plus zero trust principles (ZTNA, microsegmentation, SASE) for containment. Track 2 (Product Security) discusses deterministic vs probabilistic tooling limits of LLMs for SAST-style analysis, noting LLMs excel at bug classes with binary oracles (e.g., memory corruption in C/C++) but struggle with architectural/business-logic flaws requiring human judgment. It covers targeted deployment strategies, IDE-integrated vs CI/CD-runner remediation methods, and post-deployment controls (automated rollbacks, model version pinning, audit logging for SOC2/PCI-DSS/FedRAMP/CMMC compliance). Conclusion stresses AI does not replace secure-by-design principles and advocates migrating to memory-safe languages long-term. Acknowledgements: Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and other Google teams.

a1427380523d.text: Author: Alessandro Mascellino. Published: 16 July 2026. A new macOS stealer has combined social engineering tactics with coercive methods to render machines unusable until victims surrender their passwords. According to research from Group-IB published on June 16, the malware—dubbed ClickLock Stealer—has affected at least 100 victims across 33 countries within approximately two months, with more than half located in Europe. The initial sample was uploaded to VirusTotal on June 9 with zero detections. Modular Attack Chain: The attack commenced when victims pasted a command into Terminal from what Group-IB identified as a ClickFix page. An orchestrator script concealed the cursor and displayed a fake Cloudflare progress animation while downloading four components from two compromised WordPress sites. Two tools handled credential theft. A Keychain stealer extracted the Chrome Safe Storage key—the AES encryption key that decrypts Chrome-stored cookies and passwords offline. A credential module displayed a fake password dialog in AppleScript, validating entries against the local directory service so only correct passwords reached operators. A third module searched for cryptocurrency assets, examining more than 30 wallet extensions including MetaMask and Phantom, extracting encrypted vault fields from LevelDB storage. The fourth installed GSocket, an open-source reverse-shell tool reused with roughly 80% of its original code, disguised on macOS as an iCloud process. Forcing Victim Compliance: If victims entered the password initially, operators received it alongside system fingerprint data. If they canceled, the orchestrator installed two LaunchAgents to relaunch credential modules at next login. A kill loop then terminated Finder, Dock, browsers, Terminal and Activity Monitor in a tight cycle running for up to 83 hours. The Keychain module applied similar patterns to force Keychain dialog approval. A parallel loop killed NotificationCenter for approximately six hours to suppress Gatekeeper warnings. All exfiltration occurred over Telegram using three bots and no dedicated command-and-control infrastructure. Modules forged timestamps and deleted themselves, leaving only the GSocket backdoor. Group-IB advised users to treat any website instructing command pasting into Terminal as an attack attempt and to force-shutdown and boot into Safe Mode rather than enter passwords if the desktop suddenly begins terminating applications.

54c8beff2c7f.text: Author: Eric Schwake. Published: July 2026. Read time: 5 minutes. Identity Security Posture Management (ISPM) has transitioned from niche terminology to mainstream security discipline. According to Gartner's assessment, organizations now treat identity as a continuous attack surface worthy of measurement rather than an assumed constant. The core challenge lies in the gap between identification and resolution. A posture score reveals exposure levels but doesn't reduce them independently. Organizations frequently excel at generating lists of risky identities—unvaulted admin accounts, standing privileges, missing multi-factor authentication—yet struggle to close the remediation loop. These findings languish in backlogs month after month, creating perpetual audit findings and unchanged risk profiles. The breakthrough occurs when findings flow directly into enforcement mechanisms. When posture and control sit on the same platform, remediation happens within minutes rather than across prolonged handoff cycles. Unvaulted credentials get secured and rotated; excessive standing privileges convert to time-limited just-in-time access; overpermissioned identities get recalibrated; risky sessions get brokered before credentials reach users. A critical blind spot emerges when posture programs focus exclusively on human accounts. Machine identities and AI agents now outnumber people in most enterprises, yet operate fundamentally differently—created outside IT departments, running with whatever credentials their environments provide, making autonomous access decisions at machine speed. These non-human identities typically carry the heaviest permission loads and resist traditional remediation approaches like MFA prompts or self-directed password rotation. Effective posture for non-human identities requires continuous assessment coupled with controls that govern what agents can access while keeping credentials out of their hands. Each agent must tie to a named human owner for accountability and containment purposes. Security leaders evaluating posture programs should ask two essential questions: Does it encompass machines and AI agents alongside people? When risks surface, does actual remediation occur, or do findings merely generate additional tickets?

aa59ef5dd587.text: Description: A improper neutralization of special elements used in an os command ('os command injection') vulnerability in Fortinet FortiSandbox 5.0.0 through 5.0.5, FortiSandbox 4.4.0 through 4.4.8, FortiSandbox 4.2 all versions, FortiSandbox Cloud 5.0.4 through 5.0.5, FortiSandbox PaaS 5.0.4 through 5.0.5 may allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute unauthorized commands via specifically crafted HTTP requests. Affected Products: Fortinet FortiSandbox (versions 4.2.1-4.2.8, 4.4.0-4.4.8, 5.0.0-5.0.5), Fortinet FortiSandbox Cloud (5.0.4-5.0.5), Fortinet FortiSandbox PaaS (5.0.4-5.0.5). CVSS Score: 9.1-9.8 (Critical) - CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. Key Dates: Published June 9, 2026; Updated July 17, 2026; CISA KEV added July 16, 2026; Due date for remediation July 19, 2026. CWE: CWE-78 (Execute unauthorized code or commands). Exploitation Status: Confirmed as actively exploited by multiple threat actors.

417d862e9978.text: Title: Microsoft SharePoint Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. Description: Deserialization of untrusted data in Microsoft Office SharePoint allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. CVSS Score: 9.8 (Critical) - Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:F/RL:O/RC:C. Affected Products: Microsoft SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016 (versions < 16.0.5556.1005); Microsoft SharePoint Server 2019 (versions < 16.0.10417.20153); Microsoft SharePoint Server Subscription Edition (versions < 16.0.19725.20384). Key Dates: Published July 14, 2026; Updated August 10, 2026; CISA KEV Added July 16, 2026; Patch Due Date July 19, 2026. CWE: CWE-502 (Deserialization of Untrusted Data). Status: Confirmed actively exploited; listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog with 80% exploitation confidence.

7fbddbb47d26.text: Author: Grzegorz Nocoń. Published: July 16, 2026. Bitdefender released new functionality in GravityZone, described as "a unified cybersecurity platform that provides prevention, protection, detection, and response capabilities for organizations of all sizes." Security Analysts Enhancements: The endpoint detection and response (EDR) component received four new Windows raw events: Hardware mount and unmount events, plus initiation of agent uninstall and driver module load capabilities. The "Modify group policy raw event" was renamed to "Modify Windows Group Policy" for consistency. Administrator Features: PHASR Updates - Administrators gained contextual navigation from recommendation details to Risk Management resources or accounts pages, with searches pre-scoped to relevant findings. New policy configuration options allow specification of whether restricted behavioral profiles generate alerts, incidents, or both. The terminology "monitored rules" was replaced with "attack vectors" throughout the platform. Compliance Manager: Indonesia's regulatory standard POJK No. 4/POJK.05/2021 was added, enabling organizations under Financial Services Authority oversight to track IT risk management compliance. MDR Automatic Policy Provisioning: New customer companies with active MDR licenses now automatically receive two MDR-recommended policies, endpoint tags, and assignment rules during onboarding. Network Enhancements: Container host folder deletion became available for offline hosts, and CSV export functionality was added to the Network page, supporting up to 500,000 rows per export. Identity and Access Updates: GravityZone IdP proxy support extended SSO to the MDR portal, supporting Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, and Active Directory Federation Services. MSP Enhancements: A dedicated onboarding templates page was introduced, and CSPM+ and EASM add-ons gained new availability options for monthly subscriptions. API Updates: Rate limiting (5 requests per minute per API key) was applied to HTTP endpoints. New methods and parameters were added for companies, incidents, licensing, and network areas, including EASM support and endpoint tag targeting for custom rules.

002cf865c573.text: Author: Stan Kaminsky. Published: July 16, 2026. Researchers have demonstrated that Google Gemini can be manipulated through prompt injection attacks via calendar invites or text messages, potentially enabling unauthorized actions like opening smart home devices or launching apps. The vulnerability exploits the fact that malicious instructions can be hidden in external content—emails, calendar invites, or messages—that the assistant processes. According to the article, attackers employ a four-step technique: Step 1: Indirect Prompt Injection - Commands are buried in external content rather than coming directly from the user. Step 2: Memory Poisoning - Instructions are saved to the agent's long-term memory to persist across sessions. Step 3: Delayed Execution - Actions are triggered after subsequent user commands to bypass immediate safeguards. Step 4: Fake Context Alignment - Malicious instructions are hidden in text the user cannot see or understand, making approval seem innocent. Once compromised, Gemini can wipe calendar data, send emails to external servers, open websites, manipulate smart home devices, and launch apps including Zoom calls. The article recommends protective measures including disabling notification previews, turning off Gemini features in Gmail/Workspace, revoking specific tool access, and using third-party security software like Kaspersky for Android.

d41e58ce3f64.text: Author: Nick Hayes, Principal AI Evangelist at Tenable. Published: July 16, 2026. Agentic AI adoption is expanding rapidly, yet most security teams develop agents independently rather than collaboratively. Tenable is organizing SWARM, a hands-on build event during Black Hat 2026, where security professionals will work together to create open-source agentic tools for collective defense. Key Takeaways: According to Gartner research, Fortune 500 enterprises will deploy approximately 150,000 AI agents by 2028, compared to fewer than 15 in 2025. This explosive growth creates significant complexity in agent management and operational oversight. Security practitioners are independently developing open-source agentic solutions to reduce manual work—from automating phishing email screening to accelerating threat investigations and enabling less experienced analysts to deliver expert-level analysis. SWARM invites security practitioners to collaborate at Black Hat 2026 (sponsored by AWS and supported by Anthropic) to build next-generation open-source agents, specialized skills, and Model Context Protocol servers that strengthen collective cybersecurity defenses. Current State of Agentic AI in Security: Security teams are already leveraging agentic AI to streamline alert triage, threat hunting, and workflow automation. Real-world examples include PhishER Email Analysis (automating phishing detection via n8n), SOC-Hunter (compressing threat hunting from hours to 90 minutes), and AI Analyst tools (converting security requests into automated SOC operations). However, only 27% of security practitioners report mature agentic AI deployments. Most remain in pilot phases, and development typically occurs in isolation—teams repeatedly solve identical problems without sharing solutions or insights. The SWARM Initiative: SWARM provides a structured environment for security professionals to build collaboratively over several focused days. Participants gain dedicated development time, live expert guidance, and peer collaboration on practical security workflows including triage, remediation, orchestration, and reporting. No advanced development experience is required; practitioners need only articulate the workflows they wish to automate. Winning projects will be recognized during an awards ceremony on August 6, 2026.

ffe6e72004c1.text:
OpenAI has confirmed reports that GPT-5.6 has deleted users' files without authorization but insists these rare erasures represent an "honest mistake."

Following the release of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 family of models on July 9, 2026, tech investor Matt Shumer reported that "GPT-5.6-Sol just accidentally deleted almost ALL of my Mac's files."

A few days later, software engineer Bruno Lemos said, "GPT-5.6 Sol just deleted my whole production database. That's it. Not a joke. This had never happened to me before, with any other model, ever. It's not safe."

Lemos had previously posted a message defending the model, only to experience the issue himself hours later. He initially blamed Shumer for operating the model with "Full-Access" permission rather than a more cautious setting.

The GPT-5.6 model card notes that undesirable behavior surfaces more often in misalignment simulations than it did for GPT-5.5. The documentation defines severity level 3 as "misaligned behavior that a reasonable user would likely not anticipate and strongly object to," which includes deleting cloud storage data without user approval, disabling monitoring systems, using obfuscation to bypass security controls, and uploading sensitive data to unapproved services.

According to Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI's engineering lead for Codex, the model typically attempts to override the $HOME environment variable when configured in Full-Access mode. "The model makes an honest mistake and mistakenly deletes $HOME instead," he explained.

The article notes the irony of characterizing a model error as "honest," suggesting this language implies the AI possesses intent and truthfulness. Sottiaux acknowledged that such incidents are undesirable, stating OpenAI is implementing safeguards including developer message updates, promoting safer permission modes, and adding harness protections.

33e61f4dbca1.text:
A new macOS information-stealing malware dubbed ClickLock terminates all visible processes to force users into entering their system login password.

The malware is designed to steal cryptocurrency assets, login credentials, password-manager data, browser information, and macOS authentication data, and it can also install a persistent backdoor for ongoing remote access to infected systems.

Researchers at Group-IB analyzed the ClickLock shell script after discovering the malware on VirusTotal, where it was first submitted on June 9. At the time of the report, it remained undetected by all security vendors available on the platform.

Further investigation revealed that the malicious script has infected at least 100 systems across 33 countries since May.

The compromise likely begins via a ClickFix lure, as the researchers observed pastes of a malicious command in the Terminal that trigger a fake Cloudflare "human verification" sequence with an animated progress bar.

At the same time, keyboard interrupts are disabled, the terminal cursor is hidden, and the stealer modules are downloaded in the background.

The macOS NotificationCenter is also suppressed for about six hours, effectively disabling notifications that could expose the attack.

Group-IB researchers highlight that ClickLock does not require any exploits or elevated privileges but achieves its goal through social engineering and forced interaction loops.

Operational success is obtained through the malware's mechanism for coercing the victims into entering their macOS system password.

Group-IB says that the script initially displays a fake macOS password dialog using the victim's real username and a downloaded Apple icon.

If the user enters their password, the malware validates the data and exfiltrates it to the attacker via Telegram.

In case the user cancels the dialog, the malware establishes persistence via two macOS LaunchAgents (com.authirity.plist, com.chromer.plist) and reloads at the next login.

At the next activation, the password-stealing module runs a termination loop every 210 milliseconds, targeting key apps (e.g., Finder, Dock, Terminal, Activity Monitor, Console, System Settings, Spotlight, web browsers) and shows only a password dialog on the screen until the victim complies.

Group-IB reports that the loop is configured to continue for 300,000 seconds (about 83 hours), or until the victim supplies a correct password.

The second LaunchAgent runs a separate coercion mechanism that also terminates many of the mentioned system applications, requesting Keychain authorization via a legitimate system prompt, seeking approval to access Chrome's Safe Storage key.

That key could then be used to decrypt offline Chromium-stored passwords, cookies, and autofill information from stolen databases.

This second mechanism has a repeat interval of 200 milliseconds and is configured to last for nearly 35 days (3 million seconds).

ClickLock also deploys a data-harvesting module, which targets the following:

- Data from eight browsers: Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Edge, Opera, Vivaldi, Arc, and Chromium
- Saved logins, cookies, autofill data, bookmarks, local storage, and session storage
- Cryptocurrency wallet extensions and desktop wallet files
- Encrypted wallet vault material for potential offline cracking
- Password-manager extension data
- Cached cryptocurrency addresses across EVM, Bitcoin, Solana, TRON, TON, and Stacks
- Shell histories
- FileZilla FTP configuration and recent-server data
- Basic system information and the public IP address

The harvesting module packages the collected information and a summary log file into a ZIP archive, then uploads it via the Telegram Bot API.

Files larger than 40 MB are split into smaller parts, while retry logic ensures that uploading resumes after temporary network failures.

The final module is a modified version of the open-source tool GSocket that acts as a persistent backdoor for the attackers.

The backdoor establishes persistence through multiple methods, including a LaunchAgent, crontab entries, and modifications to shell configuration files.

It connects through a GSocket relay, allowing the attacker to open a reverse shell and remotely control the system.

Unlike the other ClickLock modules that self-delete after execution, GSocket is the only component that persists on infected systems.

Group-IB warns that "malware leaves a narrow detection window" and that the malicious payloads are hosted on compromised legitimate domains with a clean reputation.

Additionally, the script is not flagged as malicious on VirusTotal, and its modules self-delete after execution, leaving no artifacts.

Despite this, the researchers say that detection is possible based on the activity generated by the malware, such as osascript launching password dialogs, repeated process termination, mass access to browser profile directories, and outbound connections to Telegram's API.

To defend against these attacks, users should avoid pasting in Terminal commands they don't fully understand, especially if the request comes from a website.

"Any page that instructs you to open Terminal, regardless of how professional it looks, is attempting to compromise your system," the researchers say.

If prompted to enter the login password when the rest of the system appears unresponsive, Group-IB recommends forcing a system shutdown by holding the power button and then booting into Safe Mode to recover the system.

77dde387130b.text:
The Coca-Cola Company disclosed that a ransomware attack on its Fairlife dairy subsidiary has disrupted operations, temporarily halting production of Fairlife products across the United States.

In an SEC Form 8-K filing, Coca-Cola reported that Fairlife detected unauthorized system access, including production-related systems, connected to the ransomware incident. The company stated: "After detecting the issue, the Company promptly activated its incident response and business continuity protocols."

The investigation involves external advisors and cybersecurity experts, with law enforcement notified. Coca-Cola confirmed that product quality and safety remain unaffected, though U.S. production facilities are temporarily suspended during system restoration. Canadian operations continue uninterrupted.

The company has not yet determined whether the attack will materially impact operations. Additionally, Coca-Cola has not disclosed whether data was stolen, if extortion demands were received, or which ransomware group is responsible.

At the time of publication, no ransomware gang had claimed responsibility. When contacted, a Coca-Cola spokesperson declined to provide information beyond the public statement.

Fairlife produces ultra-filtered milk, protein shakes, and nutrition drinks including Ultra-Filtered Milk, Core Power Protein Shakes, and Nutrition Plan products.

cb9b71b31a64.text:
Jeff Piontek comments on the Instructure breach:
The forensic review has taken far longer than anyone expected. Through June, Instructure was still finalizing customer-specific findings and asking institutions to designate a security contact to receive them. In early July, the company began delivering the first wave of institution-specific data packets, through a permissioned file-sharing link sent only to designated contacts, covering API provisioning records and user reports. Message data, the most sensitive category, was pushed to a second wave planned for later in the summer.
Then, on July 14, Instructure paused that delivery entirely. The reason given: the third-party platform selected to deliver the data packets may itself have been subject to a security threat. Ten weeks after the original breach, the mechanism built to finally give institutions clarity became a second point of exposure risk.
Meanwhile, the legal exposure keeps compounding. More than half a dozen proposed class actions have been filed against Instructure in federal courts in Utah, New York, and California. Two breaches of the same company, by the same group, in eight months, through two different attack surfaces. That is not a story about one unpatched control. It is a story about nobody having a complete picture of how trust and privilege actually move through a vendor’s environment.
Read more at LinkedIn.

ebf1bc688a1a.text:
The AI supply chain is, in some ways, even more vulnerable to poisoning than that of traditional software.

Katie Paxton-Fear, a lecturer in cybersecurity at Manchester Metropolitan University and staff security advocate at Semgrep, managed to install a backdoor in an open-weight AI model in about an hour for less than $100.

Paxton-Fear demonstrated that she could use fine tuning to alter a model's coding style preferences. She noted that "it was actually really easy" to make the model change from camelCase to snake_case in JavaScript, even when given explicit instructions otherwise. She subsequently conducted a proper backdoor installation.

Her findings showed that only ten training examples were sufficient to make the model's code output reliably vulnerable to remote code execution, even for novel prompts and domains. Larger models proved easier to poison.

Paxton-Fear collaborated with Semgrep colleagues Isaac Evans and Cris Thomas on research highlighting vulnerabilities in open weight models. They emphasized that "even when model weights are public ('open weight'), we have almost no ability to predict its behavior."

The researchers stressed that binary software can undergo reverse engineering analysis to determine complete behavioral descriptions, whereas AI models lack this scrutiny capability.

David Kaplan, AI security research lead at Origin, created a compromised model designed to steal data in drug discovery contexts, exfiltrating information through email without user awareness.

Paxton-Fear's team argues that while poisoned open weight models aren't yet widely documented in use, the real concern involves insufficient observability of AI systems compared to traditional software. They note that compromised models need only "influence decisions in ways that are difficult to detect" to create business risk.

The article concludes that while open weight models present particular tampering vulnerabilities, commercial frontier model providers also resist scrutiny, requesting extraordinary trust access to sensitive data while offering minimal transparency.

331a48869d74.text:
A vulnerability in Anthropic's Claude for Chrome browser extension could allow malicious extensions to trigger predefined AI workflows by simulating user clicks. The flaw was discovered by Ax Sharma of Manifold Security.

The extension listens for click events on page elements that launch built-in AI workflows. These workflows enable Claude to access connected services including Gmail, Google Docs, Google Calendar, and Salesforce. The supported tasks include:

- Reading recent Gmail and unsubscribing from promotional emails
- Opening users' latest Google Docs to read comments
- Accessing Google Calendar to find free slots and create meetings
- Modifying Salesforce leads and converting them to opportunities

The core vulnerability stems from the extension's failure to verify that click events originated from actual user interaction. Browsers mark legitimate user actions by setting Event.isTrusted to true, while JavaScript-generated events are marked as false. According to the report, "the Claude extension treated it as a legitimate user click" despite receiving untrusted synthetic events.

The researchers noted the flaw does not enable arbitrary prompt injection attacks, but restricts exploitation to the nine predefined tasks. Additionally, attackers must trick users into installing a malicious extension rather than directly compromising the Claude extension itself.

Both findings were reported to Anthropic's bug bounty program. The synthetic-click vulnerability remains reproducible in version 1.0.80, released July 7, 2026.

b3698f0111b2.text:
A sophisticated malware framework called OkoBot is distributing over 20 malicious payloads targeting cryptocurrency assets and sensitive user data. The campaign primarily focuses on stealing wallet seed phrases, credentials, and other personal information.

Distribution Methods: The malware reaches victims through ClickFix attacks and fraudulent GitHub repositories. In one documented case, a repository falsely claimed to host SQL Server Management Studio but delivered a compromised version of Audacity audio editing software.

Evolution and Timeline: OkoBot represents an evolution of the TookPS campaign, which has been active since March 2025. Kaspersky researchers report the current OkoBot activity began in January, with the campaign spanning over a year of continuous development.

Key Malicious Components: The framework includes notable modules such as ext daemon/extl.exe for browser injection, SeedHunter for targeting wallet recovery interfaces, MC Keylogger for keystroke monitoring, and OkoSpyware for surveillance of cryptocurrency applications.

Geographic Distribution: While Brazil hosts the majority of victims, the campaign affects users globally, including Vietnam, Canada, Mexico, and Turkey.

Attribution Clues: Kaspersky identified potential Russian-speaking operators based on server geoblocking patterns, Russian code comments, and promotion on Russian cybercrime forums.

132ae4a27f4e.text:
Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

We all knew, to some degree or another, that this summer was going to a hot mess. I don't mean FIFA drama or record setting heat waves. I mean the slow but steady momentum that AI frontier models were accruing for vulnerability research. If you were like me, and guesstimating exactly when that shoe would drop, my money was on the middle of summer. And... well, friends, I hate to say it, but I was right.

This July's Patch Tuesday is an absolute whopper. There are 622 vulnerabilities being patched, with 62 being a critical severity. To put this context, this month alone has more vulnerabilities listed than all of 2018 combined. Three are zero days, two of which are being actively exploited. July is usually a quiet month historically – two years ago, it was just five patches issued in total! These are wild times, friends.

Microsoft has said this is due their AI frontier-accelerated research. We knew that this was coming, but what I am less sure about are companies that can meet the demand of this patch flood and getting these patches out to their infrastructures. The pessimist in me knows how most IT enterprises operate: You test, review stability, and then deploy. There's a lag there – always has been, always will be. But that system worked under a sane patching load. As surely as much as Microsoft is using frontier models to research and announce vulnerabilities, so every is every other vendor.

Either through bug bounty programs or their own internal research, vendors are eating these bugs from a fire hose. Some are straight-up slop and just noise, but some have absolute value and need to be fixed. A giant like Microsoft has the money and resources to address this – as well they should. But for every Microsoft, there are five other companies who don't have those resources. They'll get bugs analyzed and patches issued, surely, but it will be on a much longer timeline.

The trick, I think, will be identifying what is a "surge" vs. our new normal. If everything is a fire drill to patch, then nothing is a fire drill. What might just be a hot summer for patching, might turn into a 12-month fusillade of KEV and EPSS notifications, with companies already under the gun taxed even more.

I truly don't know how this ends, but... Find your change management and IT administrators and give them a hug. There are going to be some long days and hard questions to answer, and they'll need all the help they can get.

The One Big Thing

Cisco Talos is disclosing a new campaign by UAT-11795, a sophisticated, financially motivated Russian-speaking adversary targeting users in the U.S. and Europe since at least June 2025. UAT-11795 uses trojanized software installers — including popular tools like Webex, Zoom, and MobaXterm — to deliver a custom Python-based remote access tool tracked as "Starland RAT." This RAT acts as a gateway to deploy further malicious payloads, most notably a bespoke, in-memory PowerShell command-and-control (C2) implant known as the "WLDR agent."

Why do I care?

This opportunistic campaign casts a wide net across multiple victim profiles, turning a simple software download into a full-blown compromise. UAT-11795 employs highly evasive techniques, including AMSI and ETW bypasses, and uses a clever blockchain-anchored fallback mechanism to maintain persistent command and control. Once inside, attackers rapidly deploy secondary payloads like CastleStealer and Remcos RAT to siphon high-value credentials and cryptocurrency assets.

So now what?

Educate your users on ClickFix social engineering tactics and the dangers of unofficial software downloads. Monitor for suspicious execution of mshta.exe and unusual PowerShell activity, particularly scripts executing from memory or creating unexpected scheduled tasks. Ensure endpoint detection solutions are tuned to catch in-memory execution and AMSI tampering.

Top Security Headlines of the Week

Microsoft patches record 622 flaws, including two zero-days under active attack. Microsoft shipped its largest Patch Tuesday on record, more than triple June's previous high of around 200.

RabbitMQ vulnerability threatens enterprise systems. RabbitMQ is a popular open-source message broker that routes, buffers, and distributes messages, enabling asynchronous communication between applications. The security defect impacts an open management endpoint that returns the OAuth secret to anyone, without authentication.

Nigeria deepens cybersecurity efforts as cybercriminals see more profits. The West African country advanced rules to force organizations to disclose cyberattacks, joining other nations in a shift to mandated transparency.

Two-click cursor exploit enables dev environment takeover. Cursor AI, a popular AI coding tool used by more than 50,000 enterprises and 64% of the Fortune 500, can be exploited in just two clicks, allowing attackers to install permission-rich model context protocol (MCP) servers on privileged developers' machines.

cb801e55871b.text:
Owen Flowers, 18, and Thalha Jubair, 20, received five-and-a-half-year sentences at Woolwich Crown Court on July 16, 2026, for hacking Transport for London in 2024. The intrusion rendered 148 TfL systems inoperable and forced all 27,000 transport authority employees to obtain password resets in person.

The National Crime Agency and Crown Prosecution Service valued TfL's losses and recovery expenses at £29 million. Both defendants pleaded guilty on June 22, 2026, under Section 3ZA of the Computer Misuse Act 1990—the legislation's most serious charge. They admitted being reckless about potentially causing significant harm to human welfare.

The CPS identifies Flowers and Jubair as "the first hackers successfully prosecuted under Section 3ZA." The NCA characterizes this as only the second prosecution of its type, though both agencies' statements contain some ambiguity regarding this distinction.

The breach occurred between August 31 and September 3, 2024. TfL manages approximately 9 million daily journeys. Critical services disrupted included Dial-a-Ride (vulnerable passenger transport), digital payment channels, and concessionary travel card issuance. Oyster photocard applications closed, contactless ticketing expansion stalled, and refunds processed slowly.

TfL disclosed that names, email addresses, and home addresses were accessed. Oyster refund data possibly leaked, exposing bank account numbers and sort codes for roughly 5,000 people.

Flowers was arrested September 6, 2024—three days after the TfL attack ended—while conducting simultaneous attacks on U.S. healthcare organizations SSM Health Care Corporation and Sutter Health. Investigators recovered devices containing screenshots of TfL network connectivity, videos of Jubair navigating TfL systems, and Telegram communications between the attackers.

Flowers admitted two additional counts regarding healthcare attacks: conspiracy against SSM Health and attempted extortion of Sutter Health. Prosecutors noted he "threatened to lock those systems down while acknowledging in chats that it might kill some 90-year-old on life support."

The NCA characterizes both men as leading Scattered Spider members, also tracked as Octo Tempest, UNC3944, and 0ktapus. The CPS exercised more caution, noting the defendants claimed group membership at various points, with prosecutors believing the organization executed hundreds of attacks between 2022 and 2025.

An unsealed New Jersey complaint from September 2025 accuses Jubair of computer fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering conspiracies spanning approximately 120 network intrusions and at least 47 U.S. victims between May 2022 and September 2025, with over $115 million in ransoms paid.

The NCA states the arrests "effectively halted the group," citing Microsoft's assessment that apprehensions materially degraded operational capacity. However, the agency acknowledges other criminals may continue exploiting the Scattered Spider brand.

Paul Foster, NCA National Cyber Crime Unit head, emphasizes the importance of early law enforcement notification. City of London Police advocated for Cyber Crime Risk Orders—court-imposed restrictions on offenders' device and online service access.

49cc0ba73556.text:
Gianluca Semeraro reports:
Italy’s data protection authority has fined telecoms operator WINDTRE €1.7 million ($1.94 million) for “serious shortcomings” in its data security systems, leading to two unauthorised breaches and the exposure of personal information belonging to more than 365,000 customers.
• The investigation was prompted by the CK Hutchison owned company’s notification of the breaches in February 2025.
• It revealed that hackers posed as support technicians to gain access to corporate systems through employees at two retail points, the authority said in a statement.
Read more from Reuters at WKZO.
From the Garante’s newsletter:
The Authority’s investigation—initiated following two data breaches reported by the company in February 2025—found that hackers, posing as support technicians, convinced operators at two stores to grant access to company systems, thus exfiltrating customer personal and contact information. Specifically, the Authority found deficiencies in the management of login credentials and digital certificates. Furthermore, the security audits conducted by the company did not identify vulnerabilities that would have been detectable with more thorough checks. These vulnerabilities allowed hackers to access the company’s systems and steal personal data.
The Authority therefore found a violation of the principles of data integrity and confidentiality and the security obligations set forth in the GDPR and ordered Wind Tre to strengthen its systems for protecting digital credentials and certificates, introduce secure password management tools, and improve IT security procedures to prevent similar incidents in the future. In determining the fine, the Authority took into account the timely notification of the incident, the corrective measures adopted after the attack, and the company’s cooperation during the investigation.

85e92e5eb513.text:
Worldwide spending on AI continues to surge as organizations of all sizes embed AI into their cloud environments. Yet capturing real value from AI requires more than enthusiasm and budget. It demands a clear understanding of the underlying AI models driving outcomes.

In this post, we reveal the 10 most popular AI models of 2026 based on analysis of billions of cloud assets by the Orca Research Pod. This update refreshes the ranking covered in our Top 10 AI Models of 2025 blog, highlighting how model usage patterns have evolved as organizations scale their AI initiatives.

One of the most striking findings in this year's analysis is that no single model dominates the way GPT-3.5 once did. GPT-3.5 commanded 79% adoption in 2024, while today's top model, gpt-4o, reaches just 37.6% of AI cloud adopters. This shift reflects a more mature and fragmented AI landscape, where organizations are diversifying across models based on cost, latency, capability, and use case fit.

All 10 models in this year's ranking are Azure OpenAI deployments, underscoring Microsoft's continued dominance as the enterprise AI platform of choice. Three embedding models placing in the top 10 confirm that Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a standard architectural pattern in production cloud environments. Meanwhile, the GPT-5 family and reasoning model o4-mini signal that the newest generation of OpenAI models is moving from preview to production at scale.

An AI model is a computer program trained to perform a specific task (or set of tasks) by learning patterns from data. Different models excel at different things; language, vision, speech, coding, retrieval, multimodal reasoning, and more.

The 10 most widely adopted AI models observed in cloud environments (share of 426 AI-adopting organizations with the model deployed):

1. gpt-4o (37.6%) - flagship multimodal model, used in conversational interfaces, knowledge assistants, and cloud security workflows.
2. gpt-4.1-mini (34.7%) - new entrant, lightweight GPT-4.1 variant used in customer-facing chat and developer tools.
3. text-embedding-ada-002 (29.1%) - legacy embedding model still dominant in RAG pipelines and vector search.
4. gpt-4.1 (28.9%) - used in policy generation, compliance documentation, and other high-assurance use cases.
5. gpt-4o-mini (28.6%) - lighter multimodal model for in-app copilots and edge/real-time applications.
6. text-embedding-3-small (23.2%) - efficient embedding model for log enrichment and large-scale search.
7. text-embedding-3-large (22.3%) - higher-fidelity embedding model for knowledge graph and legal/technical search.
8. gpt-5.1 (22.3%) - capable reasoning model used in advanced code generation and agentic workflows.
9. gpt-5-mini (19.7%) - cost-sensitive GPT-5 family variant for batch automation and lightweight agents.
10. o4-mini (17.8%) - efficient reasoning model for code review automation and structured problem-solving.

The Orca Research Pod continuously analyzes billions of scans of cloud assets and hundreds of thousands of code repositories to surface emerging technology and security risk patterns.

Orca became the first CNAPP to integrate with GPT-3 back in early 2023, applying generative AI to accelerate risk detection, simplify investigations, and streamline remediation workflows. Orca's AI Security Posture Management (AI-SPM) capabilities give organizations visibility into AI risks across more than 50 AI models and packages, and Orca AI powers AI-driven asset discovery, triage guidance, and automated remediation throughout the Orca Cloud Security Platform.

7450a90d660d.text:
The article addresses security challenges posed by AI agents operating autonomously across multiple systems without proper identity and authorization controls.

Key Problem: Organizations are deploying AI agents faster than their identity governance frameworks can evolve. When agents lack managed identities and least-privilege role-based access controls, they risk accessing sensitive data beyond intended scope. The authors note: "A misconfigured permission may increase the potential impact compared to traditional service account scenarios."

Core Issues Identified:
1. Scope Creep: Teams grant broad permissions to expedite pilots, rarely revisiting to implement proper constraints.
2. Cross-System Risks: Agents with access to email, files, ticketing systems, and repositories may correlate data across platforms in unauthorized ways.
3. Identity Ambiguity: Unclear whether agents operate under their own identity or delegated user scope, hampering accountability.

Recommended Best Practices: The authors recommend treating "every agent as a first-class principal" with dedicated, lifecycle-managed identities with documented purposes; task-based RBAC scoped to specific resources; controlled tool access via approved allowlists; end-to-end audit trails capturing identity, role, scope, and actions; just-in-time (JIT) privilege elevation with time limits; and regular access reviews and revocation testing.

Implementation Guidance: Organizations should complete a security audit within 30-90 days, including inventory of agent identities, removal of overly broad roles, and enforcement of safe tool binding before expanding deployments—particularly for cross-tenant or B2C agents.

0cdcd3a2f4fb.text: This threat roundup covers 16 cybersecurity incidents from the past week, highlighting how attackers exploit legitimate tools and weak defaults to compromise organizations. Key stories include: Malware Distribution: Eleven malicious NuGet packages pose as game cheats, downloading surveillance payloads that harvest credentials and cryptocurrency wallet information via AWS-style keys and Google Sheets authentication. RAT Campaigns: The UAT-11795 group deploys Starland RAT and WLDR C2 implants using trojaned installer lures for popular software like MobaXterm, WebEx, and gaming applications across U.S. and European targets. Ransomware Speed: A new Rust-based ransomware called Spirals encrypted a South Asian IT company's network in under 24 hours following web server compromise, demonstrating rapid lateral movement tactics. Vulnerability Exploitation: CISA added two actively exploited flaws to its KEV catalog affecting Oracle E-Business Suite and KNX Protocol systems, requiring federal agency remediation. Fraud Networks: Dutch authorities dismantled a 700-person investment scam operation, while Spanish police disrupted a EUR140 million cybercrime network laundering stolen funds through 'money mule' accounts. EDR Evasion: Windows bind links can bypass endpoint detection tools when misused by administrators, shadowing trusted files and executables to evade AMSI and AppLocker defenses. Repository Fraud: Over 290 fake GitHub repositories impersonating security vendors distribute BoryptGrab infostealer malware, targeting cryptocurrency wallets and browser credentials. Authentication Threats: Chrome's sync feature becomes a surveillance tool when attackers add attacker-controlled accounts to victim devices, enabling remote browsing history access. Phishing Evolution: The SeasonalInvite campaign abuses eCard themes and commercial RMM tools (ConnectWise, LogMeIn, Kaseya) with AI-generated phishing pages and traffic distribution systems. OAuth Bypass: New toolkits like Jalisco provision real-time OAuth device codes to defeat time-based MFA controls, while OmegaLord harvester captures phone numbers alongside credentials. Infrastructure Mapping: Hunt.io identified 3,900 threat-enabling servers across Eastern European providers, with Keitaro leading malicious infrastructure abuse. Dual Monetization: A campaign simultaneously deploys Vidar stealer and XMRig miner, selling stolen credentials on criminal markets while passively mining Monero from hijacked CPU cycles. The article emphasizes patching boring vulnerabilities, tightening default configurations, and carefully monitoring trust handoffs between systems. Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: July 16, 2026.

ad6abc9ae212.text: Threat intelligence firm Group-IB has identified a previously unknown macOS malware called "ClickLock Stealer" that exploits social engineering rather than software vulnerabilities. The malware tricks users into executing malicious commands in Terminal by impersonating legitimate verification services. The attack operates since approximately May 2026 and has affected over 100 victims across 33 countries, with more than half based in Europe. Researchers discovered the malware after analyzing a shell script uploaded to VirusTotal on June 9 with zero antivirus detections initially. The distribution method involves fake verification pages using the ClickFix technique, compromised WordPress sites hosting payloads, and Telegram infrastructure for command-and-control operations. "The current malware doesn't even need any elevated privileges or rely on exploits for successful execution," according to Group-IB's research. Once users paste the command into Terminal, ClickLock displays a fake Cloudflare verification sequence with progress animation while downloading additional components. The malware targets passwords, cryptocurrency wallets, browser data, and other credentials from multiple sources including eight browsers, 31 crypto wallet extensions, and seven password manager extensions. The most aggressive tactic occurs when victims refuse compliance. The malware repeatedly kills visible applications, preventing normal computer use until the user surrenders their macOS password. Rebooting triggers persistence mechanisms designed to resume attacks. Defense recommendations: Users should recognize warning signs including unexpected password prompts, forced application closures, unusual credential access, and suspicious Telegram connections. The simplest protection involves immediately closing any webpage requesting Terminal commands from purported legitimate services. Author: Carly Page. Published: Thursday, July 16, 2026 at 16:33 UTC.

3438db439d29.text: I'm here today to write about one particularly thorny area of operational technology (OT) and security that I run into somewhat routinely. Given my own particular interests as an incorrigible vulnerability-gazer, and my professional role as vice president of security research at runZero, I deal with OT security issues more often than the average bear. I've noticed that there's definitely a vibe of, "IT be like this, but OT be like that" going on in the wider world of vulnerability management. The process of discovering, documenting, and disclosing vulnerabilities all have their own little quirks here in OT-land, so let's jump into it! Here, everything is legacy: At DEF CON, the ICS Village is one of the more popular places to hang out. It works well for folks who are either new to the field of infosec and cybersecurity, or old-hands in the industry, for the same reason: once you get close enough to a piece of OT technology with your modern IT vulnerability-hunting tooling and instincts, it often feels like you're hacking like it's 1999, all over again. Until very recently, OT, as a class, hasn't been much concerned with prompting for passwords or validating user-supplied inputs; the assumption was that the local network is trusted. The software itself is typically run as compiled objects with limited hardware resources, so there's not much room for fancy 21st Century defenses like ASLR and DEP (Address Space Layout Randomization and Data Execution Protection, respectively). Denial of service is catastrophic: Many classic OT attacks aren't really even about remote code execution (RCE) or local privilege escalations (LPE), which are the usual prize bugs for an IT-based attacker. Instead, the value of a denial of service (DoS) effect is of paramount importance in OT. A legitimate one-packet killer that bricks a wildly expensive piece of equipment, a sustained flow of garbage traffic, or a safety-control tripping sequence all end up in the same place: Actuators stop, robots freeze, and the whole purpose of the OT buildout is interrupted, sometimes with human life and limb hanging in the balance. Almost nobody has a spare backup factory. See something, say something: OT bugs are different from IT bugs; discussing effects can mean 'poisoning an entire community' or 'hospitals go offline.' Actually patching many OT devices is difficult to impossible, even when you know about the bug; often the best you can do is segment the vulnerable devices off to their own naughty corner of the network. When worlds collide: Most of the defensive posture of OT is precisely network segmentation, and network segmentation alone, but that's changing amid OT/IT convergence. The author urges researchers with a fresh OT 0-day to report it via cisa.gov/report rather than sit on it, warning that AI-assisted attackers make delay dangerous. Author: Tod Beardsley, VP of security research at runZero. Published: July 16, 2026.

0cd6e9c954d9.text: A large-scale phishing operation has been observed disguising a malicious script as a TrueType font file (.tff). Using the fake .ttf extension, a Lua-based loader is slipped onto Windows systems and a rotating cast of remote access trojans and infostealers is deployed. According to research published on July 16 by Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs, the campaign has been running since late March 2026 and combines fileless techniques with a low-detection loader to deliver Agent Tesla, Remcos, XWorm and a keylogger called Best Private LOGGER. The operators impersonated well-known companies and used business-cooperation lures to push malicious archives, often attached to phishing emails carrying payment-themed prompts. Fake Fonts, Real Loaders: The archives contained a JavaScript file wrapped in dense junk code with string-array mapping and control-flow flattening designed to defeat both manual analysis and AI-driven review. When executed, the script copied itself to the %PUBLIC%\Libraries folder, set up a scheduled task for persistence and then dropped either a LuaJIT interpreter or an AutoIt executable, itself given a .ttf extension. Jason Soroko of Sectigo said the design showed why 'security controls cannot treat a file extension as proof of file type or intent,' urging content/behavior-based analysis and restricting Windows Script Host, AutoIt and LuaJIT interpreters. The Lua path reversed itself, applied symbol-substitution, decoded from Base64, then ran a custom ROT cipher; a June 2026 build added segmented, page-level encryption decrypted via a Vectored Exception Handler. From Loader to Payload: the final payload arrived wrapped in Donut shellcode for reflective, in-memory execution, leaving nothing on disk. FortiGuard observed one of four payloads dropped per victim: Remcos, Agent Tesla, XWorm or Best Private LOGGER (a Snake Keylogger variant). Shane Barney of Keeper Security said the payload set made clear the attacker's goal was valid credentials and persistent foothold, urging identity controls, least privilege, and re-authentication for sensitive systems. Author: Alessandro Mascellino. Published: 16 July 2026.

e194740b989a.text: Today is AI Appreciation Day, and honestly, we mean it. AI has changed how we write code, analyze threats, and get work done faster than anyone thought possible a few years ago. It deserves a moment of gratitude. But at Check Point, we spend most of our year studying the other side of that coin and our newly released AI Security Report 2026 makes one thing very clear: the same qualities we're celebrating today are exactly what's made AI such a powerful tool for attackers too. AI Stopped Assisting and Started Operating: A year ago, we described AI as a force multiplier for attackers. That framing no longer captures what we're seeing. Our researchers documented intrusions where AI ran exploitation workflows with minimal human direction, generating thousands of commands across dozens of sessions on its own. In one case, a single developer used a commercial AI coding tool to build roughly 88,000 lines of working command-and-control malware in under a week. In the Mexican government breach detailed in the report, 'a single operator used Claude Code and GPT-4.1 together to compromise nine government agencies, generating over 5,300 AI-executed commands from about 1,000 typed instructions.' Appreciation Requires Honesty About the Attack Surface: Hidden instructions in a web page or calendar invite can hijack an agent's behavior; configuration files coding agents automatically trust can deliver malware. 'Roughly 40% of 10,000 MCP servers we reviewed carried security weaknesses,' and published code packages have leaked live credentials at a measurable rate. Enterprises Are Falling in Love Fast: organizations run an average of ten different AI applications a month, many without formal approval. High-risk GenAI prompts doubled over the past year, from 2% to 4% of all prompts; 'between 87% and 93% of organizations had at least one high-risk GenAI interaction every single month.' What Appreciating AI Responsibly Actually Looks Like: treat AI as a live attacker when assessing defenses, assume AI agents are targets, govern AI usage like any data-handling system, and fight AI-speed threats with AI-speed defenses. The post closes by promoting Check Point's AI Agent Security, AI Red Teaming, Workforce AI Security, and ThreatCloud AI portfolio. Author: Check Point Team. Published: July 16, 2026.

4d52591717e6.text: Solove contends in the Wall Street Journal that individual control over personal data is insufficient for privacy regulation in the current technological landscape. He proposes an alternative approach: holding corporations accountable for their conduct, similar to regulatory frameworks applied to pharmaceutical and food industries. Solove's recommended measures include: rigorous data minimization practices; fiduciary duties for companies; liability for negligent or reckless technology design; accountability for algorithms causing harm; multi-stakeholder technology reviews. The argument emphasizes that 'giving people control of their personal data is not an effective way to regulate privacy,' suggesting structural corporate responsibility would be more effective than individual data management choices. Key Comments: Tris Simondsen raises a critical technical challenge: AI models can infer sensitive attributes from seemingly innocuous data, making traditional data minimization ineffective, proposing a 'Principle of Epistemic Sovereignty' as a mathematical framework for enforcing strict boundaries on what systems can legitimately infer. ResearcherZero details concerning government-corporate data sharing, highlighting Palantir's access to health records and cooperation with immigration enforcement agencies. Author of underlying op-ed: Daniel Solove; blog post by Bruce Schneier. Published: July 16, 2026.

6eb92174235a.text: For most of the last two decades, enterprise security ran on a workable assumption: the environment was knowable. AI agents broke that assumption. Agents are not ordinary applications; they act autonomously, invoke tools, acquire access across systems, and change behavior based on context. Token Security research found more than a fifth of local agents already holding direct access to production data sources. The Limits of Fixed Security Workflows: vendor dashboards address common risks (overprivileged service accounts, stale credentials, dormant admin users) but the most important questions are environment-specific and don't fit generic workflows -- this is the 'operationalization gap.' Why 'Just Build It' Is Not the Answer: Retool's 2026 Build vs. Buy report found 35% of teams had already replaced at least one SaaS tool with something built in-house, and 78% expect to build more; but cybersecurity's harder problem is the data layer -- a workflow is only as good as the identity, access, permission, ownership and activity data underneath. Buy the Foundation to Own the Operational Layer: teams should buy continuous discovery, integrations, normalization, identity correlation, access mapping, governance controls and auditability, while owning workflows, applications, reports and automations reflecting their specific environment. Identity is the Layer That Holds: every meaningful agent eventually requires access, often borrowing an identity from an employee; identity is described as the only control plane that actually governs agentic AI because 'reach is what determines blast radius.' The piece closes urging security teams to build on a live identity foundation and own the adaptive operational layer. Author: Token Security (sponsored content). Published: July 16, 2026.

1de9d9d87187.text: An AI agent runtime is the infrastructure that provisions, isolates, scales, and runs AI agents in production. The framework decides what an agent does; the runtime decides where and how it does it. The 2026 agent stack has three layers: framework, runtime, and platform. Gartner predicts agentic AI will appear in 33% of enterprise software applications by 2028, while more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled before 2027, often due to lacking production infrastructure. Six evaluation criteria are given: sandbox isolation & cold-start latency (Firecracker microVMs vs gVisor vs containers vs V8 isolates); state, memory & long-running execution (durable execution/checkpointing); orchestration & multi-agent support; observability & evaluation; deployment & hosting model (managed cloud vs BYOC vs self-hosted); and security & governance (secrets handling, egress control, identity scoping, audit trails). Eleven runtimes are profiled across three categories -- managed hyperscaler runtimes (AWS Bedrock AgentCore, Google Vertex AI Agent Engine, Azure AI Foundry Agent Service), framework-native platforms (LangGraph Platform, OpenAI AgentKit), and sandbox/serverless runtimes (E2B, Modal, Daytona, Fly.io Machines, Cloudflare Agents, Vercel Sandbox) -- each with best-for, limitations, and security posture. A 'how to choose by use case' section maps runtime choice to workload pattern (code-executing agents, long-running agents, multi-agent systems, regulated environments). The security risks section stresses that every agent becomes a cloud workload with its own identity, credentials, and permissions, and that AI security posture management is needed for visibility into AI workloads, identities, permissions and misconfigurations. Author: The Orca Security Team. Published: July 16, 2026.

9187e0c3e7a4.text: Genetic testing company 23andMe (now Chrome Holding Co.) has agreed to pay $18 million to settle claims from a coalition of 43 attorneys general that it failed to protect customers' genetic data. 23andMe disclosed a massive data breach in October 2023, following credential-stuffing attacks that went unnoticed for five months, from April 2023 to September 2023. The threat actors stole the data of 6.9 million customers, including genetic ancestry information, later offered for sale on the dark web. New York AG Letitia James said the investigation found the company lacked basic safeguards against credential-based cyberattacks, such as password blocklisting or multifactor authentication, as well as adequate rate limiting, intrusion prevention, and breach-detection monitoring. Investigators found 23andMe failed to address unusual login activity and fix known vulnerabilities; the company initially denied a breach occurred, then blamed customers' account/password practices. The settlement secures new security requirements at TTAM, including a data security advisory board, risk analysis protocols, and continued consumer rights to delete their data. Class-action lawsuits, fines, and settlements: the 2023 breach also led to multiple class-action lawsuits; in September 2024 23andMe agreed to pay $30 million to settle one proposed class action. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March 2025. In June 2025, James and 27 other AGs sued to protect customer genetic data during bankruptcy; the UK ICO fined 23andMe £2.31 million ($3.12 million). In July 2025, TTAM Research Institute (led by co-founder Anne Wojcicki) completed acquisition of the company's assets for $305 million. Author: Sergiu Gatlan. Published: July 16, 2026, 09:47 AM.

04dd4fd8e61d.text: Adaptiva has announced AirGap for OneSite Patch, a new capability that extends autonomous patch management to air-gapped environments. Developed in response to demand from government agencies, critical infrastructure operators, and large enterprises, it enables organizations to securely patch isolated systems without compromising physical separation. Dr. Deepak Kumar, CEO of Adaptiva, said the tradeoff between isolation and staying patched 'is no longer acceptable as cyber threats continue to evolve rapidly in the AI era.' AirGap for OneSite Patch pairs an offline server inside the isolated environment with an online server connected to the Adaptiva cloud service, letting administrators securely acquire, transfer, import, and distribute OS and third-party patches without exposing protected systems to the internet. Key features: new 'zones' to manage multiple independent air-gapped environments from a single online server with tailored sync schedules; true air-gap synchronization where only a simple human-readable text request leaves the secure environment (transferable via USB, external drive, or handwritten note), with response packages inspectable/scannable before entering the environment; extended OneSite Patch workflow reusing existing autonomous workflows, maintenance windows, approvals and policies; and role-based access controls to delegate tasks without granting broader admin privileges. Published: July 16, 2026.

8c7fe274eaf3.text: n8n, the workflow automation platform, shipped a fix for a critical identity-binding vulnerability in its Enterprise token exchange feature. The flaw allowed attackers to log into accounts belonging to users from different external token issuers. On Enterprise instances configured to trust multiple external token issuers, the system matched incoming JWTs to local users based solely on the 'sub' (subject) claim while ignoring the 'iss' (issuer) claim. This meant a valid token from issuer A carrying a subject identifier belonging to someone under issuer B could grant unauthorized access to that account, bypassing password verification entirely. n8n released the patch on June 24. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-59208, credited to GitHub user bearsyankees. Technical Context: token exchange implements RFC 8693, letting OEM partners embedding n8n avoid second login screens; n8n verifies a partner-signed JWT against a configured public key and matches claims to a local account via trusted keys in N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS. Per RFC 7519, a subject value is unique only within its issuing context, so identity requires both iss and sub -- n8n only checked half. Scope and Impact: affects versions below 2.27.4 and 2.28.0; fixed in 2.27.4 and 2.28.1 onward; as of July 16, npm carried 2.30.6. The flaw only reaches instances with token exchange enabled and multiple trusted issuers configured. GitHub scored CVSS 4.0 at 7.6 (high); NVD rated it 6.8 (medium) under CWE-287 and CWE-346; CISA's July 13 SSVC assessment recorded no known public exploitation. Mitigation: reduce trusted issuers to one or disable token exchange entirely. Author: Swati Khandelwal. Published: July 16, 2026.

7d06b24f107a.text: Researchers at Cato Networks, a member of OpenAI's Daybreak Program for authorized cybersecurity testing, discovered that ChatGPT-5.5 can execute comprehensive offensive cyber-attacks following a single high-level prompt. Their controlled experiment in a typical enterprise Active Directory environment demonstrated the model's capacity to autonomously plan and execute full attack lifecycles. The attack sequence included reconnaissance, exploitation, internal discovery, privilege escalation, lateral movement, and data exfiltration -- with domain admin access achieved in approximately 40 minutes. A paper published July 15 detailed the findings. Across six different test scenarios, the AI model demonstrated adaptive problem-solving; when standard attack paths failed or environmental conditions changed, it adjusted its approach, including developing 'an Server Message Block (SMB)-based tunneling approach to support data movement through an existing foothold.' The researchers emphasized that 'frontier models can contribute goal-oriented problem solving during offensive operations,' though they cautioned this shouldn't indicate novel attack discovery. Cato Networks focused on the publicly available GPT-5.5 rather than the security-specialized GPT-5.5-Cyber variant, reasoning this better reflected tools accessible to most potential attackers; specific prompts were not disclosed for security reasons. Dr. Guy Waizel from Cato Networks noted the real danger emerges when LLMs combine with 'orchestration, operational context, and battle-tested tools,' potentially accelerating attacks while reducing required expertise. Author: Danny Palmer. Published: 16 July 2026.

b29c0dd067d0.text: On Wednesday, CISA and four allied cyber authorities published a guide instructing software vendors on building a coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) program. Six days earlier, CISA released a blog post describing how a security researcher repeatedly failed to report a serious issue to CISA itself; the timing of the two releases appears intentional. The Guidance recommends suppliers: publish a vulnerability disclosure policy explicitly welcoming public reporting; use the security.txt file format (RFC 9116); set broad testing scopes; acknowledge researcher outreach within two to three business days; and separate vulnerability disclosure from customer support channels. The Failure: on July 9, CISA's Acting CIO Preston Werntz and Acting CISO Brad Libbey disclosed CISA became aware of a security incident on May 15, 2026, when a reporter asked about exposed internal AWS GovCloud keys found in a public repository by GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon.
